Introduction

介绍

Walking in Memphis

在孟菲斯漫步

When he was nine years old, my godson developed a brief but freakishly intense obsession with Elvis Presley. He took to singing ‘Jailhouse Rock’ at the top of his voice, with all the low crooning and pelvis-jiggling of the King himself. He didn’t know this style had become a joke, so he offered it with all the heart-catching sincerity of a pre-teen who believes he is being cool. In the brief pauses before he started singing it all over again, he demanded to know everything (‘Everything! Everything!’) about Elvis, and so I jabbered out the rough outline of that inspiring, sad, stupid story.

我的教子九岁那年，对猫王埃尔维斯·普雷斯利产生了短暂却异常强烈的迷恋。他开始扯着嗓子唱《监狱摇滚》，模仿着猫王低沉的吟唱和扭动胯部的动作。他不知道这种唱法已经成了笑柄，所以他唱得一本正经，带着一个自以为很酷的少年特有的真挚情感。每次唱到一半，他都会停下来，缠着我问关于猫王的一切（“一切！一切！”），于是我便絮絮叨叨地把那段鼓舞人心、令人唏嘘又有点荒唐的故事大概讲了一遍。

Elvis was born in one of the poorest towns in Mississippi – a place far, far away, I said. He arrived in the world alongside his twin brother, who died a few minutes later. As he grew up, his mother told him that if he sang to the moon every night, his brother could hear his voice, so he sang and sang. He began to perform in public just as television was taking off – so in a sudden swoosh, he became more famous than anyone had ever been before. Everywhere Elvis went, people would scream, until his world became a chamber of screams. He retreated into a cocoon of his own construction, where he gloried in his possessions in place of his lost freedom. For his mother he bought a palace and named it Graceland.

埃尔维斯出生在密西西比州一个极其贫困的小镇——我说，那是一个遥远的地方。他和他的双胞胎兄弟一同来到这个世界，但兄弟却在几分钟后夭折了。在他成长的过程中，他的母亲告诉他，如果他每晚对着月亮唱歌，他的兄弟就能听到他的声音，于是他便不停地唱着。他开始公开表演的时候，电视也正蓬勃发展——于是，他突然间变得比任何人都更加出名。埃尔维斯所到之处，人们都会尖叫，直到他的世界变成了一个尖叫的牢笼。他把自己封闭在一个茧房里，在那里，他沉溺于自己的财富，以此来弥补失去的自由。他为母亲买了一座宫殿，并将其命名为“优雅园”。

I skimmed through the rest – the descent into addiction, the sweating, gurning stage-jammering in Vegas, the death at the age of forty-two. Whenever my godson, who I’ll call Adam – I’ve changed some details here to avoid identifying him – asked questions about how the story ended, I got him to duet ‘Blue Moon’ with me instead. ‘You saw me standing alone,’ he sang in his little voice, ‘without a dream in my heart. Without a love of my own.’

我略过了剩下的部分——沉沦毒瘾、在拉斯维加斯汗流浃背、扭曲着脸庞的舞台表演、以及42岁英年早逝。每当我的教子，我姑且称他为亚当（为了避免暴露他的身份，我在这里做了一些改动）问起故事的结局时，我就让他和我合唱《蓝月亮》。他用稚嫩的声音唱道：“你看到我独自一人站在那里，心中没有梦想，也没有属于自己的爱。”

One day, Adam looked at me very earnestly and asked: ‘Johann, will you take me to Graceland?’ Without really thinking, I agreed. ‘Do you promise? Do you really promise?’ I said I did. And I never gave it another thought, until everything had gone wrong.

有一天，亚当非常认真地看着我，问道：“约翰，你愿意带我去格雷斯兰吗？”我几乎没怎么思考就答应了。“你保证吗？你真的保证吗？”我说我保证。之后我再也没想过这件事，直到一切都出了差错。

Ten years later, Adam was lost. He had dropped out of school when he was fifteen, and he spent literally almost all his waking hours at home alternating blankly between screens – his phone, an infinite scroll of Whatsapp and Facebook messages, and his iPad, on which he watched a blur of YouTube and porn. At moments, I could still see in him traces of the joyful little boy who sang ‘Viva Las Vegas’, but it was like that person had broken into smaller, disconnected fragments. He struggled to stay with a topic of conversation for more than a few minutes without jerking back to a screen or abruptly switching to another subject. He seemed to be whirring at the speed of Snapchat, somewhere where nothing still or serious could reach him. He was intelligent, decent, kind – but it was like nothing could gain any traction in his mind.

十年后，亚当迷失了方向。他十五岁就辍学了，几乎醒着的所有时间都待在家里，茫然地在各种屏幕间切换——手机，无休止地滚动着WhatsApp和Facebook消息；还有iPad，上面播放着模糊的YouTube和色情视频。有时，我还能在他身上看到当年那个唱着《拉斯维加斯万岁》的快乐小男孩的影子，但仿佛那个人已经破碎成无数碎片。他很难集中精力谈论一个话题超过几分钟，总是会突然跳回屏幕，或者突然切换到另一个话题。他仿佛以Snapchat的速度飞速运转，任何平静或严肃的事情都无法触及他的内心。他聪明、善良、正直——但似乎没有什么东西能真正进入他的脑海。

During the decade in which Adam had become a man, this fracturing seemed to be happening – to some degree – to many of us. The sensation of being alive in the early twenty-first century consisted of the sense that our ability to pay attention – to focus – was cracking and breaking. I could feel it happen to me – I would buy piles of books, and I would glimpse them guiltily from the corner of my eye as I sent, I told myself, just one more tweet. I still read a lot, but with each year that passed, it felt more and more like running up a down escalator. I had just turned forty, and wherever my generation gathered, we would lament our lost capacity for concentration, as if it was a friend who had vanished one day at sea and never been seen since.

在亚当长大成人的那十年里，这种分裂似乎在某种程度上发生在了我们许多人身上。二十一世纪初的生存感受，就包括一种感觉：我们的注意力——我们的专注力——正在逐渐丧失。我能感受到这种变化发生在我身上——我会买一大堆书，然后一边心虚地用眼角瞥一眼，一边告诉自己，再发一条推文就好。我仍然读很多书，但随着时间的流逝，这种感觉越来越像是在逆行。我刚满四十岁，无论我们这一代人在哪里聚会，我们都会哀叹自己失去的专注力，仿佛一个朋友某天在海上失踪，从此杳无音讯。

Then one evening, as we lay on a large sofa, each staring at our own ceaselessly shrieking screens, I looked at Adam and felt a low dread. We can’t live like this, I said to myself.

一天晚上，我们躺在一张大沙发上，各自盯着屏幕上不停尖叫的画面，我看着亚当，感到一阵莫名的恐惧。我们不能再这样生活下去了，我对自己说。

‘Adam,’ I said softly. ‘Let’s go to Graceland.’

“亚当，”我轻声说，“我们去格雷斯兰吧。”

‘What?’

'什么？'

I reminded him of the promise I had made to him so many years before. He couldn’t even remember those ‘Blue Moon’ days, nor my pledge to him, but I could see that the idea of breaking this numbing routine ignited something in him. He looked up at me and asked if I was serious. ‘I am, ‘I said, ‘but there’s one condition. I’ll pay for us to go four thousand miles. We’ll go to Memphis, and New Orleans – we’ll go all over the South, anywhere you want. But I can’t do it if, when we get there, all you’re going to do is stare at your phone. You have to promise to leave it switched off except at nights. We have to return to reality. We have to reconnect with something that matters to us.’ He swore he would, and a few weeks later, we lifted off from London Heathrow, towards the land of the Delta blues.

我提醒他多年前我对他的承诺。他甚至记不起那些“蓝月亮”的日子，也记不起我对他的誓言，但我看得出来，打破这种麻木的日常的想法点燃了他内心的某种东西。他抬起头看着我，问我是不是认真的。“我是认真的，”我说，“但有一个条件。我会支付我们四千英里的路费。我们会去孟菲斯，去新奥尔良——我们会去南方各地，你想去哪儿都行。但如果到了那里，你只会盯着手机看，那我就做不到了。你必须答应我，除了晚上，其他时间都关机。我们必须回归现实。我们必须重新与那些对我们真正重要的东西建立联系。”他发誓他会做到，几周后，我们从伦敦希思罗机场起飞，飞往三角洲蓝调的故乡。

When you arrive at the gates of Graceland, there is no longer a human being whose job is to show you around. You are handed an iPad, and you put in little earbuds, and the iPad tells you what to do – turn left; turn right; walk forward. In each room, the iPad, in the voice of some forgotten actor, tells you about the room you are in, and a photograph of it appears on the screen. So we walked around Graceland alone, staring at the iPad. We were surrounded by Canadians and Koreans and a whole United Nations of blank-faced people, looking down, seeing nothing around them. Nobody was looking for long at anything but their screens. I watched them as we walked, feeling more and more tense. Occasionally somebody would look away from the iPad and I felt a flicker of hope, and I would try to make eye contact with them, to shrug, to say, Hey, we’re the only ones looking around, we’re the ones who travelled thousands of miles and decided to actually see the things in front of us – but every time this happened, I realised they had broken contact with the iPad only to take out their phones and snap a selfie.

当你抵达格雷斯兰庄园的大门时，不再有人类为你导览。你会拿到一台iPad，戴上耳机，iPad会告诉你该怎么做——左转；右转；向前走。每到一个房间，iPad都会用某个早已被人遗忘的演员的声音为你介绍房间，屏幕上还会显示房间的照片。于是，我们独自在格雷斯兰庄园里漫步，目光始终盯着iPad。周围都是加拿大人、韩国人，还有一大群面无表情的人，他们低着头，对周围的一切都漠不关心。除了屏幕，没有人会长时间看向别处。我一边走一边观察着他们，感觉越来越紧张。偶尔会有人把目光从 iPad 上移开，我心中燃起一丝希望，我会试着和他们进行眼神交流，耸耸肩，说：“嘿，只有我们四处看看，只有我们跋涉千里来到这里，决定好好看看眼前的风景。”——但每次发生这种情况时，我都会意识到，他们放下 iPad 只是为了拿出手机自拍。

When we got to the Jungle Room – Elvis’s favourite place in the mansion – the iPad was chattering away when a middle-aged man standing next to me turned to say something to his wife. In front of us, I could see the large fake pot plants that Elvis had bought to turn this room into his own artificial jungle. The fake plants were still there, sagging sadly. ‘Honey,’ he said, ‘this is amazing. Look.’ He waved the iPad in her direction, and then began to move his finger across it. ‘If you swipe left, you can see the Jungle Room to the left. And if you swipe right, you can see the Jungle Room to the right.’ His wife stared, smiled, and began to swipe at her own iPad.

当我们来到丛林房——猫王在豪宅里最喜欢的地方——时，iPad正叽叽喳喳地响着，这时站在我旁边的一位中年男子转过身来跟妻子说了些什么。在我们面前，我看到了猫王为了把这间房装扮成他自己的人造丛林而买的大型仿真盆栽。那些仿真植物还在那里，耷拉着，显得有些凄凉。“亲爱的，”他说，“这太棒了，你看。”他朝她挥了挥iPad，然后开始用手指在屏幕上滑动。“你向左滑动，就能看到左边的丛林房。你向右滑动，就能看到右边的丛林房。”他的妻子盯着他，笑了笑，也开始在自己的iPad上滑动。

I watched them. They swiped back and forth, looking at the different dimensions of the room. I leaned forward. ‘But, sir,’ I said, ‘there’s an old-fashioned form of swiping you can do. It’s called turning your head. Because we’re here. We’re in the Jungle Room. You don’t have to see it on your screen. You can see it unmediated. Here. Look.’ I waved my hand at it, and the fake green leaves rustled a little.

我看着他们。他们来回滑动屏幕，打量着房间的不同维度。我向前倾身。“但是，先生，”我说，“有一种老式的滑动方式，那就是转动你的头。因为我们在这里。我们身处丛林房间。您不必在屏幕上看。您可以直接看到它。来，看。”我朝它挥了挥手，人造绿叶沙沙作响。

The man and his wife backed away from me a few inches. ‘Look!’ I said, in a louder voice than I intended. ‘Don’t you see? We’re there . We’re actually there . There’s no need for your screen. We are in the Jungle Room. ’ They hurried out of the room, glancing back at me with a who’s-that-loon shake of the head, and I could feel my heart beating fast. I turned to Adam, ready to laugh, to share the irony with him, to release my anger – but he was in a corner, holding his phone under his jacket, flicking through Snapchat.

那对夫妇往后退了几英寸。“看！”我的声音比预想的要大。“你们没看到吗？我们就在那儿。我们真的在那儿。根本不需要你们的屏幕。我们就在丛林房间里。”他们匆匆走出房间，回头冲我摇了摇头，一副“这人是谁啊”的样子，我感觉自己的心跳得飞快。我转向亚当，准备大笑，想和他分享这其中的讽刺，发泄一下我的怒气——但他正躲在角落里，把手机藏在外套下面，翻看着Snapchat。

At every stage in this trip, he had broken his promise. When the plane first touched down in New Orleans two weeks before, he immediately took out his phone, while we were still in our seats. ‘You promised not to use it,’ I said. He replied: ‘I meant I wouldn’t make phone calls. I can’t not use Snapchat and texting, obviously.’ He said this with baffled honesty, as if I had asked him to hold his breath for ten days. I watched him scrolling through his phone in the Jungle Room silently. Milling past him was a stream of people also staring at their screens. I felt as alone as if I had been standing in an empty Iowa cornfield, miles from another human. I strode up to Adam and snatched his phone from his grasp.

这次旅行，他每一步都违背了自己的诺言。两周前，飞机刚降落在新奥尔良，我们还没下飞机，他就立刻掏出了手机。“你答应过不用手机的，”我说。他回答说：“我是说我不打电话。但我显然没办法不用Snapchat和短信。”他语气里带着困惑和坦诚，仿佛我让他憋气十天似的。我看着他在“丛林房”里默默地滑动着手机屏幕。从他身边走过的，也是一群人盯着自己的屏幕。我感到无比孤独，仿佛置身于爱荷华州空旷的玉米地，与世隔绝。我走到亚当面前，一把夺过他的手机。

‘We can’t live like this!’ I said. ‘You don’t know how to be present! You are missing your life! You’re afraid of missing out – that’s why you are checking your screen all the time! By doing that, you are guaranteeing you are missing out! You are missing your one and only life! You can’t see the things that are right in front of you , the things you have been longing to see since you were a little boy! None of these people can! Look at them !’

“我们不能再这样生活下去了！”我说。“你根本不懂得活在当下！你错过了你的人生！你害怕错过——所以你才总是盯着屏幕！你这样做，就是在故意错过！你错过了你独一无二的人生！你看不到就在你眼前的事物，看不到你从小就渴望看到的事物！这些人也看不到！看看他们！”

I was talking loudly, but in their iPad iSolation, most people around us didn’t even notice. Adam snatched his phone back from me, told me (not without some justification) that I was acting like a freak, and stomped away, out past Elvis’s grave, and into the Memphis morning.

我说话声音很大，但周围的人都沉浸在iPad的世界里，根本没注意到。亚当一把抢回手机，（也并非毫无道理地）说我像个怪胎，然后跺着脚走了，经过猫王的墓地，走进了孟菲斯的晨光中。

I spent hours walking listlessly between Elvis’s various Rolls-Royces, which are displayed in the adjoining museum, and finally I found Adam again as night fell in the Heartbreak Hotel across the street, where we were staying. He was sitting next to the swimming pool, which was shaped like a giant guitar, and as Elvis sang in a 24/7 loop over this scene, he looked sad. I realised as I sat with him that, like all the most volcanic anger, my rage towards him – which had been spitting out throughout this trip – was really anger towards myself. His inability to focus, his constant distraction, the inability of the people at Graceland to see the place they had travelled to, was something I felt rising within myself. I was fracturing like they were fracturing. I was losing my ability to be present too. And I hated it.

我在隔壁博物馆里漫无目的地在猫王的几辆劳斯莱斯之间徘徊了几个小时，这些车都陈列在那里。最后，夜幕降临，我在街对面的伤心旅馆（我们住的地方）再次找到了亚当。他正坐在一个形似巨型吉他的游泳池旁，猫王的歌声循环播放，仿佛24小时不间断，他看起来很悲伤。我坐在他身边，意识到，就像所有最猛烈的愤怒一样，我对他的怒火——在整个旅程中不断爆发——实际上是对自己的愤怒。他无法集中注意力，总是心不在焉，格雷斯兰庄园的人们无法真正理解他们此行的目的，这些都让我感到内心深处的某种情绪正在升腾。我像他们一样，正在崩溃。我也正在失去专注当下的能力。我恨透了这种感觉。

‘I know something’s wrong,’ Adam said to me softly, holding his phone tightly in his hand. ‘But I have no idea how to fix it.’ Then he went back to texting.

“我知道出问题了，”亚当轻声对我说，手里紧紧攥着手机，“但我不知道该怎么解决。”说完，他又继续发短信。

I took Adam away to escape our inability to focus – and what I found is that there was no escape, because this problem was everywhere. I travelled all over the world to research this book, and there was almost no respite. Even when I took time out from my research to go to see some of the world’s most famously chill and tranquil places, I found it waiting for me.

我带亚当出去是为了逃避我们无法集中注意力的问题——结果却发现根本无处可逃，因为这个问题无处不在。为了写这本书，我走遍了世界各地，却几乎没有喘息之机。即使我抽出时间去探访一些世界上最著名的宁静祥和之地，也发现这个问题依然如影随形。

One afternoon, I sat in the Blue Lagoon in Iceland, a vast and infinitely calm lake of geothermal water that bubbles up at the temperature of a hot bathtub even as snow falls all around you. As I watched the falling snowflakes gently dissolve into the rising steam, I realised I was surrounded by people wielding selfie sticks. They had put their phones into waterproof casings, and they were frantically posing and posting. Several of them were live-streaming to Instagram. I wondered if the motto for our era should be: I tried to live, but I got distracted. This thought was interrupted by a ripped German, who looked like an influencer, bellowing into his camera phone: ‘Here I am in the Blue Lagoon, living my best life!’

一天下午，我坐在冰岛的蓝湖里。蓝湖是一个广袤无垠、静谧无比的地热湖，湖水温度如同热水浴缸般温暖，即使周围雪花纷飞，湖面依然温暖如春。我看着飘落的雪花轻轻融入升腾的蒸汽中，突然意识到自己被一群拿着自拍杆的人包围了。他们都给手机套上了防水壳，正忙着摆各种姿势拍照发到网上。其中几个人还在Instagram上直播。我不禁想到，我们这个时代的座右铭是不是应该是：我努力生活，却总是分心？这时，一个身材健硕的德国人打断了我的思绪。他看起来像个网红，对着手机大声喊道：“我在蓝湖，享受人生！”

Another time, I went to see the Mona Lisa in Paris, only to find she is now permanently hidden behind a rugby scrum of people from everywhere on earth, all jostling their way to the front, only for them to immediately turn their backs on her, snap a selfie, and fight their way out again. On the day I was there, I watched the crowd from the side for more than an hour. Nobody – not one person – looked at the Mona Lisa for more than a few seconds. Her smile no longer seems like an enigma. It appears as though she is looking at us from her perch in sixteenth-century Italy and asking us: Why won’t you just look at me like you used to?

还有一次，我去巴黎看《蒙娜丽莎》，却发现她现在永远被来自世界各地的人群挡在后面，就像橄榄球赛一样，每个人都争先恐后地挤到前面，然后又立刻背过身去，拍张自拍，再挤出去。那天，我在旁边观察了人群一个多小时。没有一个人——真的没有一个人——会多看《蒙娜丽莎》几秒钟。她的微笑不再神秘莫测。她仿佛正从十六世纪意大利的画作中凝视着我们，质问我们：为什么你们不再像以前那样看着我了？

This seemed to fit with a much wider sense that had been settling on me for several years – one that went well beyond bad tourist habits. It felt like our civilisation had been covered with itching powder, and we spent our time twitching and twerking our minds, unable to simply give attention to things that matter. Activities that require longer forms of focus – like reading a book – have been in freefall for years. After my trip with Adam, I read the work of the leading scientific specialist on willpower in the world, a man named Professor Roy Baumeister, who is based at the University of Queensland in Australia, and then I went to interview him. He had been studying the science of willpower and self-discipline for more than thirty years, and he is responsible for some of the most famous experiments ever carried out in the social sciences. As I sat down opposite the sixty-six-year-old, I explained I was thinking of writing a book about why we seem to have lost our sense of focus, and how we can get it back. I looked to him hopefully.

这似乎与我多年来一直萦绕心头的一种更广泛的感受不谋而合——这种感受远不止是不良的旅游习惯那么简单。感觉我们的文明就像被一层痒粉覆盖，我们整天都在胡思乱想，无法专注于真正重要的事情。那些需要长时间集中注意力的活动——比如读书——已经持续衰落多年。和亚当旅行之后，我读了世界上研究意志力的顶尖专家罗伊·鲍迈斯特教授的著作。他任教于澳大利亚昆士兰大学，之后我去采访了他。他研究意志力和自律的科学已经超过三十年，并主持了一些社会科学领域最著名的实验。当我坐在这位六十六岁的老人对面时，我解释说我正在考虑写一本书，探讨我们为什么似乎失去了专注力，以及我们如何才能重新找回它。我满怀希望地看着他。

It was curious, he said, that I should bring up this topic with him. ‘I’m feeling like my control over my attention is weaker than it used to be,’ he said. He used to be able to sit for hours, reading and writing, but now ‘it seems like my mind jumps around a lot more’. He explained that he had realised recently that ‘when I start to feel bad, I’d play a video game on my phone, and then that got to be fun’. I pictured him turning away from his enormous body of scientific achievement to play Candy Crush Saga. He said: ‘I can see that I am not sustaining concentration in perhaps the way I used to.’ He added: ‘I’m just sort of giving in to it, and will start to feel bad.’

他说，我跟他提起这个话题，真是奇怪。“我感觉自己对注意力的控制力不如以前了，”他说。他以前能一坐就是几个小时，读书写作，但现在“感觉我的思绪更容易飘忽不定”。他解释说，他最近意识到，“心情不好的时候，我就会玩手机游戏，然后就觉得挺有意思的”。我脑海中浮现出他放下自己庞大的科学成就，转而玩《糖果传奇》的画面。他说：“我意识到自己可能无法像以前那样集中注意力了。”他补充道：“我有点儿放纵自己，然后就开始感觉不舒服。”

Roy Baumeister is literally the author of a book named Willpower , and he has studied this subject more than anyone else alive. I thought – if even he is losing some of his ability to focus, who isn’t it happening to?

罗伊·鲍迈斯特是《意志力》一书的作者，他对这个主题的研究比任何人都深入。我想——如果连他都开始失去一些专注力，那么还有谁能幸免呢？

For a long time I reassured myself by saying this crisis was really just an illusion. Previous generations felt their attention and focus were getting worse too – you can read medieval monks nearly a millennium ago complaining that they were suffering from attention problems of their own. As human beings get older, they can focus less, and they become convinced that this is a problem with the world and with the next generation, rather than with their own failing minds.

很长一段时间以来，我一直安慰自己说，这场危机其实只是一种错觉。前几代人也感觉自己的注意力越来越差——你甚至可以读到近千年前的中世纪僧侣抱怨自己注意力不集中的记录。随着年龄增长，人的注意力会逐渐下降，他们开始认为这是世界和下一代的问题，而不是自身思维衰退的问题。

The best way to know for sure would be if scientists, starting years ago, had done something simple. They could have given attention tests to random members of the public, and continued doing the same test for years and decades to track any changes that took place. But nobody did that. That long-term information was never gathered. There is, however, a different way I think we can reach a reasonable conclusion about this. As I researched this book, I learned that there are all sorts of factors that have been scientifically proven to reduce people’s ability to pay attention. There is strong evidence that many of these factors have been rising in the past few decades – sometimes dramatically. Against this, there’s only one trend I could find that might have been improving our attention. That’s why I came to believe that this is a real crisis, and an urgent one.

要确切了解情况，最好的办法是科学家们从多年前就开始做一些简单的事情。他们可以随机抽取一些公众成员进行注意力测试，并持续进行数年甚至数十年，以追踪任何变化。但没有人这样做。这种长期数据从未被收集起来。然而，我认为我们可以通过另一种方式得出合理的结论。在撰写本书的过程中，我了解到，科学已经证明，许多因素会降低人们的注意力。有强有力的证据表明，过去几十年里，其中许多因素都在上升——有时甚至急剧上升。与之相反，我只发现一个趋势可能正在改善我们的注意力。正因如此，我才相信这是一个真正的危机，而且迫在眉睫。

I also learned that the evidence about where these trends are taking us is stark. For example, a small study investigated how often an average American college student actually pays attention to anything, so the scientists involved put tracking software on their computers and monitored what they did in a typical day. They discovered that, on average, a student would switch task once every sixty-five seconds. The median amount of time they focused on any one thing was just nineteen seconds. If you’re an adult and tempted to feel superior, hold off. A different study by Gloria Mark, professor of infomatics at the University of California, Irvine – who I interviewed – observed how long on average an adult working in an office stays on one task. It was three minutes.

我还了解到，这些趋势将把我们引向何方的证据令人震惊。例如，一项小型研究调查了美国大学生平均注意力集中的频率。参与研究的科学家们在他们的电脑上安装了追踪软件，并监控他们一天的活动。他们发现，平均而言，学生每65秒就会切换一次任务。他们专注于任何一项任务的平均时间只有19秒。如果你是成年人，并且想要沾沾自喜，请三思。我采访过的加州大学欧文分校信息学教授格洛丽亚·马克（Gloria Mark）的另一项研究观察了在办公室工作的成年人平均专注于一项任务的时间。结果是三分钟。

So I went on a 30,000-mile journey to find out how we can get our focus and attention back. In Denmark I interviewed the first scientist who has, with his team, shown that our collective ability to pay attention really is rapidly shrinking. Then I met with scientists all over the world who have discovered why. In the end, I interviewed over 250 experts – from Miami to Moscow, from Montreal to Melbourne. My quest for answers took me to a crazy mixture of places, from a favela in Rio de Janeiro where attention had shattered in a particularly disastrous way, to a remote office in a small town in New Zealand where they had found a way to radically restore focus.

于是，我踏上了一段长达三万英里的旅程，探寻我们该如何重拾专注力。在丹麦，我采访了第一位科学家，他和他的团队证实了我们集体的注意力正在迅速下降。之后，我又与世界各地的科学家会面，了解他们发现的原因。最终，我采访了超过250位专家——从迈阿密到莫斯科，从蒙特利尔到墨尔本。为了寻找答案，我走访了形形色色的地方，从里约热内卢一个注意力严重分散的贫民窟，到新西兰一个小镇的偏远办公室——那里的人们找到了一种彻底恢复专注力的方法。

I came to believe that we have profoundly misunderstood what is actually happening to our attention. For years, whenever I couldn’t focus, I would angrily blame myself. I would say: You’re lazy, you’re undisciplined, you need to pull yourself together. Or I would blame my phone, and rage against it, and wish it had never been invented. Most of the people I know respond the same way. But I learned that in fact something much deeper than personal failure, or a single new invention, is happening here.

我逐渐意识到，我们对注意力究竟发生了什么有着深刻的误解。多年来，每当我无法集中注意力时，我都会愤怒地责怪自己。我会对自己说：你太懒了，你太没自律了，你得振作起来。或者我会责怪我的手机，对它大发雷霆，恨不得它从未被发明出来。我认识的大多数人都有同样的反应。但我后来明白，这背后其实蕴含着比个人失败或某项新发明更深层次的原因。

I first began to glimpse this when I went to Portland, Oregon, to interview Professor Joel Nigg, who is one of the leading experts in the world on children’s attention problems. He said it might help me grasp what’s happening if we compare our rising attention problems to our rising obesity rates. Fifty years ago there was very little obesity, but today it is endemic in the Western world. This is not because we suddenly became greedy or self-indulgent. He said: ‘Obesity is not a medical epidemic – it’s a social epidemic. We have bad food, for example, and so people are getting fat.’ The way we live changed dramatically – our food supply changed, and we built cities it’s hard to walk or bike around – and those changes in our environment led to changes in our bodies. Something similar, he said, may be happening with the changes in our attention and focus.

我第一次意识到这一点，是在我去俄勒冈州波特兰市采访乔尔·尼格教授的时候。尼格教授是世界顶尖的儿童注意力问题专家之一。他说，如果我们把日益严重的注意力问题与不断上升的肥胖率进行比较，或许能帮助我理解正在发生的事情。五十年前，肥胖症几乎不存在，但如今它在西方世界已成流行病。这并非因为我们突然变得贪婪或放纵。他说：“肥胖不是一种医学流行病，而是一种社会流行病。例如，我们吃的食物不健康，所以人们才会发胖。”我们的生活方式发生了翻天覆地的变化——食物供应发生了改变，我们建造的城市也变得难以步行或骑自行车出行——而这些环境变化导致了我们身体的变化。他说，类似的情况也可能发生在我们的注意力和专注力方面。

He told me that after studying this topic for decades, he believes we need to ask if we are now developing ‘an attentional pathogenic culture’ – an environment in which sustained and deep focus is extremely hard for all of us, and you have to swim upstream to achieve it. There’s scientific evidence for many factors in poor attention, he said, and for some people there are some causes that lie in their biology, but he told me we may also need to figure out: ‘Is our society driving people to this point so often, because we have an epidemic [that’s being] caused by specific things that are dysfunctional in our society?’

他告诉我，在研究这个课题几十年后，他认为我们需要扪心自问，我们是否正在形成一种“注意力病态文化”——在这种环境下，持续而深入的专注对我们所有人来说都极其困难，必须逆流而上才能做到。他说，有很多科学证据表明注意力不集中是由多种因素造成的，对某些人来说，某些原因可能与他们的生理状况有关，但他告诉我，我们或许还需要弄清楚：“我们的社会是否经常把人们逼到这种境地，是因为我们社会中某些特定的功能失调因素导致了这种流行病？”

Later I asked him – if I put you in charge of the world, and you wanted to ruin people’s ability to pay attention, what would you do? He thought about it for a moment, and said: ‘Probably about what our society is doing.’

后来我问他——如果我让你掌管世界，而你想破坏人们的注意力，你会怎么做？他想了一会儿，说：“大概会针对我们这个社会正在做的事情吧。”

I found strong evidence that our collapsing ability to pay attention is not primarily a personal failing on my part, or your part, or your kid’s part. This is being done to us all. It is being done by very powerful forces. Those forces include Big Tech, but they also go way beyond them. This is a systemic problem. The truth is that you are living in a system that is pouring acid on your attention every day, and then you are being told to blame yourself and to fiddle with your own habits while the world’s attention burns. I realised, when I learned all this, that there is a hole in all the existing books I had read about how to improve your focus. It was huge. They have, in the main, neglected to talk about the actual causes of our attention crisis – which lie mainly in these larger forces. Based on what I learned, I have concluded there are twelve deep forces at work that are damaging our attention. I came to believe we can only solve this problem in the long term if we understand them – and then, together, we stop them from continuing to do this to us.

我发现了强有力的证据，证明我们注意力日益下降并非主要是你、我或你孩子的个人失误。这是所有人共同面临的问题，是由一些非常强大的力量造成的。这些力量包括大型科技公司，但远不止于此。这是一个系统性问题。事实是，你生活在一个每天都在腐蚀你注意力的系统中，然后你却被告知要自责，要你去改变自己的习惯，而与此同时，全世界的注意力却在燃烧。当我了解到这一切时，我意识到我读过的所有关于如何提高注意力的书籍都存在一个巨大的漏洞。它们大多忽略了我们注意力危机的真正原因——而这些原因主要在于这些更大的力量。基于我的所学，我得出结论，有十二种深层次的力量正在损害我们的注意力。我逐渐相信，只有理解这些力量，我们才能从长远角度解决这个问题——然后，我们才能共同阻止它们继续损害我们。

There are real steps you can take as an isolated individual to reduce this problem for yourself, and throughout this book you’ll learn how to carry them out. I am strongly in favour of you seizing personal responsibility in this way. But I have to be honest with you, in a way that I fear previous books on this topic were not. Those changes will only get you so far. They will solve a slice of the problem. They are valuable. I do them myself. But unless you are very lucky, they won’t allow you to escape the attention crisis. Systemic problems require systemic solutions. We have to take individual responsibility for this problem, for sure, but at the same time, together, we have to take collective responsibility for dealing with these deeper factors. There is a real solution – one that will actually make it possible for us to start to heal our attention. It requires us to radically reframe the problem, and then to take action. I believe I have figured out how we might start to do that.

作为个体，你可以采取一些切实可行的步骤来缓解这个问题，本书将教你如何做到。我强烈支持你以这种方式承担起个人责任。但我必须坦诚地告诉你，我担心之前关于这个主题的书籍并没有做到这一点。这些改变只能让你有所改善，它们只能解决一部分问题。它们固然有价值，我自己也在实践。但除非你非常幸运，否则它们无法让你摆脱注意力危机。系统性问题需要系统性的解决方案。我们当然必须为这个问题承担个人责任，但与此同时，我们也必须共同承担起解决这些更深层次问题的集体责任。确实存在一个真正的解决方案——一个能够真正帮助我们开始治愈注意力问题的方案。它要求我们彻底重新定义问题，然后采取行动。我相信我已经找到了我们可以着手解决这个问题的方法。

There are, I think, three crucial reasons why it is worth coming on this journey with me. The first is that a life full of distractions is, at an individual level, diminished. When you are unable to pay sustained attention, you can’t achieve the things you want to achieve. You want to read a book, but you are pulled away by the pings and paranoias of social media. You want to spend a few uninterrupted hours with your child, but you keep anxiously checking your email to see if your boss is messaging you. You want to set up a business, but your life dissolves instead into a blur of Facebook posts that only make you feel envious and anxious. Through no fault of your own, there never seems to be enough stillness – enough cool, clear space – for you to stop and think. A study by Professor Michael Posner at the University of Oregon found that if you are focusing on something and you get interrupted, on average it will take twenty-three minutes for you to get back to the same state of focus. A different study of office workers in the US found most of them never get an hour of uninterrupted work in a typical day. If this goes on for months and years, it scrambles your ability to figure out who you are and what you want. You become lost in your own life.

我认为，与我一同踏上这段旅程有三个至关重要的原因。首先，充满干扰的生活会削弱个人的能力。当你无法集中注意力时，你就无法实现自己想要达成的目标。你想读书，却被社交媒体的提示音和各种焦虑所牵引；你想和孩子享受几个小时不受打扰的时光，却总是焦虑地查看邮件，生怕老板给你发了消息；你想创业，却被Facebook上那些让你感到嫉妒和焦虑的帖子所淹没。并非你的错，你似乎永远找不到足够的安静——足够的冷静、清晰的空间——让你停下来思考。俄勒冈大学的迈克尔·波斯纳教授的一项研究发现，如果你正在专注于某件事，却被打断，平均需要23分钟才能重新集中注意力。另一项针对美国办公室工作人员的研究发现，他们中的大多数人在典型的一天中从未有过一小时不受干扰的工作时间。如果这种情况持续数月甚至数年，就会扰乱你认清自我、明确人生目标的能力。你会迷失在自己的生活中。

When I went to Moscow to interview the most important philosopher of attention in the world today, Dr James Williams – who works on the philosophy and ethics of technology at Oxford University – he told me: ‘If we want to do what matters in any domain – any context in life – we have to be able to give attention to the right things … If we can’t do that, it’s really hard to do anything.’ He said that if we want to understand the situation we are in at the moment, it helps to picture something. Imagine you are driving a car, but somebody has thrown a big bucket of mud all over the windshield. You’re going to face a lot of problems in that moment – you are at risk of knocking off your rear-view mirror, or getting lost, or arriving at your destination late. But the first thing you need to do – before you worry about any of those problems – is clean your windshield. Until you do that, you don’t even know where you are. We need to deal with our attention problems before we try to achieve any other sustained goal.

当我前往莫斯科采访当今世界最重要的注意力哲学家詹姆斯·威廉姆斯博士时——他在牛津大学研究技术哲学和伦理学——他告诉我：“如果我们想在任何领域、任何生活情境中做有意义的事情，就必须能够将注意力集中在正确的事情上……如果我们做不到这一点，就很难做成任何事情。” 他说，如果我们想理解我们目前所处的境况，想象一些场景会很有帮助。想象一下，你正在开车，但有人把一大桶泥巴泼在了挡风玻璃上。那一刻你会面临很多问题——你可能会撞掉后视镜，可能会迷路，或者可能会迟到。但你首先需要做的——在你担心这些问题之前——是擦干净挡风玻璃。在你擦干净之前，你甚至不知道自己身在何处。在我们尝试实现任何其他持久目标之前，我们需要先解决我们的注意力问题。

The second reason we need to think about this subject is that this fracturing of attention isn’t just causing problems for us as individuals – it’s causing crises in our whole society. As a species, we are facing a slew of unprecedented tripwires and trapdoors – like the climate crisis – and, unlike previous generations, we are mostly not rising to solve our biggest challenges. Why? Part of the reason, I think, is that when attention breaks down, problem-solving breaks down. Solving big problems requires the sustained focus of many people over many years. Democracy requires the ability of a population to pay attention long enough to identify real problems, distinguish them from fantasies, come up with solutions, and hold their leaders accountable if they fail to deliver them. If we lose that, we lose our ability to have a fully functioning society. I don’t think it’s a coincidence that this crisis in paying attention has taken place at the same time as the worst crisis of democracy since the 1930s. People who can’t focus will be more drawn to simplistic authoritarian solutions – and less likely to see clearly when they fail. A world full of attention-deprived citizens alternating between Twitter and Snapchat will be a world of cascading crises where we can’t get a handle on any of them.

我们需要思考这个问题的第二个原因是，这种注意力分散不仅给我们个人带来问题，也给整个社会带来危机。作为一个物种，我们正面临着一系列前所未有的陷阱和陷阱——比如气候危机——而且，与前几代人不同的是，我们大多没有挺身而出解决这些最大的挑战。为什么？我认为部分原因是，当注意力分散时，解决问题的能力也会随之下降。解决重大问题需要许多人多年来的持续关注。民主要求民众能够集中足够的注意力来识别真正的问题，区分现实问题和幻想，提出解决方案，并在领导人未能兑现承诺时追究其责任。如果我们失去了这种能力，我们就失去了拥有一个运转良好的社会的能力。我认为，这场注意力危机与自20世纪30年代以来最严重的民主危机同时发生绝非巧合。注意力不集中的人更容易被简单粗暴的威权解决方案所吸引，也更难看清这些方案的失败之处。一个充斥着注意力匮乏、在推特和Snapchat之间来回切换的公民的世界，将会是一个危机层出不穷、我们根本无力应对的世界。

The third reason we need to think deeply about focus is, for me, the most hopeful. If we understand what’s happening, we can begin to change it. The writer James Baldwin – the man who is, for my money, the greatest writer of the twentieth century – said: ‘Not everything that is faced can be changed, but nothing can be changed until it is faced.’ This crisis is human-made, and it can be unmade by us too.

我们需要深入思考专注的第三个原因，对我而言，也是最令人充满希望的一点。如果我们理解了正在发生的事情，我们就能开始改变它。作家詹姆斯·鲍德温——在我看来，他是二十世纪最伟大的作家——曾说过：“并非所有面对的事情都能改变，但只有面对它，才能改变任何事情。”这场危机是人为造成的，我们也能够化解它。

I want to tell you right at the start how I gathered the evidence I’m going to present to you in this book, and why I selected it. In my research, I read a very large number of scientific studies, and then I went to interview the scientists who I thought had gathered the most important evidence. Several different kinds of scientists have studied attention and focus. One group are neuroscientists, and you’ll hear from them. But the people who have done the most work on why it is changing are social scientists, who analyse how changes in the way we live affect us, both as individuals, and as groups. I studied social and political sciences at Cambridge University, where I got a rigorous training in how to read the studies these scientists publish, how to assess the evidence they put forward, and – I hope – how to ask probing questions about it.

我想开门见山地告诉大家，我是如何收集本书中要呈现的证据，以及我选择这些证据的原因。在研究过程中，我阅读了大量的科学论文，然后采访了我认为收集到最重要证据的科学家。许多不同类型的科学家都研究过注意力和专注力。其中一类是神经科学家，你们也会听到他们的观点。但真正深入研究注意力变化原因的是社会科学家，他们分析了生活方式的改变如何影响我们，无论是作为个体还是群体。我曾在剑桥大学学习社会与政治科学，在那里我接受了严格的训练，学习如何阅读这些科学家发表的研究论文，如何评估他们提出的证据，以及——我希望——如何就此提出深入的问题。

These scientists often disagree with each other about what is happening and why. This isn’t because the science is rickety but because humans are extremely complex, and it’s really hard to measure something as complicated as what affects our ability to pay attention. This obviously presented a challenge to me as I wrote this book. If we wait for perfect evidence, we will be waiting for ever. I had to proceed, doing my best, on the basis of the best information we have – while always being conscious that this science is fallible and fragile and needs to be handled with care.

这些科学家常常对正在发生的事情及其原因各执己见。这并非因为科学本身存在缺陷，而是因为人类极其复杂，而像影响我们注意力这样复杂的因素，很难进行精确测量。这无疑给我的写作带来了挑战。如果我们等待完美的证据，那将永远无法得到答案。我只能尽我所能，基于我们掌握的最佳信息继续写作——同时始终牢记，科学并非完美无缺，它脆弱易错，需要谨慎对待。

So I have tried, at every stage in this book, to give you a sense of how controversial the evidence I am offering is. On some of the topics, the subject has been studied by hundreds of scientists, and they have achieved a broad consensus that the points I am going to put forward are correct. That’s obviously the ideal, and wherever it was possible, I sought out scientists who represent a consensus in their field and built my conclusions on the solid rocks of their knowledge. But there are some other areas where only a handful of scientists have studied the question I wanted to understand, and so the evidence I can draw on is thinner. There are a few other topics where different reputable scientists strongly disagree about what’s really going on. In those cases, I am going to tell you upfront, and try to represent a range of perspectives on the question. At every stage I have tried to build my conclusions on the strongest evidence I could find.

因此，在本书的每个阶段，我都力求让读者感受到我所提供的证据的争议性。在某些主题上，已有数百位科学家进行过研究，并达成了广泛的共识，认为我即将提出的观点是正确的。这当然是理想状态，因此，我尽可能地寻找在其领域内具有共识的科学家，并基于他们扎实的知识基础来构建我的结论。但在其他一些领域，只有少数科学家研究过我想要了解的问题，因此我能引用的证据就比较薄弱。还有一些主题，不同的权威科学家对问题的本质存在着激烈的争论。在这些情况下，我会事先说明，并努力呈现不同的观点。在每个阶段，我都力求以我能找到的最有力的证据来构建我的结论。

I have tried to always approach this process with humility. I’m not an expert on any of these questions. I’m a journalist, approaching experts, and testing and explaining their knowledge as best I can. If you want more detail on these debates, I delve much deeper into the evidence in the more than 400 endnotes I have put on the book’s website, discussing the more than 250 scientific studies I have drawn on in this book. I have also sometimes used my own experiences to help explain what I learned. My individual anecdotes obviously aren’t scientific evidence. They tell you something simpler: why I wanted to know the answers to these questions so badly.

我始终以谦逊的态度对待这个过程。我并非这些问题的专家。我是一名记者，我接触专家，尽我所能地验证并解释他们的知识。如果您想更深入地了解这些争论，我在本书网站上提供的400多条尾注中对此进行了更详尽的探讨，这些尾注讨论了我在本书中引用的250多项科学研究。有时，我也会结合自己的经历来解释我的发现。我的个人经历显然并非科学证据。它们只说明了一个简单的问题：为什么我如此渴望知道这些问题的答案。

When I came back from my trip to Memphis with Adam, I was appalled at myself. One day, I spent three hours reading the same first few pages of a novel, getting lost in distracted thoughts every time, almost as though I was stoned, and I thought – I can’t continue like this. Reading fiction had always been one of my greatest pleasures, and losing it would be like losing a limb. So I announced to my friends that I was going to do something drastic.

我和亚当从孟菲斯旅行回来后，对自己感到无比震惊。有一天，我花了三个小时反复阅读同一本小说的前几页，每次都心不在焉，几乎像吸了毒一样。我心想——我不能再这样下去了。阅读小说一直是我最大的乐趣之一，失去它就像失去一条胳膊或一条胳膊。于是，我告诉朋友们，我要采取一些激烈的措施。

I thought this was happening to me because I wasn’t disciplined enough as an individual, and because I had been taken over by my phone. So at the time, I thought the solution was obvious: be more disciplined and banish your phone. I went online and booked myself a little room by the beach in Provincetown, at the tip of Cape Cod. I am going to be there for three months, I announced triumphantly to everyone, with no smartphone, and no computer that can get online. I’m done. I’m through. For the first time in twenty years, I’m going offline. I talked to my friends about the double meaning of the word ‘wired’. It means both being in a manic, hyper mental state, and being online. They seemed to me to be tied together, these twin definitions. I was tired of being wired. I needed to clear my head. And so I did it. I quit. I set up an auto-reply saying I would be unreachable for the next three months. I abandoned the buzz in which I had vibrated for twenty years.

我当时觉得这一切发生在我身上，是因为我个人不够自律，也因为我被手机控制了。所以，我觉得解决办法显而易见：更加自律，把手机扔掉。我在网上订了一间位于科德角顶端普罗温斯敦海滩边的小房间。我得意洋洋地向所有人宣布，我要在那里待三个月，期间不带智能手机，也不带任何能上网的电脑。我彻底结束了。我彻底告别了。二十年来，我第一次要断网。我和朋友们聊起了“wired”（网络）这个词的双重含义。它既指一种亢奋、高度紧张的精神状态，也指沉迷于网络。在我看来，这两个含义密不可分。我厌倦了这种网络状态。我需要清空思绪。于是，我这么做了。我戒掉了手机。我设置了自动回复，说接下来的三个月我将无法联系。我放弃了让我沉迷了二十年的网络生活。

I tried to go into this extreme digital detox without any illusions. I knew this ditching of the entire internet couldn’t be a long-term solution for me – I wasn’t going to join the Amish and abandon technology for ever. Even more than that, I knew this approach couldn’t even be a short-term solution for most people. I come from a working-class family – my grandmother, who raised me, cleaned toilets; my dad was a bus driver – and saying to them that the solution to their attention problems would be to quit their jobs and go and live in a shack by the sea would be a spiteful insult: they literally can’t do it.

我尝试进行这种极端的数码戒断，但并没有抱任何幻想。我知道彻底戒掉网络对我来说并非长久之计——我不可能像阿米什人那样永远放弃科技。更重要的是，我知道这种方法对大多数人来说甚至连短期都无法奏效。我出身于工人阶级家庭——我的祖母是清洁工，她养育了我；我的父亲是公交车司机——如果我告诉他们，解决注意力问题的办法是辞职去海边的小棚屋里生活，那简直是对他们的侮辱：他们根本做不到。

I did it because I thought that if I didn’t, I might lose some crucial aspects of my ability to think deeply. I did it in desperation. And I did it because I felt that if I stripped everything back for a time, I might start to be able to glimpse the changes we could all make in a more sustainable way. This drastic digital detox taught me a lot of important things – including, as you’ll see, the limits of digital detoxes.

我这么做是因为我觉得如果不这么做，我可能会失去一些至关重要的深度思考能力。我是走投无路才这么做的。我这么做也是因为我觉得，如果我暂时抛开一切，或许就能开始瞥见我们所有人都能以更可持续的方式做出的改变。这次彻底的数字排毒教会了我很多重要的东西——包括，正如你将看到的，数字排毒的局限性。

It began on a morning in May when I set off for Provincetown, with the glare of the screens of Graceland haunting me. I thought the problem was in my own distractible nature and in our tech, and I was about to give my devices away – freedom, oh freedom! – for a long, long time.

那是五月的一个清晨，我出发前往普罗温斯敦，格雷斯兰庄园里刺眼的屏幕一直萦绕在我心头。我当时觉得问题出在自己容易分心的性格和我们使用的科技产品上，我打算把所有电子设备都扔掉——自由啊，自由！——很长很长一段时间都不用。

# ↩

1 Cause One: The Increase in Speed, Switching and Filtering

原因一：速度、切换和滤波的增加

‘I don’t understand what you’re asking for,’ the man in Target in Boston kept saying to me. ‘These are the cheapest phones we got. They have super-slow internet. That’s what you want, right?’ No, I said. I want a phone that can’t access the internet at all. He studied the back of the box, looking confused. ‘This would be really slow. You could probably get your email but you wouldn’t—’ Email is still the internet, I said. I am going to go away for three months, specifically so I can be totally offline.

“我不明白你想要什么，”波士顿塔吉特百货的店员不停地跟我说。“这些是我们店里最便宜的手机。它们的网速超级慢。这就是你想要的，对吧？” 不，我说。“我想要一部完全不能上网的手机。” 他仔细看了看包装盒背面，一脸困惑。“这手机网速会非常慢。你或许能收到邮件，但你根本——” “邮件也是网络啊，”我说。“我要离开三个月，就是为了彻底断网。”

My friend Imtiaz had already given me his old, broken laptop, one that had lost the ability to get online years before. It looked like it came from the set of the original Star Trek , a remnant from some aborted vision of the future. I was going to use it, I had resolved, to finally write the novel I had been planning for years. Now what I needed was a phone where I could be called in emergencies by the six people I was going to give the number to. I needed it to have no internet option of any kind, so that if I woke up at 3 a.m. and my resolve cracked and I tried to get online, I wouldn’t be able to do it, no matter how hard I tried.

我的朋友伊姆蒂亚兹已经把他的旧笔记本电脑给了我，那台电脑几年前就坏了，根本连不上网。它看起来就像是从初代《星际迷航》的片场里搬出来的，像是某个夭折的未来愿景的遗物。我下定决心要用它，终于可以写出我计划了好几年的小说了。现在我需要一部手机，这样在紧急情况下，我把号码告诉的六个人都能联系到我。我需要它完全不能上网，这样，就算我凌晨三点醒来，意志力动摇，想上网，也无论如何都做不到。

When I explained to people what I was planning, I would get one of three responses. The first was just like that of this man in Target: they couldn’t seem to process what I was saying. They thought I was saying that I was going to cut back on my internet use. The idea of going offline completely seemed to them so bizarre that I had to explain it again and again. ‘So you want a phone that can’t go online at all? ’ he said. ‘Why would you want that?’

当我向别人解释我的计划时，通常会得到三种反应。第一种就像我在Target超市遇到的那个男人一样：他们似乎无法理解我的意思。他们以为我说的是要减少上网时间。完全断网的想法在他们看来简直匪夷所思，所以我不得不一遍又一遍地解释。“所以你想要一部完全不能上网的手机？”他问道，“你为什么要这么做？”

The second response – which this man offered next – was a kind of low-level panic on my behalf. ‘What will you do in an emergency?’ he asked. ‘It doesn’t seem right.’ I asked – what emergency will require me to get online? What’s going to happen? I’m not the President of the United States – I don’t have to issue orders if Russia invades Ukraine. ‘Anything,’ he said. ‘Anything could happen.’ I kept explaining to the people my age – I was thirty-nine at the time – that we had spent half our lives without phones, so it shouldn’t be so hard to picture returning to the way we had lived for so long. Nobody seemed to find this persuasive.

接下来这个人给出的第二个回答，让我感到一丝不安。“万一发生紧急情况怎么办？”他问，“这感觉不太对劲。”我反问——什么紧急情况需要我上网？会发生什么？我又不是美国总统——就算俄罗斯入侵乌克兰，我又不用下令。“什么事都可能发生，”他说，“什么事都有可能发生。”我反复向和我同龄的人解释——当时我39岁——我们人生的一半时间都没有手机，所以重新回到过去那种生活方式应该不难想象。但似乎没人觉得这有说服力。

And the third response was envy. People began to fantasise about what they would do with all the time they spent on their phones if it was all suddenly freed up. They started by listing the number of hours that Apple’s Screen Time option told them they spent on their phones every day. For the average American, it’s three hours and fifteen minutes. We touch our phones 2,617 times every twenty-four hours. Sometimes they would wistfully mention something they loved and had abandoned – playing the piano, say – and stare off into the distance.

第三种反应是羡慕。人们开始幻想，如果突然间所有花在手机上的时间都空出来了，他们会用这些时间做什么。他们首先列出苹果“屏幕使用时间”功能显示的自己每天使用手机的时间。对于普通美国人来说，这个数字是三个小时十五分钟。我们每天触摸手机2617次。有时，他们会怅然地提起自己曾经热爱却已经放弃的事情——比如弹钢琴——然后凝视远方。

Target had nothing for me. Ironically, I had to go online to order what seemed to be the last remaining cellphone in the United States that can’t access the web. It’s called the Jitterbug. It’s designed for extremely old people, and it doubles as a medical emergency device. I opened the box and smiled at its giant buttons and told myself that there’s an added bonus: if I fall over, it will automatically connect me to the nearest hospital.

Target 商店里什么都没有。讽刺的是，我最后还是得上网订购一部似乎是全美最后一款不能上网的手机。它叫 Jitterbug，是专为老年人设计的，还能当做紧急医疗设备。我打开盒子，看着它巨大的按钮笑了，心想这手机还有个额外的好处：万一我摔倒了，它会自动帮我联系最近的医院。

I laid out on the hotel bed everything I was taking with me. I had gone through all the routine things I normally use my iPhone for, and bought objects to replace each one. So for the first time since I was a teenager, I bought a watch. I got an alarm clock. I dug out my old iPod and loaded it with audiobooks and podcasts, and I ran my finger along its screen, thinking about how futuristic this gadget seemed to me when I bought it twelve years ago; now it looked like something that Noah might have carried onto the Ark. I had Imtiaz’s broken laptop – now rendered, effectively, into a 1990s-style word processor – and next to it I had a pile of classic novels I had been meaning to read for decades, with War and Peace at the top.

我把要带的所有东西都摊在了酒店的床上。我仔细检查了平时用iPhone做的事情，然后买了东西来替代。所以，自从十几岁以来，我第一次买了一块手表。我买了一个闹钟。我翻出了我的旧iPod，往里面装了有声读物和播客，然后用手指划过屏幕，回想起十二年前买它时，我觉得它多么具有未来感；现在它看起来就像诺亚方舟上的东西。我带着伊姆蒂亚兹那台坏掉的笔记本电脑——现在它实际上变成了一台九十年代风格的文字处理器——旁边是一摞我一直想读却没读的经典小说，最上面是《战争与和平》。

I took an Uber so I could hand over my iPhone and my MacBook to a friend who lived in Boston. I hesitated before putting them on the table in her house. Quickly, I pushed a button on my phone to summon a car to take me to the ferry terminal, and then I switched it off and walked away from it fast, like it might come running after me. I felt a twinge of panic. I’m not ready for this, I thought. Then somewhere, from the back of my mind, I remembered something the Spanish writer José Ortega y Gasset said: ‘We cannot put off living until we are ready … Life is fired at us point-blank.’ If you don’t do this now, I told myself, you’ll never do it, and you’ll be lying on your deathbed seeing how many likes you got on Instagram. I climbed into the car and refused to look back.

我叫了辆优步，把我的iPhone和MacBook交给住在波士顿的朋友。把它们放在她家桌子上之前，我犹豫了一下。我迅速按下手机上的一个按钮，叫了一辆车送我去渡轮码头，然后关掉手机，快步走开，好像它会追着我似的。我感到一阵恐慌。我还没准备好，我想。这时，我突然想起西班牙作家何塞·奥尔特加·伊·加塞特说过的一句话：“我们不能等到准备好才去生活……生活就像一记近距离的炮弹，直击我们的内心。” 我告诉自己，如果现在不做，就永远没机会了，到时候躺在病床上，看着自己在Instagram上获得了多少个赞，恐怕就没机会了。我钻进车里，头也不回地走了。

I had learned years before from social scientists that when it comes to beating any kind of destructive habit, one of the most effective tools we have is called ‘ pre-commitment’. It’s right there in one of the oldest surviving human stories, Homer’s Odyssey . Homer tells of how there was once a patch of sea that sailors would always die in, for a strange reason: living in the ocean, there were two sirens – a uniquely hot blend of woman and fish – who would sing to the sailors to join them in the ocean. Then, when they clambered in for some sexy fish-based action, they’d drown. But then, one day, the hero of the story – Ulysses – figured out how to beat these temptresses. Before the ship approached the sirens’ stretch of sea, he got his crew members to tie him to the mast, hard, hand and foot. He couldn’t move. When he heard the sirens, no matter how much Ulysses yearned to dive in, he couldn’t.

多年前，我从社会科学家那里了解到，要克服任何类型的不良习惯，最有效的工具之一就是“预先承诺”。这在现存最古老的人类故事之一——荷马史诗《奥德赛》中就有记载。荷马讲述了从前有一片海域，水手们总是会在那里丧命，原因很奇怪：那里住着两个塞壬——一种人鱼结合的性感生物——她们会用歌声引诱水手们下海。然后，当水手们爬进海里，想要和她们来一场鱼腥的邂逅时，就会溺水身亡。但是，有一天，故事中的英雄——尤利西斯——找到了战胜这些诱惑者的方法。在船驶近塞壬所在的海域之前，他让船员们把他的手脚牢牢地绑在桅杆上。他动弹不得。当他听到警笛声时，无论尤利西斯多么渴望跳进去，他都做不到。

I had used this technique before when I was trying to lose weight. I used to buy loads of carbs and tell myself I would be strong enough to eat them slowly and in moderation, but then I would guzzle them at 2 a.m. So I stopped buying them. At 2 a.m., I wasn’t going to haul myself to a store to buy Pringles. The you that exists in the present – right now – wants to pursue your deeper goals, and wants to be a better person. But you know you’re fallible and likely to crack in the face of temptation. So you bind the future version of you. You narrow your choices. You tie yourself to the mast.

我以前减肥的时候也用过这招。我以前会买一大堆碳水化合物，告诉自己我会有毅力慢慢吃，适量享用，但最后还是会在凌晨两点狼吞虎咽。所以我干脆就不买了。凌晨两点，我可不想挣扎着去商店买品客薯片。现在的你——此时此刻的你——想要追求更深层次的目标，想要成为一个更好的人。但你知道自己会犯错，很容易在诱惑面前崩溃。所以你限制了未来的自己。你缩小了选择范围。你把自己绑在了桅杆上。

There has been a small range of scientific experiments to see if this really works, at least in the short term. For example, in 2013 a professor of psychology named Molly Crockett – who I interviewed at Yale – got a bunch of men into a lab and split them into two groups. All of them were going to face a challenge. They were told that they could see a slightly sexy picture right away if they wanted to, but if they were able to wait and do nothing for a little while, they would get to see a super-sexy picture. The first group was told to use their willpower, and discipline themselves in the moment. But the second group was given a chance, before they went into the lab, to ‘pre-commit’ – to resolve, out loud, that they were going to stop and wait so they could see the sexier picture. The scientists wanted to know – would the men who made a pre-commitment hold out more often, and longer, than the men who didn’t? It turned out pre-commitment was strikingly successful – resolving clearly to do something, and making a pledge that they’d stick to it, made the men significantly better at holding out. In the years since, scientists have shown the same effect in a broad range of experiments.

为了验证这种方法是否真的有效，至少在短期内有效，已经有一些科学实验。例如，2013年，一位名叫莫莉·克罗克特（Molly Crockett）的心理学教授（我在耶鲁大学采访过她）召集了一群男性进入实验室，并将他们分成两组。他们都将面临一项挑战：他们被告知，如果他们愿意，可以立即看到一张略带性感的图片；但如果他们能够等待一段时间，什么也不做，就能看到一张超级性感的图片。第一组被告知要运用他们的意志力，并在当下约束自己。而第二组在进入实验室之前，有机会“预先承诺”——大声地决定他们会停下来等待，以便看到那张更性感的图片。科学家们想知道：那些预先做出承诺的男性，是否比那些没有预先承诺的男性更能坚持下去，并且坚持的时间更长？事实证明，预先承诺的效果非常显著——明确下定决心去做某件事，并承诺坚持到底，能显著提高男性的坚持能力。此后多年，科学家们在大量实验中也证实了这一点。

My trip to Provincetown was an extreme form of pre-commitment, and like Ulysses’ victory, it also began on a boat. As the ferry to Provincetown pulled out, I looked back at Boston Harbour, where the May light was reflecting on the water. I stood towards the back of the ship, next to a wet and flapping Stars and Stripes, and watched the foam of the ocean spraying behind us. After about forty minutes, Provincetown slowly appeared on the horizon when I saw the thin spike of the Pilgrim Monument come into view.

我的普罗温斯敦之旅可谓是一次彻底的预先承诺，就像尤利西斯的胜利一样，它也始于一艘船。当前往普罗温斯敦的渡轮驶离港口时，我回头望向波士顿港，五月的阳光洒在水面上，波光粼粼。我站在船尾，旁边是一面被水浸湿、迎风飘扬的星条旗，看着海浪在我们身后激起的泡沫。大约四十分钟后，普罗温斯敦缓缓出现在地平线上，我看到了朝圣者纪念碑那纤细的尖顶。

Provincetown is a long, lush strip of sand where the United States juts into the Atlantic Ocean. It is the last stop in the Americas, the end of the road. You can stand there, the writer Henry David Thoreau said, and feel the whole of the United States at your back. I felt a giddy sense of lightness, and as the beach appeared through the foam, I began to laugh, though I didn’t know why. I was almost drunk with exhaustion. I was thirty-nine, and I had been working non-stop since I was twenty-one. I had taken almost no holidays. I fattened myself with information every waking hour to make myself a more productive writer, and I had started to think that the way I lived was a bit like the process where, in a factory farm, a foie gras goose is force-fed gross amounts in order to turn its liver into pâté. In the previous five years, I had travelled over 80,000 miles, researching, writing and talking about two books. All day, every day, I tried to inhale more information, interview more people, learn more, talk more, and I was now manically skipping between topics, like a record that has been scratched from overuse, and I was finding it hard to retain anything. I had felt tired for so long that all I knew was how to outrun it.

普罗温斯敦是一片绵延的、郁郁葱葱的沙滩，美国在此伸入大西洋。它是美洲大陆的最后一站，是路的尽头。作家亨利·大卫·梭罗曾说，你可以站在那里，感受到整个美国就在你身后。我感到一阵眩晕般的轻盈，当沙滩从浪花中显现出来时，我不禁笑了起来，尽管我不知道为什么。我几乎累得酩酊大醉。我三十九岁，从二十一岁起就没日没夜地工作，几乎没有休过假。为了让自己成为一个更高效的作家，我醒着的每一分钟都在拼命地吸收信息，我开始觉得我的生活方式有点像工厂化养殖场里，为了把鹅肝做成鹅肝酱，强迫鹅吃下大量的饲料。在过去的五年里，我为了两本书的调研、写作和宣传，旅行了超过八万英里。我整天都在努力吸收信息，采访更多的人，学习更多的知识，进行更多的交流，但现在我却像一张被过度播放而磨损的唱片一样，疯狂地在各种话题间跳跃，发现自己很难记住任何东西。我感到疲惫不堪，以至于我唯一知道的就是如何逃避这种疲惫感。

As people began to disembark, I heard the ping of an incoming text message somewhere on the ferry and reached instinctively for my pocket. I felt a panic – where’s my phone? – and then remembered, and laughed even more.

人们开始下船时，我听到渡轮上某处传来短信提示音，下意识地伸手去摸口袋。我顿时慌了——手机呢？——然后才想起来，忍不住笑了起来。

I found myself thinking, at that moment, about the first time I had ever seen a cellphone. I was around fourteen or fifteen – so this was 1993 or 1994 – and I was on the top deck of the 340 bus in London, coming home from school. A man in a suit was talking loudly into an object that in my memory is the size of a small cow. All of us on that top deck turned and looked at him. He seemed to be enjoying us looking, and he talked louder. This continued for some time, until another passenger said to him: ‘Mate?’ ‘Yes? ‘You’re a wanker.’ And the people on the bus broke the first rule of public transport in London. We looked at each other, and we smiled. These small rebellions were happening all over London, I recall, at the birth of mobile phones. We saw them as an absurd invasion.

那一刻，我突然想起了第一次见到手机的情景。我大概十四五岁——也就是1993年或1994年——当时我正坐在伦敦340路公交车的上层，放学回家。一个穿着西装的男人对着一个东西大声说话，我记得那东西跟一头小牛差不多大。上层车厢里的所有人都转头看向他。他似乎很享受我们盯着他看，于是声音更大了。这种情况持续了一会儿，直到另一个乘客对他说：“哥们儿？”“什么事？”“你个混蛋。”于是，车上的乘客们违反了伦敦公共交通的第一条规则。我们互相看了一眼，然后笑了。我记得，在手机诞生之初，这种小小的反抗在伦敦到处发生。我们当时觉得手机是一种荒谬的入侵。

I sent my first email about five years later, when I went to university. I was nineteen years old. I wrote a few sentences, and clicked send, and waited to feel something. No surge of excitement came. I wondered why there was such a fuss about this new email thing. If you had told me then that within twenty years a combination of these two technologies – that seemed initially either repellent or yawnsome – would come to dominate my life to the point where I would have to get on a boat and flee, I would have thought you had lost your mind.

大约五年后，我上了大学，才发出了我的第一封电子邮件。那时我十九岁。我写了几句话，点击发送，然后等待着某种感觉。然而，并没有涌起一股兴奋之情。我纳闷，为什么人们对电子邮件这种新玩意儿如此大惊小怪。如果当时有人告诉我，二十年后，这两种最初让我觉得要么令人反感要么乏味的技术结合起来，会主宰我的生活，以至于我不得不乘船逃离，我肯定会觉得他疯了。

I tugged my bag off the boat and pulled out the map I had printed from the internet. I hadn’t navigated anywhere without Google Maps in years, but fortunately, Provincetown consists of one long street, so there are literally only two directions you can give – go left, or go right. I had to go right, to the offices of the estate agent I had rented my sliver of a beachhouse from. Commercial Street runs through the middle of Provincetown, and I walked past the neat New England stores selling lobsters and sex toys (these are not the same shops, obviously – that’s a niche even Provincetown would shun). I remembered that I chose this place for a few reasons. A year before, I had come over for a day from Boston to visit my friend Andrew, who lives there every summer. Provincetown is like a cross between a quaint Cape Cod village in the old New England style, and a sex dungeon. For a long time, it was a working-class fishing town populated by Portuguese immigrants and their kids. Then artists started to move in, and it became a Bohemian enclave. Then it became a gay destination. Today it is a place where, in old fisherman’s cottages, there now live men whose full-time job is to dress as Ursula, the villain from The Little Mermaid , and sing songs about cunnilingus to the tourists who dominate the town in summer.

我从船上拽下包，拿出从网上打印的地图。我已经好几年没用谷歌地图导航了，不过幸运的是，普罗温斯敦只有一条长街，所以你只能给出两个方向——左转或右转。我得往右走，去我租住那间狭小海滨别墅的房产中介办公室。商业街贯穿普罗温斯敦的中心，我走过那些整洁的新英格兰商店，它们有卖龙虾的，也有卖情趣用品的（显然，这两家店不一样——即使是普罗温斯敦，也会对情趣用品这种小众商品避之不及）。我记起我选择来这里有几个原因。一年前，我从波士顿过来一天，去看望我的朋友安德鲁，他每年夏天都住在这里。普罗温斯敦就像是古朴的科德角小镇（保留着新英格兰的古老风貌）和情趣地牢的结合体。很长一段时间以来，这里都是一个以葡萄牙移民及其子女为主的工人阶级渔村。后来，艺术家们开始涌入，这里逐渐变成了波西米亚人的聚居地。之后，它又成了同性恋者的天堂。如今，在昔日渔民的小屋里，住着一些男人，他们的全职工作就是装扮成《小美人鱼》中的反派乌苏拉，为夏季涌入小镇的游客们演唱关于口交的歌曲。

I chose Provincetown because I found it charming but not complex – I felt (slightly arrogantly) that I had figured out its essential dynamics in my first twenty-four hours there. I was determined to go to a place that would not trigger my journalistic curiosity too much. If I had chosen (say) Bali, I know that I would have soon started trying to figure out how Balinese society worked, and begun interviewing people, and soon I would be back to my manic information-sucking. I wanted a pretty purgatory where I could decompress, and nothing more.

我选择普罗温斯敦是因为我觉得它很迷人，但并不复杂——我（略带自负地）觉得，仅仅24小时，我就掌握了它的基本运作模式。我决心去一个不会过度激发我新闻记者好奇心的地方。如果我选择的是（比如说）巴厘岛，我知道我很快就会开始琢磨巴厘岛的社会运作方式，开始采访当地人，很快我就会重新陷入疯狂的信息收集状态。我想要的是一个美丽的世外桃源，让我可以放松身心，仅此而已。

The estate agent, Pat, drove me out to the beachhouse. It was close to the sea, a forty-minute walk from the centre of Provincetown – almost in the neighbouring town of Truro, in fact. It was a plain wooden house, split into four different apartments. Mine was to the bottom left. I asked Pat to remove the modem – in case, in some fit of madness, I went and bought an internet-connected device – and to cut off all the cable packages on the television. I had two rooms. Beyond the house, there was a short gravel path, and at the end of it, waiting for me, was the ocean, vast and open and warm. Pat bid me good luck, and I was alone.

房产经纪人帕特开车送我到海滨别墅。别墅离海边很近，从普罗温斯敦镇中心步行四十分钟就能到——实际上几乎就在邻近的特鲁罗镇了。那是一栋普通的木屋，被隔成了四个独立的公寓。我的公寓在左下角。我让帕特把调制解调器拿走——以防我一时兴起去买了个能上网的设备——还让她把电视上的所有有线电视套餐都取消了。我住两间房。房子外面有一条短短的碎石路，路的尽头就是浩瀚无垠、温暖无比的大海。帕特祝我好运，然后我就独自一人待在那里了。

I unpacked my books and began to flick through them. I couldn’t get any traction with the one I picked up. I left it aside and walked over towards the ocean. It was early in the Provincetown season, and there were only around six other people that I could see for any direction stretching for miles. I felt then a sudden certainty – you only get these feelings a few times in a lifetime – that I had done absolutely the right thing. For so long I had been fixing my gaze on things that were very fast and very temporary, like a Twitter feed. When you fix your gaze on the speedy, you feel pensive, amped up, liable to be washed away if you don’t move, wave, shout. Now I found myself staring at something very old and very permanent. This ocean was here long before you, I thought, and it will be there long after your small concerns are forgotten. Twitter makes you feel that the whole world is obsessed with you and your little ego – it loves you, it hates you, it’s talking about you right now . The ocean makes you feel like the world is greeting you with a soft, wet, welcoming indifference. It’s never going to argue back, no matter how loud you yell.

我打开书包，开始翻阅。拿起一本，却怎么也读不进去。我把它放在一边，朝海边走去。那时普罗温斯敦的旅游旺季才刚刚开始，方圆几英里内，我能看到的只有大约六个人。那一刻，我突然感到一种莫名的确定——这种感觉一生中也就只有几次——我确信自己做的绝对正确。长久以来，我一直把目光投向那些转瞬即逝的事物，比如推特。当你盯着那些快速变化的东西时，你会感到忧郁、兴奋，仿佛如果不行动、不挥手、不呐喊，就会被冲走。而现在，我发现自己正凝视着一些古老而永恒的东西。我想，这片海洋在你之前就存在了，在你那些琐碎的烦恼被遗忘之后，它依然会在那里。推特让你觉得全世界都对你和你那点可怜的自尊心着迷——它爱你，它恨你，它此刻正在议论你。大海让你感觉世界正以一种温柔、湿润、热情而又冷漠的态度迎接你。无论你如何大声呼喊，它都不会反驳。

I stood there for a long time. There was something shocking to me about being so still – to be not scrolling, but static. I tried to remember the last time I had felt like this. I walked down towards Provincetown through the ocean with my jeans rolled up. The water was warm and my feet sank a little into the sand. Little fish swam past and around my pasty white legs. I watched crabs burrow into the sand ahead of me. Then, after about fifteen minutes, I saw something so strange that I kept staring at it, and the more I stared, the more confused I became. There was a man standing on the water, out in the middle of the ocean. He was not on a boat, nor on any floating device I could see. But he was far out at sea, and he was standing tall and firm. I wondered if, in my exhaustion, I had somehow begun to hallucinate. I waved to him; he waved back; and then he turned away, and stood with his palms out, facing the water. He stood there for a long time, and I stood there just as long, watching him. Then he began to walk towards me, seemingly on top of the ocean.

我站在那里很久。这种静止不动的感觉让我感到震惊——不是在滑动屏幕，而是静止不动。我努力回想上次有这种感觉是什么时候。我卷起牛仔裤的裤腿，沿着海向普罗温斯敦走去。海水很温暖，我的脚微微陷进沙子里。小鱼在我苍白的双腿间游来游去。我看着螃蟹在我前方的沙子里挖洞。大约过了十五分钟，我看到了一些奇怪的东西，我目不转睛地盯着它看，看得越久，我就越困惑。一个男人站在海面上，在茫茫大海的中央。他不在船上，也不在任何我能看到的漂浮物上。但他确实在遥远的海面上，而且站得笔直挺拔。我怀疑自己是不是因为疲惫而产生了幻觉。我向他挥手；他也挥手回应；然后他转过身去，双手摊开，面向大海。他站在那里很久，我也站在那里很久，看着他。然后他开始向我走来，仿佛站在海面上。

He saw my puzzled expression and explained to me that when the tide comes in in Provincetown, it covers the beach – but what you can’t see is that the sand beneath the water is uneven. Beneath its surface there are sandbars and islands of raised sand – and if you walk along them, it gives the peculiar impression to anyone watching that you are walking on water. I would see this man often after that, as the weeks and months passed, standing out in the Atlantic, his palms facing outwards, still and unmoving for hours. That, I thought to myself, is the opposite of Facebook – standing perfectly still, looking out towards the ocean, with your palms open.

他看到我困惑的表情，便向我解释说，普罗温斯敦涨潮时，海水会淹没沙滩——但你看不见的是，水下的沙子并不平整。水面下有沙洲和隆起的沙岛——如果你沿着它们走，旁观者会产生一种奇特的错觉，仿佛你在水上行走。此后数周数月，我经常看到这个人站在大西洋中，手掌朝外，一动不动地站上几个小时。我心想，这和脸书截然相反——一动不动地站着，望着大海，手掌张开。

Eventually I came to my friend Andrew’s house. One of his dogs ran to greet me. We strolled down to have dinner together. Andrew had been on a long, silent retreat the year before – no phone, no talking – and he told me to enjoy this sense of bliss, because it wouldn’t last long. It’s when you set aside your distractions, he said, that you begin to see what you were distracting yourself from. Oh, Andrew, you’re such a drama queen, I said, and we both laughed.

最后我来到了朋友安德鲁家。他的一条狗跑过来迎接我。我们一起散步去吃晚饭。安德鲁去年进行了一次漫长的静修——没有手机，不说话——他告诉我好好享受这种宁静，因为它不会持续太久。他说，当你放下所有干扰时，你才会开始看清自己究竟在逃避什么。哦，安德鲁，你真是个戏精，我说，然后我们俩都笑了。

Later, I walked down Commercial Street, past the library, and the town hall, and the AIDS monument, and the cupcake store, and the drag queens handing out flyers for their shows that night, until I heard some singing. In a pub, the Crown and Anchor, people were gathered around a piano, singing showtunes. I went in. Together with these strangers, we covered most of the soundtrack of Evita and Rent . I was struck again by a big difference – between standing in a group of strangers singing with them, and interacting with groups of strangers through screens. The first dissolves your sense of ego; the second jabs and pokes at it. The last song we sang was ‘A Whole New World’.

后来，我沿着商业街走，经过图书馆、市政厅、艾滋病纪念碑、纸杯蛋糕店，还有那些正在派发当晚演出传单的变装皇后们，直到我听到有人唱歌。在一家名为“皇冠与锚”的酒吧里，人们围坐在钢琴旁，唱着音乐剧的曲目。我走了进去。我们和这些陌生人一起，几乎唱完了《艾薇塔》和《吉屋出租》的所有歌曲。我再次感受到巨大的差异——站在一群陌生人中间和他们一起唱歌，与隔着屏幕和一群陌生人互动。前者会消解你的自我意识；后者则会不断地戳刺和挑衅它。我们唱的最后一首歌是《崭新的世界》。

I walked back to the beachhouse alone at 2 a.m. I thought about the difference between the glowing blue light I had spent so much of my life staring at, which keeps you always alert, and the natural light that had faded all around me, which seemed to say: the day is over; rest now. The beachhouse was empty. There were no texts or voice messages or emails waiting for me – or, if there were, I wouldn’t know for three months. I climbed into bed, and I fell into the deepest sleep I could remember. I didn’t wake up until fifteen hours later.

凌晨两点，我独自走回海滨小屋。我思索着，我生命中大部分时间都盯着的那种刺眼的蓝光，它让我时刻保持清醒，而周围的自然光却渐渐消失，仿佛在说：一天结束了，该休息了。小屋空无一人。没有短信、语音留言或邮件等着我——或者说，即使有，我也得等上三个月才能知道。我爬上床，进入了记忆中最沉睡的梦乡。十五个小时后，我才醒来。

I spent a week in this haze of decompression, feeling almost stoned with a mixture of exhaustion and stillness. I sat in cafés and talked to strangers. I wandered around the Provincetown library and its three bookstores, picking out yet more books I was going to read. I ate enough lobsters that, if that species ever evolves consciousness, I will be remembered as their Stalin figure, destroying them on an industrial scale. I walked all the way out to the spot where the Pilgrims first arrived on American soil, 400 years before. (They wandered around, couldn’t find much, and sailed further down, landing on Plymouth Rock.)

我整整一周都沉浸在这种放松的迷雾中，疲惫和宁静交织，感觉几乎像吸了大麻一样。我坐在咖啡馆里和陌生人聊天。我在普罗温斯敦图书馆和它的三家书店里闲逛，挑选着更多准备阅读的书籍。我吃的龙虾多到，如果这种生物有朝一日进化出了意识，我大概会被它们铭记为斯大林式的人物，大规模地消灭了它们。我一路走到400年前清教徒首次踏上美洲大陆的地方。（他们四处游荡，没找到什么，于是继续航行，最终在普利茅斯岩登陆。）

Strange things started to bubble up into my consciousness. I kept hearing in my head the opening lines of songs from the 1980s and 1990s, when I was a kid, ones I hadn’t thought about for years – ‘Cat Among the Pigeons’ by Bros, or ‘The Day We Caught the Train’ by Ocean Colour Scene. Without Spotify, I had no way to listen to the songs in full, so I sang them to myself as I walked down the beach. Every few hours, I would feel an unfamiliar sensation gurgling inside me and I would ask myself: What is that? Ah, yes. Calm. But all you’ve done is leave two lumps of metal behind; why does this feel so different? It felt like I had spent years holding two screaming, colicky babies, and now the babies had been handed over to a babysitter, and their screaming and vomiting had vanished from view.

一些奇怪的事情开始涌入我的意识。我脑海里不断回响着上世纪八九十年代的歌曲开头几句，那是我小时候常听的歌，我已经好几年没想起它们了——比如Bros乐队的《Cat Among the Pigeons》，或是Ocean Colour Scene乐队的《The Day We Caught the Train》。没有Spotify，我没办法完整地听这些歌，所以只能一边在沙滩上走一边哼唱。每隔几个小时，我就会感到体内有一种陌生的感觉在咕噜咕噜地响，我会问自己：那是什么？啊，对了。平静。但你只不过是留下了两块金属而已；为什么这种感觉如此不同？感觉就像我曾抱着两个哭闹不止、肠绞痛的婴儿好几年，现在他们被交给了保姆，他们的哭闹和呕吐声也消失了。

Everything slowed down for me. Normally I follow the news every hour or so, getting a constant drip-feed of anxiety-provoking factoids and trying to smush it together into some kind of sense. In Provincetown, I could no longer do this. Every morning, I would buy three newspapers and sit down to read them – and then I wouldn’t know what happened in the news until the next day. Instead of a constant blast running all through my waking life, I got one in-depth, curated guide to what happened, and then I could turn my attention to other things. One day, not long after I arrived, a gunman went into a newspaper office in Maryland and murdered five journalists. As a journalist myself, that’s obviously close to my heart, and in my normal life, I would have received texts from my friends as soon as it happened, and then followed it for hours on social media, absorbing garbled accounts, gradually assembling a picture. In Provincetown, the day after the massacre, I knew within ten minutes all the clear, tragic details I needed to know, from a dead tree. Suddenly, physical newspapers – the very thing this gunman had targeted – seemed to me like an extraordinarily modern invention, and one we all needed. My normal mode of consuming news, I realised, induced panic; this new style induced perspective.

一切都慢了下来。平时我几乎每隔一小时就看新闻，不断地接收着令人焦虑的零碎信息，然后努力把它们拼凑成一个大致的结论。但在普罗温斯敦，我再也无法这样做了。每天早上，我会买三份报纸，坐下来阅读——然后直到第二天才能知道新闻内容。我不再被铺天盖地的新闻轰炸，而是只收到一份经过精心筛选的深度报道，之后我就可以把注意力转移到其他事情上。我刚到不久的一天，一名枪手闯入马里兰州的一家报社，杀害了五名记者。作为一名记者，这件事自然让我感同身受。在正常情况下，事发后我会立刻收到朋友们的短信，然后花几个小时在社交媒体上追踪报道，吸收各种零散的信息，慢慢拼凑出事件的全貌。在普罗温斯敦，大屠杀发生后的第二天，我从一棵枯树上，十分钟之内就了解了所有我需要知道的清晰而悲惨的细节。突然间，纸质报纸——正是枪手袭击的目标——在我看来却是一项极其现代的发明，而且是我们所有人都需要的。我意识到，我平常获取新闻的方式只会引发恐慌；而这种新的方式却能带来更客观的视角。

I felt like something was happening in that first week that was slowly opening my receptors a little – to more attention, to more connection. But what was it? I only began to understand those first two weeks in Provincetown – and why I felt the way I did – later, when I went to Copenhagen.

在那第一周，我感觉好像有什么事情在慢慢地改变着我，让我更容易注意到周围的事物，也更容易与他人建立联系。但那究竟是什么呢？直到后来去了哥本哈根，我才开始明白在普罗温斯敦的那两周，以及我当时的感受。

Sune Lehmann’s sons jumped into his bed, and he knew – with a lurch in his gut – that there was something wrong. Every morning, his two boys would leap all over him and his wife, excitedly shrieking, glad to be awake for another day. It’s the kind of scene you picture longingly when you imagine becoming a parent, and Sune adored his sons. He knew he should be thrilled by their joy at being awake and alive – but each morning, whenever they appeared, he would instinctively stretch out his hand, not for them, but for something colder. ‘I would reach over and grab my phone to check my email,’ he told me, ‘even though these amazing, wonderful, sweet creatures are crawling around my bed.’

苏恩·莱曼的儿子们跳到他的床上，他心里一阵悸动，知道肯定出了什么事。每天早上，他的两个儿子都会兴奋地尖叫着，在他和妻子身上蹦来蹦去，为又一天的到来而高兴。这正是你想象中为人父母时会憧憬的场景，而苏恩也深爱着他的儿子们。他知道自己应该为他们醒来、活着的喜悦而感到欣慰——但每天早上，每当他们出现时，他都会下意识地伸出手，不是为了他们，而是为了某个更冰冷的东西。“我会伸手去拿手机查看邮件，”他告诉我，“即使这些可爱、美好、讨人喜欢的小家伙们正爬来爬去。”

Every time he thought about it, he felt ashamed. Sune had trained as a physicist, but after a while, he figured he was going to have to investigate – at the Technical University of Denmark, where he is a professor in the Department of Applied Mathematics and Computer Science – what was happening not just in physics, but in himself. ‘I had been obsessed with how I was losing my own ability to focus,’ he told me. ‘I was realising that, somehow, I was not able to control my own use of the internet.’ He found himself mindlessly following the small details of events like the US presidential election on social media, hour after hour, achieving nothing. This wasn’t just affecting him as a parent, but as a scientist. He says: ‘I came to this realisation that my job in a way is to think something that is different from everyone else – but I was in an environment where I was just getting all the same information as everyone else, and I was just thinking the same things as everyone else.’

每当想起这件事，他都感到羞愧。苏内曾接受过物理学训练，但过了一段时间，他意识到自己必须深入探究——在他任教的丹麦技术大学应用数学与计算机科学系——究竟发生了什么，不仅是物理学领域，还有他自身。“我一直执着于自己注意力逐渐丧失，”他告诉我，“我意识到，不知何故，我无法控制自己使用互联网。”他发现自己漫不经心地在社交媒体上关注着美国总统大选等事件的细枝末节，一连几个小时，却一无所获。这不仅影响了他作为父亲的角色，也影响了他作为科学家的身份。他说：“我逐渐意识到，我的工作在某种程度上是思考一些与众不同的东西——但我却身处一个信息爆炸的环境中，获取的信息和思考的内容都和其他人一样。”

He had a sense that the deterioration he was experiencing in his focus was happening to a lot of the people around him – but he also knew that at many points in history, people have thought they were experiencing some kind of disastrous social decline, when in fact, they were merely ageing. It’s always tempting to confuse your personal decline for the decline of the human species. Sune – who was in his late thirties at the time – asked himself: ‘Am I a grumpy old man, or is the world really changing?’ So with scientists across Europe, he launched the largest scientific study yet conducted to answer a key question – is our collective attention span really shrinking?

他隐约感觉到自己注意力下降的状况也发生在周围很多人身上——但他同时也知道，历史上很多时候，人们都以为自己正经历某种灾难性的社会衰落，而实际上，他们只是老了而已。人们总是很容易把个人的衰退误认为是人类物种的衰落。当时年近四十的苏内问自己：“我是个脾气暴躁的老头，还是世界真的在发生变化？”于是，他与欧洲各地的科学家一起，发起了一项迄今为止规模最大的科学研究，旨在解答一个关键问题——我们的集体注意力持续时间真的在缩短吗？

As a first step they drew up a list of sources of information that they could analyse. The first and most obvious was Twitter. The site had launched in 2006 and Sune began this work in 2014 – so there was eight years of data to draw on. On Twitter, you can track what topics people are talking about and how long they discuss them for. The team began to do a massive analysis of the data. How long do people talk about a topic on Twitter for? Has the length of time they focus, collectively, on any one thing changed? Do people talk about the topics that obsess them – the trending hashtags – for more or less time now, compared to in the recent past? What they found is that in 2013 a topic would remain in the top fifty most-discussed subjects for 17.5 hours. By 2016 that had dropped to 11.9 hours. This suggested that together, on that site, we were focusing on any one thing for ever-shorter periods of time.

作为第一步，他们列出了可以分析的信息来源清单。最直接、最显而易见的来源是推特。该网站于2006年上线，而苏恩于2014年开始这项工作——这意味着他们有八年的数据可供参考。在推特上，你可以追踪人们正在讨论的话题以及他们讨论的时长。团队开始对这些数据进行大规模分析。人们在推特上讨论一个话题会持续多久？他们集体关注某个话题的时间长度是否发生了变化？与过去相比，人们现在讨论那些让他们着迷的话题——热门话题标签——的时间是更长了还是更短了？他们的发现是，2013年，一个话题在最热门的50个话题中停留的时间平均为17.5小时。到2016年，这个数字下降到了11.9小时。这表明，在这个网站上，我们集体关注任何单一话题的时间越来越短。

Okay, they thought, that’s striking, but maybe this was a quirk of Twitter. So they started to look at a whole range of other data sets. They looked at what people search for on Google – what’s the rate of churn in that? They analysed movie-ticket sales – how long did people carry on going to the cinema to watch a movie after it became a hit? They studied Reddit – how long did topics last there? All the data suggested that, as time passed, we were focusing less on any one individual topic. (The one exception, intriguingly, was Wikipedia, where the level of attention on topics has held steady.) With almost every data set they looked at, the pattern was the same. Sune said: ‘We looked at a lot of different systems … and we see that in every system, there is an accelerating trend.’ It is ‘faster to reach peak popularity’, and then there is ‘a faster drop again’.

他们心想，这确实令人惊讶，但也许只是推特的特例。于是，他们开始研究一系列其他数据集。他们研究了人们在谷歌上的搜索内容——用户流失率是多少？他们分析了电影票销售情况——一部电影走红后，人们会持续去电影院观看多久？他们研究了Reddit——上面的话题能持续多久？所有数据都表明，随着时间的推移，我们对任何单一话题的关注度都在下降。（有趣的是，维基百科是个例外，人们对各个话题的关注度一直保持稳定。）几乎他们研究的每个数据集都呈现出相同的模式。苏恩说：“我们研究了很多不同的系统……我们发现，在每个系统中，都存在一种加速的趋势。”它“更快地达到人气巅峰”，然后“迅速回落”。

The scientists wanted to know how long this has been happening for – and that’s when they made a really eye-opening discovery. They turned to Google Books, which has scanned the full text of millions of books. Sune and his team decided to analyse books that were written between the 1880s and the present day using a mathematical technique – the scientific term for it is ‘detecting n-grams’ – that can spot the rise and fall of new phrases and topics in the text. It’s the equivalent of finding hashtags from the past. The computers could detect new phrases as they appear – think of, say, ‘the Harlem renaissance’, or ‘no-deal Brexit’ – and they could see how long they were discussed for, and how quickly they faded from discussion. It was a way of finding out how long the people who came before us talked about a fresh topic for. How many weeks and months did it take for them to get bored and move on the next thing? When they looked at the data, they found that the graph looked remarkably similar to Twitter’s. With each decade that passed, for more than 130 years, topics have come and gone faster and faster.

科学家们想知道这种情况持续了多久——就在这时，他们有了令人大开眼界的发现。他们求助于谷歌图书，该平台已经扫描了数百万本书籍的全文。苏恩和他的团队决定使用一种数学技术——科学术语称之为“n-gram检测”——来分析19世纪80年代至今出版的书籍。这种技术可以识别文本中新词组和话题的兴衰。这相当于寻找过去的标签。计算机可以检测到新词组的出现——例如“哈莱姆文艺复兴”或“无协议脱欧”——并观察这些词组被讨论的时间长短以及它们从讨论中消失的速度。这是一种了解前人讨论一个新话题的时间长短的方法。他们需要多少周或多少个月才会感到厌倦并转向下一个话题？当他们查看数据时，发现图表与推特的图表惊人地相似。 130多年来，每过十年，各种话题的兴衰更迭速度就越来越快。

When he saw the results, Sune told me, he thought: ‘Goddammit, it really is true … Something is changing. It’s not just the same-old, same-old.’ This was the first proof gathered anywhere in the world that our collective attention spans have been shrinking. Crucially, this has been happening not just since the birth of the web, but for the whole of my life, my parents’ lives and my grandparents’ lives. Yes, the internet had rapidly accelerated the trend – but, crucially, this scientific team had discovered it was not the sole cause.

苏恩告诉我，当他看到结果时，他心想：“该死，这竟然是真的……有些事情正在改变。不再是老一套了。”这是全世界首次有证据表明，我们的集体注意力持续时间正在缩短。至关重要的是，这种情况并非始于互联网诞生之时，而是贯穿了我的一生，我的父母和祖父母的一生。没错，互联网加速了这一趋势——但关键在于，这个科研团队发现，互联网并非唯一原因。

Sune and his colleagues wanted to understand what has been driving this change, so they built a complex mathematical model to try to figure it out. It’s a bit like the systems that climate scientists construct to successfully predict changes in the weather. (The full technical details of how they did it, if you’re interested, are in their published research.) It was designed to see what you could do to data to make it rise and fall at faster and faster rates in ways that resembled the decline in collective attention they had been documenting. What they discovered is that there is one mechanism that can make this happen every time. You just have to flood the system with more information. The more information you pump in, the less time people can focus on any individual piece of it.

苏恩和他的同事们想要了解这种变化背后的驱动力，于是他们构建了一个复杂的数学模型来尝试找出答案。这有点像气候科学家构建的用于成功预测天气变化的系统。（如果您感兴趣，他们的完整技术细节可以在他们发表的论文中找到。）该模型旨在研究如何通过对数据进行处理，使其以越来越快的速度波动，从而模拟他们一直在记录的集体注意力下降的趋势。他们的发现是，有一种机制可以每次都实现这一点。你只需要向系统中输入更多信息。输入的信息越多，人们就越难集中精力关注其中的任何一条信息。

‘It’s a fascinating explanation of why this acceleration is happening,’ Sune told me. Today, ‘There’s just more information in the system. So if you think about one hundred years ago, literally it would take time for news to travel. If there was some kind of huge catastrophe in a Norwegian fjord, they would have to get up from the fjord down to Oslo, someone would have to write it up,’ and it would slowly wend its way across the globe. Compare that with the 2019 massacre in New Zealand, when a depraved racist began to murder Muslims in a mosque and it was ‘literally streaming live’, so anyone could watch it, anywhere.

“这真是对这种加速现象的一个绝妙解释，”苏恩告诉我。如今，“系统中的信息量更大了。想想一百年前，新闻传播确实需要时间。如果挪威峡湾发生了什么巨大的灾难，人们必须从峡湾一路南下到奥斯陆，有人才能把它写下来，”然后新闻才会慢慢传遍全球。相比之下，2019年新西兰发生的大屠杀，一个丧心病狂的种族主义者在清真寺里开始屠杀穆斯林，而整个过程“实际上是现场直播”，任何人都可以随时随地观看。

One way of thinking about this, Sune said, is that at the moment, it is like we’re ‘drinking from a fire-hose – there’s too much coming at us’. We are soaked in information. The raw figures on this have been analysed by two other scientists, Dr Martin Hilbert at the University of Southern California and Dr Priscilla López at the Open University of Catalonia. Picture reading an eighty-five-page newspaper. In 1986, if you added up all the information being blasted at the average human being – TV, radio, reading – it amounted to forty newspapers-worth of information every day. By 2007, they found it had risen to the equivalent of 174 newspapers per day. (I’d be amazed if it hadn’t gone up further since then.) The increase in the volume of information is what creates the sensation of the world speeding up.

苏恩说，我们可以这样理解：目前我们就像“被消防水管喷水一样——信息太多了”。我们被信息淹没。南加州大学的马丁·希尔伯特博士和加泰罗尼亚开放大学的普里西拉·洛佩兹博士两位科学家分析了这方面的原始数据。想象一下阅读一份85页的报纸。1986年，如果把普通人每天接收到的所有信息——电视、广播、阅读——加起来，相当于每天40份报纸的信息量。到了2007年，他们发现这个数字已经上升到每天174份报纸的水平。（如果此后没有继续增长，我会感到惊讶。）信息量的激增正是造成世界节奏加快的根源。

How is this change affecting us? Sune smiled when I asked. ‘There’s this thing about speed that feels great … Part of why we feel absorbed in this is that it’s awesome, right? You get to feel that you are connected to the whole world, and you feel that anything that happens on the topic, you can find out about it and learn about it.’ But we told ourselves we could have a massive expansion in the amount of information we are exposed to, and the speed at which it hits us, with no costs. This is a delusion: ‘It becomes exhausting.’ More importantly, Sune said, ‘What we are sacrificing is depth in all sorts of dimensions … Depth takes time. And depth takes reflection. If you have to keep up with everything and send emails all the time, there’s no time to reach depth. Depth connected to your work in relationships also takes time. It takes energy. It takes long timespans. And it takes commitment. It takes attention, right? All of these things that require depth are suffering. It’s pulling us more and more up onto the surface.’

这种变化对我们有什么影响？我问苏恩时，她笑了。“速度确实让人感觉很棒……我们沉迷其中的部分原因在于它很棒，对吧？你会感觉自己与整个世界相连，感觉任何与此相关的事情，你都能了解和学习。”但我们告诉自己，我们可以以零成本大幅扩展我们接触的信息量，并以极快的速度接收信息。这是一种错觉：“它会让人筋疲力尽。”更重要的是，苏恩说，“我们牺牲的是各个层面的深度……深度需要时间。深度需要反思。如果你必须跟上所有事情的步伐，不停地发邮件，就没有时间去深入思考。与人际关系相关的深度也需要时间。它需要精力。它需要长时间的投入。它需要专注，对吧？所有这些需要深度的事情都在遭受损失。”它正把我们越来越往水面拉。

There was a phrase in Sune’s scientific paper, summarising his findings, that kept rattling around in my head. It said that we are, collectively, experiencing ‘a more rapid exhaustion of attention resources’. When I read this, I realised what I had experienced in Provincetown. I was – for the first time in my life – living within the limits of my attention’s resources.
