I was absorbing as much information as I could actually process, think about, and contemplate – and no more. The firehose of information was turned off. Instead, I was sipping water at the pace I chose.

苏恩的科学论文中总结他的研究成果时，有一句话一直在我脑海里挥之不去。这句话说，我们集体正经历着“注意力资源更快耗尽”的现象。读到这句话时，我意识到自己在普罗温斯敦的经历。我生平第一次真正体验到了注意力资源的极限。我尽可能多地吸收信息，只要这些信息是我能够处理、思考和消化的——仅此而已。信息洪流停止了。取而代之的是，我按照自己的节奏，细细品味着信息。

Sune is a smiling, affable Dane, but when I asked him about how these trends will develop in the future, his body stiffened, and his smile turned to a tight pucker. ‘We’ve been accelerating for a very long time, and for sure, we’re getting closer and closer to whatever limits we have,’ he said. This acceleration, he said, ‘can’t continue indefinitely. There’s some physical limit to how fast things can move. It must stop at some point. But I don’t see any slowing down right now.’

苏恩是个笑容可掬、和蔼可亲的丹麦人，但当我问及这些趋势未来将如何发展时，他的身体僵硬起来，笑容也变得僵硬起来。“我们已经加速发展了很长时间，而且可以肯定的是，我们正越来越接近自身的极限，”他说。他接着说，这种加速“不可能无限持续下去。事物发展的速度是有物理极限的，总有一天会停止。但就目前而言，我看不出有任何减速的迹象。”

Shortly before I met with him, Sune had seen a photograph of Mark Zuckerberg, the founder of Facebook, standing in front of a room of people who were all wearing virtual-reality headsets. He was the only person standing in actual reality, looking at them, smiling, pacing proudly around. When he saw it, Sune said, ‘I was like – holy shit, this is a metaphor for the future.’ If we don’t change course, he fears we are headed towards a world where ‘there’s going to be an upper class of people that are very aware’ of the risks to their attention and find ways to live within their limits, and then there will be the rest of the society with ‘fewer resources to resist the manipulation, and they’re going to be living more and more inside their computers, being manipulated more and more’.

就在我与苏恩见面之前不久，他看到一张照片，照片上是Facebook创始人马克·扎克伯格站在一群戴着虚拟现实头盔的人面前。他是唯一一个站在现实世界中的人，他看着他们，面带微笑，骄傲地踱步。看到这张照片后，苏恩说：“我当时就想——我的天哪，这简直就是未来的隐喻。”他担心，如果我们不改变方向，我们将走向这样一个世界：一部分人“非常清楚”注意力面临的风险，并会想方设法在自身能力范围内生活；而其余的人“缺乏抵御操控的资源，他们将越来越沉迷于电脑，越来越容易受到操控”。

Once he had learned all this, Sune deeply changed his own life. He stopped using all social media, except Twitter, which he checks only once a week, on Sundays. He stopped watching TV. He stopped getting his news from social media, and instead took out a newspaper subscription. He read many more books instead. ‘As you know, everything with self-discipline is not like it’s a thing you fix and then it’s fixed for ever,’ he said. ‘I think the first thing you have to realise is it’s an ongoing battle.’ But he told me it had helped to trigger a philosophical shift in how he approached life. ‘In general, we want to take the easy way out, but what makes us happy is doing the thing that’s a little bit difficult. What’s happening with our cellphones is that we put a thing in our pocket that’s with us all the time that always offers an easy thing to do, rather than the important thing.’ He looked at me and smiled. ‘I wanted to give myself a chance at choosing something that’s more difficult.’

了解了这一切之后，苏恩彻底改变了自己的生活。他停止使用所有社交媒体，只在每周日查看一次推特。他不再看电视，也不再从社交媒体获取新闻，而是订阅了一份报纸。他读了很多书。“你知道，自律不像其他事情那样，一旦解决了就永远有效，”他说，“我认为你首先要意识到，这是一场持久战。”但他告诉我，这促使他转变了人生观。“通常，我们都想走捷径，但真正让我们快乐的是去做那些有点困难的事情。我们现在用手机，就是把一个东西揣在兜里，时刻陪伴着我们，它总是提供一些容易的事情，而不是真正重要的事情。”他看着我，笑了笑。“我想给自己一个机会，去选择一些更难的事情。”

Sune’s study is pioneering, so it only provides us with a small base of evidence – but, as I dug deeper, I found two related areas of scientific investigation that helped me to understand this more. The first comes, intriguingly, from studies investigating if we can really learn how to speed-read. Several teams of scientists have spent years figuring out – can you make humans read things really, really fast? They found that you can – but it always comes at a cost. These teams took ordinary people and got them to read much faster than they ordinarily would; with training, and with practice, it sort of works. They can run their eyes over the words quickly and retain something of what they are seeing. But if you then test them on what they read, you’ll discover that the faster you make them go, the less they will understand. More speed means less comprehension. Scientists then studied professional speed-readers – and they discovered that even though they are obviously better at it than the rest of us, the same thing happens. This showed there’s just a maximum limit for how quickly humans can absorb information, and trying to bust through that barrier simply busts your brain’s ability to understand it instead.

苏恩的研究是开创性的，因此它提供的证据基础还很有限——但是，随着我深入研究，我发现了两个相关的科学研究领域，它们帮助我更好地理解了这个问题。第一个领域很有意思，它源于一些研究，这些研究旨在探究我们是否真的能够学会快速阅读。几个科学家团队花费数年时间研究——我们能否让人类的阅读速度变得非常非常快？他们发现答案是肯定的——但这总是要付出代价的。这些团队招募普通人，让他们以远超正常速度的速度阅读；经过训练和练习，这种方法在某种程度上是有效的。他们可以快速浏览文字，并记住一些内容。但是，如果你测试他们阅读的内容，你会发现，速度越快，他们理解得就越少。速度越快，理解越差。科学家们随后研究了专业的速读者——他们发现，即使他们显然比我们其他人更擅长阅读，同样的情况仍然会发生。这表明人类吸收信息的速度是有限的，试图突破这个障碍只会破坏大脑理解信息的能力。

The scientists investigating this also discovered that if you make people read quickly, they are much less likely to grapple with complex or challenging material. They start to prefer simplistic statements. After I read this, I looked again at my own habits. When I read a physical newspaper, I’ll often be drawn to the stories that I don’t understand yet – why, say, is there an uprising in Chile? But when I read the same newspaper online, I usually skim those stories, and click on the simpler, more scannable stories related to the stuff I already know. After I noticed this, I wondered if in some ways, we are increasingly speed-reading life, skimming hurriedly from one thing to another, absorbing less and less.

研究此问题的科学家们还发现，如果让人们快速阅读，他们就更不愿意费力去理解复杂或有挑战性的内容。他们会开始偏爱简单明了的表述。读到这篇文章后，我重新审视了自己的阅读习惯。当我阅读纸质报纸时，我常常会被那些我还不理解的新闻所吸引——比如说，智利为什么会发生起义？但当我在线阅读同一份报纸时，我通常会略读这些新闻，然后点击那些更简单、更容易浏览的、与我已知内容相关的文章。注意到这一点后，我不禁思考，在某种程度上，我们是否正越来越多地“速读”生活，匆匆地从一件事跳到另一件事，吸收的信息却越来越少。

One day, in my webless summer, after slowly reading a book, slowly eating a meal, and slowly wandering around town, I wondered if, in my normal life, I suffer from a kind of mental jet lag. When you fly into a distant time zone, you feel like you’ve moved too fast and now you are out of sync with the world around you. The British writer Robert Colville says we are living through ‘the Great Acceleration’, and like Sune, he argues it’s not simply our tech that’s getting faster – it’s almost everything. There’s evidence that a broad range of important factors in our lives really are speeding up: people talk significantly faster now than they did in the 1950s, and in just twenty years, people have started to walk 10 percent faster in cities.

一天，在我那段没有网络的夏日时光里，我慢悠悠地读完一本书，慢悠悠地吃完一顿饭，慢悠悠地在城里闲逛之后，我开始思考，在我的日常生活中，我是否也像其他人一样，患有某种精神上的时差反应。当你飞入一个遥远的时区时，你会感觉自己行动得太快，与周围的世界失去了同步。英国作家罗伯特·科尔维尔（Robert Colville）说，我们正经历着“大加速”，和苏恩（Sune）一样，他认为不仅仅是科技在加速——几乎所有事物都在加速。有证据表明，我们生活中许多重要的因素确实在加速：人们现在的语速比20世纪50年代快得多，短短二十年间，人们在城市里的步行速度就提高了10%。

Usually, this acceleration is sold to us in a spirit of celebration – the original BlackBerry advertising slogan was ‘anything worth doing is worth doing faster’. Internally, at Google, their unofficial motto among the staff is ‘if you’re not fast, you’re fucked’.

通常，这种加速是以庆祝的心态来推销的——黑莓最初的广告语是“凡事值得做，就值得做得更快”。而在谷歌内部，员工之间不成文的座右铭是“速度不够快，你就完蛋了”。

But there’s a second way in which scientists have learned how this societal slamming on of the accelerator is affecting our attention. It comes from studying what happens to focus not when we speed up, but when we deliberately slow down. One of the leading experts on this topic is Guy Claxton, professor of learning sciences at the University of Winchester, who I went to interview in Sussex, in England. He has analysed what happens to a person’s focus if they engage in deliberately slow practices, like yoga, or tai chi, or meditation, as discovered in a broad range of scientific studies, and he has shown they improve your ability to pay attention by a significant amount. I asked him why. He said that ‘we have to shrink the world to fit our cognitive bandwidth’. If you go too fast, you overload your abilities, and they degrade. But when you practise moving at a speed that is compatible with human nature – and you build that into your daily life – you begin to train your attention and focus. ‘That’s why those disciplines make you smarter. It’s not about humming or wearing orange robes.’ Slowness, he explained, nurtures attention, and speed shatters it.

但科学家们还通过第二种方式了解到，这种社会加速运转的趋势正在影响我们的注意力。这种方式源于研究当我们刻意放慢速度而非加速时，注意力会发生什么变化。这方面的权威专家之一是温彻斯特大学学习科学教授盖伊·克拉克斯顿，我曾前往英国苏塞克斯采访他。他分析了人们在进行瑜伽、太极或冥想等刻意放慢节奏的活动时，注意力会发生什么变化——这些活动已在大量科学研究中得到证实——并表明这些活动能显著提高注意力。我问他为什么。他说：“我们必须缩小世界，使其适应我们的认知带宽。” 如果速度过快，就会超出自身能力的承受范围，导致能力下降。但当你练习以符合人性的速度行动——并将这种速度融入日常生活——你就能开始训练你的注意力和专注力。“这就是为什么这些训练能让你更聪明。” “这无关乎哼歌或穿橙色长袍。”他解释说，“慢节奏能培养注意力，而快节奏则会分散注意力。”

At some level, in Provincetown, I sensed this was true – so I decided to try these slow practices. The first time I went to see my yoga teacher, Stefan Piscitelli, I said to him: ‘This is going to be like teaching yoga to Stephen Hawking. After his death.’ I explained that I was an immobilised lump of flesh designed only to read, write and occasionally walk. He laughed and said: ‘We’ll see what we can do.’ And so every day, for an hour, under his guidance, I slowly moved my body in ways I had never done before. At first I found it extraordinarily boring, and I tried to draw Stefan into arguing about politics or philosophy. He would always gently guide me back to trying to move into some weird pretzel shape I had never tried before. By the end of the summer, I was able to be silent for an hour, and to stand on my head. Afterwards, sometimes with Stefan’s guidance, I would meditate for twenty minutes – a practice I had tried at various points in my life but always let lapse. I felt a kind of slowness spreading through my body. I felt my heartbeat slow down, and my shoulders – which are normally in a kind of permanent hunch – relax gently.

在普罗温斯敦，我隐约感觉到这是真的——于是我决定尝试这些缓慢的练习。第一次去见我的瑜伽老师斯特凡·皮西泰利时，我对他说：“这就像教斯蒂芬·霍金练瑜伽一样，只不过是在他去世之后。”我解释说，我就像一团僵硬的肉，除了读书、写字和偶尔走走之外，什么都不会。他笑着说：“我们看看能做到什么程度。”于是，每天一个小时，在他的指导下，我缓慢地活动身体，尝试一些我从未做过的动作。起初，我觉得这极其枯燥，于是试图把斯特凡拉过来，跟他讨论政治或哲学。但他总是会温和地引导我回到练习中，尝试一些我从未尝试过的奇特姿势。到了夏天结束的时候，我已经能够安静地待上一个小时，还能倒立。之后，有时在斯特凡的指导下，我会冥想二十分钟——我人生中曾多次尝试过冥想，但总是半途而废。我感到一种缓慢的感觉蔓延至全身。我的心跳渐渐慢了下来，平时总是微微耸起的肩膀也轻轻地放松了下来。

But even when I felt the physical relief from this slowness, it was always followed by a kind of bubbling guilt. I thought – how can I explain this to my sped-up, stressed-out friends back home? How can we all change our lives so we feel more like this? How do you slow down in a world that is speeding up?

但即便我感受到这种慢节奏带来的身体上的放松，随之而来的总是一种难以言喻的愧疚感。我想——我该如何向那些生活节奏飞快、压力山大的朋友们解释这一切？我们该如何改变自己的生活，让自己也拥有这种感觉？在这个节奏越来越快的世界里，我们该如何慢下来？

I started to ask myself an obvious question. If life has accelerated, and we have become overwhelmed by information to the point that we are less and less able to focus on any of it, why has there been so little pushback? Why haven’t we tried to slow things down to a pace where we can think clearly? I was able to find the first part of an answer to this question – and it’s only the first part – when I went to interview Professor Earl Miller. He has won some of the top awards in neuroscience in the world, and he was working at the cutting edge of brain research when I went to see him in his office at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT). He told me bluntly that instead of acknowledging our limitations and trying to live within them, we have – en masse – fallen for an enormous delusion.

我开始问自己一个显而易见的问题：如果生活节奏加快，我们被信息淹没到越来越难以集中注意力，为什么几乎没有人对此提出异议？为什么我们不尝试放慢节奏，让自己能够清晰地思考？当我采访厄尔·米勒教授时，我找到了这个问题的答案——而且仅仅是答案的一部分。米勒教授曾获得世界神经科学领域的一些顶级奖项，我去麻省理工学院（MIT）拜访他时，他正处于脑科学研究的前沿。他直言不讳地告诉我，我们非但没有正视自身的局限性并努力适应，反而集体陷入了一个巨大的错觉之中。

There’s one key fact, he said, that every human being needs to understand – and everything else he was going to explain flows from that. ‘Your brain can only produce one or two thoughts’ in your conscious mind at once. That’s it. ‘We’re very, very single-minded.’ We have ‘very limited cognitive capacity’. This is because of the ‘fundamental structure of the brain’, and it’s not going to change. But rather than acknowledge this, Earl told me, we invented a myth. The myth is that we can actually think about three, five, ten things at the same time. To pretend this was the case, we took a term that was never meant to be applied to human beings at all. In the 1960s, computer scientists invented machines with more than one processor, so they really could do two things (or more) simultaneously. They called this machine-power ‘multitasking’. Then we took the concept and applied it to ourselves.

他说，有一个关键事实是每个人都需要理解的——他接下来要解释的一切都由此展开。“你的大脑一次只能产生一到两个想法。”仅此而已。“我们非常非常专注。”我们的“认知能力非常有限”。这是因为“大脑的基本结构”，而且这种结构不会改变。但厄尔告诉我，我们并没有承认这一点，而是编造了一个神话。这个神话是，我们实际上可以同时思考三件、五件甚至十件事。为了假装这是真的，我们借用了一个原本根本不适用于人类的术语。在20世纪60年代，计算机科学家发明了拥有多个处理器的机器，因此它们确实可以同时执行两项（或更多）任务。他们把这种机器能力称为“多任务处理”。然后，我们把这个概念应用到了自己身上。

When I first learned about Earl’s claim that our ability to think about several things at once is a delusion, I bristled – he couldn’t be right, I thought, because I have done several things at the same time myself. In fact, I do it often. Here’s the first example that came to mind: I have checked my email while thinking about the next draft of my book and planning out an interview I was going to do later that day. I did them all from the same toilet seat. (I apologise for putting this image in your head.) Where’s the fantasy in that?

当我第一次听说厄尔声称我们同时思考多件事的能力是一种错觉时，我感到非常恼火——他不可能说得对，我想，因为我自己也经常同时做几件事。事实上，我经常这样做。我脑海中浮现的第一个例子是：我一边查看邮件，一边思考我书稿的下一稿，同时还在计划当天晚些时候要进行的采访。而我做这一切都是在同一个马桶上完成的。（很抱歉让你想到这个画面。）这有什么梦幻之处呢？

Some scientists used to side with my initial gut instinct – they believed it was possible for people to do several complex tasks at once. So they started to get people into labs, and they told them to do lots of things at the same time, and they monitored how well it went. What the scientists discovered is that, in fact, when people think they’re doing several things at once, they’re actually – as Earl explained – ‘juggling. They’re switching back and forth. They don’t notice the switching because their brain sort of papers it over, to give a seamless experience of consciousness, but what they’re actually doing is switching and reconfiguring their brain moment to moment, task to task – [and] that comes with a cost.’

有些科学家曾经赞同我最初的直觉——他们相信人们可以同时完成几项复杂的任务。于是，他们开始招募人员进入实验室，让他们同时做很多事情，并观察他们的表现。科学家们发现，事实上，当人们认为自己同时做几件事时，他们实际上是在“杂耍”。正如厄尔解释的那样，他们在“杂耍”。他们来回切换。他们没有注意到这种切换，因为他们的大脑会将其掩盖，从而提供一种无缝的意识体验，但实际上，他们正在做的是每时每刻、每项任务地切换和重新配置他们的大脑——而这需要付出代价。

There are three ways, he explained, in which this constant switching degrades your ability to focus. The first is called the switch cost effect. There is broad scientific evidence for this. Imagine you are doing your tax return and you receive a text, and you look at it – it’s only a glance, taking five seconds – and then you go back to your tax return. In that moment, ‘Your brain has to reconfigure, when it goes from one task to another,’ he said. You have to remember what you were doing before, and you have to remember what you thought about it, ‘and that takes a little bit of time’. When this happens, the evidence shows that ‘your performance drops. You’re slower. All as a result of the switching.’

他解释说，这种频繁切换会从三个方面降低你的专注力。第一种是切换成本效应，这方面有大量的科学证据支持。想象一下，你正在填写纳税申报表，这时收到一条短信，你瞥了一眼——只是一眼，大概五秒钟——然后你又回到纳税申报表。他说，在那一刻，“你的大脑需要重新配置，才能从一项任务切换到另一项任务”。你必须记住之前在做什么，以及你当时的想法，“这需要一些时间”。证据表明，当这种情况发生时，“你的表现会下降，速度会变慢。这一切都是切换造成的。”

So if you check your texts often while trying to work, you aren’t only losing the little bursts of time you spend looking at the texts – you are also losing the time it takes to refocus afterwards, which can be much longer. He said: ‘If you’re spending a lot of your time not really thinking, but wasting it on switching, that’s just wasted brain-processing time.’ This means that if your Screen Time shows you are using your phone four hours a day, you are losing much more time than that in lost focus.

所以，如果你在工作时频繁查看短信，你不仅会浪费那些零碎的浏览时间，还会浪费之后重新集中注意力所需的时间，而这可能需要更长的时间。他说：“如果你把大量时间浪费在切换手机上，而不是真正思考，那纯粹是浪费大脑处理时间。” 这意味着，如果你的屏幕使用时间显示你每天使用手机四个小时，那么你因注意力不集中而损失的时间远远不止这些。

When Earl said this, I thought – yes, but it must be a small effect, a tiny drag on your attention. But when I went and read the relevant research, I learned there is some science suggesting the effect can be surprisingly large. For example, a small study commissioned by Hewlett-Packard looked at the IQ of some of their workers in two situations. At first they tested their IQ when they were not being distracted or interrupted. Then they tested their IQ when they were receiving emails and phone calls. The study found that ‘technological distraction’ – just getting emails and calls – caused a drop in the workers’ IQ by an average of ten points. To give you a sense of how big that is: in the short term, that’s twice the knock to your IQ that you get when you smoke cannabis. So this suggests in terms of being able to get your work done, you’d be better off getting stoned at your desk than checking your texts and Facebook messages a lot.

厄尔这么说的时候，我心想——没错，但这影响肯定很小，只会稍微分散你的注意力。但当我去查阅相关研究后，我发现一些科学研究表明，这种影响可能出乎意料地大。例如，惠普公司委托进行的一项小型研究，考察了部分员工在两种情况下的智商。首先，他们在员工不受干扰的情况下测试了他们的智商。然后，他们又在员工接收电子邮件和电话的情况下测试了他们的智商。研究发现，“技术干扰”（仅仅是接收电子邮件和电话）就会导致员工的智商平均下降10分。为了让你更好地理解这个数字有多大：短期来看，这相当于吸食大麻对智商造成的损害的两倍。所以，就工作效率而言，与其频繁查看短信和Facebook消息，还不如在办公桌前吸点大麻来得更有效率。

From there, the research shows, it gets worse. The second way switching harms your attention is what we might call the screw-up effect. When you switch between tasks, errors that wouldn’t have happened otherwise start to creep in, because – Earl explained – ‘your brain is error-prone. When you switch from task to task, your brain has to backtrack a little bit and pick up and figure out where it left off’ – and it can’t do that perfectly. Glitches start to occur. ‘Instead of spending critical time really doing deep thinking, your thinking is more superficial, because you’re spending a lot of time correcting errors and backtracking.’

研究表明，情况会从这里开始变得更糟。切换任务损害注意力的第二个方面，我们可以称之为“失误效应”。当你切换任务时，原本不会发生的错误开始悄然出现，因为——正如厄尔解释的那样——“你的大脑容易出错。当你从一个任务切换到另一个任务时，你的大脑必须稍微回溯一下，重新开始并弄清楚上次中断的地方”——而它无法完美地完成这项工作。于是，各种小故障开始出现。“你的思考不再像以前那样深入，而是变得更加肤浅，因为你把大量时间都花在了纠正错误和回溯上。”

Then there’s a third cost to believing you can multitask, one that you’ll only notice in the medium or longer term – which we might call the creativity drain. You’re likely to be significantly less creative. Why? ‘Because where do new thoughts [and] innovation come from?’ Earl asked. They come from your brain shaping new connections out of what you’ve seen and heard and learned. Your mind, given free undistracted time, will automatically think back over everything it absorbed, and it will start to draw links between them in new ways. This all takes place beneath the level of your conscious mind, but this process is how ‘new ideas pop together, and suddenly, two thoughts that you didn’t think had a relationship suddenly have a relationship’. A new idea is born. But if you ‘spend a lot of this brain-processing time switching and error-correcting’, Earl explained, you are simply giving your brain less opportunity to ‘follow your associative links down to new places and really [have] truly original and creative thoughts’.

相信自己可以同时处理多项任务还有第三个代价，这个代价只有在中长期才会显现——我们可以称之为“创造力损耗”。你的创造力很可能会显著下降。为什么呢？“因为新想法和创新从何而来？”厄尔问道。它们源于你的大脑将你所见、所闻、所学的一切重新连接起来。当你的大脑拥有不受干扰的自由时间时，它会自动回顾所有吸收的信息，并以新的方式将它们联系起来。这一切都发生在你的意识层面之下，但正是这个过程让“新想法迸发而出，突然间，两个你原本认为毫无关联的想法突然有了联系”。一个新想法就此诞生。但厄尔解释说，如果你“把大量的大脑处理时间都花在切换和纠错上”，你实际上就减少了大脑“沿着联想深入探索，产生真正原创和创造性想法”的机会。

I later learned about a fourth consequence, based on a smaller amount of evidence – which we might call the diminished memory effect. A team at UCLA got people to do two tasks at once, and tracked them to see the effects. It turned out that afterwards they couldn’t remember what they had done as well as people who did just one thing at a time. This seems to be because it takes mental space and energy to convert your experiences into memories, and if you are spending your energy instead on switching very fast, you’ll remember and learn less.

后来，我了解到第四种后果，虽然证据较少，但我们可以称之为“记忆力减弱效应”。加州大学洛杉矶分校的一个研究团队让参与者同时完成两项任务，并追踪他们的反应以观察其影响。结果发现，事后他们无法像一次只做一件事的人那样清楚地记住自己做过的事情。这似乎是因为将经历转化为记忆需要占用心理空间和能量，如果你把这些能量用于快速切换任务，那么你记住和学习的内容就会减少。

So if you spend your time switching a lot, then the evidence suggests you will be slower, you’ll make more mistakes, you’ll be less creative, and you’ll remember less of what you do. I wanted to know: how often are most of us engaging in switching like this? Professor Gloria Mark, at the Department of Infomatics at the University of California, Irvine, who I interviewed, has discovered that the average American worker is distracted roughly once every three minutes. Several other studies have shown a large chunk of Americans are almost constantly being interrupted and switching between tasks. The average office worker now spends 40 percent of their work time wrongly believing they are ‘multitasking’ – which means they are incurring all these costs for their attention and focus. In fact, uninterrupted time is becoming rare: one study found that most of us working in offices never get a whole hour uninterrupted in a normal day. I had to look again at that figure several times before I really absorbed it: most office workers never get an hour to themselves without being interrupted. This is happening at every level of businesses – the average CEO of a Fortune 500 company, for example, gets just twenty-eight uninterrupted minutes a day.

所以，如果你经常切换任务，那么有证据表明，你的速度会变慢，犯的错误会更多，创造力会下降，而且对做过的事情的记忆也会变差。我想知道：我们大多数人究竟有多频繁地进行这样的切换？我采访了加州大学尔湾分校信息学系的格洛丽亚·马克教授，她发现美国普通员工平均每三分钟就会分心一次。其他几项研究也表明，很大一部分美国人几乎总是被打断，在不同任务之间切换。如今，普通上班族有40%的工作时间都错误地认为自己是在“多任务处理”——这意味着他们正在为注意力和专注力付出代价。事实上，不受干扰的时间正变得越来越少：一项研究发现，我们大多数在办公室工作的人，在正常的一天中，从来没有一个小时是完全不受干扰的。我不得不反复查看这个数字，才真正理解它的含义：大多数上班族从来没有一个小时是完全属于自己的，总是被打断。这种情况在企业的各个层面都在发生——例如，财富 500 强公司的 CEO 平均每天只有 28 分钟不受干扰的时间。

Whenever this problem is talked about in the media, it’s described as ‘multitasking’ – but I think using this old computing term is a mistake. When I picture multitasking, I picture a 1990s single mother trying to feed a baby while also taking a work call and preventing the food she’s cooking from catching fire. (I watched a lot of bad sitcoms in the 1990s.) I don’t picture somebody taking a work call while also checking their text messages. We now use our phones so habitually that I don’t think we consider doing a task and checking our phones at the same time as multitasking, any more than we think scratching your butt during a work call is multitasking. But it is. Simply having your phone switched on and receiving texts every ten minutes while you try to work is itself a form of switching – and these costs start to kick in for you too. One study at the Carnegie Mellon University’s Human Computer Interaction Lab took 136 students and got them to sit a test. Some of them had to have their phones switched off, and others had their phones on and received intermittent text messages. The students who received messages performed, on average, 20 percent worse. Other studies in similar scenarios have found even worse outcomes of 30 percent. It seems to me that almost all of us with a smartphone are losing that 20 to 30 percent, almost all the time. That’s a lot of brainpower for a species to lose.

每当媒体谈到这个问题时，都会用“多任务处理”来形容——但我认为使用这个过时的计算机术语是个错误。我脑海中浮现的“多任务处理”画面，是一位上世纪90年代的单身母亲，她一边喂孩子，一边接工作电话，还要防止正在做饭的食物着火。（我90年代看过不少烂情景喜剧。）我不会想象有人一边接工作电话一边查看短信。如今我们使用手机已经成了习惯，以至于我们根本不会把同时做一件事和查看手机视为多任务处理，就像我们不会认为在工作电话中挠屁股是多任务处理一样。但事实的确如此。即使只是在工作时手机开着，每隔十分钟就收到一条短信，这本身也是一种切换——而这些切换也会带来相应的成本。卡内基梅隆大学人机交互实验室的一项研究招募了136名学生，并让他们参加了一项测试。有些学生必须关机，而另一些学生则保持手机开机状态，并间歇性地接收短信。结果显示，接收短信的学生平均成绩下降了20%。其他类似研究发现，成绩下降幅度甚至高达30%。在我看来，几乎所有拥有智能手机的人都在时时刻刻损失这20%到30%的脑力。这对人类来说，损失如此巨大的脑力实在令人难以接受。

If you want to understand how much harm this does, Earl told me, just look at one of the fastest rising causes of death in the world: distracted driving. The cognitive neuroscientist Dr David Strayer at the University of Utah conducted detailed research where he got people to use driving simulators and tracked how safe their driving was when they were distracted by technology – something as simple as their phone receiving texts. It turned out their level of impairment was ‘very similar’ to if they were drunk. It’s worth dwelling on that: persistent distractions have as bad an effect on your attention on the road as consuming so much alcohol that you got drunk. The distraction all around us isn’t just annoying, it’s deadly: around one in five car accidents is now due to a distracted driver.

厄尔告诉我，如果你想了解这种行为的危害有多大，只需看看世界上增长最快的死因之一：分心驾驶。犹他大学的认知神经科学家大卫·斯特雷耶博士进行了一项详细的研究，他让人们使用驾驶模拟器，并追踪他们在受到科技产品（比如手机接收短信）分心时驾驶的安全性。结果发现，他们的驾驶能力受损程度与醉酒驾驶“非常相似”。这一点值得深思：持续的分心对驾驶注意力的影响，与饮酒过量导致醉酒一样严重。我们周围的各种干扰因素不仅令人烦恼，而且致命：现在大约五分之一的交通事故都是由于分心驾驶造成的。

The evidence is clear, Earl told me: there’s no alternative, if you want to do things well, to focusing carefully on one thing at a time. As I learned all this, I realised that my desire to absorb a tsunami of information without losing my ability to focus was like my desire to eat at McDonald’s every day and stay trim – an impossible dream. The size and capacity of the human brain hasn’t significantly changed in 40,000 years, Earl explained, and it isn’t going to upgrade any time soon. Yet we are deluded about this fact. Dr Larry Rosen, a professor of psychology at California State University, discovered that the average teen and young adult genuinely believes they can follow six or seven forms of media at once. We are not machines. We cannot live by the logic of machines. We are humans, and we work differently.

厄尔告诉我，证据很明确：要想把事情做好，就必须一次只专注于一件事，别无他法。当我明白这一切后，我意识到，我渴望吸收海量信息而不丧失专注力，就像我渴望每天吃麦当劳却保持身材一样——一个不可能实现的梦想。厄尔解释说，人类大脑的体积和容量在过去四万年里并没有发生显著变化，而且短期内也不会升级。然而，我们却对此深信不疑。加州州立大学心理学教授拉里·罗森博士发现，普通青少年和年轻人真心相信自己可以同时关注六七种媒体。我们不是机器。我们不能按照机器的逻辑生活。我们是人，我们的运作方式不同。

When I learned all this, I realised another crucial reason why I had felt so good – and so mentally restored – in Provincetown. For the first time in a long time, I was allowing myself to focus on one thing at a time for long stretches. It felt like I had had an enormous boost in my mental capacity – because I was respecting my mind’s limitations. I asked Earl if, given what we know about the brain, it was fair to conclude that attention problems today really are worse than at some points in the past. He replied: ‘Absolutely.’ We have, he believes, created in our culture ‘a perfect storm of cognitive degradation, as a result of distraction’.

当我了解了这一切之后，我意识到我在普罗温斯敦感觉如此之好——精神状态如此焕然一新——的另一个关键原因。很久以来，我第一次允许自己长时间专注于一件事。感觉我的思维能力得到了极大的提升——因为我尊重了自己思维的局限性。我问厄尔，鉴于我们对大脑的了解，是否可以得出这样的结论：如今的注意力问题确实比过去某些时期更为严重。他回答说：“绝对如此。”他认为，我们文化中的种种干扰，造成了“认知能力退化的完美风暴”。

This was hard to take on board. It’s one thing to have a hunch that there’s a crisis. It’s another thing to hear one of the leading neuroscientists in the world tell you we are living in a ‘perfect storm’ that’s degrading your capacity to think. ‘The best we can do now,’ Earl had told me, ‘is try to get rid of the distractions as much as possible.’ At one point in our conversation, he sounded quite optimistic, suggesting that we can all achieve progress on this, starting today. He said: ‘The brain is like a muscle. The more you use certain things, the stronger the connection’s getting, and the better things work.’ If you are struggling to focus, he says, just try monotasking for ten minutes, and then allow yourself to be distracted for a minute, then monotask for another ten minutes, and so on. ‘As you do it, it becomes more familiar, your brain gets better and better at it, because you’re strengthening the [neural] connections involved in that behaviour. And pretty soon you can do it for fifteen minutes, twenty minutes, half an hour, you know? … Just do it. Practise at it … Start slow, but practise, and you’ll get there.’

这很难让人接受。隐约感觉到危机存在是一回事，但亲耳听到世界顶尖神经科学家之一告诉你，我们正生活在一场“完美风暴”中，这场风暴正在削弱你的思考能力，又是另一回事。“我们现在能做的最好的事情，”厄尔告诉我，“就是尽可能地消除干扰。”在我们的谈话中，他一度听起来相当乐观，认为我们所有人都能在这方面取得进步，从今天开始。他说：“大脑就像肌肉。你越是使用某些东西，连接就越牢固，效果也就越好。”如果你难以集中注意力，他建议你尝试专注于一项任务十分钟，然后允许自己分心一分钟，然后再专注于一项任务十分钟，如此反复。“随着你不断练习，你会越来越熟悉这种模式，你的大脑也会越来越擅长，因为你正在强化与这种行为相关的神经连接。”很快你就能坚持十五分钟、二十分钟、半小时了，你知道吗？……去做吧。练习……慢慢来，但要练习，你就能做到。

To achieve this, he says you have to separate yourself – for increasing periods of time – from the sources of your distraction. It’s a mistake, he said, to ‘try to monotask by force of will – because it’s too hard to resist that informational tap on the shoulder’. When I asked him about how, as a society, we could find a way to do this, he told me that he’s not a sociologist, and I’d have to look elsewhere for answers to that.

他表示，要做到这一点，你必须逐渐延长与干扰源的隔离时间。他说，试图“靠意志力强迫自己只做一件事——因为很难抵挡住信息推送的诱惑”是错误的。当我问他，作为一个社会，我们该如何做到这一点时，他告诉我他不是社会学家，我需要从其他领域寻找答案。

Our brains are not only overloaded now with switching – I learned they are also overloaded with something else. Adam Gazzaley, who is a professor of neurology, physiology and psychiatry at the University of California, helped me to understand it when I sat down with him in a coffee shop in San Francisco. He explained that you should think of your brain as like a nightclub where, standing at the front of that club, there’s a bouncer. The bouncer’s job is to filter out most of the stimuli that are hitting you at any given moment – the traffic noise, the couple having an argument across the street, the cellphone ringing in the pocket of the person next to you – so that you can think coherently about one thing at a time. The bouncer is essential: this ability to filter out irrelevant information is crucial if you are going to be able to attend to your goals. And that bouncer in your head is strong and ripped: he can fight off two, four, maybe even six people trying to barge into your brain at a time. He can do a lot. The part of your brain doing this is known as the prefrontal cortex.

我们的大脑不仅现在被各种信息切换搞得焦头烂额——我还了解到，它还被其他东西搞得不堪重负。加州大学神经学、生理学和精神病学教授亚当·加扎利（Adam Gazzaley）在旧金山一家咖啡馆里和我坐下来聊天时，帮我理解了这一点。他解释说，你应该把你的大脑想象成一个夜总会，门口站着一个保安。保安的工作就是过滤掉你此刻接收到的大部分刺激——交通噪音、街对面情侣的争吵、旁边人口袋里的手机铃声——这样你才能一次只专注于一件事。保安至关重要：如果你想专注于你的目标，这种过滤无关信息的能力至关重要。而且你大脑里的这个保安非常强壮有力：他可以同时击退两三个，甚至六个试图闯入你大脑的人。他能做到很多事情。大脑中负责这项工作的部位被称为前额叶皮层。

But today, Adam believes, the bouncer is besieged in an unprecedented way. In addition to switching tasks like never before, our brains are also being forced to filter more frantically than at any point in our past. Think about something as simple as noise. There’s broad scientific evidence that if you are sitting in a noisy room, your ability to pay attention deteriorates, and your work gets worse. For example, children in noisy classrooms have worse attention than kids in quiet classrooms. Yet many of us are surrounded by high levels of noise, working in open-plan offices, sleeping in crowded cities, and tapping away on our laps in crammed coffee shops like the one we were sitting in at that moment. Rising noise pollution is just one example – we live surrounded by shrieking distractions calling for our attention, and the attention of others. That’s why, Adam said, the bouncer has to work ‘way harder’ to keep out distractions. He’s exhausted. And so a lot more is fighting its way past him, into your mind – interfering with the flow of your thoughts.

但亚当认为，如今，这位“保安”正面临着前所未有的困境。除了前所未有地频繁切换任务外，我们的大脑也被迫以前所未有的速度进行过滤。就拿噪音来说吧。大量的科学证据表明，如果你身处嘈杂的房间，你的注意力就会下降，工作效率也会降低。例如，在嘈杂教室里的孩子比在安静教室里的孩子注意力更差。然而，我们中的许多人却被高噪音环境包围：在开放式办公室工作，在拥挤的城市里睡觉，在像我们此刻正坐的那种拥挤的咖啡馆里敲击键盘。日益严重的噪音污染只是其中一个例子——我们生活在各种刺耳的干扰之中，这些干扰不仅吸引着我们的注意力，也吸引着他人的注意力。正因如此，亚当说，保安不得不“更加努力”地工作来抵御干扰。他已经筋疲力尽了。因此，更多的信息会越过他，进入你的脑海——干扰你的思维流动。

As a result, a lot of the time, he can’t filter like he used to. The bouncer is overwhelmed, and the nightclub becomes full of rowdy assholes disrupting the normal dancing. ‘We have fundamental limitations,’ Adam added. ‘We could ignore them, and pretend we’re capable of everything we would wish – or we can acknowledge them, and live our lives in a better way.’

结果，很多时候，他无法像以前那样控制自己的言行。保安应接不暇，夜店里挤满了喧闹的家伙，扰乱了正常的跳舞秩序。“我们都有根本性的局限，”亚当补充道，“我们可以无视它们，假装自己无所不能——或者我们可以正视它们，更好地生活。”

In my first two weeks in Provincetown, I felt I had finally stepped out of the madness. I had gone to live in a monotasking world that wasn’t forcing on me the mental pressure of switching and filtering. This is how my summer is going to be, I thought to myself. An oasis of calm. An example of how to live differently. I ate cupcakes and laughed with strangers. I felt light, and free.

在普罗温斯敦的头两周，我感觉自己终于摆脱了喧嚣。我来到了一个可以专注于单一任务的世界，不再需要承受切换信息和筛选信息的压力。我心想，我的夏天就该这样过。一片宁静的绿洲。一种截然不同的生活方式。我吃着纸杯蛋糕，和陌生人谈笑风生。我感到轻松自在，无比自由。

And then something happened that I didn’t expect. On the fourteenth day I woke up, and my hand reached immediately for the nightstand to grab my iPhone, as it had done every morning since I arrived. It found only my dumb-phone, on which there were no messages, only the option to tell the nearest hospital I had fallen over. I could hear the ocean whispering in the distance. I turned and saw all the books I had been longing to read, waiting for me. And I felt an intense sensation – something I couldn’t quite place. And at that moment, the worst week I had experienced in years began.

然后，一件意想不到的事情发生了。第十四天，我醒来，下意识地伸手去拿床头柜上的iPhone，就像我来到这里后每天早上都会做的那样。结果，我摸到的只有一部功能机，里面没有任何信息，只有一个选项可以通知最近的医院我摔倒了。我能听到远处海浪的低语。我转过身，看到所有我一直渴望阅读的书，它们都在那里等着我。我感到一种强烈的、难以言喻的感觉。就在那一刻，我多年来经历过的最糟糕的一周开始了。

# ↩

2 Cause Two: The Crippling of Our Flow States

原因二：心流状态的削弱

On the first day of my mental free-fall, I walked down the beach and saw the same thing that had been scratching at me since Memphis. Almost everyone was staring at their screens. People seemed to be using Provincetown simply as a backdrop for selfies, rarely looking up, at the ocean, or each other. Except this time, the itch I felt wasn’t to yell: You’re wasting your lives, put the damn phone down. It was to yell: Give me that phone! Mine !

在我精神崩溃的第一天，我沿着海滩漫步，看到了自孟菲斯以来就一直萦绕在我心头的景象：几乎每个人都盯着自己的屏幕。人们似乎只是把普罗温斯敦当作自拍的背景，很少抬头看看大海，或者彼此交流。只是这一次，我内心的冲动不再是呐喊：“你们在浪费生命，放下该死的手机！”而是呐喊：“把手机给我！我的！”

Every time I switched on my iPod to listen to an audiobook or some music, I also had to switch on my noise-cancelling headphones, and they would say: ‘Searching for Johann’s iPhone. Searching for Johann’s iPhone.’ The Bluetooth was trying to connect, but it couldn’t, so then it would say sadly: ‘Connection cannot be made.’ That was how it felt. The French philosopher Simone de Beauvoir said that when she became an atheist, it felt like the world had fallen silent. When my phone was taken away, I felt like a large part of the world had vanished. As that first week ended, its absence flooded me with an angry panic. I wanted my phone. I wanted my email. And I wanted them at once. Every time I left the beachhouse, I instinctively patted my pocket to make sure my phone was there, and I always felt a lurch when I realised it was missing. It was like I had lost part of my own body. I turned to my piles of books, thinking idly of how, all through my teens and twenties, I would spend days on end lying in a bed, doing nothing but reading in one great gulp. But in Provincetown up to that point, I had been reading in a rushed, hyperactive way – I was scanning Charles Dickens the way you might scan a blog for vital information. My reading was manic and extractive. Okay, I’ve got it, he’s an orphan: what’s your point? I could see this was foolish, but I couldn’t stop. I couldn’t slow my mind in the way that yoga slowed my body.

每次我打开iPod听有声书或音乐时，都得同时戴上降噪耳机，耳机里就会响起：“正在搜索约翰的iPhone。正在搜索约翰的iPhone。”蓝牙尝试连接，但总是失败，然后耳机里就会无奈地响起：“连接失败。”那种感觉就像那样。法国哲学家西蒙娜·德·波伏娃说过，当她成为无神论者时，感觉世界仿佛陷入了寂静。手机被拿走后，我感觉世界的一部分也随之消失了。第一周结束时，手机的缺失让我感到一阵愤怒和恐慌。我想要我的手机。我想要我的邮箱。而且我想要同时拥有它们。每次离开海滨别墅，我都会下意识地拍拍口袋，确认手机还在，而一旦发现手机不见了，我总会感到一阵莫名的失落。感觉就像失去了自己身体的一部分。我转向我那堆积如山的书籍，漫不经心地想着，在我十几岁到二十几岁的那些日子里，我常常一连几天躺在床上，什么也不做，只是如饥似渴地阅读。但在普罗温斯敦，直到那时为止，我的阅读方式都十分匆忙、亢奋——我阅读查尔斯·狄更斯的作品，就像浏览博客寻找关键信息一样。我的阅读狂热而又充满提取性。“好了，我知道了，他是个孤儿：那你想表达什么？”我知道自己这样做很愚蠢，但我停不下来。我无法像瑜伽那样让我的思绪慢下来，让我的身体也慢下来。

At a loss, I took to taking out my comically large medical-device phone and stabbing at its massive buttons. I stared at it helplessly. An image came into my head of a wildlife documentary I had seen as a kid, of a penguin whose baby died. She kept nudging it with her beak for hours, hoping it would come to life. But no matter how much I prodded it, my chunky Jitterbug could not access the web.

我束手无策，只好掏出那台滑稽的巨型医疗设备手机，胡乱地按着它巨大的按键。我无助地盯着它。脑海中浮现出小时候看过的一部野生动物纪录片，一只企鹅的幼崽夭折了。她用喙不停地轻推幼崽，几个小时过去了，希望它能复活。可是无论我怎么按，我那台笨重的Jitterbug手机都连不上网。

All around me, I could see reminders of why I had cast aside my phone in the first place. I sat in Café Heaven, a lovely little place in the West End of Provincetown, and ate an eggs Benedict. Next to me there were two men in, I guess, their mid-twenties. I shamelessly eavesdropped on their conversation while pretending to read David Copperfield . It was clear they had met on an app, and this was the first time they had seen each other in person. There was something about their conversation that seemed odd to me, and I couldn’t place it at first. Then I realised they weren’t, in fact, having a conversation at all. What would happen is the first one, who was blond, would talk about himself for ten minutes or so. Then the second one, who was dark-haired, would talk about himself for ten minutes. And they alternated in this way, interrupting each other. I sat next to them for two hours, and at no point did either of them ask the other person a question. At one point, the dark-haired man mentioned that his brother had died a month before. The blond didn’t even offer a cursory ‘I’m so sorry to hear that’: he simply went back to talking about himself. I realised that if they had met up simply to read out their own Facebook status updates to each other in turn, there would have been absolutely no difference.

周围的一切都在提醒我，当初为什么要把手机扔到一边。我坐在普罗温斯敦西区一家名为“天堂咖啡馆”的可爱小店里，吃着班尼迪克蛋。旁边坐着两个男人，我猜他们大概二十五六岁。我假装在读《大卫·科波菲尔》，却厚着脸皮偷听他们的谈话。很明显，他们是在交友软件上认识的，这是他们第一次见面。他们的谈话让我觉得有点奇怪，但我一开始说不上来。后来我才意识到，他们根本就不是在聊天。通常的情况是，第一个金发男会先讲自己十分钟左右，然后第二个黑发男再讲自己十分钟左右。他们就这样轮流讲，互相打断。我在他们旁边坐了两个小时，他们俩竟然一次也没问过对方一个问题。谈话中，黑发男子提到他哥哥一个月前去世了。金发男子连一句客套的“我很遗憾听到这个消息”都没说，就继续聊起自己。我意识到，如果他们见面只是为了轮流朗读各自的Facebook状态更新，结果也完全一样。

I felt like everywhere I went, I was surrounded by people who were broadcasting but not receiving. Narcissism, it occurred to me, is a corruption of attention – it’s where your attention becomes turned in only on yourself and your own ego. I don’t say this with any sense of superiority. I am embarrassed to describe what I realised in that week that I missed most about the web. Every day in my normal life – sometimes several times a day – I would look at Twitter and Instagram to see how many followers I had. I didn’t look at the feed, the news, the buzz – just my own stats. If the figure had gone up, I felt glad – like a money-obsessed miser checking the state of his personal stocks and finding he was slightly richer than yesterday. It was as if I was saying to myself, See? More people are following you. You matter. I didn’t miss the content of what they said. I just missed the raw numbers, and the sense that they were growing.

我感觉无论走到哪里，身边的人都在忙着发泄，却不接收信息。我突然意识到，自恋是对注意力的一种腐蚀——它让你的注意力只集中在自己和自己的虚荣心上。我这么说并非出于优越感。我甚至不好意思描述那一周我意识到自己最怀念的网络世界。在日常生活中，我每天都会查看推特和Instagram，有时一天好几次，看看自己有多少粉丝。我不看动态、新闻或热门话题——只看自己的数据。如果粉丝数增加了，我就会很高兴——就像一个守财奴查看自己的股票，发现自己比昨天多了一些财富一样。我仿佛在对自己说：“看！更多人关注你了。你很重要。”我并不怀念他们说的内容。我只是怀念那些数字，以及它们不断增长的感觉。

I found that I had started to panic about irrational things. I kept wondering how, when I left Provincetown and took the boat back to Boston, I was going to get to my friend’s house to retrieve my phone and laptop. What if there were no taxis at the dock? Would I be stranded? Would I never get to my phone? I have been around a lot of addiction in my life, and I knew what I was feeling – the addicted person’s craving for the thing that numbs their nagging sense of hollowness.

我发现自己开始对一些非理性的事情感到恐慌。我一直在想，离开普罗温斯敦乘船返回波士顿后，我该怎么去朋友家取回我的手机和笔记本电脑？万一码头没有出租车怎么办？我会不会被困在那里？我会不会永远都拿不到手机？我这辈子接触过很多有成瘾问题的人，我知道自己现在的感受——就像成瘾者渴望某种东西来麻痹他们挥之不去的空虚感。

One day, I lay on the beach, using puffy dried seaweed as a pillow, trying to read, and I started to angrily reproach myself for not being relaxed, for not being focused, for not starting to write the novel I had been planning for so long. Here you are in paradise, I kept saying to myself; you ditched the phone; now focus. Focus, damn you. I thought back to this moment when, over a year later, I interviewed Professor Gloria Mark, who has spent years studying the science of interruptions. She explained to me that if you have spent long enough being interrupted in your daily life, you will start to interrupt yourself even when you are set free from all these external interruptions. I kept looking at things and imagining how I would describe them in a tweet, and then imagining what people would say in response.

有一天，我躺在沙滩上，用蓬松的干海藻当枕头，试图看书。我却开始愤怒地责备自己不够放松，不够专注，没有开始写我计划已久的小说。我不断地对自己说：“你身处天堂，你扔掉了手机，现在就集中注意力。集中注意力，该死的！”一年多后，我采访了格洛丽亚·马克教授，她多年来一直研究干扰的科学。我回想起这一刻。她向我解释说，如果你在日常生活中长期受到干扰，即使摆脱了所有这些外部干扰，你也会开始自我干扰。我不断地观察事物，想象着我会如何用推特描述它们，然后再想象人们会如何回应。

I realised I had, for over twenty years now, been sending out and receiving signals with large numbers of people all throughout the day. Texts, Facebook messages, phone calls – they were all little ways in which the world seemed to say: I see you. I hear you. We need you. Signal back. Signal more. Now the signals were gone, and it felt like the world was saying – you don’t matter. The absence of these insistent signals seemed to suggest an absence of meaning. I would start conversations with people – on the beach, in bookstores, in cafés – and they were often friendly, but the conversations seemed to have a low social temperature compared to the web-based ones I had lost. No stranger is going to flood you with hearts and tell you you’re great. For years I had derived a large part of my meaning in life from the thin, insistent signals of the web. Now they were gone, and I could see how paltry and lacking in substance they were. But, still, I missed them.

我意识到，二十多年来，我每天都在与很多人进行着各种形式的交流。短信、Facebook消息、电话——这些都是世界似乎在说“我看到你了，我听到了，我们需要你”的细微方式。回复我，多发点信号。如今，这些信号消失了，感觉世界仿佛在说——你无关紧要。这些持续不断的信号的缺失，似乎暗示着意义的缺失。我会和人攀谈——在海滩上、书店里、咖啡馆里——他们通常都很友好，但与我失去的那些网络交流相比，这些对话的社交氛围似乎淡了很多。不会再有陌生人给你送上无数爱心，告诉你你很棒。多年来，我从网络上那些细微却持续不断的信号中汲取了生活意义的很大一部分。现在它们消失了，我才意识到它们是多么的微不足道，多么的空洞。但是，即便如此，我仍然怀念它们。

I now faced a choice. I told myself: By leaving that world behind, you’ve created a vacuum. If you’re going to stay away from it, now you need to fill the vacuum with something. It was only in the third week – after feeling wretched – that I began to find a way to do this. I found a way out of my funk by returning to the research of a remarkable man who opened up a whole new field of psychology in the 1960s, and whose work I had studied over the years. He made a breakthrough – this man identified a way human beings can access their own powers of focus, in a way that makes it possible to concentrate for long periods without it feeling like a huge effort.

我当时面临一个选择。我告诉自己：离开那个世界，就等于留下了一个真空。既然要远离它，现在就必须用什么东西来填补这个真空。直到第三周——在那段痛苦不堪的日子里——我才开始找到方法。我重新研读了一位杰出人物的研究，他于上世纪六十年代开创了心理学的一个全新领域，而我多年来也一直在研究他的著作。他取得了突破性的发现——他找到了一种方法，使人类能够调动自身的专注力，从而长时间集中注意力而不会感到吃力。

To understand how it works, I think it helps to first hear the story of how he made this discovery. I learned a lot of this story from him directly, later, when I went to visit him in Claremont, California. It begins with him as an eight-year-old boy, fleeing Nazi bombs at the height of the Second World War, in a city on the coast of Italy, alone.

为了理解它的运作原理，我认为首先听听他是如何发现这一发现的很有帮助。后来，我去加州克莱蒙特拜访他时，直接从他那里了解到了很多这个故事。故事要从他八岁时说起，二战正酣，他独自一人在意大利沿海的一座城市里躲避纳粹的轰炸。

Mihaly had to run, but he had no idea where to go. The air-raid siren was making a familiar shrieking sound, warning the townspeople that soon there would be Nazi planes overhead. These planes were flying from Germany to Africa, and everybody in the town – even a kid like Mihaly – knew that if the planes couldn’t make it across because of bad weather, they had a plan B. It was to drop their bombs right here, onto this small town. Mihaly tried to get into the nearest air-raid shelter, but it was full. Go next door, he thought, to the butcher’s shop – you could hide in there. Its shutters were down. A few grown-ups managed to find the key, and they all hurried inside.

米哈伊不得不逃跑，但他不知道该往哪里去。空袭警报发出熟悉的尖锐声响，警告镇上的人们，纳粹的飞机很快就会从头顶飞过。这些飞机正从德国飞往非洲，镇上的每个人——甚至像米哈伊这样的孩子——都知道，如果飞机因为恶劣天气无法飞抵非洲，他们还有备用计划。那就是把炸弹投到这里，投在这个小镇上。米哈伊试图躲进最近的防空洞，但那里已经满了。他想，去隔壁的肉铺吧——那里可以躲起来。肉铺的卷帘门是关着的。几个大人找到了钥匙，他们都赶紧跑了进去。

In the darkness, it became clear something was dangling down from the ceiling. It was hanging meat. But they saw this wasn’t an animal – it was the wrong shape. As their eyes refocused, they realised it was the bodies of two men. They recognised them as the butchers themselves, sagging from their own meat-hooks. Mihaly ran again, deeper into the shop – only to run into the hanging body of a third man. They had been suspected of being collaborators with the fascists, so they had been killed. The air-raid siren was still sounding, and Mihaly hid there, close to the corpses.

黑暗中，他们隐约看到天花板上垂着什么东西。那是挂着的肉。但他们发现那不是动物——形状不对。当他们的目光重新聚焦时，他们意识到那是两具男人的尸体。他们认出那是屠夫本人，正从自己的肉钩上耷拉着身子。米哈伊再次跑了起来，往店里深处跑去——却撞见了第三具悬挂着的尸体。他们被怀疑是法西斯分子的同伙，所以被杀了。空袭警报还在响，米哈伊躲在尸体附近。

It had seemed to the boy for some time that the adult world had lost its mind. Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi (pronounced cheek-sent-me-high-ee) was born in 1934 in Fiume, an Italian town close to the Yugoslavian border. His father was a diplomat there for the Hungarian government, so Mihaly grew up on a street where people routinely spoke three or four languages. It was a family where people came up with big, sometimes mad projects: one of his big brothers was the first person ever to hang-glide from Russia to Austria. But when Mihaly was six, the war began, and ‘the collapse happened’, he told me. He was not allowed to play outside on the street, so he invented worlds of play within his own home. He would stage elaborate battles with toy soldiers that went on for weeks, planning out every move in this fantasy war. He spent a lot of his nights in chilly bomb shelters, sitting under blankets, terrified. ‘You never knew what was actually happening,’ he recalled. When the all-clear sounded in the mornings, people would leave politely and go to work.

在男孩看来，大人的世界似乎早已失去了理智。米哈里·契克森米哈赖（Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi，发音为cheek-sent-me-high-ee）1934年出生于意大利小镇阜姆，靠近南斯拉夫边境。他的父亲是匈牙利政府驻当地的外交官，因此米哈里从小生活在一条人们习以为常地讲着三四种语言的街道上。这是一个充满奇思妙想的家庭，人们常常会提出一些宏大甚至疯狂的计划：他的一位哥哥是第一个从俄罗斯滑翔到奥地利的人。但米哈里六岁那年，战争爆发了，“一切都崩溃了，”他告诉我。他被禁止在街上玩耍，于是便在家中构建起属于自己的游戏世界。他会用玩具士兵进行精心设计的战斗，持续数周之久，在这场幻想战争中，他会精心策划每一个行动。许多个夜晚，他都躲在冰冷的防空洞里，裹着毯子，恐惧不已。 “你永远不知道实际发生了什么，”他回忆道。每天早上解除警报后，人们都会礼貌地离开去上班。

Italy was getting too dangerous, so his family took him to a seaside town across the border named Opatija – but before long, the town was besieged from all sides. Partisans would come down and kill anyone suspected of collaborating with the invaders, while the Nazis bombarded from the air. ‘Now, nothing was getting safe,’ Mihaly told me. ‘I never found a stable world in which I [could] live.’ By the time the war ended, Europe was in ruins, and his family had lost everything. They got word that one of his brothers had been killed in the fighting, and another, Moricz, had been taken by Stalin to a Siberian concentration camp. ‘By the time I was ten years old,’ he remembered years later, ‘I was convinced that grown-ups didn’t know how to live a good life.’

意大利局势变得过于危险，于是他的家人带他去了边境另一侧的海滨小镇奥帕蒂亚——但没过多久，小镇就被四面围困。游击队员会下来杀害任何被怀疑与侵略者合作的人，而纳粹则从空中进行轰炸。“现在，一切都不安全了，”米哈伊告诉我，“我再也找不到一个可以安身立命的稳定世界。”战争结束时，欧洲满目疮痍，他的家人失去了一切。他们得知他的一个兄弟在战斗中阵亡，另一个兄弟莫里茨被斯大林送往西伯利亚集中营。“到了十岁的时候，”多年后他回忆道，“我确信大人根本不懂得如何好好生活。”

After the war, he and his parents ended up in a refugee camp, which he found squalid, and lacking in hope. One day, in these ruins of a life, Mihaly was told that he was going to join a Scout troop for boys in the camp, and he started going out into the wilderness with them. He discovered that he felt most alive when he was doing something difficult, like navigating a steep ascent, or finding his way through a ravine. He thinks this experience saved him.

战后，他和父母流落到一个难民营，那里环境恶劣，毫无希望。一天，在这片破败的土地上，米哈伊得知自己将加入营地里的一支童子军队伍，于是他开始和他们一起到野外探险。他发现，在做一些具有挑战性的事情时，比如攀登陡峭的山坡或穿越峡谷，他才能真正感受到生命的活力。他认为正是这段经历拯救了他。

When he was thirteen, he quit school, because he couldn’t see how all this adult wisdom was going to help him when it had driven European civilisation off a cliff. He found his own way to Rome, and he started working as a translator in that trashed, half-starved city. He wanted to get back out into the mountains, so he saved up for a long time to go to Switzerland. When he was fifteen, he was finally able to take the train to Zurich, and while he was waiting around for the transport to the Alps, he saw an advertisement for a psychology lecture. The lecturer was Carl Jung, a legendary Swiss psychoanalyst, and while Mihaly wasn’t drawn to the content of Jung’s ideas, he was thrilled by the idea of looking at how the human mind works in a scientific way. He decided to become a psychologist, but it turned out there were no psychology degrees in Europe. He learned, though, that the subject existed in a distant country he had only seen in the movies: the United States.

十三岁那年，他辍学了，因为他看不出这些成年人的智慧对他有什么用，毕竟它们已经把欧洲文明推向了悬崖。他独自前往罗马，在那座破败不堪、饥荒肆虐的城市里做起了翻译。他渴望回到山区，于是攒了很久的钱，准备去瑞士。十五岁那年，他终于坐上了去苏黎世的火车。在等候前往阿尔卑斯山的交通工具时，他看到了一则心理学讲座的广告。主讲人是卡尔·荣格，一位传奇的瑞士精神分析学家。虽然米哈里对荣格的思想内容并不感兴趣，但他却对用科学的方法研究人类思维运作方式的想法感到兴奋不已。他决定成为一名心理学家，但后来发现欧洲并没有心理学学位。不过，他了解到，在一个他只在电影里见过的遥远国度——美国——存在着心理学专业。

Finally, after years of saving, he made it there – only to get a nasty shock when he arrived. American psychology was dominated by one big idea, epitomised by a famous scientist. A Harvard professor named B. F. Skinner had become an intellectual celebrity by discovering something strange. You can take an animal that seems to be freely making up its own mind about what to pay attention to – like a pigeon, or a rat, or a pig – and you can get it pay attention to whatever you choose for it. You can control its focus, as surely as if it was a robot and you had created it to obey your whims. Here’s an example of how Skinner did it that you can try for yourself. Take a pigeon. Put it in a cage. Keep it until it is hungry. Then introduce a bird feeder that releases seed into the cage when you push a button. Pigeons move around a lot – so wait until the pigeon makes a random movement that you have chosen in advance (like, say, jerking its head up high, or sticking out its left wing), and at that precise moment, release some pellets. Then wait for it to make the same random movement again, and give it more pellets.

经过多年的积蓄，他终于抵达了目的地——却在抵达后大吃一惊。当时的美国心理学界被一个核心理念所主导，而这个理念的代表人物是一位著名的科学家。哈佛大学教授B·F·斯金纳发现了一些奇特的现象，并因此声名鹊起。你可以控制一种看似能够自由决定关注什么的动物——比如鸽子、老鼠或猪——让它关注你选择的任何事物。你可以像操控机器人一样控制它的注意力，就像你创造了一个机器人来服从你的意志一样。以下是斯金纳的一个例子，你可以亲自尝试一下。找一只鸽子，把它关进笼子里，直到它饿了。然后，在笼子里放一个喂鸟器，按下按钮就能让鸟食掉进笼子里。鸽子活动范围很大——所以，等到鸽子做出你事先选定的随机动作（比如，高高抬起头，或者伸出左翼），就在那一刻，投放一些饲料颗粒。然后，等待它再次做出同样的随机动作，再投放一些饲料颗粒。

If you do this a few times, the pigeon will quickly learn that if it wants pellets, it should carry out the random gesture you have chosen – and it will start to do it a lot. If you manipulate it correctly, its focus will come to be dominated by the twitch that you chose to reward. It will come to jerk up its head or stick out its left wing obsessively. When Skinner discovered this, he wanted to figure out – how far can you take this? How elaborately can you program an animal using these reinforcements? He discovered you can take it really far. You can teach a pigeon to play ping-pong. You can teach a rabbit to pick up coins and put them into piggy banks. You can teach a pig to vacuum. Many animals will focus on very complex – and, to them, meaningless – things, if you reward them right.

如果你这样做几次，鸽子很快就会明白，如果想要食物，就应该做出你随机选择的那个动作——而且它会开始频繁地这样做。如果你正确地引导它，它的注意力就会被你选择奖励的那个动作所占据。它会开始不停地抬起头或伸出左翼。斯金纳发现这一点后，他想弄清楚——这种方法能做到什么程度？你能用这些强化手段对动物进行多精细的训练？他发现这种方法可以做到非常精细。你可以教鸽子打乒乓球。你可以教兔子捡硬币放进存钱罐。你可以教猪吸尘。如果你给予正确的奖励，许多动物都会专注于非常复杂——对它们来说毫无意义——的事情。

Skinner became convinced that this principle explained human behaviour almost in its entirety. You believe that you are free, and that you make choices, and you have a complex human mind that is selecting what to pay attention to – but it’s all a myth. You and your sense of focus are simply the sum total of all the reinforcements you have experienced in your life. Human beings, he believed, have no minds – not in the sense that you are a person with free will making your own choices. You can be reprogrammed in any way that a clever designer wants. Years later, the designers of Instagram asked: If we reinforce our users for taking selfies – if we give them hearts and likes – will they start to do it obsessively, just like the pigeon will obsessively hold out its left wing to get extra seed? They took Skinner’s core techniques, and applied them to a billion people.

斯金纳深信，这一原理几乎可以解释人类行为的全部。你以为自己是自由的，可以做出选择，拥有复杂的思维，能够选择关注什么——但这都是迷思。你和你的专注力，不过是你一生中所经历的所有强化作用的总和。他认为，人类没有思维——并非指拥有自由意志、能够自主选择。你可以被任何聪明的“设计师”以任何方式重新编程。多年后，Instagram 的设计师们提出了这样一个问题：如果我们鼓励用户自拍——比如给他们点赞和爱心——他们会不会像鸽子那样，为了获得更多种子而痴迷地伸出左翼？他们借鉴了斯金纳的核心理论，并将其应用于十亿用户。

Mihaly learned that these ideas ruled American psychology, and they were hugely influential in American society too. Skinner was a star, featured on the front page of Time magazine. He was so famous that by 1981, 82 percent of the American college-educated public could identify who he was.

米哈里了解到，这些思想主导了美国心理学界，并且对美国社会也产生了巨大的影响。斯金纳是位明星人物，曾登上《时代》杂志的封面。他名气之大，以至于到1981年，82%的美国大学毕业生都能认出他。

To Mihaly, this seemed like a bleak and limited view of human psychology. It clearly yielded some results – but he believed it was missing most of what it means to be human. He decided he wanted to explore the aspects of human psychology that were positive, and nourishing, and generated something more than hollow mechanical responses. But there weren’t many people in American psychology that thought like this. To begin, he decided to study something that seemed to him to be one of the great achievements of human beings – the making of art. He had seen destruction; now it was time to study creation. So, in Chicago, he persuaded a group of painters to let him witness their process over many months, so he could try to figure out the underlying psychological processes that were driving the unusual kind of focus they had chosen to dedicate their lives to. He watched one artist after another focusing on a single image and attending to it with great care.

在米哈里看来，这似乎是一种对人类心理学的悲观而狭隘的看法。它显然取得了一些成果，但他认为这种看法忽略了人性的大部分本质。他决定探索人类心理学中那些积极的、滋养的方面，以及那些能够产生超越空洞机械反应的更深层次的东西。然而，在美国心理学界，很少有人持有这种观点。为了着手研究，他决定从他认为人类最伟大的成就之一——艺术创作入手。他目睹了毁灭，现在是时候研究创造了。于是，在芝加哥，他说服了一群画家，让他观察他们几个月的创作过程，以便他能够探究驱动他们如此专注、并将毕生精力投入其中的潜在心理过程。他观察着一位又一位艺术家，他们专注于单一的画面，并全神贯注地进行创作。

Mihaly was struck by one thing above all else – for the artist, when they were in the process of creation, time seemed to fall away. They almost appeared to be in a hypnotic trance. It was a deep form of attention that you rarely see elsewhere.

米哈里印象最深刻的是一点——对于艺术家而言，创作时时间仿佛静止。他们几乎进入了一种催眠般的恍惚状态。这是一种你很少在其他地方见到的深度专注。

Then he noticed something puzzling. After investing all this time in creating their paintings, when they were finished, the artists didn’t triumphantly gaze at what they had made and show it off and seek out praise for it. Almost all of them simply put the painting away and started working on another one. If Skinner was right – that human beings do things just to gain rewards and avoid punishments – this made no sense. You’d done the work; now here’s the reward, right in front of you, for you to enjoy. But creative people seemed mostly uninterested in rewards; even money didn’t interest most of them. ‘When they finished,’ Mihaly said to an interviewer later, ‘the object, the outcome was not important.’

然后他注意到一件令人费解的事。艺术家们投入了大量时间创作画作，完成后，他们并没有得意洋洋地欣赏自己的作品，炫耀一番，寻求赞扬。几乎所有人都只是把画收起来，开始创作下一幅。如果斯金纳的观点——人类做事只是为了获得奖励、避免惩罚——是正确的，那么这种现象就说不通了。你已经完成了工作；现在奖励就在眼前，等着你去享受。但富有创造力的人似乎对奖励漠不关心；甚至金钱也无法吸引他们中的大多数人。“当他们完成作品时，”米哈里后来对一位采访者说，“作品本身，结果，并不重要。”

He wanted to understand what was actually driving them. What made it possible for them to focus on just one thing for so long? It became clear to Mihaly that ‘what was so enthralling about painting was’ something about ‘the process of painting itself’. But what? To try to understand this better, Mihaly started to study adults who engaged in other activities – people who were long-distance swimmers, or rock climbers, or chess players. He only looked at first at non-professionals. Often they were doing things that were physically uncomfortable, exhausting, and even dangerous, for no obvious reward – yet they loved it. He talked to them about how they felt when they were doing the thing that drew this extraordinary focus out of them. He noticed that although these activities were very different, the way the people described how they felt had striking similarities. One word kept cropping up again and again. They kept saying things like: ‘I was carried on by the flow.’

他想了解究竟是什么在驱使他们。是什么让他们能够如此长时间地专注于一件事？米哈里逐渐明白，“绘画如此引人入胜的原因”在于“绘画过程本身”。但究竟是什么呢？为了更好地理解这一点，米哈里开始研究从事其他活动的成年人——比如长距离游泳运动员、攀岩者或棋手。起初，他只关注非专业人士。这些人常常从事一些身体上不舒服、筋疲力竭甚至危险的活动，而且似乎没有明显的回报——但他们却乐在其中。他与他们交谈，了解他们在从事那些让他们如此专注的活动时的感受。他注意到，尽管这些活动截然不同，但人们描述自身感受的方式却有着惊人的相似之处。一个词反复出现。他们总是说：“我被一股力量裹挟着前进。”

One rock climber told him later: ‘The mystique of rock-climbing is climbing; you get to the top of a rock glad it’s over but really wish it could go on forever. The justification of climbing is climbing, like the justification of poetry is writing. You don’t conquer anything except things in yourself … The act of writing justifies poetry. Climbing is the same: recognising you are a flow. The purpose of flow is to keep on flowing, not looking for a peak or utopia but staying in the flow. It is not a moving up but a continuous flowing; you move up to keep the flow going.’

一位攀岩者后来告诉他：“攀岩的魅力就在于攀登本身；当你到达岩顶时，你会庆幸攀登结束了，但又真心希望它能永远持续下去。攀登的意义就在于攀登本身，就像诗歌的意义在于写作一样。你征服的并非任何东西，而是你内心的挑战……写作赋予诗歌意义。攀岩也是如此：认识到你本身就是一股流动。流动的目的在于保持流动，而不是寻找顶峰或乌托邦，而是保持在流动之中。这不是向上攀升，而是持续流动；你向上攀升是为了保持流动。”

Mihaly began to wonder if these people were in fact describing a fundamental human instinct that had not been studied by scientists before. He called it a ‘flow state’. This is when you are so absorbed in what you are doing that you lose all sense of yourself, and time seems to fall away, and you are flowing into the experience itself. It is the deepest form of focus and attention that we know of. When he began to explain to people what a flow state is and asked if they had ever experienced something like it, 85 percent of them recognised and remembered at least one time they’d felt this way – and they often said these moments were the highlights of their lives. It didn’t matter if they got there by performing brain surgery or strumming the guitar or making great bagels – they described their flow states with wonder. He found himself thinking back to being a child on the floor of a war-smashed city, planning elaborate battles with his toy soldiers, and then to himself at the age of thirteen, exploring the hills and mountains around his refugee camp.

米哈里开始思考，这些人是否实际上描述的是一种此前科学家从未研究过的人类基本本能。他称之为“心流状态”。在这种状态下，你会完全沉浸于正在做的事情中，以至于忘记了自己，时间仿佛静止，你完全融入到体验本身。这是我们所知的最深层次的专注和注意力状态。当他开始向人们解释什么是心流状态，并询问他们是否体验过类似的状态时，85%的人都表示至少有过一次这样的经历——而且他们常常说，这些时刻是他们生命中最美好的回忆。无论他们是通过进行脑外科手术、弹奏吉他还是制作美味的百吉饼进入这种状态，他们都带着惊奇的心情描述着自己的心流状态。他不禁回想起自己还是个孩子时，在饱受战争蹂躏的城市里，坐在地板上用玩具士兵策划着复杂的战斗；然后又想起自己十三岁时，在难民营周围的山丘和山脉间探索的场景。

He was discovering that if human beings drill down in the right way, we can hit a gusher of focus inside ourselves – a long surge of attention that will flow forth and carry us through difficult tasks in a way that feels painless, and in fact pleasurable. So the obvious question is: where do we drill to get it? How can we bring about flow states? At first, most people assume they will achieve flow simply by relaxing into it – you picture yourself lying by the pool in Vegas sipping a cocktail. But when he studied it, he found that in fact, relaxing rarely gets you into a flow state. You have to get there by a different route.

他发现，如果人类以正确的方式深入钻研，就能激发内在的专注力——一种持久的注意力涌动，它将带领我们轻松愉快地完成各种艰巨任务。那么，显而易见的问题是：我们应该从哪里入手才能获得这种专注力？如何才能进入心流状态？起初，大多数人认为只要放松就能进入心流状态——想象一下自己躺在拉斯维加斯的泳池边，啜饮着鸡尾酒。但他的研究发现，事实上，放松很少能让人进入心流状态。你需要另辟蹊径才能达到那种状态。

Mihaly’s studies identified many aspects of flow, but it seemed to me – as I read over them in detail – that if you want to get there, what you need to know boils down to three core components. The first thing you need to do is to choose a clearly defined goal. I want to paint this canvas; I want to run up this hill; I want to teach my child how to swim. You have to resolve to pursue it, and to set aside your other goals while you do. Flow can only come when you are monotasking – when you choose to set aside everything else and do one thing. Mihaly found that distraction and multitasking kill flow, and nobody will reach flow if they are trying to do two or more things at the same time. Flow requires all of your brainpower, deployed towards one mission.

米哈里的研究揭示了心流的诸多方面，但当我仔细研读他的研究后，我认为，要想进入心流状态，你需要了解的其实只有三个核心要素。首先，你需要选择一个明确的目标。比如，我想画这幅画；我想跑上这座山；我想教我的孩子游泳。你必须下定决心去追求它，并在过程中暂时放下其他目标。心流只能在你专注于一件事的时候出现——当你选择放下其他一切，专心做一件事的时候。米哈里发现，分心和多任务处理会扼杀心流，试图同时做两件或更多事情的人是无法进入心流状态的。心流需要你将所有的脑力都投入到一项任务中。

Secondly, you have to be doing something that is meaningful to you. This is part of a basic truth about attention: we evolved to pay attention to things that are meaningful to us. As Roy Baumeister, the leading expert on willpower I quoted in the introduction, put it to me: ‘A frog will look at a fly it can eat much more than a stone it can’t eat.’ To a frog, a fly is meaningful and a stone is not – so it easily pays attention to a fly, and rarely pays attention to a stone. This, he says, ‘goes back to the design of the brain … It’s designed to pay attention to the stuff that matters to you.’ After all, ‘the frog who sat around all day looking at stones would have starved’. In any situation, it will be easier to pay attention to things that are meaningful to you, and harder to pay attention to things that seem meaningless. When you are trying to make yourself do something that lacks meaning, your attention will often slip and slide off it.

其次，你必须做对你有意义的事情。这是关于注意力的一个基本真理：我们进化成关注对我们有意义的事物。正如我在引言中引用的意志力研究权威罗伊·鲍迈斯特（Roy Baumeister）对我说的那样：“青蛙会更关注它能吃的苍蝇，而不是它吃不下的石头。”对青蛙来说，苍蝇有意义，石头没有意义——所以它很容易关注苍蝇，却很少关注石头。他说，这“可以追溯到大脑的设计……大脑的设计就是为了让你关注对你重要的事情。”毕竟，“整天盯着石头看的青蛙会饿死”。在任何情况下，关注对你有意义的事情都更容易，而关注那些看似毫无意义的事情则更难。当你试图强迫自己去做一些缺乏意义的事情时，你的注意力往往会游离。

Thirdly, it will help if you are doing something that is at the edge of your abilities, but not beyond them. If the goal you choose is too easy, you’ll go into autopilot – but if it’s too hard, you’ll start to feel anxious and off-kilter and you won’t flow either. Picture a rock climber who has medium-ranking experience and talent. If she clambers up any old brick wall at the back of a garden, she’s not going to get into flow because it’s too easy. If she’s suddenly told to climb the side of Mount Kilimanjaro, she won’t get into flow either because she’ll freak out. When she needs is a hill or mountain that is, ideally, slightly higher and harder than the one she did last time.

第三，做一些力所能及的事情会很有帮助，但不要超出你的能力范围。如果目标太容易，你会进入自动驾驶模式；但如果太难，你会开始感到焦虑和失衡，也无法进入心流状态。想象一下一位经验和天赋都中等的攀岩者。如果她只是爬上花园后面的普通砖墙，她不会进入心流状态，因为这太容易了。如果突然让她去攀登乞力马扎罗山，她也不会进入心流状态，因为她会惊慌失措。她需要的是一座比上次攀登的山丘或山峰更高更难的山。

So: to find flow, you need to choose one single goal; make sure your goal is meaningful to you; and try to push yourself to the edge of your abilities. Once you have created these conditions, and you hit flow, you can recognise it because it’s a distinctive mental state. You feel you are purely present in the moment. You experience a loss of self-consciousness. In this state it’s like your ego has vanished and you have merged with the task – like you are the rock you are climbing.

所以，要想进入心流状态，你需要选择一个单一的目标；确保这个目标对你意义重大；并努力挑战自己的极限。一旦你创造了这些条件，进入心流状态，你就能识别出来，因为这是一种独特的心理状态。你会感觉自己完全沉浸在当下。你会体验到自我意识的丧失。在这种状态下，你的自我仿佛消失了，你与任务融为一体——就像你就是你要攀登的那块岩石。

By the time I met him, Mihaly was eighty-seven, and he had spent more than five decades studying flow states. He – along with scientists all over the world – had built up a broad and robust body of scientific evidence to show flow states are a real and deep form of human attention. They have also shown that the more flow you experience, the better you feel. Until his research, professional psychology in the US had been focused either on when things go wrong – when you’re mentally distressed – or on the manipulative vision of B. F. Skinner. Mihaly made the case for ‘positive psychology’: that we should primarily focus on the things that make life worth living, and find ways to boost them.

我见到米哈里时，他已八十七岁高龄，五十多年来一直致力于研究心流状态。他与世界各地的科学家一道，积累了大量可靠的科学证据，证明心流状态是人类注意力的一种真实而深刻的形式。他们还发现，心流体验越丰富，感觉就越好。在他的研究出现之前，美国的专业心理学要么关注事情出错时——也就是人们感到精神痛苦的时候——要么关注B·F·斯金纳那种带有操控性的理论。米哈里提出了“积极心理学”的理念：我们应该主要关注那些让生活充满意义的事物，并找到增强这些事物的方法。

This disagreement seemed to me to lay the groundwork for one of the defining conflicts in the world today. We now live in a world dominated by technologies based on B. F. Skinner’s vision of how the human mind works. His insight – that you can train living creatures to desperately crave arbitrary rewards – has come to dominate our environment. Many of us are like those birds in cages being made to perform a bizarre dance to get rewards, and all the while we imagine we are choosing it for ourselves – the men I saw in Provincetown obsessively posting selfies to Instagram started to look to me like Skinner’s pigeons with a six-pack and a pina colada. In a culture where our focus is stolen by these surface-level stimuli, Mihaly’s deeper insight has been forgotten: that we have within us a force that makes it possible to focus for long stretches and enjoy it, and it will make us happier and healthier, if only we create the right circumstances to let it flow.

在我看来，这场分歧似乎为当今世界最根本的冲突之一埋下了伏笔。我们现在生活在一个被基于斯金纳关于人类思维运作方式的理论的技术所主导的世界。他的洞见——你可以训练生物体对任意奖励产生强烈的渴望——已经主宰了我们的环境。我们中的许多人就像笼中鸟，被迫跳着怪异的舞蹈来获得奖励，而我们却一直以为这是我们自己的选择——我在普罗温斯敦看到的那些痴迷于在Instagram上发布自拍的男人，在我看来就像是斯金纳笔下那些拿着六块腹肌和一杯椰林飘香的鸽子。在一个我们的注意力被这些肤浅刺激所窃取的文化中，米哈里的更深层次的洞见已被遗忘：我们体内蕴藏着一种力量，它使我们能够长时间集中注意力并享受其中，如果我们创造合适的条件让它发挥作用，它就会让我们更快乐、更健康。

Once I knew this, I understood why, when I felt constantly distracted, I didn’t just feel irritated – I felt diminished. We know, at some level, that when we are not focusing, we are not using one of our greatest capacities. Starved of flow, we become stumps of ourselves, sensing somewhere what we might have been.

一旦我明白了这一点，我就明白了为什么当我感到持续分心时，我不仅会感到烦躁，还会感到自身能力的下降。我们内心深处都知道，当我们无法集中注意力时，我们就无法发挥自身最强大的能力之一。一旦失去了专注力，我们就会变成行尸走肉，只能在某个地方隐约感觉到自己本该成为的样子。

As an old man, something strange happened to Mihaly. After the Second World War was over, his older brother, Moricz, had been taken to a Stalinist concentration camp in Russia, and people who vanished into these gulags were often never heard from again – but after many years of silence, in which everyone assumed he was dead, Moricz reappeared. Released at last into a thawing Soviet Union, he struggled to find work: survivors of the gulags were marked as inherently suspect. Eventually he found employment as a stoker on the railways, even though he had advanced degrees from Switzerland. He didn’t complain.

米哈伊晚年时，发生了一件怪事。二战结束后，他的哥哥莫里茨被送往苏联的斯大林集中营。那些被关进古拉格的人往往杳无音信——但多年杳无音讯，人人都以为他已经去世后，莫里茨却突然出现了。他最终被释放到逐渐解冻的苏联，却难以找到工作：古拉格的幸存者天生就被视为可疑人物。尽管他拥有瑞士的高等学位，最终还是在铁路找到了一份司炉工的工作。他没有抱怨。

When Moricz was in his eighties, Mihaly went to Budapest, in Hungary, to be reunited with him. Moricz’s ability to find flow had been cut off in the most brutal ways, but Mihaly discovered that, very late in his life, his brother had been able, for the first time, to pursue something he had always loved. He was fascinated by crystals. He began to collect these sparkling rocks, and he had gathered examples from every continent. He went to meet dealers, he attended conventions, he read magazines about them. When Mihaly went to his home, it looked like a museum of crystals running from the ceiling to the floor, with special lighting fitted to show off their sparkle. Moricz handed Mihaly a crystal the size of a child’s fist and said: ‘I was looking at this thing just yesterday. It was nine in the morning when I put it under the microscope. Outside, it was sunny, just like today. I kept turning the rock around, looking at all the fissures, the intrusions, the dozen or so different crystal formations inside and around … then I looked up, and thought that a storm must be coming, because it had gotten so dark … then I realised it was not overcast, but the sun had been setting – it was seven in the evening.’ Mihaly thought the crystal was gorgeous, but wondered – ten hours?

莫里茨八十多岁时，米哈伊前往匈牙利的布达佩斯与他重聚。莫里茨的创作灵感早已被残酷地切断，但米哈伊发现，在他生命的最后阶段，他的哥哥第一次得以追求他一直以来热爱的事物——水晶。他痴迷于水晶，开始收集这些闪闪发光的石头，他的收藏遍及各大洲。他拜访水晶商，参加水晶展，阅读相关的杂志。米哈伊来到他家时，那里简直像一座水晶博物馆，从天花板到地板都摆满了水晶，还特意安装了灯光来衬托它们的璀璨光芒。莫里茨递给米哈伊一块拳头大小的水晶，说道：“我昨天才看过这东西。早上九点，我把它放在显微镜下观察。外面阳光明媚，就像今天一样。”我不停地转动着那块岩石，观察着所有的裂缝、侵入体，以及内部和周围十几种不同的晶体结构……然后我抬头望去，心想一定是暴风雨要来了，因为天色已经很暗了……后来我才意识到，不是阴天，而是太阳正在落山——当时是晚上七点。米哈伊觉得那块晶体非常漂亮，但他不禁疑惑——这花了十个小时？

Then he realised. Moricz had learned how to read the rocks – to see where it came from, and its chemical composition. It was a chance for him to use his skills. For him, this triggered a flow state. All his life Mihaly had been learning how flow states can save us. Now he saw it in the face of his own gulag-starved brother, as they stared together into a shimmering crystal.

然后他恍然大悟。莫里茨学会了如何解读岩石——辨别岩石的来源和化学成分。这对他来说是一个运用这项技能的机会。对他而言，这触发了一种心流状态。米哈里一生都在学习心流状态如何拯救我们。现在，当他和自己饱受折磨、饥肠辘辘的弟弟一起凝视着一块闪闪发光的晶体时，他从弟弟的脸上看到了这一点。

The more he studied flow states, the more Mihaly noticed something else crucial about them. They are extraordinarily fragile and easily disrupted. He wrote: ‘Many forces, both within ourselves and in the environment, stand in the way’ of flow. In the late 1980s, he discovered that staring at a screen is one of the activities we take part in that on average provides the lowest amount of flow. (He warned that ‘surrounded by an astonishing panoply of recreational gadgets … most of us go on being bored and vaguely frustrated.’) But as I reflected on this in Provincetown, I realised that even though I had set aside my screens, I was still making a basic mistake. ‘To have a good life, it is not enough to remove what is wrong with it,’ Mihaly has explained. ‘We also need a positive goal; otherwise why keep going?’

米哈里对心流状态研究得越深入，就越注意到其另一个关键特性：心流极其脆弱，极易被打断。他写道：“许多力量，既来自我们自身，也来自环境，都会阻碍心流的到来。” 20世纪80年代末，他发现，盯着屏幕是我们参与的活动中，平均而言最难以获得心流体验的一项。（他警告说：“我们被琳琅满目的娱乐设备包围着……但大多数人仍然感到无聊和莫名的沮丧。”） 但在普罗温斯敦反思此事时，我意识到，即使我已经放下了屏幕，我仍然犯了一个根本性的错误。“要想拥有美好的生活，仅仅消除生活中的弊端是不够的，”米哈里解释道，“我们还需要一个积极的目标；否则，我们为什么要继续下去呢？”

In our normal lives, many of us try to seek relief from distraction simply by crashing – we try to recover from a day of overload by collapsing in front of the TV. But if you only break away from distraction into rest – if you don’t replace it with a positive goal you are striving towards – you will always be pulled back to distraction sooner or later. The more powerful path out of distraction is to find your flow.

在日常生活中，我们很多人为了摆脱干扰，往往会选择彻底放松——比如，一天工作下来，筋疲力尽地瘫倒在电视机前。但如果你只是暂时摆脱干扰，休息片刻，却没有用积极的目标来取代它，那么迟早你还是会被干扰拉回来。摆脱干扰更有效的方法是找到自己的“心流”状态。

So at the end of that third week in Provincetown, I asked myself – why did you come here? It wasn’t just to get away from the phone and the Skinnerian reinforcements of constant likes and retweets and shares. You came here to write. Writing and reading have always been the primary sources of flow in my life. I had been nurturing an idea for a novel for a long time, and I told myself I would get round to it one day, when I had the time. Well, I thought, here is the time. Drill there. See if it brings you flow. This seemed to fit perfectly into Mihaly’s model for how to create flow states – it required me to set aside my other goals; it was something meaningful to me; and it was something at the edge of my comfort zone, but not, I hoped, beyond it. So on the first day of my third week, in my panicked funk, I sat on the sofa in my little corner of the beachhouse. I nervously opened the broken old laptop my friend Imtiaz had loaned me, and I wrote the first line of my novel. And I wrote the second line. And it became a paragraph, then a page. It was hard. I didn’t particularly enjoy it. But the next day, conscious that I had to retrain my habits, I made myself do the same. And so it went on, day after day. I struggled. I disciplined myself.

所以在普罗温斯敦的第三周结束时，我问自己——你为什么来这里？不仅仅是为了逃离手机，逃离斯金纳式的点赞、转发和分享带来的持续不断的“精神强化”。你来这里是为了写作。写作和阅读一直是我生活中心流的主要来源。我酝酿一个小说构思很久了，我告诉自己总有一天会有时间把它写出来。好吧，我想，现在就是时候了。就从这里开始吧。看看它能否让你进入心流状态。这似乎完美契合了米哈里关于如何创造心流状态的模型——它要求我放下其他目标；它对我来说意义非凡；它处于我的舒适区边缘，但我希望它不会超出我的舒适区。所以在第三周的第一天，我带着焦虑和低落的情绪，坐在海滨小屋角落里的沙发上。我忐忑不安地打开朋友伊姆蒂亚兹借给我的那台破旧的笔记本电脑，写下了小说的第一句话。然后是第二句。接着是一段，然后是一页。这很艰难。我并不享受这个过程。但第二天，我意识到自己必须改变写作习惯，于是强迫自己继续下去。就这样，日复一日，我坚持不懈。我努力克服困难，严格自律。

By the end of the fourth week, the flow states started to come. And so it ran, into the fifth and sixth weeks – and soon, I was hurrying to my laptop, hungry to do it. Everything Mihaly had described was there – the loss of ego; the loss of time; the sense that I was growing into something bigger than I had been before. Flow was carrying me through the difficult patches, the frustrations. It had unlocked my focus.

到了第四周结束时，心流状态开始出现。就这样，心流持续到了第五周和第六周——很快，我便迫不及待地奔向电脑，渴望投入其中。米哈里所描述的一切都出现了——放下自我；时间仿佛静止；感觉自己正在成长为一个比以往更强大的人。心流帮助我度过了难关和挫折。它让我能够全神贯注。

I noticed that if I spent a day where I experienced three hours of flow early on, for the rest of the day, I felt relaxed and open and able to engage – to walk along the beach, or start chatting to people, or read a book, without feeling cramped, or irritable, or phone-hungry. It was like the flow was relaxing my body and opening my mind – perhaps because I knew I had done my best. I felt myself falling into a different rhythm. I realised then that to recover from our loss of attention, it is not enough to strip out our distractions. That will just create a void. We need to strip out our distractions and to replace them with sources of flow.

我发现，如果一天中早些时候能体验到三个小时的心流状态，那么接下来的时间里，我都会感到放松、心境平和，并且能够全身心地投入到各种活动中——比如在海滩漫步、与人聊天、阅读书籍，而不会感到局促、烦躁或渴望玩手机。这种心流状态仿佛放松了我的身体，打开了我的心扉——或许是因为我知道自己已经尽力了。我感觉自己进入了一种不同的节奏。我意识到，要想从注意力不集中的状态中恢复过来，仅仅消除干扰是不够的。那样只会造成一种空虚感。我们需要消除干扰，并用能够带来心流的事物来取代它们。

After three months in Provincetown, I had written 92,000 words of my novel. They might be terrible, but in one sense, I didn’t care. The reason why became clear to me when one day, shortly before I left Provincetown, I placed my deckchair in the ocean so the sea was lapping at my feet and I finished the third volume of War and Peace . As I closed its last page, I realised I had been sitting there for most of the day. I had been reading like this, day after day, for weeks. And I thought suddenly – it came back! My brain came back! I feared my brain had been broken, and this experiment might just reveal I was a permanently degenerated blob. But I could see now that healing was possible. I cried with relief.

在普罗温斯敦待了三个月后，我写了九万两千字的小说。它们或许很糟糕，但某种程度上，我并不在意。离开普罗温斯敦前不久的一天，我把躺椅搬到海里，让海水轻拍我的脚，读完了《战争与和平》的第三卷。合上最后一页时，我才意识到自己几乎一整天都坐在那里。就这样，我日复一日地读了好几个星期。突然，我意识到——它回来了！我的大脑回来了！我曾害怕我的大脑已经崩溃，害怕这次“实验”会证明我已彻底退化成一团残骸。但现在我明白了，一切皆有可能。我如释重负，喜极而泣。

I thought to myself – I never want to go back to email. I never want to go back to my phone. What a waste of time! What a waste of life! I felt this as strongly as I have ever felt anything. It might seem odd to describe something as immaterial as the internet as heavy, but that’s how it felt to me in that moment – like there had been a vast weight on my back, and I had sloughed it off.

我心想——我再也不想用电子邮件了。我再也不想用手机了。真是浪费时间！真是浪费生命！这种感觉我从未如此强烈。或许你会觉得用“沉重”来形容互联网这种虚无缥缈的东西很奇怪，但那一刻我的确有这种感觉——就像背上压着一块巨石，而我把它卸了下来。

And then I immediately felt uncomfortable with all these thoughts, and guilty. How will this sound, I wondered, when I describe it to people back home? It won’t sound like a liberation to them. It will sound like a taunt. Yes, I managed to get away and find flow in a blissful way, but my situation in Provincetown was so radically different from the lives of anyone I knew – so wildly privileged – that I wondered for a while if it had anything to teach anyone else. I realised that this experience would only be meaningful if we could all find ways to integrate these experiences into our everyday lives. Later, in a very different place, I learned how this could be done.

然后，我立刻对这些想法感到不适和内疚。我心想，如果我把这些经历告诉家乡的人，他们会怎么想？在他们听来，这不会是一种解脱，而是一种嘲讽。没错，我的确逃离了喧嚣，找到了内心的平静，但我在普罗温斯敦的经历与我认识的任何人的生活都截然不同——我享有如此巨大的特权——以至于我一度怀疑，这段经历是否能给其他人带来什么启示。我意识到，只有当我们都能找到方法将这些经历融入日常生活时，这段经历才有意义。后来，在另一个截然不同的地方，我学会了如何做到这一点。

When I said goodbye to Mihaly, it was clear he was unwell. His eyes were heavy, and he told me he had been sick lately. At one point in our conversation, a little stream of ants began to crawl across his desk, and he stopped and stared at them for a while. He was in his late eighties, and it seemed likely he was approaching the end of his life. But his eyes lit up when he told me: ‘The best experiences in life that I had, when I thought back on it, came from times when I had been in the mountains climbing … climbing and doing something really kind of difficult and dangerous – but within the scope of what I could do.’ When you are approaching death, I thought to myself, you won’t think about your reinforcements – the likes and retweets; you’ll think about your moments of flow.

我向米哈里道别时，他显然身体不适。他眼皮沉重，告诉我他最近一直生病。我们谈话间，一群蚂蚁爬过他的桌子，他停下来盯着它们看了好一会儿。他已年近九旬，似乎已接近生命的尽头。但当他告诉我：“回想起来，我人生中最美好的经历都来自登山……攀登，做一些真正艰难危险的事情——但都在我能力范围之内。”时，他的眼睛闪闪发光。我心想，当你临近死亡时，你不会再想着那些点赞和转发之类的东西；你会想起那些心流涌动的时刻。

I felt in that moment that we all have a choice now between two profound forces – fragmentation, or flow. Fragmentation makes you smaller, shallower, angrier. Flow makes you bigger, deeper, calmer. Fragmentation shrinks us. Flow expands us. I asked myself – do you want to be one of Skinner’s pigeons, atrophying your attention on dancing for crude rewards, or Mihaly’s painters, able to concentrate because you have found something that really matters?

那一刻，我感到我们每个人都面临着两种深刻力量的选择——碎片化，或流动。碎片化让你变得渺小、肤浅、易怒；流动让你变得宏大、深邃、平静。碎片化使我们萎缩，流动使我们扩展。我问自己——你想成为斯金纳笔下的鸽子，为了粗浅的回报而麻木地跳舞，还是想成为米哈里笔下的画家，因为找到了真正重要的东西而能够全神贯注？

# ↩

3 Cause Three: The Rise of Physical and Mental Exhaustion

原因三：身心疲惫加剧

The first thing I heard when I opened my eyes was the sound of the ocean lapping in the distance. Then I felt the sun flooding my bed, bathing me in light. Every morning in Provincetown, when this happened, I felt something strange in my body. It took me more than a month to realise what it was.

我睁开眼的第一件事，听到的便是远处海浪拍岸的声音。接着，我感到阳光洒满床铺，将我沐浴在温暖的光芒中。在普罗温斯敦的每个清晨，每当这般景象出现时，我都会感到身体里有种异样的感觉。我花了整整一个月才明白那究竟是什么。

Ever since I went through puberty, I’d thought of sleep as something I wrestled myself into and fought my way out of. I would go to bed sometime between one and three in the morning and immediately bunch up the pillows so they supported my hunched shoulders. Then I would try to stop my mind jangling as it ran through all the things that had happened that day, and all the things I would need to do when I woke up, and all the things to worry about in the world. To take my mind off this internal electrical storm, I’d usually watch a noisy TV show on my laptop.
