Sometimes that would lull me to sleep, but more often, it would awaken a new wave of anxious energy, and I would start emailing or researching again for another few hours. Finally, on most nights, I would power down by taking a few melatonin gummies, and pass out.

自从青春期以来，我就觉得睡觉就像一场搏斗，挣扎着才能入睡，挣扎着才能醒来。我通常会在凌晨一到三点之间上床，然后立刻把枕头堆成一团，支撑着我弓着的肩膀。接着，我会努力让自己的思绪平静下来，不再让它像脱缰的野马般地奔涌，一遍遍地回想着当天发生的一切，醒来后要做的事情，以及这世上所有让我担忧的事情。为了摆脱这种内心的风暴，我通常会用笔记本电脑看一些嘈杂的电视节目。有时候这能让我昏昏欲睡，但更多时候，它会唤醒新一轮的焦虑，然后我又会开始回复邮件或查阅资料，再持续几个小时。最后，大多数晚上，我会吃几颗褪黑素软糖来放松身心，然后沉沉睡去。

Once I was in Zimbabwe and I spoke to some rangers who – as part of their jobs – had to knock out rhinos in order to give them medical treatment. They explained that they did it by darting them with a very powerful tranquilliser. As they described how the rhinos would stagger about in a panicked funk and then crash to the ground, I thought – hey, that’s my sleep routine too.

有一次我在津巴布韦，和一些护林员聊了聊。他们的工作之一是给犀牛注射麻醉剂，以便进行治疗。他们解释说，他们用一种强效麻醉剂麻醉犀牛。当他们描述犀牛惊恐地踉跄几步，然后重重地摔倒在地时，我心想——嘿，这不就是我的睡眠模式吗？

After my chemical crash, I would be woken up six or seven hours later by a tag team of loud alarms. First, a radio alarm playing the BBC World Service would jolt me with the horrors of the day’s news; then ten minutes later my phone would play a loud clanging alert; then ten minutes after that another alarm clock would howl. When my ability to out-sleep all three finally wore off, I would stagger to my feet and immediately douse myself with enough caffeine to kill a small herd of cows. I lived on the permanent cliff-edge of exhaustion.

药物作用消退后，六七个小时后，我会被一连串刺耳的闹钟声吵醒。先是BBC世界广播电台的闹铃声，用当天新闻的种种骇人听闻的内容把我吓了一跳；十分钟后，我的手机会发出刺耳的提示音；再过十分钟，另一个闹钟就会发出凄厉的鸣叫。当我终于无法再睡过这三个闹钟时，我会踉跄着站起来，立刻狂饮咖啡，摄入的咖啡因足以毒死一小群牛。我仿佛永远生活在精疲力竭的边缘。

In Provincetown, when night fell, I would return to my little rooms to find there was no noise to rouse me and no portal to let in the wider world. I would go to lie in my bedroom, where the only source of light was a small reading lamp next to a pile of books. I would lie there reading and feel the paroxysms of the day slowly wend their way out of my body as I gently eased out of consciousness. I realised I had left my melatonin unused in the bathroom cabinet.

在普罗温斯敦，夜幕降临后，我回到自己的小房间，发现没有一丝声响唤醒我，也没有通往外界的通道。我躺在卧室里，唯一的光源是一盏小台灯，旁边堆着一摞书。我躺在那里读书，感觉白天的种种烦躁和疲惫慢慢从体内消散，我渐渐进入梦乡。这时我才意识到，我把褪黑素忘在浴室的柜子里了。

One day I woke up without any alarms after sleeping for nine hours and realised that I didn’t want any coffee. This was such an alien sensation that it made me stop for a moment and stand there in my boxer shorts in the kitchen in front of the unboiling kettle, staring at it. Then it finally occurred to me what I was feeling – I had awoken from my sleep feeling fully refreshed. My body didn’t feel heavy. I was alert. As the weeks passed, I realised that I felt like this every day now. The last time I remembered feeling like this was when I was a child.

有一天，我睡了九个小时，醒来时没有闹钟，却发现自己不想喝咖啡。这种感觉如此陌生，让我愣住了，穿着四角裤站在厨房里，面对着还没烧开的水壶，盯着它发呆。这时我才恍然大悟——我醒来后感觉神清气爽，身体轻盈，精神抖擞。几周过去了，我发现现在每天都是如此。我上次有这种感觉，还是在孩提时代。

For a long time, I had been trying to live by the rhythms of machines – going endlessly, day or night, until finally the battery conked out. Now I was living by the rhythm of the sun. As the sky went dark, I gradually wound down and finally rested, and when the sun came up, I woke naturally.

长久以来，我一直试图按照机器的节奏生活——日夜不停地运转，直到电池最终耗尽。现在，我却按照太阳的节奏生活。当夜幕降临，我逐渐放松下来，最终休息；当太阳升起，我自然醒来。

This was making something shift in my understanding of my body. I could see now it craved far more sleep than I normally allowed it, and when sleep came without any chemical nudging, my dreams were more vivid. It was as though my body and my mind were unclenching, and then replenishing.

这让我对身体的认知发生了转变。我现在意识到，它渴望的睡眠远比我平时允许的要多得多，而且当睡眠自然而然地到来时，我的梦境也更加生动。仿佛我的身心都在放松，然后得到滋养。

I wondered if this was playing a role in why I was able to think more clearly, and for much longer stretches, than I had for years. I decided to explore the best scientific evidence about how the mysterious long stretches of unconsciousness our bodies crave – and that we so often deny them – might affect our ability to pay attention.

我很好奇，这是否是我多年来思维更加清晰、持续时间更长的原因之一。我决定探究关于这种神秘的、长时间的无意识状态（我们身体渴望却又常常拒绝）如何影响我们注意力能力的最佳科学证据。

In 1981, in a lab in Boston, a young research scientist was keeping people awake all through the night and all through the following day, in long, yawn-strewn stretches. His job was to make sure they stayed conscious and, as he did it, to give them tasks to carry out. They had to add up numbers, and then sort cards into different groups, and then take part in memory tests. For example, he would show them a picture, then take it away, and ask: what colour was the car in the picture I just showed you? Charles Czeisler – a tall, long-limbed man with wire-framed glasses and a deep voice – had, until this moment, never been interested in studying sleep. He had been taught in his medical training that when you are asleep, you are mentally ‘switched off’. This is how lots of us see sleep – as a purely passive process, a mental dead zone in which nothing of consequence happens. Who, he shrugged, would want to study switched-off people? He was researching something he thought was much more important – it was a technical investigation of what time of day certain specific hormones are released in the human body. This required keeping people awake.

1981年，在波士顿的一间实验室里，一位年轻的研究科学家让受试者整夜保持清醒，直到第二天，期间他们还打着哈欠，昏昏欲睡。他的工作是确保他们保持清醒，并在清醒的过程中给他们布置任务。他们需要计算数字，将卡片分类，然后参加记忆测试。例如，他会给他们看一张图片，然后拿走，问：我刚才给你看的图片里的车是什么颜色的？查尔斯·切斯勒——一个身材高挑、四肢修长、戴着金属框眼镜、嗓音低沉的男人——在此之前从未对睡眠研究感兴趣。他在医学训练中学到的是，人睡觉时大脑会“关闭”。我们很多人都这样看待睡眠——一个纯粹被动的过程，一个大脑的空白区域，什么重要的事情都不会发生。他耸耸肩，心想，谁会想研究一个大脑“关闭”的人呢？他当时正在研究一项他认为更为重要的课题——一项关于人体特定激素在一天中特定时间释放的技术调查。这需要让人们保持清醒。

But as the days and nights went on, Charles couldn’t help but notice something. When people are kept awake, ‘One of the first things to go is the ability to focus our attention,’ he told me, in a teaching room at Harvard. He had been giving his test subjects really basic tasks, but with each hour that passed, they were losing their ability to carry them out. They couldn’t remember things he’d just told them or focus enough to play very simple card games. He told me: ‘I was just stunned by how performance would deteriorate. It’s one thing to say that the average performance on a memory task would be 20 percent worse, or 30 percent worse. But it’s another thing to say that your brain is so sluggish that is takes ten times longer for your brain to reply to something.’ As people stayed awake, it seemed their ability to focus fell off a cliff. In fact, if you stay awake for nineteen hours straight, you become as cognitively impaired – as unable to focus and think clearly – as if you had got drunk. He found that when they were kept awake for one whole night and continued walking about the next day, instead of taking a quarter of a second to respond to a prompt, the participants in his experiment were taking four, five or six seconds. ‘It’s kind of amazing,’ he said.

但随着日夜交替，查尔斯不禁注意到了一些事情。在哈佛大学的一间教室里，他告诉我，当人们被强迫熬夜时，“最先丧失的能力之一就是注意力集中能力”。他给受试者布置了一些非常简单的任务，但随着时间的推移，他们完成这些任务的能力每过一个小时就下降一个小时。他们记不住他刚刚告诉他们的事情，也无法集中注意力玩一些非常简单的纸牌游戏。他告诉我：“我简直不敢相信他们的表现会下降得如此之快。说他们在记忆任务上的平均表现下降了20%或30%是一回事，但说你的大脑反应如此迟钝，以至于你的大脑需要十倍的时间才能做出反应，则是另一回事。”人们熬夜的时间越长，他们的注意力似乎就越低。事实上，如果你连续19个小时不睡觉，你的认知能力就会像喝醉了一样受损——无法集中注意力，也无法清晰思考。他发现，当实验参与者被整夜不睡，第二天继续活动时，他们对提示的反应时间不再是四分之一秒，而是四秒、五秒甚至六秒。“这真是太神奇了，”他说。

Charles was intrigued. Why would this be? He switched to studying sleep, and over the next forty years he would go on to become one of the leading figures in the world on this question, making several key breakthroughs. He runs the unit on sleep problems at one of the major hospitals in Boston, teaches at Harvard Medical School, and advises everyone from the Boston Red Sox to the US Secret Service. He came to believe that, as a society, we are currently getting sleep all wrong – and it is ruining our focus.

查尔斯对此很感兴趣。这是为什么呢？他转而研究睡眠，并在接下来的四十年里，成为该领域世界顶尖专家之一，取得了多项关键突破。他在波士顿一家大型医院负责睡眠问题研究，在哈佛医学院任教，并为包括波士顿红袜队和美国特勤局在内的各界人士提供咨询。他逐渐意识到，作为一个社会，我们目前的睡眠方式完全错误——这正在损害我们的注意力。

With each passing year, he warned, this has become more urgent. Today 40 percent of Americans are chronically sleep-deprived, getting less than the necessary minimum of seven hours a night. In Britain, an incredible 23 percent are getting less than five hours a night. Only 15 percent of us wake up from our sleep feeling refreshed. This is new. Since 1942, the average amount of time a person sleeps has been slashed by an hour a night. Over the past century, the average child has lost eighty-five minutes of sleep every night. There’s a scientific debate about the precise scale of our sleep loss, but the National Sleep Foundation has calculated that the amount of sleep we get has dropped by 20 percent in just a hundred years.

他警告说，随着时间的推移，这个问题变得越来越紧迫。如今，40%的美国人长期睡眠不足，每晚睡眠时间不足7小时。在英国，令人震惊的是，23%的人每晚睡眠时间不足5小时。只有15%的人醒来后感觉精神焕发。这种情况是前所未有的。自1942年以来，人均睡眠时间每晚减少了1小时。过去一个世纪，儿童平均每晚睡眠时间减少了85分钟。关于我们睡眠不足的具体程度，科学界仍存在争议，但美国国家睡眠基金会计算得出，短短一百年间，我们的睡眠时间就减少了20%。

One day Charles had an idea. He wondered if, when you are tired, you begin to experience what he called ‘attentional blinks’. This is where, initially for just a fraction of a second, you lose your ability to pay attention. To see if this was true, he started to study both alert and tired people using sophisticated technology that can track their eyes to see what they are focusing on – and at the same time, it can also scan your brain, to see what is happening there. He discovered something remarkable. As you become tired, your attention will indeed blink out, for a simple reason. People think you’re either awake or a sleep, he told me, but he found that even if your eyes are open and you are looking around you, you can lapse – without knowing it – into a state called ‘local sleep’. This is where ‘part of the brain is awake, and part of the brain is asleep’. (It’s called local sleep because the sleep is local to one part of the brain.) In this state, you believe you are alert and mentally competent – but you aren’t. You are sitting at your desk and you look awake, but parts of your brain are asleep, and you are not able to think in a sustained way. When he studied people in this state, he found ‘amazingly, sometimes their eyes were open, but they couldn’t see what was in front of them’.

有一天，查尔斯突然想到一个问题。他想知道，当你疲惫时，是否会开始经历他所谓的“注意力短暂中断”。这种中断是指，最初只是短暂的几分之一秒，你会失去集中注意力的能力。为了验证这个想法，他开始利用先进的技术研究清醒和疲惫的人。这项技术可以追踪他们的眼球运动，观察他们的注意力集中在什么地方，同时还能扫描他们的大脑，了解大脑中正在发生的事情。他发现了一些惊人的现象。当你感到疲惫时，你的注意力确实会短暂中断，原因很简单。他告诉我，人们通常认为你要么清醒，要么睡着，但他发现，即使你睁着眼睛环顾四周，你也会在不知不觉中进入一种叫做“局部睡眠”的状态。在这种状态下，“大脑的一部分处于清醒状态，而另一部分处于睡眠状态”。（之所以称为局部睡眠，是因为睡眠仅限于大脑的某个特定区域。）在这种状态下，你会觉得自己很清醒，思维敏捷——但实际上并非如此。你坐在办公桌前，看起来清醒，但你的大脑部分区域却处于睡眠状态，无法进行持续思考。当他研究处于这种状态的人时，他发现“令人惊讶的是，有时他们的眼睛是睁着的，但却看不到眼前的事物”。

The effects of sleep deprivation, Charles found, are especially terrible for children. Adults usually respond by becoming drowsy, but kids usually respond by becoming hyperactive. He said: ‘We’re chronically sleep-depriving them, so it’s no shock they’re exhibiting all the symptoms of sleep deficiency – the first and foremost of which is the [in]ability to pay attention.’

查尔斯发现，睡眠不足对儿童的影响尤其严重。成年人通常会感到困倦，而儿童则通常会变得过度活跃。他说：“我们长期剥夺他们的睡眠，所以他们出现所有睡眠不足的症状也就不足为奇了——其中最主要的症状就是注意力不集中。”

There has now been a lot of scientific investigation into this, and there’s a broad scientific consensus that if you sleep less, your attention will likely suffer. I went to the University of Minneapolis to interview professor of neuroscience and psychology Roxanne Prichard, who has produced some cutting-edge work on these questions. When she started teaching college students full-time in 2004, the first thing that struck her, she told me, was ‘just how exhausted young adults were’. They would often fall asleep the moment the lecture-theatre lights were dimmed, and they were visibly struggling to stay awake and focused on anything. She began to study how much sleep they were getting. She discovered that on average, a typical student has the same sleep quality as an active-duty soldier or a parent of a newborn baby. As a result, the majority of them were ‘constantly fighting off this drive to sleep … They’re not able to access their neural resources.’

目前已有大量科学研究对此进行了探讨，科学界普遍认为，睡眠不足会影响注意力。我前往明尼阿波利斯大学采访了神经科学和心理学教授罗克珊·普里查德，她在这些问题上做出了开创性的研究。她告诉我，2004年她开始全职教大学生时，最让她震惊的是“年轻人的疲惫程度”。他们常常在教室灯光调暗的瞬间就睡着了，而且明显难以保持清醒和集中注意力。她开始研究他们的睡眠情况。她发现，普通学生的平均睡眠质量与现役军人或新生儿父母的睡眠质量相当。因此，他们中的大多数人“一直在与困倦作斗争……他们无法充分利用自身的神经资源”。

She decided to teach them the science of why their bodies need sleep – but she found herself in a strange position. The students knew they were bone-tired, but ‘the problem is – they’ve been accustomed to that since puberty, basically’. They have seen their parents and grandparents chronically sleep-depriving themselves too. ‘They’ve grown up being accustomed to being exhausted and trying to medicate that away [with caffeine or other stimulants] as a state of normal. So I’m fighting against a current that says it’s normal to be exhausted all the time.’ She started to show them some experiments. You can test the time it takes for a person to react to something – a picture that changes on a screen, say, or a ball that’s thrown to them. ‘The people with the quickest reaction times are the ones sleeping the most,’ she shows them – and the less they sleep, the less they see or react. This is just one way, of many, that shows that ‘you are more efficient when you are rested – that it takes you less time to do things. That you don’t need to have six screens or tabs open when you’re doing your homework just to keep yourself awake.’

她决定教他们身体为什么需要睡眠的科学原理——但她发现自己处境尴尬。学生们知道自己筋疲力尽，但“问题是——他们基本上从青春期就开始习惯这种状态了”。他们也目睹了父母和祖父母长期睡眠不足。“他们从小就习惯了精疲力竭，并试图用咖啡因或其他兴奋剂来缓解这种状态，认为这是正常的。所以我正在与一种认为一直疲惫不堪才是正常的观念作斗争。”她开始给他们展示一些实验。你可以测试一个人对某些事物的反应时间——比如屏幕上变化的图片，或者扔过来的球。“反应最快的人往往是睡眠时间最长的人，”她告诉他们——睡眠越少，他们的视觉感知和反应能力就越差。这只是众多证明“休息充足时效率更高——做事所需时间更短。做作业时，你不需要打开六个屏幕或标签页来让自己保持清醒”的众多方式之一。

At first, when I talked with Charles and Roxanne and other sleep experts, I thought – yes, this is bad, but they are talking about really exhausted people, an outlying group of the truly knackered. But they kept explaining to me that it only takes a small amount of sleep loss for these negative effects to kick in. Roxanne showed me that if you stay awake for eighteen hours – so you woke up at 6 a.m. and went to sleep at midnight – by the end of the day, your reactions are equivalent to if you had 0.05 percent blood alcohol. She said: ‘Stay up another three hours, and you’re [the equivalent of being] legally drunk.’ Charles explained: ‘Many people say, “Well, I don’t stay up all night, so I’m fine,” but in fact, if you miss a couple of hours sleep every night and you do this night after night, within a week or two, you’re at the same level of performance and impairment as you would be staying up all night. Everybody falls apart with two nights of missed sleep – or you can get to that same point by sleeping four or five hours a night and going for a couple of weeks.’ As he said this, I remembered: 40 percent of us live on the brink of that.

起初，当我与查尔斯、罗克珊和其他睡眠专家交谈时，我想——是的，这很糟糕，但他们谈论的是非常疲惫的人，是真正精疲力竭人群中的一小部分。但他们不断向我解释说，即使睡眠不足时间很短，这些负面影响也会显现出来。罗克珊向我演示，如果你连续18个小时不睡觉——也就是早上6点起床，午夜才睡——到一天结束时，你的反应就相当于血液酒精浓度达到0.05%。她说：“再熬三个小时，你就相当于达到法定醉酒标准了。”查尔斯解释说：“很多人会说，‘我不会熬夜，所以我没事’，但事实上，如果你每晚少睡几个小时，而且日复一日地如此，一两周之内，你的表现和受损程度就会和熬夜一样。”任何人连续两晚没睡好觉都会崩溃——或者，如果你每晚只睡四五个小时，持续两周，也会达到同样的程度。’ 他说这话的时候，我想起来了：我们当中有 40% 的人生活在崩溃的边缘。

‘If you’re not sleeping well, your body interprets that as an emergency,’ Roxanne said. ‘You can deprive yourself of sleep and live. We could never raise children if we couldn’t drop down on our sleep, right? We’d never survive hurricanes. You can do that – but it comes at a cost. The cost is [that] your body shifts into the sympathetic nervous system zone – so your body is like, “Uh oh, you’re depriving yourself of sleep, must be an emergency, so I’m going to make all these physiological changes to prepare yourself for that emergency. Raise your blood pressure. I’m going to make you want more fast food, I’m going to make you want more sugar for quick energy. I’m going to make your heart-rate [rise]” … So it’s like all this shifts, to say – I’m ready.’ Your body doesn’t know why it’s staying awake. ‘Your brain doesn’t know you’re sleep-deprived because you’re goofing off and watching Schitt’s Creek , right? It doesn’t know why you’re not sleeping – but the net effect is a physiological sort of alarm bell.’

“如果你睡眠不足，你的身体会将其解读为紧急情况，”罗克珊说。“你可以剥夺自己的睡眠，也能活下去。如果我们不能减少睡眠时间，就无法养育孩子，对吧？我们也无法在飓风中幸存下来。你可以这样做——但这是有代价的。代价是你的身体会进入交感神经系统活跃期——你的身体会想，‘糟糕，你剥夺了自己的睡眠，一定是紧急情况，所以我要做出所有这些生理变化来为紧急情况做好准备。我会让你的血压升高。我会让你更想吃快餐，我会让你更想摄入糖分来快速补充能量。我会让你的心率加快……’所以就像所有这些变化都在说——我准备好了。”你的身体不知道自己为什么会保持清醒。 “你的大脑并不知道你因为在闲逛看《富家穷路》而睡眠不足，对吧？它不知道你为什么不睡觉——但最终的结果是一种生理上的警报。”

In this bodily emergency, your brain doesn’t just cut back on immediate short-term focus. It cuts off resources to other longer-term forms of focus too. When we sleep, our minds start to identify connections and patterns from what we’ve experienced during the day. This is one of the key sources of our creativity – it’s why narcoleptic people, who sleep a lot, are significantly more creative. Sleep deprivation damages memory as well. When you go to bed tonight, your mind will start to transfer the things you have learned during the day into your long-term memory. Xavier Castellanos, who I interviewed at New York University, where he is a professor of child and adolescent psychiatry, explained to me that you can get rats to learn a maze, and that night, you can monitor what happens in their brains as they sleep. What you find is that they are retracing their steps in the maze, one by one, encoding them into their long-term memory. The less you sleep, the less this happens, and the less you will be able to recall.

在这种生理紧急情况下，你的大脑不仅会减少对短期事物的即时关注，还会减少对其他长期关注的资源投入。当我们睡觉时，大脑会开始识别白天经历的各种联系和模式。这是我们创造力的关键来源之一——这也是为什么嗜睡症患者（他们睡眠时间很长）的创造力显著更强。睡眠不足也会损害记忆力。今晚入睡后，你的大脑会开始将白天学到的东西转移到长期记忆中。我在纽约大学采访了儿童和青少年精神病学教授泽维尔·卡斯特拉诺斯，他向我解释说，你可以让老鼠学习迷宫，然后在晚上观察它们睡眠时大脑的活动。你会发现，它们会一步一步地重走迷宫，并将这些步骤编码到长期记忆中。睡眠越少，这种情况发生的频率就越低，你的记忆力也会越差。

These effects are especially powerful for children. If you deprive kids of sleep, they begin to show attention problems rapidly, and often go into a manic state.

这些影响对儿童尤其强烈。如果剥夺孩子的睡眠，他们很快就会出现注意力不集中的问题，而且常常会进入躁狂状态。

For years I believed I could cheat my way into getting all the benefits of proper sleep through technical fixes. The most obvious is caffeine. I once heard an almost certainly apocryphal story about Elvis – that in the last years of his life, his doctor would wake him up by injecting caffeine directly into his veins. When I heard this, I didn’t think – how awful. I thought – where’s that doctor been all my life? For years I reasoned – okay, I don’t sleep enough, but I make up for it with coffee, Coke Zero and Red Bull. But Roxanne explained to me what I was really doing when I drank all this. Throughout the day, in your brain, a chemical is building up called adenosine, and it signals to you when you are sleepy. Caffeine blocks the receptor that picks up on the level of adenosine. ‘I liken it to putting a Post-it note over your fuel-gauge indicator. You’re not giving yourself more energy – you’re just not realising how empty you are. When the caffeine wears off, you’re doubly exhausted.’

多年来，我一直以为可以通过一些“作弊”的方法来获得充足睡眠带来的所有益处。最显而易见的就是咖啡因。我曾经听过一个关于猫王的故事，虽然很可能是杜撰的——据说在他生命的最后几年，他的医生会直接往他静脉里注射咖啡因来唤醒他。听到这个故事时，我并没有觉得“太可怕了”，而是想“我以前怎么没遇到这样的医生？”多年来，我一直这样安慰自己：好吧，我睡眠不足，但我可以用咖啡、零度可乐和红牛来弥补。但罗克珊向我解释了我喝这些东西的真正目的。白天，你的大脑中会积累一种叫做腺苷的化学物质，它会在你犯困时发出信号。咖啡因会阻断接收腺苷信号的受体。“我把它比作在油表指示器上贴一张便签。你并没有给自己补充能量——你只是没有意识到自己有多空。”咖啡因的作用消退后，你会感到双倍疲惫。

The less you sleep, the more the world blurs in every way – in your immediate focus, in your ability to think deeply and make connections, and in your memory. Charles told me that even if nothing else was changing in our society, this decline in how much we sleep is on its own enough to prove that our crisis in focusing and paying attention is real. ‘It’s very sad to watch this play out and not be able to stop this,’ he said. ‘It’s like watching a crash that’s happening.’

睡眠越少，世界就越模糊——你的注意力、深度思考和建立联系的能力，以及记忆力都会受到影响。查尔斯告诉我，即使社会其他方面没有改变，睡眠时间的减少本身就足以证明，我们注意力和专注力的危机是真实存在的。“眼睁睁看着这一切发生却无能为力，真是令人悲哀，”他说，“这就像眼睁睁地看着一场车祸发生。”

Every expert I spoke to said this transformation explains, in part, our declining attention. Dr Sandra Kooij is one of the leading experts on adult ADHD in Europe, and when I went to interview her in The Hague, she told me bluntly: ‘Our Western society is a bit ADHD-ish because we’re all sleep-deprived … It’s huge. And it means something for us. So we’re all in a hurry, we’re all impulsive, we’re easily irritated in traffic. You see it everywhere around you … This has been studied and proven in laboratories: you think you’re thinking clearly, but you’re not. You’re much less clear than you could be.’ She added that ‘when we sleep better, a lot of problems get less – like mood disorders, like obesity, like concentration problems … It repairs a lot of damage.’

我采访过的每一位专家都表示，这种转变在一定程度上解释了我们注意力下降的原因。桑德拉·库伊博士是欧洲成人多动症领域的顶尖专家之一。我去海牙采访她时，她直言不讳地告诉我：“我们的西方社会有点像多动症患者，因为我们都睡眠不足……这影响巨大，而且对我们意义重大。所以我们都行色匆匆，都容易冲动，在交通拥堵时也容易烦躁。你到处都能看到这种情况……实验室已经研究并证实了这一点：你以为自己思路清晰，但其实不然。你的思维远没有达到应有的清晰程度。”她补充道：“当我们睡眠充足时，很多问题都会减少——比如情绪障碍、肥胖、注意力不集中……它能修复很多损伤。”

As I learned all this, I had some obvious questions. The first was – why does our lack of sleep damage our ability to focus so much? Surprisingly, this is a relatively new research question. Roxanne told me: ‘In 1998, when I chose [the subject of sleep] to focus on for my dissertation, there wasn’t a lot of research on what sleep was for. We knew what it was and we all do it … and it’s kind of mysterious. You’re spending a third of your life unconscious, not engaging with the world … It was just this mystery – it seems like a waste of resources.’

了解了这些之后，我自然而然地产生了一些疑问。第一个问题是——为什么睡眠不足会如此严重地损害我们的注意力？令人惊讶的是，这竟然是一个相对较新的研究课题。罗克珊告诉我：“1998年，当我选择睡眠作为我博士论文的研究方向时，关于睡眠的作用的研究并不多。我们知道睡眠是什么，也都知道睡眠的重要性……但它本身却有点神秘。你一生中有三分之一的时间处于无意识状态，没有与外界互动……这简直是个谜——感觉像是在浪费资源。”

Charles had been told when he was a young man there was no point studying sleep because it’s a passive process – but in fact, he learned, sleep is an incredibly active process. When you go to sleep, all sorts of activities take place in your brain and body – and these are necessary for you to be able to function and focus. One of the things that happens is that during sleep, your brain cleans itself of waste that has accumulated during the day. ‘During slow-wave sleep, your cerebral spinal fluid channels open up more and remove metabolic waste from your brain,’ Roxanne explained to me. Every night, when you go to sleep, your brain is rinsed with a watery fluid. This cerebrospinal fluid washes through your brain, flushing out toxic proteins and carrying them down to your liver to get rid of them. ‘So when I’m talking to college students, I call this brain-cell poop. If you can’t focus well, it might be you have too much brain-cell poop circulating.’ That can explain why, when you are tired, ‘you get a hung-over sort of feeling’ – you are literally clogged up with toxins.

查尔斯年轻时曾被告知，研究睡眠毫无意义，因为它是一个被动的过程——但事实上，他后来了解到，睡眠是一个极其活跃的过程。当你入睡时，你的大脑和身体会发生各种各样的活动——这些活动对于你的正常运转和集中注意力至关重要。其中一项活动就是在睡眠期间，你的大脑会清除白天积累的废物。“在慢波睡眠期间，你的脑脊液通道会更加畅通，并将代谢废物从大脑中排出，”罗克珊向我解释道。每天晚上，当你入睡时，你的大脑都会被一种水状液体冲洗。这种脑脊液会流经你的大脑，冲刷掉有毒的蛋白质，并将它们输送到肝脏进行代谢。“所以当我跟大学生们讲解时，我把这叫做‘脑细胞排泄物’。”如果你无法集中注意力，可能是因为你的大脑里循环着太多的“脑细胞粪便”。这可以解释为什么当你疲倦时，“你会感觉像宿醉一样”——你实际上是被毒素堵塞了。

This positive kind of brainwashing can only happen when you are asleep. Dr Maiken Nedergaard, at the University of Rochester, told one interviewer: ‘The brain only has limited energy at its disposal, and it appears that it must choose between two different functional states – awake and aware, or asleep and cleaning up. You can think of it as like having a house party. You can either entertain the guests or clean up the house, but you can’t really do both at the same time.’ A brain that hasn’t been through this necessary cleaning process becomes more clogged and less able to concentrate. Some scientists suspect this is why people who are under-slept are at greater risk, in the long-term, of developing dementia. When you are sleeping, Roxanne says, ‘You’re repairing.’

这种积极的“洗脑”只能在睡眠时发生。罗切斯特大学的迈肯·内德加德博士在接受采访时说：“大脑可利用的能量有限，它似乎必须在两种不同的功能状态之间做出选择——清醒且意识清醒，或者睡眠并进行清理。你可以把它想象成举办家庭聚会。你可以招待客人，也可以打扫房子，但你不可能同时做这两件事。” 一个没有经历过这种必要清理过程的大脑会变得更加堵塞，注意力也更难集中。一些科学家怀疑，这就是为什么睡眠不足的人长期患痴呆症的风险更高。罗克珊说，当你睡觉时，“你就在进行修复。”

Another thing that happens during sleep is that your energy levels are restored and replenished. Charles told me that ‘the prefrontal cortex is the judgement area of the brain, and that seems to be particularly sensitive to sleep loss … You see that, with even one night of sleep loss, that area of the brain is just not utilising glucose, which is the main energy source of the brain. It’s sort of going stone cold.’ Without renewing your sources of energy, you can’t think clearly.

睡眠期间，你的能量水平也会得到恢复和补充。查尔斯告诉我，“前额叶皮层是大脑的判断区域，它似乎对睡眠不足特别敏感……你会发现，即使只缺睡一晚，大脑的这一区域也无法利用葡萄糖，而葡萄糖是大脑的主要能量来源。它就像完全停止运转了一样。” 如果能量来源得不到补充，你就无法清晰地思考。

But for me, the most intriguing process that happens when we sleep is that we dream – and this, I learned, also performs an important function. In Montreal, I went to interview Tore Nielsen, who is a professor of psychiatry there. He often tells people he has a ‘dream job’ and asks them to guess what it is. After they’ve run through the list – racing-car driver? Chocolate-taster? – he tells them: he runs the Dream Lab at the University of Montreal. He told me that some scientists in the field believe that ‘dreaming somehow helps you to adapt emotionally to waking events’. When you dream, you can revisit stressful moments, but without stress hormones flooding your system. Over time, those scientists believe this can make it easier to handle stress – which we know makes it easier to focus. Tore emphasises that there seems to be some evidence supporting this theory and some contradicting it, and we need to know more to be sure.

但对我来说，睡眠中最引人入胜的过程莫过于做梦——而且我发现，做梦也发挥着重要的作用。在蒙特利尔，我采访了精神病学教授托雷·尼尔森。他经常告诉别人他有一个“梦想职业”，然后让他们猜是什么。在人们列举完各种职业之后——赛车手？巧克力品鉴师？——他会告诉他们：他在蒙特利尔大学运营着一个梦境实验室。他告诉我，该领域的一些科学家认为，“做梦在某种程度上可以帮助你更好地适应清醒时的情绪变化”。做梦时，你可以重温那些压力时刻，但不会像做梦那样让压力激素涌入你的身体。这些科学家认为，随着时间的推移，这可以让人更容易应对压力——而我们知道，压力越小，注意力就越容易集中。托雷强调，目前似乎有一些证据支持这一理论，也有一些证据与之相悖，我们需要了解更多信息才能确定。

But if it is correct, then we have a problem – because as a society, we are dreaming less and less. Dreams occur most during the stage known as rapid-eye movement (REM) sleep. Tore told me: ‘The longest and most intense REM periods are the ones that occur toward the seven- or eight-hour mark of the sleep cycle. So if you’re curtailing your sleep down to five or six hours, chances are good that you’re not getting those long, intense REM periods.’ As he said this, I wondered: What does it mean to be a society and culture so frantic that we don’t have time to dream?

但如果这是真的，那我们就面临一个问题——因为作为一个社会，我们做梦的时间越来越少。梦境大多发生在快速眼动睡眠（REM）阶段。托雷告诉我：“最长、最强烈的REM睡眠阶段通常出现在睡眠周期的七八小时左右。所以，如果你把睡眠时间缩短到五六个小时，很可能就无法体验到那些漫长而强烈的REM睡眠阶段。” 听到这番话，我不禁思考：一个如此忙碌的社会和文化，以至于我们连做梦的时间都没有，这究竟意味着什么？

As we find ourselves wired and unable to sleep, more and more of us are turning to drugs to knock ourselves out – whether it’s melatonin or alcohol or Ambien. Nine million Americans – 4 percent of adults – are using prescription sleeping pills, and vastly more are using over-the-counter sleep aids, like I did for many years. But Roxanne told me bluntly: ‘If you chemically induce sleep, it’s not the same kind of sleep.’ Remember – sleep is an active process, in which your brain and body do lots of things. Many of these things don’t happen, or happen far less, in drugged or drunk sleep. The different ways of artificially inducing sleep can have different effects. If you take 5 mg of melatonin – which is often a standard dose that’s sold over the counter in the US – Roxanne said you risk ‘blowing out your melatonin receptors’, which would make it harder to sleep without them.

当我们精神亢奋却难以入眠时，越来越多的人开始求助于药物来让自己入睡——无论是褪黑素、酒精还是安眠药。900万美国人——占成年人口的4%——正在服用处方安眠药，而服用非处方助眠药的人则更多，就像我多年来一直服用的那样。但罗克珊直言不讳地告诉我：“如果你用药物诱导睡眠，那和自然睡眠完全不同。”记住，睡眠是一个积极的过程，在这个过程中，你的大脑和身体会进行许多活动。在药物或酒精的作用下，许多这样的活动要么不会发生，要么发生得少得多。不同的人工诱导睡眠的方式会产生不同的效果。罗克珊说，如果你服用5毫克褪黑素——这通常是美国非处方药的标准剂量——你可能会“破坏你的褪黑素受体”，这将使你更难入睡。

Bigger effects kick in with the harder stuff. Of Ambien and the other prescribed sedatives, she warns: ‘Sleep is a really important balance of many, many neurotransmitters, and if you artificially … pump up one, it changes the balance of that sleep.’ You will likely have less REM sleep, and fewer dreams, and so you lose all the benefits that come from this crucial stage. You are likely to be groggy throughout the day – which is why sleeping pills increase your risk of death from all causes: you’re more likely to get into a car accident, for example. ‘If you’ve ever had surgery and recovered from that, like coming off anaesthesia,’ Roxanne said, you don’t say, ‘Oh, I feel so refreshed.’ Knocking yourself out is like taking a minor anaesthetic. Your body doesn’t rest and clean and refresh and dream like it needs to.

服用更强效的药物会带来更严重的副作用。她警告说，对于安眠药和其他处方镇静剂，“睡眠是多种神经递质之间非常重要的平衡，如果你人为地……增加其中一种，就会改变睡眠的平衡。”你的快速眼动睡眠（REM睡眠）可能会减少，做梦也会减少，从而失去这个关键阶段带来的所有益处。你很可能整天都昏昏沉沉——这就是为什么安眠药会增加各种原因导致的死亡风险：例如，你更容易发生车祸。“如果你做过手术，并且从麻醉中恢复过来，”罗克珊说，“你不会说，‘哦，我感觉神清气爽。’让自己昏睡过去就像服用了轻微的麻醉剂。你的身体无法像它需要的那样休息、清洁、恢复和做梦。”

Roxanne told me that there are some legitimate uses for sleeping pills – for example, taking them for a short time after you’ve had a traumatic bereavement might be sensible. But she warned ‘it’s definitely not the solution for insomnia,’ and that’s why doctors are not supposed to prescribe them over the long term.

罗克珊告诉我，安眠药也有一些合理的用途——例如，在经历丧亲之痛后短期服用可能是明智之举。但她警告说，“这绝对不是治疗失眠的办法”，所以医生不应该长期开安眠药。

It’s a sign of how dysfunctional we have become when it comes to sleep that the people who should be warning us most about this crisis – doctors – are in fact required to become sleep-deprived to get their qualifications. As part of their medical training, doctors have to do gruelling twenty-four-hour shifts on call – they nickname it ‘doing a Jack Bauer’, after the TV show 24 , where Kiefer Sutherland can’t sleep because he’s chasing terrorists. This endangers their patients. But we have become a culture where even the people who should know best about sleep fetishise staying sleepless beyond the point of reason, just like the rest of us.

睡眠问题已经严重失调，最应该警告我们这场危机的群体——医生——实际上却需要长期睡眠不足才能获得执业资格，这足以说明我们在这方面有多么失调。作为医学培训的一部分，医生必须轮值24小时，他们戏称这种做法为“杰克·鲍尔式值班”，源自电视剧《24小时》，剧中基弗·萨瑟兰饰演的杰克·鲍尔因为追捕恐怖分子而彻夜难眠。这会危及他们的病人。然而，我们如今的文化却让连最了解睡眠的人也像我们其他人一样，沉迷于不眠不休，甚至到了痴迷的地步。

The second question I found myself asking was: Given that lack of sleep is so harmful, and at some level we all know it, why are we doing it less? Why would we give up on one of our most basic needs?

我问自己的第二个问题是：既然睡眠不足危害如此之大，而且在某种程度上我们都明白这一点，为什么我们反而睡眠不足了呢？为什么我们要放弃我们最基本的需求之一呢？

There’s a big scientific debate about this, and several factors seem to be having an effect. Some are going to come up later in this book. One of them – unexpectedly – is our relationship with physical light. Charles made some of the key breakthroughs on this. Until the nineteenth century, the lives of almost all humans were shaped primarily by the rise and fall of the sun. Our natural rhythms evolved to match it – we would get a rush of energy when it got light, and we would feel sleepy after it got dark. For almost all of human history, our ability to intervene in this cycle was pretty limited – we could light fires, but that was it. As a result, humans evolved to be as sensitive to changes of light, Charles says, as algae and cockroaches. But suddenly, with the invention of the electric lightbulb, we gained the power to control the light we are exposed to – and this power has started to scramble our internal rhythms.

关于这一点，科学界存在着激烈的争论，似乎有几个因素在起作用。本书后面会提到其中一些因素。其中一个因素——出乎意料地——是我们与光的关系。查尔斯在这方面取得了一些关键性的突破。直到19世纪，几乎所有人类的生活都主要受太阳升起和落下的影响。我们的自然节律进化以适应这种变化——天亮时我们会精力充沛，天黑后我们会感到困倦。在人类历史的大部分时间里，我们干预这一循环的能力非常有限——我们只能生火，仅此而已。因此，查尔斯说，人类进化得对光线的变化像藻类和蟑螂一样不敏感。但突然之间，随着电灯泡的发明，我们获得了控制光线的能力——而这种能力开始扰乱我们的内在节律。

Here’s a clear example. We evolved to get a rush of energy – a ‘surge of waking drive’, Charles says – when the sun began to set. This was very helpful to our ancestors. Imagine you’re out camping, and the sun starts to fall – it’s very useful if you then feel a rush of wakefulness, because then you’ll be able to set up your tent before it’s too dark to do it. In the same way, our ancestors got a fresh rush of energy just as the light waned so they could safely get back to their tribe and finish the things they needed to do that day. But now we control the light. We decide when sunset happens. So if we keep bright lights switched on right until the moment we decide to go to sleep, or we watch TV on our phones in bed, when we switch them off we accidentally trigger a physical process – our bodies think this sudden waning of the light is the arrival of sunset, so they release a rush of fresh energy to help you get back to your cave.

这里有一个很好的例子。我们进化出一种机制，在日落时分获得一股能量——查尔斯称之为“觉醒的冲动”。这对我们的祖先来说非常有用。想象一下，你正在露营，太阳开始西沉——如果你这时感到一股清醒，那就非常有用，因为这样你就能在天黑之前搭好帐篷。同样地，我们的祖先在光线渐弱时会获得一股新的能量，这样他们就能安全地回到部落，完成当天需要做的事情。但现在我们控制着光线。我们决定日落的时间。所以，如果我们一直开着明亮的灯直到我们决定睡觉的那一刻，或者在床上用手机看电视，当我们关掉灯的时候，我们无意中触发了一个生理过程——我们的身体会把光线的突然减弱误认为是日落的到来，于是释放出一股新的能量，帮助你回到洞穴。

‘Now this surge of waking drive, instead of happening at three or four o’clock in the afternoon before the sun sets at six, is now happening at ten, eleven, midnight,’ Charles says. ‘You have the surge of waking energy at the time you’re deciding whether to go to sleep. Now you get up in the morning; you feel like you’re going to die. You swear to God that you’re going to get more sleep the next day, but you’re not tired the next evening,’ because you’ve watched more TV on your laptop in bed, and triggered the same process all over again. ‘The surge is very powerful, and so people are like, “I’m fine,” and the morning is a blur that they’ve forgotten.’ Charles believes that – as he said to another interviewer – ‘every time we turn on a light, we are inadvertently taking a drug that affects how we will sleep.’ This goes on day after day. ‘That’s a major contributing factor to this epidemic of sleep deficiency – because we’re exposing ourselves to light later and later,’ he explained. Indeed, 90 percent of Americans look at a glowing electronic device in the hour before they go to bed – triggering precisely this process. We are now exposed to ten times the amount of artificial light that people were exposed to just fifty years ago.

“现在，这种清醒时的兴奋感，不再像以前那样在下午三四点，也就是日落前（六点）出现，而是出现在晚上十点、十一点，甚至午夜，”查尔斯说道。“在你决定是否入睡的时候，你会突然感到精力充沛。早上醒来，你感觉自己快要死了。你向上帝发誓第二天一定要多睡一会儿，但到了晚上你却一点也不觉得累，”因为你又在床上用笔记本电脑看了会儿电视，再次触发了同样的兴奋过程。“这种兴奋感非常强烈，所以人们会觉得‘我没事’，然后早上醒来的记忆就模糊不清了。”查尔斯认为——正如他之前对另一位采访者所说——“我们每次开灯，都相当于在不知不觉中服用了一种影响睡眠的药物。”这种情况日复一日地发生着。 “这是导致睡眠不足流行的主要原因之一——因为我们接触光线的时间越来越晚，”他解释道。事实上，90%的美国人在睡前一小时内都会看发光的电子设备——这正是引发睡眠不足的原因。我们现在接触到的人造光量是五十年前的十倍。

I wondered if one of the reasons why I slept so much better on Cape Cod was because I returned to something closer to this natural rhythm. When the sun sets on Provincetown, the town gets much darker, and by my beachhouse, there was almost no artificial light, barely even a street lamp. The orange haze of air pollution that lights up the sky in every place I have ever lived was gone, and there was only the gentle light of the moon and the stars.

我一直在想，我在科德角睡得这么好，是不是因为我重新适应了这种更接近自然的作息规律。普罗温斯敦的太阳落山后，小镇变得格外昏暗，而我的海滨小屋附近几乎没有人造光源，连路灯都很少见。在我居住过的任何地方，那种笼罩着天空的橙色空气污染都消失了，取而代之的是柔和的月光和星光。

But Charles told me you can only really understand our crisis of sleep if you understand it in a much bigger context. At first glance, he says, what we are doing is crazy: ‘We wouldn’t deprive children of nutrition. We wouldn’t think of doing that. Why are we depriving them of sleep?’ But it makes a dark kind of sense when you see it as part of a broader picture. In a society dominated by the values of consumer capitalism, ‘Sleep is a big problem,’ he told me. ‘If you’re asleep, you’re not spending money, so you’re not consuming anything. You’re not producing any products.’ He explained that ‘during the last recession [in 2008]… they talked about global output going down by so many percent, and consumption going down. But if everybody were to spend [an] extra hour sleeping [as they did in the past], they wouldn’t be on Amazon. They wouldn’t be buying things.’ If we went back to sleeping a healthy amount – if everyone did what I did in Provincetown – Charles said ‘it would be an earthquake for our economic system, because our economic system has become dependent on sleep-depriving people. The attentional failures are just roadkill. That’s just the cost of doing business.’ I only really understood how significant this point was towards the end of writing this book.

但查尔斯告诉我，只有从更广阔的视角来理解我们面临的睡眠危机，才能真正理解它。他说，乍一看，我们现在的做法简直疯狂：“我们不会剥夺孩子的营养，我们根本不会想到这么做。那我们为什么要剥夺他们的睡眠呢？”但当你把它放在更广阔的背景下看待时，就会发现其中蕴含着一种令人不安的道理。在一个被消费资本主义价值观主导的社会里，“睡眠是个大问题，”他告诉我。“如果你在睡觉，你就无法消费，也就无法生产任何产品。”他解释说，“在上次经济衰退（2008年）期间……人们都在谈论全球产出和消费下降了多少个百分点。但如果每个人都像过去那样多睡一个小时，他们就不会在亚马逊上购物了。” “他们就不会买东西了。”查尔斯说，如果我们恢复到健康的睡眠时间——如果每个人都像我在普罗温斯敦那样——“那将对我们的经济体系造成地震般的冲击，因为我们的经济体系已经依赖于睡眠不足的人。注意力不集中就像路边的死尸。这就是做生意的代价。”直到写这本书的最后，我才真正理解这一点的重要性。

All this leads to one last big question about sleep – how do we solve this crisis? There are several layers to the solution. The first is personal and individual. As Charles explains, you need to radically limit your exposure to light before you go to sleep. He believes you should have no sources of artificial light in your bedroom at all, and you should avoid the blue light of screens for at least two hours before you go to bed.

这一切引出了关于睡眠的最后一个重要问题——我们该如何解决这场危机？解决方案包含多个层面。首先是个人层面的。正如查尔斯解释的那样，你需要在睡前大幅减少接触光线。他认为，卧室里应该完全没有人工光源，并且在睡前至少两小时内避免接触电子屏幕的蓝光。

We also need, all the sleep experts told me, to have different relationships with our phones. Roxanne told me that to lots of us, ‘It’s like your baby, right? So as a new parent, you’re like – I’ve got to be vigilant for this thing. I’ve got to pay attention. I’m not sleeping as deeply. Or you are like a firefighter who’s listening for a call.’ We’re constantly a little tensed to see ‘did something happen?’ She says your phone should always recharge overnight in a different room, where you can’t see or hear it. Then you need to make sure your room is the right temperature – it should be cool, almost cold. This is because your body needs to cool its core to send you to sleep, and the harder that is, the longer it takes.

所有睡眠专家都告诉我，我们需要改变与手机的关系。罗克珊告诉我，对我们很多人来说，“手机就像你的孩子，对吧？所以作为新手父母，你会觉得——我必须时刻警惕它。我必须注意它。我的睡眠质量也因此下降。或者你就像一个时刻准备着接听电话的消防员。”我们总是有点紧张，生怕“发生什么事了？”她说，手机应该放在另一个房间里充电，这样你既看不到也听不到它。然后，你需要确保房间温度适宜——应该凉爽，甚至有点冷。这是因为你的身体需要降低核心温度才能入睡，而降温越困难，入睡所需的时间就越长。

These are helpful (and relatively well-known) tips – but, as every expert I spoke to acknowledged, they are not enough for most people. We live in a culture that is constantly amping us up with stress and stimulation. You can tell people all this, and explain the health benefits of a good long night in bed, and they will agree, and then they say, ‘Do you want me to list everything I need to do in the next twenty-four hours? And you want me to spend nine hours sleeping too?’

这些建议很有帮助（也比较常见），但正如我采访过的每一位专家都承认的那样，对大多数人来说，这些还远远不够。我们生活在一个不断被压力和刺激所包围的文化中。你可以告诉人们这些，解释睡个好觉对健康的益处，他们也会表示赞同，然后他们会说：“难道你想让我列出接下来24小时要做的事情吗？你还想让我睡上9个小时？”

As I learned about several of the things we need to do to improve our focus, I realised that we live in an apparent paradox. Many of the things we need to do are so obvious they are banal: slow down, do one thing at a time, sleep more. But even though at some level we all know them to be true, we are in fact moving in the opposite direction: towards more speed, more switching, less sleep. We live in a gap between what we know we should do and what we feel we can do. The key question, then, is: what’s causing that gap? Why can’t we do the obvious things that would improve our attention? What forces are stopping us? I spent a large part of the rest of my journey uncovering the answers.

当我了解到一些提升专注力的方法后，我意识到我们生活在一个看似矛盾的境地。许多我们需要做的事情显而易见，甚至显得老生常谈：放慢速度，一次只做一件事，多睡觉。但即便我们内心深处都明白这些道理，我们实际上却在朝着相反的方向发展：追求更快的速度、更频繁的切换和更少的睡眠。我们生活在“应该做什么”和“感觉能做什么”之间的鸿沟之中。那么，关键问题是：是什么造成了这种鸿沟？为什么我们做不到那些显而易见的、能够提升专注力的事情？究竟是什么力量在阻碍我们？在接下来的旅程中，我花费了大量时间来探寻这些问题的答案。

# ↩

4 Cause Four: The Collapse of Sustained Reading

原因四：持续阅读的崩溃

In the West End of Provincetown there’s a gorgeous bookstore named Tim’s Used Books. You walk in and you immediately inhale the tangy must that comes from having old books stacked everywhere. I went in almost every other day that summer to buy another book to read. There was a young woman who worked at the cash register who was really smart, and I took to chatting with her. I noticed that every time I went in, she was reading a different book – one day Vladimir Nabokov, another day Joseph Conrad, another day Shirley Jackson. Wow, I said, you read fast. Oh, she replied, I don’t. I can only read the first chapter or two of a book. I asked: Really? Why? She said: I guess I can’t focus. Here was an intelligent young woman with lots of time, surrounded by many of the best books ever written, and with a desire to read them – but she could only get through the first chapter or two, and then her attention puttered out, like a failing engine.

在普罗温斯敦西区，有一家名为“蒂姆二手书店”的漂亮书店。你一走进去，就能立刻闻到一股浓郁的旧书气息，那是书堆里散发出来的。那年夏天，我几乎隔一天就去一次，买本书来读。收银台有个年轻姑娘，非常聪明，我便和她聊了起来。我注意到，每次我去，她都在读不同的书——今天读弗拉基米尔·纳博科夫，明天读约瑟夫·康拉德，后天读雪莉·杰克逊。哇，我说，你读得真快。哦，她回答说，我读得并不快。我只能读一本书的前一两章。我问：真的吗？为什么？她说：我想我无法集中注意力。这位聪明的年轻女子，时间充裕，身边摆满了各种经典名著，而且她也渴望阅读它们——但她却只能读完前一两章，然后注意力就涣散了，就像一台快要熄火的发动机。

I have lost count of how many people I know who have told me this. When I first met him, David Ulin, who was a book critic and editor at the Los Angeles Times for more than thirty years, told me that he had lost his ability to read deeply over long periods, because whenever he tried to settle down, he kept being drawn back to the buzz of the online conversation. This is an incredibly smart man whose whole life had been books. It was disconcerting.

我已经数不清有多少人跟我说过类似的话了。我第一次见到大卫·乌林时，他曾在《洛杉矶时报》担任书评人和编辑三十余年，他告诉我，他已经失去了长时间深度阅读的能力，因为每当他试图静下心来阅读时，总会被网络上的热烈讨论所吸引。他是一位才华横溢、毕生致力于书籍的人。这真令人不安。

The proportion of Americans who read books for pleasure is now at its lowest level ever recorded. The American Time Use Survey – which studies a representative sample of 26,000 Americans – found that between 2004 and 2017 the proportion of men reading for pleasure had fallen by 40 percent, while for women, it was down by 29 percent. The opinion-poll company Gallup found that the proportion of Americans who never read a book in any given year tripled between 1978 and 2014. Some 57 percent of Americans now do not read a single book in a typical year. This has escalated to the point that by 2017, the average American spent seventeen minutes a day reading books and 5.4 hours on their phone. Complex literary fiction is particularly suffering. For the first time in modern history, less than half of Americans read literature for pleasure. It’s been less well studied, but there seem to be similar trends in Britain and other countries: between 2008 and 2016 the market for novels fell by 40 percent. In one single year – 2011 – paperback fiction sales collapsed by 26 percent.

美国人休闲阅读的比例已降至历史最低水平。美国时间利用调查（American Time Use Survey）——该调查选取了26000名具有代表性的美国人样本——发现，2004年至2017年间，男性休闲阅读的比例下降了40%，女性下降了29%。民意调查公司盖洛普（Gallup）的调查显示，1978年至2014年间，从未读过任何书籍的美国人比例增长了两倍。如今，约有57%的美国人一年内一本书都不读。这种情况愈演愈烈，到2017年，美国人平均每天只花17分钟读书，却花5.4小时玩手机。复杂的文学作品尤其受到冲击。现代史上，休闲阅读的美国人首次不足半数。虽然相关研究较少，但英国和其他国家似乎也出现了类似的趋势：2008年至2016年间，小说市场萎缩了40%。 2011年一年内，平装小说销量暴跌了26%。

Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi had discovered in his research that one of the simplest and most common forms of flow that people experience in their lives is reading a book – and, like other forms of flow, it is being choked off in our culture of constant distraction. I thought a lot about this. For many of us, reading a book is the deepest form of focus we experience – you dedicate many hours of your life, coolly, calmly, to one topic, and allow it to marinate in your mind. This is the medium through which most of the deepest advances in human thought over the past 400 years have been figured out and explained. And that experience is now in freefall.

米哈里·契克森米哈赖在他的研究中发现，人们生活中体验到的最简单、最常见的“心流”形式之一就是阅读——然而，和其他形式的“心流”一样，它在我们这个充满干扰的文化中正逐渐消失。我对此进行了深入思考。对我们许多人来说，阅读是我们体验到的最深度的专注——你投入数小时的时间，冷静、沉着地专注于一个主题，让它在你的脑海中慢慢沉淀。过去400年来，人类思想中大多数最深刻的进步都是通过阅读这一媒介得以理解和阐释的。而如今，这种体验正在急剧减少。

In Provincetown I noticed I wasn’t just reading more – I was reading differently. I was becoming much more deeply immersed in the books I had chosen. I got lost in them for really long stretches, sometimes whole days – and I felt like I was understanding and remembering more of what I read. I seemed like I travelled further in that deckchair by the sea, reading book after book, than I had in the previous five years of shuttling frantically around the world: I went from fighting on the battlefields of the Napoleonic wars, to being an enslaved person in the Deep South, to being an Israeli mother trying to avoid hearing the news that her son has been killed. As I reflected on this, I started to think again about a book I had read ten years before: The Shallows by Nicholas Carr – a landmark work that really alerted people to a crucial aspect of the growing attention crisis. He warned that the way we are reading seems to be changing as we migrate to the internet – so I went back to one of the key experts he drew on, to see what she has learned since.

在普罗温斯敦，我发现自己不仅读的书更多了——而且阅读方式也变了。我更加沉浸于自己选择的书籍之中。我常常长时间地沉浸在书中，有时甚至整整几天——而且我感觉自己对读过的内容理解得更透彻，记忆也更深刻。仿佛在那张海边的躺椅上，一本接一本地阅读，比过去五年在世界各地奔波劳碌的经历还要精彩：我仿佛从拿破仑战争的战场上走来，到美国南部腹地的奴隶，再到一位以色列母亲努力不去听儿子阵亡的消息。反思这一切，我不禁想起十年前读过的一本书：《浅薄》（The Shallows），作者是尼古拉斯·卡尔（Nicholas Carr）。这是一部里程碑式的作品，它真正地提醒人们注意日益严重的注意力危机的一个关键方面。卡尔警告说，随着我们转向互联网，我们的阅读方式似乎正在发生变化——于是我又去找了卡尔引用的一位重要专家，看看她这些年来又有哪些新的发现。

Anne Mangen is a professor of literacy at Stavanger University in Norway, and she explained to me that in two decades of researching this subject, she has proved something crucial. Reading books trains us to read in a particular way – in a linear fashion, focused on one thing for a sustained period. Reading from screens, she has discovered, trains us to read in a different way – in a manic skip and jump from one thing to another. ‘We’re more likely to scan and skim’ when we read on screens, her studies have found – we run our eyes rapidly over the information to extract what we need. But after a while, if we do this long enough, she told me that ‘this scanning and skimming bleeds over. It also starts to colour or influence how we read on paper … That behaviour also becomes our default, more or less.’ It was precisely what I had noticed when I tried to settle into Dickens when I arrived in Provincetown and found myself rushing ahead of him, as if it was a news article and I was trying to push for the key facts.

安妮·曼根是挪威斯塔万格大学的读写能力教授。她向我解释说，她二十年来对这个课题的研究证明了一个至关重要的事实：阅读纸质书会训练我们以一种特定的方式阅读——线性阅读，长时间专注于一件事。而她发现，在屏幕上阅读则会训练我们以一种不同的方式阅读——疯狂地跳跃式地从一个内容跳到另一个内容。她的研究发现，我们在屏幕上阅读时“更倾向于浏览和略读”——我们的目光快速扫过信息，提取所需内容。但她告诉我，一段时间后，如果我们一直这样做，“这种浏览和略读的习惯会蔓延开来。它也会开始影响我们阅读纸质书的方式……这种行为或多或少会成为我们的默认行为。” 这正是我在普罗温斯敦尝试阅读狄更斯作品时所注意到的。我发现自己总是抢在他前面阅读，就像在读一篇新闻报道，而我正努力抓住关键事实一样。

This creates a different relationship with reading. It stops being a form of pleasurable immersion in another world and becomes more like dashing around a busy supermarket to grab what you need and then get out again. When this flip takes place – when our screen-reading contaminates our book-reading – we lose some of the pleasures of reading books themselves, and they become less appealing.

这会改变我们与阅读的关系。阅读不再是一种令人愉悦的沉浸式体验，而更像是匆匆忙忙地在熙熙攘攘的超市里抢购所需物品，然后匆匆离开。当这种转变发生——当我们的屏幕阅读污染了纸质阅读——我们便失去了阅读本身的一些乐趣，书籍也变得不再那么吸引人。

It has other knock-on effects. Anne has conducted studies that split people into two groups, where one is given information in a printed book, and the other is given the same information on a screen. Everyone is then asked questions about what they just read. When you do this, you find that people understand and remember less of what they absorb on screens. There’s broad scientific evidence for this now, emerging from fifty-four studies, and she explained that it’s referred to as ‘screen inferiority’. This gap in understanding between books and screens is big enough that in elementary-school children, it’s the equivalent of two-thirds of a year’s growth in reading comprehension.

它还会产生其他连锁反应。安妮曾进行过一些研究，将参与者分成两组，一组阅读纸质书籍，另一组则在屏幕上阅读相同的信息。之后，研究人员会询问所有参与者关于他们刚刚阅读的内容的问题。研究发现，人们对屏幕上的信息理解和记忆程度较低。目前已有54项研究证实了这一点，并提供了广泛的科学证据。安妮解释说，这种现象被称为“屏幕劣势”。书籍和屏幕之间的理解差距非常大，对于小学生来说，这相当于他们一年阅读理解能力提升的三分之二。

As she spoke, I realised that the collapse in reading books is in some ways a symptom of our atrophying attention, and in some ways a cause of it. It’s a spiral – as we began to move from books to screens, we started to lose some of the capacity for the deeper reading that comes from books, and that, in turn, made us less likely to read books. It’s like when you gain weight, and it gets harder and harder to exercise. As a result, Anne told me she was worried we are now losing ‘our ability to read long texts any more’, and we are also losing our ‘cognitive patience … [and] the stamina and the ability to deal with cognitively-challenging texts’. When I was at Harvard conducting interviews, one professor told me that he struggled to get his students there to read even quite short books, and he increasingly offered them podcasts and YouTube clips they could watch instead. And that’s Harvard. I started to wonder what happens to a world where this form of deep focus shrinks so far and so fast. What happens when that deepest layer of thinking becomes available to fewer and fewer people, until it is a small minority interest, like opera, or volleyball?

听她说话的时候，我意识到，读书人数的锐减在某种程度上是我们注意力衰退的征兆，某种程度上也是造成注意力衰退的原因。这是一个恶性循环——当我们开始从纸质书转向电子屏幕时，我们开始失去一些从书籍中获得的深度阅读能力，而这反过来又让我们更不愿意读书。这就像你体重增加后，锻炼变得越来越困难一样。因此，安妮告诉我，她担心我们现在正在失去“阅读长篇文本的能力”，我们也正在失去“认知耐心……以及处理认知挑战性文本的耐力和能力”。我在哈佛大学做采访时，一位教授告诉我，他很难让学生阅读哪怕是很短的书籍，他越来越多地向他们推荐播客和YouTube视频。而这仅仅是哈佛的情况。我开始思考，如果这种深度专注能力如此迅速地萎缩，世界将会变成什么样子。当这种最深层次的思考方式越来越少人能够接触到，直到它变成像歌剧或排球一样的小众爱好时，会发生什么？

As I wandered the streets of Provincetown contemplating some of these questions, I found myself thinking back over a famous idea that I now realised I had never really understood before – one that was also mulled, in a different way, by Nicholas Carr in his book. In the 1960s, the Canadian professor Marshall McLuhan talked a lot about how the arrival of television was transforming the way we see the world. He said these changes were so deep and so profound that it was hard to really see them. When he tried to distil this down into a phrase, he explained that ‘the medium is the message’. What he meant, I think, was that when a new technology comes along, you think of it as like a pipe – somebody pours in information at one end, and you receive it unfiltered at the other. But it’s not like that. Every time a new medium comes along – whether it’s the invention of the printed book, or TV, or Twitter – and you start to use it, it’s like you are putting on a new kind of goggles, each with their own special colours and lenses. Each set of goggles you put on makes you see things differently.

当我在普罗温斯敦的街头漫步，思考着这些问题时，我不禁回想起一个著名的观点，而我意识到自己以前从未真正理解过它——尼古拉斯·卡尔在他的书中也以不同的方式探讨过这个观点。上世纪60年代，加拿大教授马歇尔·麦克卢汉曾多次谈到电视的出现如何改变了我们看待世界的方式。他说，这些变化如此深刻，如此巨大，以至于我们很难真正察觉。当他试图用一句话来概括时，他解释说：“媒介即信息”。我认为，他的意思是，当一项新技术出现时，人们会把它想象成一根管道——有人从一端注入信息，而你则从另一端接收未经过滤的信息。但事实并非如此。每当一种新的媒介出现——无论是纸质书、电视还是推特的发明——当你开始使用它时，就像戴上了一副新的护目镜，每副护目镜都有其独特的颜色和镜片。你戴上的每一副护目镜都会让你以不同的视角看待事物。

So (for example) when you start to watch television, before you absorb the message of any particular TV show – whether it’s Wheel of Fortune or The Wire – you start to see the world as being shaped like television itself. That’s why McLuhan said that every time a new medium comes along – a new way for humans to communicate – it has buried in it a message. It is gently guiding us to see the world according to a new set of codes. The way information gets to you, McLuhan argued, is more important than the information itself. TV teaches you that the world is fast; that it’s about surfaces and appearances; that everything in the world is happening all at once.

所以（举例来说），当你开始看电视时，在你真正理解某个电视节目的信息之前——无论是《幸运之轮》还是《火线》——你就会开始觉得整个世界都像电视本身一样。这就是为什么麦克卢汉说，每当一种新的媒介出现——一种新的人类交流方式——它都蕴含着某种信息。它悄然引导我们用一套新的编码来看待世界。麦克卢汉认为，信息传递给你的方式比信息本身更重要。电视教会你，世界瞬息万变；它关乎表面和表象；世界上的一切都在同时发生。

This made me wonder what the message is that we absorb from social media, and how it compares to the message that we absorb from printed books. I thought first of Twitter. When you log in to that site – it doesn’t matter whether you are Donald Trump or Bernie Sanders or Bubba the Love Sponge – you are absorbing a message through that medium and sending it out to your followers. What is that message? First: that you shouldn’t focus on any one thing for long. The world can and should be understood in short, simple statements of 280 characters. Second: the world should be interpreted and confidently understood very quickly. Third: what matters most is whether people immediately agree with and applaud your short, simple, speedy statements. A successful statement is one that lots of people immediately applaud; an unsuccessful statement is one that people immediately ignore or condemn. When you tweet, before you say anything else, you are saying that at some level you agree with these three premises. You are putting on those goggles and seeing the world through them.

这让我不禁思考，我们从社交媒体中吸收的信息是什么，它与我们从纸质书籍中吸收的信息有何异同。我首先想到的是推特。当你登录这个网站时——无论你是唐纳德·特朗普、伯尼·桑德斯，还是“爱心海绵”巴布——你都在通过这个媒介吸收信息，并将其传递给你的粉丝。那么，这个信息是什么呢？第一：你不应该长时间专注于任何一件事。世界可以而且应该用280个字符的简短语句来理解。第二：世界应该被迅速解读并自信地理解。第三：最重要的是人们是否立即同意并赞赏你简短、简洁、快速的语句。成功的语句是很多人立即赞同的语句；失败的语句是人们立即忽略或谴责的语句。当你发推文时，在你发表任何其他言论之前，你就已经表明你在某种程度上同意这三个前提。你戴上了这副“眼镜”，透过它来看待世界。

How about Facebook? What’s the message in that medium? It seems to be first: your life exists to be displayed to other people, and you should be aiming every day to show your friends edited highlights of your life. Second: what matters is whether people immediately like these edited and carefully selective highlights that you spend your life crafting. Third: somebody is your ‘friend’ if you regularly look at their edited highlight reels, and they look at yours – this is what friendship means.

那么Facebook呢？这个平台传递的信息是什么？似乎有三点：第一，你的生活是为了展示给别人看的，你应该每天都努力向朋友们展示你精心剪辑的生活亮点。第二，重要的是人们是否会立刻喜欢这些你花费大量时间精心挑选和编辑的精彩瞬间。第三，如果你经常查看对方精心剪辑的精彩瞬间，而对方也经常查看你的，那么这个人就是你的“朋友”——这就是友谊的意义。

How about Instagram? First: what matters is how you look on the outside. Second: what matters is how you look on the outside. Third: what matters is how you look on the outside. Fourth: what matters is whether people like how you look on the outside. (I don’t mean this glibly or sarcastically: that really is the message the site offers.)

就拿Instagram来说吧。首先：重要的是你的外表。其次：重要的是你的外表。第三：重要的是你的外表。第四：重要的是别人是否喜欢你的外表。（我这么说并非轻率或讽刺：这确实是该网站传递的信息。）

I realised one of the key reasons why social media makes me feel so out of joint with the world, and with myself. I think all of these ideas – the messages implicit in these mediums – are wrong. Let’s think about Twitter. In fact, the world is complex. To reflect that honestly, you usually need to focus on one thing for a significant amount of time, and you need space to speak at length. Very few things worth saying can be explained in 280 characters. If your response to an idea is immediate, unless you have built up years of expertise on the broader topic, it’s most likely going to be shallow and uninteresting. Whether people immediately agree with you is no marker of whether what you are saying is true or right – you have to think for yourself. Reality can only be understood sensibly by adopting the opposite messages to Twitter. The world is complex and requires steady focus to be understood; it needs to be thought about and comprehended slowly; and most important truths will be unpopular when they are first articulated. I realised that the times in my own life when I’ve been most successful on Twitter – in terms of followers and retweets – are the times when I have been least useful as a human being: when I’ve been attention-deprived, simplistic, vituperative. Of course there are occasional nuggets of insight on the site – but if this becomes your dominant mode of absorbing information, I believe the quality of your thinking will rapidly degrade.

我意识到社交媒体让我感到与世界、与自己如此格格不入的关键原因之一。我认为所有这些想法——这些媒介中隐含的信息——都是错误的。就拿推特来说吧。事实上，世界是复杂的。要诚实地反映这一点，你通常需要长时间专注于一件事，并且需要足够的空间来畅所欲言。很少有值得说的话能用280个字符解释清楚。如果你对某个想法的反应过于迅速，除非你在这个更广泛的领域积累了多年的专业知识，否则你的反应很可能肤浅而乏味。人们是否立即同意你的观点并不能说明你所说的是真是假——你必须独立思考。只有摒弃与推特截然相反的观念，才能理性地理解现实。世界是复杂的，需要持续的专注才能理解；需要慢慢地思考和领悟；而且大多数重要的真理在最初提出时都会不受欢迎。我意识到，在我自己生活中，我在推特上最成功的时候——无论是粉丝数量还是转发量——恰恰是我作为一个人最无用的时候：那时我注意力匮乏、思维简单、言辞粗鲁。当然，这个网站上偶尔也会有一些真知灼见——但如果它成为你获取信息的主要方式，我相信你的思考质量会迅速下降。

The same goes for Instagram. I like looking at pretty people, like everyone else. But to think that life is primarily about these surfaces – getting approval for your six-pack or how you look in a bikini – is a recipe for unhappiness. And the same goes for a lot of how we interact on Facebook too. It’s not a friendship to pore jealously over another person’s photos and boasts and complaints, and to expect them to do the same for you. In fact, that’s pretty much the opposite of friendship. Being friends is about looking into each other’s eyes, doing things together in the world, an endless exchange of gut laughs and bear hugs, joy and grief and dancing. These are all the things Facebook will often drain from you by dominating your time with hollow parodies of friendship.

Instagram也是如此。我和其他人一样，喜欢看漂亮的人。但如果认为生活主要就是关注这些表面现象——比如你的六块腹肌是否得到认可，或者你穿比基尼的样子是否好看——那注定会不快乐。我们在Facebook上的很多互动也是如此。嫉妒地盯着别人的照片、炫耀和抱怨，并期望别人也这样做，这根本不是友谊。事实上，这几乎与友谊背道而驰。真正的朋友是彼此凝视，一起经历生活中的点点滴滴，开怀大笑，互相拥抱，分享喜悦、悲伤和欢笑。而Facebook却常常用空洞的友谊模仿来占据你的时间，让你失去所有这些美好的情感。

After thinking all this, I would return to the printed books I was piling up against the wall of my beachhouse. What, I wondered, is the message buried in the medium of the printed book? Before the words convey their specific meaning, the medium of the book tells us several things. Firstly, life is complex, and if you want to understand it, you have to set aside a fair bit of time to think deeply about it. You need to slow down. Secondly, there is a value in leaving behind your other concerns and narrowing down your attention to one thing, sentence after sentence, page after page. Thirdly, it is worth thinking deeply about how other people live and how their minds work. They have complex inner lives just like you.

思考了这一切之后，我又回到了堆在海滨小屋墙边的那些书本前。我不禁思索，纸质书这种媒介究竟蕴含着怎样的信息？在文字传递其具体含义之前，书籍本身就告诉我们几件事。首先，生活是复杂的，如果你想理解它，就必须留出相当多的时间去深入思考。你需要放慢脚步。其次，放下其他琐事，将注意力集中于一件事上，逐句逐页地阅读，这本身就很有价值。第三，深入思考他人的生活方式和思维模式也值得我们去做。他们和你一样，拥有复杂而丰富的内心世界。

I realised that I agree with the messages in the medium of the book. I think they are true. I think they encourage the best parts of human nature – that a life with lots of episodes of deep focus is a good life. It is why reading books nourishes me. And I don’t agree with the messages in the medium of social media. I think they primarily feed the uglier and shallower parts of my nature. It is why spending time on these sites – even when, by the rules of the game, I am doing well, gaining likes and followers – leaves me feeling drained and unhappy. I like the person I become when I read a lot of books. I dislike the person I become when I spend a lot of time on social media.

我意识到我认同书中所传递的信息。我认为它们是真理。我认为它们鼓励人性中最美好的一面——充满专注时刻的生活才是美好的生活。这就是为什么读书能滋养我。但我并不认同社交媒体所传递的信息。我认为它们主要滋养了我性格中丑陋和肤浅的一面。这就是为什么即使按照游戏规则，我在这些网站上表现良好，获得了点赞和关注，但花时间在这些网站上仍然会让我感到精疲力竭、不快乐。我喜欢读书后成为的自己。我不喜欢长时间沉迷于社交媒体后变成的自己。

But I wondered if I was getting carried away – these were just my hunches, after all – so later, I went to the University of Toronto to interview Raymond Mar, who is a professor of psychology there. Raymond is one of the social scientists who has done most in the world to study the effects that reading books has on our consciousness, and his research has helped to open up a distinctive way of thinking about this question.

但我怀疑自己是不是想得太多了——毕竟这只是我的直觉——所以后来，我去了多伦多大学采访了心理学教授雷蒙德·马尔。雷蒙德是世界上研究阅读对意识影响的社会科学家之一，他的研究为我们思考这个问题开辟了一种独特的视角。

When he was a little boy, Raymond read obsessively – but it had never occurred to him to try to figure out how reading itself might affect the way in which our minds work until he was a grad student, and one day, his mentor, Professor Keith Oatley, put a thought to him. When you read a novel, you are immersing yourself in what it’s like to be inside another person’s head. You are simulating a social situation. You are imagining other people and their experiences in a deep and complex way. So maybe, he said, if you read a lot of novels, you will become better at actually understanding other people off the page. Perhaps fiction is a kind of empathy gym, boosting your ability to empathise with other people – which is one of the most rich and precious forms of focus we have. Together, they decided to begin to study this question scientifically.

雷蒙德小时候酷爱读书，但他从未想过阅读本身会如何影响我们的思维方式，直到他读研究生时，他的导师基思·奥特利教授提出了一个问题。奥特利教授说，读小说时，你会沉浸在另一个人的内心世界里，模拟一种社交情境，以一种深刻而复杂的方式想象他人及其经历。因此，奥特利教授认为，如果你读很多小说，或许就能更好地理解现实生活中的他人。也许小说就像一个“同理心健身房”，能够提升你对他人的同理心——而同理心正是我们拥有的最宝贵、最丰富的专注力之一。于是，他们决定共同对这个问题进行科学研究。

It’s a tricky thing to study. Some other scientists had developed a technique where you give somebody a passage to read, and then immediately afterwards you test their empathy. But to Raymond, this was flawed. If reading affects us, it reshapes us over the longer term – it’s not like coming up on ecstasy, where you swallow it and experience immediate effects for a few hours.

这很难研究。一些科学家开发了一种方法，让受试者阅读一段文字，然后立即测试他们的同理心。但雷蒙德认为这种方法有缺陷。如果阅读对我们产生影响，那么它对我们的塑造是长期的——这不像服用摇头丸那样，吞下后几个小时内就能感受到效果。

With his colleagues he came up with a clever three-stage experiment, designed to see if this longer-term effect existed. If you took part in the test, you were brought into a lab and you were shown a list of names. Some were famous novelists; some were famous non-fiction writers; and some were random people who aren’t writers at all. You were asked to circle the names of the novelists, and then, separately, you were asked to circle the names of the non-fiction writers. Raymond reasoned that people who had read more novels over their lifetime would be able to recognise the names of more fiction writers. He also now had an interesting comparison group – people who had read a lot of non-fiction books.

他和同事们设计了一个巧妙的三阶段实验，旨在验证这种长期效应是否存在。实验中，参与者会被带到实验室，并看到一份名单。名单上的名字有：一些是著名小说家；一些是著名非虚构作家；还有一些是与写作无关的普通人。参与者需要圈出小说家的名字，然后再分别圈出非虚构作家的名字。雷蒙德认为，一生中阅读小说较多的人应该能够认出更多小说家的名字。此外，他还找到了一个有趣的对照组——阅读过大量非虚构类书籍的人。

Then he gave everyone two tests. The first used a technique that’s sometimes used to diagnose autism. You are shown lots of pictures of people’s eye areas, and you are asked: what is this person thinking? It’s a way of measuring how good you are at reading the subtle signals that reveal the emotional state of another person. In the second test, you sat down and watched several videos of real people in real situations like, for example, two men who had just played a squash game talking to each other. You had to figure out: what’s going on here? Who won the game? What’s the relationship between them? How do they feel? Raymond and the experimenters knew the real answer – and so they could see who, in the test, was best at reading the social signals and figuring it out.

然后他给每个人做了两项测试。第一项测试采用了一种有时用于诊断自闭症的技术。测试中，你会看到很多人物眼部区域的图片，然后被问到：这个人正在想什么？这是一种衡量你解读他人情绪状态细微信号能力的方法。在第二项测试中，你坐下来观看几段真实人物在真实情境下的视频，例如，两个刚打完壁球的男人正在交谈。你需要弄清楚：这里发生了什么？谁赢了？他们之间是什么关系？他们的感受如何？雷蒙德和实验人员知道真正的答案——所以他们能够看出谁在测试中最擅长解读社交信号并做出判断。

When they got the results, they were clear. The more novels you read, the better you were at reading other people’s emotions. It was a huge effect. This wasn’t just a sign that you were better educated – because, reading non-fiction books, by contrast, had no effect on your empathy.

当他们拿到结果时，结论很明确：小说读得越多，就越能更好地理解他人的情绪。这种影响非常显著。这不仅仅表明你受过更好的教育——因为相比之下，阅读非虚构类书籍对你的同理心没有任何影响。

I asked Raymond – why? Reading, he told me, creates a ‘unique form of consciousness … While we’re reading, we’re directing attention outwards towards the word on the page and, at the same time, enormous amounts of attention is going inwards as we imagine and mentally simulate.’ It’s different from if you just close your eyes and try to imagine something off the top of your head. ‘It’s being structured – but our attention is in a very unique place, fluctuating both out towards the page, towards the words, and then inwards, towards what those words represent.’ It’s a way of combining ‘outwardly directed attention and inwardly directed attention’. When you read fiction in particular, you imagine what it is like to be another person. You find yourself, he says, ‘trying to understand the different characters, their motivations, their goals, tracking those different things. It’s a form of practice. We’re probably using the same kinds of cognitive processes that we would use to understand our real peers in the real world.’ You simulate being another human being so well that fiction is a far better virtual-reality simulator than the machines currently marketed under that name.

我问雷蒙德——为什么？他告诉我，阅读创造了一种“独特的意识状态……当我们阅读时，我们的注意力一方面向外集中于书页上的文字，另一方面，我们也会投入大量的注意力进行想象和心理模拟。”这与闭上眼睛凭空想象截然不同。“阅读是有结构的——但我们的注意力处于一种非常独特的状态，它既向外集中于书页上的文字，又向内集中于这些文字所代表的意义。”这是一种结合“向外指向的注意力和向内指向的注意力”的方式。尤其是在阅读小说时，你会想象自己是另一个人。你会发现自己“试图理解不同的角色，他们的动机，他们的目标，并追踪这些不同的事物。这是一种练习。”我们可能正在使用与理解现实世界中的同龄人相同的认知过程。你对扮演另一个人的模拟如此出色，以至于小说比目前市面上以该名称销售的机器更能有效地模拟虚拟现实。

Each of us can only ever experience a small sliver of what it’s like to be a human being alive today, Raymond told me, but as you read fiction, you see inside other people’s experiences. That doesn’t vanish when you put down the novel. When you later meet a person in the real world, you’ll be better able to imagine what it’s like to be them. Reading a factual account may make you more knowledgeable, but it doesn’t have this empathy-expanding effect.

雷蒙德告诉我，我们每个人只能体验到当今人类生活的一小部分，但当你阅读小说时，你就能深入了解他人的经历。这种体验并不会随着你放下小说而消失。当你日后在现实生活中遇到某个人时，你会更能设身处地地去感受他们的处境。阅读纪实作品或许能让你增长知识，但它却不具备这种拓展同理心的效果。

There have now been dozens of other studies replicating the core effect that Raymond discovered. I asked Raymond what would happen if we discovered a drug that boosted empathy as much as reading fiction has been shown to in his work. ‘If it had no side effects,’ he said, ‘I think that it would be a very popular drug.’ The more I talked with him, the more I reflected that empathy is one of the most complex forms of attention we have – and the most precious. Many of the most important advances in human history have been advances in empathy – the realisation by at least some white people that other ethnic groups have feelings and abilities and dreams just like them; the realisation by some men that the way they have exerted power over women was illegitimate and caused real suffering; the realisation by many heterosexuals that gay love is just like straight love. Empathy makes progress possible, and every time you widen human empathy, you open the universe a little more.

现在已有数十项研究重复验证了雷蒙德发现的核心效应。我问雷蒙德，如果我们发现一种药物，其增强同理心的效果能像阅读小说一样显著，那会怎么样？他回答说：“如果它没有副作用，我想它会成为一种非常受欢迎的药物。” 我和他交谈越多，就越发意识到同理心是我们拥有的最复杂、最珍贵的注意力形式之一。人类历史上许多最重要的进步都源于同理心的提升——至少一些白人意识到其他族群也拥有和他们一样的情感、能力和梦想；一些男性意识到他们过去对女性施加权力的方式是不正当的，并且造成了真正的痛苦；许多异性恋者意识到同性恋之爱与异性之爱并无二致。同理心使进步成为可能，每一次人类同理心的拓展，都意味着宇宙的更多可能性。

But – as Raymond is the first to point out – these results can be interpreted in a very different way. It could be that reading fiction, over time, boosts your empathy. But it could also be that people who are already empathetic are simply more drawn to reading novels. This makes his research controversial, and contested. He told me that it’s likely that both are true – that reading fiction boosts your empathy, and that empathetic people are more drawn to reading fiction. But there’s a hint, he said, that reading fiction really does have a significant effect: one of his studies found that the more a child is read storybooks – something their parents, more than the kid, choose – the better they are at reading other people’s emotions. This suggests that the experience of stories really does expand their empathy.

但正如雷蒙德首先指出的那样，这些结果可以有截然不同的解读。或许阅读小说会随着时间的推移增强你的同理心。但也可能是那些本身就富有同理心的人更容易被小说吸引。这使得他的研究颇具争议。他告诉我，这两种说法可能都成立——阅读小说确实能增强同理心，而富有同理心的人也更容易被小说吸引。但他表示，有迹象表明阅读小说确实会产生显著影响：他的一项研究发现，孩子读故事书的次数越多（这更多是由父母而非孩子自己选择的），他们就越能更好地理解他人的情绪。这表明，阅读故事确实能够拓展他们的同理心。

If we have reasons to believe that reading fiction boosts our empathy, do we know what the forms that are largely replacing it – like social media – are doing to us? Raymond said it’s easy to be snobbish about social media and to fall into a moral panic, and he finds that way of thinking silly. There’s a lot that is good about social media, he stressed. The effects he is describing aren’t to do primarily with the printed page, he said – they are to do with being immersed in a complex narrative that simulates the social world. His studies have found that long TV series are just as effective, he said. But there’s a catch. One of his studies showed that children are more empathetic if they read storybooks or watch movies, but not if they watch shorter shows. This seems to fit, it seemed to me, with what we see on social media – if you see the world through fragments, your empathy often doesn’t kick in, in the way that it does when you engage with something in a sustained, focused way.

如果我们有理由相信阅读小说能增强我们的同理心，那么我们是否了解那些正在大量取代小说的阅读形式——比如社交媒体——对我们产生了怎样的影响？雷蒙德说，人们很容易对社交媒体抱有偏见，甚至陷入道德恐慌，而他认为这种想法很愚蠢。他强调，社交媒体有很多优点。他所描述的这些影响主要并非源于纸质书籍，而是源于沉浸于模拟社会世界的复杂叙事之中。他的研究发现，长篇电视剧同样有效。但这里有个问题。他的一项研究表明，如果孩子们阅读故事书或观看电影，他们的同理心会更强，但如果观看短篇节目则不会。在我看来，这似乎与我们在社交媒体上看到的现象相吻合——如果你只能通过碎片化的信息来了解世界，你的同理心往往无法像持续、专注地参与其中时那样被激发出来。

As I talked with him, I thought: We internalise the texture of the voices we’re exposed to. When you expose yourself to complex stories about the inner lives of other people over long periods of time, that will repattern your consciousness. You too will become more perceptive, open and empathetic. If, by contrast, you expose yourself for hours a day to the disconnected fragments of shrieking and fury that dominate social media, your thoughts will start to be shaped like that. Your internal voices will become cruder, louder, less able to hear more tender and gentle thoughts. Take care what technologies you use, because your consciousness will, over time, come to be shaped like those technologies.

与他交谈时，我想到：我们会内化所接触到的声音的质感。当你长时间接触他人内心世界的复杂故事时，你的意识模式就会被重塑。你也会变得更加敏锐、开放和富有同理心。相反，如果你每天花几个小时沉浸在社交媒体上那些支离破碎的尖叫和愤怒之中，你的思想也会开始被塑造成那样。你内心的声音会变得更加粗粝、喧闹，难以听到那些温柔细腻的想法。谨慎选择你使用的科技产品，因为随着时间的推移，你的意识最终会受到这些科技产品的影响。

Before I said goodbye to Raymond, I asked him why he had spent so much time studying the effects of reading fiction on human consciousness. Up to the moment when I asked this, he had been something of a data geek, explaining his methods in great detail. But as he answered, his face opened up. ‘We’re all on the same ball of mud and water that is heading towards a catastrophic end potentially. If we are going to solve these problems, we can’t do it alone,’ he said. ‘That’s why I think empathy is so valuable.’

在和雷蒙德道别之前，我问他为什么花了这么多时间研究阅读小说对人类意识的影响。在此之前，他一直是个数据控，详细地解释着他的研究方法。但当他回答这个问题时，他的表情豁然开朗。“我们都身处同一颗泥石流中，而这颗泥石流正朝着灾难性的结局驶去。如果我们想要解决这些问题，单凭一己之力是行不通的，”他说，“这就是为什么我认为同理心如此宝贵。”

# ↩

5 Cause Five: The Disruption of Mind-Wandering

第五个原因：走神造成的干扰

For more than one hundred years, there has been one image – a metaphor – that has, above all others, dominated how experts think about attention. Picture the Hollywood Bowl, crammed with tens of thousands of people, with all the laughing and jostling and yelling that takes place as people saunter in and wait for the show. Then, suddenly, the lights go down, and on the stage, a spotlight appears. It lights up one individual: Beyoncé. Or Britney. Or Bieber. Suddenly all the chatter and clatter cease, and the focus of that room narrows to one person and their awesome power. In 1890 the founder of modern American psychology, William James, wrote – in the most influential text ever (in the Western world, at least) on this subject – that ‘everyone knows what attention is’. Attention, he said, is a spotlight. To put it in our terms, it’s the moment Beyoncé appears, alone, on the stage, and everyone else around you seems to vanish.

一百多年来，有一个意象——一个比喻——凌驾于其他所有比喻之上，主导着专家们对注意力的思考。想象一下好莱坞露天剧场，成千上万的人挤满了人，欢声笑语、熙熙攘攘、喧闹嘈杂，人们涌入剧场，等待演出开始。突然，灯光暗了下来，舞台上出现了一束聚光灯。它照亮了一个人：碧昂丝。或者布兰妮。或者贾斯汀·比伯。突然间，所有的喧闹声都消失了，整个房间的焦点都集中在一个人身上，以及她那令人敬畏的魅力。1890年，现代美国心理学的奠基人威廉·詹姆斯在他关于注意力的最具影响力的著作（至少在西方世界是如此）中写道：“每个人都知道什么是注意力”。他说，注意力就像一束聚光灯。用我们的话来说，就是碧昂丝独自一人出现在舞台上的那一刻，你周围的人仿佛都消失了。

James himself offered other images at the time too, and psychologists have tried other ways of thinking about it – but ever since, the study of attention has primarily been the study of the spotlight. This image, I realised when I stopped to think about it, dominated how I thought about attention too. Attention is usually defined as a person’s ability to selectively attend to something in the environment. So when I said I was distracted, I meant that I couldn’t narrow the spotlight of my attention down to the one thing I want to focus on. I want to read a book, but the light of my attention won’t fade from my phone, or from the people talking in the street outside, or from my anxieties about work. There’s a lot of truth in this way of thinking about attention – but I learned that, in fact, this is only one form of attention that you need in order to function fully. It exists alongside other forms of attention that are just as essential for you to be able to think coherently – and those forms are under even greater threat right now than your spotlight.

詹姆斯本人当时也提出了其他一些比喻，心理学家也尝试过其他方法来思考这个问题——但自那以后，注意力的研究主要集中在聚光灯上。当我停下来思考时，我意识到这个比喻也主导了我对注意力的理解。注意力通常被定义为一个人选择性地关注环境中某事物的能力。所以，当我说我分心时，我的意思是，我无法将注意力集中在我想关注的那件事上。我想看书，但我的注意力却无法从手机、街上人们的谈话声，或是我对工作的焦虑中转移开来。这种关于注意力的思考方式有很多道理——但我了解到，事实上，这只是你正常运转所需的众多注意力形式之一。它与其他同样重要的注意力形式并存，而这些注意力形式对于你连贯地思考至关重要——而且它们现在面临的威胁甚至比你的聚光灯还要大。

In my life before I fled to Cape Cod, I lived in a tornado of mental stimulation. I would never go for a walk without listening to a podcast or talking on the phone. I would never wait two minutes in a store without looking at my phone or reading a book. The idea of not filling every minute with stimulation panicked me, and I found it weird when I saw other people not doing it. On long train or bus journeys, whenever I would see somebody just sit there for six hours, doing nothing but stare out of the window, I would feel an urge to lean over to them and say, ‘I’m sorry to disturb you. It’s none of my business, but I just wanted to check – you do realise that you have a limited amount of time in which to be alive, and the clock counting down towards death is constantly ticking, and you’ll never get back these six hours you are spending doing nothing at all? And when you are dead, you’ll be dead forever ? You know that, right?’ (I never did this, as you can tell from the fact I am not writing this book from a psychiatric institution, but it crossed my mind.)

在逃往科德角之前，我的生活就像一场精神风暴。我出门散步时，总会听播客或打电话。在商店里，哪怕只等两分钟，我也总是低头看手机或读书。一想到不能让每一分钟都充满刺激，我就感到恐慌，看到别人不这样做，我反而觉得很奇怪。在漫长的火车或巴士旅途中，每当我看到有人一坐就是六个小时，什么也不做，只是盯着窗外发呆时，我就会忍不住想凑过去说：“不好意思打扰您了。这本来不关我的事，但我只是想问问——您难道不知道自己的生命有限吗？死亡的倒计时一直在滴答作响，您浪费的这六个小时一去不复返了？而且，一旦死了，就永远消失了。”你知道的，对吧？（我从来没这么做过，因为我写这本书的时候并没有待在精神病院里，这一点你也能看出来，但我确实想过这个问题。）

So I thought that in Provincetown, stripped of distractions, I would gain one benefit – I would be able to be even more stimulated, for even longer periods, and retain even more of what I inhaled. I can listen to longer podcasts! I can read longer books! That did happen – but it occurred alongside something else, something I didn’t see coming. One day I left my iPod at home, and I decided to simply go for a walk along the beach. I walked for two hours, and I let my thoughts float, without my spotlight settling on anything. I felt my mind roam – from looking at the little crabs on the beach, to memories of my childhood, to ideas for books I might write years from now, to the shapes of the men sunning themselves in Speedos. My consciousness drifted like the boats I could see bobbing on the horizon.

所以我想，在普罗温斯敦，抛开一切干扰，我或许能获得一个好处——我可以更长时间地保持高度专注，并且更好地记住我所吸收的信息。我可以听更长的播客！我可以读更长的书！这些确实发生了——但与此同时，也发生了一些我始料未及的事情。有一天，我把iPod留在了家里，决定去海滩散步。我走了两个小时，任思绪飘荡，没有刻意关注任何事物。我的思绪漫游开来——从沙滩上的小螃蟹，到童年的回忆，到多年后我可能会写的书的构思，再到穿着泳裤晒太阳的男人们的身影。我的意识就像地平线上摇曳的小船一样，随波逐流。

At first I felt guilty. You came here to focus, I said to myself, and to learn about focus. But what you are indulging in is its opposite – a mental detumescence. But I continued. Before long, I was doing this every day, and my periods of meandering started to stretch to three, four, sometimes even five hours. This would have been unthinkable to me in my normal life. But in that time, I felt more creative than I had since I was a child. Ideas started spinning out of my head. When I would get home and write them down, I realised I was having more creative ideas – and making more connections – in a single three-hour walk than I usually had in a month. I started to let smaller moments of mind-wandering in too. When I finished reading a book, I would just lie there for twenty minutes, thinking about it, staring out to sea.

起初我感到内疚。我对自己说，你来这里是为了集中注意力，学习如何集中注意力。但你现在沉溺的却是截然相反的事情——精神的放纵。但我还是继续下去了。不久之后，我每天都这样做，我的漫无目的的走神时间开始延长到三四个小时，有时甚至五个小时。这在我的日常生活中是不可想象的。但在那段时间里，我感觉自己比孩提时代更有创造力。各种想法开始涌入我的脑海。当我回家把它们写下来时，我意识到，短短三个小时的散步，我产生的创意——以及建立的联系——比我通常一个月产生的还要多。我也开始允许一些更短时间的走神。读完一本书后，我会躺在那里二十分钟，思考书中的内容，凝视着大海。

Weirdly, it seemed like letting my spotlight disappear entirely was improving my ability to think and to focus in some way I couldn’t articulate. How could that be? I only began to understand what was happening when I learned that over the past thirty years, there has been a sudden bubbling up of research into this very topic: mind-wandering.

奇怪的是，似乎完全摆脱外界关注反而提升了我的思考和专注能力，但我却无法用语言来形容这种感觉。这怎么可能呢？直到我了解到，过去三十年来，关于“走神”这一主题的研究突然兴起，我才开始明白是怎么回事。

In the 1950s, in the small town of Aberdeen in Washington state, a high-school chemistry teacher named Mr Smith had a problem with one of his students, a teenage boy named Marcus Raichle. He called in the boy’s parents and explained sternly that he was doing something bad. ‘Your son has a habit of daydreaming,’ he said. We all know this is one of the worst things you can do at school.

上世纪五十年代，在华盛顿州阿伯丁小镇，一位名叫史密斯的高中化学老师遇到了一个问题：他的一个学生，一个名叫马库斯·雷克尔的十几岁男孩，做起了坏事。他把男孩的父母叫来，严厉地解释说，他儿子正在做一件不好的事。“你儿子有爱做白日梦的习惯，”他说。我们都知道，这是在学校里最糟糕的事情之一。

Thirty years later, their son helped to make a breakthrough on this very topic – one that Mr Smith would not have approved of. Marcus became a prominent neuroscientist and won the Kavli Prize, a leading honour in the field. In the 1980s, a whole new way of seeing what was happening in people’s brains – the PET ( positron emission tomography) scan – evolved right outside his office, where the technology was being applied for the first time, by him and his colleagues. I stood on that very spot, in the Washington School of Medicine in St Louis, Missouri, when I went to interview him. He was one of the first scientists who was able to use this new tool, and when he switched it on with a patient inside, he was able to see into a living human brain in a way almost nobody ever had before.
