三十年后，他们的儿子在这个领域取得了突破性进展——而史密斯先生生前绝不会赞同这一做法。马库斯成为了一位杰出的神经科学家，并荣获了卡弗里奖，这是该领域的最高荣誉。上世纪80年代，一种全新的观察人脑活动的方式——正电子发射断层扫描（PET）——在他办公室外蓬勃发展，他和他的同事们正是在这里首次应用了这项技术。我去采访他时，就站在那个地方，位于密苏里州圣路易斯的华盛顿医学院。他是最早能够使用这项新技术的科学家之一，当他启动设备，让病人接受扫描时，他得以用一种几乎前所未有的方式观察活体人脑。

Back in his medical training, Marcus had been confidently told that we know what’s happening inside your head in the moments when you are not focusing. Your brain is ‘lying there dormant, quiet, doing nothing, like muscles do until you start to move them’, he was told. But one day Marcus noticed something odd. He had some patients strapped in for a PET scan, and those patients were waiting for him to give them a task and just letting their minds wander. As he got the task ready, he glanced at the machine, and he was puzzled. Their brains, it seemed, were not inactive, as his med-school tutors had said they should be. Activity had shifted from one part of the brain to another – but the brain was still highly active. Surprised, he began to study this in detail. He named the region of the brain that becomes more active when you think you’re not doing much ‘the default mode network’ – and as he studied this more, analysing what people’s brains do when they seem to be doing nothing, he could physically see this region light up on the brain scans. As he looked at them, Marcus said, ‘God, there she was. The whole thing. It was just stunning.’

在接受医学训练时，马库斯曾被自信地告知，我们知道在你注意力不集中的时候，你的大脑内部发生了什么。他被告知，你的大脑“处于休眠状态，安静地待在那里，什么也不做，就像肌肉一样，直到你开始活动它们”。但有一天，马库斯注意到了一些奇怪的事情。他让一些病人做PET扫描，这些病人正等着他布置任务，任由思绪飘荡。当他准备好任务时，他瞥了一眼机器，感到困惑。他们的大脑似乎并没有像他的医学院导师所说的那样处于休眠状态。大脑的活动从一部分转移到了另一部分——但大脑仍然非常活跃。他感到惊讶，于是开始详细研究这一现象。他将大脑中在你感觉无所事事时变得更加活跃的区域命名为“默认模式网络”。随着他深入研究，分析人们看似无所事事时大脑的活动，他能够通过脑部扫描图像亲眼看到这个区域的活跃度。看着这些图像，马库斯说道：“天哪，它就在那里。整个过程都展现了出来。真是太令人震惊了。”

It was a paradigm shift in what scientists thought happens inside our brains, and it triggered an explosion of scientific research into dozens of topics all over the world. One of them was a sudden surge of interest in the science of mind-wandering, asking: what happens when our thoughts float freely, without any immediate focus to anchor them? We can see something is happening – but what? As the debate developed over decades, some scientists came to think that the default mode network is the part of the brain that becomes most active during mind-wandering, and others strongly disagreed – it’s an ongoing debate. But Marcus’s findings led to a rush of scientific research into why our minds wander at all, and what benefits it might produce.

这彻底改变了科学家们对我们大脑内部运作机制的认知，并引发了全球范围内数十个主题的科学研究热潮。其中之一便是对走神科学的突然关注，人们不禁要问：当我们的思绪自由飘荡，没有任何即时的焦点来锚定它们时，究竟发生了什么？我们能感觉到某种变化正在发生——但究竟是什么呢？随着这场争论持续数十年，一些科学家认为默认模式网络是走神时大脑中最活跃的部分，而另一些科学家则强烈反对——这至今仍是一场争论。但马库斯的发现引发了一场科学研究热潮，旨在探究我们为何会走神，以及走神可能带来的益处。

To understand this better, I went to Montreal in Quebec to interview Nathan Spreng, who is a professor of neurology and neurosurgery at McGill University, and to York in England to interview Jonathan Smallwood, who is a professor of psychology at the university there. They are two of the people who have studied this question in most depth. It is a relatively new field of science, so some of its basic ideas are still quite contested, and more will become clear in the coming decades. But in their dozens of scientific studies, they had discovered – it seemed to me – three crucial things that are happening during mind-wandering.

为了更好地理解这个问题，我前往加拿大魁北克省蒙特利尔采访了麦吉尔大学神经病学和神经外科教授内森·斯普伦格，又前往英国约克采访了该校心理学教授乔纳森·斯莫伍德。他们是研究这个问题最深入的两位学者。这是一个相对较新的科学领域，因此一些基本概念仍存在争议，未来几十年内会有更多内容得到阐明。但就我个人而言，他们数十项科学研究已经发现了——在走神过程中发生的三个关键事件。

Firstly, you are slowly making sense of the world. Jonathan gave me an example. When you read a book – as you are doing now – you obviously focus on the individual words and sentences, but there’s always a little bit of your mind that is wandering. You are thinking about how these words relate to your own life. You are thinking about how these sentences relate to what I said in previous chapters. You are thinking about what I might say next. You are wondering if what I am saying is full of contradictions, or whether it will all come together in the end. Suddenly you picture a memory from your childhood, or from what you saw on TV last week. ‘You draw together the different parts of the book in order to make sense of the key theme,’ he said. This isn’t a flaw in your reading. This is reading. If you weren’t letting your mind wander a little bit right now, you wouldn’t really be reading this book in a way that would make sense to you. Having enough mental space to roam is essential for you to be able to understand a book.

首先，你正在慢慢理解这个世界。乔纳森给我举了个例子。当你读书时——就像你现在正在做的那样——你当然会专注于单个的词句，但你的思绪总会有些游离。你在思考这些文字与你自身生活的联系。你在思考这些句子与我之前章节的内容有何关联。你在思考我接下来会说什么。你在琢磨我说的这些话是否自相矛盾，或者最终是否会水落石出。突然间，你想起了童年的一段记忆，或者上周在电视上看到的情景。“你把书中不同的部分串联起来，从而理解其核心主题，”他说。这并不是你阅读的缺陷。这才是阅读。如果你现在不让你的思绪稍微游离一下，你就无法真正理解这本书。拥有足够的思维空间来漫游，对于理解一本书至关重要。

This isn’t just true of reading. It is true of life. Some mind-wandering is essential for things to make sense. ‘If you couldn’t do it,’ Jonathan told me, ‘so many other things would go out of the window.’ He has found that the more you let your mind wander, the better you are at having organised personal goals, being creative, and making patient, long-term decisions. You will be able to do these things better if you let your mind drift, and slowly, unconsciously, make sense of your life.

这不仅适用于阅读，也适用于生活。适度的思绪游离对于理解事物至关重要。“如果你做不到这一点，”乔纳森告诉我，“很多其他事情都会变得一团糟。”他发现，你越是让思绪自由驰骋，就越能更好地制定有条理的个人目标，越能发挥创造力，越能做出耐心而长远的决策。如果你让思绪自由飘荡，慢慢地、不知不觉地理解你的人生，你就能更好地做到这些。

Secondly, when your mind wanders, it starts to make new connections between things – which often produces a solution to your problems. As Nathan put it to me, ‘I think what’s happening is that, when there’s unresolved issues, the brain tries to make things fit,’ if it’s just given the space to do it. He gave me a famous example: the nineteenth-century French mathematician Henri Poincaré was wrestling with one of the hardest problems in maths, and he had narrowed his spotlight down onto every squiggle of it for ages, and he was getting nowhere. Then one day when he was away on a trip, suddenly, as he was stepping into a bus, the solution came to him in a flash. It was only when he turned off the spotlight of his focus, and let his mind wander on its own, that he could connect the pieces, and finally answer the problem. In fact, when you look back over the history of science and engineering, many great breakthroughs don’t happen during periods of focus – they happen during mind-wandering.

其次，当你的思绪游离时，它会开始在事物之间建立新的联系——这往往会为你解决问题带来答案。正如内森对我说的那样，“我认为，当存在未解决的问题时，大脑会试图将各种事物联系起来”，只要给它足够的空间。他给我举了一个著名的例子：19世纪的法国数学家亨利·庞加莱一直在苦苦思索数学中最难的问题之一，他长时间地将注意力集中在方程的每一个细节上，却毫无进展。然后有一天，当他外出旅行时，就在他登上公交车的那一刻，答案突然闪现在他的脑海中。只有当他不再刻意关注某个细节，让思绪自由驰骋时，他才能将各个部分连接起来，最终解答了这个问题。事实上，回顾科学和工程的历史，许多伟大的突破并非发生在专注的时期，而是发生在走神的时候。

‘Creativity is not [where you create] some new thing that’s emerged from your brain,’ Nathan told me. ‘It’s a new association between two things that were already there.’ Mind-wandering allows ‘more extended trains of thought to unfold, which allows for more associations to be made.’ Henri Poincaré couldn’t have come up with his solution if he had remained narrowly focused on the math problem he was trying to solve, or if he had been totally distracted. It took mind-wandering to get him there.

“创造力并非凭空产生某种新事物，”内森告诉我，“而是将两个原本就存在的事物联系起来。” 走神能让“更长的思路得以展开，从而建立更多联系”。如果亨利·庞加莱始终专注于他正在解决的数学问题，或者完全心不在焉，他就不可能找到答案。正是走神让他找到了答案。

Thirdly, during mind-wandering, your mind will – Nathan said – engage in ‘mental time-travel’, where it roams over the past and tries to predict the future. Freed from the pressures of thinking narrowly about what’s right in front of you, your mind will start to think about what might come next – and so it will help to prepare you for it.

第三，正如内森所说，在走神的时候，你的思维会进行“精神时间旅行”，它会漫游过去并试图预测未来。摆脱了局限于眼前事物的思维束缚，你的思维会开始思考接下来可能发生的事情——从而帮助你做好准备。

Up until I met these scientists, I thought that mind-wandering – what I was doing in Provincetown so much, and so pleasurably – was the opposite of attention, and that’s why I felt guilty about doing it. I realised I was wrong. It is actually a different form of attention – and a necessary one. Nathan told me that when we narrow our attention down into a spotlight to focus on one thing, that takes ‘a certain amount of bandwidth’, and when we turn off the spotlight, ‘we still have the same bandwidth – it’s just we can allocate more of those resources’ towards other ways of thinking. ‘So it’s not like attention necessarily goes down – it just shifts,’ to other, crucial forms of thinking.

在遇到这些科学家之前，我一直认为走神——我在普罗温斯敦时经常做，而且乐在其中——与专注截然相反，所以我才会为此感到内疚。后来我意识到自己错了。走神实际上是一种不同的专注形式，而且是必要的。内森告诉我，当我们把注意力集中到一件事上时，会占用“一定的带宽”，而当我们关掉聚光灯时，“我们仍然拥有相同的带宽——只是我们可以把更多的资源分配给其他思考方式”。“所以，这并不是说注意力减少了——它只是转移了，”转移到其他至关重要的思考方式上。

This, I realised, is quite challenging to the whole way I had been raised to think about productivity. I feel instinctively like I’ve done a good hard day of work when I have been sitting at my laptop, spotlight-focused on tapping out words – at the end of it, I feel a little Puritan rush of pride at my productivity. Our whole culture is built around this belief. Your boss wants to see you sitting at your desk every hour of the day; this is what she thinks work is. This way of thinking is implanted in us from a very young age when, like Marcus Raichle, we are told off at school for daydreaming. That’s why, on the days I spent simply wandering aimlessly on the beaches of Provincetown, I didn’t feel productive. I thought I was slacking, being lazy, indulging myself.

我意识到，这与我从小接受的关于效率的固有观念截然不同。我本能地觉得，只要坐在电脑前，全神贯注地敲击键盘，就等于完成了一天卓有成效的工作——一天结束时，我会感到一种清教徒式的自豪感，为自己的效率感到骄傲。我们的整个文化都建立在这种信念之上。你的老板希望你一天24小时都坐在办公桌前；这就是她眼中的工作。这种思维方式从小就根深蒂固，就像马库斯·雷克尔一样，我们在学校里因为走神而被训斥。正因如此，当我漫无目的地在普罗温斯敦的海滩上闲逛时，我并不觉得自己是在工作。我觉得自己是在偷懒，是在懈怠，是在放纵自己。

But Nathan – after studying all this – had found that to be productive, you can’t aim simply to narrow your spotlight as much as possible. He said: ‘I try to go for a walk every day and just let my mind kind of sort things out… I don’t think our full conscious control of our thoughts is necessarily our most productive way of thinking. I think loose patterns of association can lead to unique insight.’ Marcus agreed. Focusing on what’s right in front of you, he told me, gives you ‘some of the raw material that has to be digested, but at some point, you need to stand back from that’. He warned: ‘If we’re just frantically running around focusing on the external world exclusively, we miss the opportunity to let the brain digest what’s been going on.’

但内森在研究了这一切之后发现，要想提高效率，你不能仅仅追求尽可能缩小关注范围。他说：“我尽量每天都出去散步，让思绪自由流动……我认为完全有意识地控制自己的想法未必是最高效的思考方式。我认为松散的联想模式反而能带来独特的洞见。” 马库斯对此表示赞同。他告诉我，专注于眼前的事物能让你“获得一些需要消化的原始素材，但有时你需要跳出这个局限”。他警告说：“如果我们只是疯狂地奔波，只关注外部世界，就会错失让大脑消化所发生的一切的机会。”

As he said this, I thought about the people I had looked at on the train, staring out the window for hours. I had been silently judging them for their lack of productivity – but now I realised they may have been more meaningfully productive than me, as I frantically took notes on one book after another, without taking time to sit back and digest. The kid in the class who is staring out of the window mind-wandering might be doing the most useful thinking.

他这么说的时候，我想起了我在火车上看到的那些人，他们一连几个小时都盯着窗外发呆。我当时一直在默默地评判他们缺乏效率——但现在我意识到，他们或许比我更有意义地高效，因为我当时正疯狂地在一本书又一本书上做笔记，却从未停下来好好思考。班上那个望着窗外、心不在焉的孩子，或许正在进行最有价值的思考。

I thought back over all the scientific studies I had read about how we spend our time rapidly switching between tasks, and I realised that in our current culture, most of the time we’re not focusing, but we’re not mind-wandering either. We’re constantly skimming, in an unsatisfying whirr. Nathan nodded when I asked about this, and told me he is constantly trying to figure out how to get his phone to stop sending him notifications for things he doesn’t want to know. All this frenetic digital interruption is ‘pulling our attention away from our thoughts’, and ‘suppressing your default mode network… I think we’re almost in this constant stimulus-driven, stimulus-bound environment, moving from one distraction to the next.’ If you don’t remove yourself from that, it will ‘suppress whatever train of thought you had’.

我回想起读过的所有科学研究，它们都指出我们如何把时间浪费在快速切换任务上。我意识到，在当今社会，我们大部分时间都无法集中注意力，但也没有走神。我们只是不断地浏览，陷入一种令人不满足的嗡嗡声中。当我问起这件事时，内森点了点头，告诉我他一直在想办法让手机停止推送那些他不想知道的信息通知。所有这些疯狂的数字干扰都在“分散我们的注意力，让我们无法思考”，并且“抑制了我们的默认模式网络……我认为我们几乎一直处于一种刺激驱动、刺激受限的环境中，不断地从一个干扰跳到另一个干扰。”如果你不让自己摆脱这种状态，它就会“抑制你原本的思路”。

So we aren’t just facing a crisis of lost spotlight focus – we are facing a crisis of lost mind-wandering. Together they are degrading the quality of our thinking. Without mind-wandering, we find it harder to make sense of the world – and in the jammed-up state of confusion that creates, we become even more vulnerable to the next source of distraction that comes along.

因此，我们面临的不仅仅是注意力分散的危机，更是思维漫游能力的丧失。两者共同降低了我们的思考质量。缺乏思维漫游，我们就更难理解这个世界——而由此产生的混乱状态，又使我们更容易受到下一个干扰源的影响。

When I interviewed him, Marcus Raichle – who made the breakthrough that opened up this whole area of science – had just given up playing in a symphony orchestra, at the age of eighty. He was an oboe player, and his favourite piece to perform was Dvořák’s Ninth Symphony. If you want to think about thinking itself, he told me, you should see it as like a symphony. ‘You’ve got two violin sections, violas, cellos, basses, woodwinds, brass, percussion – but it operates as a whole. It has rhythms.’ You need space in your life for the spotlight of focus – but alone, it would be like a solo oboe player on a bare stage, trying to play Beethoven. You need mind-wandering to activate the other instruments and to make the sweetest music. I thought I had come to Provincetown to learn to focus. I realised that, in fact, I was learning to think – and that required much more than the spotlight of focus.

我采访他的时候，马库斯·雷克尔——这位突破性发现开启了整个科学领域的先驱——刚刚在八十岁高龄时放弃了交响乐团的演奏生涯。他曾是一名双簧管演奏家，最喜欢演奏的曲目是德沃夏克的第九交响曲。他告诉我，如果你想思考思维本身，就应该把它想象成一首交响曲。“它有两个小提琴声部、中提琴、大提琴、低音提琴、木管乐器、铜管乐器、打击乐器——但它作为一个整体运作。它有节奏。”你需要生活中留出空间来集中注意力——但如果只有这样，就像一个独奏双簧管的演奏家站在空荡荡的舞台上，试图演奏贝多芬。你需要思绪游离来激活其他乐器，才能奏出最美妙的乐章。我原以为我来普罗温斯敦是为了学习如何集中注意力。但我意识到，事实上，我是在学习如何思考——而这需要的远不止是集中注意力。

On the long walks I try to go on now without any devices at all, I spend a lot of time reflecting on Marcus’s metaphor. A few days ago, I wondered if it could be taken further. If thinking is like a symphony that requires all these different kinds of thought, right now, the stage has been invaded. One of those heavy-metal bands who bite the heads off bats and spit them at the audience has charged the stage, and they are standing in front of the orchestra, screaming.

现在，我尽量不带任何电子设备进行长时间的散步，花很多时间思考马库斯的比喻。几天前，我在想这个比喻是否可以进一步延伸。如果思考就像一场交响乐，需要各种不同的思维方式，那么此刻，舞台已经被入侵了。一群重金属乐队冲上了舞台，他们冲在乐队前面，对着乐池大喊大叫，就像那种会咬掉蝙蝠头然后吐向观众的乐队一样。

And yet, as I dug deeper into the research on mind-wandering, I learned there is an exception to what I just explained – and it’s a big one. In fact, it is one you have probably experienced.

然而，当我深入研究走神现象时，我发现我刚才解释的情况存在一个例外——而且是一个很大的例外。事实上，你可能已经经历过这种情况。

In 2010 the Harvard scientists Professor Dan Gilbert and Dr Matthew Killingsworth developed a web app to study how people feel when they do all sorts of everyday things, from commuting to watching TV to exercising. People would get random prompts from the app that would ask: ‘What are you doing now?’ They would then be asked to rank how they felt. One of the things Dan and Matthew tracked was how often people found themselves mind-wandering – and what they discovered was surprising, given everything I had just learned. In general, when people are mind-wandering in our culture, they rank themselves as less happy than when they are doing almost any other activity. Even housework, for example, is associated with higher levels of happiness. They concluded: ‘A wandering mind is an unhappy mind.’

2010年，哈佛大学的科学家丹·吉尔伯特教授和马修·基林斯沃思博士开发了一款网络应用程序，用于研究人们在进行各种日常活动时的感受，例如通勤、看电视和锻炼。该应用程序会随机向用户提出问题：“你现在在做什么？”然后，用户需要对自己的感受进行评分。丹和马修追踪的一项指标是人们走神的频率——考虑到我刚刚了解到的所有信息，他们的发现令人惊讶。总的来说，在我们的文化中，当人们走神时，他们的幸福感低于进行几乎任何其他活动时。例如，即使是做家务，也会让人感到更快乐。他们的结论是：“走神的人不快乐。”

I thought about this a lot. Given that mind-wandering has been shown to have so many positive effects, why does it so often make us feel bad? There is a reason for this. Mind-wandering can easily descend into rumination. Most of us have had that feeling at some point or another – if you stop focusing and let your mind drift, you become jammed up with stressful thoughts. I thought back to my life at many points before Provincetown. When I was sitting on those trains, clucking in my own mind at the people who could sit staring out of the window while I manically worked and worked and worked, what was my mental state? Often, I saw now, I was loaded with stress and anxiety. Any attempt to relax my thinking would have let those bad feelings flood in. In Provincetown, by contrast, I had no stresses, and I felt safe – so my mind-wandering could float freely and do its positive work.

我反复思考过这个问题。既然研究表明走神有这么多积极作用，为什么它又常常让我们感觉不好呢？这其中是有原因的。走神很容易陷入沉思。我们大多数人或多或少都有过这种感觉——如果你停止专注，任由思绪飘荡，就会被各种压力重重的想法所困扰。我回想起去普罗温斯敦之前的许多人生阶段。当我坐在火车上，一边在心里暗骂那些可以悠闲地望着窗外的人，一边疯狂地工作、工作、再工作时，我的精神状态是怎样的呢？现在看来，我常常感到压力和焦虑。任何试图放松思考的尝试都会让这些负面情绪涌上心头。相比之下，在普罗温斯敦，我没有压力，感到很安全——所以我的思绪可以自由飘荡，发挥它积极的作用。

In situations of low stress and safety, mind-wandering will be a gift, a pleasure, a creative force. In situations of high stress or danger, mind-wandering will be a torment.

在压力较小且安全的环境下，走神是一种恩赐、一种乐趣、一种创造力。在压力较大或危险的环境下，走神则是一种折磨。

On the beach in the centre of Provincetown, just off the long strip of Commercial Street, there is a comically large blue wooden chair that faces the ocean. It must be eight feet tall, as if it is waiting for a giant. I would often sit on that chair, looking tiny as darkness fell, talking with people I had befriended around the town. Sometimes we would be silent, and simply watch the light change. The light in Provincetown is unlike the light anywhere else I have ever been. You are on a thin, narrow sandbar in the middle of the ocean, and as you sit on that beach, you are facing east. The sun is setting behind you in the west – but its light is flowing forward, onto the water in front of you, and reflecting back into your face. You seem to be flooded with the waning light of two sunsets. I watched it with the people I met, and I felt radically open, to them, and to the sun, and to the ocean.

在普罗温斯敦中心的海滩上，就在商业街那条长长的街道旁，摆放着一把滑稽的大蓝色木椅，正对着大海。它足有八英尺高，仿佛在等待着一位巨人。我常常坐在那把椅子上，夜幕降临时，我显得格外渺小，和我在镇上结识的朋友们聊天。有时我们会沉默不语，只是静静地看着光线的变化。普罗温斯敦的光线与我去过的任何其他地方都截然不同。你身处海洋中央一条狭长的沙洲上，坐在沙滩上，面向东方。太阳在你身后的西方缓缓落下——但它的光芒却向前流动，洒落在你面前的海面上，又反射回你的脸上。你仿佛被两场日落的余晖所包围。我和遇到的朋友们一起欣赏着这美景，我感到自己彻底敞开了心扉，敞开了心扉，敞开了心扉，敞开了心扉，敞开了心扉，敞开了心扉，敞开了心扉，敞开了心扉，敞开了心扉，敞开了心扉，敞开心扉，敞开心扉，敞开心扉。

One day, about ten weeks into my time in Provincetown, I was sitting alone in my friend Andrew’s house with one of his dogs, Bowie, at my feet. I was reading a novel and occasionally looking out towards the ocean, when I noticed that Andrew had left his laptop on a chair, open and glowing. On its screen, there was an internet browser. It had no password. There was the World Wide Web, glowing at me. You could look at the internet now, I thought to myself. You could look at anything you want – your social media, your email, the news. The thought made me feel heavy, and I made myself leave Andrew’s house.

在普罗温斯敦待了大约十周后的一天，我独自坐在朋友安德鲁的家里，他的狗鲍伊趴在我的脚边。我正读着小说，偶尔望向大海，这时我注意到安德鲁把笔记本电脑放在椅子上，屏幕开着，闪着光。屏幕上显示着一个浏览器，没有密码。万维网就在那里，闪闪发光地对着我。现在你可以上网了，我心想。你可以看任何你想看的东西——社交媒体、电子邮件、新闻。想到这里，我感到一阵沉重，于是强迫自己离开了安德鲁的家。

But the clock kept running down, and before long, I realised I had only two weeks left. I knew I had to go online to book a hotel for when I went back to Boston. In the Provincetown Library, there is a small bank of six computers that are open to the public. I had walked past them many times and I always averted my gaze, as if they were a toilet stall somebody had accidentally left open. I logged on and booked the hotel in two minutes, and then opened my email. I thought I knew what was about to happen. I spend around half an hour a day dealing with email in my normal life, spread from morning to night (and sometimes it’s drastically more). So I calculated that in the time I had been away, I had clocked up thirty-five hours’ worth of emails that I would now have to plough through over the next few months, scrambling to catch up. (When I had gone away, I left an auto-reply saying I was totally uncontactable.) I didn’t want it. I felt exhausted just thinking about it.

但时间一分一秒地流逝，很快我就意识到只剩下两周了。我知道我必须上网预订回波士顿的酒店。普罗温斯敦图书馆里有一小排六台电脑，对外开放。我以前无数次路过那里，总是刻意避开目光，仿佛它们是有人不小心没关的厕所隔间门。我登录电脑，两分钟就订好了酒店，然后打开邮箱。我想我大概知道接下来会发生什么。平时我每天要花大约半小时处理邮件，从早到晚都有（有时甚至更多）。所以我算了一下，在我离开的这段时间里，我积攒了相当于35个小时的邮件，接下来几个月我得拼命地处理这些邮件，才能赶上进度。（我离开的时候设置了自动回复，说我完全联系不上。）我不想这样。光是想想就觉得精疲力竭。

But then something strange happened. I opened my inbox nervously and skimmed through my emails – and there was hardly anything there. In two hours, I had seen everything. The world had accepted my absence with a shrug. I realised that email breeds email, and if you just stop, it stops. I would like to say I felt calmed and soothed by this. In truth, I felt affronted – like my ego had been poked with a knitting needle. All this mania, all these demands on my time, I realised, made me feel important. I wanted in a sudden rush to send emails in order to get emails back – to feel needed again. I clicked over to my Twitter feed. I had precisely the same number of Twitter followers that I had when I left. My absence had been entirely unnoticed. I wandered away from the library and returned to the things that had given me nourishment in Provincetown – long passages of writing flowed from me; the ocean washed over my feet; my friends sat with me and talked all night. I tried to forget the wound to my ego.

但随后发生了一件奇怪的事。我忐忑不安地打开邮箱，快速浏览邮件——结果发现几乎什么都没有。短短两个小时，我已经把所有邮件都看完了。世界仿佛耸耸肩，接受了我的缺席。我意识到，邮件会滋生更多邮件，如果你停止发送，它就会停止。我想说，这让我感到平静和放松。但实际上，我感到受到了冒犯——就像我的自尊心被一根毛衣针戳了一下。我意识到，所有这些忙碌，所有这些对我时间的占用，都让我觉得自己很重要。我突然很想发送邮件，以便收到回复——再次感受到被需要。我打开了推特。我的推特粉丝数量和我离开时一模一样。我的缺席似乎完全无人察觉。我离开了图书馆，回到了普罗温斯敦那些滋养我的事物中——长篇大论的文字从我笔下流淌而出；海水轻抚着我的双脚；朋友们陪我彻夜长谈。我试图忘记自尊心受到的伤害。

On my last day in Provincetown, I took a boat out to Long Point, which is the tip of the tip of Cape Cod, a yellow crest of sand and sea. There, I could look back over the whole of the place where I had spent my summer, stretching from the Pilgrim Monument all the way down to Hyannis. It was a peculiar feeling, to see the boundaries of my summer in one single scan of the horizon. I felt more still and centred than I ever had before in my life.

在普罗温斯敦的最后一天，我乘船前往长岬，那是科德角最南端的尖端，一片金黄色的沙滩与海水交织而成的岬角。在那里，我可以回望整个夏天我度过的地方，从朝圣者纪念碑一直延伸到海恩尼斯。那种感觉很奇妙，只需一眼就能看到我整个夏天的边界。我感到前所未有的平静和安宁。

You can’t just go back and live the way you used to, I told myself, sitting in the shadow of the lighthouse. It’s not hard. This summer has shown you how to do it. I demonstrated pre-commitment by cutting myself off. You can show pre-commitment in your everyday life now. I already owned the tools. On my laptop, I have a program called Freedom. It’s easy – you download it, and you tell it you want it to deny you access to a specific website, or to the entire internet, for an amount of time you designate, from five minutes to a week. You hit the button, and no matter what you do, your laptop won’t get online. And for my phone, I owned something called a kSafe. Again, it’s simple – it’s a little plastic safe that opens at the top. You put your phone in it, and you put the lid on, and you twist the top to determine how long you want to shut your phone away for. Then it’s gone – locked away, so you’d have to smash it with a hammer to get the phone out. Using these two devices, I said to myself, you can recreate Provincetown wherever you are. You can use your phone and the internet part of your laptop for maybe ten or fifteen minutes a day.

“你不能再像以前那样生活了，”我坐在灯塔的阴影下对自己说。“这并不难。这个夏天已经教会了我该怎么做。我通过切断与外界的联系来展现预先承诺。你现在就可以在日常生活中展现预先承诺。我已经拥有了所需的工具。我的笔记本电脑上有一个叫做Freedom的程序。它很简单——你下载它，然后告诉它你想在指定的时间内（从五分钟到一周不等）禁止访问某个特定的网站，或者整个互联网。你点击按钮，无论你做什么，你的笔记本电脑都无法上网。我的手机上有一个叫做kSafe的东西。同样，它很简单——它是一个顶部可以打开的小塑料保险箱。你把手机放进去，盖上盖子，然后旋转顶部来决定你想把手机锁起来多长时间。”然后它就没了——被锁起来了，你得用锤子砸开才能把手机取出来。我心想，有了这两样东西，无论身在何处，你都能重现普罗温斯敦的氛围。你每天只需用手机和笔记本电脑上网十分钟或十五分钟就行了。

That evening, I gave away the small mountain of books I had read, and boarded the ferry to Boston. I got violently seasick on the journey back, and it felt like a rude metaphor for how I felt about returning to the online world. I reclaimed my phone from my friend the next day, and I lay on my hotel bed staring at it. It seemed strangely alien now – even the Apple font looked unfamiliar. I found myself flicking between icons, looking at various programs and websites. I looked at social media and thought, I don’t want this. I flicked through Twitter and felt like I had stood on a termites’ nest. When I looked up, three hours had gone.

那天晚上，我把读过的书堆成小山似的都送人了，然后登上了去波士顿的渡轮。回程的路上我晕船晕得厉害，这感觉就像是对我重返网络世界的一种粗暴的隐喻。第二天我从朋友那里拿回了手机，躺在酒店的床上盯着它看。现在它看起来如此陌生——就连苹果的字体都让我觉得很不熟悉。我不由自主地在各种图标间切换，浏览着不同的程序和网站。我看了看社交媒体，心想：我不想要这些。我快速浏览了一下推特，感觉就像踩到了白蚁窝。当我抬起头时，三个小时已经过去了。

I left it behind and went to eat. When I got back, people had started replying to my emails and texts, and despite myself, I felt a little rush of affirmation. In the next few weeks, I started to post on social media – and I felt myself become cruder and meaner than I had been in the summer. I made snarky comments. The complexity and compassion I had felt in Provincetown was, I felt, being replaced by something thinner. At moments I didn’t like what I was saying. And then I felt the slow rush of approval, the retweets, the likes. I want to tell you that I learned the lessons of my time in Provincetown in a linear and life-affirming way, but that would be a lie. What happened was more complex. I left Provincetown in August, and I used Freedom and the kSafe, and slowly it slipped, and by December, the Screen Time on my iPhone indicated that I was spending four hours a day on my phone. I told myself that includes using Google Maps to navigate the city, and the hours I spent listening to podcasts and the radio and audiobooks. But I felt ashamed when I thought of it. I wasn’t quite back to where I had been at the start, but I had clearly slid into distraction and disruption.

我把手机留在了那里，去吃饭了。回来后，人们开始回复我的邮件和短信，我不由自主地感到一丝被认可的感觉。接下来的几周，我开始在社交媒体上发帖——我感觉自己比夏天的时候更加粗鲁刻薄。我发表了一些尖酸刻薄的评论。我在普罗温斯敦感受到的那种复杂和同情心，我觉得正在被某种更单薄的东西所取代。有时，我不喜欢自己说的话。然后，我又感受到了缓慢涌来的认可，转发，点赞。我想告诉你，我在普罗温斯敦的经历是以一种线性且积极的方式让我学到东西的，但这并非事实。实际情况要复杂得多。我八月份离开了普罗温斯敦，开始使用Freedom和kSafe，但情况逐渐恶化，到了十二月，我iPhone上的屏幕使用时间显示，我每天在手机上花费四个小时。我告诉自己，这其中也包括使用谷歌地图导航，以及我花在听播客、广播和有声读物上的时间。但想到这些，我还是感到羞愧。我还没完全恢复到最初的状态，但我显然已经陷入了分心和混乱之中。

I felt like a failure. I had a strong sensation that something was pulling me down. Then I told myself: You’re making excuses for yourself. You are doing this, nobody else. These are your failings. And I felt weak. I had gained a lot of insights in Provincetown – but I felt they were fragile, and easily broken by something bigger, something I didn’t quite yet understand.

我感觉自己像个失败者。我强烈地感觉到有什么东西在拉扯着我。然后我告诉自己：你是在为自己找借口。这一切都是你自己造成的，与他人无关。这些都是你的失败。我感到自己很脆弱。我在普罗温斯敦学到了很多东西——但我感觉它们很脆弱，很容易被某种更大的、我尚未完全理解的东西击垮。

I wanted to know what was preventing me from doing what I wanted, in the better part of myself, to do. I discovered that the answer is more complex than we have been led to believe, and has many facets – and I learned about the first of them when I went to Silicon Valley.

我想知道究竟是什么阻碍了我去做我内心真正想做的事。我发现答案远比我们之前认为的要复杂得多，它包含许多方面——而我去硅谷的经历，让我了解了其中的第一个方面。

# ↩

6 Cause Six: The Rise of Technology That Can Track and Manipulate You (Part One)

第六个原因：能够追踪和操控你的技术的兴起（第一部分）

James Williams told me I had made a fundamental mistake in Provincetown. He was a senior Google strategist for many years, and he left, horrified, to go to Oxford University, to study human attention, and figure out what his colleagues in Silicon Valley have done to it. He told me a digital detox is ‘not the solution, for the same reason that wearing a gas mask for two days a week outside isn’t the answer to pollution. It might, for a short period of time, keep, at an individual level, certain effects at bay. But it’s not sustainable, and it doesn’t address the systemic issues.’ He said our attention is being deeply altered by huge invasive forces in the wider society. Saying the solution is primarily to personally abstain is just ‘pushing it back onto the individual’, he said, when ‘it’s really the environmental changes that will really make the difference’.

詹姆斯·威廉姆斯告诉我，我在普罗温斯敦犯了一个根本性的错误。他曾是谷歌的高级战略师多年，后来他震惊地离开了谷歌，前往牛津大学研究人类注意力，试图弄清硅谷的同行们究竟对人类注意力做了什么。他告诉我，数字排毒“并非解决之道，就像每周在户外戴两天防毒面具并不能解决污染问题一样。它或许能在短期内，从个人层面缓解某些影响，但这不可持续，也无法解决系统性问题。” 他说，我们的注意力正受到更广泛的社会中巨大侵入性力量的深刻影响。他认为，把解决方案主要放在个人戒除电子产品上，只是“把责任推回给个人”，而“真正能带来改变的是环境的改变”。

For a long time I didn’t really understand what this meant. What would changing our environment entail, when it came to attention, if not each of us trying to change our own personal behaviour? The answer slowly became clear to me when I met with many people who had designed crucial aspects of the world in which we now live. In the hills of San Francisco and the hot, arid streets of Palo Alto, I realised that there are six ways in which our technology, as it currently works, is harming our ability to pay attention – and that these causes are united by one deeper underlying force that needs to be overcome.

很长一段时间，我都不太明白这意味着什么。如果我们每个人都不去改变自己的行为，那么在注意力方面，改变环境又意味着什么呢？当我与许多参与设计我们如今生活世界关键方面的人士会面时，答案才逐渐清晰起来。在旧金山的山丘上，在帕洛阿尔托炎热干燥的街道上，我意识到，我们目前的技术运作方式正在从六个方面损害我们的注意力——而这些原因都源于一个更深层次的潜在力量，我们需要克服它。

One of the first people to guide me on this journey was Tristan Harris, another former Google engineer, who, after I had been interviewing him for several years, became globally famous for appearing in the viral Netflix documentary The Social Dilemma . That film explored a whole range of ways in which social media, as it is currently designed, can be destructive. I wanted to tease out something the film largely didn’t explore – its effect on our focus. To grasp it, I think it helps to know Tristan’s own story, and what he witnessed at the heart of the machine that is repatterning the world’s attention.

在我的这段探索之旅中，最早给予我指导的人之一是特里斯坦·哈里斯，他也是一位前谷歌工程师。在我采访他几年之后，他因出演Netflix爆款纪录片《社交困境》而名声大噪。这部影片探讨了社交媒体目前的设计方式可能带来的种种破坏性影响。而我想挖掘的是影片中鲜少涉及的一点——它对我们注意力的影响。为了理解这一点，我认为了解特里斯坦的个人经历，以及他在重塑世界注意力的这台机器核心所目睹的一切，会很有帮助。

In the early 1990s, in the town of Santa Rosa, California, a little boy with a bowl haircut and a bright golden bow tie was learning magic. Tristan was seven years old when he first tried out one of the most basic tricks. He would ask you to hand him a coin, and then – poof! It was gone. After he mastered more tricks, he put on a magic show for his elementary-school class, and then – to his glee – he was selected to go to a magic camp out in the hills, where he was taught for a week by professional magicians. It seemed to him like a real-life Jedi training camp.

上世纪九十年代初，在加利福尼亚州圣罗莎镇，一个留着锅盖头、系着金色领结的小男孩正在学习魔术。特里斯坦七岁时第一次尝试了一个最基本的魔术：他会让你递给他一枚硬币，然后——噗！硬币就消失了。掌握了更多魔术后，他为小学班级表演了一场魔术，之后——令他欣喜若狂的是——他被选中去山里参加一个魔术训练营，在那里接受专业魔术师为期一周的指导。对他来说，这简直就像一个现实版的绝地武士训练营。

He discovered, at this young age, the most important fact about magic. He explained years later: ‘It’s really about the limits of attention.’ The job of a magician is – at heart – to manipulate your focus. That coin didn’t really vanish – but your attention was somewhere else when the magician moved it, so when your focus comes back to the original spot, you’re amazed. To learn magic is to learn to manipulate someone’s attention without them even realising it – and once the magician controls their focus, Tristan realised, he can do what he wants. One of the things that he was taught at camp is that a person’s susceptibility to magic has nothing to do with their intelligence. ‘It’s about something more subtle,’ he said later. It’s ‘about the weaknesses, or the limits, or the blind spots, or the biases that we’re all trapped inside of’.

他在年幼时就发现了魔术最重要的真相。多年后他解释说：“这其实关乎注意力的极限。”魔术师的工作——本质上——就是操控你的注意力。那枚硬币并没有真的消失——只是当魔术师移动它时，你的注意力转移到了别处，所以当你的注意力重新回到原点时，你会感到惊讶。学习魔术就是学会如何在不知不觉中操控他人的注意力——一旦魔术师控制了他们的注意力，特里斯坦意识到，他就能为所欲为。他在夏令营学到的一点是，一个人对魔术的敏感度与智力无关。“这关乎一些更微妙的东西，”他后来说道，“关乎我们每个人都身陷其中的弱点、局限、盲点或偏见。”

Magic, in other words, is the study of the limits of the human mind. You think you control your attention; you think that if somebody messes with it, you will know, and you’ll be able to spot and resist it right away, but, in reality, we are fallible sacks of meat, and we are fallible in predictable ways that can be figured out by magicians and messed with.

换句话说，魔术是对人类思维极限的研究。你以为你能掌控自己的注意力；你以为如果有人干扰你的注意力，你会立刻察觉并加以抵抗，但实际上，我们不过是会犯错的血肉之躯，而且我们的错误方式是可以预测的，魔术师可以摸清这些规律并加以利用。

As he got to know better and better magicians – eventually befriending one of the best in the world, Derren Brown – Tristan learned something he found both remarkable and disconcerting. It is possible to manipulate your attention to such a degree that a magician can, in many cases, turn you into his puppet. He can make you choose whatever he wants you to choose, while all along you think you’re simply using your own free will. When Tristan first said this to me, I thought he was overstating his case, so he introduced me to another of his magician friends, James Brown. Tristan told me James would show me what it meant. I’ll give you one example. When we sat together, James showed me a standard pack of cards. He said See? Some of them are red, and some of them are black, and they are all mixed up together. Then he turned the cards so the colours were facing towards him, and I couldn’t see them any more. He told me he was going to get me to sort them neatly into two piles – one black, one red – without me ever getting to look at the colour of the cards for myself. It was, obviously, impossible. How could I sort cards I couldn’t see?

随着他结识的魔术师越来越多——最终与世界顶尖魔术师之一的德伦·布朗成为了朋友——特里斯坦了解到一些令他既惊叹又不安的事情。魔术师可以如此巧妙地操控你的注意力，以至于在很多情况下，他们能把你变成自己的傀儡。他可以让你做出他想让你做的任何选择，而你却一直以为自己是在行使自由意志。特里斯坦第一次跟我说起这件事时，我觉得他有点夸张，于是他又把我介绍给了他的另一位魔术师朋友詹姆斯·布朗。特里斯坦告诉我，詹姆斯会向我展示这意味着什么。我举个例子。我们坐在一起时，詹姆斯给我看了一副普通的扑克牌。他说：“看到了吗？有些是红色的，有些是黑色的，它们都混在一起了。”然后他把牌翻过来，让颜色朝向他，我就再也看不到颜色了。他告诉我，他要让我把这些牌整齐地分成两堆——一堆是黑色的，一堆是红色的——而且我根本没机会自己看牌的颜色。这显然是不可能的。我怎么可能把看不见的牌分类呢？

He told me to look into his eyes, and – entirely using my own free will – to tell him whether to put the next card into a pile on the left, or a pile on the right. So I gave him my orders – left, left, right, and so on – according to what I was confident were my own random whims. At the end, he lifted up the piles of cards and showed them to me. The red cards were neatly in one pile; the black cards were in the other.

他让我看着他的眼睛，然后——完全凭我的自由意志——告诉他下一张牌应该放在左边的牌堆还是右边的牌堆。于是我按照自己确信是随意的想法，不断地给他下达指令——左边、左边、右边，如此反复。最后，他拿起牌堆给我看。红牌整齐地放在一堆，黑牌放在另一堆。

I was baffled. How did he do it? He eventually told me he had been subtly guiding my choices. He did it again, and said he would do it a little more crudely this time, to see if I could spot it. Finally – and he had to be pretty blatant – I saw it. When he told me to pick at the next card, he indicated very slightly with his eyes to the left or to the right – and I always chose in the way he unconsciously guided me to. Everyone always does, he told me. Later, Tristan explained to me that this is a core insight of magic – you can manipulate people and they don’t even know it’s happening. They will swear to you that they made their own free choices – as I would have about those cards.

我当时百思不得其解。他是怎么做到的？他最终告诉我，他一直在暗中引导我的选择。他又试了一次，说这次会更明显一些，看看我能不能发现。最后——他不得不表现得相当露骨——我终于明白了。当他让我选下一张牌时，他用眼神轻轻地向左或向右示意——而我总是按照他无意识引导的方向去选。他告诉我，每个人都会这样。后来，特里斯坦向我解释说，这是魔术的核心要义——你可以操纵别人，而他们甚至都不知道发生了什么。他们会信誓旦旦地告诉你，他们的选择都是出于自己的自由意志——就像我当初选择那些牌一样。

One morning, in his office in San Francisco, Tristan leaned forward and said to me: ‘How does a magician do their work? It works because they don’t have to know your strengths – they just have to know your weaknesses. How well do you know your weaknesses?’ I wanted to believe I understood my weaknesses very well, but Tristan shook his head gently. ‘If people did know their weaknesses,’ he said, ‘then magic wouldn’t work.’

一天早上，在旧金山的办公室里，特里斯坦俯身靠近我，问道：“魔术师是怎么表演的？他们的表演之所以有效，是因为他们不需要了解你的优点——他们只需要了解你的缺点。你对自己的缺点了解多少？” 我想相信自己非常了解自己的缺点，但特里斯坦轻轻地摇了摇头。“如果人们真的了解自己的缺点，”他说，“那么魔术就行不通了。”

Magicians play on these weaknesses to delight and entertain us. As Tristan grew up, he became part of another group of people who were figuring out our weaknesses to manipulate us – but they had very different goals.

魔术师正是利用这些弱点来取悦和娱乐我们。随着特里斯坦长大，他也加入了另一群人，这些人也在研究我们的弱点并试图操纵我们——但他们的目的却截然不同。

It was in his first year at Stanford University, in 2002, that Tristan first heard whispers of a course on campus that took place in a mysterious-sounding place known as the Persuasive Technologies Lab. It was, the rumours went, a place where scientists were figuring out how to design technology that could change your behaviour – without you even knowing you were being changed. In his teens Tristan had become obsessed with coding, and he had already been an intern at Apple after his freshman year at Stanford, designing a piece of code that is still used in many of your devices today. This secretive and much-discussed course, he learned, was about taking everything scientists had discovered over the twentieth century about how to change other people’s behaviour, and figuring out how the students could integrate these forms of persuasion into their code.

2002年，特里斯坦在斯坦福大学一年级时，第一次听说校园里有一门课，授课地点听起来很神秘，叫做“说服技术实验室”。据说，科学家们在那里研究如何设计一种能够改变人们行为的技术——而且人们甚至不会意识到自己正在被改变。特里斯坦十几岁时就痴迷于编程，在斯坦福大学一年级结束后，他曾在苹果公司实习，编写了一段至今仍在许多设备中使用的代码。他了解到，这门神秘而又备受关注的课程，是将科学家们在20世纪发现的所有关于如何改变他人行为的知识，与学生们如何将这些说服技巧融入到他们的代码中。

The course was taught by a warm, upbeat Mormon behavioural scientist in his forties named Professor B.J. Fogg. At the start of each day, he would take out a stuffed frog and a cuddly monkey and introduce them to the class, and then he would play on his ukulele. Whenever he wanted the group to break or wrap up, he would tap on a toy xylophone. B.J. explained to students that computers had the potential to be far more persuasive than people. They can, he believed, ‘be more persistent than human beings, [and] offer greater anonymity’, and ‘go where humans cannot go or may not be welcome’. Soon, he was sure, they would be changing the lives of everyone – persuading us persistently, throughout the day. He had previously worked on a course dedicated to ‘the psychology of mind control’. He assigned to Tristan and his other students a small mound of books which explained hundreds of psychological insights and tricks that had been discovered about how to manipulate human beings and to get them to do what you want. It was a treasure trove. Many of them were based on the philosophy of B.F. Skinner, the man who, as I had learned earlier, had found a way to get pigeons and rats and pigs to do whatever he wanted by offering the right ‘reinforcements’ for their behaviour. After years of falling out of fashion, his ideas were back with full force.

这门课是由一位四十多岁、热情开朗的摩门教行为科学家B.J.福格教授教授的。每天上课伊始，他都会拿出一只毛绒青蛙和一只毛绒猴子，向学生们介绍它们，然后弹奏他的尤克里里。每当他想让大家休息或结束课程时，他就会敲击一个玩具木琴。B.J.向学生们解释说，计算机比人类更有说服力。他认为，计算机“比人类更执着，[并且]能提供更高的匿名性”，而且“可以去到人类去不了或不受欢迎的地方”。他确信，不久之后，计算机就会改变每个人的生活——整天不断地影响着我们。他之前曾开设过一门专门研究“精神控制心理学”的课程。他给特里斯坦和其他学生布置了一小堆书，这些书解释了数百种关于如何操纵人类并让他们按照你的意愿行事的心理学见解和技巧。那简直是个宝库。其中许多内容都基于B.F.斯金纳的哲学思想。我之前了解到，斯金纳找到了一种方法，通过提供适当的“强化物”来让鸽子、老鼠和猪按照他的意愿行事。他的思想在沉寂多年后，如今又强势回归。

‘It really woke up the magic part of me,’ Tristan told me. ‘I was like – oh wow, there really are these invisible rules that govern what people do. And if there are rules that govern what people do, that’s power. That’s like Isaac Newton discovering the laws of physics. It felt like somebody’s showing me the code – the code of how you can influence people. I remember the experience of sitting there in the graduate area of campus reading those books over the weekends, and underlining furiously these passages, and just being like – oh my God, I can’t even believe that works.’ He was so intoxicated by the excitement of it that, he says, ‘I will admit, I don’t think the ethical bells were firing in my brain yet.’

“它真的唤醒了我内心深处的魔法，”特里斯坦告诉我。“我当时想——哇，原来真的存在一些无形的规则支配着人们的行为。如果真的存在支配人们行为的规则，那就是力量。这就像艾萨克·牛顿发现了物理定律一样。感觉就像有人在向我展示密码——影响他人的密码。我记得当时周末坐在校园的研究生区里读那些书，疯狂地划着重点，然后就想——我的天哪，我简直不敢相信这真的有效。” 他说，他当时完全沉浸在兴奋之中，“我承认，我当时脑子里还没有响起任何道德警钟。”

As part of the class, he was paired with a young man named Mike Krieger, and they were tasked with designing an app. Tristan had been thinking for a while about something named seasonal affective disorder – a condition where, if you are stuck in gloomy weather for a long time, you are more likely to become depressed. How, they asked, could technology help with that? They came up with an app called Send the Sunshine. Two friends would choose to be connected through it, and it would track where they both were and the online weather reports for their locations. If the app realised that your friend was starved of sunshine, and you had some, it would prompt you to take a photo of the sun and send it to him. It showed that somebody cared; and it sent some sunshine your way. It was sweet, and simple, and it helped to spur Mike and another person on the course, named Kevin Systrom, to think about the power of sharing photographs online. They were already thinking about another of the key lessons of the class, taken from B. F. Skinner: build in immediate reinforcements. If you want to shape the user’s behaviour, make sure he gets hearts and likes right away. Using these principles, they launched a new app of their own. They named it Instagram.

作为课程的一部分，他与一位名叫迈克·克里格的年轻人结对，他们的任务是设计一款应用程序。特里斯坦一直在思考一种叫做季节性情感障碍的疾病——如果长时间处于阴雨天气中，就更容易患上抑郁症。他们思考着，科技能如何帮助解决这个问题？他们开发了一款名为“传递阳光”的应用程序。两位朋友可以通过这款应用连接，应用会追踪他们的位置以及各自所在地的在线天气预报。如果应用检测到你的朋友渴望阳光，而你正好有阳光，它就会提示你拍一张太阳的照片并发送给他。这既表达了你的关心，也为你带来了阳光。这款应用既温馨又简单，它启发了迈克和另一位名叫凯文·斯特罗姆的同学思考在线分享照片的力量。他们已经开始思考这门课程的另一个关键要点，这个要点来自B·F·斯金纳：建立即时强化机制。如果你想引导用户的行为，就要确保他能立刻获得点赞和喜爱。他们运用这些原则，推出了自己的新应用，并将其命名为 Instagram。

The class was filled with people who were going to use the techniques B.J. taught to change how we live our lives, and B.J. was quickly dubbed ‘the millionaire maker’. But something was starting to nag at Tristan. After a while, he noticed he had become obsessed with checking his email. He would do it repetitively, mindlessly, again and again, and he felt his attention span was beginning to atrophy. He realised, he told me, that the email app he was using ‘operates on a bunch of different levers, and it’s very powerful, and it sucks, and it’s super-stressful, and it ruins hours and hours of people’s lives’. He had been learning in the Persuasive Technologies Lab to hack people, but he came to ask a disconcerting question: am I somehow being hacked by other tech designers myself? He wasn’t yet sure how they might be doing it – but he began to have a strange feeling about it. B.J. taught his students that they should only use these powers for good, and he laced ethical debates throughout his course. Yet Tristan was going to start to wonder – were these secrets, this code, actually being used ethically in the real world?

班上坐满了准备运用B.J.教授的技巧来改变生活方式的人，B.J.很快就被冠以“百万富翁制造者”的称号。但特里斯坦开始感到有些不安。过了一段时间，他发现自己对查看电子邮件产生了痴迷。他会一遍又一遍地、机械地重复查看，感觉自己的注意力开始逐渐丧失。他告诉我，他意识到自己使用的邮件应用程序“运作机制复杂，功能强大，但同时也很糟糕，让人压力巨大，浪费了人们大量的时间”。他一直在说服技术实验室学习如何“入侵”他人，但现在他却产生了一个令人不安的问题：我是否也被其他技术设计师“入侵”了？他还不确定他们是如何做到的——但他开始对此感到一种莫名的不安。 B.J.教导学生们应该只将这些力量用于行善，并在他的课程中穿插了许多伦理辩论。然而，特里斯坦开始怀疑——这些秘密，这些准则，在现实世界中真的能被合乎伦理地使用吗？

In the final class Tristan attended, all the students discussed ways in which these persuasive technologies could be used in the future. One of the other groups had come up with an eye-catching plan. They asked: ‘What if in future you had a profile of every single person on earth?’ As a designer, you would track all the information they offer up on social media and build up a detailed profile of them. It’s not just the simple stuff – their gender, or age, or interests. It would be something deeper. This would be a psychological profile – figuring out how their personality works, and the best ways to persuade them. It would know if the user was an optimist or pessimist, if they were open to new experiences or they were prone to nostalgia – it would figure out dozens of characteristics they have.

在特里斯坦参加的最后一节课上，所有学生都讨论了这些说服性技术在未来可能的应用方式。其中一个小组提出了一个引人注目的方案。他们问道：“如果未来你能拥有地球上每个人的个人资料，会怎么样？”作为一名设计师，你需要追踪他们在社交媒体上发布的所有信息，并建立起一份详细的个人档案。这不仅仅是性别、年龄或兴趣等基本信息，而是更深层次的心理分析——了解他们的性格特点，以及如何才能更好地说服他们。这份档案会知道用户是乐观主义者还是悲观主义者，是乐于接受新鲜事物还是容易怀旧——它会分析出用户数十种不同的性格特征。

Think, the class wondered out loud, about how you could target people if you knew this much about them. Think about how you could change them. When a politician or a company wants to persuade you, they could pay a social-media company to perfectly target their message just for you. It was the birth of an idea. Years later, when it was revealed that the campaign for Donald Trump had paid a company named Cambridge Analytica to do exactly that, Tristan would think of that final class in Stanford. ‘This was the class that freaked me out,’ he told me. ‘I remember saying – this is horribly concerning.’

同学们纷纷议论纷纷，思考着：如果对一个人了解这么多，该如何精准地进行宣传？该如何改变他们？当政客或公司想要说服你时，他们可以付费给社交媒体公司，让他们精准地向你推送信息。一个想法由此诞生。多年后，当唐纳德·特朗普的竞选团队被曝出曾付费给一家名为剑桥分析（Cambridge Analytica）的公司来做同样的事情时，特里斯坦想起了他在斯坦福的最后一堂课。“这堂课让我感到毛骨悚然，”他告诉我，“我记得当时我说——这太令人担忧了。”

But Tristan had a deep belief in the power of tech to do good. So he took what he had learned at Stanford and designed an app with a straightforward positive purpose. He was trying to stop one of the ways the web screws with our attention. Let’s say you are checking out the CNN site, and you start to read a news story about Northern Ireland, a topic you don’t know much about. Normally, you will then open a new window and begin googling for info – and before you know it, you vanish down a rabbit hole and emerge half an hour later, lost in articles and videos about a totally different topic (usually cats playing the piano). Tristan’s app was designed so that in this situation, you could do something different: you highlight any phrase (say, ‘Northern Ireland’), and it would pull up a simple pop-up window giving you a straightforward summary of the topic. No clicking away from the site; no rabbit holes. Your attention is preserved. The app did well – it started to be used by thousands of websites, including the New York Times , and quite soon, Google made a substantial offer to buy the whole thing and for Tristan to come and work for them. They told him it was so he could integrate it into their web browser, Chrome, and make people less distracted. He jumped at the chance.

但特里斯坦深信科技拥有造福人类的力量。于是，他运用在斯坦福大学所学的知识，设计了一款目标明确、旨在造福大众的应用程序。他试图阻止网络分散我们注意力的一种方式。假设你正在浏览CNN网站，开始阅读一篇关于北爱尔兰的新闻报道，而你对这个话题并不了解。通常情况下，你会打开一个新窗口，开始搜索相关信息——结果不知不觉就陷入了无尽的搜索，半小时后才从中抽身，发现自己沉浸在完全不同的主题（通常是猫弹钢琴）的文章和视频中。特里斯坦的应用程序旨在解决这种情况：你可以选择选中任何短语（比如“北爱尔兰”），它会弹出一个简单的窗口，为你提供该主题的简明摘要。无需离开网站；无需陷入无尽的搜索。你的注意力得以保留。这款应用发展势头良好——数千家网站开始使用它，其中包括《纽约时报》。很快，谷歌就开出了高价，不仅想收购整个应用，还想让特里斯坦加入他们。谷歌告诉他，这样做是为了让他把应用整合到他们的浏览器Chrome中，从而减少用户的注意力分散。特里斯坦欣然接受了这个机会。

It is hard to convey, Tristan believes, quite what it was like to go to work for Google at that moment in history, in 2011. Every day, the company he worked for – from its base, the Googleplex in Palo Alto – was shaping and reshaping how 1 billion people navigated their way through the world: what they got to see, and what they didn’t. He told one audience later: ‘I want you to imagine walking into a room. A control room, with a bunch of people, a hundred people, hunched over a desk with little dials – and that that control room will shape the thoughts and feelings of a billion people. This might sound like science fiction, but this actually exists right now, today. I know, because I used to work in one of those control rooms.’

特里斯坦认为，很难用语言来描述2011年那个历史时刻在谷歌工作是怎样的感受。他所在的公司——总部设在帕洛阿尔托的谷歌园区——每天都在塑造和重塑着10亿人看待世界的方式：他们能看到什么，看不到什么。他后来对一群听众说：“想象一下，你走进一个房间。一个控制室，里面挤满了人，一百来个人，都弓着背坐在摆满小旋钮的桌子前——而这个控制室将塑造10亿人的思想和情感。这听起来像是科幻小说，但它现在就真实存在。我知道，因为我曾经在其中一个控制室工作过。”

Tristan was assigned for a while to work on the development of Gmail, Google’s email system – precisely the app that was driving him wild, and that he suspected might be using some manipulative tricks he hadn’t yet figured out. Even as he worked on it, he would obsessively check his email, making him less focused, and whenever he looked at a new message, he found it took him a long time to get his mind back to where it had been before. He started trying to think through how you might design a system of email that was less prone to nuking your attention – but whenever he tried to discuss this idea with his colleagues, the conversation didn’t seem to go far. At Google, he quickly learned, success was measured, in the main, by what was called ‘engagement’ – which was defined as minutes and hours of eyeballs on the product. More engagement was good; less engagement was bad. This was for a simple reason. The longer you make people look at their phones, the more advertising they see – and therefore the more money Google gets. Tristan’s co-workers were decent people, struggling with their own tech distractions – but the incentives seemed to lead only one way: you should always design products that ‘engage’ the maximum number of people, because engagement equals more dollars, and disengagement equals fewer dollars.

特里斯坦曾被安排参与谷歌电子邮件系统Gmail的开发工作一段时间——而这正是让他抓狂的应用，他怀疑它可能使用了某些他尚未发现的操控手段。即使在开发过程中，他也会不停地查看邮件，导致注意力难以集中。每当他查看一封新邮件时，他都发现自己需要很长时间才能回过神来。他开始思考如何设计一个不易分散用户注意力的电子邮件系统——但每当他试图与同事讨论这个想法时，对话似乎都进展缓慢。在谷歌，他很快了解到，衡量成功的主要标准是所谓的“用户参与度”——也就是用户在产品上花费的时间（以分钟或小时为单位）。用户参与度越高越好，用户参与度越低越糟糕。原因很简单：用户盯着手机的时间越长，他们看到的广告就越多——因此，谷歌赚的钱也就越多。特里斯坦的同事们都是好人，他们也都在努力应对科技带来的种种干扰——但激励机制似乎只指向一个方向：你应该始终设计能够“吸引”最多人的产品，因为参与度越高，收入就越多；而缺乏参与度则意味着收入减少。

With each month that passed, Tristan became more startled by the casualness with which the attention of a billion people was being corroded at Google and the other Big Tech companies. One day he would hear an engineer excitedly saying: ‘Why don’t we make it buzz your phone every time we get an email?’ Everyone would be thrilled – and a few weeks later, all over the world, phones began to buzz in pockets, and more people found themselves looking at Gmail more times a day. The engineers were always looking for new ways to suck eyeballs onto their program and keep them there. Day after day, he would watch as engineers proposed more interruptions to people’s lives – more vibrations, more alerts, more tricks – and they would be congratulated.

随着时间推移，特里斯坦越来越震惊于谷歌和其他大型科技公司是如何轻而易举地侵蚀十亿用户的注意力。有一天，他听到一位工程师兴奋地说：“为什么我们不让手机在每次收到邮件时都震动一下呢？”大家都为此欢呼雀跃——几周后，世界各地的人们开始在口袋里听到手机震动，越来越多的人发现自己每天查看Gmail的次数也越来越多。工程师们总是想方设法吸引用户的眼球，并让他们长时间停留在他们的程序上。日复一日，他眼睁睁地看着工程师们提出更多干扰人们生活的方案——更多的震动、更多的提醒、更多的花招——而他们却总是受到赞扬。

As the number of people using Google and Gmail continued to spike up, Tristan started to ask his colleagues: ‘How do you ethically persuade two billion people’s minds?… How do you ethically structure two billion people’s attention?’ But instead, he found that most other people in the company were being pushed to ask simply, ‘How can we make this more engaging?’ And that meant more attention-sucking, more interrupting; on and on it went, with better techniques being discovered every week. One day, when we were walking in San Francisco, Tristan said to me: ‘Things look pretty bad from the outside, but when you’re on the inside, things can look even worse.’ Tristan was starting to realise: it’s not your fault you can’t focus. It’s by design. Your distraction is their fuel.

随着谷歌和Gmail用户数量的持续飙升，特里斯坦开始问他的同事：“如何才能合乎道德地影响20亿人的思想？……如何才能合乎道德地引导20亿人的注意力？” 但他发现，公司里的大多数人却被要求问：“我们怎样才能让它更有吸引力？” 这意味着更多的注意力分散，更多的打断；如此循环往复，每周都有新的技巧被发现。有一天，我们一起在旧金山散步时，特里斯坦对我说：“从外面看，情况已经很糟糕了，但当你身处其中时，情况可能更糟。” 特里斯坦开始意识到：你无法集中注意力并非你的错。这是有意为之。你的分心正是他们的燃料。

After working intensively on the Gmail team, Tristan saw that when it came to questioning what they were doing to people’s attention, ‘the conversation was not happening’. He looked out across his friends now working in every part of Silicon Valley, and this grab-and-raid approach to our focus was being taken in almost all the companies they worked in. ‘What started to really concern me over the years,’ he told me, ‘was just watching my friends who had originally gotten into this business because they thought they could make the world better, [and now] were caught in this arms race to manipulate human nature.’

在Gmail团队深度工作之后，特里斯坦发现，当涉及到质疑他们如何吸引人们的注意力时，“根本没有进行任何讨论”。他环顾四周，发现硅谷各行各业的朋友们几乎都在采用这种攫取和掠夺用户注意力的策略。“这些年来，真正让我担忧的是，”他告诉我，“我的朋友们最初进入这个行业是因为他们认为可以改变世界，而现在却陷入了这场操纵人性的军备竞赛。”

To pluck one example out of dozens Tristan could offer, his friends Mike and Kevin had launched Instagram, and after a little while, ‘They added these filters, because it was a cool thing. So you could take a photo, and just have it look artistic instantly.’ It didn’t cross their minds, he’s sure, that it would start a race with Snapchat and others to see who could ‘provide better beautification filters’ – and that this would, in turn, change how people thought of their own bodies so much that today there’s a whole category of people who undergo surgery so they can look more like their filters. He could see that his friends were setting in motion changes that were transforming the world in ways they couldn’t predict or control. ‘The reason we have to be so careful about the way that we design technology,’ he said, is that ‘they squeeze, they squish, the entire world down into that medium – and out the other end comes a different world.’

特里斯坦能举出几十个例子，他举个例子：他的朋友迈克和凯文创办了Instagram，没过多久，“他们就添加了滤镜，因为这很酷。这样你拍张照片，就能立刻拥有艺术感。”他确信，他们当时肯定没想到，这会引发一场与Snapchat等平台的竞赛，看谁能“提供更好的美颜滤镜”——而这反过来又会彻底改变人们对自身形象的看法，以至于如今有一大批人会去做整容手术，只为了让自己看起来更像滤镜里的样子。他意识到，他的朋友们正在引发一场变革，这场变革正以他们无法预测或控制的方式改变着世界。“我们必须如此谨慎地设计技术，”他说，“原因在于，它们会把整个世界压缩到这个媒介里——而最终呈现出来的，却是一个截然不同的世界。”

But here was Tristan, at the centre of the machine unleashing these transformations, and he could see that behind closed doors, the dials in the control room were being set to ten.

但特里斯坦身处这台机器的中心，正释放着这些变革，他看到在紧闭的门后，控制室里的旋钮被调到了十。

After a few years at the heart of the Googleplex, Tristan couldn’t take it any more, and he decided to leave. As a final gesture, he put together a slide show for the people he worked with, to appeal to them to think about these questions. The first slide said simply: ‘I’m concerned about how we’re making the world more distracted.’ He explained: ‘Distraction matters to me, because time is all we have in life… Yet hours and hours can get mysteriously lost here.’ He showed a picture of a Gmail inbox. ‘And [on] feeds that suck huge chunks of time away here.’ He showed a Facebook feed. He said he was worried that the company – and others like it – were inadvertently ‘destroy[ing] our kids’ ability to focus’, pointing out that the average child between the ages of thirteen and seventeen in the US was sending one text message every six minutes they were awake. People were, he warned, living ‘on a treadmill of continuous checking’.

在谷歌总部核心部门工作几年后，特里斯坦再也无法忍受，决定离开。作为最后的告别，他为同事们制作了一份幻灯片，呼吁他们思考这些问题。第一张幻灯片上写着：“我担心我们正在让世界变得更加容易分心。”他解释说：“分心对我来说很重要，因为时间是我们生命中唯一拥有的东西……然而，几个小时却会在这里悄然流逝。”他展示了一张Gmail收件箱的图片。“还有那些吞噬我们大量时间的信息流。”他又展示了一张Facebook信息流的图片。他说，他担心谷歌——以及其他类似的公司——正在无意中“摧毁孩子们的专注力”，并指出美国13至17岁的孩子平均每醒着六分钟就会发送一条短信。他警告说，人们正生活在“不断查看信息的跑步机”上。

He asked: We know that interruptions cause a deterioration in people’s ability to focus and think clearly – so why are we ramping up the interruptions? Why are we finding better and better ways to do it all the time? ‘Think about that,’ he told his colleagues. ‘We should feel an enormous responsibility to get this right.’ All humans have natural vulnerabilities, and instead of exploiting those vulnerabilities – like a malign magician – Google should be respecting them. He suggested some modest changes as a place to start. Instead of notifying someone every time they have a new email, he suggested, we could notify them once a day, in a batch – so it’d be like getting a newspaper in the morning, instead of constantly following the rolling news. Every time we prompt somebody to click over to a new photo their friend has posted, we could warn them – on the same screen – that the average person who clicks on a photo is pulled away for twenty minutes before they get back to their task. We could tell them: You think it’ll only take a second, but it won’t.

他问道：我们知道，干扰会降低人们的专注力和清晰思考能力——那么，我们为什么要不断增加干扰？为什么我们总是想方设法地制造更多干扰？“好好想想，”他告诉同事们，“我们应该感到肩负着重大的责任，确保这件事得到妥善解决。”所有人都有天生的弱点，谷歌不应该像个邪恶的魔术师一样利用这些弱点，而应该尊重它们。他建议从一些小的改变入手。比如，与其每次收到新邮件都通知用户，不如每天集中通知一次——这样就像早上收到一份报纸，而不是不停地追看滚动新闻。每次我们提示用户点击查看朋友发布的新照片时，我们可以在同一屏幕上提醒他们：普通人点击一张照片后，平均需要二十分钟才能回到工作中。我们可以告诉他们：你以为只需要一秒钟，但实际上并非如此。

He suggested giving users a chance to pause every time they click to do something potentially seriously distracting, to check: are you sure you want to do this? Do you know how much time it will take from you? ‘Humans make different decisions when we pause and consider,’ he said.

他建议，每次用户点击进行可能严重分散注意力的操作时，都应该给他们一个暂停的机会，让他们思考：你确定要这样做吗？你知道这会占用你多少时间吗？他说：“人们在停下来思考后，会做出不同的决定。”

He was trying to give his colleagues a sense of the weight of the decisions they made every day: ‘We shape more than eleven billion interruptions to people’s lives every day . This is nuts!’ The people sitting around you in the Googleplex, he explained, control more than 50 percent of all the notifications on all the phones in the whole world. We are ‘creating an arms race that causes companies to find more reasons to steal people’s time’, and it ‘destroys our common silence and ability to think’. He asked: ‘Do we really know what we’re doing to people?’

他试图让同事们意识到他们每天所做的决定有多么重要：“我们每天对人们的生活造成超过110亿次的干扰。这太疯狂了！”他解释说，坐在你周围的谷歌员工控制着全世界所有手机上超过50%的通知。我们正在“制造一场军备竞赛，迫使公司想方设法窃取人们的时间”，这“破坏了我们共同的宁静和思考能力”。他问道：“我们真的知道我们正在对人们做什么吗？”

This was an almost insanely bold thing to do. At the heart of the machine that was changing the world, here was a smart and talented but fairly junior engineer, still only twenty-nine years old, saying something that directly challenged the whole direction of the company. It would be like a junior exec in 1975 standing up in front of the whole of ExxonMobil and telling them that they were responsible for global warming by showing them images of the melting of the Arctic. Everyone in Silicon Valley was scrambling to get into and suck up to Google. But here was Tristan, with the ability to stay at its heart for ever and make a lot of money, writing what seemed to be his own professional death certificate, because he believed somebody, somewhere, had to say something.

这几乎是件疯狂至极的事。在改变世界的这台机器的核心，一位聪明才智过人但资历尚浅的工程师，年仅29岁，却发表了直接挑战公司整体发展方向的言论。这就像1975年一位初级主管站在埃克森美孚全体员工面前，向他们展示北极冰川融化的图片，并指责他们应对全球变暖负责一样。当时硅谷的每个人都争先恐后地想加入谷歌，并竭力讨好它。而特里斯坦，一个有能力永远留在公司核心并赚取巨额财富的人，却仿佛亲手写下了自己的职业生涯“死亡证明”，因为他相信总得有人站出来发声。

He shared his slide show with his colleagues, and went home, depressed. Then something unexpected happened.

他与同事们分享了幻灯片，然后沮丧地回家了。这时，意想不到的事情发生了。

With each hour that passed, more and more Google employees shared Tristan’s slide show. The next day, he was inundated with messages from within the company enthusing about it. It turned out he had tapped into a latent mood. Just because you design these products, it doesn’t mean you are more insulated than anyone else from becoming hooked on them. The workers at the Googleplex could feel this tsunami of distractions hitting them too. Many of them wanted to have a serious conversation about what they were doing to the world. People were drawn in particular to the question Tristan had put to them: ‘What if we designed [our products] to minimise stress and create calmer states of mind?’

随着时间的推移，越来越多的谷歌员工分享了特里斯坦的幻灯片。第二天，他收到了公司内部无数条信息，大家都对幻灯片赞不绝口。事实证明，他触及到了员工们内心深处的一种情绪。即便你设计了这些产品，也不意味着你比其他人更能免受其害，不会沉迷其中。谷歌园区的员工们也感受到了这股注意力分散的浪潮。他们中的许多人都想认真探讨一下，他们正在对这个世界造成怎样的影响。人们尤其关注特里斯坦提出的问题：“如果我们设计产品的目的是为了减轻压力，创造更平静的心境，那会怎样？”

There was some pushback too. A few of his colleagues said that every new technology brings with it a panic where people say it’ll trash the world – after all, Socrates said writing things down would ruin people’s memories. We were told that everything from the printed book to television would trash the minds of the young, but here we are, and the world survived. Some others responded from a libertarian perspective, saying that what he was suggesting would invite government regulation, which they believed was contrary to the whole spirit of cyberspace.

当然，也有一些反对的声音。他的几位同事说，每项新技术都会引发恐慌，人们总说它会毁了世界——毕竟，苏格拉底就说过，把事情写下来会毁掉人们的记忆。我们曾被告知，从印刷书籍到电视，一切都会摧残年轻人的思想，但事实并非如此，世界依然运转良好。另一些人则从自由主义的角度回应，认为他提出的方案会招致政府监管，而他们认为这违背了网络空间的精神。

Tristan’s presentation caused such a ruction within Google that he was asked to stay in a special new position, created just for him. They offered him the role of being Google’s first ‘design ethicist’. He was thrilled. Here was a chance to think through some of the most challenging questions of our time, in a place where – if he could get people to listen – he could make an enormous difference. For the first time in a long time, he felt optimistic. He thought his new appointment meant Google was serious about exploring these questions. He knew there was enthusiasm for it among his fellow workers, and he believed in the good faith of his bosses.

特里斯坦的演讲在谷歌内部引起了巨大反响，以至于公司特地为他设立了一个新职位，并邀请他留下来担任。他们邀请他担任谷歌首位“设计伦理学家”。他欣喜若狂。这是一个绝佳的机会，让他能够深入思考当今时代最具挑战性的问题，而且如果他能让人们倾听他的想法，他就能在这个领域产生巨大的影响。他很久以来第一次感到如此乐观。他认为，这项新任命意味着谷歌认真对待这些问题。他知道同事们对此充满热情，而且他也相信老板们的诚意。

He was assigned a desk, and – in effect – left to think. So he started to research the effects of many things. For example, he looked at the way Snapchat hooks teenagers. The app had an option called ‘Snapchat streaks’, where two friends – almost always teens – would check in with each other every day through the app. Every day they checked in, their streak got longer, so you would aim to build up a streak of 200, 300, 400 days, all on a brightly coloured display full of emojis. If you missed a single day, it would reset to zero. It was a perfect way to take the desire of teens for social connection and manipulate it to get them hooked. You came every day to extend your streak, and you stuck around to scroll, often for hours.

他被分配了一张办公桌，实际上，就是让他自己思考。于是，他开始研究各种事物的影响。例如，他研究了Snapchat是如何吸引青少年的。这款应用有一个名为“Snapchat连续签到”的功能，两个朋友——几乎都是青少年——每天通过应用互相签到。每次签到，他们的连续签到天数就会增加，所以他们的目标是积累200天、300天、400天的连续签到，所有这些都显示在一个色彩鲜艳、充满表情符号的屏幕上。如果错过一天，连续签到天数就会清零。这完美地利用了青少年渴望社交的心理，并加以操纵，让他们沉迷其中。你每天都来延长你的连续签到天数，然后长时间地浏览，往往一待就是几个小时。

But whenever he came up with a specific proposal for how Google’s own products could be less interrupting and presented it to people above him, he was told, in effect: ‘This is hard, it’s confusing, and it’s often at odds with our bottom line.’ Tristan realised he was bumping up against a core contradiction. The more people stared at their phones, the more money these companies made. Period. The people in Silicon Valley did not want to design gadgets and websites that would dissolve people’s attention spans. They’re not the Joker, trying to sow chaos and make us dumb. They spend a lot of their own time meditating and doing yoga. They often ban their own kids from using the sites and gadgets they design, and send them instead to tech-free Montessori schools. But their business model can only succeed if they take steps to dominate the attention spans of the wider society. It’s not their goal, any more than ExxonMobil deliberately wants to melt the Arctic. But it’s an inescapable effect of their current business model.

但每当他提出如何让谷歌的产品减少干扰的具体方案并向上级汇报时，得到的回复几乎都是：“这很难，很复杂，而且往往与我们的盈利目标相悖。” 特里斯坦意识到自己正面临着一个核心矛盾。人们盯着手机的时间越长，这些公司赚的钱就越多。就这么简单。硅谷的那些人并不想设计会分散人们注意力的设备和网站。他们不是小丑，不是想制造混乱、让我们变笨。他们自己会花很多时间冥想和练习瑜伽。他们经常禁止自己的孩子使用他们设计的网站和设备，而是把他们送到没有科技产品的蒙特梭利学校。但他们的商业模式只有在他们采取措施掌控大众注意力的情况下才能成功。这并非他们的本意，就像埃克森美孚公司并非故意要融化北极一样。但这却是他们现有商业模式不可避免的后果。

When Tristan warned about these negative effects, most people inside the company sympathised and agreed. When he suggested alternatives, people changed the subject. To give you a sense of the money involved: the personal wealth of Larry Page, one of the founders of Google, is $102 billion; his colleague Sergey Brin is worth $99 billion; and their colleague Eric Schmidt is worth $20.7 billion. That’s separate from Google’s wealth as a company, which as I write stands at $1 trillion. These three men alone are worth roughly the same as the total combined wealth of every single person, building and bank account in the oil-rich country of Kuwait, and Google is worth roughly the entire wealth of the whole of Mexico or Indonesia. Telling them to distract people less was like telling an oil company not to drill for oil – they didn’t want to hear it. ‘You don’t even really get to make that ethical decision’ to improve people’s attention spans, Tristan realised, ‘because your business model and your incentives are making that decision for you’. Years later, testifying before the US Senate, he explained: ‘I failed because companies don’t [currently] have the right incentive to change.’

当特里斯坦警告这些负面影响时，公司内部大多数人表示同情并表示赞同。但当他提出替代方案时，人们却避而不谈。为了让大家对其中涉及的金额有所了解：谷歌创始人之一拉里·佩奇的个人财富为1020亿美元；他的同事谢尔盖·布林身价990亿美元；另一位同事埃里克·施密特身价207亿美元。这还不包括谷歌公司的财富，截至我撰写本文时，谷歌的市值已达1万亿美元。仅这三人的财富就大致相当于石油资源丰富的科威特所有居民、所有房产和所有银行账户的总和，而谷歌的市值则大致相当于整个墨西哥或印度尼西亚的财富总和。让他们少打扰员工，就像劝石油公司不要开采石油一样——他们根本不想听。特里斯坦意识到，“你甚至根本没有机会做出改善人们注意力持续时间的道德抉择，因为你的商业模式和激励机制已经替你做出了决定。”多年后，他在美国参议院作证时解释说：“我失败了，因为企业（目前）缺乏改变的正确动力。”

Tristan was in the ethicist job for two years, and towards the end, as he told an audience later, ‘I felt completely hopeless. There were literally days when I went to work and I would read Wikipedia all day and check my email and I would have no idea, once you see something as massive as the attention economy and its perverse incentives, how could a system this big ever change? I truly felt hopeless. I felt depressed.’ So, finally, he quit Google, and went out into a Silicon Valley where, as he put it to me, ‘everything is a race for attention’. In that lonely time in Tristan’s life, he was about to team up with another person who felt depressed and lost – and who felt guilty about what he personally had done to you, me, and everyone we know.

特里斯坦在谷歌担任伦理学家两年，临近退休时，正如他后来对听众所说：“我感到彻底绝望。有好几天，我上班后整天都在看维基百科，查看邮件，却始终无法理解，当你看到注意力经济及其扭曲的激励机制如此庞大的体系时，它究竟该如何改变？我真的感到绝望，非常沮丧。”最终，他辞去了谷歌的工作，来到了硅谷。正如他告诉我的，那里“一切都在争夺注意力”。在特里斯坦人生中那段孤独的时光里，他即将与另一位同样感到沮丧和迷茫的人携手合作——这个人也为自己曾经对你、我以及我们认识的每个人所做的一切感到愧疚。

You probably haven’t heard of Aza Raskin, but he has directly intervened in your life. He will, in fact, probably affect how you spend your time today. Aza grew up in the most elite sliver of Silicon Valley, at the height of its confidence that it was making the world better. His dad was Jef Raskin, the man who invented the Apple Macintosh for Steve Jobs, and he built it around one core principle: that the user’s attention is sacred. The job of technology, Jef believed, was to lift people up and make it possible to achieve their higher goals. He taught his son: ‘What is technology for? Why do we even make technology? We make technology because it takes the parts of us that are most human and it extends them. That’s what a paintbrush is. That’s what a cello is. That’s what language is. These are technologies that extend some part of us. Technology is not about making us superhuman. It’s about making us extra-human.’

你或许没听说过阿扎·拉斯金，但他却直接影响了你的生活。事实上，他很可能会影响你今天如何度过时间。阿扎成长于硅谷最精英的地区，那时硅谷正处于鼎盛时期，人们自信满满地认为自己正在让世界变得更美好。他的父亲是杰夫·拉斯金，正是他为史蒂夫·乔布斯发明了苹果Macintosh电脑，而他设计这款电脑的核心原则只有一个：用户的注意力神圣不可侵犯。杰夫认为，科技的使命是提升人们的生活，使他们能够实现更高的目标。他教导儿子：“科技的目的是什么？我们为什么要创造科技？我们创造科技，是因为它能将我们身上最人性化的部分延伸出去。画笔、大提琴、语言都是如此。这些科技延伸了我们自身的某些特质。科技的目的不是让我们成为超人，而是让我们超越人类。”

Aza became a precocious young coder, and he gave his first talk about user interfaces when he was ten years old. By the time he was in his early twenties, he was at the forefront of designing some of the first internet browsers, and he was the creative lead on Firefox. As part of this work, he designed something that distinctly changed how the web works. It’s called ‘infinite scroll’. Older readers will remember that it used to be that the internet was divided into pages, and when you got to the bottom of one page, you had to decide to click a button to get to the next page. It was an active choice. It gave you a moment to pause and ask: Do I want to carry on looking at this? Aza designed the code that means you don’t have to ask that question any more. Imagine you open Facebook. It downloads a chunk of status updates for you to read through. You scroll down through it, flicking your finger – and when you get to the bottom, it will automatically load another chunk for you to flick through. When you get to the bottom of that, it will automatically download another chunk, and another, and another, forever. You can never exhaust it. It will scroll infinitely.

阿扎从小就展现出过人的编程天赋，十岁时就发表了关于用户界面的首次演讲。二十出头时，他已站在设计早期互联网浏览器的最前沿，并担任火狐浏览器的创意总监。在这项工作中，他设计了一项彻底改变网络运作方式的技术，名为“无限滚动”。年纪稍长的读者或许还记得，以前的互联网页面是按页划分的，当你翻到一页底部时，必须点击按钮才能跳转到下一页。这是一个主动选择，让你有时间停下来思考：我还要继续浏览吗？阿扎设计的代码让你无需再为此烦恼。想象一下，你打开Facebook，它会加载一段状态更新供你阅读。你向下滚动，手指轻轻滑动——当你到达底部时，它会自动加载下一段状态更新供你浏览。当你到达底部时，它会自动下载下一个数据块，再下一个，再下一个，永无止境。你永远也无法穷尽它。它会无限滚动。

Aza was proud of the design. ‘At the outset, it looks like a really good invention,’ he told me. He believed he was making life easier for everyone. He had been taught that increased speed and efficiency of access were always advances. His invention quickly spread all over the internet. Today, all social media and lots of other sites use a version of infinite scroll. But then Aza watched as the people around him changed. They seemed to be unable to pull themselves away from their devices, flicking through and through and through, thanks in part to the code he had designed. He found himself infinitely scrolling through what he often realised afterwards was crap, and he wondered if he was making a good use of his life.

阿扎对自己的设计引以为豪。“一开始，这看起来真是一个很棒的发明，”他告诉我。他相信自己正在让每个人的生活更轻松。他从小就被灌输，访问速度和效率的提升永远都是进步。他的发明迅速在互联网上传播开来。如今，所有社交媒体和许多其他网站都使用某种形式的无限滚动。但随后，阿扎发现周围的人发生了变化。他们似乎无法从电子设备中抽身，不停地滑动屏幕，这在一定程度上要归功于他设计的代码。他发现自己也在无休止地滚动浏览着一些事后才意识到是垃圾的内容，他开始怀疑自己是否在有效地利用生命。

One day, when he was thirty-two, Aza sat down and did a calculation. At a conservative estimate, infinite scroll makes you spend 50 percent more of your time on sites like Twitter. (For many people, Aza believes, it’s vastly more.) Sticking with this low-ball percentage, Aza wanted to know what it meant, in practice, if billions of people were spending 50 percent more on a string of social media sites. When he was done, he stared at the sums. Every day, as a direct result of his invention, the combined total of 200,000 more total human lifetimes – every moment from birth to death – is now spent scrolling through a screen. These hours would otherwise have been spent on some other activity.

有一天，32岁的阿扎坐下来做了个计算。保守估计，无限滚动功能会让你在Twitter等网站上花费的时间增加50%。（阿扎认为，对很多人来说，实际花费的时间远不止这些。）阿扎坚持这个保守估计，想知道如果数十亿人每天在社交媒体网站上花费的时间增加50%，这在实际生活中意味着什么。计算完成后，他盯着这些数字。由于他的发明，每天，相当于20万个人类生命周期——从出生到死亡的每一刻——都被浪费在了屏幕上。这些时间原本可以用于其他活动。

When he described this to me, he still sounded a little stunned. That time is ‘just completely gone. It’s like their entire life – poof. That time, which could have been used for solving climate change, for spending time with their family, for strengthening social bonds. For whatever is it that makes their life well-lived. It just…’ He trailed off. I pictured my young godson Adam and all his teenage friends, scrolling, scrolling, infinitely scrolling.

他跟我描述这件事的时候，听起来仍然有些震惊。他说，那段时间“就这么彻底地消失了。就像他们的整个人生——砰的一声就没了。那段时间，本来可以用来解决气候变化，可以用来陪伴家人，可以用来加强社交联系。可以用来做任何能让他们的生活更有意义的事情。它就……”他的声音渐渐低了下去。我仿佛看到了我的教子亚当和他的所有青少年朋友们，不停地滑动屏幕，无休止地滑动。

Aza told me he felt ‘sort of dirty’. He realised: ‘These things we do, they really can change the world. Then the question immediately follows: in what way did we change the world?’ He realised he thought making tech easier to use meant the world would get better. But he began to think that ‘one of my biggest learnings as a designer or technologist is – making something easy to use doesn’t mean it’s good for humanity’. He thought about his father – who had since died – and his commitment to make tech that set people free to be better, and he wondered if he was living up to his dad’s vision. He began to ask if he and his generation in Silicon Valley were actually ‘mak[ing] technology that tears us, rips us, and breaks us’.

阿扎告诉我，他感觉“有点脏”。他意识到：“我们做的这些事，真的可以改变世界。然后问题就接踵而至：我们究竟以何种方式改变了世界？”他意识到，他曾以为让科技更易于使用就意味着世界会变得更好。但他开始思考，“作为一名设计师或技术人员，我最大的感悟之一就是——让某样东西易于使用并不意味着它对人类有益”。他想起了已经去世的父亲，以及父亲致力于开发能够解放人们、让他们变得更好的科技的决心，他不禁思考自己是否实现了父亲的愿景。他开始质疑，他和硅谷的同代人是否真的在“制造撕裂我们、摧毁我们、毁灭我们的科技”。

He carried on designing more things in the vein of infinite scroll, and getting more and more uncomfortable. ‘It was about the time that we were getting to be really successful at this that my stomach started to drop,’ he told me. He felt that he was seeing people become more unempathetic, angry and hostile as their social-media use went up. At the time, he was running an app he had designed named Post-Social, which was a social-media site designed to help people interact more in the real world, away from their devices. He was trying to raise money for the next phase of its development, and all any investor wanted to know was: how much of people’s attention do you capture and run through your app? How often? How many times a day? That’s not what Aza wanted to be – a person who thought solely about how to drain away people’s time. But ‘you could see this gravity, pulling this product back to everything that we were trying to fight against.’

他继续设计更多类似无限滚动的产品，却越来越感到不安。“就在我们即将取得真正成功的时候，我的胃开始翻江倒海，”他告诉我。他感觉随着人们使用社交媒体的时间越来越长，他们变得越来越冷漠、愤怒和敌对。当时，他正在运营一款名为Post-Social的应用程序，这是一个他自己设计的社交媒体网站，旨在帮助人们在现实世界中更多地互动，而不是依赖电子设备。他正试图为下一阶段的开发筹集资金，而所有投资者都只想知道：你的应用程序能吸引多少用户的注意力？使用频率如何？一天多少次？这并非Aza想要成为的样子——一个只想着如何消耗人们时间的人。但“你能感觉到一股引力，将这款产品拉回到我们一直试图对抗的一切。”

The logic of the underlying system was being laid bare for Aza. Silicon Valley sells itself by articulating ‘a big, lofty goal – connecting everyone in the world, or whatever it is. But when you’re actually doing the day-to-day work, it’s about increasing user numbers.’ What you are selling is your ability to grab and hold attention. When he tried to discuss this, he thwacked into raw denial. ‘Say you were baking bread,’ he said to me, ‘and you had this incredible bread, and you used this secret substance – and all of a sudden, you’re making free bread for the world, and everyone’s eating it. Then one of your scientists comes and says – by the way, we think it causes cancer, this secret substance. What do you do? You would almost certainly say – that can’t be right. We need more research. Maybe it’s something [else] that the people out there are doing. Maybe there’s some other factor.’

阿扎彻底看清了这套底层系统的逻辑。硅谷的营销手段是描绘一个“宏伟的目标——连接全世界所有人”之类的愿景。但实际上，日常工作的核心是增加用户数量。你卖的其实是你吸引和留住用户注意力的能力。当他试图讨论这一点时，却断然否认。“假设你在烤面包，”他对我说，“你烤出了非常棒的面包，还用了一种秘密配方——突然之间，你开始免费为全世界提供面包，每个人都在吃。然后你的一个科学家跑来说——顺便说一句，我们认为这种秘密配方会致癌。你会怎么做？你几乎肯定会说——这不可能。我们需要更多研究。也许是其他人做了什么别的事情。也许还有其他因素。”

All throughout the industry, Aza kept meeting people who were going through similar crises. ‘There were a number of dark nights of the soul that I personally witnessed,’ he says. He watched as Silicon Valley’s own inhabitants seemed to be hijacked by their own creations, and then tried to escape. When I met with several of these tech dissidents, it struck me how young they were – like they were almost children who had invented toys and watched their toys conquer the world. Everyone was scrambling to meditate in an attempt to resist the programs they had invented. He realised ‘one of the ironies is there are these incredibly popular workshops at Facebook and Google about mindfulness – about creating the mental space to make decisions non-reactively – and they are also the biggest perpetrators of non-mindfulness in the world’.

在整个行业里，阿扎不断遇到经历类似危机的人。“我亲眼目睹了许多人陷入深深的痛苦挣扎，”他说。他眼看着硅谷的居民们似乎被自己创造的产品所控制，然后又试图逃离。当我与几位科技异见人士会面时，我惊讶地发现他们竟然如此年轻——就像发明了玩具并眼睁睁看着玩具征服世界的孩子一样。每个人都在努力冥想，试图抵抗自己创造的程序。他意识到，“讽刺的是，Facebook和谷歌举办的关于正念的研讨会非常受欢迎——这些研讨会旨在创造心理空间，让人们能够不带反应地做出决策——而他们同时也是世界上最大的不正念传播者。”

When Tristan and Aza started to speak out, they were ridiculed as wildly over-the-top Cassandras. But then, one by one, all over Silicon Valley, people who had built the world we now live in were beginning to declare in public that they had similar feelings. For example, Sean Parker, one of the earliest investors in Facebook, told a public audience that the creators of the site had asked themselves from the start: ‘How do we consume as much of your time and conscious attention as possible?’ The techniques they used were ‘exactly the kind of thing that a hacker like myself would come up with, because you’re exploiting a vulnerability in human psychology … The inventors, creators – it’s me, it’s Mark [Zuckerberg], it’s Kevin Systrom on Instagram, it’s all of these people – understood this consciously. And we did it anyway.’ He added: ‘God only knows what it’s doing to our children’s brains.’ Chamath Palihapitiya, who had been Facebook’s vice president of growth, explained in a speech that the effects are so negative that his own kids ‘aren’t allowed to use that shit’. Tony Fadell, who co-invented the iPhone, said: ‘I wake up in cold sweats every so often thinking, what did we bring to the world?’ He worried that he had helped create ‘a nuclear bomb’ that can ‘blow up people’s brains and reprogram them’.

当特里斯坦和阿扎开始公开表达他们的担忧时，他们被嘲笑为危言耸听的预言家。但随后，在硅谷各地，那些缔造了我们如今所处世界的人们开始一个接一个地公开表示，他们也有类似的感受。例如，Facebook 的早期投资者之一肖恩·帕克曾公开表示，该网站的创建者从一开始就在问自己：“我们如何才能尽可能多地占用你的时间和注意力？”他们使用的技巧“正是像我这样的黑客会想到的那种，因为你是在利用人类心理的弱点……发明者、创造者——包括我、马克·扎克伯格、Instagram 的凯文·斯特罗姆，以及所有这些人——都清楚地意识到了这一点。” “但我们还是这么做了。”他补充道：“只有上帝才知道这会对我们孩子的脑子造成什么影响。”曾任Facebook增长副总裁的查马斯·帕里哈皮蒂亚在一次演讲中解释说，其负面影响如此之大，以至于他自己的孩子“都不被允许使用那玩意儿”。iPhone的联合发明人托尼·法德尔说：“我时不时会惊醒，冷汗涔涔，心想我们到底给世界带来了什么？”他担心自己参与制造了一颗“核弹”，这颗核弹会“炸毁人们的大脑，并重新编程”。

Many Silicon Valley insiders predicted that it would only get worse. One of its most famous investors, Paul Graham, wrote: ‘Unless the forms of technological progress that produced these things are subject to different laws than technological progress in general, the world will get more addictive in the next forty years than it did in the last forty.’

许多硅谷内部人士预测情况只会越来越糟。其中一位最著名的投资者保罗·格雷厄姆写道：“除非产生这些东西的技术进步遵循与一般技术进步不同的规律，否则未来四十年世界将比过去四十年更容易让人上瘾。”

One day, James Williams – the former Google strategist I met – addressed an audience of hundreds of leading tech designers and asked them a simple question. ‘How many of you want to live in the world you are designing?’ There was a silence in the room. People looked around them. Nobody put up their hand.

有一天，我认识的那位前谷歌战略家詹姆斯·威廉姆斯，在数百位顶尖科技设计师面前发表了演讲，并问了他们一个简单的问题：“你们当中有多少人想生活在你们所设计的世界里？” 房间里一片寂静。人们环顾四周，却无人举手。

# ↩

7 Cause Six: The Rise of Technology That Can Track and Manipulate You (Part Two)

原因六：能够追踪和操纵你的技术的兴起（第二部分）

Tristan said to me that if you want to understand the deeper problems in the way our tech currently works – and why it is undermining our attention – a good place to start is with what seems like a simple question.

特里斯坦对我说，如果你想了解我们当前科技运作方式中存在的更深层次的问题——以及它为何会削弱我们的注意力——一个好的起点就是一个看似简单的问题。

Imagine you are visiting New York and you want to know which of your friends are around in the city so you can hang out with them. You turn to Facebook. The site will alert you about lots of things – a friend’s birthday, a photo you’ve been tagged in, a terrorist attack – but it won’t alert you to the physical proximity of somebody you might want to see in the real world. There’s no button that says ‘I want to meet up – who’s nearby and free?’ This isn’t technologically tricky.
