It would be really easy for Facebook to be designed so that when you opened it, it told you which of your friends were close by and which of them would like to meet for a drink or dinner that week. The coding to do that is simple: Tristan and Aza and their friends could probably write it in a day. And it would be hugely popular. Ask any Facebook user – would you like Facebook to physically connect you to your friends more, instead of keeping you endlessly scrolling?

想象一下，你正在纽约旅行，想知道哪些朋友在城里，好约他们出去玩。你打开Facebook。这个网站会提醒你很多事情——朋友的生日、你被标记的照片、恐怖袭击——但它不会告诉你哪些你想在现实生活中见到的朋友就在附近。没有一个按钮可以让你说“我想见面——谁在附近而且有空？”。这在技术上并不难。Facebook完全可以设计成这样：当你打开它时，它会告诉你哪些朋友在附近，以及哪些朋友想在本周一起喝一杯或吃顿饭。实现这个功能的代码很简单：Tristan、Aza和他们的朋友可能一天就能写出来。而且它肯定会大受欢迎。问问任何一个Facebook用户——你希望Facebook能让你和朋友们更多地进行线下联系，而不是让你无休止地滑动屏幕吗？

So – it’s an easy tweak, and users would love it. Why doesn’t it happen? Why won’t the market provide it? To understand why, Tristan and his colleagues explained to me, you need to step back and understand more about the business model of Facebook and the other social-media companies. If you follow the trail from this simple question, you will see the root of many of the problems we are facing.

所以，这只是一个简单的调整，用户肯定会喜欢。为什么它没有实现？为什么市场不提供这种功能？要理解其中的原因，特里斯坦和他的同事向我解释说，你需要退后一步，深入了解Facebook和其他社交媒体公司的商业模式。如果你从这个简单的问题入手，就能找到我们面临的许多问题的根源。

Facebook makes more money for every extra second you are staring through a screen at their site, and they lose money every time you put the screen down. They make this money in two ways. Until I started to spend time in Silicon Valley, I had only naively thought about the first and the most obvious. Clearly – as I wrote in the last chapter – the more time you look at their sites, the more advertisements you see. Advertisers pay Facebook to get to you and your eyeballs. But there’s a second, more subtle reason why Facebook wants you to keep scrolling and desperately doesn’t want you to log off. When I first heard about this reason, I scoffed a little – it sounded far-fetched. But then I kept talking with people in San Francisco and Palo Alto, and every time I expressed scepticism about it, they looked at me like I was a maiden aunt in the 1850s who had just heard the details of sex for the first time. How, they asked, did you think it worked?

你每多盯着Facebook的网站看一秒钟，他们就能赚更多钱；而你每放下屏幕一秒钟，他们就会损失一部分钱。他们赚钱的方式有两种。在我开始在硅谷待一段时间之前，我天真地只想到第一种，也是最显而易见的。显然——正如我在上一章里写到的——你浏览他们网站的时间越长，看到的广告就越多。广告商付钱给Facebook，就是为了让你的眼球被他们看到。但Facebook想让你不停地滑动屏幕，拼命不让你退出登录，还有第二种更微妙的原因。我第一次听到这个原因时，有点不以为然——听起来太牵强了。但后来我和旧金山以及帕洛阿尔托的人们不断交流，每次我对此表示怀疑时，他们都用一种仿佛我是19世纪50年代第一次听到性知识的处女般的眼神看着我。他们问，你觉得这套系统是怎么运作的？

Every time you send a message or status update on Facebook, or Snapchat, or Twitter, and every time you search for something on Google, everything you say is being scanned and sorted and stored. These companies are building up a profile of you, to sell to advertisers who want to target you. For example, starting in 2014, if you used Gmail, Google’s automated systems would scan through all your private correspondence to generate an ‘ advertising profile’ exactly for you. If (say) you email your mother telling her you need to buy diapers, Gmail knows you have a baby, and it knows to target ads for baby products straight to you. If you use the word ‘arthritis’, it’ll try to sell you arthritis treatments. The process that had been predicted in Tristan’s final class back in Stanford was beginning.

每次你在Facebook、Snapchat或Twitter上发送消息或更新状态，每次你在Google上搜索内容，你说的每一句话都会被扫描、整理和存储。这些公司正在建立你的个人档案，以便出售给想要精准投放广告的广告商。例如，从2014年开始，如果你使用Gmail，Google的自动化系统会扫描你所有的私人邮件，为你生成一个专属的“广告档案”。假设你发邮件告诉你妈妈你需要买尿布，Gmail就知道你有个宝宝，并会向你推送婴儿用品的广告。如果你在邮件中使用了“关节炎”这个词，它就会尝试向你推销关节炎治疗产品。特里斯坦在斯坦福大学最后一堂课上预言的这个过程，如今已经开始了。

Aza explained it to me by saying that I should imagine that ‘inside of Facebook’s servers, inside of Google’s servers, there is a little voodoo doll, [and it is] a model of you. It starts by not looking much like you. It’s sort of a generic model of a human. But then they’re collecting your click trails [i.e., everything you click on], and your toenail clippings, and your hair droppings [i.e., everything you search for, every little detail of your life online]. They’re reassembling all that metadata you don’t really think is meaningful, so that doll looks more and more like you. [Then] when you show up on [for example] YouTube, they’re waking up that doll, and they’re testing out hundreds of thousands of videos against this doll, seeing what makes its arm twitch and move, so they know it’s effective, and then they serve that to you.’ It seemed like such a ghoulish image that I paused. He went on: ‘By the way – they have a doll like that for one in four human beings on earth.’

阿扎向我解释说，我应该想象一下，“在Facebook的服务器里，在谷歌的服务器里，有一个小小的巫毒娃娃，它是你的模型。一开始它看起来不太像你，只是一个普通的人类模型。但后来，他们会收集你的点击轨迹（也就是你点击的每一个东西）、你的脚趾甲屑、你的头发屑（也就是你搜索的每一个东西，你在网上生活的每一个细节）。他们会重新组合所有这些你认为无关紧要的元数据，让这个娃娃越来越像你。然后，当你出现在（比如）YouTube上时，他们会唤醒这个娃娃，并用成千上万个视频来测试它，看看什么能让它的手臂抽搐、移动，从而确定这种方法有效，然后把这些视频推送给你。” 这画面太可怕了，我愣了一下。他接着说：“顺便一提——地球上每四个人中就有一个人拥有这样的玩偶。”

At the moment these voodoo dolls are sometimes crude and sometimes startlingly specific. We’ve all had one kind of experience of searching online for something. I recently tried to buy an exercise bike, and a month later, I am still endlessly being served advertisements for exercise bikes by Google and Facebook, until I want to scream, ‘I bought one already!’ But the systems are getting more sophisticated every year. Aza told me: ‘It’s getting to be so good that whenever I give a presentation, I’ll ask the audience how many think Facebook is listening to their conversations, because there’s some ad that’s been served that’s just too accurate. It’s about a specific thing they never mentioned before [but they happen to have talked about offline] to a friend the day before. Now, it’s generally one half to two-thirds of the audience that raises their hands. The truth is creepier. It’s not that they are listening and then they can do targeted ad serving. It’s that their model of you is so accurate that it’s making predictions about you that you think are magic.’

目前这些“巫毒娃娃”有时粗糙简陋，有时却精准得令人震惊。我们都曾有过类似的经历：在网上搜索东西时，总是被广告轰炸。我最近想买一辆健身车，一个月过去了，谷歌和脸书仍然不停地给我推送健身车的广告，我都快要崩溃了，恨不得大喊：“我已经买过了！” 但这些系统每年都在变得更加精密复杂。阿扎告诉我：“现在的技术越来越高超，以至于我每次做演讲都会问听众，有多少人认为脸书在监听他们的对话，因为有些广告的精准度实在太高了。广告内容往往与他们之前从未提及过的事情有关（但他们前一天可能在线下跟朋友聊过）。现在，通常会有一半到三分之二的听众举手。但真相更令人毛骨悚然。他们并非真的在监听，然后进行定向广告投放。”问题在于，他们对你的建模非常精准，以至于做出的预测让你觉得神奇。

It was explained to me that whenever something is provided by a tech company for free, it’s always to improve the voodoo doll. Why is Google Maps free? So the voodoo doll can include the details of where you go every day. Why are Amazon Echo and Google Nest Hubs sold for as cheap as $30 (£22), far less than they cost to make? So they can gather more info; so the voodoo doll can consist not just of what you search for on a screen but what you say in your home.

有人向我解释说，科技公司免费提供的任何服务，都是为了完善他们的“巫毒娃娃”。谷歌地图为什么免费？因为这样“巫毒娃娃”就能收集你每天的出行记录。亚马逊 Echo 和谷歌 Nest Hub 的售价低至 30 美元（22 英镑），远低于制造成本，这是为什么？因为这样它们就能收集更多信息；这样“巫毒娃娃”就不仅包含你在屏幕上搜索的内容，还能包含你在家里说的话。

This is the business model that built and sustains the sites on which we spend so much of our lives. The technical term for this system – coined by the brilliant Harvard Professor Shoshana Zuboff – is ‘ surveillance capitalism’. Her work has made it possible for us to understand a lot of what is happening now. Of course, there have been increasingly sophisticated forms of advertising and marketing for over a hundred years – but this is a quantum leap forward. A billboard didn’t know what you googled at three in the morning last Thursday. A magazine ad didn’t have a detailed profile of everything you’ve ever said to your friends on Facebook and email. Trying to give me a sense of this system, Aza said to me: ‘Imagine if I could predict all your actions in chess before you made them. It would be trivial for me to dominate you. That’s what is happening on a human scale now.’ Sometimes, a few of their specific practices have been banned by law. For example, in 2017 the European Union blocked some forms of tracking of internet users – they can’t scan your Gmail any more in that territory – but the wider invasive machinery rolls on.

正是这种商业模式构建并维系着我们生活中花费大量时间的网站。哈佛大学杰出的教授肖莎娜·祖博夫（Shoshana Zuboff）创造了一个专门描述这套系统的专业术语——“监控资本主义”。她的研究使我们能够理解当下正在发生的许多事情。当然，一百多年来，广告和营销的形式一直在不断演变，日趋复杂——但这无疑是一次质的飞跃。广告牌不会知道你上周四凌晨三点在谷歌上搜索了什么。杂志广告也不会详细记录你在Facebook和电子邮件上与朋友说过的每句话。为了让我更好地理解这套系统，阿扎（Aza）对我说：“想象一下，如果我能预测你下棋之前的所有行动，那我就能轻而易举地战胜你。这就是现在人类社会正在发生的事情。”有时，他们的一些具体做法已被法律禁止。例如，2017 年欧盟禁止了一些形式的互联网用户跟踪——在欧盟境内，他们不能再扫描你的 Gmail 了——但更广泛的侵入性机制仍在继续运转。

Once you understand all this, you can see why there is no button that suggests you meet up with your friends and family away from the screen. Instead of getting us to maximise screen time, that would get us to maximise face-to-face time. Tristan said: ‘If people used Facebook just to quickly get on, so they could find the amazing thing to do with their friends that night, and get off, how would that [affect] Facebook’s stock price? The average amount of time people spend on Facebook today is something like fifty minutes a day … [But] if Facebook acted that way, people would spend barely a few minutes on there per day, in a much more fulfilling way.’ Facebook’s share price would collapse; it would be, for them, a catastrophe. This is why these sites are designed to be maximally distracting. They need to distract us, to make more money.

一旦你理解了这一切，你就能明白为什么Facebook上没有一个按钮会建议你远离屏幕，与亲朋好友相聚。与其让我们尽可能多地使用屏幕，不如鼓励我们尽可能多地面对面交流。特里斯坦说：“如果人们使用Facebook只是为了快速登录，找到当晚和朋友们一起做的精彩活动，然后就退出，这会对Facebook的股价产生什么影响？如今人们平均每天在Facebook上花费大约50分钟……但如果Facebook真的像他们说的那样运作，人们每天只需花几分钟时间在上面，就能获得更有意义的体验。” Facebook的股价将会暴跌；对他们来说，这将是一场灾难。这就是为什么这些网站被设计成尽可能分散用户注意力。他们需要分散我们的注意力，才能赚更多的钱。

Tristan has seen, on the inside, how these business incentives work in practice. Imagine this, he said to me: an engineer proposes a tweak that improves people’s attention, or gets them to spend more time with their friends. ‘Then what happens is they will wake up two weeks to four weeks later, and there’ll be some review on their dashboard looking at the metrics. [Their manager will] be saying, “Hey, why did time spent [on the site] go down about three weeks ago? Oh, it’ll be [because] we added these features. Let’s just roll back some of those features, to figure out how we get that number back up.” ’ This isn’t some conspiracy theory, any more than it’s a conspiracy theory to explain that KFC wants you to eat fried chicken. It’s simply an obvious result of the incentive structure that has been put in place and that we allow to continue. ‘Their business model,’ he says, ‘is screen time, not life time.’

特里斯坦亲眼目睹了这些商业激励机制在实践中的运作方式。他跟我说，想象一下：一位工程师提出一项改进方案，可以提高用户的注意力，或者让他们花更多时间陪伴朋友。“然后，两周到四周后，他们醒来，发现仪表盘上出现了一些指标分析。[他们的经理会]说，‘嘿，为什么大约三周前用户在网站上的停留时间下降了？哦，那是因为我们添加了这些功能。我们先把其中一些功能撤回，看看怎么才能把停留时间拉回来。’”这并非什么阴谋论，就像肯德基想让你吃炸鸡一样，这并非阴谋论。这只是现有激励机制的必然结果，而我们却允许这种机制继续存在下去。“他们的商业模式，”他说，“是屏幕时间，而不是生命时间。”

It was at this point in learning Tristan’s story – from him, his friends, his colleagues and his critics – that I realised something so simple that I am almost embarrassed to say it. For years, I had blamed my deteriorating powers of attention simply on my own failings or on the existence of the smartphone itself as a technology. Most of the people I know do the same. We tell ourselves: The phone arrived, and it ravaged me. I believed any smartphone would have done the same. But what Tristan was showing is that the truth is more complicated. The arrival of the smartphone would always have increased to some degree the number of distractions in life, to be sure, but a great deal of the damage to our attention spans is being caused by something more subtle. It’s not the smartphone in and of itself; it is the way the apps on the smartphone and the sites on our laptops are designed.

正是在了解特里斯坦的故事——从他本人、他的朋友、同事和批评者那里——的过程中，我意识到了一件简单到让我几乎不好意思说出口的事情。多年来，我一直把注意力不集中归咎于自身的缺点，或者归咎于智能手机这项技术本身。我认识的大多数人也都是如此。我们告诉自己：手机一出现，就毁了我。我当时认为任何一款智能手机都会如此。但特里斯坦的经历表明，真相远比这复杂。诚然，智能手机的出现总会在一定程度上增加生活中的干扰因素，但我们注意力持续时间的下降很大程度上是由一些更为微妙的因素造成的。问题不在于智能手机本身，而在于智能手机上的应用程序和笔记本电脑上的网站的设计方式。

Tristan taught me that the phones we have, and the programs that run on them, were deliberately designed by the smartest people in the world to maximally grab and maximally hold our attention. He wants us to understand that this design is not inevitable. I had to really think this over, because, of all the things I learned from him, this seemed the most important.

特里斯坦告诉我，我们现在用的手机以及手机上运行的程序，都是世界上最聪明的人精心设计的，目的就是为了最大限度地吸引和留住我们的注意力。他想让我们明白，这种设计并非必然。我不得不认真思考这句话，因为在他教给我的所有东西中，这似乎是最重要的。

The way our tech works now to corrode our attention was and remains a choice – by Silicon Valley, and by the wider society that lets them do it. Humans could have made a different choice then, and they can make a different choice now. You could have all this technology, Tristan told me, but not design it to be maximally distracting. In fact, you could design it with the opposite goal: to maximally respect people’s need for sustained attention, and to interrupt them as little as possible. You could design the technology not so that it pulls people away from their deeper and more meaningful goals, but so that it helps them to achieve them.

如今科技侵蚀我们注意力的方式，过去是、现在仍然是硅谷以及纵容他们这样做的整个社会的选择。人类过去可以做出不同的选择，现在也可以。特里斯坦告诉我，你可以拥有所有这些科技，但不必将其设计成最大程度地分散人们的注意力。事实上，你可以以相反的目标来设计它：最大限度地尊重人们对持续注意力的需求，并尽可能减少对他们的干扰。你可以设计出这样的科技：它不是让人们偏离更深层次、更有意义的目标，而是帮助他们实现这些目标。

This was shocking to me. It’s not just the phone: it’s the way the phone is currently designed. It’s not just the internet: it’s the way the internet is currently designed – and the incentives for the people designing it. You could keep your phone and your laptop, and you could keep your social-media accounts – and have much better attention, if they were designed around a different set of incentives.

这让我很震惊。问题不仅仅在于手机本身，而在于手机目前的设计方式。问题不仅仅在于互联网，而在于互联网目前的设计方式——以及设计者的激励机制。你可以继续使用手机、笔记本电脑和社交媒体账号，但如果它们的设计遵循不同的激励机制，你就能更好地集中注意力。

Once you see it in this different way, Tristan came to believe, it opens up a very different path forward, and the beginnings of a way out of our crisis. If the existence of the phone and the internet is the sole driver of this problem, we’re trapped and in deep trouble – because as a society, we’re not going to discard our tech. But if it’s the current design of the phones and the internet and the sites we run on them that is driving a lot of the problem, and there’s a very different way they could work, that would put us all in a very different position.

特里斯坦逐渐意识到，一旦你换个角度看待问题，就能找到一条截然不同的前进道路，并开启摆脱危机的希望。如果手机和互联网的存在是造成这个问题的唯一原因，那我们就真的陷入了困境——因为作为一个社会，我们不会轻易放弃科技。但如果问题的根源在于手机、互联网以及我们通过它们访问的网站的现有设计，而它们本可以以截然不同的方式运作，那么我们所有人的处境都将截然不同。

After you’ve adjusted your perspective in this way, seeing this as a debate between whether you are pro-tech or anti-tech is bogus and lets the people who stole your attention off the hook. The real debate is: what tech, designed for what purposes, in whose interests?

当你调整了视角之后，再把这场辩论看作是支持科技还是反对科技之争，那就大错特错了，也让那些窃取你注意力的人逃脱了责任。真正的辩论是：什么样的科技？它的设计目的是什么？它服务于谁的利益？

But when Tristan and Aza said that these sites are designed to be as distracting as possible, I still didn’t really understand how. It seemed like a big claim. To grasp it, I had to first learn something else embarrassingly basic. When you open your Facebook feed, you see a whirr of things for you to look at – your friends, their photos, some news stories. When I first joined Facebook back in 2008, I naively thought that these things appeared simply in the order in which my friends had posted them. I’m seeing my friend Rob’s photo because he just put it up; then my auntie’s status update comes next because she posted it before him. Or maybe, I thought, they were selected randomly. In fact, I learned over the years – as we all became more informed about these questions – that what you see is selected for you according to an algorithm.

但当特里斯坦和阿扎说这些网站的设计目的就是为了尽可能地分散用户的注意力时，我仍然不太明白其中的原理。这听起来有点夸张。为了理解这一点，我首先需要了解一些非常基础的知识。当你打开Facebook动态消息时，你会看到各种各样的内容——你的朋友、他们的照片、一些新闻报道。2008年我刚加入Facebook时，天真地以为这些内容只是按照朋友发布信息的顺序排列的。我看到朋友罗布的照片是因为他刚刚上传的；然后紧接着是我阿姨的状态更新，因为她比他先发布。或者，我当时想，这些内容可能是随机选择的。事实上，这些年来，随着我们对这些问题了解的加深，我逐渐意识到，你看到的内容是根据算法为你选择的。

When Facebook (and all the others) decide what you see in your news feed, there are many thousands of things they could show you. So they have written a piece of code to automatically decide what you will see. There are all sorts of algorithms they could use – ways they could decide what you should see, and the order in which you should see them. They could have an algorithm designed to show you things that make you feel happy. They could have an algorithm designed to show you things that make you feel sad. They could have an algorithm to show you things that your friends are talking about most. The list of potential algorithms is long.

当Facebook（以及其他所有社交媒体平台）决定你在动态消息中看到什么内容时，他们有成千上万种选择。因此，他们编写了一段代码来自动决定你会看到什么。他们可以使用各种各样的算法——决定你该看到什么，以及看到它们的顺序。他们可以设计一个算法来向你展示让你感到快乐的内容。他们可以设计一个算法来向你展示让你感到悲伤的内容。他们可以设计一个算法来向你展示你的朋友们正在热议的内容。潜在的算法种类繁多。

The algorithm they actually use varies all the time, but it has one key driving principle that is consistent. It shows you things that will keep you looking at your screen. That’s it. Remember: the more time you look, the more money they make. So the algorithm is always weighted towards figuring out what will keep you looking, and pumping more and more of that on to your screen to keep you from putting down your phone. It is designed to distract. But, Tristan was learning, that leads – quite unexpectedly, and without anyone intending it to – to some other changes, which have turned out to be incredibly consequential.

他们实际使用的算法一直在变化，但有一个关键的驱动原则始终不变：它会向你展示让你盯着屏幕的东西。就是这样。记住：你看的时间越长，他们赚的钱就越多。所以，算法始终致力于找出什么能让你一直盯着看，并不断地把这类内容推送到你的屏幕上，让你无法放下手机。它的设计目的就是分散你的注意力。但是，特里斯坦逐渐意识到，这——出乎意料地，而且并非任何人的本意——会导致一些其他的变化，而这些变化最终产生了极其深远的影响。

Imagine two Facebook feeds. One is full of updates, news and videos that make you feel calm and happy. The other is full of updates, news and videos that make you feel angry and outraged. Which one does the algorithm select? The algorithm is neutral about the question of whether it wants you to be calm or angry. That’s not its concern. It only cares about one thing: will you keep scrolling? Unfortunately, there’s a quirk of human behaviour. On average, we will stare at something negative and outrageous for a lot longer than we will stare at something positive and calm. You will stare at a car crash longer than you will stare at a person handing out flowers by the side of the road, even though the flowers will give you a lot more pleasure than the mangled bodies in a crash. Scientists have been proving this effect in different contexts for a long time – if they showed you a photo of a crowd, and some of the people in it were happy, and some angry, you would instinctively pick out the angry faces first. Even ten-week-old babies respond differently to angry faces. This has been known about in psychology for years and is based on a broad body of evidence. It’s called ‘negativity bias’.

想象一下两个Facebook信息流。一个充满了让你感到平静和快乐的更新、新闻和视频。另一个则充满了让你感到愤怒和愤慨的更新、新闻和视频。算法会选择哪一个呢？算法对你想让自己平静还是愤怒这个问题并不在意。这不是它关心的。它只关心一件事：你会不会继续滑动屏幕？不幸的是，人类行为有一个怪癖。平均而言，我们会盯着一些负面和令人愤慨的内容看的时间，比盯着一些积极和平静的内容看的时间要长得多。你会盯着车祸现场看的时间，比盯着路边分发鲜花的人看的时间要长，即使鲜花带给你的愉悦感远胜于车祸现场的残肢断骸。科学家们已经在不同的情境下证实了这种效应——如果他们给你看一张人群的照片，照片里有些人看起来很开心，有些人很生气，你会本能地先注意到那些生气的面孔。即使是十周大的婴儿对生气的面孔也会有不同的反应。心理学界对此早已有所了解，并有大量证据支持。它被称为“消极偏见”。

There is growing evidence that this natural human quirk has a huge effect online. On YouTube, what are the words that you should put into the title of your video, if you want to get picked up by the algorithm? They are – according to the best site monitoring YouTube trends – words such as ‘hates, obliterates, slams, destroys’. A major study at New York University found that for every word of moral outrage you add to a tweet, your retweet rate will go up by 20 percent on average, and the words that increased your retweet rate most were ‘attack’, ‘bad’ and ‘blame’. A study by the Pew Research Center found that if you fill your Facebook posts with ‘indignant disagreement’, you’ll double your likes and shares. So an algorithm that prioritises keeping you glued to the screen will – unintentionally but inevitably – prioritise outraging and angering you. If it’s more enraging, it’s more engaging.

越来越多的证据表明，这种人类与生俱来的怪癖在网络上有着巨大的影响。在YouTube上，如果你想让算法选中你的视频，应该在标题中使用哪些词语呢？根据监测YouTube趋势的最佳网站的说法，应该使用“憎恨”、“摧毁”、“抨击”、“破坏”等词语。纽约大学的一项重要研究发现，你在推文中添加的每多一个表达道德义愤的词语，你的转发率平均就会提高20%，而最能提升转发率的词语是“攻击”、“糟糕”和“指责”。皮尤研究中心的一项研究发现，如果你在Facebook帖子中充斥着“义愤填膺的反对意见”，你的点赞和分享量将会翻倍。因此，一个优先考虑让你沉迷于屏幕的算法，会——尽管并非有意为之，但却不可避免地——优先考虑那些让你感到愤怒和愤怒的内容。而越是激怒你，就越能吸引你的注意力。

If enough people are spending enough of their time being angered, that starts to change the culture. As Tristan told me, it ‘turns hate into a habit’. You can see this seeping into the bones of our society. When I was a teenager, there was a horrific crime in Britain, where two ten-year-old children murdered a toddler named Jamie Bulger. The Conservative prime minister at the time, John Major, responded by publicly saying that he believed we need ‘to condemn a little more, and understand a little less’. I remembered thinking then, at the age of fourteen, that this was surely wrong – that it’s always better to understand why people do things, even (perhaps especially) the most heinous acts. But today, this attitude – condemn more, understand less – has become the default response of almost everyone, from the right to the left, as we spend our lives dancing to the tune of algorithms that reward fury and penalise mercy.

如果足够多的人把足够多的时间花在愤怒上，文化就会开始改变。正如特里斯坦告诉我的那样，这会“把仇恨变成一种习惯”。你可以看到这种现象正在渗透到我们社会的骨子里。我十几岁的时候，英国发生了一起骇人听闻的罪案，两名十岁的孩子谋杀了名叫杰米·布尔格的幼童。当时的保守党首相约翰·梅杰公开回应说，他认为我们需要“多谴责一些，少理解一些”。我记得当时十四岁的我心想，这肯定是错的——理解人们做事的原因总是更好的，即使（也许尤其）是那些最令人发指的罪行。但如今，这种态度——多谴责，少理解——几乎成了所有人的默认反应，从右翼到左翼皆是如此，我们终其一生都在按照算法的节奏跳舞，这些算法奖励愤怒，惩罚仁慈。

In 2015 a researcher named Motahhare Eslami, as part of a team at the University of Illinois, took a group of ordinary Facebook users and explained to them how the Facebook algorithm works. She talked them through how it selects what they see. She discovered that 62 percent of them didn’t know their feeds were filtered at all, and they were astonished to learn about the algorithm’s existence. One person in the study compared it to the moment in the film The Matrix , when the central character, Neo, discovers he is living in a computer simulation.

2015年，伊利诺伊大学的研究员莫塔哈雷·伊斯兰米(Motahhare Eslami)与团队成员合作，招募了一群普通的Facebook用户，并向他们解释了Facebook算法的运作原理。她详细讲解了算法如何筛选用户看到的内容。她发现，62%的用户完全不知道他们的信息流经过过滤，得知算法的存在后，他们都感到非常震惊。一位参与者将这种体验比作电影《黑客帝国》中主角尼奥发现自己生活在计算机模拟世界中的场景。

Since I started work on this book in 2018, awareness of these questions has been growing rapidly, not least thanks to Tristan’s work – but I called several of my relatives and asked them if they knew what an algorithm was. None of them – including the teenagers – did. I asked my neighbours. They looked at me blankly. It’s easy to assume most people know about this, but I don’t think it’s true. And even if you know all about it, that alone gives you no protection at all.

自从我2018年开始着手写这本书以来，人们对这些问题的关注度迅速提升，这很大程度上要归功于特里斯坦的研究——但我还是给几个亲戚打了电话，问他们是否知道什么是算法。结果，包括青少年在内，没有一个人知道。我又问了邻居，他们一脸茫然地看着我。人们很容易想当然地认为大多数人都了解算法，但我认为并非如此。即使你对算法了如指掌，也无法从中获得任何保护。

When I pieced together the evidence I’d learned, I could see that – when I broke it down – the people I interviewed had presented evidence for six distinct ways in which this machinery, as it currently operates, is harming our attention. (I will come to the scientists who dispute these arguments in

# ↩

Chapter Eight : as you read this, remember that some of it is controversial.)

当我把收集到的证据拼凑起来后，我发现——仔细分析之后——我采访的人提出了六种不同的证据，证明这套机制目前的运作方式正在损害我们的注意力。（我将在第八章讨论那些反驳这些论点的科学家：阅读时请记住，其中一些观点存在争议。）

First, these sites and apps are designed to train our minds to crave frequent rewards. They make us hunger for hearts and likes. When I was deprived of them in Provincetown, I felt bereft, and had to go through a painful withdrawal. Once you have been conditioned to need these reinforcements, Tristan told one interviewer, ‘It’s very hard to be with reality, the physical world, the built world – because it doesn’t offer as frequent and as immediate rewards as this thing does.’ This craving will drive you to pick up your phone more than you would if you had never been plugged into this system. You’ll break away from your work and your relationships to seek a sweet, sweet hit of retweets.

首先，这些网站和应用程序旨在训练我们的大脑，使其渴望频繁的奖励。它们让我们对点赞和关注趋之若鹜。在普罗温斯敦，当我无法获得这些奖励时，我感到无比失落，不得不经历痛苦的戒断反应。特里斯坦曾对一位采访者说，一旦你习惯了需要这些“奖励”，你就很难再面对现实、面对物质世界、面对现实世界——因为它们无法像这些东西一样提供如此频繁和即时的奖励。这种渴望会驱使你比从未接触过这个系统的人更频繁地拿起手机。你会为了获得转发的快感而放弃工作和人际关系。

Second, these sites push you to switch tasks more frequently than you normally would – to pick up your phone, or click over to Facebook on your laptop. When you do this, all the costs to your attention caused by switching – as I discussed in

# ↩

Chapter One – kick in. The evidence there shows this is as bad for the quality of your thinking as getting drunk or stoned.

其次，这些网站会促使你比平时更频繁地切换任务——比如拿起手机，或者点击笔记本电脑上的Facebook。当你这样做时，切换任务所造成的注意力损耗——正如我在第一章中讨论的那样——就会显现出来。那里的证据表明，这种行为对思维质量的损害程度不亚于醉酒或吸毒。

Third, these sites learn – as Tristan put it – how to ‘frack’ you. These sites get to know what makes you tick, in very specific ways – they learn what you like to look at, what excites you, what angers you, what enrages you. They learn your personal triggers – what, specifically, will distract you . This means that they can drill into your attention. Whenever you are tempted to put your phone down, the site keeps drip-feeding you the kind of material that it has learned, from your past behaviour, keeps you scrolling. Older technologies – like the printed page, or the television – can’t target you in this way. Social media knows exactly where to drill. It learns your most distractible spots and targets them.

第三，正如特里斯坦所说，这些网站会学习如何“操控”你。它们会以非常具体的方式了解你的喜好——它们会学习你喜欢看什么、什么让你兴奋、什么让你生气、什么让你愤怒。它们会了解你的个人触发点——具体来说，是什么会让你分心。这意味着它们可以牢牢抓住你的注意力。每当你想要放下手机时，网站就会不断地向你推送它根据你过去的行为习得的内容，让你继续滑动屏幕。像纸质书籍或电视这样的传统技术无法以这种方式精准定位你。社交媒体知道该如何精准地锁定你的注意力。它会了解你最容易分心的地方，并针对这些地方进行攻击。

Fourth, because of the way the algorithms work, these sites make you angry a lot of the time. Scientists have been proving in experiments for years that anger itself screws with your ability to pay attention. They have discovered that if I make you angry, you will pay less attention to the quality of arguments around you, and you will show ‘decreased depth of processing’ – that is, you will think in a shallower, less attentive way. We’ve all had that feeling – you start prickling with rage, and your ability to properly listen goes out the window. The business models of these sites are jacking up our anger every day. Remember the words their algorithms promote – attack, bad, blame.

第四，由于算法的运作方式，这些网站常常让你生气。多年来，科学家们通过实验证明，愤怒本身会影响你的注意力。他们发现，如果我让你生气，你就会减少对周围论点质量的关注，并且会出现“处理深度降低”——也就是说，你的思维会变得肤浅、注意力不集中。我们都有过这种感觉——怒火中烧，完全丧失了倾听的能力。这些网站的商业模式每天都在加剧我们的愤怒。记住他们的算法所推广的关键词——攻击、糟糕、指责。

Fifth, in addition to making you angry, these sites make you feel that you are surrounded by other people’s anger. This can trigger a different psychological response in you. As Dr Nadine Harris, the Surgeon General of California, who you’ll meet later in this book, explained to me: Imagine that one day you are attacked by a bear. You will stop paying attention to your normal concerns – what you’re going to eat tonight, or how you will pay the rent. You become vigilant. Your attention flips to scanning for unexpected dangers all around you. For days and weeks afterwards, you will find it harder to focus on more everyday concerns. This isn’t limited to bears. These sites make you feel that you are in an environment full of anger and hostility, so you become more vigilant – a situation where more of your attention shifts to searching for dangers, and less and less is available for slower forms of focus like reading a book or playing with your kids.

第五，除了让你生气之外，这些网站还会让你感觉自己被他人的愤怒所包围。这会引发你不同的心理反应。正如加州卫生局局长纳丁·哈里斯博士（你会在本书后面读到她）向我解释的那样：想象一下，有一天你被熊袭击了。你会不再关注那些日常琐事——比如今晚吃什么，或者怎么交房租。你会变得高度警惕。你的注意力会转移到扫描周围所有意想不到的危险上。在接下来的几天甚至几周里，你会发现自己很难再专注于日常琐事。这种情况并不局限于熊。这些网站会让你感觉自己身处一个充满愤怒和敌意的环境中，因此你会变得更加警惕——在这种情况下，你的注意力更多地转移到寻找危险上，而用于阅读或与孩子玩耍等更轻松的专注活动的时间则越来越少。

Sixth, these sites set society on fire. This is the most complex form of harm to our attention, with several stages, and I think probably the most harmful. Let’s go through it slowly.

第六，这些网站正在引燃社会。这是对我们注意力最复杂的危害形式，它包含多个阶段，而且我认为可能是危害最大的。让我们慢慢来。

We don’t just pay attention as individuals: we pay attention together, as a society. Here’s an example. In the 1970s, scientists discovered that all over the world, people were using hairsprays that contained a group of chemicals named CFCs. These chemicals were then entering the atmosphere and having an unintended but disastrous effect – they were damaging the ozone layer, a crucial part of the atmosphere that protects us from the sun’s rays. Those scientists warned that, over time, this could pose a serious threat to life on earth. Ordinary people absorbed this information and saw that it was true. Then activist groups – made up of ordinary citizens – formed, and demanded a ban. These activists persuaded their fellow citizens that this was urgent and made it into a big political issue. This put pressure on politicians and that pressure was sustained until those politicians banned CFCs entirely. At every stage, averting this risk to our species required us to be able to pay attention as a society – to absorb the science; to distinguish it from falsehood; to band together to demand action; and to pressure our politicians until they act.

我们不仅要作为个体关注，更要作为一个社会共同关注。举个例子。20世纪70年代，科学家发现世界各地的人们都在使用含有氟氯化碳（CFCs）的发胶。这些化学物质进入大气层，造成了意想不到的灾难性后果——它们破坏了臭氧层，而臭氧层是大气层的重要组成部分，保护我们免受太阳辐射的侵害。科学家警告说，随着时间的推移，这可能会对地球上的生命构成严重威胁。普通民众接受了这些信息，并意识到这是事实。随后，由普通公民组成的行动团体成立，要求禁止使用氟氯化碳。这些行动者说服了他们的同胞，让他们意识到此事迫在眉睫，并将其上升为一个重要的政治议题。这给政客们施加了压力，这种压力持续不断，直到政客们最终彻底禁止使用氟氯化碳。在每个阶段，为了避免人类面临这种风险，我们都需要作为一个社会共同关注——理解科学；辨别真伪；团结起来要求采取行动；并向我们的政治家施压，直到他们采取行动。

But there is evidence that these sites are now severely harming our ability to come together as a society to identify our problems and to find solutions in ways like this. They are damaging not just your attention as an individual, but our collective attention. At the moment false claims spread on social media far faster than the truth, because of the algorithms that spread outraging material faster and further. A study by the Massachussetts Institute of Technology found that fake news travels six times faster on Twitter than real news, and during the 2016 US presidential elections, flat-out falsehoods on Facebook outperformed the top stories at nineteen mainstream news sites put together. As a result, we are being pushed all the time to pay attention to nonsense – things that just aren’t so. If the ozone layer was threatened today, the scientists warning about it would find themselves being shouted down by bigoted viral stories claiming the threat was all invented by the billionaire George Soros, or that there’s no such thing as the ozone layer anyway, or that the holes were really being made by Jewish space lasers.

但有证据表明，这些网站正在严重损害我们作为一个社会团结起来，共同识别问题并寻找解决方案的能力。它们不仅损害了个人的注意力，也损害了我们集体的注意力。目前，由于算法会更快、更广泛地传播耸人听闻的内容，虚假信息在社交媒体上的传播速度远远超过真相。麻省理工学院的一项研究发现，假新闻在推特上的传播速度是真实新闻的六倍；在2016年美国总统大选期间，脸书上的彻头彻尾的谎言的传播速度甚至超过了19家主流新闻网站所有头条新闻的总和。结果，我们不断被引导去关注无稽之谈——那些根本不存在的事情。如果今天臭氧层受到威胁，发出警告的科学家们将会被充满偏见的病毒式传播信息所淹没，这些信息声称臭氧层的威胁是亿万富翁乔治·索罗斯捏造的，或者根本就不存在臭氧层，又或者臭氧层空洞实际上是犹太人用太空激光器制造的。

If we are lost in lies, and constantly riled up to be angry with our fellow citizens, this sets off a chain reaction. It means we can’t understand what is really going on. In those circumstances, we can’t solve our collective challenges. This means our wider problems will get worse. As a result, the society won’t just feel more dangerous – it will actually be more dangerous. Things will start to break down. And as real danger rises, we will become more and more vigilant.

如果我们深陷谎言，不断被煽动起来对同胞充满愤怒，就会引发连锁反应。这意味着我们无法理解事情的真相。在这种情况下，我们无法解决共同面临的挑战。这意味着我们更广泛的问题将会恶化。结果，社会不仅会让人感到更加危险——实际上也会变得更加危险。社会秩序将开始崩溃。随着真正的危险加剧，我们会变得越来越警惕。

One day, Tristan was shown how this dynamic works when he was approached by a man named Guillaume Chaslot, who had been an engineer designing and administering the algorithm that picks out the videos that are recommended to you on YouTube when you watch a video there. Guillaume wanted to tell him what was happening behind closed doors. Just like Facebook, YouTube makes more money the longer you watch. That’s why they designed it so that when you stop watching one video, it automatically recommends and plays another one for you. How are those videos selected? YouTube also has an algorithm – and it too has figured that that you’ll keep watching longer if you see things that are outrageous, shocking and extreme. Guillaume had seen how it works, with all the data YouTube keeps secret – and he saw what it meant in practice.

有一天，特里斯坦遇到了一个名叫纪尧姆·沙洛特的人，他向特里斯坦展示了这种动态是如何运作的。纪尧姆曾是一名工程师，负责设计和管理YouTube推荐视频的算法。他想告诉特里斯坦一些幕后运作的真相。就像Facebook一样，YouTube的盈利模式是用户观看时间越长，它赚的钱就越多。因此，他们设计了一个系统，当用户停止观看一个视频时，系统会自动推荐并播放另一个视频。这些视频是如何被选中的呢？YouTube也有一个算法——它也发现，如果用户看到一些耸人听闻、令人震惊和极端的内容，他们就会继续观看更长时间。纪尧姆亲眼目睹了这一切，包括YouTube隐藏的所有数据——他也看到了这在实际应用中的意义。

If you watched a factual video about the Holocaust, it would recommend several more videos, each one getting more extreme, and within a chain of five or so videos, it would usually end up automatically playing a video denying the Holocaust happened. If you watched a normal video about 9/11, it would often recommend a ‘9/11 truther’ video in a similar way. This isn’t because the algorithm (or anyone at YouTube) is a Holocaust denier or 9/11 truther. It was simply selecting whatever would most shock and compel people to watch longer. Tristan started to look into this, and concluded: ‘No matter where you start, you end up more crazy.’

如果你观看了一段关于大屠杀的客观视频，它会推荐更多类似的视频，每个视频都越来越极端。通常情况下，在观看五六个视频后，它会自动播放一段否认大屠杀的视频。如果你观看了一段关于9/11事件的普通视频，它通常也会以类似的方式推荐一段“9/11阴谋论”视频。这并非因为算法（或YouTube的任何员工）是否认大屠杀或鼓吹9/11阴谋论的人。它只是选择那些最能引起人们震惊并促使他们观看更长时间的内容。特里斯坦开始研究这个问题，并得出结论：“无论你从哪里开始，最终都会变得更加疯狂。”

It turned out, as Guillaume leaked to Tristan, that YouTube had recommended videos by Alex Jones and his website InfoWars 15 billion times. Jones is a vicious conspiracy theorist who has claimed that the 2012 Sandy Hook massacre was faked, and that the grieving parents are liars whose children had never even existed. As a result, some of those parents were inundated with death threats and had to flee their homes. When they sued him, he admitted in court that the massacre was real, and said he had been suffering from ‘a form of psychosis’ when he denied it. This is just one of many insane claims he has made. Tristan has said: ‘Let’s compare that – what is the aggregate traffic of the New York Times , the Washington Post , the Guardian ? All that together is not close to fifteen billion views.’

正如吉约姆向特里斯坦透露的那样，YouTube竟然向亚历克斯·琼斯及其网站InfoWars推荐了150亿次视频。琼斯是一位恶毒的阴谋论者，他声称2012年桑迪胡克小学枪击案是伪造的，那些悲痛欲绝的父母都是骗子，他们的孩子根本不存在。结果，一些遇难父母收到了大量死亡威胁，被迫逃离家园。当他们起诉琼斯时，他在法庭上承认枪击案是真实的，并声称自己之前否认时患有“某种精神病”。这只是他众多荒谬言论中的一个。特里斯坦说：“我们来比较一下——《纽约时报》、《华盛顿邮报》和《卫报》的总流量是多少？加起来也远不到150亿次观看。”

The average young person is soaking up filth like this day after day. Do those feelings of anger go away when they put down their phone? The evidence suggests that for lots of people, they don’t. A major study asked white nationalists how they became radicalised, and a majority named the internet – with YouTube as the site that most influenced them. A separate study of far-right people on Twitter found that YouTube was by far the website they turned to the most. ‘Just watching YouTube radicalises people,’ Tristan explained. Companies like YouTube want us to think ‘we have a few bad apples’, he explained to the journalist Decca Aitkenhead, but they don’t want us to ask: ‘Do we have a system that is systematically, as you turn the crank every day, pumping out more radicalisation? We’re growing bad apples. We’re a bad-apple factory. We’re a bad-apple farm.’

普通年轻人每天都在吸收着这样的污秽信息。当他们放下手机时，这些愤怒的情绪就会消失吗？证据表明，对很多人来说，答案是否定的。一项大型研究询问白人至上主义者是如何变得激进的，大多数人提到了互联网——其中YouTube是对他们影响最大的网站。另一项针对推特上极右翼人士的研究发现，YouTube是他们访问最多的网站。“仅仅是观看YouTube就能使人激进化，”特里斯坦解释道。他向记者德卡·艾特肯黑德解释说，像YouTube这样的公司想让我们认为“我们只有几个害群之马”，但他们不想让我们问：“我们是否拥有一个系统，它每天都在有条不紊地生产更多的激进分子？我们正在培育害群之马。我们是一个害群之马工厂。我们是一个害群之马农场。”

I saw a vision of where this could take us all in 2018, when I went to Brazil in the run-up to their presidential election, in part to see my friend Raull Santiago, a remarkable young man I got to know when I was writing the Brazilian edition of my book about the war on drugs, Chasing the Scream .

2018 年，在巴西总统选举前夕，我去了巴西，部分原因是去看望我的朋友劳尔·圣地亚哥，一位杰出的年轻人。我在撰写关于禁毒战争的书籍《追逐尖叫》的巴西版时认识了他。那时，我看到了这件事可能带给我们所有人的愿景。

Raull grew up in a place named Complexo do Alemão, which is one of the biggest and poorest favelas in Rio. It’s a huge, jagged ziggurat of concrete and tin and wire that stretches far up on the hills, way above the city, until it seems to be almost in the clouds. At least 200,000 people live there, in narrow concrete alleyways that are criss-crossed with makeshift wires providing electricity. The people here built this whole world brick by brick, with little support from the state. The alleyways of Alemão are surreally beautiful: they look like Naples after some undefined apocalypse. As a child, Raull would fly kites high above the favela with his best friend Fabio, where they could see out all across Rio, towards the ocean and the statue of Christ the Redeemer.

劳尔在阿莱芒贫民窟长大，那是里约热内卢最大、最贫困的贫民窟之一。它像一座巨大的、参差不齐的混凝土、铁皮和电线构成的金字塔，高耸于山丘之上，远高于城市，仿佛直插云霄。至少有20万人居住在那里，狭窄的混凝土巷道纵横交错，简易的电线纵横交错地提供电力。这里的人们一砖一瓦地建造了这个世界，几乎没有得到政府的任何支持。阿莱芒的巷道美得令人惊叹：仿佛是经历了一场未知的末日浩劫后的那不勒斯。小时候，劳尔经常和他的好朋友法比奥一起在贫民窟上空放风筝，在那里他们可以俯瞰整个里约热内卢，远眺大海和基督救世主雕像。

Often the authorities would send tanks rolling into the favela. The attitude of the Brazilian state towards the poor was to keep them suppressed with periodic threats of extreme violence. On their way to school, Raull and Fabio would regularly see bodies in the alleyways. Everyone in Alemão knew that the cops could shoot poor kids and claim they were drug dealers, and plant drugs or guns on them. In practice, the police had a licence to murder the poor, and everyone knew it.

当局经常派坦克开进贫民窟。巴西政府对待穷人的态度是，时不时地以极端暴力相威胁，以此压制他们。劳尔和法比奥上学路上经常看到巷子里躺着尸体。阿莱芒的每个人都知道，警察可以枪杀穷孩子，然后谎称他们是毒贩，并在他们身上栽赃毒品或枪支。实际上，警察拥有杀害穷人的特权，而且人人都知道这一点。

Fabio always seemed like the kid most likely to get away from all of this – he was great at maths, and determined to raise money for his mother and disabled sister. He was always figuring out deals – he persuaded the local bars to let him buy their bottles so he could sell them on in bulk, for example. But then, one day, Raull was told something terrible: Fabio had – like so many kids before him – been shot dead by the police. He was fifteen years old.

法比奥似乎总是最有可能摆脱这一切的孩子——他数学很好，而且决心要为母亲和残疾的妹妹筹钱。他总是能想出各种交易的办法——比如，他能说服当地的酒吧让他买下他们的酒瓶，然后再批量转售。但是，有一天，劳尔听到了一个可怕的消息：法比奥——就像之前的许多孩子一样——被警察枪杀了。他才十五岁。

Raull decided he couldn’t just watch his friends being killed one by one – so, as the years passed, he decided to do something bold. He set up a Facebook page named Coletivo Papo Reto, which gathers cell phone footage from across Brazil of the police killing innocent people and planting drugs or guns on them. It became huge with their videos regularly going viral. Even some people who had defended the police began to see their real behaviour and oppose it. It was an inspiring story about how the internet made it possible for people who have been treated like third-class citizens to find a voice, and to mobilise and fight back.

劳尔无法眼睁睁地看着朋友们一个个被杀害——于是，随着时间的推移，他决定采取大胆的行动。他创建了一个名为“Coletivo Papo Reto”（挑战警察集体）的Facebook页面，专门收集巴西各地警察杀害无辜民众并栽赃毒品或枪支的手机视频。该页面迅速走红，视频经常在网络上疯传。甚至一些曾经为警察辩护的人也开始看清警察的真面目，并开始反对他们。这是一个鼓舞人心的故事，讲述了互联网如何让那些被视为三等公民的人们发出自己的声音，并团结起来进行反抗。

But at the same time as the web was having this positive effect, the social-media algorithms were having the opposite effect – they were supercharging anti-democratic forces in Brazil. A former military officer named Jair Bolsonaro had been a marginal figure for years. He was way outside the mainstream, because he kept saying vile things and attacking large parts of the population in extreme ways. He praised people who had carried out torture against innocent people when Brazil was a dictatorship. He told his female colleagues in the Senate that they were so ugly he wouldn’t bother raping them, and that they weren’t ‘worthy’ of it. He said he would rather learn his son was dead than learn his son was gay. Then YouTube and Facebook became one of the main ways people in Brazil got their news. Their algorithms prioritised angry outrageous content – and Bolsonaro’s reach dramatically surged. He became a social-media star. He ran for president openly attacking people like the residents of Alemão, saying the country’s poorer, blacker citizens ‘are not even good for breeding’, and should ‘go back to the zoo’. He promised to give the police even more power to launch intensified military attacks on the favelas – a licence for wholesale slaughter.

然而，在互联网产生积极影响的同时，社交媒体算法却产生了截然相反的效果——它们极大地助长了巴西的反民主势力。一位名叫雅伊尔·博尔索纳罗的前军官多年来一直是个边缘人物。他完全游离于主流之外，因为他不断发表恶毒言论，并以极端的方式攻击广大民众。他赞扬那些在巴西独裁统治时期对无辜民众施以酷刑的人。他告诉参议院的女同事，她们丑陋到他懒得强奸她们，她们“不配”被强奸。他说，他宁愿得知儿子去世，也不愿得知儿子是同性恋。后来，YouTube和Facebook成为巴西民众获取新闻的主要渠道之一。它们的算法优先推送愤怒、耸人听闻的内容——博尔索纳罗的影响力因此急剧上升。他一跃成为社交媒体明星。他竞选总统时公开攻击像阿莱芒贫民窟居民这样的群体，声称该国较贫穷、肤色较深的公民“甚至不配繁衍后代”，应该“滚回动物园”。他还承诺赋予警方更大的权力，对贫民窟发动更猛烈的军事打击——这无异于一场大规模屠杀的许可。

Here was a society with huge problems that urgently needed to be solved – but social media algorithms were boosting far-right-wingers and wild disinformation. In the run-up to the election, in favelas like Alemão, many people were deeply worried about a story that had been circulating online. Supporters of Bolsonaro had created a video warning that his main rival, Fernando Haddad, wanted to turn all the children of Brazil into homosexuals, and that he had developed a cunning technique to do it. The video showed a baby sucking a bottle, only there was something peculiar about it – the teat of the bottle had been painted to look like a penis. This, the story that circulated said, is what Haddad will distribute to every kindergarten in Brazil. This became one of the most-shared news stories in the entire election. People in the favelas explained indignantly that they couldn’t possibly vote for somebody who wanted to get babies to suck these penis-teats, and so they would have to vote for Bolsonaro instead. On these algorithm-pumped absurdities, the fate of the whole country turned.

这是一个问题重重、亟待解决的社会——然而社交媒体算法却助长了极右翼分子和虚假信息的传播。在大选前夕，像阿莱芒这样的贫民窟里，许多人对网上流传的一则消息忧心忡忡。博索纳罗的支持者制作了一段视频，警告说他的主要竞争对手费尔南多·哈达德想要把巴西所有的孩子都变成同性恋，而且他为此发明了一种狡猾的手段。视频中，一个婴儿正在吮吸奶瓶，但奶瓶却有些蹊跷——奶嘴被涂成了阴茎的形状。流传的消息称，哈达德将把这种奶瓶分发给巴西的每一所幼儿园。这则消息迅速成为整个大选期间传播最广的新闻之一。贫民窟的人们愤慨地解释说，他们不可能投票给一个想让婴儿吸吮这些阴茎乳头的人，所以他们只能投票给博索纳罗。整个国家的命运，就此由这些算法驱动的荒谬之举所改变。

When Bolsonaro unexpectedly won the presidency, his supporters chanted ‘Facebook! Facebook! Facebook!’ They knew what the algorithms had done for them. There were, of course, many other factors at work in Brazilian society – this is only one – but it is the one Bolsonaro’s gleeful followers picked out first.

博索纳罗意外赢得总统大选时，他的支持者高喊着“脸书！脸书！脸书！”他们深知算法为他们做了什么。当然，巴西社会还有许多其他因素在起作用——这只是其中之一——但这却是博索纳罗那些欣喜若狂的追随者们首先想到的。

Not long afterwards, Raull was in his home in Alemão when he heard a noise that sounded like an explosion. He ran outside and saw that a helicopter was hovering above the favela and firing down at the people below – precisely the kind of violence Bolsonaro had pledged to carry out. Raull screamed for his kids to hide, terrified. When I spoke to Raull on Skype later, he was more shaken than I had seen him before. As I write, this violence is being ramped up more and more.

不久之后，劳尔在阿莱芒的家中听到一声巨响，听起来像是爆炸。他跑到屋外，看到一架直升机盘旋在贫民窟上空，向下扫射人群——这正是博索纳罗誓言要实施的那种暴力。劳尔惊恐万分，大声呼喊孩子们躲起来。后来我通过Skype与劳尔通话时，他比我之前见到的任何时候都更加惊魂未定。就在我写下这些文字的时候，这种暴力还在不断升级。

When I thought about Raull, I could see the deeper way the rage-driven algorithms of social media and YouTube damage attention and focus. It’s a cascading effect. These sites harm people’s ability to pay attention as individuals. Then they pump the population’s heads full of grotesque falsehoods, to the point where they can’t distinguish real threats to their existence (an authoritarian leader pledging to shoot them) from non-existent threats (their children being made gay by penises painted on baby bottles). Over time, if you expose any country to all this for long enough, it will become so lost in rage and unreality that it can’t make sense of its problems and it can’t build solutions. This means that the streets and the skies actually become more dangerous – so you become hypervigilant, and this wrecks your attention even more.

当我想到劳尔时，我更深刻地体会到社交媒体和YouTube上那些由愤怒驱动的算法是如何损害人们的注意力和专注力的。这是一种连锁反应。这些网站首先损害了人们作为个体集中注意力的能力。然后，它们又向民众灌输大量荒谬的谎言，以至于人们无法区分真正威胁生存的因素（例如，一个独裁领导人扬言要枪毙他们）和根本不存在的威胁（例如，他们的孩子因为奶瓶上画着阴茎而被“掰弯”）。久而久之，如果一个国家长期暴露在这种环境下，就会被愤怒和虚假信息所淹没，以至于无法理解自身的问题，也无法找到解决办法。这意味着街道和天空实际上会变得更加危险——于是人们变得过度警惕，而这反过来又会进一步损害他们的注意力。

This could be the future for all of us if we continue with these trends. Indeed, what happens in Brazil alone directly affects your life and mine. Bolsonaro has dramatically stepped up the destruction of the Amazon rainforest – the lungs of the planet. If this continues for much longer, it will tip us into an even worse climate disaster.

如果我们继续沿用这些趋势，这可能就是我们所有人的未来。事实上，仅巴西发生的事情就直接影响着你我的生活。博索纳罗大幅加剧了对亚马逊雨林——地球之肺——的破坏。如果这种情况持续下去，我们将面临更加严重的气候灾难。

When I was discussing all this with Tristan one day back in San Francisco, he ran his fingers through his hair and said to me that these algorithms are ‘debasing the soil of society … You need … a social fabric, and if you debase it, you don’t know what you are going to wake up to.’

有一天我在旧金山和特里斯坦讨论这些事情时，他一边用手指梳理着头发一边对我说，这些算法“正在破坏社会的土壤……你需要……社会结构，如果你破坏了它，你不知道醒来后会看到什么。”

This machinery is systematically diverting us – at an individual and a social level – from where we want to go. James Williams, the former Google strategist, said to me we should imagine ‘if we had a GPS and it worked fine the first time. But the next time, it took you a few streets away from where you wanted to go. And then later, it took you to a different town.’ All because the advertisers who funded GPS had paid for this to happen. ‘You would never keep using that.’ But social media works exactly this way. There’s a ‘destination we want to get to, and most of the time, it doesn’t actually get us there – it takes us off track. If it was actually navigating us not through informational space but through physical space, we would never keep using it. It would be, by definition, defective.’

这套机制正在系统性地将我们——无论是在个人层面还是社会层面——引离我们真正想去的地方。谷歌前战略家詹姆斯·威廉姆斯曾对我说，我们可以想象一下：“如果我们有一个GPS，第一次用起来很顺畅。但第二次，它却把你带到离目的地几条街远的地方。再后来，它甚至把你带到了另一个城镇。”这一切都是因为资助GPS的广告商花钱促成了这种情况。“你肯定不会继续使用它。”但社交媒体的运作方式恰恰如此。我们有一个“想要到达的目的地，但大多数时候，它实际上并不能带我们到达那里——反而会把我们引向歧途。如果它实际上是在物理空间而非信息空间中引导我们，我们肯定不会继续使用它。从定义上讲，它就是有缺陷的。”

Tristan and Aza started to believe that all these effects, when you add them together, are producing a kind of ‘human downgrading.’ Aza said: ‘I think we’re in the process of reverse-engineering ourselves. [We discovered a way to] open up the human skull, find the strings that control us, and start pulling on our own marionette strings. Once you do that, an accidental jerk in one direction causes your arm to jerk further, which pulls your marionette string further … That’s the era that we’re headed into now.’ Tristan believes that what we are seeing is ‘the collective downgrading of humans and the upgrading of machines’. We are becoming less rational, less intelligent, less focused.

特里斯坦和阿扎开始相信，所有这些影响加在一起，会造成一种“人类退化”。阿扎说：“我认为我们正在进行自我逆向工程。[我们发现了一种方法]打开人类的头骨，找到控制我们的线索，然后开始拉扯我们自己的傀儡线。一旦你这么做了，一个不经意的拉扯就会导致你的手臂进一步抖动，从而进一步拉扯你的傀儡线……这就是我们现在正走向的时代。”特里斯坦认为，我们正在目睹的是“人类的集体退化和机器的集体升级”。我们变得越来越不理性、越来越不聪明、越来越不专注。

Aza told me: ‘Imagine if you have worked your entire career towards a technology that you feel is good. It’s making democracy stronger. It’s changing the way you live. Your friends value you because of these things you’ve made. All of a sudden you’re like – that thing I’ve been working on my entire life is not just meaningless. It’s tearing apart the things you love the most.’

阿扎告诉我：“想象一下，你毕生致力于一项你认为很棒的技术。它让民主更加强大，改变了你的生活方式。你的朋友因为你的这些成就而珍视你。突然间，你发现——我毕生致力于的东西不仅毫无意义，而且还在摧毁你最珍视的一切。”

He told me that literature is full of stories where humans create something in a burst of optimism and then lose control of their creation. Dr Frankenstein creates a monster only for it to escape from him and commit murder. Aza began to think about these stories when he talked with his friends who were engineers working for some of the most famous websites in the world. He would ask them basic questions, like why their recommendation engines recommend one thing over another and, he said to me, ‘They’re like: we’re not sure why it’s recommending those things.’ They’re not lying – they have set up a technology that is doing things they don’t fully comprehend. He always says to them: ‘Isn’t that exactly the moment, in the allegories, where you turn the thing off – [when] it’s starting to do things you can’t predict?’

他告诉我，文学作品中充满了这样的故事：人类在一时乐观的驱使下创造出某种东西，然后却失去了对它的控制。弗兰肯斯坦博士创造了一个怪物，结果它逃脱了他的掌控，并犯下了谋杀罪。阿扎开始思考这些故事，是因为他和他的朋友们——一些在世界知名网站工作的工程师——聊天时，他会问他们一些基本问题，比如为什么他们的推荐引擎会推荐某些东西而不是其他东西。他告诉我：“他们会说：‘我们也不确定它为什么会推荐这些东西。’”他们并没有撒谎——他们开发的技术正在做一些他们自己也无法完全理解的事情。他总是对他们说：“这不正是寓言故事里那种应该关掉机器的时刻吗？——当机器开始做出你无法预料的事情时？”

When Tristan testified about this before the Senate, he asked: ‘How can we solve the world’s most urgent problems if we’ve downgraded our attention spans, downgraded our capacity for complexity and nuance, downgraded our shared truth, downgraded our beliefs into conspiracy-theory thinking, where we can’t construct shared agendas to solve our problems? This is destroying our sense-making, at a time when we need it the most. And the reason why I’m here is because every day it’s incentivised to get worse.’ He said he was especially worried about this, he told me later, because we are now, as a species, facing our biggest challenge ever – the fact that we are destroying the ecosystem we depend on for life by triggering the climate crisis. If we can’t focus, what possible hope do we have to solve global warming?

特里斯坦在参议院就此作证时问道：“如果我们注意力持续时间缩短，理解复杂性和细微差别的能力下降，对共同真理的认知退化，甚至沉迷于阴谋论，以至于无法构建解决问题的共同议程，我们又该如何解决世界上最紧迫的问题呢？这正在摧毁我们理解事物的能力，而我们恰恰最需要这种能力。我之所以站在这里，是因为这种情况每天都在恶化。”他后来告诉我，他对此尤其担忧，因为我们人类正面临着前所未有的挑战——我们正在通过引发气候危机来破坏我们赖以生存的生态系统。如果我们无法集中精力，又有什么希望解决全球变暖问题呢？

So Tristan and Aza started to ask with increasing urgency: How, in practice, do we change the machinery that is stealing our attention?

因此，特里斯坦和阿扎开始越来越迫切地提出这样一个问题：在实践中，我们如何改变正在窃取我们注意力的机制？

# ↩

8 Cause Seven: The Rise of Cruel Optimism (or: Why Individual Changes are an Important Start, But Not Enough)

8. 原因七：残酷乐观主义的兴起（或：为什么个人改变是一个重要的开始，但还不够）

‘I was with my daughter that afternoon,’ the Israeli-American tech designer Nir Eyal said to me, as he looked back on the day that it hit him that something had gone really wrong. ‘We had this beautiful afternoon planned’ – they were going through a daddy-and-daughter book, and she got to a page that asked: if you could have any superpower, which one would you choose? As she was contemplating this, Nir received a text, and ‘I started looking at my phone, as opposed to being fully present with her.’ When he looked up, she was gone.

“那天下午我和女儿在一起，”以色列裔美国科技设计师尼尔·埃亚尔（Nir Eyal）回忆起那天，突然意识到事情出了大问题。“我们原本计划了一个美好的下午，”他们正在一起看一本父女书，女儿翻到一页，上面写着：如果你能拥有任何一种超能力，你会选择哪一种？就在她思考这个问题的时候，尼尔收到了一条短信，“我开始看手机，而不是全心全意地陪伴她。”当他抬起头时，女儿已经不见了。

A childhood is made up of small moments of connection between a child and their parent. If you miss them, you don’t ever get them back. Nir realised with a lurch: ‘She got the message that whatever was on my phone was more important than she was.’

童年是由孩子与父母之间那些细微的情感联结构成的。一旦错过，就再也找不回来了。尼尔猛然意识到：“她明白了我的意思，我手机里的东西比她更重要。”

This wasn’t the first time. ‘I realised – wow, I really need to reconsider my relationship with distraction.’ Except Nir’s relationship to the technology causing this was different from yours or mine in a crucial way. Like Tristan, he studied with B. J. Fogg in his lab of ‘persuasive technologies’ at Stanford, and he went on to work with some of the most influential companies in Silicon Valley, helping them figure out how to get their users ‘hooked’. Now he was seeing it happen even to his own young daughter. She would scream at him: ‘iPad time! iPad time!’ and demand to go online. Nir realised he needed to figure out a strategy for how to overcome this – for her, for himself, and for all of us.

这并非第一次。“我意识到——哇，我真的需要重新审视自己与分心事物的关系。”然而，尼尔与导致这种分心的科技之间的关系，与你我之间存在着关键性的差异。和特里斯坦一样，他曾在斯坦福大学B·J·福格的“说服性技术”实验室学习，之后又在硅谷一些最具影响力的公司工作，帮助他们找到让用户“上瘾”的方法。如今，他发现这种情况甚至发生在自己的小女儿身上。她会冲他大喊：“玩iPad！玩iPad！”，非要上网。尼尔意识到，他需要找到一个克服这种分心的方法——为了她，为了他自己，也为了我们所有人。

He offers one particular way of dealing with this crisis that I want to engage with in detail. It is very different from the approach that Tristan and Aza have developed. Nir’s approach is important because it’s pretty clear this is going to be the approach that the wider tech industry offers us for the attention problems they are, in part, causing.

他提出了一种应对这场危机的独特方法，我想详细探讨一下。这与Tristan和Aza提出的方法截然不同。Nir的方法之所以重要，是因为很明显，这很可能是整个科技行业为了解决他们自身造成的注意力问题而提出的方案。

Somewhere at the back of his mind, Nir already had a template for what he believed he had to do. When he was young, Nir had been seriously overweight – something that shocked me when he said it, because he is now lean, bordering on buff. He was sent to ‘fat camp’, and tried all sorts of diets and detoxes, stripping out sugar or fast food. Nothing worked. Then, finally, he realised: ‘As much as I would have loved to blame McDonald’s for the problem, that wasn’t the problem. I was eating my feelings. I was using food as a coping mechanism.’ Once he knew this, he said, he could ‘actually tackle the problem’. He got in touch with his own anxieties and unhappiness, and he took up wrestling, and slowly began to change his body. ‘Clearly, food had a role,’ he said, ‘but it wasn’t the root cause of my problem.’ He said he had learned a key lesson: ‘In my life, I had something that felt like it controlled me, and I controlled it.’

在尼尔的潜意识深处，他早已有了自己必须做的事情的蓝图。年轻时，尼尔严重超重——他提起这件事时，我感到很惊讶，因为他现在身材精瘦，甚至可以说是健壮。他曾被送去“减肥营”，尝试过各种各样的节食和排毒方法，戒掉糖和快餐。但这些都无济于事。最终，他意识到：“尽管我很想把问题归咎于麦当劳，但那并不是问题的根源。我是在用食物来排解情绪。我把食物当作了一种应对机制。” 他说，一旦明白了这一点，他就能“真正解决问题”。他开始正视自己的焦虑和不快乐，并开始练习摔跤，慢慢地改变了自己的体型。 “很显然，食物起了一定作用，”他说，“但它并不是我问题的根源。” 他说他学到了一个重要的教训：“在我的生活中，我感觉自己被某种东西控制了，但我最终控制了它。”

Nir came to believe that if we are going to overcome this process of becoming hooked to our apps and devices, we have to develop individual skills to resist the part inside all of us that succumbs to these distractions. He argues that to do that, we primarily have to look inwards – to the reasons why we want to use them compulsively in the first place. People like Tristan and Aza, he said, ‘tell me about how bad these companies are. I say, well, what have you tried? Right? What have you done? Often, it’s nothing.’ He believes individual changes should be ‘the first line of defence’, and ‘it has to begin with a bit of introspection, with a bit of understanding ourselves’. Yes, he says, the environment changed: ‘You [the average tech user] didn’t make the iPhone. It’s not your fault. I never said it’s your fault. I’m saying it’s your responsibility. This stuff isn’t going away. In some form or other, it’s here to stay. What choice do we have? We have to adapt. That’s our only option.’

尼尔逐渐意识到，如果我们想要克服对应用程序和设备的依赖，就必须培养个人技能，抵制内心深处那些容易被这些干扰所诱惑的部分。他认为，要做到这一点，我们首先要反省自身——探究我们最初为何会如此痴迷地使用它们。他说，像特里斯坦和阿扎这样的人会“告诉我这些公司有多糟糕”。我会问他们：“你们尝试过什么？对吧？你们做过什么？通常情况下，什么都没做。”他认为，个人的改变应该是“第一道防线”，而且“必须从一些内省开始，从一些自我认知开始”。他承认，环境确实发生了变化：“你（普通科技用户）并没有制造iPhone。这不是你的错。我从来没说过这是你的错。我说的是，这是你的责任。这些东西不会消失。它们会以某种形式长期存在。我们还有别的选择吗？”我们必须适应。这是我们唯一的选择。

So how can we adapt? What can we do? He began to read through the social-science literature, to find evidence for individual changes you can make. He laid out what he sees as the best answers in his book Indistractible . There is one tool in particular that he believes can get us out of this problem. All of us have ‘ internal triggers’ – moments in our lives that push us to give in to bad habits. Nir realised that for him, it’s ‘when I’m writing – it’s never come easy. It’s always difficult.’ When he sat at his laptop and tried to write, he would often start to feel bored or stressed. ‘All of these bad things come bubbling up when I’m writing.’ When that happened, it would trigger something inside him. To get away from these uncomfortable feelings, he would tell himself there was something else he had to do, for just a moment. ‘The easiest thing to do would be – let me just check email real quick. Let me just open my phone real quick.’ He said: ‘I would think of every single conceivable excuse.’ He would compulsively check the news, telling himself that’s what a good citizen does. He would google a fact supposedly relevant to his writing, and two hours later he would find himself at the bottom of a rabbit hole, looking at something totally irrelevant.

那么我们该如何适应？我们能做些什么？他开始阅读社会科学文献，寻找个人可以做出改变的证据。他在他的著作《专注力》（Indistractible）中阐述了他认为的最佳答案。他特别相信有一种工具可以帮助我们摆脱困境。我们每个人都有“内在触发点”——生活中某些时刻会驱使我们屈服于坏习惯。尼尔意识到，对他而言，触发点是“写作的时候——写作从来都不是一件容易的事。它总是很困难。”当他坐在笔记本电脑前尝试写作时，他常常会感到无聊或压力。“写作时，所有这些不好的事情都会涌上心头。”每当这种情况发生时，都会触发他内心的某种东西。为了摆脱这些不舒服的感觉，他会告诉自己，他必须去做点别的事情，哪怕只是一小会儿。“最简单的做法就是——让我快速查看一下电子邮件。” “我这就打开手机看看。”他说：“我会想尽一切可能的借口。”他会强迫性地查看新闻，告诉自己这是好公民该做的。他会搜索一些自认为与写作相关的信息，结果两个小时后，他发现自己陷入了无底洞，浏览着一些完全无关的内容。

‘An internal trigger is an uncomfortable emotional state,’ he told me. ‘It’s all about avoidance. It’s all about – how do I get out of this uncomfortable state?’ He believes we all need to explore our triggers non-judgementally, think about them, and find ways to disrupt them. So whenever he felt that prickling feeling or boredom or stress come to him, he identified what was happening, and picked up a pack of Post-It notes, and he wrote on it what he wanted to know. Later, when he had finished a good stretch of writing, he would let himself google it – but only then.

“内在触发因素是一种不舒服的情绪状态，”他告诉我。“关键在于逃避。关键在于——我该如何摆脱这种不舒服的状态？”他认为我们都需要以不带评判的眼光去探索自己的触发因素，思考它们，并找到方法来打破它们。所以，每当他感到那种刺痛感、无聊或压力袭来时，他就会找出原因，然后拿起一包便利贴，把想知道的问题写下来。之后，当他写够了一段时间后，他才会允许自己上网搜索——但仅限于此。

It worked for him. This taught Nir that ‘we’re not beholden to habits. They can be interrupted. They get interrupted all the time. We can change habits. The way we change a habit is by understanding what the internal trigger is, and making sure that there’s some kind of break between the impulse to do a behaviour and the behaviour itself.’ He developed a range of techniques like this. He believes we should all try adopting a ‘ten-minute rule’ – if you feel the urge to check your phone, wait ten minutes. He says you should ‘time-box’ – which means you should draw up a detailed schedule of what you are going to do each day, and stick to it. He recommends changing the notification settings on your phone, so that your apps can’t interrupt you and kill your focus throughout the day. He says you should delete all the apps you can from your phone, and if you have to keep some, then you should schedule the time you are willing to spend on them in advance. He advises that you unsubscribe from email lists, and – if you can – have ‘office hours’ on your email, when you check them a few times a day, and ignore them the rest of the time.

这对他很有效。这让尼尔明白，“我们不必受制于习惯。习惯是可以被打断的。事实上，习惯经常被打断。我们可以改变习惯。改变习惯的方法是了解内在的触发因素，并确保在冲动和实际行为之间留有一段间隔。” 他开发了一系列类似的技巧。他认为我们都应该尝试“十分钟法则”——如果你想查看手机，就等十分钟。他还建议我们“设定时间限制”——这意味着你应该制定一份详细的每日计划，并严格执行。他建议更改手机的通知设置，这样你的应用程序就不会在一天中不断打断你，分散你的注意力。他建议你尽可能删除手机上的所有应用程序，如果必须保留一些，那么你应该提前安排好使用它们的时间。他建议你取消订阅电子邮件列表，并且——如果可以的话——在你的电子邮件中设定“办公时间”，每天查看几次，其余时间忽略它们。

By laying out these tools, he told me, ‘I wanted to empower people to realise – look, this isn’t that hard. It’s not that tough. If you know what to do, it’s pretty simple how to handle distraction.’ He seemed puzzled that more people don’t do it: ‘Two-thirds of people with a smartphone never change their notification settings. What? Right? This is not hard stuff. We just need to do this kind of stuff.’ Instead of railing against the tech companies, he says, we need to ask what we have done as individuals. He asked me: ‘Why isn’t the beginning of the discussion – okay, have we exhausted everything you can do right now? Can we do that stuff first? … Change your notification settings! Come on, this is basic stuff, right? Turn off the fucking Facebook notifications every five minutes! How about planning your day, you know? How many of us plan our day? We just let our time be usurped by the news or whatever’s on Twitter or whatever’s happening in the world outside us, as opposed to saying – actually what do I want to do with my time?’

他告诉我，通过提供这些工具，“我希望人们能够意识到——你看，这并不难。这并不难。如果你知道该怎么做，应对干扰其实很简单。” 他似乎很困惑为什么更多的人没有这样做：“三分之二的智能手机用户从来不更改通知设置。什么？对吧？这根本不是什么难事。我们只需要做这些就行了。” 他说，我们不应该一味指责科技公司，而应该反思我们作为个体做了些什么。他问我：“为什么讨论的开头不是——好吧，我们是不是已经尝试了所有你能做的事情？我们能不能先做这些？……更改你的通知设置！拜托，这都是基本常识，对吧？每五分钟就关掉该死的Facebook通知！还有，计划一下你的一天怎么样？我们当中有多少人会计划自己的一天呢？”我们任由自己的时间被新闻、推特上的内容或外界发生的事情所占据，而不是去思考——我到底想用我的时间做什么？

I felt conflicted as Nir explained this to me. I realised he was articulating precisely the logic that had taken me to Provincetown. Something deep inside me thought like this. Like him, I believed: this is a problem in you, and you need to change yourself. There was clearly some truth in it. Every specific intervention Nir recommends is, I believe, helpful. I tried each one of them after going through his work, and several of them made a small but real difference to me.

尼尔向我解释这一切时，我内心很矛盾。我意识到，他阐述的正是我当初去普罗温斯敦的逻辑。我内心深处也曾有过这样的想法。和他一样，我相信：这是你自身的问题，你需要改变自己。这其中显然包含着一些真理。我相信，尼尔推荐的每一个具体方法都很有帮助。在阅读了他的著作之后，我尝试了其中的每一种方法，其中一些确实给我带来了虽小但却切实的改变。

But there was something about what he said that made me feel uncomfortable, and for a while, I couldn’t articulate it. Nir’s approach is absolutely in line with how the tech companies want us to think about our attention problems. They can no longer deny the crisis, so they are doing something else: subtly urging us to see it as an individual problem that has to be solved with greater self-restraint on my part and yours, not theirs. That’s why they began to offer tools they argued would help you to strengthen your willpower. All new iPhones have an option where you could be told how much Screen Time you spent that day and that week, and a Do Not Disturb function where you can block out incoming messages. Facebook and Instagram introduced their own modest equivalents. Mark Zuckerberg even started using Tristan’s slogan, promising that time on Facebook would be ‘time well spent’ – except for him, it was all about Nir-style tools where you reflect on what’s gone wrong with your own motives. I am writing this chapter about Nir not because he is unusual, but because he is the most candid of the people putting forward the dominant view in Silicon Valley about what you and I should do now.

但他的话让我感到有些不舒服，一时之间，我却说不清这种感觉。尼尔的做法与科技公司希望我们看待注意力问题的方式完全一致。他们再也无法否认这场危机，于是他们另辟蹊径：巧妙地敦促我们将其视为个人问题，需要我们每个人通过更强的自制力来解决，而不是依靠他们。这就是为什么他们开始提供各种工具，声称可以帮助你增强意志力。所有新款iPhone都提供一项功能，可以显示你当天和当周的屏幕使用时间，还有一个“勿扰模式”，可以屏蔽来电信息。Facebook和Instagram也推出了各自类似的简化版功能。马克·扎克伯格甚至开始使用特里斯坦的口号，承诺在Facebook上花费的时间将是“物有所值”的——只不过对他来说，这一切都与尼尔式的工具有关，让你反思自己的动机出了什么问题。我写这一章是关于尼尔的，不是因为他很特别，而是因为在硅谷提出主流观点的人中，他是最坦诚的，而主流观点是关于你我如今应该做什么的。

Nir kept insisting that the tech companies have done a lot to make it easy for us to unplug. To explain this, he gave the example of a company boardroom he had been to where the boss took out his phone in a meeting, so everyone else felt free to do it. ‘I don’t know why that’s the tech company’s responsibility. In fact, if anything, the tech company gives you this beautiful little function here that [says] “do not disturb”. The tech company gave us a button. All you have to do is that. What more responsibility do we want from Apple? For God’s sake, push the fucking button that says “do not disturb” for an hour if you’re going to have a meeting with your colleagues. Is that so difficult?’

尼尔一直坚持认为，科技公司已经做了很多工作，让我们更容易摆脱电子设备的束缚。为了解释这一点，他举了一个例子：他曾去过一家公司的会议室，老板在会议上拿出手机，所以其他人也都觉得可以这么做。“我不明白为什么这是科技公司的责任。事实上，科技公司已经提供了‘勿扰模式’这个很棒的小功能。他们给了我们一个按钮，你只需要按一下就行了。我们还要苹果公司承担什么责任？拜托，如果你要和同事开会，就按一下‘勿扰模式’按钮，设置一个小时的勿扰模式好吗？这很难吗？”

My unease about this approach only became clear to me when I turned to the book Nir wrote a few years before he produced his work about how to beat distraction. It was written for an audience of tech designers and engineers, and it was named Hooked: How to Build Habit-Forming Products . He described it as a ‘cookbook’ containing ‘a recipe for human behaviour’. Reading Hooked as an ordinary user of the internet is strange – it’s like the moment in an old Batman movie when the villain is caught and reveals everything he did all along, step by step. Nir writes: ‘Let’s admit it: we are all in the persuasion business. Innovators build products meant to persuade people to do what we want them to do. We call these people users and even if we don’t say it aloud, we secretly wish every one of them would become fiendishly hooked to whatever we’re making.’

我对这种方法的疑虑，直到我翻阅了尼尔几年前写的那本书才真正显现出来。那本书是为科技设计师和工程师写的，书名是《上瘾：如何打造习惯养成型产品》。他把这本书描述为一本“烹饪书”，里面包含了“人类行为的配方”。作为一个普通的互联网用户，读《上瘾》的感觉很奇怪——就像老版蝙蝠侠电影里，反派被抓后，一步步地揭露自己所有的所作所为。尼尔写道：“让我们承认吧：我们都在从事说服工作。创新者打造的产品旨在说服人们去做我们想让他们做的事。我们称这些人是用户，即使我们不说出口，我们也暗自希望他们每个人都能对我们开发的产品上瘾。”

He lays out the methods to achieve this, which he describes as ‘mind manipulation’. The goal, Nir says, is to ‘create a craving’ in human beings – and he cites B. F. Skinner as a model for how to do it. His approach can be summarised by the headline on one of his blog posts: ‘Want to hook your users? Drive them crazy’.

他详细阐述了实现这一目标的方法，并将其称为“精神操控”。尼尔表示，其目标是在人类心中“制造渴望”，并以B·F·斯金纳为例来说明如何做到这一点。他的方法可以用他一篇博客文章的标题来概括：“想让你的用户上瘾？让他们疯狂。”

The goal of the designer is to create an ‘ internal trigger’ (remember them?) that will keep the user coming back again and again. To help the designer picture the kind of person they are targeting, he says they should imagine a user he names Julie, who ‘fears being out of the loop’. He comments: ‘Now we’ve got something! Fear is a powerful internal trigger, and we can design our solution to help calm Julie’s fear.’ Once you have succeeded in playing on feelings like this, ‘a habit is formed, [and so] the user is automatically triggered to use the product during routine events such as wanting to kill time while waiting in line,’ he writes approvingly.

设计师的目标是创造一种“内在触发点”（还记得这个概念吗？），让用户不断重复使用。为了帮助设计师想象目标用户群体，他建议他们想象一个名叫朱莉的用户，她“害怕被排除在外”。他评论道：“这下我们找到方向了！恐惧是一种强大的内在触发点，我们可以设计解决方案来帮助朱莉消除这种恐惧。”他赞许地写道，一旦成功利用了这种情感，“用户就会养成习惯，在诸如排队等候等日常情况下，他们会自动触发使用产品。”

Designers should get you and me ‘to repeat behaviours for long periods, ideally for the rest of their lives’, he writes. He says he believes this makes people’s lives better, but he also notes: ‘Habits can be very good for the bottom line.’ Nir says there should be some ethical limits to this: it is wrong to target children, and he believes designers need to ‘get high on their own supply’ and use their own apps themselves. He is not opposed to all regulations – he believes it should be a legal requirement that if you spend more than thirty-five hours on Facebook a week, you should see a pop-up saying you might have a problem and directing you towards a place to get help.

他写道，设计师应该引导你我“长期重复某些行为，理想情况下，最好是终生如此”。他认为这能改善人们的生活，但也指出：“习惯对企业的盈利也大有裨益。”尼尔认为这应该有一些道德上的限制：以儿童为目标群体是错误的，而且他认为设计师需要“充分发挥自身优势”，亲自使用自己开发的应用程序。他并非反对所有监管措施——他认为，如果用户每周在Facebook上花费超过35小时，就应该弹出提示，告知用户可能存在问题，并引导用户寻求帮助。

But as I read all this, I was troubled. Nir’s ‘cookbook’ for how to design apps became hugely successful – the CEO of Microsoft, for example, held it aloft and told her staff to read it, and Nir is a hugely popular speaker at tech conferences. Many apps were built inspired by his techniques. Nir was one of the people who led Silicon Valley in the charge to ‘drive them crazy’ – and yet when people like my godson Adam were, in fact, driven crazy, he told me that the solution is primarily to change our individual behaviour, not the actions of the tech companies.

但读到这些，我感到很困惑。尼尔的“应用设计秘籍”大获成功——例如，微软首席执行官曾高举这本书，要求员工阅读；尼尔本人也是科技大会上备受欢迎的演讲嘉宾。许多应用的设计灵感都源自他的技巧。尼尔是引领硅谷“逼疯科技公司”浪潮的领军人物之一——然而，当像我的教子亚当这样的人真的被逼疯时，他却告诉我，解决之道主要在于改变我们个人的行为，而不是改变科技公司的做法。

When we talked, I explained to him that, for me, it seemed like there was a worrying mismatch between his two books. In Hooked he talks about using ferociously powerful machinery to get us ‘fiendishly hooked’ and in ‘pain’ until we get our next techno-fix. Yet in Indistractible he tells us that when we feel distracted by this machinery, we should try gentle personal changes. In the first book, he describes big and powerful forces used to hook us; in the second, he describes fragile little personal interventions that he says will get us out.

我们交谈时，我向他解释说，在我看来，他的两本书之间存在着令人担忧的矛盾。在《上瘾》（Hooked）一书中，他谈到利用极其强大的机器让我们“上瘾”，并让我们“痛苦不堪”，直到我们获得下一次科技满足。然而，在《专注力》（Indistractible）一书中，他却告诉我们，当我们感到被这种机器分散注意力时，应该尝试一些温和的个人改变。在第一本书中，他描述了用来让我们上瘾的强大力量；在第二本书中，他却描述了一些脆弱而微小的个人干预措施，并声称这些措施可以让我们摆脱这种依赖。

‘I see exactly the opposite, in fact,’ he said in response. ‘Everything I talked about in Hooked , you can turn off with the tap of one thumb. Fuck them.’

“事实上，我看到的恰恰相反，”他回应道。“我在《上瘾》里提到的所有东西，你只需动动手指就能关掉。去他妈的。”

I understood my growing discomfort with Nir’s approach more fully when I talked it over with several other people. One was Ronald Purser, who is professor of management at San Francisco State University. He introduced me to an idea I hadn’t heard before – a concept named ‘ cruel optimism’. This is when you take a really big problem with deep causes in our culture – like obesity, or depression, or addiction – and you offer people, in upbeat language, a simplistic individual solution. It sounds optimistic, because you are telling them that the problem can be solved, and soon – but it is, in fact, cruel, because the solution you are offering is so limited, and so blind to the deeper causes, that for most people, it will fail.

当我与其他人讨论此事时，我对尼尔的做法越来越感到不安，这种不安感也更加深刻。其中一位是旧金山州立大学的管理学教授罗纳德·珀瑟。他向我介绍了一个我以前从未听说过的概念——“残酷的乐观主义”。这种乐观主义指的是，当你面对一个根植于我们文化深处的重大问题——比如肥胖、抑郁或成瘾——并用乐观的语言向人们提供一个过于简单的个人解决方案时，就会产生这种现象。这听起来很乐观，因为你告诉他们问题可以解决，而且很快就能解决——但实际上却很残酷，因为你提供的解决方案过于局限，而且忽略了问题的深层原因，对大多数人来说，它注定会失败。

Ronald gave lots of examples of this idea, which was first coined by the historian Lauren Berlant. I started to really grasp this idea when he applied this concept to an idea that’s related to attention but separate to it – stress. I think it’s worth taking a little time to go through it, because I believe it can help us to see a mistake that Nir – and many us – are making when it comes to focus.

罗纳德举了很多例子来佐证这个观点，这个观点最初是由历史学家劳伦·贝兰特提出的。当他把这个概念应用到一个与注意力相关但又有所区别的概念——压力——时，我才真正理解了这个观点。我认为值得花点时间仔细研究一下，因为我相信这能帮助我们发现尼尔——以及我们很多人——在专注力方面犯的一个错误。

Ronald talked to me about a best-selling book by a New York Times reporter that tells its readers: ‘Stress isn’t something imposed on us. It’s something we impose on ourselves.’ Stress is a feeling. Stress is a series of thoughts. If you just learn how to think differently – to quiet down your rattling thoughts – your stress will melt away. So you just need to learn to meditate. Your stress comes from a failure to be mindful.

罗纳德跟我聊起一本畅销书，作者是《纽约时报》的一位记者，书中写道：“压力不是别人强加给我们的，而是我们自己给自己施加的。”压力是一种感觉，是一系列念头。如果你学会换个角度思考——让纷乱的思绪平静下来——压力就会消失。所以，你只需要学习冥想。你的压力源于缺乏正念。

This message sings off the page with optimistic promise – but Ronald points out that in the real world, the top causes of stress in the US have been identified by scientists at Stanford Graduate School of Business in a major study. They are ‘a lack of health insurance, the constant threat of lay-offs, lack of discretion and autonomy in decision-making, long working hours, low levels of organisational justice, and unrealistic demands’. If you don’t have health insurance and you have diabetes and you can’t afford insulin, or if you are forced to work sixty hours a week by a bullying boss, or if you are watching your colleagues get laid off one by one and you suspect with a sickening feeling that you will be next, your stress is not ‘something we impose on ourselves’. It is something imposed on you.

这段话听起来充满乐观的希望，但罗纳德指出，在现实世界中，斯坦福商学院的科学家们在一项大型研究中指出，美国人压力的主要来源是“缺乏医疗保险、持续面临裁员威胁、缺乏决策自主权和自由裁量权、工作时间过长、组织公平性低下以及不切实际的要求”。如果你没有医疗保险，又患有糖尿病却买不起胰岛素；或者你被迫每周工作六十个小时，因为你的老板是个恶霸；又或者你眼睁睁地看着同事们一个个被裁员，并且隐隐觉得下一个可能就是自己，那么你的压力并非“我们自己强加的”，而是别人强加给你的。

Ronald thinks that meditation can help some people, and I agree, but that this typical best-selling book, which tells you to meditate your way through stress and humiliation, is ‘bullshit … Tell it to Hispanic women working three jobs with four kids.’ The people who say stress is just a matter of changing your thoughts are, he says, talking ‘from a privileged position. It’s easy for them to say that.’ He gave me the example of a company that was cutting back on providing healthcare to some people – and was, at the same time, congratulated by the same New York Times writer for providing meditation classes to its employees. You can see clearly how this is cruel. You tell somebody there’s a solution to their problem – just think differently about your stress and you’ll be fine! – and then leave them in a waking nightmare. We won’t give workers insulin, but we’ll give them classes on how to change their thinking. It’s the twenty-first-century version of Marie Antoinette saying, ‘Let them eat cake.’ Let them be present.

罗纳德认为冥想对某些人有帮助，我也同意，但他认为那些畅销书——教你通过冥想来缓解压力和羞辱——纯属“胡扯……去跟那些身兼三份工作、还要照顾四个孩子的拉丁裔女性说说看。” 他说，那些声称压力只需改变想法就能解决的人“站在特权阶层的角度说话。他们这么说当然容易。” 他举了一个例子：一家公司削减了部分员工的医疗保健支出，与此同时，同一位《纽约时报》的撰稿人却称赞该公司为员工提供冥想课程。这显然很残酷。你告诉别人问题有解决办法——只要换个角度看待压力，一切都会好起来！——然后却让他们继续活在噩梦中。我们不会给员工提供胰岛素，但我们会教他们如何改变思维方式。这是二十一世纪版的玛丽·安托瓦内特名言：“让他们吃蛋糕吧。”让他们在场。

While at first glance, cruel optimism seems kind and optimistic, it often has an ugly after-effect. It ensures that when the small, cramped solution fails, as it will most of the time, the individual won’t blame the system – she will blame herself. She will think she screwed up and she just wasn’t good enough. Ronald told me, ‘It deflects attention away from the social causes of stress,’ like overwork, and it can quite quickly turn into a form of ‘victim-blaming’. It whispers: the problem isn’t in the system; the problem is in you.

乍看之下，残酷的乐观主义似乎既仁慈又乐观，但它往往会带来丑陋的后果。它确保了当狭隘的解决方案失败时（这种情况几乎总是会发生），个人不会责怪体制，而是会责怪自己。她会认为自己搞砸了，自己不够优秀。罗纳德告诉我：“它转移了人们对压力社会根源的关注”，比如过度劳累，而且它很容易演变成一种“受害者有罪论”。它悄悄地告诉你：问题不在于体制，而在于你。

As he said this, I thought about Nir again, and the wider Silicon Valley approach he exemplifies. He makes his living from marketing and promoting a digital model that ‘hooks’ us and plays on our fears and which even he says is designed to make us ‘crazy’. That model, in turn, hooked him. But because he is in a position of incredible privilege – in terms of wealth, and knowledge of these systems – he was able to use his own techniques to regain some sense of control. Now he thinks the solution is simply for all of us to do the same.

他说这话的时候，我又想起了尼尔，以及他所代表的硅谷模式。他靠营销和推广一种“诱导”我们沉迷、利用我们恐惧的数字模式谋生，他自己也承认这种模式旨在让我们“发疯”。反过来，这种模式也让他沉迷其中。但由于他拥有巨大的特权——财富和对这些系统的了解——他得以运用自己的技巧重新掌控局面。现在他认为，解决办法很简单，就是我们所有人都要效仿。

Set aside the fact that it’s very convenient for him if we all blame ourselves rather than tackling the deeper problems – after all, his income depends on the tech industry. Look at something more basic. The truth is that it’s not so easy for everyone else to do what he has done. This is one of the problems with cruel optimism – it takes exceptional cases, usually achieved in exceptional circumstances, and acts as if they can be commonplace. It’s easier to find serenity through meditation when you haven’t just lost your job and you aren’t wondering how you’re going to avoid being evicted next Tuesday. It’s easier to say no to the next hamburger, or the next Facebook notification, or the next tab of OxyContin if you aren’t exhausted and stressed, and in desperate need of some kind of salve to get you through the next few stress-filled hours. To tell people – as Nir does, and as the wider tech industry increasingly does – that it’s ‘pretty simple’ and that they should just ‘push the fucking button’ is to deny the reality of most people’s lives.

先不说如果我们都责怪自己而不是去解决更深层次的问题对他来说有多方便——毕竟，他的收入依赖于科技行业。让我们看看更基本的问题。事实是，并非每个人都能像他那样做到。这就是残酷乐观主义的问题之一——它把那些通常在特殊情况下取得的特例当作常态。如果你没有刚刚失业，也不用担心下周二会被赶出家门，那么通过冥想更容易获得内心的平静。如果你不是精疲力竭、压力山大，急需某种慰藉来度过接下来几个小时的压力，那么就更容易对下一个汉堡包、下一个Facebook通知或下一粒奥施康定说“不”。告诉人们——就像 Nir 所做的那样，以及像更广泛的科技行业越来越多地所做的那样——这“很简单”，他们应该“按下该死的按钮”，这是否认大多数人生活的现实。

And, most importantly, people shouldn’t have to do it. Cruel optimism takes it for granted that we can’t significantly change the systems that are wrecking our attention, so we have to mainly focus on changing our isolated selves. But why should we accept these systems as a given? Why should we accept an environment full of programs designed to ‘hook’ us and drive us ‘crazy’?

而且，最重要的是，人们本不应该被迫这样做。残酷的乐观主义想当然地认为，我们无法从根本上改变那些正在摧毁我们注意力的系统，所以我们只能主要专注于改变我们孤立的自我。但我们为什么要接受这些系统的存在？我们为什么要接受一个充斥着旨在“诱使我们上瘾”并最终让我们“发疯”的程序的环境？

I could see this most clearly when I thought about Nir’s own analogy with the obesity experienced when he was a kid. I think it’s worth taking a moment to think through this comparison, because I think it tells us a lot about where we are going wrong now. It seems incredible to us today, but fifty years ago, there was very little obesity in the Western world. Look at a photograph of a beach taken back then: everyone is, by our standards, slim. Then a whole series of changes took place. We replaced a food-supply system based around fresh, nutritious food with one consisting mainly of processed junk. We massively stressed out our populations, making comfort eating a whole lot more appealing. We built cities that it’s often impossible to walk or bike around. In other words, the environment changed, and that – not any individual failing on the part of you or me – changed our bodies. We gained mass, en masse. The average weight gain for an adult between 1960 and 2002 was 24 lbs, or 1.7 stone.

当我想到尼尔用他小时候经历的肥胖来类比时，我对此有了最清晰的理解。我认为值得花点时间仔细思考一下这个比喻，因为它揭示了我们现在的问题所在。在今天看来或许难以置信，但五十年前，西方世界的肥胖现象非常普遍。看看当时拍摄的海滩照片：以我们今天的标准来看，每个人都很苗条。之后，一系列的变化接踵而至。我们用以加工垃圾食品为主的食品供应体系取代了以新鲜营养食品为基础的体系。我们给民众带来了巨大的压力，使得人们更容易通过暴饮暴食来寻求慰藉。我们建造的城市往往难以步行或骑自行车出行。换句话说，环境发生了变化，而正是这种变化——并非你我任何个人的过错——改变了我们的身体。我们集体增重。1960年至2002年间，成年人的平均体重增加了24磅，也就是1.7英石。

Then what happened? Rather than acknowledge the wider forces that have done this to us, take them on, and build a healthy environment in which it’s easier to avoid obesity, we were taught by the diet industry to blame ourselves as individuals. We learned to think: I got fat because of a personal failing. I chose the wrong food. I got greedy, I got lazy, I didn’t get a handle on my feelings properly, I’m not good enough. We resolved to count the calories better next time. (I’ve been there.) Individual diet books and diet plans became the primary answer offered by the culture to a crisis with primarily social causes.

然后发生了什么？我们没有去正视造成我们肥胖的更广泛的因素，也没有去对抗它们，更没有去构建一个更容易避免肥胖的健康环境，而是被减肥产业教导要责怪自己。我们学会了这样想：我变胖是因为我个人的失败。我选错了食物。我变得贪婪，我变得懒惰，我没有好好控制自己的情绪，我做得不够好。我们下定决心下次要更精确地计算卡路里。（我也有过这样的经历。）个人减肥书籍和减肥计划成了社会文化针对这场主要由社会因素引发的危机提供的主要解决方案。

How is that working out for us? The scientists who have studied it discovered that 95 percent of people in our culture who lose weight on a diet regain it within one to five years.
