That’s nineteen out of every twenty people. Why? It’s because it misses most of why you (and I) gained weight in the first place. It has no systemic analysis. It doesn’t talk about the crisis in our food supply, which surrounds us with addictive, highly processed foods that bear no relationship to what previous generations of humans ate. It doesn’t explain the crisis of stress and anxiety that drives us to overeat. It doesn’t address the fact that we live in cities where you have to squeeze yourself into a steel box to get anywhere. Diet books ignore the fact that you live in a society and culture that are shaping and pushing you, every day, to act in certain ways. A diet doesn’t change your wider environment – and it’s the wider environment that is the cause of the crisis. Your diet ends, and you’re still in an unhealthy environment that’s pushing you to gain weight. Trying to lose weight in the environment we’ve built is like trying to run up an escalator that is constantly carrying you down. A few people might heroically sprint to the top – but most of us will find ourselves back at the bottom, feeling like it’s our fault.

这种方法对我们来说效果如何呢？研究此问题的科学家发现，在我们这个文化中，95%通过节食减肥的人会在一到五年内反弹。也就是说，每20个人中就有19个会反弹。为什么？因为节食忽略了你（和我）最初体重增加的大部分原因。它缺乏系统性的分析。它没有谈到我们食品供应的危机，我们周围充斥着令人上瘾的、高度加工的食品，这些食品与前几代人的饮食习惯截然不同。它没有解释压力和焦虑危机如何驱使我们暴饮暴食。它也没有提及我们生活在城市里，为了去任何地方，你都不得不把自己挤进一个个狭小的空间。减肥书籍忽略了一个事实：你生活在一个社会和文化中，它们每天都在塑造和推动你以特定的方式行事。节食并不能改变你所处的环境——而正是这个环境才是危机的根源。节食结束了，你仍然身处一个不健康的环境，这个环境会驱使你体重增加。在如今这种环境下减肥，就像试图冲上一部不断向下倾斜的自动扶梯。或许有人能英勇地冲到顶端，但大多数人最终都会回到底部，感觉都是自己的错。

If we listen to Nir and the people like him, I fear we will respond to the rise of attention problems in the same way that we responded to the rise in weight problems – and we will end up with the same disastrous outcomes. It’s not just Silicon Valley that pushes this approach. Almost all the existing books about attention problems (and I read a lot as research for this book) present them simply as individual flaws requiring individual tweaks. They are digital diet books. But diet books didn’t solve the obesity crisis and digital diet books won’t solve the attention crisis. We have to understand the deeper forces at work here.

如果我们听信尼尔和像他一样的人，恐怕我们会像应对体重问题那样应对注意力问题的日益严重——最终导致同样的灾难性后果。推动这种做法的并非只有硅谷。几乎所有现有的关于注意力问题的书籍（为了撰写本书，我阅读了大量相关资料）都将其简单地视为需要个体调整的缺陷。它们就像是数字减肥指南。但减肥指南并没有解决肥胖危机，数字减肥指南也无法解决注意力危机。我们必须理解这背后更深层次的原因。

There was a different way we could have reacted to the obesity crisis when it began forty or so years ago. We could have listened to the evidence that purely practising individual restraint – in an unchanged environment – rarely works for long, except in one in twenty cases like Nir’s. We could have looked instead at what does work: changing the environment in specific ways. We could have used government policy to make fresh, nutritious food cheap and accessible, and sugar-filled junk expensive and inaccessible. We could have reduced the factors that cause people to be so stressed that they comfort eat. We could have built cities people can easily walk or bike through. We could have banned the targeting of junk food ads at children, shaping their tastes for life. That’s why countries that have done some of this – like Norway, or Denmark, or the Netherlands – have much lower levels of obesity, and countries that have focused on telling individual overweight people to pull themselves together, like the US and UK, have very high levels of obesity. If all the energy people like me had put into shaming and starving ourselves had been put instead into demanding these political changes, there would be far less obesity now, and a lot less misery.

四十多年前肥胖危机爆发之初，我们本可以采取不同的应对方式。我们本可以听取证据，认识到单纯依靠个人节制——在环境不变的情况下——很少能长期奏效，只有像尼尔那样的少数例外，约占二十分之一。我们本可以着眼于真正有效的方法：通过具体的方式改变环境。我们可以利用政府政策，让新鲜营养的食物价格低廉且易于获取，同时让含糖垃圾食品价格昂贵且难以获得。我们可以减少导致人们压力过大而用食物来缓解焦虑的因素。我们可以建造便于步行或骑行的城市。我们可以禁止针对儿童投放垃圾食品广告，以免影响他们终生的饮食习惯。正因如此，像挪威、丹麦和荷兰这样采取了上述部分措施的国家，肥胖率要低得多；而像美国和英国这样只关注于劝诫超重者控制饮食的国家，肥胖率却居高不下。如果像我这样的人把原本用来羞辱自己、让自己挨饿的精力，用来要求这些政治变革，那么现在的肥胖症患者就会少得多，痛苦也会少得多。

Tristan believes we need a similar shift in consciousness around tech. When he testified before the Senate, he told them: ‘You can try having self-control, but there are a thousand engineers on the other side of the screen working against you.’ This precisely what Nir refuses to fully acknowledge – even though he has been one of those designers himself. I stress again: I am in favour of each individual piece of advice he offers. You really should take out your phone now and turn off your notifications. You really should figure out your internal triggers. And on, and on. (Tristan believes this too). But it’s not ‘pretty simple’ to get from that to being able to pay attention in an environment designed – in part by Nir himself – to invade and raid your focus.

特里斯坦认为，我们需要在科技领域进行类似的意识转变。他在参议院作证时曾说过：“你可以尝试自律，但屏幕另一端有成千上万的工程师在暗中与你作对。” 这正是尼尔拒绝完全承认的——尽管他自己也曾是这些设计师之一。我再次强调：我赞同他提出的每一条建议。你真的应该现在就拿出手机，关闭通知。你真的应该找出你内心的触发点。等等等等。（特里斯坦也这么认为）。但是，要从这些建议过渡到能够在这样一个环境中集中注意力，并非易事——而这个环境的设计，部分正是尼尔自己设计的，旨在侵入和分散你的注意力。

My discussion with Nir got a little heated as we spoke more. Because this is one of the few contentious interviews in this book, to be fair to him, I have posted the full audio on the book’s website, so you can hear his responses – including the ones I don’t have space to quote here – in full. Our conversation clarified my thinking in a really helpful way. He made me realise that to get our attention back, we are going to have to adopt some individual solutions, to be sure – but we have to be honest enough to tell people that they alone probably won’t be enough to get most of us out of this hole. We are also going to have to collectively take on the forces that are stealing our focus and compel them to change.

我和尼尔的谈话随着深入而变得有些激烈。由于这是本书中为数不多的几篇颇具争议的访谈之一，为了公平起见，我已将完整音频发布在本书网站上，以便大家可以完整地听到他的回应——包括那些我在这里篇幅有限无法引用的内容。我们的对话以一种非常有益的方式理清了我的思路。他让我意识到，为了重新集中注意力，我们当然需要采取一些个人解决方案——但我们也必须坦诚地告诉大家，这些方案本身可能不足以让我们大多数人摆脱困境。我们还需要共同对抗那些分散我们注意力的势力，并迫使它们做出改变。

The alternative to cruel optimism – telling people a simplistic story that sets them up to fail – isn’t pessimism, the idea that you can’t change anything. It’s authentic optimism. This is where you honestly acknowledge the barriers that stand in the way of your goal and establish a plan to work together with other people to dismantle those barriers, step by step.

残酷的乐观主义——那种用过于简单化的故事误导他人、让他们注定失败的做法——的反面并非悲观主义（认为你无能为力），而是真正的乐观主义。真正的乐观主义意味着你要坦诚地承认阻碍你实现目标的障碍，并制定计划，与他人携手合作，一步步地消除这些障碍。

Then I realised I was now left with a really difficult question. How, precisely, do we start to do that?

然后我意识到，我现在面临着一个非常棘手的问题：我们究竟该如何着手去做这件事？

# ↩

9 The First Glimpses of the Deeper Solution

9 更深层次解决方案的初步发现

After learning so much about how our technology works, I was left with two clear and urgent questions. Firstly: what are the specific changes to this invasive tech that could be made, in practice, to prevent it harming our attention and focus? And secondly: how do we compel these huge corporations to introduce these changes in the real world?

在深入了解了我们技术的运作方式之后，我心中留下了两个清晰而紧迫的问题。首先：为了防止这种侵入性技术损害我们的注意力和专注力，我们究竟可以做出哪些具体的改变？其次：我们如何才能迫使这些大型企业在现实世界中做出这些改变？

Tristan and Aza – drawing on their own experiences, and the essential work of Professor Shoshana Zuboff – believe that if we are going to find a lasting solution, we need to go right to the root cause of the problem. That’s why, one morning, Aza said to me starkly: ‘We could just ban surveillance capitalism.’ I paused to try to process what he was saying. This would mean, he explained, that the government would ban any business model that tracks you online in order to figure out your weaknesses and then sells that private data to the highest bidder so they can change your behaviour. This model is, Aza says, ‘just fundamentally anti-democratic and anti-human’, and it has to go.

特里斯坦和阿扎——结合他们自身的经历以及肖莎娜·祖博夫教授的重要研究——认为，如果我们想要找到持久的解决方案，就必须直击问题的根源。因此，一天早上，阿扎直截了当地对我说：“我们可以直接禁止监控资本主义。”我停顿了一下，试图理解他的话。他解释说，这意味着政府将禁止任何通过网络追踪用户、找出用户弱点并将这些私人数据出售给出价最高者以改变用户行为的商业模式。阿扎说，这种模式“从根本上来说是反民主、反人性的”，必须被废除。

This sounded dramatic and frankly impossible when I first heard it, but Tristan and Aza explained that there are plenty of historical precedents for something becoming so widespread, only for society to discover it actually causes a lot of harm and ban the market in it. Think about lead paint. It was in a majority of American homes – then it was discovered to damage the brains of kids and adults, making it harder for them to focus. As one of Tristan’s mentors, Jaron Lanier, pointed out to me, when we found that out, we didn’t say nobody could paint their homes ever again. We just banned the lead in the paint. Your home is still painted today – just with much better products. Or think about CFCs. As I mentioned before, when I was a child in the hairspray-obsessed 1980s, it was discovered that a substance in hairsprays was destroying the ozone layer that protects us from the sun’s rays. It terrified us all. We banned CFCs. We still have hairsprays, they just work differently, and today, the ozone layer is healing. There are all sorts of things that we have decided, as a civilised society, can’t be bought and sold, like (for example) human organs.

我第一次听到这个说法时，觉得很夸张，甚至难以置信。但特里斯坦和阿扎解释说，历史上有很多先例，某种东西曾经非常普遍，但后来人们发现它实际上危害很大，于是取缔了它的市场。想想含铅油漆吧。它曾经遍布美国大多数家庭——后来人们发现它会损害儿童和成人的大脑，使他们难以集中注意力。正如特里斯坦的导师之一贾伦·拉尼尔向我指出的那样，当我们发现这一点时，我们并没有禁止任何人再粉刷房屋。我们只是禁止在油漆中使用铅。如今，你的房子仍然在粉刷——只是使用了更好的产品。再想想氟氯化碳（CFC）。正如我之前提到的，在我还是个孩子的时候，也就是上世纪80年代，那时人们痴迷于发胶，后来发现发胶中的一种物质会破坏保护我们免受太阳辐射的臭氧层。这让我们所有人都感到恐惧。我们禁止了氟氯化碳的使用。我们仍然在使用发胶，只是使用方法不同了。如今，臭氧层正在修复。作为一个文明社会，我们已经决定很多东西不能买卖，比如（举例来说）人体器官。

So, I asked them, let’s say we banned surveillance capitalism. What would happen to my Facebook and Twitter accounts the following day, the following week, the following year? ‘I think they would have a crisis moment, in the same way that Microsoft had a crisis moment,’ Aza told me. In 2001, Microsoft was ruled by the US government to have become a monopoly. That company reinvented itself, and now ‘They’re sort of like the benevolent adult in the room. I think the same transformation would happen to Facebook.’

于是，我问他们，假设我们禁止了监控资本主义，我的Facebook和Twitter账号在第二天、下周、明年会发生什么？“我认为它们会经历一次危机，就像微软当年经历的危机一样，”阿扎告诉我。2001年，美国政府认定微软已成为垄断企业。这家公司进行了重组，现在“它们就像房间里那位仁慈的成年人。我认为Facebook也会经历同样的转变。”

In practice, the day after a ban, these companies would have to find different ways to fund themselves. There is one model that is obvious, and an alternative form of capitalism that everyone reading this will have some experience of – subscription. Let’s imagine each of us had to pay fifty cents or a dollar every month to use Facebook. Suddenly, Facebook would no longer be working for advertisers and offering up your secret wishes and preferences as their real product. No. It would be working for you. Its job – for the first time – would be to actually figure out what makes you happy, and to give it to you – instead of figuring out what makes advertisers happy, and how they can manipulate you to give it to them. So if, like most people, you want to be able to focus, the site would have to be redesigned to facilitate that. If you want to be socially connected, instead of isolated in front of your screen, it would have to figure out how to make that possible.

实际上，一旦禁令生效，这些公司就必须另寻资金来源。有一种显而易见的模式，也是所有读者都略有体验的另一种资本主义形式——订阅制。试想一下，如果我们每个人每月都要支付50美分或1美元才能使用Facebook，那么Facebook就不再为广告商服务，也不再将你的秘密愿望和偏好当作其真正的产品。不，它将为你服务。它的职责——第一次——将真正变成弄清楚什么能让你快乐，并满足你的需求——而不是弄清楚什么能取悦广告商，以及如何操纵你把钱花在他们身上。因此，如果你像大多数人一样，希望能够集中注意力，那么网站就必须重新设计以方便你做到这一点。如果你想与他人保持联系，而不是孤立地坐在屏幕前，那么它就必须找到实现这一目标的方法。

There’s another obvious way that these companies could survive, which is for them to be bought by the government and taken into public ownership. This would take social media out of the capitalist part of the economy. This can sound drastic, but every single person reading this book benefits today, directly, from exactly the same model. We all agree we need to have sewers – they are an unavoidable necessity, unless we want to go back to the world of cholera outbreaks and faeces in the streets. So in virtually every country, the government owns, maintains and regulates the sewers, and even hardcore anti-government activists agree that this is a good use of state power.

这些公司还有另一种显而易见的生存之道，那就是被政府收购，收归国有。这将使社交媒体脱离资本主义经济体系。这听起来或许有些极端，但如今每一位读者都直接受益于同样的模式。我们都认同下水道系统必不可少——除非我们想回到霍乱肆虐、粪便遍地的时代，否则下水道系统是不可避免的。因此，几乎每个国家都由政府拥有、维护和监管下水道系统，就连最激进的反政府人士也认为这是国家权力的合理运用。

Using the same model, our governments could acknowledge that social media is now an essential public utility, and explain that when it is run according to the wrong incentives, it causes the psychological equivalents of cholera outbreaks. It would be a bad idea for the government to run it – it’s easy to imagine how authoritarian leaders could abuse that. Fortunately, there’s a better option: you can have public ownership, independent of the government. In Britain, the BBC is owned and funded by the British public, and it is run in the interests of the British public – but its day-to-day running is independent of the government. It’s not perfect, but this model works so well that it is the most respected media organisation in the world.

运用同样的模式，各国政府可以承认社交媒体如今已成为一项重要的公共事业，并解释如果其运营受到错误激励，就会引发堪比霍乱爆发的心理危机。政府运营社交媒体绝非明智之举——不难想象专制领导人会如何滥用权力。幸运的是，还有更好的选择：公共所有制，独立于政府之外。在英国，BBC由英国公众所有并资助，其运营也服务于英国公众的利益——但其日常运作独立于政府。这种模式并非完美无缺，但其运作效果显著，使其成为世界上最受尊敬的媒体机构。

Once the financial incentives are changed – through subscription, or public ownership, or another model – then the nature of these sites can change, in ways we can actually begin to envision already. Aza told me that ‘it’s actually technically not hard’ to redesign the major social-media sites so that, instead of trashing your attention span and our societies, they would be designed to heal them, once the financial incentives to do that are in place. This was difficult for me to grasp at first, so I asked what social media would look like after the changes they would like to see. Tristan, Aza and others began by explaining minor changes, then built up to big changes, and then told me what has to happen to make any of these changes happen.

一旦经济激励机制发生改变——无论是通过订阅制、公有制还是其他模式——这些网站的性质就会发生改变，而我们现在实际上已经开始设想这种改变。阿扎告诉我，重新设计主流社交媒体网站“在技术上其实并不难”，这样一来，一旦相应的经济激励机制到位，它们就不会再消耗用户的注意力，也不会破坏我们的社会，而是会起到修复社会的作用。起初我很难理解这一点，所以我问他们，在他们希望看到的改变之后，社交媒体会是什么样子。特里斯坦、阿扎和其他人先解释了一些小的改变，然后逐步过渡到大的改变，最后告诉我要实现这些改变需要做些什么。

They started by talking about how these companies could, overnight, remove a lot of the aspects of these apps and sites that deliberately scramble our heads and keep us online longer than we really want. Aza said: ‘For instance, Facebook tomorrow could start batching your notifications, so you only get one push notification a day … They could do that tomorrow.’ (This was something Tristan had proposed in his explosive slide show back when he was still at Google.) So instead of getting ‘this constant drip of behavioural cocaine’, telling you every few minutes that somebody liked your picture, commented on your post, has a birthday tomorrow, and on and on and on – you would get one daily update, like a newspaper, summarising it all. You’d be pushed to look once a day, instead of being interrupted several times an hour.

他们首先讨论了这些公司如何在一夜之间移除这些应用和网站中许多故意扰乱我们思绪、让我们长时间沉迷其中的功能。阿扎说：“例如，Facebook 明天就可以开始批量推送通知，这样你每天只会收到一条推送通知……他们明天就能做到。”（特里斯坦还在谷歌工作时，就曾在他那场精彩的幻灯片演示中提出过这个建议。）这样一来，你就不会再像现在这样，每隔几分钟就收到“行为快感”的刺激，比如有人点赞了你的照片、评论了你的帖子、明天有人过生日等等，没完没了——你每天只会收到一条更新，就像一份报纸，概括所有内容。你每天只需查看一次，而不是每小时被打断好几次。

‘Here’s another one,’ he said. ‘Infinite scroll.’ That’s his invention, where when you get to the bottom of the screen, it automatically loads more and more, forever. ‘What’s going on there is it’s catching your impulses before your brain has a chance to really get involved and make a decision.’ Facebook and Instagram and the others could simply turn off infinite scroll – so that when you get to the bottom of the screen, you have to make a conscious decision to carry on scrolling.

“再来一个，”他说，“无限滚动。”这是他的发明，当你滚动到屏幕底部时，它会自动加载更多内容，永无止境。“它的原理是，在你大脑真正有机会参与并做出决定之前，就抓住了你的冲动。”Facebook、Instagram 和其他应用完全可以关闭无限滚动功能——这样，当你滚动到屏幕底部时，就必须有意识地决定是否继续滚动。

Similarly, these sites could simply switch off the things that have been shown to most polarise people politically, stealing our ability to pay collective attention. Since there’s evidence YouTube’s recommendation engine is radicalising people, Tristan told one interviewer: ‘Just turn it off. They can turn it off in a heartbeat.’ It’s not as if, he points out, the day before recommendations were introduced, people were lost and clamouring for somebody to tell them what to watch next.

同样，这些网站完全可以关闭那些已被证明最容易引发政治极化的内容，从而剥夺我们集中注意力的能力。鉴于有证据表明YouTube的推荐引擎正在使人们走向极端，特里斯坦曾对一位采访者说：“直接关掉它就行了。他们可以毫不费力地把它关掉。” 他指出，并非在推荐系统推出前一天，人们就茫然不知所措，急切地想要有人告诉他们接下来该看什么。

Once the most obvious forms of mental pollution have been stopped, they said, we can begin to look deeper, at how these sites could be redesigned to make it easier for you to restrain yourself and think about your longer-term goals. ‘It doesn’t take much work to start imagining what would be different interfaces,’ Aza said. The most obvious example takes us back to where I started with Tristan, in our very first conversation: there could be a button that says ‘here are all your friends who are nearby and are indicating they’d like to meet up today’. You click it, you connect, you put down your phone and hang out with them. Instead of being a vacuum sucking up your attention and keeping it away from the outside world, social media would become a trampoline, sending you back into that world as efficiently as possible, matched with the people you want to see.

他们说，一旦最明显的精神污染形式被制止，我们就可以开始深入思考，如何重新设计这些网站，让你更容易控制自己，思考你的长远目标。“想象不同的界面并不难，”阿扎说。最明显的例子可以追溯到我和特里斯坦的第一次谈话：可以设置一个按钮，上面写着“以下是附近所有想今天见面的朋友”。你点击它，连接，放下手机，和他们一起玩。社交媒体不再像一个吸尘器，吸走你的注意力，让你远离外面的世界，而是变成一个蹦床，尽可能高效地把你送回那个世界，让你见到你想见的人。

Similarly, when you set up (say) a Facebook account, it could ask you how much time you want to spend per day or per week on the site. You might name ten minutes, or two hours – it’s up to you – and then the website could help you to achieve your goal. One way could be that when you hit that limit, the website could radically slow down. In tests, Amazon found that even 100 milliseconds of delay in the pace at which a page loads results in a substantial drop-off in people sticking around to buy the product. Aza said: ‘It just gives your brain a chance to catch up to your impulse and [ask] – do I really want to be here? No.’

同样，当你注册（比如）Facebook账号时，它可能会询问你每天或每周想在网站上花费多少时间。你可以设定十分钟，也可以设定两小时——完全由你决定——然后网站可以帮助你达成目标。一种方法是，当你达到这个时间限制时，网站速度会大幅降低。亚马逊的测试发现，即使页面加载速度延迟100毫秒，也会导致用户停留购买商品的意愿显著下降。Aza说：“这能让你的大脑有机会跟上你的冲动，然后问自己——我真的想待在这里吗？不。”

In addition, Facebook could ask you at regular intervals – what changes do you want to make to your life? Maybe you want to exercise more, or take up gardening, or become vegetarian, or start a heavy-metal band. It could then match you up with other people nearby – friends, or friends of friends, or interested strangers in your neighbourhood – who say they also want to make that change and have indicated they are looking for the equivalent of gym buddies. Facebook would become, Aza says, ‘a way of socially surrounding yourself with the behaviour that you want’. A battery of scientific evidence shows that if you want to succeed in changing something, you should meet up with groups of people doing the same.

此外，Facebook 还可以定期询问你——你想在生活中做出哪些改变？也许你想多运动，或者开始园艺，或者成为素食主义者，或者组建一支重金属乐队。然后，它会将你与附近的其他人匹配——可能是你的朋友、朋友的朋友，或者你社区里感兴趣的陌生人——这些人也表示他们想要做出同样的改变，并且正在寻找类似健身伙伴的人。Aza 表示，Facebook 将成为“一种让你在社交环境中接触到你想要的行为的方式”。大量的科学证据表明，如果你想成功改变某些事情，你应该与正在做同样事情的人们聚集在一起。

At the moment, they said, social media is designed to grab your attention and sell it to the highest bidder, but it could be designed to understand your intentions and to better help you achieve them. Tristan and Aza told me that it’s just as easy to design and program this life-affirming Facebook as the life-draining Facebook we currently have. I think that most people, if you stopped them in the street and painted them a vision of these two Facebooks, would say they wanted the one that serves your intentions. So why isn’t it happening? It comes back, Tristan and Aza said, to the business model. If right now these social-media companies made the changes that you just read about, they would lose an enormous amount of money. Within the existing economic structure of the companies, they can’t do the right thing by your attention span or the wider society. This – above everything else – is the rock-solid reason why you have to change the business model, if you want to change the way social media affects us.

他们说，目前社交媒体的设计目的在于抓住你的注意力，然后卖给出价最高的人，但它本可以设计成理解你的意图，并更好地帮助你实现这些意图。特里斯坦和阿扎告诉我，设计和开发一个能激励人心的Facebook，和设计一个消耗人心的Facebook一样容易。我想，如果你在街上拦住一个人，向他描述这两个Facebook的景象，大多数人都会说他们想要一个能服务于自身意图的Facebook。那么，为什么这种情况没有发生呢？特里斯坦和阿扎说，问题归根结底在于商业模式。如果这些社交媒体公司现在就做出你刚才读到的那些改变，它们将会损失惨重。在公司现有的经济结构下，它们无法真正做到既符合你的注意力，又对整个社会有益。这——凌驾于其他一切之上——才是你必须改变商业模式的根本原因，如果你想改变社交媒体对我们的影响。

The business model can only be changed by regulation imposed on these companies by governments, they said. Then the changes I just described would cease to be impossible threats to the bottom line and start to become very exciting ways to tempt subscribers. At the moment there is a fundamental clash between your interests – to be able to focus, to have friends you see offline, to be able to discuss things calmly – and the interests of the social-media companies. With the introduction of a ban on surveillance capitalism and a move to a different business model, that clash ends. As Tristan put it, you’d be paying for the interests to be aligned between you and the product you use. Suddenly that team of Silicon Valley engineers behind the screen wouldn’t be working against you and your deeper intentions; they’d be working for you and trying to serve your deeper intentions.

他们说，只有政府对这些公司实施监管，才能改变其商业模式。届时，我刚才描述的那些改变将不再是难以逾越的盈利威胁，而是会变成吸引用户的令人兴奋的新方式。目前，你的利益——能够集中精力、与线下朋友见面、能够冷静地讨论事情——与社交媒体公司的利益之间存在着根本性的冲突。随着对监控资本主义的禁令以及商业模式的转变，这种冲突将会结束。正如特里斯坦所说，你将付费购买的是你和你使用的产品之间的利益一致性。突然之间，屏幕后面的硅谷工程师团队将不再与你和你的深层意图作对；他们将为你服务，努力满足你的深层意图。

One day, Aza said to me: ‘The fundamental thing is that no one likes the way that they are spending time or making decisions with the way technology currently is. It’s hard to get from that hill to this hill, because we have to go through a valley. That’s the role of regulation – to help making crossing that valley easier. But the hill on the other side is much, much nicer.’

有一天，阿扎对我说：“根本问题在于，没有人喜欢他们现在利用科技的方式去消磨时间或做决定。从这座山到那座山很难，因为我们必须穿过一个山谷。这就是监管的作用——帮助我们更容易地跨越这个山谷。但山谷另一边的山要美好得多。”

I found so much of what Aza and Tristan had taught me persuasive – but I was wary about their argument that we need to use the law to stop these companies from continuing as they are. There were several reasons why. Firstly, I wondered if they were overstating the problem. When I spoke with Nir Eyal, he said: ‘Every generation has these moral panics, where we only want to look at the negative sides’ of an issue. He told me ‘Tristan is reading, literally verbatim, from the 1950s about the comic-book debate,’ when many people believed that children were being made violent by a new wave of gory comics. In the 1950s, ‘People like Tristan went to the Senate and told the senators that comic books are turning children into addicted, hijacked [zombies] – literally, it’s the same stuff … Today, we think of comic books as so innocuous.’

阿扎和特里斯坦教给我的很多东西都很有说服力，但我对他们提出的“我们需要用法律手段阻止这些公司继续这样下去”的观点持保留态度。原因有几个。首先，我怀疑他们是否夸大了问题。我和尼尔·埃亚尔交谈时，他说：“每一代人都会经历这种道德恐慌，我们只想看到问题的负面一面。”他告诉我，“特里斯坦正在逐字逐句地朗读上世纪五十年代关于漫画书的辩论”，当时许多人认为，一股新的血腥漫画浪潮正在使孩子们变得暴力。在上世纪五十年代，“像特里斯坦这样的人去参议院，告诉参议员们，漫画书正在把孩子们变成上瘾的、被控制的‘僵尸’——说真的，情况就是这样……而今天，我们认为漫画书是如此无害。”

On this basis, he argues – and here he’s not alone – that the science that Tristan and Aza and other critics of the current tech business model draw on is incorrect. He believes that some of the social science I have drawn on in the past two chapters is garbled or wrong.

基于此，他认为——而且他并非孤军奋战——特里斯坦、阿扎以及其他批评当前科技商业模式的人士所引用的科学是错误的。他认为我在前两章中引用的一些社会科学理论是歪曲事实或错误的。

I’ll give you one detailed example, so you get a sense of this controversy. Tristan argues YouTube is radicalising people, based on an array of evidence I mentioned before. Nir responds by pointing to a recent study by the coder Mark Ledwich that suggested in fact, watching YouTube had a slightly deradicalising effect on its users. Tristan, in response, directs people towards the Princeton academic Professor Arvind Narayanan, and many other critics of this study, who say that the research Nir is citing here is worthless. Let’s go through this, step by step. The people who say YouTube radicalises you argue that this effect happens over time. You create a profile, you log in, and gradually YouTube builds up knowledge of your preferences, and to keep you watching, the content it feeds you gets more extreme. But the research Nir cites didn’t study any logged-in users. All they did was go to a video on YouTube – say, Boris Johnson giving a speech – and without logging in, they looked at the recommendations that appeared along the side. If you use YouTube in this highly unusual way, the videos don’t become more extreme over time, and it might be fair to say YouTube is deradicalising. But huge numbers of YouTube users do log in. (We don’t know exactly how many, because YouTube keeps that information secret.)

我举一个详细的例子，以便你们了解这场争议。特里斯坦认为YouTube正在使人们走向极端，他列举了我之前提到的一系列证据。尼尔则回应说，程序员马克·莱德维奇最近的一项研究表明，观看YouTube实际上对用户有轻微的去极端化作用。特里斯坦反驳说，普林斯顿大学教授阿文德·纳拉亚南以及许多其他批评这项研究的学者都认为尼尔引用的研究毫无价值。我们来一步步分析一下。那些认为YouTube会使人走向极端的人认为，这种影响是随着时间的推移而发生的。你创建个人资料，登录，YouTube会逐渐了解你的偏好，为了让你继续观看，它推送的内容会变得越来越极端。但尼尔引用的研究并没有调查任何登录用户。他们只是在YouTube上观看一个视频——比如鲍里斯·约翰逊的演讲——而且没有登录，只是查看了侧边栏的推荐内容。如果你以这种非常规的方式使用 YouTube，视频内容并不会随着时间的推移而变得更加极端，甚至可以说 YouTube 正在起到去极端化的作用。但确实有大量的 YouTube 用户登录。（我们不知道确切的数字，因为 YouTube 对此信息保密。）

For every conceivable way the tech companies could be screwing with us, there is a back-and-forth like this, with Tristan and Nir each citing rigorous social scientists who have reached opposing conclusions. Tristan draws on academics from Yale and New York University and Harvard; Nir draws on academics like Professor Andrew Przybylski at Oxford University, who agrees with Nir that Tristan’s warnings are overheated. So what’s happening? It’s not that either of them is being disingenuous – it’s that measuring the changes these sites are triggering is really complicated, and hard to figure out. We have to be honest that we are making decisions based on a lot of uncertainty here. In the long sweep of history, there will likely be some areas where it turns out Nir is right, and some where Tristan is right. That still leaves us with a basic dilemma. Right now, we need to make choices about whether to let social-media companies continue behaving as they have been. We have to figure out the balance of risk.

科技公司可能以各种方式操纵我们，而特里斯坦和尼尔则各自引用了得出相反结论的严谨社会科学家的观点，展开了一场类似的争论。特里斯坦引用了耶鲁大学、纽约大学和哈佛大学的学者；尼尔则引用了牛津大学安德鲁·普日比尔斯基教授等学者的观点，普日比尔斯基教授同意尼尔的看法，认为特里斯坦的警告有些过激。那么，究竟发生了什么？并非他们两人都言不由衷——而是衡量这些网站引发的变化实在太复杂，难以捉摸。我们必须承认，我们现在的决策很大程度上是基于不确定性的。从长远的历史来看，或许有些领域最终会证明尼尔是对的，而有些领域则会证明特里斯坦是对的。但这仍然给我们留下了一个根本性的难题。眼下，我们需要做出选择：是否要允许社交媒体公司继续像以往那样行事？我们必须找到风险的平衡点。

There are two things that helped me make up my mind about what I think we should do next. One was a thought experiment, and the other was hard evidence from inside Facebook itself.

有两件事帮助我决定了我们下一步应该做什么。一件是思想实验，另一件是来自Facebook内部的确凿证据。

Let’s imagine Nir is wrong, and we all follow his advice anyway – we allow surveillance capitalism to continue getting us ‘fiendishly hooked’, with only light regulation. Then let’s imagine Tristan is wrong, and we all follow his advice anyway – we regulate the Big Tech companies to stop their invasive practices.

假设尼尔的观点是错误的，而我们仍然听从他的建议——我们放任监控资本主义继续让我们“上瘾”，只采取轻微的监管措施。再假设特里斯坦的观点是错误的，而我们仍然听从他的建议——我们对大型科技公司进行监管，以阻止它们侵犯用户隐私的行为。

If Tristan is wrong and we still follow his advice, you would have been tricked into creating a world where you get targeted with a lot less advertising, you spend less, you get spied on less, and in return, you have to pay a small sum each month to subscribe to a few social-media companies, or those companies have in some way been taken over as public utilities run in our collective interests, like the sewers or the highways. Now imagine if we did what Nir wants. What happens if he’s wrong? What are we left with? Attention shrinks even more, political extremism expands, and the disturbing trends we see around us continue to rise.

如果特里斯坦错了，而我们仍然听从他的建议，那么你就会被诱骗去创造一个这样的世界：广告投放量大大减少，你的消费支出减少，你受到的监视也减少，而作为回报，你却需要每月支付少量费用订阅几家社交媒体公司，或者这些公司已经以某种方式被接管，成为像下水道或高速公路一样服务于我们集体利益的公共事业。现在想象一下，如果我们按照尼尔的意愿去做，会发生什么？如果他错了呢？我们会面临什么？人们的注意力会进一步分散，政治极端主义会愈演愈烈，我们周围那些令人不安的趋势也会持续加剧。

The second thing that persuaded me was even more decisive. One day, in the spring of 2020, it was revealed what Facebook actually thinks about these questions, in private, when they think we will never be able to hear them. A large number of internal Facebook documents and communications were leaked to the Wall Street Journal . It turned out that behind closed doors, the company had responded to the claims that their algorithms had damaged our collective attention and helped the rise of Trump and Brexit by convening a team of some of their best scientists and tasking them with figuring out if this was really true, and if it was, to figure out what they could do about it. The unit was called Common Ground.

第二件让我信服的事更加关键。2020年春天的一天，Facebook私下里对这些问题的真实想法被曝光，他们认为我们永远不会听到这些。大量Facebook内部文件和通信被泄露给了《华尔街日报》。结果显示，在闭门会议中，针对算法损害公众注意力、助长特朗普崛起和英国脱欧的指控，Facebook召集了一批顶尖科学家组成团队，负责调查这些指控是否属实，如果属实，又该如何应对。这个团队名为“共同立场”（Common Ground）。

After studying all the hidden data – the stuff that Facebook doesn’t release to the public – the company’s scientists reached a definite conclusion. They wrote: ‘Our algorithms exploit the human brain’s attraction to divisiveness,’ and ‘if left unchecked’, the site would continue to pump its users with ‘more and more divisive content in an effort to gain user attention and increase time on the platform’. A separate internal Facebook team, whose work also leaked to the Journal , had independently reached the same conclusions. They found that 64 percent of all the people joining extremist groups were finding their way to them because Facebook’s algorithms were directly recommending them. This meant across the world, people were seeing in their Facebook feeds racist, fascist and even Nazi groups next to the words: ‘Groups You Should Join.’ They warned that in Germany, one-third of all the political groups on the site were extremist. Facebook’s own team was blunt, concluding: ‘Our recommendation systems grow the problem.’

在研究了所有隐藏数据——也就是Facebook不向公众公开的数据——之后，该公司科学家得出了一个明确的结论。他们写道：“我们的算法利用了人脑对分裂的偏好”，并且“如果不加以控制”，该网站会继续向用户推送“越来越多具有分裂性的内容，以吸引用户注意力并增加用户在平台上的停留时间”。另一个Facebook内部团队的研究成果也泄露给了《华尔街日报》，他们独立得出了相同的结论。他们发现，加入极端主义团体的人中，有64%是因为Facebook的算法直接推荐才加入的。这意味着，在世界各地，人们会在Facebook动态消息中看到种族主义、法西斯主义甚至纳粹团体，旁边还配有“你应该加入的团体”的字样。他们警告说，在德国，该网站上所有政治团体中有三分之一是极端主义团体。Facebook自己的团队直言不讳地总结道：“我们的推荐系统加剧了这个问题。”

After carefully analysing all the options, Facebook’s scientists concluded there was one solution: they said Facebook would have to abandon its current business model. Because their growth was so tied up with toxic outcomes, the company should abandon attempts at growth. The only way out was for the company to adopt a strategy that was ‘anti-growth’ – deliberately shrink, and choose to be a less wealthy company that wasn’t wrecking the world.

在仔细分析了所有方案后，Facebook的科学家们得出结论：只有一个解决办法。他们认为，Facebook必须放弃目前的商业模式。由于其增长与诸多有害后果紧密相连，公司应该放弃增长的尝试。唯一的出路是采取“反增长”战略——刻意缩减规模，选择成为一家不那么富有但也不会对世界造成破坏的公司。

Once Facebook was shown – in plain language, by their own people – what they were doing, how did the company’s executives respond? According to the Journal ’s in-depth reporting, they mocked the research, calling it an ‘Eat Your Veggies’ approach. They introduced some minor tweaks, but dismissed most of the recommendations. The Common Ground team was disbanded and has ceased to exist. The Journal reported dryly: ‘ Zuckerberg also signalled he was losing interest in the effort to recalibrate the platform in the name of the social good … asking that they not bring him something like that again.’ I read this and I thought of my friend Raull Santiago, in his favela in Rio, being terrorised by helicopters sent by the far-right government that was elected with the help of these algorithms – algorithms so powerful that Bolsonaro’s supporters responded to his victory by chanting, ‘Facebook! Facebook!’

当Facebook的员工用通俗易懂的语言向他们展示了他们的所作所为后，公司高管们作何反应？据《华尔街日报》的深度报道，他们嘲笑这项研究，称之为“吃蔬菜”式的做法。他们做出了一些细微的调整，但对大多数建议置之不理。“共同立场”团队被解散，从此不复存在。《华尔街日报》冷冷地报道说：“扎克伯格也表示，他对以社会公益之名重新调整平台的努力失去了兴趣……并要求他们不要再给他类似的方案。”读到这里，我想起了我的朋友劳尔·圣地亚哥，他住在里约热内卢的贫民窟里，饱受极右翼政府派出的直升机的骚扰。而这个政府正是靠着这些算法当选的——这些算法如此强大，以至于博索纳罗的支持者们在他胜选时高喊着“Facebook！Facebook！”

I realised that if Facebook won’t change the fact that their algorithm unintentionally promotes fascism – that it promotes Nazism in Germany – they will never care about protecting your focus and attention. These companies will never restrain themselves. The risks of letting them continue behaving the way they have are greater than the risks of overreacting. They have to be stopped. They have to be stopped by us.

我意识到，如果Facebook不改变其算法无意中助长法西斯主义——也就是在德国助长纳粹主义——的事实，他们就永远不会在意保护你的注意力。这些公司永远不会克制自己。放任他们继续这种行为的风险远大于反应过度的风险。必须阻止他们。必须由我们来阻止他们。

I was daunted. For a while, I felt I had no idea how we could achieve such a goal. Many people go this far in the argument, and then sputter to a pessimistic halt. They say – yes, this system is messing with us in terrible ways, but we’ll just have to adjust, because nothing and nobody can stop it. We live in a culture where there is a sense of deep political fatalism at every turn. I saw this when I wrote my book about the war on drugs, Chasing the Scream , and I travelled all over the world talking about it. Especially in the US, I kept hearing: Yes, you’re right that the drug war is a disaster and a failure. (Over 80 percent of Americans agree.) Yes, you’re right that decriminalisation or legalisation would be better. But no, it will never happen – so do you know a good lawyer or rehab facility for an addicted relative? Political pessimism keeps people trapped in a search for purely personal and individual solutions.

我感到畏惧。有一段时间，我觉得我们根本不知道该如何实现这样的目标。很多人在论证过程中走到这一步，然后就陷入了悲观的泥沼。他们说——没错，这个体制正在以各种可怕的方式折磨我们，但我们只能适应，因为没有任何人或事能够阻止它。我们生活在一个处处弥漫着根深蒂固的政治宿命论的文化中。我在撰写关于毒品战争的著作《追逐尖叫》时就深有体会，我为此走遍世界各地。尤其是在美国，我不断听到这样的说法：是的，你说得对，毒品战争是一场灾难，是一场失败。（超过80%的美国人同意这一点。）是的，你说得对，非刑事化或合法化会更好。但是，不，这永远不会发生——那么，你认识什么好的律师或戒毒机构可以帮帮你的吸毒亲戚吗？政治上的悲观主义让人们陷入了寻求纯粹个人解决方案的困境。

But here’s the truth: this despair isn’t just self-defeating; I think it’s actually empirically wrong. I reminded myself – forces as powerful as the tech companies have been defeated many times in human history, and it always happens in the same way. It is when ordinary people form movements and demand something better, and they don’t give up until they have achieved it. I know that could sound vague or idealistic, so I want to give a very practical example of a change that happened in my family, and very likely in your family, in the past three generations.

但事实是：这种绝望不仅无济于事，而且我认为它实际上与经验相悖。我提醒自己——像科技公司这样强大的势力在人类历史上已被击败过无数次，而且每次都是以同样的方式。那就是普通民众组成运动，要求更好的生活，并且坚持不懈直到实现目标。我知道这听起来可能有些空泛或理想化，所以我想举一个非常实际的例子，来说明过去三代人中发生在我家（很可能也发生在你家）的这种变化。

I am forty-one years old. My grandmothers were the age I am now in the year 1962. In that year, my Scottish grandmother, Amy McRae, was living in a working-class tenement in Scotland, and my Swiss grandmother, Lydia Hari, was living on a mountain in the Swiss Alps. Amy had been forced to leave school when she was thirteen, because nobody thought it was worth educating girls. While her brother stayed in education, she was sent to work cleaning toilets, which she did all her working life. She had wanted to work with homeless people, but in practice women were locked out of jobs like that, and she was told to know her place as a woman and shut up. Lydia grew up in a Swiss village, and as a teenager she was constantly drawing and painting. She wanted to be an artist. She was told that girls couldn’t be artists. She got married young, and was told to obey her husband. I would sit in their kitchen years later, when her husband would hold out an empty mug and yell ‘ Kaffee! ’ (coffee) and she was expected to scramble to fetch it. She would sometimes sketch, but she said it made her depressed, because it reminded her of what her life might have been.

我今年四十一岁。我的祖母们在1962年时和我一样大。那一年，我的苏格兰祖母艾米·麦克雷住在苏格兰一栋工人阶级的廉租公寓里，而我的瑞士祖母莉迪亚·哈里则住在瑞士阿尔卑斯山的一座山上。艾米十三岁就被迫辍学，因为当时没有人认为女孩接受教育是值得的。她的哥哥继续读书，而她却被送去打扫厕所，这份工作她做了一辈子。她原本想去帮助无家可归的人，但实际上，女性被排除在这类工作之外，她被告知要安分守己，闭嘴。莉迪亚在瑞士的一个村庄长大，十几岁时她就经常画画。她想成为一名艺术家。但她被告知女孩不能当艺术家。她很早就结婚了，并被要求服从丈夫。多年后，我坐在他们家的厨房里，她丈夫会拿着空杯子喊“咖啡！”，然后她就得赶紧去拿。她有时会画画，但她说这让她很沮丧，因为这让她想起自己原本可能的生活。

My grandmothers lived in a society in which women were excluded from almost all systems of power and almost all choices about their lives. In 1962 there were no women in the British cabinet, the US cabinet or the Swiss government. Women made up less than 4 percent of the members of British parliament and the US Senate, and less than 1 percent in Switzerland’s Federal Assembly, where women weren’t even allowed to vote in seventeen out of the country’s twenty cantons (including the one where my grandmother lived). This meant that the rules were written by men for men. American and British women were banned from getting mortgages or opening bank accounts unless they were married and had written permission from their husbands. Swiss women were banned from getting jobs at all without the written permission of their spouse. There were no domestic-violence shelters anywhere on earth, and it was legal everywhere for a man to rape his wife. (When, in the 1980s, there were moves to ban rape within marriage, one California Assembly member objected, saying, ‘But if you can’t rape your wife, who can you rape?’) In practice, men could beat their wives, because the police did not regard this as a crime, and they could molest their daughters, since it was so taboo to speak out about this that nobody ever went to the police to report it.

我的祖母们生活在一个女性几乎被排除在所有权力体系之外，几乎无法自主选择人生道路的社会里。1962年，英国、美国和瑞士政府的内阁中都没有女性成员。英国议会和美国参议院的女性议员比例均不足4%，瑞士联邦议会的女性议员比例更是不足1%。在瑞士20个州中，有17个州（包括我祖母居住的州）甚至没有女性投票权。这意味着规则是由男性制定，也服务于男性。美国和英国的女性必须结婚并获得丈夫的书面许可才能申请抵押贷款或开设银行账户。瑞士的女性未经配偶书面许可，根本无法工作。当时世界上没有任何家庭暴力庇护所，而且男性强奸妻子在任何地方都是合法的。 （20 世纪 80 年代，当有人提议禁止婚内强奸时，一位加州议员提出反对，说：“如果你不能强奸你的妻子，那你能强奸谁呢？”）实际上，男人可以殴打妻子，因为警察不认为这是犯罪；他们也可以猥亵女儿，因为谈论这种事是如此禁忌，以至于没有人会去报警。

As I type out those facts, I keep thinking about my fifteen-year-old niece. Like her great-grandmother, she loves to draw and paint, and every time I see her doing it, I think of Lydia, doing the same thing in her Swiss village eighty-five years before. Lydia was told to stop wasting her time and start serving men. My niece is told: You’re going to be a great artist – let’s start looking at art schools. My niece never met my grandmother, but I believe that Lydia would have been happy to know the ways in which feminism changed the world.

我一边敲下这些文字，一边想着我十五岁的外甥女。她像她的曾祖母一样，热爱绘画。每次看到她画画，我都会想起八十五年前在瑞士小村庄里做着同样事情的莉迪亚。莉迪亚被告知不要浪费时间，应该去服侍男人。而我的外甥女却被告知：你会成为一名伟大的艺术家——我们开始考虑艺术院校吧。我的外甥女从未见过我的祖母，但我相信，如果莉迪亚知道女权主义如何改变了世界，她一定会很高兴。

I know it’s exceptionally irritating for a male to mansplain this topic in this way, especially when so much sexism and misogyny remains, and when women still face huge barriers. I know the advance of women’s rights is far from won, and many of the advances that have been made are under threat. I know only one thing here that is definitely true: the difference between the lives of my grandmothers and the life of my niece is a stunning achievement, and it happened for one reason, and one reason only. There was an organised movement of ordinary women who banded together and fought for it, and continued fighting even when it was really hard.

我知道，一个男人以这种方式对这个话题进行“男性说教”会让人非常恼火，尤其是在性别歧视和厌女症依然盛行，女性仍然面临巨大障碍的当下。我知道女性权利的进步远未结束，许多已取得的成果也岌岌可危。但我唯一确信的是：我祖母的生活和我侄女的生活之间的巨大差异，是一个惊人的成就，而这一切的发生只有一个原因。那就是一群普通的女性团结起来，为之奋斗，即使在最艰难的时刻也从未放弃。

There are, of course, many differences between the fight for feminism and the fight for our focus. But nonetheless, I kept returning to this example in my mind for a very basic reason. The feminist movement teaches us that huge and seemingly immovable forces can be challenged by ordinary people – and that when they do, it can lead to real change. The concentrated power of men in 1962 was vastly greater than the power of Big Tech as I write this in 2021. Men controlled almost everything – every parliament, every corporation, every police force – and they had for as long as those institutions had existed. It would have been very easy, in that situation, to say – nothing can change; give up; women will just have to learn to live a life of subordination. Many people are tempted to think that now, when they contemplate the huge forces stealing our focus. But that’s the thing about the pessimistic belief that we are powerless and can’t change anything. It’s false.

当然，争取女权主义和争取关注点之间存在诸多差异。但即便如此，我脑海中仍然反复出现这个例子，原因很简单。女权运动告诉我们，普通人也可以挑战看似不可撼动的巨大力量——而当他们这样做时，就能带来真正的改变。1962年男性集中的权力远比我2021年写下这些文字时大型科技公司的权力要大得多。男性几乎控制了一切——每一个议会、每一家公司、每一支警察部队——而且只要这些机构存在，他们就一直如此。在那种情况下，人们很容易说——一切都无法改变；放弃吧；女性只能学会忍受从属的生活。现在，当人们思考那些占据我们关注点的巨大力量时，许多人也容易产生这种想法。但这就是悲观主义的本质：认为我们无能为力，无法改变任何事情。这是错误的。

Think about another historical example. I’m gay. In 1962, I would have been put in jail for it. Now I can get married. Homophobia ruled for 2,000 years, and then it didn’t. The difference – the only difference – was a movement of ordinary people demanding an end to the forces thwarting their lives. I am free because the people who came before us didn’t give up; they got up. Again, of course, there’s big differences between the struggle for equality for gay people, and this fight. But there is a key parallel: no source of power, no set of ideas, is so large it can’t be challenged. Big Tech would love us to believe that their power is impregnable and there’s no point fighting for change because that never works. These companies are as fragile as every other powerful force that was torn down in the end.

想想另一个历史例子。我是同性恋。在1962年，我会因此被关进监狱。现在我可以结婚了。恐同症统治了两千年，然后它就消失了。区别——唯一的区别——在于普通民众发起了一场运动，要求结束那些阻碍他们生活的势力。我之所以自由，是因为前人没有放弃；他们奋起反抗。当然，同性恋者争取平等的斗争与这场斗争之间存在着巨大的差异。但两者之间存在一个关键的相似之处：没有任何权力来源，没有任何一套思想体系强大到不可挑战。大型科技公司想让我们相信他们的权力坚不可摧，争取变革毫无意义，因为变革永远不会奏效。这些公司和其他最终被摧毁的强大势力一样脆弱。

If we don’t form a movement and fight, what is the alternative? Tristan and Aza warned me that right now, we are only at the start of what unregulated surveillance capitalism will do to us. It is only going to become more sophisticated and more invasive. They gave me lots of examples. Here’s one. There’s a technology that exists called ‘style transfer’. If you use it, you can show a computer lots of paintings by Van Gogh and then you point it at a new scene, and it can recreate it in the style of Van Gogh. Aza told me how ‘style transfer’ could quite soon be used against you or me: ‘ Google today could read all of your Gmail, come up with a model that can mimic your style, and then sell that to an advertiser. [You, as the user] don’t even know what’s going on,’ but you will start to receive emails that are unusually welcoming and persuasive, because they sound just like you. Even worse, in Aza’s opinion, ‘they could look at all of your Gmail, look at all the emails you responded to quickly and positively, and learn that style. So [they] learn the style that is uniquely persuasive to you. There is nothing illegal about that. There are no laws to protect you against that. Is it breaking your privacy? They’re not selling your data. They’re just selling an asymmetric knowledge about how you work – even more than you know about yourself – to the highest bidder.’

如果我们不发起运动、奋起反抗，还有什么出路？特里斯坦和阿扎警告我说，我们现在所看到的，仅仅是不受监管的监控资本主义对我们造成的后果的开端。它只会变得越来越复杂、越来越具有侵入性。他们给我举了很多例子。这里举一个例子。有一种叫做“风格迁移”的技术。如果你使用这项技术，你可以给电脑展示很多梵高的画作，然后让它指向一个新的场景，它就能用梵高的风格重新创作出来。阿扎告诉我，“风格迁移”很快就会被用来对付你我：“谷歌现在就可以读取你所有的Gmail邮件，建立一个能够模仿你风格的模型，然后把这个模型卖给广告商。[作为用户，你]甚至都不知道发生了什么，”但你会开始收到一些异常热情、极具说服力的邮件，因为它们听起来就像是你写的。更糟糕的是，在阿扎看来，“他们可以查看你所有的Gmail邮件，查看你所有快速且积极回复的邮件，并学习你的回复风格。这样一来，他们就能了解哪种风格对你特别有说服力。这并不违法。也没有任何法律保护你免受这种侵害。这侵犯了你的隐私吗？他们并没有出售你的数据。他们只是将关于你工作方式的不对称信息——甚至比你自己对自己的了解还要多——出售给出价最高的人。”

It’s an asymmetry so extreme that it will hack vulnerabilities you don’t even know are vulnerabilities. There are technological innovations coming that will make the current forms of surveillance capitalism look as crude as Space Invaders looks to a kid raised on Fortnite. Facebook, in 2015, filed a patent for technology that will be able to detect your emotions from the cameras on your laptop and phone. If we don’t regulate, Aza warns, ‘Our supercomputers are going to test their way to finding all our vulnerabilities, without anyone ever stopping to ask – is that right? It’ll feel to us a little bit like we’re still making our own decisions,’ but it will be ‘a direct attack against agency and free will’.

这种不对称性如此极端，以至于它会利用你甚至都不知道是漏洞的弱点。即将到来的技术创新将使当前的监控资本主义形式显得如同太空侵略者游戏在玩《堡垒之夜》的孩子眼中一样粗糙简陋。2015年，Facebook申请了一项专利，该技术能够通过笔记本电脑和手机上的摄像头检测你的情绪。阿扎警告说，如果我们不进行监管，“我们的超级计算机将通过测试来发现我们所有的漏洞，而没有人会停下来问——这样做对吗？我们可能会感觉自己仍然在自主做决定，”但这实际上是“对自主性和自由意志的直接攻击”。

Tristan’s mentor, Jaron Lanier – a veteran Silicon Valley engineer – told me he used to be a consultant for loads of dystopian Hollywood movies, like Minority Report , but he had to stop because he kept designing ever-more-frightening technologies to warn people of what was coming – and designers kept responding by saying: that’s so cool; how do we make that?

特里斯坦的导师，资深硅谷工程师贾伦·拉尼尔告诉我，他曾经是许多反乌托邦好莱坞电影的顾问，比如《少数派报告》，但他不得不停止这项工作，因为他不断设计越来越可怕的技术来警告人们即将发生的事情——而设计师们的回应却是：这太酷了；我们该如何实现它？

‘Sometimes I hear people say it’s too late to make certain changes to the web or platforms or digital technology,’ James Williams told me. But the axe, he said, existed for 1.4 million years before anybody thought to put a handle on it. The web, by contrast, ‘is less than ten thousand days old’.

“我有时会听到有人说，现在对网络、平台或数字技术进行某些改变已经太晚了，”詹姆斯·威廉姆斯告诉我。但他指出，斧头存在了140万年，直到有人想到给它装上斧柄。相比之下，互联网“诞生至今还不到一万天”。

We are, I realised, in a race. To one side there is the rapidly escalating power of invasive technologies, which are figuring out how we work and fracking our attention. On the other side there needs to be a movement demanding technologies that work for us, not against us; technologies that feed our ability to focus, instead of fracturing it. At the moment, the movement for humane technology consists of a few brave people like Professor Shoshana Zuboff, Tristan and Aza. They are the equivalent of the scattered bands of brave feminists of the early 1960s. We all need to decide – are we going to join them and put up a fight? Or are we going to let the invasive technologies win by default?

我意识到，我们正身处一场竞赛之中。一方面，侵入性技术的影响力正迅速增长，它们正在摸清我们的运作方式，并不断蚕食我们的注意力。另一方面，我们需要一场运动，要求技术为我们服务，而不是与我们对抗；要求技术增强我们的专注力，而不是削弱它。目前，倡导人道技术的运动由少数勇敢的人组成，例如肖莎娜·祖博夫教授、特里斯坦和阿扎。他们就像上世纪六十年代初那些分散的勇敢女权主义者一样。我们都需要做出抉择——我们是要加入他们，奋起反抗？还是要眼睁睁地看着侵入性技术默认获胜？

# ↩

10 Cause Eight: The Surge in Stress and How It Is Triggering Vigilance

原因八：压力激增及其如何引发警觉

When I first admitted to myself I had an attention problem and fled to Provincetown, I had a simple story about what happened to my focus – the internet and cellphones broke it. I now knew that this was too simplistic – that the business model behind the tech was more important than the tech itself – but I was about to learn something even more important. These technologies arrived in our lives at a moment when we were unusually vulnerable to being hijacked by them – when our collective immune system was down, for reasons that are totally separate from the technology and its design.

当我第一次承认自己注意力不集中，并逃到普罗温斯敦时，我对注意力不集中的原因给出了一个简单的解释——互联网和手机破坏了我的专注力。现在我知道这种解释过于简单——科技背后的商业模式比科技本身更重要——但我即将学到更重要的东西。这些科技进入我们的生活时，我们正处于一个异常脆弱、容易被它们“劫持”的时期——那时我们的集体免疫系统处于低迷状态，而这背后的原因与科技本身及其设计完全无关。

At some level, many of us can sense some of the reasons for this. In early 2020 I decided to team up with the Council for Evidence-Based Psychiatry, and together we commissioned YouGov – one of the world’s leading polling companies – to carry out (so far as I can tell) the first scientific opinion poll ever conducted into attention, in both the US and Britain. The poll identified people who felt their attention was getting worse, and then it asked them why they believed this was happening. It gave them ten options to choose from, and asked them to select any and all that they felt applied to them. The number-one reason people gave for their problems was not their phones. It was stress, which was chosen by 48 percent. The number-two reason was a change in life circumstances, like having a baby or getting older, also chosen by 48 percent. The number-three problem was difficult or disturbed sleep, which was named by 43 percent. Phones came fourth, chosen by 37 percent.

在某种程度上，我们很多人都能感受到造成这种现象的原因。2020年初，我决定与循证精神病学委员会合作，共同委托世界领先的民意调查公司之一YouGov，在美国和英国开展了（据我所知）有史以来首次针对注意力问题的科学民意调查。该调查首先识别出那些感觉自己注意力越来越差的人，然后询问他们认为造成这种情况的原因。调查提供了十个选项，并要求他们选择所有他们认为适用于自己的选项。人们给出的首要原因并非手机，而是压力，48%的人选择了压力。第二大原因是生活环境的变化，例如生孩子或变老，同样有48%的人选择了压力。第三大问题是睡眠困难或睡眠紊乱，43%的人选择了睡眠问题。手机排在第四位，有37%的人选择了手机。

When I started to study the science of this in more detail, I learned that the hunches of ordinary people are not wrong. There are deeper forces than our phones and the web at work – and those forces led us, in turn, to develop a dysfunctional relationship with the web.

当我开始更深入地研究这方面的科学原理时，我发现普通人的直觉并非错误。除了手机和网络之外，还有更深层次的力量在起作用——而正是这些力量反过来导致我们与网络之间产生了不健康的关系。

I began to understand the first dimension of this when I spent time with the woman who later became the Surgeon General of California, who has made a key breakthrough on these questions. Of all the people I met for this book, she is perhaps the one I most admire. At first, when you read her story, it might like seem the situation she is describing is so extreme that it doesn’t have much to do with your own life – but stick with me, because what she discovered can help us to understand a force that is fracturing the attention of many of us.

当我与后来成为加州卫生局局长、并在这些问题上取得关键突破的那位女士相处一段时间后，我开始理解这个问题的第一个层面。在我为这本书采访的所有人中，她或许是我最敬佩的人。起初，当你读到她的故事时，你可能会觉得她所描述的情况如此极端，与你的生活似乎毫不相干——但请继续读下去，因为她的发现可以帮助我们理解一种正在分散我们许多人注意力的力量。

In the 1980s, in the suburbs of Palo Alto in California, a young Black girl named Nadine felt anxious as she made her way home from school. She loved her mother – her mom had taught her some ferocious moves on the tennis court, and she was always telling Nadine to get herself an education, because once you have it, nobody can take it away from you. But there were times when – through no fault of her own – her mother behaved very differently. ‘The problem was,’ Nadine wrote later, ‘that we never knew which mother we were going to get. Every day after school it was a guessing game – are we coming home to happy Mom or scary Mom?’

上世纪80年代，在加州帕洛阿尔托郊区，一个名叫娜丁的年轻黑人女孩放学回家时总是感到焦虑。她爱她的母亲——母亲教过她一些网球场上的绝招，也总是告诉娜丁要努力学习，因为一旦拥有了知识，就没人能把它夺走。但有时——并非娜丁的错——母亲的行为却截然不同。“问题是，”娜丁后来写道，“我们永远不知道会见到怎样的妈妈。每天放学回家都像是在猜谜——我们会看到一个和蔼可亲的妈妈，还是一个令人害怕的妈妈？”

Two decades later, Dr Nadine Burke Harris looked at the two children sitting in front of her in her examination room and felt something in her body – an old, familiar ache. The kids were seven and eight years old, and a few hours before, their father had pulled them into his car, deliberately failed to put on their seatbelts, and driven off, until he found a wall. Then he aimed his car at it and drove forward as fast as he could. Nadine watched the kids and thought about how afraid they must have been. ‘I knew intuitively what that type of fear felt like,’ she told me when we sat together. ‘I could empathise on a physiological level, if that makes any sense. I know what happens in those moments.’ These children, it turned out, also had a parent with paranoid schizophrenia.

二十年后，纳丁·伯克·哈里斯医生看着诊室里坐在她面前的两个孩子，心中涌起一股熟悉的、久违的痛楚。孩子们当时七岁和八岁，几个小时前，他们的父亲把他们拉进车里，故意不给他们系安全带，然后开车离开，直到找到一堵墙。接着，他把车对准墙，以最快的速度冲了过去。纳丁看着孩子们，想着他们当时一定非常害怕。“我凭直觉就知道那种恐惧是什么感觉，”我们坐在一起时，她告诉我，“如果这能说得通的话，我能从生理层面感同身受。我知道在那种时刻会发生什么。”后来发现，这两个孩子的父母中也有一位患有偏执型精神分裂症。

Nadine had coped with her mother’s mental illness by always being an A student, just as her mom, in her healthier moments, had taught her to. She got into Harvard, and then she studied public health and paediatrics. When it came to making a decision about what to do with everything she had learned, she realised she wanted to help children. While many of her classmates went on to provide medicine for rich people, Nadine went to Bayview, one of the last non-gentrified parts of San Francisco, which is a really poor, struggling neighbourhood with a lot of violence. Not long after she started there, Nadine was with some friends when she heard a cracking sound. She ran towards it, and found a seventeen-year-old boy who had been shot and was bleeding out. She learned that grandmothers in her new neighbourhood sometimes slept in their bathtubs because they were afraid of stray bullets hitting them in their sleep. She reflected later on what it’s like to live in the middle of random violence like this all the time. To live in Bayview, she realised, was to constantly soak up fear and stress.

娜丁一直努力学习，力求在母亲的精神疾病面前保持优异的成绩，就像母亲在她身体健康时教导她的那样。她考入了哈佛大学，主修公共卫生和儿科学。当她面临如何运用所学知识的抉择时，她意识到自己想帮助孩子。许多同学后来都从事医疗行业，为富人服务，而娜丁则去了旧金山湾景社区——旧金山最后一片尚未被高档化的地区之一，一个非常贫困、生活艰难且暴力频发的社区。搬到湾景不久，娜丁和朋友们在一起时，突然听到一声枪响。她循声跑去，发现一个十七岁的男孩中枪倒地，血流不止。她了解到，新社区里的一些老奶奶有时会睡在浴缸里，因为她们害怕被流弹击中。后来，她反思了生活在这样一个充满随机暴力的环境中究竟是怎样一种感受。她意识到，住在湾景镇就意味着要不断地承受恐惧和压力。

One day, a fourteen-year-old boy who had been diagnosed with ADHD, who I’ll call Robert, was brought to see Nadine. (I have also changed some other details throughout this chapter, at Nadine’s request, to protect the medical confidentiality of her patients.) For a while, Robert had been prescribed the stimulant drug Ritalin, but it didn’t seem to be making any difference for him. He said he didn’t like how it made him feel, and he wanted to stop, but his previous doctors had insisted that he carry on taking it at higher and higher doses.

一天，一个被诊断患有注意力缺陷多动障碍（ADHD）的十四岁男孩，我姑且称他为罗伯特，被带到娜丁面前。（应娜丁的要求，为了保护她病人的医疗隐私，我在本章中也修改了一些细节。）罗伯特之前一直服用兴奋剂利他林，但似乎并没有什么效果。他说他不喜欢这种药的感觉，想停药，但他之前的医生坚持让他继续服用，而且剂量越来越大。

Nadine asked Robert and his mother when his attention problems had first begun. It was when he was ten. She asked: what happened then? Well, they explained, that was when he was sent to live at his dad’s house. They talked about the divorce, and the boy’s life in general – and then Nadine asked gently: why was Robert sent to live with his dad? It took a while for them to tell the story, but in fits and starts, it tumbled out. Robert’s mother had a boyfriend, and one day when she came home, she found him in the shower, sexually abusing her son. She had been sexually abused all throughout her own childhood, and she had been groomed to be terrified of abusive men and to submit to their demands. In that moment, she felt powerless – so she did something she was deeply ashamed of. Instead of calling the police, she sent her son away to live with his dad. Whenever Robert came back to visit, his abuser was still there, waiting.

娜丁问罗伯特和他的母亲，他的注意力问题是什么时候开始的。他们说是十岁的时候。娜丁又问：后来发生了什么？他们解释说，那时他被送到他父亲家住。他们谈到了父母离婚，以及罗伯特的生活——然后娜丁轻声问道：为什么罗伯特要被送到他父亲家？他们花了些时间才把事情说完，断断续续地，最终还是把真相倾泻而出。罗伯特的母亲有个男朋友，有一天她回家时，发现他正在浴室里性侵她的儿子。她自己童年时期也遭受过性侵，从小就被灌输了对施暴男人的恐惧，并被教导要顺从他们的要求。那一刻，她感到无能为力——于是她做了一件让她深感羞耻的事情。她没有报警，而是把儿子送到他父亲家去住。每当罗伯特回来探望时，施暴者仍然在那里等着他。

Nadine thought a lot about this case, and she began to wonder if it might connect to a wider problem she was seeing. When she arrived at the medical centre in Bayview, she had noticed that the kids there were being diagnosed as having attention problems at a staggering rate – dramatically higher than in wealthier neighbourhoods – and that the first and usually only response was to drug them with very powerful stimulants like Ritalin or Adderall. Nadine is a believer in the power of medication to solve all sorts of problems – it’s why she went into medicine – but she started to wonder: what if we are misdiagnosing the problem a lot of these kids are facing?

娜丁反复思考这个病例，开始怀疑它是否与她观察到的一个更广泛的问题有关。当她来到湾景医疗中心时，她注意到那里的孩子被诊断出注意力缺陷的比例高得惊人——远高于富裕社区——而医生通常唯一的应对措施就是给他们服用利他林或阿德拉等强效兴奋剂。娜丁相信药物可以解决各种问题——这也是她选择从医的原因——但她开始思考：如果我们误诊了许多孩子面临的问题呢？

Nadine knew that decades before, scientists had discovered something significant. When human beings are in a terrifying environment – like a war zone – we often flip into a different state. She gave me an example, one I briefly referred to a little earlier. Imagine that you are walking in the woods and you are confronted by a grizzly bear that looks like it’s angry and about to attack you. In that moment, your brain stops worrying about what you’re going to eat that night, or how you’re going to pay the rent. It becomes narrowly and entirely focused on one thing: danger. You track every movement of the bear, and your mind starts scanning for ways to get away from it. You become highly vigilant.

娜丁知道，几十年前，科学家们就发现了一个重要的现象。当人类身处可怕的环境——比如战区——时，我们往往会进入一种不同的状态。她给我举了一个例子，我之前也简单提过。想象一下，你正在树林里散步，突然遇到一头看起来很愤怒、随时准备攻击你的灰熊。那一刻，你的大脑不再担心晚上吃什么，也不再担心怎么交房租。它完全专注于一件事：危险。你会密切关注熊的一举一动，你的大脑开始搜索逃离的方法。你会变得高度警惕。

Now imagine that these bear attacks happen a lot. Imagine if three times a week, an angry bear suddenly appeared on your street and swiped one of your neighbours. If this happened, you would likely develop a state known as ‘ hypervigilance’. You would start to look out for danger all the time – whether there’s a bear right in front of you or not. Nadine explained to me: ‘Hypervigilance is essentially when you’re looking out for the bear around every corner. Your attention is focused on cues for potential danger, as opposed to being focused on being present with what’s going on, or the lesson you’re supposed to be learning, or doing the work you were supposed to be doing. It’s not that [people in this state are] not paying attention. It’s that they’re paying attention to any cues or signs of threat or danger in their environment. That is where their focus is.’

现在想象一下，如果熊袭击事件频繁发生。想象一下，如果每周三次，一只愤怒的熊突然出现在你家门口，袭击你的邻居。如果这种情况发生，你很可能会进入一种被称为“过度警觉”的状态。你会开始时刻警惕危险——无论熊是否就在你眼前。娜丁向我解释说：“过度警觉本质上就是你时刻提防着熊出现在你眼前。你的注意力集中在潜在危险的迹象上，而不是专注于当下发生的事情，或者你应该学习的课程，或者你应该做的工作。这并不是说（处于这种状态的人）没有注意力。而是说，他们会关注环境中任何威胁或危险的迹象或信号。他们的注意力就集中在那里。”

She pictured Robert sitting in a classroom trying to learn math, but knowing that in a few days he will be seeing the man who sexually abused him and might do it again. How, Nadine wondered, could he bring the power of his mind to bear on sums in these circumstances? It was primed instead to do one thing – to detect danger. This wasn’t a failing in his brain – it was a natural and necessary response to intolerable circumstances. She wanted to know how many of the kids she was treating, who were being told they had some inherent defect, might in fact be in a position like this. With the team at her clinic, she decided to scientifically investigate this question. She began to read the relevant scientific studies, and she learned that there was a standard way to identify if a child has been traumatised, and by how much. It’s named the Adverse Childhood Experiences Study. It’s quite straightforward. It asks: Have you experienced any of these ten bad things in your childhood – factors like physical abuse, cruelty and neglect? Then it asks about any problems you might be having now – like obesity, addiction and depression.

她想象着罗伯特坐在教室里努力学习数学，但他知道几天后他就会见到那个性侵他的男人，而且他很可能会再次遭到性侵。纳丁心想，在这种情况下，他怎么可能集中精力做数学题呢？他的大脑本能地去做一件事——察觉危险。这并非大脑的缺陷，而是面对难以忍受的处境时自然而必要的反应。她想知道，在她治疗的那些被告知患有某种先天缺陷的孩子中，有多少人实际上可能也处于类似的境地。于是，她和诊所的团队决定用科学的方法研究这个问题。她开始阅读相关的科学研究，并了解到有一种标准方法可以识别儿童是否遭受过创伤，以及创伤的程度。这种方法被称为“童年逆境经历研究”（Adverse Childhood Experiences Study）。它非常简单明了。它会问：你的童年是否经历过以下十种糟糕的事情——例如身体虐待、残忍对待和忽视？然后它会询问你现在可能遇到的任何问题——例如肥胖、成瘾和抑郁。

Nadine decided her team was going to study all of the more than 1,000 children in their care in this way, to figure out how much childhood trauma they had experienced, and to see if that correlated with any of the other problems they might be having – including headaches, abdominal pains, and (crucially) attention problems. With every child, they went through this detailed assessment.

纳丁决定让她的团队用这种方法研究他们照顾的1000多名儿童，以了解他们经历过多少童年创伤，并观察这是否与他们可能存在的其他问题相关——包括头痛、腹痛以及（至关重要的）注意力问题。他们对每个孩子都进行了这种详细的评估。

Children who had experienced four or more types of trauma were 32.6 times more likely to have been diagnosed with attention or behaviour problems than children who had not experienced any trauma. Other scientists across the US have backed up the broad finding that kids are far more likely to have problems focusing if they experience trauma. For example, Dr Nicole Brown, in a separate body of research, found that childhood trauma tripled the development of ADHD symptoms. A large study by the British Office of National Statistics found that if there’s a financial crisis in the family, a child’s chances of being diagnosed with attention problems go up 50 percent. If there’s a serious illness in the family, it goes up 75 percent. If a parent has to make a court appearance, it goes up nearly 200 percent. This evidence base is small, but it is growing, and it seems to broadly back up what Nadine found in Bayview.

经历过四种或四种以上创伤的儿童，被诊断出注意力或行为问题的可能性是未经历过任何创伤儿童的32.6倍。美国其他科学家也证实了这一普遍发现：经历过创伤的儿童更容易出现注意力问题。例如，妮可·布朗博士在另一项研究中发现，童年创伤使多动症症状的发生率增加了两倍。英国国家统计局的一项大型研究发现，如果家庭出现经济危机，儿童被诊断出注意力问题的几率会增加50%；如果家庭成员患有重病，则会增加75%；如果父母一方需要出庭，则会增加近200%。虽然目前这方面的证据还比较少，但正在不断增加，而且似乎与纳丁在贝维尤的发现大体上相符。

She believed she had uncovered a key truth about focus: to pay attention in normal ways, you need to feel safe. You need to be able to switch off the parts of your mind that are scanning the horizon for bears or lions or their modern equivalents, and let yourself sink down into one secure topic. In Adelaide, in Australia, I met with a child psychiatrist named Dr Jon Jureidini who has specialised in this question, and he told me that narrowing your focus is ‘a really good strategy in a safe environment, because it means you can learn things and flourish and develop. But if you are in a dangerous environment, selective attention [where you focus on just one thing] is a really dumb strategy. What you need instead is to evenly spread vigilance around your environment, looking for cues for danger.’

她认为自己发现了关于专注力的一个关键真理：要想正常地集中注意力，你需要感到安全。你需要能够关闭大脑中那些时刻警惕着周围环境、寻找熊、狮子或其他现代威胁的思维模式，让自己沉浸在一个安全的话题中。在澳大利亚阿德莱德，我拜访了一位名叫乔恩·朱雷迪尼的儿童精神科医生，他专门研究这个问题。他告诉我，在安全的环境中，缩小注意力范围“确实是一个很好的策略，因为这意味着你可以学习新知识、茁壮成长。但如果你身处危险的环境，选择性注意力（只专注于一件事）就是一个非常愚蠢的策略。你需要做的是将警惕性均匀地分散到周围环境中，寻找危险的迹象。”

After she learned this, Nadine realised that with Robert, the response by his previous doctors had been a serious error. She told me: ‘Guess what? Ritalin does not treat sexual assault.’ For these kids, ‘The medications are treating the surface symptoms and not the root cause … If a child is having horrific behaviour, most of the time, it’s the child’s really great way of alerting the system that something is not right.’ She came to believe that when children can’t pay attention, that’s often a signal that they are under terrible stress. Jon, the doctor in Adelaide who specialised in this subject, told me: ‘If you’re medicating a child in that situation, you’re colluding with them remaining in a violent or unacceptable situation.’ One study compared children who had been sexually abused with a group of children the same age who hadn’t been abused, and found that the sexual-abuse survivors had double the usual rate of diagnosable ADHD. (This is not the only cause of ADHD – I’ll come to the others later.)

得知此事后，娜丁意识到，罗伯特之前的医生们的治疗是一个严重的错误。她告诉我：“你猜怎么着？利他林根本治不好性侵。”对于这些孩子来说，“药物只能缓解表面症状，而无法根治病因……如果一个孩子出现可怕的行为，大多数情况下，这恰恰是孩子在提醒系统出了问题。”她逐渐相信，当孩子无法集中注意力时，这往往是他们承受巨大压力的信号。阿德莱德一位专攻此领域的医生乔恩告诉我：“如果你在这种情况下给孩子用药，就等于是在纵容他们继续身处暴力或不可接受的环境中。”一项研究对比了遭受性虐待的儿童和一组同龄但未遭受虐待的儿童，发现性虐待幸存者被诊断出患有注意力缺陷多动障碍（ADHD）的比例是普通儿童的两倍。 （这并非多动症的唯一病因——我稍后会谈到其他病因。）

The approach that was taken to Robert can lead to horrendous outcomes. In Norway, I went to interview the politician Inga Marte Thorkildsen, who started to investigate these questions – and wrote a book about it – after she was shaken by the case of one of her constituents. He was an eight-year-old boy whose teachers identified him as showing all the signs of hypervigilance. He wouldn’t sit still; he was running around all the time; he refused to do what he was told. So he was diagnosed with ADHD, and given stimulants. Not long afterwards he was found dead, with a seventeen-centimetre gap in his skull. He had been murdered by his father, who, it emerged, had been violently abusing him all along. When I sat with her in Oslo, Inge told me: ‘Nobody did anything because they just said, wow, he has problems with attention, blah blah. They didn’t even talk to him during [the period when he was being given] medication.’

对罗伯特采取的那种做法可能会导致可怕的后果。在挪威，我采访了政治家英格·玛特·托基尔森，她因一位选民的遭遇而深受触动，并开始调查这些问题，还为此写了一本书。这位选民年仅八岁，老师们发现他表现出过度警觉的所有迹象。他坐不住，总是跑来跑去，不听话。于是他被诊断为多动症，并开始服用兴奋剂。不久之后，人们发现他已经死亡，头骨上有一个十七厘米的缺口。他是被父亲杀害的，而后来发现，他的父亲一直以来都在虐待他。我在奥斯陆采访英格时，她告诉我：“没有人采取任何行动，因为他们只是说，哇，他注意力有问题，等等等等。在他服药期间，他们甚至都没跟他谈过话。”

Nadine began to ask, If that is the wrong approach, what’s the right way to respond? How could she help Robert, and all the other kids in her care like him? She told me that she starts by explaining to parents: ‘I believe this [inability to focus] is being caused by your [child’s] body making too many stress hormones. So here’s how we fix them. We have to create an environment. We have to limit the amount of scary or stressful things that your [child] is experiencing and witnessing. And we have to layer on lots of buffering, lots of caregiving, lots of nurturing. In order for you to be able to do that, you, Mom, have to recognise and address your own history of what’s gone on in your life.’

娜丁开始问，如果这种方法不对，那正确的应对方式是什么？她该如何帮助罗伯特，以及所有像他一样需要她照顾的孩子？她告诉我，她首先会向家长解释：“我相信孩子注意力不集中是因为体内压力激素分泌过多。所以我们要这样解决。我们必须创造一个良好的环境。我们必须减少孩子经历和目睹的恐惧或压力事件。而且，我们必须给予孩子充分的缓冲、关爱和呵护。为了做到这一点，妈妈，你必须正视并处理自己过往的人生经历。”

There’s no point saying this if you can’t then offer them practical ways to do it. So she worked really hard to get funding from Bay Area philanthropists so that she could turn this proposal into a reality. In a case like Robert’s, Nadine explained, there are lots of steps that have to be taken. They had to help the mother get therapy, so she could understand why she felt powerless to challenge his abuser. They had to connect the family with legal help so they could get a restraining order on the abuser, so he was out of Robert’s life for ever. They had to prescribe yoga for both the abused child and mother, so they could reconnect with their bodies. They had to help them to improve their sleep and their nutrition.

如果你不能提供切实可行的方法，光说这些毫无意义。所以她非常努力地从湾区的慈善家那里筹集资金，以便将这个提议变成现实。纳丁解释说，像罗伯特这样的案例，需要采取很多步骤。他们必须帮助母亲接受心理治疗，让她明白自己为什么无力反抗施虐者。他们必须为这个家庭联系法律援助，以便申请针对施虐者的限制令，让他永远离开罗伯特的生活。他们必须为受虐儿童及其母亲制定瑜伽计划，帮助她们重新与自己的身体建立联系。他们还必须帮助她们改善睡眠和营养状况。

Nadine told me that you have to ‘scale the tools that you offer to be the same scale as the problems folks are having’. These deeper solutions are, she stressed, really hard work – but she has seen them transform children. ‘I think it’s easy for people to hear that when you’ve experienced childhood trauma, you’re broken or damaged,’ but in reality, ‘we have an ability to change.’ She sees it all the time in her practice: ‘The number of kids who have gone from failing to honour roll when they have the right diagnosis and the right support is nuts.’ That’s why, for her, this is ‘joyful work’, because ‘it shows us the profound potential for change. That’s what I see in my clinical practice. This is eminently treatable. It’s nuts how treatable it is. And there’s so much low-hanging fruit.’ She believes that if we work hard enough to inform people, ‘We’re going to get there: we’re going to get to the place where we’ve transformed the landscape of how society and medicine – all of us – respond to this issue.’

娜丁告诉我，你必须“调整你提供的工具的规模，使其与人们面临的问题规模相匹配”。她强调，这些更深层次的解决方案确实需要付出艰辛的努力——但她亲眼见证了它们如何改变孩子。“我认为人们很容易认为，经历过童年创伤的人就破碎或受损了，”但实际上，“我们有能力改变。”她在临床实践中经常看到这种情况：“当孩子们得到正确的诊断和支持后，他们从不及格到成绩优异的转变之多，简直令人难以置信。”这就是为什么对她来说，这是一份“充满喜悦的工作”，因为“它向我们展示了改变的巨大潜力。这就是我在临床实践中看到的。这种情况完全可以治疗。它的可治疗性之高令人难以置信。” “而且还有很多唾手可得的成果。”她认为，如果我们足够努力地向人们普及相关知识，“我们就能成功：我们就能改变社会和医学界——我们所有人——应对这一问题的面貌。”

Nadine believes she can only do this work because of the scared child she was in the suburbs of Palo Alto all those years before. She told me: ‘There’s a Buddhist saying – be grateful for your suffering, because it allows you to empathise with the suffering of others.’

娜丁认为，她之所以能从事这项工作，完全是因为多年前在帕洛阿尔托郊区度过的那个充满恐惧的童年。她告诉我：“佛教有一句格言——要感恩你所遭受的苦难，因为它能让你体会他人的痛苦。”

Not long before I saw her last, Nadine had just been appointed Surgeon General of California, the most senior medical position in the state. But as prestigious and powerful as that is, she told me she is more proud of something else. She had recently met with Robert and his mother. She saw how – as a result of the extensive help they have been given – they were slowly changing. He was no longer drugged for attention problems, nor was he showing difficulty focusing. They were developing empathy for each other. They were healing at a deep level, in a way that drugging the child could never have achieved. Robert’s mother was able to see how her own sexual abuse had left her unable to protect her own child, and she was able, for the first time in her life, to see herself differently – and to have compassion for herself. This in turn meant she could start to have compassion for her son. They are both, Nadine said, ‘recognising how the story can unfold differently’ from now on.

就在我上次见到她不久前，娜丁刚刚被任命为加州卫生局局长，这是该州最高的医疗职位。但尽管这个职位声望显赫、权力巨大，她却告诉我，她更引以为豪的是另一件事。她最近见了罗伯特和他的母亲。她看到，在他们接受的大量帮助下，他们正在慢慢改变。罗伯特不再因为注意力问题而服用药物，也不再出现注意力不集中的情况。他们开始彼此理解，并在一个深层次上得到疗愈，这是给孩子服用药物永远无法实现的。罗伯特的母亲终于意识到，自己曾遭受的性虐待让她无法保护自己的孩子，她生平第一次能够以不同的视角看待自己，并对自己产生怜悯之心。这反过来也意味着她可以开始对儿子产生怜悯之心。娜丁说，他们俩都“意识到，从现在开始，故事可以有不同的发展”。

Nadine could see that the severe trauma that Robert experienced had been devastating, but she also came to believe that ordinary life in Bayview – with all the stress that entails – corrodes attention. Her patients who weren’t being abused as kids were still worried a lot of the time about being evicted, or going hungry, or being shot. They were under constant low-level pressure.

娜丁能看出罗伯特遭受的严重创伤令人痛彻心扉，但她也逐渐意识到，湾景镇的日常生活——以及随之而来的各种压力——会逐渐侵蚀人的注意力。她的病人中，即使没有遭受过童年虐待的人，也常常担心被驱逐、挨饿或被枪击。他们一直承受着持续的、低度的压力。

When she explained this to me, I wanted to understand – do other forms of stress affect attention? How about ones that are vastly less harrowing than sexual abuse? I found that the scientific evidence on this is a little bit complicated. The evidence in labs shows if you are put under mild-to-moderate stress, you will perform better on some tasks that require attention in the short term. We’ve all had that experience: before I go on stage to give a speech, I feel a surge of pressure, but it makes me wake up, pull myself together, and perform at my best.

她跟我解释这件事的时候，我很想知道——其他形式的压力也会影响注意力吗？那些远没有性虐待那么可怕的压力呢？我发现这方面的科学证据有点复杂。实验室的证据表明，如果你处于轻度到中度的压力之下，短期内你在某些需要集中注意力的任务上表现会更好。我们都有过类似的经历：每次上台演讲之前，我都会感到一阵压力，但这反而让我清醒过来，调整好状态，发挥出最佳水平。

But what if that stress is protracted? In those circumstances, even mild levels of stress ‘can significantly alter attentional processes’, as one scientific team found in a typical study. The science is so clear on this that a recent summary explained: ‘It is now obvious that stress can cause structural changes in the brain with long-term effects.’

但如果压力持续存在呢？在这种情况下，即使是轻微的压力“也会显著改变注意力过程”，正如一个科研团队在一项典型研究中发现的那样。科学对此已非常明确，最近的一份总结报告解释道：“现在很明显，压力会导致大脑结构发生变化，并产生长期影响。”

I started to ask – why would this be? One reason is that stress often triggers other problems that we know undermine attention. For example, Professor Charles Nunn, a leading evolutionary anthropologist, investigated the rise of insomnia, and found that we struggle to sleep when we experience ‘stress and hyper-vigilance’. If you don’t feel safe, then you’ll be unable to wind down, because your body is saying to you – you’re in danger; stay alert. So the inability to sleep, he explained, isn’t a malfunction – it’s ‘an adaptive trait, under circumstances of perceived threat’. To really deal with insomnia, Charles concluded we ‘need to alleviate the sources of the anxiety and stress to effectively treat insomnia.’ They have to get to grips with the causes.

我开始思考——为什么会这样？其中一个原因是，压力常常会引发其他一些我们知道会损害注意力的问题。例如，著名进化人类学家查尔斯·纳恩教授研究了失眠症的兴起，发现当我们经历“压力和过度警觉”时，就难以入睡。如果你感到不安全，就无法放松下来，因为你的身体会告诉你——你身处危险之中；保持警惕。因此，他解释说，失眠并非功能障碍，而是“在感知到威胁的情况下的一种适应性特征”。查尔斯总结道，要真正解决失眠问题，我们“需要缓解焦虑和压力的根源，才能有效治疗失眠”。他们必须找到失眠的根本原因。

What might those deeper causes be? Here’s one. Six out of every ten US citizens have less than $500 in savings for if a crisis comes along, and many other countries in the Western world are moving in the same direction. As a result of big structural changes in the economy, the middle class is collapsing. I wanted to understand: what happens to your ability to think clearly when you become more financially stressed? I learned that this has been studied carefully by Sendhil Mullainathan, professor of computational science at the University of Chicago. He was part of a team that studied sugarcane harvesters in India. They tested their thinking skills before the harvest (when they were broke), and after the harvest (when they had a fair bit of money). It turned out that when they had the financial security that came at the end of the harvest, they were on average thirteen IQ points smarter – an extraordinary gap. Why would that be? Anyone reading this who’s ever been financially stressed knows part of the answer instinctively. When you are worried about how to survive financially, everything – from a broken washing machine to a child’s lost shoe – becomes a threat to your ability to get through the week. You become more vigilant, just like Nadine’s patients.

这些更深层次的原因可能是什么？这里有一个例子。十个美国公民中，有六个人没有足够的积蓄来应对危机，而西方世界的许多其他国家也正朝着同样的方向发展。由于经济结构的巨大变化，中产阶级正在崩溃。我想了解的是：当你面临更大的经济压力时，你的清晰思考能力会发生什么变化？我了解到，芝加哥大学计算科学教授森迪尔·穆莱纳坦（Sendhil Mullainathan）对此进行了深入研究。他所在的团队研究了印度的甘蔗收割工人。他们在收割前（当时他们身无分文）和收割后（当时他们手头宽裕）分别测试了他们的思维能力。结果发现，在收割结束后，当他们拥有了经济保障时，他们的智商平均提高了13分——这是一个惊人的差距。这是为什么呢？任何曾经经历过经济压力的人，都会本能地知道部分答案。当你为生计担忧时，任何事——从坏掉的洗衣机到孩子丢了一只鞋——都会威胁到你能否撑过这一周。你会变得更加警惕，就像娜丁的病人一样。

As I studied this big cause of stress, I kept thinking about something Nadine said to me: you have to ‘scale the tools that you offer to be the same scale as the problems folks are having’. I wondered: what would this mean if we applied it to our financial stress? It turns out there is a place that answered that very question. In Finland in 2017, a coalition government, consisting of both centrist and right-wing parties, decided to try an experiment. Every now and then, politicians and citizens across the world have suggested that we should give everyone a small guaranteed basic income every month. The government would say to you: we’re giving you a small amount of money to cover the basics (food, housing, heat), but no more. You don’t have to do anything for it – we just want you to be secure and have the basic minimum necessary to survive. This idea has been mooted by everyone from Republican President Richard Nixon to the Democratic presidential candidate Andrew Yang.

在研究这个巨大的压力源时，我一直在想娜丁跟我说过的一句话：你必须“调整你提供的工具的规模，使其与人们面临的问题规模相匹配”。我心想：如果我们把这句话应用到财务压力上，又会意味着什么呢？结果发现，有一个地方正好可以解答这个问题。2017年，芬兰一个由中间派和右翼政党组成的联合政府决定尝试一项实验。世界各地的政客和民众时不时会提出这样的建议：我们应该每月给每个人发放一笔数额不大的基本收入保障。政府会这样说：我们会给你一小笔钱来支付基本生活所需（食物、住房、取暖），仅此而已。你不需要为此付出任何努力——我们只是希望你能安心，拥有维持生存所需的最低限度保障。从共和党总统理查德·尼克松到民主党总统候选人安德鲁·杨，几乎所有人都曾提出过这个想法。

Finland decided to stop talking and actually try it. They selected 2,000 of their citizens at random, aged between twenty-five and fifty-eight, and told them: for the next two years, every month, we’re going to give you 560 euros (which is about $650 US, or £500), no strings attached. The government set up alongside it a rigorous scientific programme to see what happened next, and once the project was over, the results were published. I interviewed two of the lead scientists who worked on it: Olavi Kangas, who is a professor in the Department of Social Research at the University of Turku, and Dr Signe Jauhilinen, and they talked me through their findings.

芬兰决定不再空谈，而是付诸行动。他们随机抽取了2000名年龄在25岁至58岁之间的公民，并告诉他们：在接下来的两年里，每个月都会收到560欧元（约合650美元或500英镑），没有任何附加条件。芬兰政府同时启动了一项严谨的科学研究项目，以观察后续反应。项目结束后，研究结果得以公布。我采访了两位参与该项目的主要科学家：图尔库大学社会研究系的奥拉维·康加斯教授和西格内·尧希利宁博士，他们向我详细介绍了他们的研究发现。

Olavi told me that when it came to attention and focus, ‘the differences were very significant’ – once people received a basic income, their ability to focus improved significantly. Signe said they couldn’t figure out the exact reason why, but they found that ‘problems with money are really not good for concentration … If you have to worry about your financial situation … it takes a lot of the capacity of your brain. If you don’t have to worry, then it improves your capacity to think about other things.’

奥拉维告诉我，在注意力和专注力方面，“差异非常显著”——一旦人们获得了基本收入，他们的专注力就显著提高了。西格妮说，他们无法确定确切的原因，但他们发现“经济问题确实不利于集中注意力……如果你不得不担心自己的财务状况……就会占用你大量的脑力。如果你不必担心，那么你思考其他事情的能力就会提高。”

What the guaranteed basic income seems to have done – even though it was quite small – is give the recipients a sense they were standing on stable ground at last. How many people in the world feel that at the moment? Anything that reduces stress improves our ability to pay deep attention. Finland showed that a universal basic income – enough to give a baseline of security, but not so much that it disincentivises work – improves people’s focus by dealing with one of the causes of our hypervigilance.

保障基本收入——即便数额不大——似乎也让受益者感到终于有了立足之地。如今世界上有多少人有这种感觉呢？任何能减轻压力的事物都能提升我们的专注力。芬兰的经验表明，全民基本收入——足以提供基本的安全保障，但又不会高到让人失去工作动力——能够解决导致我们过度警觉的根源之一，从而提升人们的专注力。

This made me think again about our problems with our phones and with the web. The internet arrived for most of us in the late 1990s, into a society where the middle class was starting to crumble, and where financial insecurity was rising, and we were sleeping an hour less than people did in 1945. A more stressed society will be less able to resist distractions. It would always have been hard to resist the sophisticated human-hacking of surveillance capitalism, but it appeared we were already getting weaker, and we were easier to hack than we would have been otherwise. I was about to investigate other causes that also made us increasingly vulnerable.

这让我再次思考我们与手机和网络之间的问题。对我们大多数人来说，互联网是在上世纪90年代末期才出现的，当时的社会中产阶级开始瓦解，经济不安全感日益加剧，人们的睡眠时间甚至比1945年的人还少了一个小时。一个压力更大的社会更难抵御各种干扰。要抵挡住监控资本主义下精心设计的黑客攻击一直都很困难，但我们似乎已经变得越来越脆弱，也更容易受到攻击。我即将探究其他导致我们日益脆弱的原因。

I want to be honest here about something that complicates the argument I am putting forward in this book. There’s one way in which what Nadine had to teach me – and the wider science of stress that I learned later – is a challenge to the broader thrust of what I’m writing here.

我想坦诚地谈谈一些使我在本书中提出的论点变得复杂的问题。纳丁教给我的东西——以及我后来学到的更广泛的压力科学知识——在某种程度上挑战了我在这里所写的整体主旨。

As you saw in the introduction, I believe it is reasonable to argue that our attention problems are getting worse, even though we don’t have any long-term studies tracking changes in people’s ability to focus over time. I came to this conclusion because we can prove that there are several factors that damage focus and attention, and those factors are rising.

正如引言中所述，我认为，尽管目前尚无长期研究追踪人们注意力随时间的变化，但我们有理由认为，我们的注意力问题正在恶化。我得出此结论的原因是，我们可以证明，有几个因素会损害注意力和专注力，而且这些因素的影响正在加剧。
