But there’s one counterargument to that. You might ask: what if there are counterveiling trends, happening at the same time, which make our attention better? Nadine has shown that experiencing violence damages your ability to focus. But over the past century, there has been a big fall in violence in the Western world. I know this runs contrary to what we read in the news, but it’s true – Professor Stephen Pinker, in his book The Better Angels of Our Nature , lays out the evidence for this very clearly. This seems counterintuitive, in part because we are constantly fed images of violent and threat on television and the web, but it is a fact that you are far less likely to be violently attacked or murdered than your ancestors. Not very long ago, the whole world – in terms of violence and fear – looked more like Bayview, or worse.

但对此还有一种反驳观点。你可能会问：如果同时存在一些相反的趋势，让我们的注意力更加集中呢？纳丁的研究表明，经历暴力会损害你的专注力。但在过去一个世纪里，西方世界的暴力事件大幅下降。我知道这与我们在新闻中读到的内容相悖，但这是事实——史蒂芬·平克教授在他的著作《人性中的善良天使》中对此进行了非常清晰的阐述。这似乎有悖常理，部分原因是电视和网络上充斥着暴力和威胁的画面，但事实是，你遭受暴力袭击或谋杀的可能性远低于你的祖先。不久之前，整个世界——就暴力和恐惧而言——看起来更像是贝维尤，甚至更糟。

The threat of being beaten up or killed is surely the largest source of stress any person can face. Since that has fallen, we would expect this trend to have improved attention and focus. I want to be candid about this fact.

遭受殴打或杀害的威胁无疑是任何人面临的最大压力来源。既然这种威胁有所下降，我们理应预期人们的注意力和专注力会因此得到提升。我想坦诚地说明这一点。

Do I think this sole – but highly significant – trend improving our focus outweighs all the other factors dragging it down? Does it outweigh the effects of a huge increase in switching, a decline in sleep, the effects of vast machinery of surveillance capitalism, the rise in financial insecurity? I think – on balance – it doesn’t. But this isn’t something we can put into a computer and crunch the numbers on – it’s too hard to quantify and compare each of these effects. So reasonable people could disagree with me. It is possible that Nadine’s evidence suggests our attention, as a society, should be improving.

我是否认为，这一唯一但意义重大的趋势能够提升我们的专注力，从而抵消所有其他拖累专注力的因素？它是否能够抵消信息切换频率大幅增加、睡眠时间减少、庞大的监控资本主义机器的影响以及日益加剧的经济不安全感？我认为，总的来说，并非如此。但这并非我们可以用电脑进行数据分析的事情——量化和比较每一种影响都太难了。因此，理性的人可能会不同意我的观点。纳丁提供的证据表明，作为一个社会，我们的注意力应该有所提高。

But I then learned about another attention-wrecking force in our culture – one that has been rising throughout my lifetime.

但后来我了解到，在我们的文化中还有另一种分散注意力的力量——这种力量在我有生之年一直在崛起。

As a culture, in the Western world, we work longer with each decade that passes. Ed Deci, a professor of psychology who I interviewed at the University of Rochester in upstate New York, has shown that an extra month per year has been tacked on to what, in 1969, was considered a full-time job. As the twenty-first century began, the Canadian health service decided to study how people in their country spent their time at work. They studied over 30,000 people in over one hundred workplaces – public and private, large and small – and they ended up producing some of the most detailed research anywhere on how we work. They explained that as work hours swell and swell, people get more distracted and less productive, and concluded: ‘These workloads are not sustainable.’

在西方世界，随着时间的推移，我们的工作时间越来越长。我采访了纽约州北部罗切斯特大学的心理学教授埃德·德西，他指出，如今人们每年的工作时间比1969年时增加了一个月。进入21世纪，加拿大卫生服务部门决定研究加拿大人的工作时间分配情况。他们对一百多个工作场所（包括公共和私营部门、大型和小型机构）的三万多名员工进行了调查，最终得出了迄今为止最详尽的工作方式研究成果。他们解释说，随着工作时间的不断增加，人们更容易分心，工作效率也越来越低，并得出结论：“这样的工作量是不可持续的。”

I only understood the full implications of this for our attention when I went to two places that had experimented with ways to radically reduce the amount of stress people experience at work. They are 10,000 miles apart, and their experiments are quite different – but I believe they have big implications for how we could reverse the damage that is being done to our attention today.

直到我去了两个地方，亲身尝试用各种方法大幅降低人们在工作中承受的压力，我才真正理解这件事对我们注意力的全部影响。这两个地方相距一万英里，实验方法也截然不同——但我相信，它们对于我们如何扭转如今注意力所遭受的损害具有重要的启示意义。

# ↩

11 The Places That Figured Out How to Reverse the Surge in Speed and Exhaustion

11个成功逆转速度与疲劳激增现象的地方

Andrew Barnes never stopped. He was working in the City of London – Britain’s Wall Street – in the aftermath of the financial sector being deregulated in 1987. So companies could really let rip, and there was an explosion of financial swagger, with men in suits yelling at each other across the floor of the Stock Exchange as they traded billions. In this world, you were a wimp if you arrived later than 7.30 a.m., and you were a fool if you left before 7.30 p.m. So for half of the year, Andrew woke up in the dark and arrived home in the dark. He missed feeling the sun on his face.

安德鲁·巴恩斯从未停歇过。1987年金融业放松管制后，他便在伦敦金融城——英国的华尔街——工作。公司可以放开手脚，金融界一片浮躁，西装革履的人们在证券交易所里一边交易数十亿，一边互相叫喊。在这个世界里，早上7点半以后到公司就是个懦夫，晚上7点半以前走就是个傻瓜。因此，一年中有半年时间，安德鲁都是摸黑起床，摸黑回家。他怀念阳光洒在脸上的感觉。

In the City, everyone believed working better meant working more, until work consumed your whole life. He moved between various ball-breaking corporations. At one of them, all the new employees were called in on their first day to find that on the table in front of them there was a pre-typed resignation letter. They were ordered to sign it, and they were told: if you ever displease the boss, we’ll pull out this letter, and you will be out. Andrew slowly realised that he hated this exhausting existence. ‘If I look back, I sacrificed my twenties on the altar of ambition, and later in life, I probably sacrificed my family,’ he told me. His wild overwork ‘cost me some relationships along the way’, and it was only many years later that ‘I’m now having to build relationships with my kids.’

在伦敦金融城，人人都认为工作效率越高，工作时间就越长，直到工作占据了你生活的全部。他辗转于几家压榨员工的大公司。在其中一家公司，所有新员工在上班第一天就被叫到办公室，发现桌上放着一份预先打印好的辞职信。他们被要求签字，并被告知：如果你们哪天惹老板不高兴，我们就拿出这封信，你们就得走人。安德鲁渐渐意识到，他厌恶这种精疲力竭的生活。“回首往事，我把二十多岁都献给了野心，后来，我可能又牺牲了我的家庭，”他告诉我。他疯狂的过度工作“让我失去了一些人际关系”，直到多年以后，“我才开始重新建立与孩子们的关系。”

Andrew left England for Australia and New Zealand, where over time he became really successful, rising to own a series of large businesses. When I went to see him, we met in his penthouse apartment looking out over the city of Auckland – but the memory of those sunless years in the City of London never left him.

安德鲁离开英国前往澳大利亚和新西兰，在那里他逐渐取得了巨大的成功，最终拥有了一系列大型企业。我去拜访他时，我们在他的顶层公寓见面，公寓可以俯瞰奥克兰市——但伦敦金融城那些阴暗岁月的记忆始终萦绕在他心头。

One day, in 2018, he was on a plane when he happened to see a report in a business magazine about research into productivity at work. It contained some figures that intrigued him. The average British worker, the research had found, was only actually engaged with their job for less than three hours a day. This meant that most of the time people were at work, they were mentally checked out. They were in the office for a lot of hours, with their lives passing them by, but they weren’t getting much done.

2018年的一天，他在飞机上偶然看到一本商业杂志上刊登的关于工作效率研究报告。报告中的一些数据引起了他的兴趣。研究发现，英国普通员工每天真正投入工作的时间不到三个小时。这意味着，人们在工作的大部分时间里，精神都处于游离状态。他们长时间待在办公室，眼睁睁地看着自己的人生从指缝间流逝，却没能完成多少工作。

Andrew kept thinking about this. The company he ran in New Zealand, named Perpetual Guardian, had over a dozen offices employing over 240 people, in a business that drew up wills and ran and managed trusts. He wondered if these poor productivity figures applied to his own staff. In this situation, everyone is losing out. The workers are bored and distracted and worried about other things, particularly the families they don’t get to see as much as they should. At the same time, the employer isn’t getting a workforce that’s focused on the task in hand. At the back of Andrew’s mind, there was a memory of the years he himself had worked in a dysfunctional way, and he felt his own focus and judgement had been thrown off.

安德鲁一直在思考这个问题。他在新西兰经营着一家名为“永恒守护者”（Perpetual Guardian）的公司，拥有十几个办事处，雇佣了240多名员工，主要业务是起草遗嘱、运营和管理信托。他不禁怀疑，这种低迷的生产力是否也适用于他自己的员工。在这种情况下，每个人都是输家。员工们感到无聊、心不在焉，并且忧心忡忡，尤其是那些他们无法像应该的那样多陪伴家人的家人。与此同时，雇主也无法获得一支专注于手头工作的员工队伍。安德鲁的脑海中浮现出自己曾经在效率低下的工作环境中挣扎的记忆，他感觉自己的专注力和判断力也受到了影响。

So one day he asked himself: what if I changed my entire company so that from now on, every employee worked only four days a week, for the same wages? It would free up time for them to rest, have a proper social life, and to be with their families – the things they are often trying to squeeze into the cracks of their work time. What if giving them all this meant that, in return, the workers were able to focus on their tasks for just forty-five minutes more a day? His back-of-the-envelope calculations suggested to him that, in this scenario, the company’s productivity would actually go up. Giving people more time to rest and enjoy life might mean they worked more productively when they were in the office.

有一天，他问自己：如果我彻底改变公司的工作模式，让所有员工每周只工作四天，工资不变，会怎么样？这样一来，他们就能腾出时间休息、享受社交生活、陪伴家人——这些都是他们常常在工作间隙挤出来的事情。如果给予他们这些时间，作为回报，员工每天只需多专注工作45分钟，又会怎样呢？他粗略估算了一下，在这种情况下，公司的生产力实际上会提高。让员工有更多时间休息和享受生活，或许意味着他们在办公室时会更加高效。

To see if this could be right, he started to look back over the history of experiments in changing people’s work hours. For example, in Britain during the First World War, there had been a munitions factory that made people work seven days a week. When they cut back to six days, they found, the factory produced more overall. How far, Andrew wondered, could that principle be extended?

为了验证这个想法是否正确，他开始回顾以往关于改变人们工作时间的实验历史。例如，第一次世界大战期间，英国有一家军工厂要求工人每周工作七天。当他们将工作时间减少到六天时，工厂发现整体产量反而更高了。安德鲁想知道，这个原理究竟可以推广到什么程度？

So he decided to try something bold. He arranged a conference call and told all his employees that starting soon, they were going to be paid the same wage they currently got for a five-day week, but they would only be asked to work four days. However, he told them – in return, you have to find ways to genuinely get the job done. My hunch is you’ll be more productive – but you have to show me I’m right. We’ll try this change for two months. If, in that period, we don’t see a fall in productivity, I will make the four-day week permanent. ‘I was like – what? Am I hearing this right?’ I was told by Amber Taare when I went to interview everyone at the offices Perpetual has in a town named Rotorua, which is well away from the corporate headquarters. The workers were excited but wary. How could a plan like this really succeed? Was there some catch they couldn’t see? Gemma Mills, who also works in the Rotorua offices, told me: ‘I didn’t have a lot of faith that it was going to work.’ Andrew’s management team was also highly sceptical. ‘My head of HR literally fell over,’ Andrew said. The managers felt sure that productivity would be dented, and the blame would come back to them.

于是他决定尝试一项大胆的举措。他安排了一次电话会议，告诉所有员工，从不久的将来，他们的工资将与目前五天工作制的工资相同，但每周只需工作四天。不过，他告诉他们——作为交换，你们必须想方设法真正把工作做好。我的直觉是你们的效率会更高——但你们必须证明我的直觉是对的。我们将试行这项改革两个月。如果在这段时间内，我们的生产力没有下降，我将把每周四天工作制永久化。“我当时就懵了——什么？我没听错吧？”当我去采访Perpetual公司位于罗托鲁瓦镇（距离公司总部很远）的办公室时，Amber Taare这样告诉我。员工们既兴奋又谨慎。这样的计划真的能成功吗？是不是有什么他们没看到的陷阱？在罗托鲁瓦办公室工作的杰玛·米尔斯告诉我：“我当时并不看好这个项目。”安德鲁的管理团队也持高度怀疑态度。“我的人力资源主管当时简直惊呆了，”安德鲁说。管理层确信生产力会受到影响，而最终的责任会落到他们头上。

He gave the company a month to prepare, in which everyone had to think about how they could work better, and he called in a team of academic researchers to measure the real outcomes. Niggling drains on productivity that had been dragging on for years were identified and finally dealt with. One person, for example, had a job where she had to enter data, and it was wasting an hour of her day to have to enter it twice because two different systems weren’t talking to each other. Now she went to IT and insisted they sort it out. There were hundreds of changes like this happening across the company. In another office, the staff bought a little pot of flags, and everyone agreed that if you didn’t want to be interrupted, you put a flag on your desk from now on, to show you are focusing.

他给了公司一个月的时间准备，期间每个人都必须思考如何才能更高效地工作，他还邀请了一支学术研究团队来评估实际成效。多年来一直存在的、影响生产力的细微问题终于被发现并得到解决。例如，一位员工的工作是录入数据，但由于两个不同的系统无法互通，她不得不重复录入数据，每天浪费一个小时。现在，她去找了IT部门，坚持要求他们解决这个问题。公司里发生了数百起类似的变革。在另一个办公室，员工们买了一小罐小旗子，大家一致同意，从现在开始，如果你不想被打扰，就在桌子上插一面小旗子，表示你在专注工作。

‘It took a while to get your head around the concept, because it’s so challenging,’ I was told by Russell Bridge, another Perpetual Guardian employee. ‘If you’ve worked on an eight-to-five model for so long, it’s so ingrained and entrenched.’ But the change happened. With a whole extra day to themselves, people spent this time in different ways. Amber took her three-year-old daughter out of day care for one day a week, and played with her more. Gemma said ‘it just gives you that extra day to recuperate,’ and as a result, ‘I just felt genuinely better overall.’ Russell started to do DIY repairs around his home, and spent ‘quality time with the family’. He told me it helped him to realise that ‘the way humans are designed is to have downtime and [then] you will be more productive’. He found that when he came back to work, he was ‘fresher’.

“要理解这个概念确实需要一段时间，因为它太有挑战性了，”另一位Perpetual Guardian的员工Russell Bridge告诉我，“如果你长期遵循朝九晚五的工作模式，这种习惯已经根深蒂固了。” 但改变终究发生了。多出一天属于自己的时间后，大家以不同的方式利用它。Amber每周有一天把她三岁的女儿从托儿所接回家，多陪她玩。Gemma说，“这让你多了一天时间来恢复精力”，结果，“我感觉整个人都好多了。” Russell开始在家做一些DIY维修，并“花更多的时间陪伴家人”。他告诉我，这让他意识到“人类天生就需要休息，休息之后才能更高效”。他发现，当他回到工作岗位时，他“精神焕发”。

Almost everyone I spoke to who went through this experiment stressed that they noticed one change above all the others. As Gemma put it to me: ‘I was less likely to be distracted.’ Why? She said that, for her, it was about decompression. ‘I think your brain doesn’t necessarily switch off as easily if you’re going, going, going. You don’t take that time to switch off and relax… Your brain becomes accustomed to thinking constantly.’ But she found that with ‘that extra day to relax’, she could start to wind down – and so when she came back to work, her mind was clearer.

几乎所有参与过这项实验的人都强调，他们注意到一个最显著的变化。正如杰玛告诉我的那样：“我更不容易分心了。” 为什么呢？她说，对她而言，关键在于放松。“我觉得如果你一直忙个不停，大脑就很难停下来。你没有时间休息放松……你的大脑会习惯于持续思考。” 但她发现，有了“额外的一天放松时间”，她就能开始放松下来——所以当她回到工作岗位时，头脑更加清醒。

Of course, the workers had a vested reason to believe this – they wanted to keep the extra time off. What mattered more was more objective measurements. What did the academics who studied the changes find? All signs of distraction, they found, were radically down. For example, the time people spent on social media at work – which was measured by monitoring their computers – fell by 35 percent. At the same time, levels of engagement, teamwork and stimulation at work – some of which were measured by observing the workers, and some by how the workers described themselves – went up by between 30 and 40 percent. Stress levels were down by 15 percent. People told me they slept more, rested more, read more, relaxed more. Andrew’s management team – who had initially been highly sceptical – reached a surprising conclusion: they conceded that the company was achieving as much in four days as they had before in five. The changes have now been made permanent.

当然，员工们有充分的理由相信这一点——他们想保留额外的休息时间。但更重要的是更客观的衡量标准。研究这些变化的学者们发现了什么呢？他们发现，所有分散注意力的迹象都大幅下降。例如，人们在工作中使用社交媒体的时间（通过监控他们的电脑来衡量）下降了35%。与此同时，工作中的投入度、团队合作和激励程度（部分指标通过观察员工来衡量，部分指标则通过员工的自我描述来衡量）提高了30%到40%。压力水平下降了15%。人们告诉我，他们睡得更多、休息得更多、阅读得更多、放松得更多。安德鲁的管理团队——起初他们对此持高度怀疑态度——得出了一个令人惊讶的结论：他们承认，公司现在四天的工作效率相当于以前五天的工作效率。这些改变现在已成为永久性措施。

Dr Helen Delaney, who studied these changes as part of her work in the Faculty of Business and Economics at the University of Auckland, told me with a laugh: ‘It wasn’t a monstrous failure – I think we can say that. The work got done, clients were happy, staff were happy.’ When she interviewed them in depth, she found that ‘overwhelmingly, employees really liked their four-day workweek … They loved it. Who wouldn’t?’ Helen found this extra time gave them two things. Firstly, it ‘allowed them to nurture relationships with other people that are lost in the frenzy of modern living’. One senior manager told her he had struggled to connect with his son, but now he had started spending a lot of his freed-up time with him, he ‘realised actually I like being with my son, and he quite likes me, and this is a nice time to be together’. Secondly, ‘they also talked a lot about having what they called “me time” ’. They told her ‘with no one around me, no kids, no partner, no one – I got to be myself’.

海伦·德莱尼博士曾在奥克兰大学商学院从事研究这些变革的工作，她笑着告诉我：“这并非彻底的失败——我想我们可以这么说。工作完成了，客户满意，员工也满意。” 她对员工进行了深入访谈，发现“绝大多数员工都非常喜欢每周四天的工作制……他们很喜欢。谁会不喜欢呢？” 海伦发现，这额外的时间给他们带来了两方面的好处。首先，它“让他们能够维系与他人的关系，而这些关系在现代生活的忙碌中往往被忽略”。一位高级经理告诉她，他之前很难与儿子建立联系，但现在他开始花很多空闲时间陪伴儿子，他“意识到我其实很喜欢和儿子在一起，儿子也很喜欢我，这是个美好的亲子时光”。其次，“他们也经常谈到所谓的‘个人时间’”。他们告诉她，“身边没有别人，没有孩子，没有伴侣，什么都没有——我可以做我自己”。

Something similar has been tried in many other places, and even though the experiments are quite different, they keep finding similar outcomes. In 1920s Britain, W. G. Kellogg – the manufacturer of cereals – cut his staff from an eight-hour day to a six-hour day, and workplace accidents (a good measure of attention) fell by 41 percent. In 2019 in Japan, Microsoft moved to a four-day week, and they reported a 40 percent improvement in productivity. In Gothenberg in Sweden around the same time, a care home for elderly people went from an eight-hour day to a six-hour day with no loss of pay, and as a result, their workers slept more, experienced less stress, and took less time off sick. In the same city, Toyota cut two hours per day off the work week, and it turned out their mechanics produced 114 percent of what they had before, and profits went up by 25 percent.

类似的尝试在许多其他地方都进行过，尽管实验的具体情况各不相同，但结果却大同小异。20世纪20年代的英国，谷物制造商W. G. Kellogg将员工的工作时间从每天八小时缩短到六小时，结果工伤事故（衡量员工注意力集中程度的重要指标）下降了41%。2019年，微软在日本实行了每周四天工作制，并报告称生产力提高了40%。大约在同一时期，瑞典哥德堡一家养老院将员工的工作时间从每天八小时缩短到六小时，工资没有减少，结果员工睡眠时间更长，压力更小，病假也更少。在同一座城市，丰田汽车每周每天减少两小时工作时间，结果发现其维修技师的生产力提高了114%，利润也增长了25%。

All this suggests that when people work less, their focus significantly improves. Andrew told me we have to take on the logic that more work is always better work. ‘There’s a time for work, and there’s a time for not having work,’ he said, but today, for most people, ‘the problem is that we don’t have time. Time, and reflection, and a bit of rest to help us make better decisions. So, just by creating that opportunity, the quality of what I do, of what the staff does, improves.’ Andrew followed his own advice. Now he takes every weekend off – something he had never done before in his life – and goes away to his home on a nearby island without any devices connected to the internet. Gemma, one of the workers who told me that she had been wary at the start, said to me gently: ‘You know, there’s so much more than working until twelve o’clock at night … You’ve got to have a life outside of it.’

这一切都表明，人们工作时间减少时，注意力会显著提高。安德鲁告诉我，我们必须接受“工作越多，工作质量就越好”这种逻辑。“工作有工作的时候，休息也有休息的时候，”他说，“但如今，对大多数人来说，问题在于我们没有时间。我们需要时间，需要时间反思，需要一点休息来帮助我们做出更好的决定。所以，只要创造这样的机会，我和员工的工作质量就会提高。”安德鲁身体力行地践行了自己的建议。现在，他每个周末都休息——这是他以前从未做过的事——然后去附近岛屿上的家，不带任何联网设备。杰玛是其中一位员工，她告诉我她一开始很犹豫，她温和地对我说：“你知道，除了工作到晚上十二点之外，还有很多其他的事情……你必须拥有工作之外的生活。”

Later, at Stanford University, I discussed these questions with Jeffrey Pfeffer, who is a professor of organisational behaviour there. He said the reason it works is blindingly obvious. Ask any sports fan, he said. ‘If I want to win a football game, [or] if I want to win a baseball game, do I really want my team to be exhausted?’ He let this question hang in the air. Why, he asked, would the rest of us be any different?

后来，在斯坦福大学，我和组织行为学教授杰弗里·普费弗讨论了这些问题。他说，这种方法奏效的原因显而易见。他接着说，随便问问哪个体育迷，“如果我想赢一场足球比赛，或者一场棒球比赛，我真的希望我的球队筋疲力尽吗？”他让这个问题悬在空中，然后反问道，我们其他人又有什么不同呢？

One day I went for a walk along the shore in Auckland, thinking about what I had seen – and it struck me that this was the first place I had been to that had directly challenged the logic of our ever-accelerating society. We live in a culture that gets us to walk faster, talk faster, work longer, and we are taught to think that is where productivity and success come from. But here was a group of people saying: No. We are going to slow down and create more space for rest and attention.

有一天，我在奥克兰的海岸边散步，回想着我所看到的——我突然意识到，这是我到过的第一个地方，它直接挑战了我们这个日益加速的社会的逻辑。我们生活在一个让我们走得更快、说得更快、工作时间更长的文化中，我们被灌输了一种观念：这就是生产力和成功之道。但在这里，一群人却说：不。我们要慢下来，为休息和专注创造更多空间。

At the moment, this sane decision looks like an impossible luxury to the majority of us. Most people can’t slow down, because they fear that if they do, they’ll lose their jobs or their status. Today, only 56 percent of Americans take even one week of vacation a year. This is why telling people what they need to do to improve their attention – do one thing at a time, sleep more, read more books, let your mind wander – can so easily curdle into cruel optimism. The way our society works at the moment means they can’t do those things. But it doesn’t have to be this way. Our society can change. As I reflected on this, I felt a little uneasy, because there’s a few reasons why telling you the story of what happened in New Zealand in this way could leave you with a misleading impression. I like Andrew Barnes a lot – he’s an unusually enlightened and decent employer – but I don’t want you to imagine you too can wait for your boss to have an epiphany and hand you a four-day week. If we want this change to happen, you will very likely have to take a different route.

目前，对我们大多数人来说，这种理智的决定似乎是一种遥不可及的奢侈。大多数人无法放慢脚步，因为他们害怕一旦放慢脚步，就会失去工作或地位。如今，只有56%的美国人每年会休一周假。这就是为什么告诉人们如何提高注意力——一次只做一件事、多睡觉、多读书、让思绪自由驰骋——很容易变成一种残酷的乐观主义。我们目前的社会运作方式意味着他们无法做到这些。但情况并非必须如此。我们的社会是可以改变的。当我思考这个问题时，我感到有些不安，因为以这种方式讲述新西兰发生的事情可能会给你留下误导性的印象，原因有几个。我很喜欢安德鲁·巴恩斯——他是一位难得的开明且体面的老板——但我不想让你以为你也可以等着你的老板突然顿悟，然后给你每周四天的工作时间。如果我们想要实现这一改变，你很可能需要另辟蹊径。

Think about the weekend, which for a more than a hundred years gave most workers a guaranteed slice of rest and reflection. How did that come to pass? In the eighteenth century, as the Industrial Revolution surged, many workers found themselves forced by their employers to work for ten hours a day, six days a week. It was breaking them, physically and mentally. So they began to band together and demanded time to live. The first strike demanding shorter working hours took place in Philadelphia in 1791. The police beat the workers to a pulp, and afterwards, many of them were fired. But the workers didn’t give up. They fought harder. By 1835 they were organising a General Strike for an eight-hour day. Only decades of campaigns like this finally yielded an eight-hour day and a weekend for almost everyone.

想想周末，一百多年来，它为大多数劳动者提供了一段有保障的休息和反思时间。这一切是如何发生的呢？十八世纪，随着工业革命的蓬勃发展，许多工人被迫每天工作十小时，每周工作六天。这让他们身心俱疲。于是，他们开始团结起来，要求获得休息时间。第一次要求缩短工时的罢工发生在1791年的费城。警察对工人进行了残酷的殴打，事后许多人被解雇。但工人们没有放弃。他们更加努力地抗争。到了1835年，他们组织了一场争取八小时工作制的总罢工。正是经过数十年的不懈努力，才最终为几乎所有人争取到了八小时工作制和周末。

With a few honourable exceptions like Andrew, the owners of corporations will not voluntarily take less of your time, any more than Facebook will. They have to be compelled to do it. The introduction of the weekend was the biggest challenge to the speeding-up of society that has ever happened. Only a comparable fight will deliver a four-day week.

除了像安德鲁这样少数值得尊敬的例外，企业老板们不会自愿减少你占用你的时间，就像Facebook不会一样。他们必须被迫这样做。周末的引入是对社会加速运转的最大挑战。只有类似的斗争才能促成每周四天工作制的实现。

This insight is connected to another big obstacle to achieving this goal. A four-day week can be applied to salaried workers – but increasingly, many people are being forced into the ‘gig economy’, where they scramble to do several jobs without any contracts or fixed work hours at all. This is happening as a result of a very specific change: in countries like the US and Britain, governments broke up and largely destroyed labour unions. They made it harder and harder for workers to band together and demand things like contracts and fixed work hours. The only long-term solution to this is to steadily rebuild unions – so people have the power to demand these basic rights. This has already begun. For example, all over the US, workers in fast-food restaurants are unionising and demanding a $15 minimum wage per hour, with incredible success. They have secured wage rises for over 22 million workers and have pulled off the difficult job of winning majority support both in states that voted for Donald Trump and in states that voted for Joe Biden.

这一洞察与实现这一目标面临的另一个重大障碍密切相关。每周四天工作制可以适用于领固定薪水的员工，但越来越多的人被迫进入“零工经济”，他们不得不四处奔波，身兼数职，没有任何合同或固定工时。这种情况的出现源于一个非常具体的变化：在美国和英国等国家，政府解散并几乎摧毁了工会。这使得工人越来越难以联合起来，争取诸如合同和固定工时等权益。解决这个问题的唯一长期方案是逐步重建工会，使人们拥有争取这些基本权利的能力。这项工作已经开始。例如，在美国各地，快餐店的员工正在组建工会，要求每小时15美元的最低工资，并取得了令人瞩目的成功。他们为超过2200万工人争取到了加薪，并且成功地在支持唐纳德·特朗普和支持乔·拜登的州都赢得了多数支持，这是一项艰巨的任务。

But I think we won’t only have to take on employers – we’ll also have to fight something inside ourselves. When I spent time with the workers at Perpetual Guardian, I found what they said persuasive – but in my gut, I kept pushing back, looking for flaws in what they were telling me. At first I couldn’t figure out why. Then I realised that I often only feel I have worked enough if, at the end of the day, I am bone-tired and wrung out. The team who designed the original Macintosh computer wore T-shirts boasting ‘Working 90 hours a week and loving it!’ This could be the insane slogan for our professional class. Many of us have built our identities around working to the point of exhaustion. We call this success. In a culture built on ever-increasing speed, slowing down is hard, and most of us will feel guilty about doing it. That’s one reason why it’s important we all do it together – as a societal, structural change.

但我认为，我们不仅要与雇主抗争，还要与内心深处的某些东西作斗争。当我与Perpetual Guardian的员工们相处时，我发现他们的话很有说服力——但我的内心却不断质疑，试图找出他们话语中的漏洞。起初我百思不得其解。后来我意识到，我常常只有在一天结束时筋疲力尽、精疲力竭时，才会觉得自己的工作已经足够了。设计初代Macintosh电脑的团队穿着印有“每周工作90小时，乐在其中！”字样的T恤。这或许可以成为我们这个职业阶层的疯狂口号。我们中的许多人已经将自己的身份认同建立在工作到精疲力竭的程度之上。我们称之为成功。在一个以不断加速为核心的文化中，慢下来很难，而且我们大多数人都会为此感到内疚。正因如此，我们才更需要共同努力——进行一场社会结构性的变革。

When Covid-19 spread across the world, lots of people thought – amid all the tragedy and horror – that there might at least be one good outcome. Many people (not all) were freed from the daily commute and from the pressure to be seen at their desks all the time. So it was assumed that there might be a little space created for more rest. But work hours actually went up during Covid – in the first month and a half of lockdown alone, the average US worker clocked in three extra hours a day. In France, Spain and Britain, people worked two hours more a day on average. It’s not totally clear why. Some people think it’s because Zoom meetings take so damn long; others reckon it’s because, given all the economic insecurity, people were even more keen to show they were working so they didn’t get laid off.

当新冠疫情席卷全球时，许多人——在种种悲剧和恐怖之中——认为或许至少还有一线希望。许多人（并非所有人）摆脱了每日通勤，也不再需要时刻待在办公桌前。因此，人们理所当然地认为，这或许能带来一些休息时间。然而，疫情期间工作时间实际上却增加了——仅在封锁的头一个半月，美国普通员工每天的工作时间就增加了三个小时。在法国、西班牙和英国，人们平均每天的工作时间也增加了两个小时。个中缘由尚不完全清楚。有人认为是因为Zoom会议耗时过长；也有人认为，这是因为在经济形势不明朗的情况下，人们更加渴望证明自己仍在工作，以免被解雇。

What this shows is that no big outside force is going to come along and free us from the ratchet to work more and more hours – not even a global pandemic. We will only get it through a collective struggle to change the rules.

这表明，没有任何强大的外力能够让我们摆脱不断加班的恶性循环——即使是全球疫情也不行。我们只能通过集体斗争来改变规则。

But Covid also showed us something else that is relevant to a four-day week. It demonstrated that businesses can change their working practices radically, in a very short period of time, and continue to function well. When I caught up with him on Zoom in early 2021, Andrew Barnes said to me: ‘If a chief executive of a British bank had said, “We could run a 60,000-person bank from home,” a year and a half ago you’d have said – no chance. Right?’ And yet it happened, pretty seamlessly. ‘So … surely you can run a business in four days, not five?’ Andrew told me other managers used to say to him that a four-day week couldn’t possibly work because they wouldn’t be able to trust their staff if they couldn’t see them. Andrew called them back and said they should think again now: ‘They all work from home. Amazingly, the work got done.’

但新冠疫情也向我们展示了与每周四天工作制相关的另一件事。它表明，企业可以在很短的时间内彻底改变工作方式，并继续高效运转。2021年初，我通过Zoom与安德鲁·巴恩斯（Andrew Barnes）进行了一次视频通话，他告诉我：“如果一年半前，一位英国银行的首席执行官说，‘我们可以让一家拥有6万名员工的银行在家办公’，你肯定会说——不可能。对吧？”然而，这一切却发生了，而且非常顺利。“所以……你肯定可以在四天内运营一家公司，而不是五天吧？”安德鲁告诉我，其他一些经理过去曾对他说，每周四天工作制根本行不通，因为如果看不到员工，他们就无法信任员工。安德鲁给他们回了电话，告诉他们现在应该重新考虑一下：“他们都在家办公。令人惊讶的是，工作竟然完成了。”

The way we work seems fixed and unchangeable – until it changes, and then we realise it didn’t have to be like that in the first place.

我们的工作方式似乎是固定不变的——直到它发生了改变，然后我们才意识到它原本不必是这样的。

Ten thousand miles away, in Paris, workers had come up with a parallel proposal to help slow their lives down. Before the rise of smartphones, it was unusual for a boss to contact her worker once she had left the office and gone home. As a kid, plenty of my friends had parents with demanding jobs – but I almost never saw them get phoned by their employer once they got home. It was rare in the 1980s: when work was over, it was over. The only people who lived on permanent call were doctors, presidents and prime ministers.

远在万里之外的巴黎，工人们也提出了类似的方案，旨在放慢生活节奏。在智能手机普及之前，老板很少会在员工下班回家后联系她。我小时候，很多朋友的父母工作都很忙——但我几乎没见过他们下班回家后接到老板的电话。这在20世纪80年代非常罕见：工作结束，一切就结束了。只有医生、总统和总理才需要随时待命。

But since our work lives came to be dominated by email, there’s a growing expectation that workers will respond at any time, day or night. One study found that a third of French professionals felt they could never unplug, for fear of missing out on an email they were expected to reply to. Another study found that just the expectation that you should be on call causes workers anxiety, even if they don’t actually get contacted on any given night. In effect, the idea of work hours has disappeared, and we are all on call all the time. By 2015, French doctors explained they were seeing an explosion in patients suffering from ‘ le burnout ’, and voters started to demand action – so the French government commissioned Bruno Mettling, the head of the telecoms company Orange, to study the evidence and figure out a solution. He concluded that this constantly-on-call way of working was disastrous for people’s health and their ability to do their jobs. He proposed a significant reform: he said that everyone should have a ‘right to disconnect’.

但自从我们的工作生活被电子邮件主导以来，人们越来越期望员工随时待命，无论白天黑夜。一项研究发现，三分之一的法国专业人士感觉自己永远无法“断网”，因为他们害怕错过需要回复的邮件。另一项研究发现，仅仅是“随时待命”这种预期就会让员工感到焦虑，即使他们实际上在某个晚上并没有接到任何联系。实际上，工作时间的概念已经消失，我们所有人都在时刻处于待命状态。到2015年，法国医生表示，他们发现患有“职业倦怠”的患者数量激增，选民也开始要求采取行动——因此，法国政府委托电信公司Orange的首席执行官布鲁诺·梅特林（Bruno Mettling）研究相关证据并寻找解决方案。他得出结论，这种持续待命的工作方式对人们的健康和工作能力都造成了灾难性的后果。他提出了一项重大改革：他认为每个人都应该拥有“断网权”。

This right is simple. It says: you are entitled to clearly defined work hours – and you are entitled, when those work hours are over, to unplug and not have to look at email, or to have any other work contact. So in 2016, the French government passed this into law. Now any company with more than fifty people has to formally negotiate with its workers to agree the hours in which they can be contacted – and all other hours are out of bounds. (Smaller companies can draw up their own charters but don’t have to formally consult their workers.) Since then, several companies have faced penalties for trying to force people to respond to email out of hours. For example, the pest-control company Rentokil had to pay a local branch manager €60,000 (around $70,000 in the US and £50,000 in the UK) in compensation after it had complained he didn’t respond to out-of-hours emails.

这项权利很简单。它规定：您有权享有明确的工作时间——并且，在工作时间结束后，您有权完全放松，不必查看电子邮件或进行任何其他工作联系。因此，法国政府于2016年将此权利立法。现在，任何拥有50名以上员工的公司都必须与员工正式协商，确定可以联系他们的工作时间——其他所有时间均不属于工作时间。（规模较小的公司可以制定自己的章程，但无需正式咨询员工。）自此之后，一些公司因试图强迫员工在非工作时间回复电子邮件而受到处罚。例如，害虫防治公司Rentokil在投诉其当地分公司经理未回复非工作时间的电子邮件后，不得不向该经理支付6万欧元（约合7万美元，5万英镑）的赔偿金。

In practice, when I went to Paris and spoke to my friends who work for companies there, they said change is happening too slowly on this – the law is not being enforced by a tough regulator, so most French people haven’t yet experienced a big shift. But it’s a first step in the direction we all need to travel.

实际上，当我去巴黎和在当地公司工作的朋友们交谈时，他们说这方面的变革进展太慢——法律没有得到强有力的监管，所以大多数法国人还没有感受到显著的变化。但这却是我们朝着共同目标迈出的第一步。

Sitting in a café in Paris, I thought about what I had seen. There’s no point giving people sweet self-help lectures about the benefits of unplugging unless you give them a legal right to do it. In fact, lecturing people who aren’t allowed to unwind by their bosses about the benefits of unwinding becomes a kind of maddening taunt – it’s like lecturing famine victims on how they’d feel better if they had dinner at the Ritz. If you have an independent fortune and you don’t need to work, then you can probably make these changes now. But for the rest of us, we need to be part of a collective struggle in order to reclaim the time and space that has been taken from us – so we can finally rest, and sleep, and restore our attention.

坐在巴黎的一家咖啡馆里，我回想起我所看到的。除非赋予人们合法的权利，否则给他们灌输关于“断网”益处的那些甜言蜜语毫无意义。事实上，对那些被老板禁止放松的人进行“断网”教育，简直是一种令人恼火的嘲讽——就像对饥荒受害者说，如果他们去丽兹酒店吃顿饭，心情就会好很多。如果你拥有独立的财富，无需工作，那么你现在或许就能做出这些改变。但对于我们其他人来说，我们需要参与到一场集体斗争中，才能夺回被剥夺的时间和空间——这样我们才能最终休息、睡眠，恢复注意力。

12 Causes Nine and Ten: Our Deteriorating Diets and Rising Pollution

12个原因之九和第十：我们日益恶化的饮食和日益严重的污染

For every summer of my childhood and my teenage years, I was banished from my home in suburban London to a place that seemed as alien to me as the rings of Saturn. My dad had been born in a wooden farmhouse on a mountain in the Swiss Alps. ‘You must go to the farm,’ my father yelled, ‘it will teach you how to be a man!’ And so, for six weeks of the year, I would be woken up every morning by the crowing of a cockerel, in a fog of deep confusion, in the tiny room my father had shared as a kid with his four brothers.

在我童年和少年时期的每个夏天，我都会被“流放”出伦敦郊区的家，到一个对我来说如同土星环般陌生的地方。我父亲出生在瑞士阿尔卑斯山上的一座木制农舍里。“你必须去农场，”父亲吼道，“它会教会你如何成为一个真正的男人！”于是，每年有六个星期，每天早上我都会被一声鸡鸣吵醒，在父亲小时候和四个兄弟挤在一起的那间狭小房间里，我迷迷糊糊地醒来。

The first summer I spent alone with my Swiss grandparents was when I was nine years old. I learned that all through their lives, they had mostly eaten food that they had grown, raised or killed themselves. They had a huge garden, where they planted their own fruit and vegetables, and they raised their own animals for meat. But when they put their food on the table in front of me, I stared at it and struggled to recognise that it was even edible. Back home, my mother and my other grandmother were working-class Scottish women, and they had raised me on a diet of chips, fried food, supermarket-bought processed meals and vast amounts of Kinder Egg chocolate. We got a microwave when I was about seven, and from that point on I lived primarily on radiated pizza and zapped French fries. So for the first few weeks I was in Switzerland, I pleaded for chips, pizza, anything that I saw as food, and I refused to eat what my grandmother prepared. ‘ Ce n’est pas nourriture! ’ I said sincerely: ‘It’s not food.’

我九岁那年，第一次独自和瑞士的祖父母一起度过夏天。我了解到，他们一生中大部分时间都吃自己种植、饲养或宰杀的食物。他们有一个很大的花园，种着自己的水果蔬菜，还养着牲畜。但当他们把食物摆在我面前时，我盯着它们看了好一会儿，才意识到它们竟然能吃。在我的家乡，我的母亲和另一位祖母都是苏格兰的工薪阶层女性，她们从小就让我吃薯条、油炸食品、超市买的加工食品和大量的健达奇趣蛋巧克力。我七岁左右的时候家里才有了微波炉，从那时起，我的生活几乎就只剩下微波炉加热的披萨和炸薯条了。所以，在瑞士的头几个星期，我总是央求他们给我薯条、披萨，任何我能认出是食物的东西，而我拒绝吃祖母做的饭菜。“Ce n’est pas nourriture!”（这不是食物！）我真诚地说。

My grandparents were baffled. One day my grandmother caved in and took me to the city several hours away for a McDonald’s. She didn’t order anything for herself, and she watched me eat my Big Mac and fries with a look of compassionate disgust. Years later, in Las Vegas, I stumbled one day upon a very mentally unwell homeless person who was eating rotting maggot-filled food from the garbage behind the Rio casino. I realised my facial expression was exactly the same as my grandmother’s had been that day in the McDonald’s in Zurich.

我的祖父母百思不得其解。有一天，奶奶终于妥协，带我去了几个小时车程外的城市吃麦当劳。她自己什么也没点，看着我吃着巨无霸和薯条，脸上带着既同情又厌恶的神情。多年后，在拉斯维加斯，有一天我偶然遇到一个精神状况极差的流浪汉，他正在里约赌场后面的垃圾堆里吃着腐烂的、爬满蛆虫的食物。我突然意识到，我当时的表情和奶奶那天在苏黎世麦当劳里的表情一模一样。

In the two generations that had passed from my grandparents to me, there had been a dramatic transformation in one of the most basic elements of being a human – what we put into our bodies for fuel. All over the world I interviewed experts who said that we all know this change has been bad for our waistlines and our hearts, but we have been neglecting another key effect: it is stealing large parts of our ability to pay attention.

从我祖父母到我，两代人的时间里，人类最基本的要素之一——我们摄入的食物——发生了翻天覆地的变化。我采访了世界各地的专家，他们都说，我们都知道这种变化对我们的腰围和心脏健康不利，但我们却忽略了另一个关键影响：它正在削弱我们集中注意力的能力。

Dale Pinnock is one of the best-known nutritionists in Britain, and when we sat down together for a meal in London, I tried not to look at the juicy hamburgers on the menu, and ordered tofu and vegetables instead, just to impress him. He told me that if you want to understand why so many of us are struggling to focus, you might want to think about it this way. ‘If you put shampoo into a car engine, you’re not going to scratch your head when the thing conks out,’ he said. Yet every day, all over the Western world, we are putting into our bodies substances ‘which are so far removed from what was intended for human fuel’. Achieving sustained attention, he said, is a physical process that requires your body to be able to do certain things. So if you disrupt your body – by depriving it of the nutrients it needs, or by pumping it full of pollutants – your ability to pay attention will also be disrupted.

戴尔·平诺克是英国最知名的营养学家之一。我们在伦敦共进晚餐时，我特意没去看菜单上那些诱人的汉堡，而是点了豆腐和蔬菜，想给他留下好印象。他告诉我，如果你想了解为什么这么多人难以集中注意力，不妨这样想：“如果你往汽车引擎里加洗发水，车子熄火的时候你肯定不会挠头。”他说。然而，在西方世界，我们每天都在往身体里摄入“与人体所需能量相去甚远”的物质。他解释说，保持专注是一个生理过程，需要身体具备某些功能。所以，如果你扰乱了身体的正常运转——比如缺乏必要的营养，或者摄入过多的污染物——你的注意力也会受到影响。

Dale, and other experts on this question I spent time with across the world, went on to outline three broad ways in which the way we eat now is harming our focus. The first is that we currently eat a diet that causes regular energy spikes and energy crashes. If you eat (say) a Twinkie, he said, your ‘ blood sugar is going through the roof, and then crashing back down again. That’s going to affect how you can actually physically focus, because if your energy is through the floor, you’re not going to be able to give things your full attention.’ But most of us now start the day with the equivalent of a Twinkie, though we don’t realise it. ‘Think about that typical pattern. People will eat maybe a bowl of cereal and a slice of toast in the morning. It’s usually Frosties and white bread.’ Because there’s very little fibre in there, glucose – which gives you energy – ‘will be released very, very rapidly. So your blood sugar goes really high, really quickly, which is great – for about twenty minutes.’ Then ‘it crashes down, and when it crashes down, that’s when you’re knackered’ and at this point, ‘you get brain fog’.

戴尔以及我与世界各地其他专家就此问题交流后，他们概述了我们现在的饮食方式正在损害我们注意力的三大方面。首先，我们目前的饮食习惯会导致能量频繁地飙升和骤降。他说，如果你吃一块甜甜圈（比如一块奶油夹心蛋糕），你的“血糖会飙升，然后又迅速下降。这会影响你的注意力，因为如果你的能量低到谷底，你就无法全神贯注。” 但我们大多数人现在每天早上都以相当于一块甜甜圈的食物开始新的一天，尽管我们自己并没有意识到。“想想那种典型的饮食模式。人们早上可能会吃一碗麦片和一片吐司。通常是麦片和白面包。” 因为这些食物中纤维含量很低，所以葡萄糖——也就是能量来源——“会非常非常迅速地释放出来。”所以你的血糖会迅速升高，这很好——大约持续二十分钟。然后血糖会骤降，血糖骤降的时候，你就会感到筋疲力尽，这时，你会感到头脑昏沉。

When that happens, you sit at your desk and you struggle to think. Your child experiences that crash sitting at school, and she isn’t able to listen to the teacher. This is where ‘you have very, very low energy, and you constantly feel like you need a pick-me-up … That is the blood sugar crashing.’ When this happens, you and your kid want more sugary-carby treats in order to get another short burst of focus. ‘If every mealtime you’re consuming those cheap, shitty carbohydrates, then you’re going to be going on that rollercoaster over and over again.’ He added that if you’re consuming those kinds of foods with caffeine, the effect on blood sugar is exaggerated even further: ‘If you had a croissant on its own, your blood sugar would obviously spike, but if you had it with a coffee, it would spike even higher, and you would get a much more aggressive crash.’ These spikes and crashes take place throughout the day, leaving us so depleted that we can’t focus well for long stretches. He said that all this – shifting metaphor slightly – is ‘like putting rocket fuel into a Mini. It would just burn out and bust very quickly – because it can’t handle that. But put in the petrol it’s designed to take, and it’ll go along nicely.’

当这种情况发生时，你坐在书桌前，却难以集中注意力。你的孩子在学校也会经历这种崩溃，无法专心听老师讲课。这时你会感到“非常非常疲惫，总觉得需要提神……这就是血糖骤降”。这时，你和你的孩子会想要更多含糖碳水化合物的零食，以便再次短暂地集中注意力。“如果每餐都吃这些廉价劣质的碳水化合物，那么你就会一遍又一遍地经历这种血糖过山车般的波动。”他还补充说，如果同时摄入咖啡因，对血糖的影响会更加显著：“如果你单独吃一个羊角面包，血糖肯定会飙升，但如果再配上一杯咖啡，血糖会飙升得更高，而且会经历更剧烈的骤降。”这种血糖的飙升和骤降会在一天中反复发生，让我们精疲力竭，无法长时间集中注意力。他说，这一切——稍微换个比喻——“就像往迷你车里加火箭燃料。它会很快烧毁，因为它承受不了。但如果加它设计使用的汽油，它就能顺利行驶。”

There is such a strong scientific consensus that our current diets cause these energy crashes that the British National Health Service’s carefully fact-checked official website warns about it. So, Dale said, if we want to improve our kids’ focus and attention, our first step should be to ‘stop feeding them fucking Coke for breakfast and a bowl of sugar and milk. Try giving them proper food first.’ If we do, he said we’ll see rapid results, because ‘the developing brain is so responsive to change’. (He later explained that, at the moment, parents have to fight against an army of advertisers trying to get their kids to eat badly, and a food-supply system that is designed to hack our weaknesses – I’ll come to that soon.)

科学界对此已达成高度共识，认为我们目前的饮食习惯会导致能量骤降，以至于英国国家医疗服务体系（NHS）经过严格事实核查的官方网站都对此发出警告。因此，戴尔说，如果我们想提高孩子的专注力，第一步应该是“别再给他们早餐吃可乐和一碗糖加牛奶了。先试试给他们吃正餐。” 他说，如果我们这样做，就会看到立竿见影的效果，因为“发育中的大脑对变化非常敏感”。（他后来解释说，目前，家长们不得不与铺天盖地的广告商作斗争，这些广告商试图诱导孩子们吃不健康的食物，还要对抗一个旨在利用我们弱点的食品供应系统——我稍后会谈到这一点。）

The second way in which our diets affect our focus is that most of us now eat in a way that deprives us of the nutrients we need for our brains to develop and function fully. For almost all of our history, human beings ate, roughly, like my grandparents – they consumed fresh food that they knew the origin of. As the great food writer Michael Pollan, who’s a big influence on Dale, has explained, in the two generations between them and me, food went through a profound degeneration. In the mid-twentieth century there was a rapid move from fresh food towards pre-cooked, processed food that was sold in supermarkets and created in order to be reheated. This food had to be prepared for sale in a completely different way. It was pumped full of stabilisers and preservatives to make sure it didn’t go off as it sat on supermarket shelves, and this industrial process has, it turns out, stripped food of a lot of its nutritional value.

饮食影响我们注意力的第二个方面是，我们现在大多数人的饮食方式剥夺了大脑发育和正常运作所需的营养。在人类历史的大部分时间里，人们的饮食方式大致与我的祖父母辈相似——他们食用来源可靠的新鲜食物。正如对戴尔影响颇深的著名美食作家迈克尔·波伦所解释的那样，在我祖父母辈和我之间两代人的生活中，食物经历了深刻的退化。20世纪中期，人们迅速从食用新鲜食物转向食用超市里出售的预制加工食品，这些食品的设计初衷就是为了方便加热食用。这类食品的加工方式与新鲜食物截然不同。为了确保食品在超市货架上不会变质，它们被添加了大量的稳定剂和防腐剂。事实证明，这种工业化生产过程剥夺了食物的大量营养价值。

Then, as we became more accustomed to food that was radically different to what had gone before, the food industry began to find more and more sophisticated ways to directly target our primitive pleasure centres. They pumped our foods full of sugars in quantities that never occur in nature, and trans fats, and various unprecedented new inventions. In the US and Britain, most of what we eat now falls into the category of ‘ultra-processed food’ – which is, as Michael Pollan has pointed out, so removed from anything in nature that it’s very hard to figure out what the original ingredients even were.

随着我们逐渐习惯了与以往截然不同的食物，食品工业开始寻找越来越巧妙的方法来直接触动我们原始的快感中枢。他们往食物里添加了大量自然界根本不存在的糖分、反式脂肪以及各种前所未有的新成分。在美国和英国，我们现在吃的大部分食物都属于“超加工食品”的范畴——正如迈克尔·波伦所指出的，这类食品与自然界的任何成分都相去甚远，以至于我们很难弄清楚它们最初的成分是什么。

There’s some uncertainty about precisely how this has affected our focus, but we have some pretty strong clues. Since the 1970s there have been several scientific studies designed to figure out what happens to your attention when you change your diet. To give one example, in 2009 a team of Dutch scientists took a group of twenty-seven children who had been identified as having trouble focusing, and they split them into two groups. Fifteen of them were assigned to an ‘eliminationist’ diet, which meant they couldn’t consume the junk most of us eat every day – preservatives, additives, synthetic dyes – and so instead they had to eat the kind of food my grandparents would have recognised. The other twelve carried on eating the usual Western diet. The team then monitored them for several weeks to see what happened. It turned out that more than 70 percent of the kids who cut out the preservatives and dyes improved their ability to pay attention, and the average improvement was a remarkable 50 percent.

虽然目前尚不确定这种改变究竟如何影响我们的注意力，但我们掌握了一些相当有力的线索。自20世纪70年代以来，已有数项科学研究旨在探究改变饮食习惯对注意力的影响。举例来说，2009年，一个荷兰科学家团队招募了27名被诊断为注意力不集中的儿童，并将他们分成两组。其中15名儿童被安排进行“排除法”饮食，这意味着他们不能食用我们大多数人每天摄入的垃圾食品——防腐剂、添加剂、合成色素——而是必须食用我祖父母辈熟悉的那种食物。另外12名儿童则继续食用典型的西式饮食。研究团队随后对他们进行了数周的观察，以了解他们的注意力变化。结果发现，超过70%的戒除防腐剂和色素的儿童注意力有所提高，平均提高幅度高达50%。

But this was a small study – so the same team decided to follow up. This time, they took a hundred children, and they did the experiment again, following kids over five weeks. Once again, it turned out that most of the kids who stuck to the eliminationist diet saw a big improvement in their attention and focus, and more than half got dramatically better.

但这项研究规模较小，因此同一研究团队决定进行后续研究。这一次，他们招募了100名儿童，再次进行了实验，并跟踪观察了孩子们五周的情况。结果再次表明，大多数坚持排除饮食法的儿童在注意力和专注力方面都有了显著改善，超过一半的儿童的改善尤为显著。

The scientists doing these studies have mostly been investigating the notion that these kids can’t focus because they are allergic to something in our everyday diets. That’s possible. But their experiments seem to me more likely to fit with this wider way of thinking that I was learning about: that when you consume the kind of foods we evolved to eat, your brain will function better. In New York, I went for breakfast with Dr Drew Ramsay, who’s one of the pioneers of ‘ nutritional psychiatry’ – a new field that is teasing out the connection between the way we eat and our psychological challenges. He said if anyone doubts these insights, he would ask them where ‘they think attention comes from … The brain gets built from foods. So there’s that very fundamental connection.’ Your brain, he told me, can only grow and thrive if it gets a broad range of key nutrients. To give one well-studied example, if you eat a diet that’s deprived of omega-3s – which are largely found in fish – your brain will suffer. And it’s not good enough to replace these foods with supplements – your body absorbs nutrients much more effectively from real food than from capsules.

进行这些研究的科学家们主要调查的是，这些孩子无法集中注意力是否是因为他们对我们日常饮食中的某些食物过敏。这并非不可能。但我觉得他们的实验更符合我正在了解的一种更广泛的思维方式：当我们食用我们进化过程中适应的食物时，我们的大脑功能会更好。在纽约，我和德鲁·拉姆齐博士共进早餐，他是“营养精神病学”的先驱之一——这是一个新兴领域，旨在揭示我们的饮食方式与心理问题之间的联系。他说，如果有人质疑这些见解，他会问他们“他们认为注意力从何而来……大脑是由食物构建的。所以这其中存在着非常根本的联系。”他告诉我，只有摄入各种关键营养素，大脑才能生长发育。举一个经过充分研究的例子，如果你的饮食缺乏omega-3脂肪酸（主要存在于鱼类中），你的大脑就会受到影响。仅仅用补充剂代替这些食物是不够的——你的身体从真正的食物中吸收营养比从胶囊中吸收要有效得多。

The third reason is different. Our current diets aren’t just lacking in what we need – they also actively contain chemicals that seem to act on our brains almost like drugs. For example, in 2007 a group of scientists in Southampton in Britain got 297 normal kids, who were either three-year-olds or aged between eight and nine, and they split them into two groups. One group was given a drink containing common food additives that appear regularly in our diets, and the other group was given a drink that didn’t contain them. They were then monitored to see how they behaved. The kids who drank the food dyes were significantly more likely to become hyperactive. The evidence for this was strong and decisive enough that in the aftermath of this discovery, many European countries banned these dyes – but the US regulators refused to, and they are still being consumed every day in some of the country’s most popular cereals and snacks. I wondered if this could help to explain some of the gap in ADHD rates between Europe and the US.

第三个原因有所不同。我们目前的饮食不仅缺乏必需营养，而且还含有一些化学物质，这些物质似乎会像毒品一样作用于我们的大脑。例如，2007年，英国南安普顿的一组科学家招募了297名正常的儿童，年龄在三岁或八九岁之间，并将他们分成两组。一组喝了一种含有常见食品添加剂的饮料，这些添加剂经常出现在我们的日常饮食中；另一组则喝了一种不含这些添加剂的饮料。之后，研究人员观察了孩子们的行为。结果发现，喝了含有食用色素饮料的孩子更容易出现多动症症状。这一发现的证据非常充分且确凿，以至于在这一发现之后，许多欧洲国家禁止使用这些色素——但美国监管机构却拒绝这样做，这些色素至今仍然存在于美国一些最受欢迎的谷物和零食中。我不禁思考，这是否能解释欧洲和美国多动症发病率差异的部分原因。

Dale told me that if you want to understand what’s really going on here, you should look out across the world at the places where people are physically and mentally fitter than us, with lower levels of diagnosed ADHD and dementia. If you do that, he said, at first it’ll seem puzzling, because the diets they eat are actually very different – some of them are heavy on fish, some have very little fish; some have a lot of plants, some don’t have many plants; some have lots of carbohydrates and some have none at all. If you’re looking for a magic ingredient, you won’t find it. But ‘there’s one thing that unifies every single one of them. They’re all leaving out the crap that’s making us sick in the first place. They’re all leaving out the refined carbohydrates, the processed food, the junk oils. They’re all building their foundations on whole foods … That’s the key. That’s the magic bullet – just go back to whole foods. Foods as they were originally intended.’ He quoted Michael Pollan, who says we should eat only food that our grandparents would have recognised as food, and we should shop primarily around the outer edges of the supermarket – the fruit and veg at the front, and the meat and fish at the back. The stuff in the middle, he warned, isn’t really food at all.

戴尔告诉我，如果你想了解这里到底发生了什么，你应该放眼世界，看看那些人们身心比我们更健康、多动症和痴呆症诊断率更低的地方。他说，如果你这么做，一开始你会觉得很困惑，因为他们的饮食习惯截然不同——有些人吃很多鱼，有些人吃得很少；有些人吃很多植物，有些人吃得很少；有些人摄入大量碳水化合物，有些人则完全不吃。如果你想寻找某种神奇的秘诀，你肯定找不到。但是，“有一点是他们共同的。他们都摒弃了那些让我们生病的垃圾食品。他们都摒弃了精制碳水化合物、加工食品和劣质油脂。他们都以天然食物为基础……这就是关键。这就是灵丹妙药——回归天然食物。” “食物就应该是它们原本的样子。”他引用了迈克尔·波伦的话，波伦认为我们应该只吃祖父母辈会认可的食物，而且购物时应该主要在超市的外围区域——前面是水果蔬菜，后面是肉类和鱼类。他警告说，中间那些东西根本算不上真正的食物。

Yet instead of promoting healthy food to children, we often push the worst food on them. In Boston another nutritional psychiatrist, Dr Umadevi Naidoo, told me that a few years before, the funding for school lunches in the US had been cut, and ‘the food companies moved in and provided vending machines’. Now, ‘the obvious connection is that if they’re getting candy bars and cookies, which were processed’, there will ‘definitely’ be a link to the rise in attention problems in children. These reasons – and many more – are why Professor Joel Nigg, the ADHD expert I interviewed in Portland, has written: ‘A sea change is under way … If you think your child’s ADHD may have something to do with food, science now agrees with you.’

然而，我们非但没有向孩子们推广健康食品，反而常常强迫他们吃最不健康的食物。在波士顿，另一位营养精神科医生乌玛德维·奈杜博士告诉我，几年前，美国削减了学校午餐的经费，“食品公司趁机涌入，提供了自动售货机”。如今，“显而易见的联系是，如果孩子们吃的是加工过的糖果和饼干”，那么这“肯定”与儿童注意力问题的增加有关。正是基于这些原因——以及其他诸多原因——我在波特兰采访的注意力缺陷多动症专家乔尔·尼格教授写道：“一场巨变正在发生……如果你认为孩子的注意力缺陷多动症可能与食物有关，那么科学现在也认同你的观点。”

I liked all the people I was meeting – but part of me felt really uncomfortable as I had these conversations. So many of my emotions are tied up with the foods that they were explaining to me are focus-killers. I was raised to find comfort in unhealthy food. I pine for it when I feel down. As I reflected on how this diet might be affecting me, I started to think again about my time in Provincetown. There are no fast-food chains there – no McDonald’s! No KFC! Not even Burger King! There’s only a single pizza place, Spiritus Pizza. So for three months, I ate almost nothing but healthy, fresh food – which is two months and thirty days longer than at any other point in my life, other than those long Swiss summers. I wondered if that, too, had played a role in why I focused so easily and so well there.

我喜欢遇到的所有人——但在这些对话中，我内心深处却感到很不自在。我的很多情绪都与他们所说的那些会让我注意力涣散的食物息息相关。我从小就被教育要从不健康的食物中寻求慰藉。心情低落的时候，我就会特别想吃。当我反思这种饮食方式可能会对我产生什么影响时，我又想起了我在普罗温斯敦的那段日子。那里没有快餐连锁店——没有麦当劳！没有肯德基！甚至连汉堡王都没有！只有一家披萨店，Spiritus Pizza。所以，整整三个月，我几乎只吃健康新鲜的食物——这比我人生中除了漫长的瑞士夏季之外的任何其他时期都要长两个月零三十天。我不禁想，这是否也是我在那里能够如此轻松、如此高效地集中注意力的原因之一。

As I investigated all this, I kept thinking about the last time I ever saw my Swiss grandmother. She was in her mid-eighties, and we walked up her mountain together, with her walking faster than me. She led me into her huge garden, and she tended to it – ripping out weeds, observing the progress of her carrots and leeks – while her chickens scratched freely all around us. Then, with brisk hand movements, she picked out the food we were going to eat together that night, and I watched her cook it. To her, this was as natural as breathing. To me, I realise now, it should have been a revelation.

在调查这一切的过程中，我不断想起最后一次见到瑞士祖母的情景。她当时八十多岁，我们一起爬上她家所在的山，她走得比我快。她领我走进她那巨大的花园，开始照料起来——拔除杂草，观察胡萝卜和韭菜的生长——而她的鸡群则在我们周围自由自在地刨土。然后，她动作利落地挑选出我们当晚要一起吃的食材，我看着她烹饪。对她来说，这就像呼吸一样自然。而现在我意识到，对我而言，这本该是一次全新的体验。

Yet I can imagine presenting this evidence to people in a way that reeks of cruel optimism. You can picture Instagram influencers taking these points and posting: Look! Just change what you eat and your focus will return! I did it! Now you can too! But the truth is that this is – like so much of what I was learning about for this book – primarily a structural problem. Nobody I know has a mountain and a farm like my grandparents did – they have to get their food at supermarkets. Those supermarkets are full of cheap processed food which is promoted to us from the moment we are born by enormous advertising budgets. If we are going to overcome this problem, there is some role for each of us making individual changes, but there’s a bigger need to deal with the larger forces behind it. Today, just like – as Tristan had taught me – every time you try to put down your phone there’s a thousand engineers behind the screen trying to get you to pick it up again, every time you try to give up processed food, there’s a team of expert marketers trying to get you to crack and come back to it. From long before you were even consciously aware of it, they have been working at getting you to associate positive feelings with unhealthy food. They programmed me perfectly to feed their profit margins rather than my brain health, and I’m not alone. That machinery needs to be turned off, so it can’t distort the tastes and steal the focus of another generation.

然而，我可以想象，如果有人用一种近乎残酷的乐观主义来向人们展示这些证据，会是什么样子。你可以想象那些Instagram网红会抓住这些要点，然后发帖说：看！只要改变饮食习惯，你的注意力就会重新集中起来！我做到了！你也一样可以！但事实是，这——就像我在这本书里学到的很多东西一样——本质上是一个结构性问题。我认识的人里，没有人像我的祖父母那样拥有一座山和一个农场——他们只能去超市买食物。而这些超市里充斥着廉价的加工食品，从我们出生起，就被巨额广告预算不断地推销。如果我们想要解决这个问题，每个人都需要做出一些改变，但更重要的是要解决其背后更大的问题。就像特里斯坦教我的那样，今天，每当你试图放下手机，屏幕背后就有成千上万的工程师想方设法让你重新拿起它；每当你试图戒掉加工食品，就有一群营销专家想方设法让你屈服，重新回到加工食品的怀抱。早在你意识到之前，他们就一直在努力让你把积极的情绪与不健康的食物联系起来。他们完美地操控了我，让我为了利润而非我的大脑健康而改变饮食习惯，而且我并非孤例。这种操控机制必须被关闭，否则它将继续扭曲下一代的口味，转移他们的注意力。

The next cause of our attention crisis is, out of all the factors I have written about in this book, potentially the biggest. We all know that being exposed to pollution and to industrial chemicals – in the air, or on the products we buy – is bad for us. If you’d asked me when I started researching this book, I could have explained to you, in pretty basic terms, that air pollution causes asthma and other breathing problems, for example. But I was startled to learn that there is growing evidence suggesting that this pollution is seriously damaging our ability to focus.

导致我们注意力危机的下一个原因，或许是本书中我所探讨的所有因素中最主要的。我们都知道，接触污染和工业化学物质——无论是空气中的还是我们购买的产品中的——都对我们有害。如果在我刚开始研究这本书的时候你问我，我可以用非常浅显易懂的方式解释，比如空气污染会导致哮喘和其他呼吸系统疾病。但令我震惊的是，越来越多的证据表明，这种污染正在严重损害我们的注意力。

To understand this, I read widely about the science surrounding this question, and I interviewed scientists who have been at the cutting edge of discovering these effects. Professor Barbara Demeneix – a prestigious scientist in France who has won several major awards, including the Légion d’honneur, the country’s highest civilian prize – explained to me: ‘At every stage of your life, different forms of pollution will affect your attention span,’ and she has concluded this is a factor in why ‘we’ve got neurodevelopmental disease increasing exponentially … [including] ADHD across the board.’ She said that we are now surrounded by so many pollutants that ‘there is no way we can have a normal brain today’.

为了理解这一点，我广泛阅读了与此问题相关的科学文献，并采访了多位在发现这些影响方面处于前沿的科学家。芭芭拉·德梅内克斯教授是一位在法国享有盛誉的科学家，曾荣获包括法国最高平民荣誉——荣誉军团勋章在内的多项重要奖项。她向我解释说：“在你人生的每个阶段，不同形式的污染都会影响你的注意力。”她认为，这正是“神经发育疾病呈指数级增长……（包括）注意力缺陷多动障碍（ADHD）”的原因之一。她指出，我们现在被如此多的污染物包围，“以至于我们今天根本无法拥有正常的大脑”。

The form of pollution we, as ordinary citizens, know most about is in the air all around us, so I interviewed Barbara Maher, who is a professor of environmental science at the University of Lancaster in England, and has been carrying out potentially game-changing research on how it is affecting our brains. She explained to me that if you live in a major city today, every day you are breathing in a chemical soup – a mixture of many different contaminants, including those spewed from car engines. Your brain did not evolve to absorb these chemicals, like iron, through the respiratory system, and it doesn’t know how to handle them. So just by living in a polluted city, she said, you are experiencing a ‘repeated chronic insult to your brain’, and it will react by becoming inflamed. I asked her: what happens if that goes on for months and years? She said it ‘is going to lead to damage to the nerve cells, to the neurons. Depending on the dose [i.e. how bad the pollution is], depending on your genetic susceptibility, eventually, over time, your brain cells will be damaged.’

作为普通公民，我们最熟悉的污染形式莫过于空气污染。为此，我采访了英国兰卡斯特大学环境科学教授芭芭拉·马赫，她一直在进行一项可能具有颠覆性意义的研究，探讨空气污染如何影响我们的大脑。她向我解释说，如果你现在生活在大城市里，你每天都在呼吸着一种化学混合物——其中包含多种不同的污染物，包括汽车引擎排放的废气。你的大脑并没有进化到能够通过呼吸系统吸收这些化学物质（例如铁），它也不知道如何处理它们。因此，她说，仅仅生活在一个污染严重的城市，你的大脑就会遭受“反复的慢性损伤”，而大脑会通过炎症来做出反应。我问她：如果这种情况持续数月甚至数年会怎样？她说，这“会导致神经细胞和神经元受损。具体损伤程度取决于剂量（即……）。污染程度有多严重，最终，根据你的遗传易感性，你的脑细胞会随着时间的推移而受损。

She has found that the worse the pollution, the worse the damage to your brain. After soaking up this damage for years, you are more likely to develop one of the worst forms of brain degeneration, dementia. In Canada, a study found that people who live within fifty metres of a major road were 15 percent more likely to develop dementia than people who didn’t. But I asked Barbara: What does that inflammation do to your mental functioning earlier in life? ‘It’s probable that if there’s a chronic impact, that can cause aggression, loss of control, attention deficit.’

她发现污染越严重，对大脑的损害就越大。长期遭受这种损害后，更容易患上最严重的脑退化症之一——痴呆症。加拿大的一项研究发现，居住在主干道五十米范围内的人患痴呆症的几率比居住在其他地方的人高出15%。但我问芭芭拉：这种炎症会对年轻时的认知功能造成什么影响？“如果长期受到污染的影响，可能会导致攻击性、失控和注意力缺陷。”

The evidence is especially worrying when it comes to children’s brains, which are still developing, she said. ‘We’ve now seen evidence for the onset of these degenerative diseases in really, really young children in highly polluted environments. That’s your next generation … My colleague in Mexico [has] been doing MRI scans, and they can already see shrinking volumes of brain tissue in badly affected young people.’ The more polluted an area is, the worse the harm – to the point where some have ‘lesions. You can actually see plaques and tangles [in the brain, as in dementia patients], even in very young cases.’ A scientist in Barcelona, Professor Jordi Sunyer, tested school children’s ability to pay attention across the city – and found that the worse the pollution, the worse the kids performed.

她说，尤其令人担忧的是儿童大脑的状况，因为儿童的大脑仍在发育。“我们现在已经发现，在污染严重的地区，一些非常年幼的儿童也出现了这些退行性疾病。他们是我们的下一代……我在墨西哥的同事一直在进行核磁共振扫描，他们已经可以看到受影响严重的年轻人的脑组织体积正在萎缩。”污染越严重，危害就越大——甚至有些人的大脑会出现“病变”。“你甚至可以看到斑块和缠结（就像痴呆症患者一样），即使是非常年幼的儿童也会出现这种情况。”巴塞罗那的科学家乔迪·苏尼尔教授测试了全市学龄儿童的注意力能力，发现污染越严重，孩子们的表现就越差。

This seemed really daunting. It told me there’s a focus-killer literally all around us, and I felt overwhelmed. How can we fight it? I began to get some clues once I had learned some history. I started by looking at the effect of one specific pollutant on our attention: lead. As far back as ancient Rome, it was known that lead was poisonous to human beings. The architect Vitruvius, for example, begged the Roman authorities to not use it to build the city’s pipes. Yet for centuries lead was used to paint homes and in water pipes, and then in the early twentieth century it was added to petrol, which meant it was pumped into the air of every city in the world and breathed in by its inhabitants. Scientists warned almost at once that leaded gasoline was likely to produce disaster. When in 1925 General Motors announced that putting lead in gasoline was a ‘gift of God’, its CEO was warned by Dr Alice Hamilton, the leading expert on lead in the US, that he was playing with fire. ‘Where there is lead,’ she said, ‘some case of lead poisoning sooner or later develops.’ It was clear this could have a terrible effect on people’s brains: in high doses, lead poisoning makes people hallucinate, lose their minds or die. The factories where leaded petrol was developed had outbreaks of staff members going violently insane and dying because of their exposure to it.

这看起来确实令人望而生畏。它告诉我，我们身边到处都存在着一种注意力杀手，我感到不知所措。我们该如何对抗它呢？了解了一些历史之后，我开始找到一些线索。我首先研究了一种特定污染物对我们注意力的影响：铅。早在古罗马时期，人们就知道铅对人体有毒。例如，建筑师维特鲁威就曾恳求罗马当局不要用铅来建造城市管道。然而，几个世纪以来，铅一直被用于粉刷房屋和制造水管，到了20世纪初，它又被添加到汽油中，这意味着它被泵入世界各地城市的空气中，被居民吸入。科学家们几乎立刻就警告说，含铅汽油可能会造成灾难。1925年，通用汽车公司宣称在汽油中添加铅是“上帝的恩赐”，但其首席执行官却受到了美国铅污染问题权威专家爱丽丝·汉密尔顿博士的警告，称他是在玩火。 “凡是有铅的地方，”她说，“迟早都会出现铅中毒病例。” 显然，这会对人的大脑造成可怕的影响：高剂量的铅中毒会导致人出现幻觉、精神错乱甚至死亡。生产含铅汽油的工厂就曾爆发过员工因长期接触铅而精神失常甚至死亡的事件。

There was always a non-leaded form of gasoline available that didn’t carry these risks, but the big corporations resisted it fiercely, seemingly for a commercial reason: they could patent the leaded version, and so make more money from it. For forty years, the lead industry funded all the scientific research into whether it was safe – and assured the world that their scientists had discovered it was.

一直以来都有不含铅的汽油，不存在这些风险，但大型企业却极力抵制，表面上是出于商业目的：他们可以为含铅汽油申请专利，从而赚取更多利润。四十年来，铅业资助了所有关于无铅汽油安全性的科学研究，并向世人保证，他们的科学家已经证明无铅汽油是安全的。

It turns out this decision to allow leaded petrol to dominate the market stole a large amount of focus from people all over the world. I went to interview Bruce Lanphear, who is professor of health sciences at Simon Fraser University in Canada. He explained that as a young academic in the 1980s, he was offered a position in Rochester in upstate New York to study the effects of lead on children’s cognitive abilities. He knew that kids were still being exposed to a lot of lead, even though leaded paint had been banned in 1978, because millions of people still lived in homes full of it, and leaded petrol continued to be used everywhere. He wanted to know what this was doing to them.

事实证明，允许含铅汽油主导市场的决定分散了全世界人们的大量注意力。我采访了加拿大西蒙弗雷泽大学的健康科学教授布鲁斯·兰菲尔。他解释说，上世纪80年代，作为一名年轻的学者，他受邀前往纽约州北部的罗切斯特市，研究铅对儿童认知能力的影响。他知道，尽管含铅涂料早在1978年就被禁用，但孩子们仍然大量接触铅，因为数百万人仍然居住在充满含铅涂料的房屋中，而且含铅汽油仍然随处可见。他想知道这会对孩子们造成什么影响。

As part of the project he worked with, all the kids in Rochester were given blood tests to see just how much lead they were carrying in their bodies. When Bruce saw the results, he was taken aback. One in three of the children in the town had lead poisoning. For Black children, it was one in two. Rochester wasn’t unusual – separate research a few years before found that modern Americans by the 1970s were carrying more than 600 times more lead in their bodies than pre-industrial humans, and the Environmental Protection Agency estimates that 68 million children were exposed to toxic levels of lead in the US from leaded petrol alone between 1927 and 1987.

作为他参与的项目的一部分，罗切斯特的所有孩子都接受了血液检测，以确定他们体内的铅含量。当布鲁斯看到结果时，他震惊了。镇上三分之一的孩子铅中毒。黑人儿童的铅中毒率更是高达二分之一。罗切斯特的情况并非个例——几年前的另一项研究发现，到20世纪70年代，现代美国人体内的铅含量是工业化前人类的600多倍。美国环境保护署估计，仅在1927年至1987年间，美国就有6800万儿童因含铅汽油而接触到有毒浓度的铅。

Bruce and other scientists showed that lead severely stunts your ability to focus and pay attention. If you are exposed to lead as a child, he explained to me, you are ‘two and a half times more likely to meet criteria for ADHD.’ The effect becomes even bigger if it is combined with other forms of pollution. For example, if your mother was exposed to lead during pregnancy and she smoked cigarettes, you are eight times more likely to be diagnosed with ADHD.

布鲁斯和其他科学家发现，铅会严重损害人的注意力和专注力。他向我解释说，如果儿童时期接触过铅，患多动症的几率会“增加2.5倍”。如果铅与其他污染形式同时存在，影响会更大。例如，如果母亲在怀孕期间接触过铅并且吸烟，那么你患多动症的几率会增加8倍。

Before Bruce arrived, the mothers of Rochester – like mothers across the United States — had been warned about the dangers of lead poisoning, and then told that it was their fault. The authorities said to them – your kids are being exposed in this way because, as mothers, you have failed to dust your homes enough. Do more housework and get your kids to wash their hands more. This was part of a wider push: the lead industry itself claimed the problem lay mainly with ‘uneducable Negro and Puerto Rican’ parents who ‘failed’ to protect their kids from the lead in their homes.

在布鲁斯到来之前，罗切斯特的母亲们——就像全美各地的母亲们一样——都曾被警告过铅中毒的危害，但随后却被告知这是她们的错。当局对她们说：“你们的孩子之所以会接触到铅，是因为作为母亲的你们没有充分清洁房屋。多做家务，让孩子们多洗手。” 这只是更广泛宣传的一部分：铅业公司声称，问题主要出在“未受过教育的黑人和波多黎各裔”父母身上，他们“未能”保护孩子免受家中铅的侵害。

But when Bruce studied it, he found that all this dusting and handwashing made no difference at all. He could see that a whole town, and a whole generation of children, had been poisoned, and the families had been told it was down to them because they weren’t clean enough. Some scientists had gone even further in blaming the victims. They said the problem wasn’t that the families were living with high levels of a brain-damaging metal, but that the children had a mental illness. They said the kids had a psychological disorder named ‘pica’, which was making toddlers irrationally stick chunks of lead paint in their mouths. These children were labelled as having a ‘perverted appetite’, and it was (again) claimed that this problem seemed to be suffered mainly by Black and Brown children.

但布鲁斯研究后发现，所有这些除尘和洗手根本无济于事。他看到整个城镇，整整一代儿童都受到了毒害，而这些家庭却被告知这是他们自己的错，因为他们不够干净。一些科学家甚至更进一步，指责受害者。他们说问题不在于这些家庭生活在高浓度的致脑金属环境中，而在于孩子们患有精神疾病。他们说孩子们患有一种名为“异食癖”的心理疾病，这种疾病会导致幼儿非理性地将铅漆块塞进嘴里。这些孩子被贴上了“食欲异常”的标签，而且（再次）有人声称，这个问题似乎主要发生在黑人和棕色人种的孩子身上。

At every stage, right from the 1920s onwards, the lead industry created and encouraged these diversionary tactics. They also bought the loyalty of some scientists, who systematically cast doubt on the evidence that lead harmed people’s brains. Right at the start, in the 1920s, one scientist, named Thomas Midgley, announced at a press conference that it was perfectly safe to use leaded products. He didn’t tell the gathered journalists he had just recovered from a terrible dose of lead poisoning himself, caused by the very products he was now promoting. At every stage, the lead industry insisted, in effect – if there is any doubt about the danger, we should be allowed to carry on pumping lead into people’s bodies.

从20世纪20年代开始，铅业在每个阶段都制造并鼓励这些转移视线的伎俩。他们还收买了一些科学家，这些科学家系统性地质疑铅会损害大脑的证据。早在20世纪20年代初期，一位名叫托马斯·米奇利的科学家就在一次新闻发布会上宣布，使用含铅产品完全安全。他没有告诉在场的记者，他自己刚刚从一次严重的铅中毒中康复，而罪魁祸首正是他现在正在推广的这些产品。事实上，铅业在每个阶段都坚持——如果对铅的危害有任何疑问，我们就应该被允许继续往人们体内注入铅。

All through the research for this book, I had an ongoing struggle to hold clearly in my mind the structural nature of our attention crisis. We live in an extremely individualistic culture, where we are constantly pushed to see our problems as individual failings, and to seek out individual solutions. You’re unable to focus? Overweight? Poor? Depressed? We are taught in this culture to think: That’s my fault. I should have found a personal way to lift myself up and out of these environmental problems. Now, whenever I feel that way, I think about the mothers in Rochester whose kids were being poisoned by lead, and they were simply told they should dust their homes more, or that their kids had a ‘perverted’ desire to suck on chunks of lead paint. We can see clearly now there was a huge problem with a deep cause in the environment – and yet the primary response was to tell people to throw all their energy into a frantic individual displacement activity that made no difference at all, or (even worse) to blame their own poisoned children.

在本书的研究过程中，我一直努力厘清我们注意力危机的结构性本质。我们生活在一个极端个人主义的文化中，不断被灌输要将问题视为个人失败，并寻求个人解决方案。你无法集中注意力？超重？贫穷？抑郁？在这种文化中，我们被教导要这样想：这是我的错。我应该找到个人方法让自己摆脱这些环境问题。现在，每当我有这种感觉时，我就会想起罗切斯特那些孩子铅中毒的母亲们，她们却被告知应该多打扫房屋，或者她们的孩子有“变态”的欲望去吮吸含铅油漆块。我们现在清楚地看到，环境问题根源深远，而主要的应对措施却是让人们把所有精力投入到一种毫无作用的疯狂的个人转移活动中，或者（更糟糕的是）责怪自己中毒的孩子。

When the problem was blamed on isolated individuals, and they were told to solve it by simply tweaking their own behaviour, the problem only got worse. So I investigated – what did end it? I learned it was one thing, and one thing only. It stopped when ordinary citizens learned the scientific evidence and banded together to demand their governments change the law to stop these companies from poisoning them. In Britain, for example, the campaign against leaded petrol was led by a housewife named Jill Runnette, who succeeded in getting the government to cut the amount of lead in petrol by two-thirds in 1981. (It was later banned altogether.) She did it to protect herself and the children of her society.

当问题被归咎于个别个人，并被告知只需改变自身行为就能解决时，问题反而愈演愈烈。于是我展开调查——究竟是什么终结了这一切？我发现答案只有一个，也只有这一个。当普通民众了解了科学证据，并团结起来要求政府修改法律，阻止这些公司毒害他们时，这一切才得以停止。例如，在英国，反对含铅汽油的运动是由一位名叫吉尔·鲁内特的家庭主妇领导的。她成功地促使政府在1981年将汽油中的铅含量减少了三分之二（后来汽油被彻底禁用）。她这样做是为了保护自己和她所在社会的孩子们。

In a way, this felt to me like a metaphor for our whole attention crisis. Our attention and focus has been raided, pillaged and poisoned by huge external forces – and we have been told to do the equivalent of dusting our homes and washing our hands more, when we should have been doing the equivalent of banning lead paint and petrol all along. In many ways, the story of resistance to lead poisoning is a model for us to follow now. The dangers were clear for decades – Dr Alice Hamilton accurately documented them in the mid-1920s – but things only changed when there was a dedicated democratic movement of ordinary citizens taking on the forces that stole their focus. In 1975 the average Americans had a blood lead level of 15 micrograms per decilitre. Today it’s 0.85 micrograms per decilitre. The IQ of the average pre-schooler is estimated by scientists at the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention to have risen by five points as a result of the ban. It’s proof that it’s possible to make dramatic progress on fighting an attention-killer.

在某种程度上，这感觉就像是我们整个注意力危机的隐喻。我们的注意力和专注力被巨大的外部力量掠夺、掠夺和毒害——而我们却被告知要做一些类似于打扫房屋和勤洗手的事情，而我们真正应该做的，却是像禁止使用含铅油漆和汽油那样的事情。在很多方面，抵制铅中毒的故事可以作为我们如今效仿的榜样。几十年来，铅的危害显而易见——爱丽丝·汉密尔顿博士在20世纪20年代中期就准确地记录了这些危害——但只有当普通公民发起一场致力于对抗那些窃取他们注意力的力量的民主运动时，情况才发生了改变。1975年，美国人的平均血铅水平为每分升15微克。如今，这一数字已降至每分升0.85微克。美国疾病控制与预防中心的科学家估计，由于这项禁令的实施，学龄前儿童的平均智商提高了5分。这证明，在对抗注意力杀手方面，我们有可能取得显著进展。

But Barbara Demeneix warned me that since then, ‘there are so many other [attention-damaging] chemicals that … are increasing on the market’ that she fears it is now dwarfing the benefit of ditching lead. So I asked her – what chemicals are we being exposed to today that have potential effects on attention? ‘Let’s start with the main culprits: pesticides. Plasticisers. Flame-retardants. Cosmetics.’ She said ‘of over two hundred pesticides on the market in Europe, about two-thirds affect either brain development or thyroid hormone signalling’. When monkeys are exposed to the same level of the common pollutant polychlorinated biphenyls ( PCBs) as humans currently are, they develop serious problems with their working memory and mental development. A team of scientists studied the amount of a pollutant named bisphenol A, or BPA – which is used to coat 80 percent of metal cans – that mothers are exposed to. They found that exposure to the chemical predicts which of them will have kids with behaviour problems.

但芭芭拉·德梅内克斯警告我说，自那以后，“市面上出现了太多其他[损害注意力的]化学物质……数量还在不断增加”，她担心这些化学物质的危害已经远远超过了弃用铅带来的益处。所以我问她——我们现在接触到的哪些化学物质可能会影响注意力？“让我们先从罪魁祸首说起：杀虫剂、增塑剂、阻燃剂、化妆品。”她说，“在欧洲市场上两百多种杀虫剂中，大约三分之二会影响大脑发育或甲状腺激素信号传导。”当猴子接触到与人类目前相同浓度的常见污染物多氯联苯（PCBs）时，它们的记忆力和认知发育会出现严重问题。一个科学家团队研究了母亲们接触到的一种名为双酚A（BPA）的污染物的含量——这种污染物被用于涂覆80%的金属罐。他们发现，接触这种化学物质可以预测哪些人的孩子会有行为问题。

Barbara has been engaged for nearly twenty years in developmental neurotoxicity testing – the science that figures out how the chemicals we are exposed to, both on the products that we buy and in the food that we eat, affect the development of foetuses and babies. She was commissioned by the European Parliament to do major research on this question, and she has co-ordinated many other research projects – and in the course of her research, there was one area in particular that worried her most. She explained to me that from the moment you are conceived, your development is shaped by hormones, which ‘regulate early development’. So she began to research whether these chemicals have any effect on these endocrine signals. What she discovered is that many of them create an effect that’s like ‘radio interference’, screwing with the system that guides how a human should develop, especially the brain, and making parts of it go astray. This affects attention, she explained, because this whole system guides how a person’s brain will develop. If your brain doesn’t develop normally, your attention can seriously suffer.

芭芭拉从事发育神经毒性测试近二十年——这门科学旨在探究我们接触到的化学物质（包括我们购买的产品和食用的食物中的化学物质）如何影响胎儿和婴儿的发育。她受欧洲议会委托，就此问题开展了一项重要的研究，并协调了许多其他研究项目。在她的研究过程中，有一个领域尤其令她担忧。她向我解释说，从受孕的那一刻起，你的发育就受到激素的影响，这些激素“调节早期发育”。因此，她开始研究这些化学物质是否会对这些内分泌信号产生任何影响。她的发现是，许多化学物质会产生类似“无线电干扰”的影响，扰乱指导人类发育（尤其是大脑发育）的系统，并导致部分功能紊乱。她解释说，这会影响注意力，因为整个系统指导着大脑的发育。如果大脑发育异常，注意力就会受到严重影响。

Between 2005 and 2012, she tested many common substances that are all around us – and the more substances her team tested, the more evidence she gathered that the endocrine system is being messed with by our current environment. She warns that all children today are being born ‘precontaminated’ by a ‘toxic cocktail’.

2005年至2012年间，她测试了许多我们周围常见的物质——她的团队测试的物质越多，她收集到的证据就越多，表明内分泌系统正受到我们当前环境的干扰。她警告说，如今所有的孩子出生时都已“预先受到”一种“有毒混合物”的污染。

This is disputed: some scientists believe that these dangers are being hugely overstated. For example, the American Council of Science and Health has ridiculed Barbara’s claims, arguing that you would have to be exposed to a massive dose of some of these chemicals for them to have the effects she describes. According to Mother Jones magazine, this group has allegedly been funded by chemical companies and large agricultural corporations with a vested interest in this debate (although the group denies these claims), which means we should handle their scepticism with some scepticism of our own – but it doesn’t necessarily mean they are wrong. There needs to be more funding to study these questions in detail.

这一点存在争议：一些科学家认为这些危险被大大夸大了。例如，美国科学与健康委员会就对芭芭拉的说法嗤之以鼻，认为只有接触到大量此类化学物质才会产生她所描述的影响。据《琼斯母亲》杂志报道，该组织据称接受了化学公司和大型农业企业的资助，而这些企业与这场辩论有着既得利益（尽管该组织否认了这些指控），这意味着我们应该对他们的质疑保持一定的怀疑态度——但这并不一定意味着他们错了。我们需要更多资金来深入研究这些问题。

It sometimes seems like the same story that played out with lead is now happening with other attention-damaging chemicals. The industries that profit from using them fund the vast majority of the research into them; they systematically promote doubt about the possible harms; and they argue that if there’s any doubt at all about the danger of their products, they should be allowed to carry on using them.

铅中毒事件的悲剧似乎正在其他损害注意力的化学物质身上重演。那些从中获利的行业资助了绝大部分相关研究；他们系统性地散布对这些物质潜在危害的怀疑；并且他们辩称，只要人们对其产品的危险性存在任何疑虑，就应该允许他们继续使用。

I felt tempted, when I heard all this, to keep asking the scientists I interviewed: Okay, what products contain these pollutants, and how do I cut them out of my life? You say BPA coats metal cans – should I avoid metal cans? But Barbara Demeneix told me that trying to personally avoid pollutants today, at an individual level, is largely a fool’s errand in a landscape so filled with them. ‘We can eat bio [i.e. organic]. We can air our homes as often as possible. [We can] live in the countryside.’ But when it comes to these endocrine disruptors, ‘there’s no escape. There’s no escape.’ Not at the level of the isolated individual.

听到这些，我真想继续追问那些受访的科学家们：到底哪些产品含有这些污染物？我该如何才能避免接触它们？你们说金属罐上涂有双酚A（BPA）——那我应该避免使用金属罐吗？但芭芭拉·德梅内克斯告诉我，在如今污染物如此泛滥的环境下，个人层面上试图完全避免接触污染物几乎是徒劳的。“我们可以吃有机食品，可以尽可能多地通风换气，可以住在乡下。”但对于这些内分泌干扰物来说，“根本无处可逃。根本无处可逃。”就个人而言，根本无法避免。

To understand what we can actually do to solve the damage pollution is doing to our attention, I went to meet up with Bruce Lanphear by the rocks in Horseshoe Bay, on the West Coast of Canada, on a foggy day. He had just been out kayaking, and in the water in front of us, there were seals flapping around and vanishing under the waves. ‘Look at that,’ he said. ‘The clouds. The water. The greenery.’

为了了解我们究竟能做些什么来解决污染对我们注意力造成的损害，在一个雾蒙蒙的日子里，我去加拿大西海岸的马蹄湾，在岩石边与布鲁斯·兰菲尔见面。他刚刚划完皮划艇，在我们面前的水中，海豹扑腾着翅膀，消失在波浪之下。“看看那，”他说，“云朵，海水，还有绿意盎然的植被。”

From our conversation, I learned that there were two ways we need to respond now. Firstly, when it comes to new chemicals, we need a new approach. He told me that at the moment, ‘chemicals are assumed to be innocent until study after study shows they’re toxic’. So if you want to put a product on the market containing a new chemical, you can use whatever you want, and, in the years that follow, poorly funded scientists have to scramble to figure out if it’s safe. ‘That’s because who’s calling the shots? Industry.’ We need to do it differently, he said. ‘Basically, we should treat new chemicals, new pollutants, as though they are like drugs.’ The chemical should have to be tested for safety before it starts being used by ordinary people – and only if it passes stringent tests should it end up in your home and in your bloodstream.

从我们的谈话中，我了解到我们现在需要从两个方面来应对。首先，对于新型化学物质，我们需要一种新的方法。他告诉我，目前的情况是，“化学物质被认为是无害的，直到一项又一项的研究表明它们有毒”。因此，如果你想将一种含有新型化学物质的产品推向市场，你可以随意使用，而接下来的几年里，资金匮乏的科学家们不得不疲于奔命地去弄清楚它是否安全。“这是因为谁说了算？是工业界。” 他说，我们需要改变这种做法。“基本上，我们应该像对待毒品一样对待新型化学物质和新型污染物。” 化学物质在被普通人使用之前，必须经过安全测试——只有通过严格的测试，它才能最终进入你的家中，进入你的血液。

Second, for the chemicals that are already widely used, we need to do these tests, and this research needs to be carried out by scientists who are not funded by industry. Then, if we discover that any of them are harmful, we need to band together as citizens and demand that it be prohibited, like lead is – finally – today. Later, Barbara Demeneix told me bluntly: ‘We’ve got to get this under control very soon.’

其次，对于已经广泛使用的化学品，我们需要进行这些测试，而且这项研究必须由不接受工业界资助的科学家来完成。然后，如果我们发现其中任何一种有害，我们就需要团结起来，作为公民要求禁止使用，就像铅最终被禁用一样。后来，芭芭拉·德梅内克斯直言不讳地告诉我：“我们必须尽快控制住局面。”

Barbara Maher told me that when it comes to her area of expertise, air pollution, we need to pressure our governments to bring forward the transition to electric cars by law, because they massively reduce this problem. She stressed, in addition, that there are interim steps we can push our leaders to take: if we plant trees in pollution hotspots, they will soak up a lot of the contamination, and clean the air of many toxins.

芭芭拉·马赫告诉我，就她所专长的空气污染领域而言，我们需要向政府施压，通过立法加快向电动汽车的过渡，因为电动汽车能大幅减少空气污染问题。她还强调，我们可以敦促领导人采取一些过渡性措施：在污染热点地区植树造林，树木可以吸收大量污染物，净化空气中的多种毒素。

As I absorbed all this, I kept thinking about what Barbara Demeneix said to me: ‘There is no way we can have a normal brain today.’ It’s possible that a hundred years from now, when they look back at us and ask why we struggled to pay attention, they will say, ‘They were surrounded by pollutants and chemicals that inflamed their brains and harmed focus. They walked around exposed to BPA and PCBs, and breathing in metals. Their scientists knew what it did to their brains and their ability to focus. Why were they surprised they struggled to pay attention?’ Those people in the future will know whether, after learning this, we banded together to protect our brains – or whether we allowed them to continue to degrade.

当我消化这些信息时，我一直在想芭芭拉·德梅内克斯对我说的话：“如今，我们的大脑不可能正常运转。” 或许一百年后，当人们回顾我们，问我们为何难以集中注意力时，他们会说：“他们生活在充满污染物和化学物质的环境中，这些物质会刺激大脑，损害注意力。他们长期暴露在双酚A和多氯联苯中，呼吸着金属。他们的科学家早就知道这些物质对大脑和注意力的影响。他们又何必惊讶于自己难以集中注意力呢？” 未来的人们将会知道，在了解这一切之后，我们是否团结起来保护我们的大脑——还是任由它继续退化。

# ↩
