13 Cause Eleven: The Rise of ADHD and How We Are Responding to It

第13章 第十一个原因：多动症的兴起以及我们的应对措施

Something strange started to happen around fifteen years ago, when my nephews were small. Their teachers believed that large numbers of kids in their classes were becoming more restless and unable to focus. They didn’t want to sit still or attend to their lessons. Around this time, an idea that didn’t exist in Britain when I was a child – or, at least, was exceptionally rare – started to spread through the country. It was argued by some researchers and doctors that these children had a biological disorder, and that is why they weren’t paying attention. This idea proliferated with incredible speed across the English-speaking world. Between 2003 and 2011 alone, diagnoses of attention deficit hyperactivity disorder ( ADHD) soared in the United States by 43 percent overall, and by 55 percent among girls. It has now reached the point that 13 percent of adolescents in the US have been given this diagnosis, and of them, a majority are given powerful stimulant drugs as a result.

大约十五年前，我的侄子们还小的时候，发生了一件奇怪的事情。他们的老师发现班里很多孩子变得越来越躁动不安，无法集中注意力。他们不愿安静地坐着，也不愿认真听课。大约在同一时期，一种在我小时候的英国并不存在的观念——或者至少是极其罕见的观念——开始在英国蔓延开来。一些研究人员和医生认为，这些孩子患有某种生物学上的疾病，这才是他们注意力不集中的原因。这种观念在英语世界迅速传播开来。仅在2003年至2011年间，美国注意力缺陷多动障碍（ADHD）的诊断率就飙升了43%，女孩的诊断率更是增长了55%。如今，美国已有13%的青少年被诊断患有ADHD，其中大多数人因此服用强效兴奋剂药物。

In Britain, the increase has also been extraordinary: for every child who was diagnosed with ADHD when I was seven years old, in 1986, there are now one hundred kids in this position. Between 1998 and 2004 alone, the number of children being given stimulants doubled.

在英国，这一增长也十分惊人：1986年我七岁时，每有一个孩子被诊断出患有注意力缺陷多动障碍（ADHD），如今就有100个孩子面临同样的情况。仅在1998年至2004年间，服用兴奋剂的儿童人数就翻了一番。

When it comes to our own attention problems as adults, we often readily acknowledge a whole range of influences on us – the rise of invasive technologies, stress, lack of sleep, and so on. But when our children face the same challenges, over the past twenty years we have been drawn to a starkly simple story: that this problem is largely the result of a biological disorder. I wanted to investigate this in depth. Of all the chapters in this book, this is the one I’ve found hardest to write, because it’s the topic about which serious scientists disagree the most. By interviewing them, I learned that they don’t agree on even the most basic questions – including whether ADHD actually exists in the way most people have been told it does, as a biological illness. So I want to go through this chapter slowly and carefully. This is the topic where I interviewed the most experts – over thirty of them – and I kept going back with more questions for a long time.

当我们成年人遇到注意力问题时，我们往往很容易意识到各种因素的影响——侵入性技术的兴起、压力、睡眠不足等等。但当我们的孩子面临同样的挑战时，过去二十年来，我们却倾向于一个极其简单的说法：这个问题很大程度上是由生物疾病引起的。我想深入探究这个问题。在本书的所有章节中，这一章是我写得最难的，因为这是严肃的科学家们争论最激烈的话题。通过采访他们，我发现他们甚至在一些最基本的问题上都存在分歧——包括多动症是否真的像大多数人被告知的那样，是一种生物疾病。因此，我想仔细而缓慢地探讨这一章。在这个主题上，我采访了最多的专家——超过三十位——而且在很长一段时间里，我不断地向他们提出更多的问题。

But I want to make clear a few things at the start that every expert I spoke with agreed on: everyone being diagnosed with ADHD has a real problem. They aren’t making it up or faking it. Whatever the cause, if you or your child is struggling to focus, it’s not your fault: you’re not incompetent or undisciplined or any of the other stigmatising labels that might have been applied to you. You deserve compassion and practical help to find solutions. Most experts believed that for some children, there can be a biological contribution to their poor focus – though they disagreed on how large a contribution that was. We should be able to have a calm and honest conversation about the other aspects of the ADHD controversy while holding these truths in our minds.

但我想首先澄清几点，这些也是我咨询过的所有专家都认同的：所有被诊断为多动症的人都存在实际问题。他们并非捏造或装病。无论病因是什么，如果您或您的孩子难以集中注意力，这不是您的错：您并非无能、缺乏自律，或者被贴上了其他任何带有歧视性的标签。您值得得到关怀和切实可行的帮助来找到解决方案。大多数专家认为，对于某些孩子来说，注意力不集中可能存在生物学因素——尽管他们对这种因素的影响程度存在分歧。我们应该在牢记这些事实的同时，冷静而坦诚地讨论多动症争议的其他方面。

The question of whether kids who can’t focus have a biological problem is, in fact, a fairly new debate, and it has changed a lot in the past few years. In 1952 the American Psychiatric Association first wrote a guide to all the things that can go wrong with a person’s mental health, and the idea that kids who struggle to focus are suffering from a biological disorder was not included. By 1968, the idea had gained enough popularity among psychiatrists that they added it, but they believed it applied to a tiny number of children. With each passing year, the number of kids identified as having this problem has soared, to the point that in many parts of the South in the United States, 30 percent of boys are now diagnosed with ADHD by the time they turn eighteen. As I write, it is swelling even further – huge numbers of adults are now being told they have this disability, with over 3 million of them already being prescribed stimulants. The market for prescribing stimulants is now worth at least $10 billion.

关于注意力不集中的孩子是否患有生理疾病的问题，实际上是一个相对较新的争论，并且在过去几年中发生了很大的变化。1952年，美国精神病学会首次编写了一份关于所有可能影响心理健康问题的指南，其中并未包含注意力不集中的孩子患有生理疾病这一观点。到了1968年，这一观点在精神科医生中获得了足够的认可，因此被纳入指南，但他们认为这种情况只适用于极少数儿童。然而，随着时间的推移，被诊断患有注意力缺陷多动障碍（ADHD）的儿童人数逐年激增，以至于在美国南部许多地区，30%的男孩在18岁时就被诊断出患有ADHD。在我撰写本文时，这一数字还在进一步增长——大量成年人被告知患有这种疾病，其中超过300万人已被处方兴奋剂。如今，兴奋剂处方市场的价值至少为100亿美元。

As all this has exploded, a polarised argument has broken out over it. On one side, there are people saying ADHD is a disorder caused overwhelmingly by something going wrong within the individual’s genes and brain, and that very large numbers of children and adults should be taking these stimulants to treat it. This side has largely prevailed in the US. On the other side, there are people saying that attention problems are real and painful, but it is incorrect and harmful to see them as a biological disorder that requires the mass prescription of drugs, and we should be offering different forms of help. This side has largely prevailed in places like Finland.

随着这一切的爆发，一场两极分化的争论也随之而来。一方认为，多动症主要是一种由个体基因和大脑异常引起的疾病，因此应该让大量的儿童和成人服用兴奋剂进行治疗。这种观点在美国占据了主导地位。另一方则认为，注意力问题确实存在且令人痛苦，但将其视为需要大量药物治疗的生物学疾病是错误且有害的，我们应该提供其他形式的帮助。这种观点在芬兰等地占据了主导地位。

Let’s start with the purely biological story, and why so many people find truth and relief in it. One day, on an Amtrak train, I got talking to a woman who asked me what I did for a job. When I told her I was writing a book about why people struggle to pay attention, she started to tell me about her son. I didn’t write it down at the time, so I only remember the broad details of what she said – but he had a typical experience. Years before, he had been really struggling at school – he wasn’t able to pay attention in class, and he was in trouble a lot. She felt concerned for him, and judged by the other parents. Finally, the school’s teachers urged her to take him to the doctor. Their doctor spoke to her son and then told her that he had diagnosed him with ADHD. He told her that it meant her son had different genetics from other kids, and that as a result, he had developed a different kind of brain, one that wasn’t like most people’s. This meant he found it much harder to sit still and focus. Stephen Hinshaw, a professor of psychology at Stanford University, similarly told me that genetics account for ‘75 to 80 percent’ of ADHD, a ballpark figure that is based on a large series of scientific studies.

让我们先从纯粹的生物学角度来谈起，以及为什么这么多人能从中找到真理和慰藉。有一天，在美铁列车上，我和一位女士聊了起来，她问我是做什么工作的。当我告诉她我正在写一本关于人们为什么难以集中注意力的书时，她开始跟我讲她儿子的故事。当时我没有记下来，所以只记得她讲述的大概内容——但她儿子的经历很典型。几年前，他在学校里学习很吃力——上课无法集中注意力，经常惹麻烦。她很担心儿子，也觉得其他家长对他指指点点。最后，学校的老师们劝她带儿子去看医生。医生和她儿子谈过之后，告诉她儿子被诊断出患有注意力缺陷多动障碍（ADHD）。医生解释说，这意味着她儿子的基因与其他孩子不同，因此，他的大脑发育方式也与众不同，与大多数人的大脑不同。这意味着他很难静下心来集中注意力。斯坦福大学心理学教授斯蒂芬·欣肖也告诉我，遗传因素占多动症的“75%到80%”，这是一个基于大量科学研究得出的粗略数字。

It’s distressing to be told your child has a disability. She felt shocked – but at the same time as they are offered this message, parents are also told lots of positive things: your son’s behaviour isn’t your fault. In fact, you deserve sympathy: you’ve been coping with something really hard. And best of all, there is a solution. Her son was prescribed the stimulant drug Ritalin. When he started to take it, he stopped being so restless and bouncing off the walls. He said he didn’t like how it made him feel, though – one child I know told me that he felt like his brain was turned off when he took the drug – so his mother felt genuinely conflicted. Ultimately, she decided to continue to give him the stimulants until he turned eighteen, because she felt that at least this would stop him being thrown out of school. There’s no dramatic aspect to this story: he didn’t have a heart attack or start using meth. On balance, she thought she was doing the right thing.

得知孩子有残疾，父母会感到非常痛苦。她感到震惊——但与此同时，父母们也听到了很多积极的信息：你儿子的行为不是你的错。事实上，你值得同情：你一直在努力应对非常艰难的事情。最重要的是，有解决办法。她的儿子被开了利他林这种兴奋剂。开始服用后，他不再那么焦躁不安、到处乱跑了。但他表示不喜欢这种药带来的感觉——我认识的一个孩子告诉我，他服用这种药后感觉大脑好像停止运转了——所以他的母亲内心非常矛盾。最终，她决定继续给他服用兴奋剂直到他十八岁，因为她觉得至少这样可以避免他被学校开除。这个故事并没有什么戏剧性的情节：他没有心脏病发作，也没有开始吸食冰毒。总的来说，她认为自己做的是对的。

I feel a lot of sympathy for her. But there are several reasons why I also feel worried about the fact that there are more and more people like her, who now believe this is an overwhelmingly genetic problem that needs to be dealt with primarily with stimulants. I think the best way to start to explain why might be to step sideways for a moment, and to look at what happened when the concept of ADHD spread beyond kids, and even beyond adults, to a whole new category of living creatures.

我非常同情她。但同时，我也感到担忧，因为越来越多的人像她一样，认为多动症完全是遗传问题，需要主要用兴奋剂来治疗。我想，要解释个中缘由，或许可以先退一步，看看当多动症的概念从儿童甚至成人扩展到其他人群时，究竟发生了什么。

One day in the 1990s, a nine-year-old beagle named Emma was led into a vet’s surgery. Her stressed-out owner explained that she had a problem. The dog was anxious all the time – she ate constantly, and there were times when she would suddenly go ballistic, ricocheting off the walls and barking incessantly. If she was left alone in the house, the dog would freak out even more. The owner kept using one word to describe Emma: hyperactive. She implored the vet to help her figure out what to do.

上世纪九十年代的某一天，一只名叫艾玛的九岁比格犬被带进了兽医诊所。她焦虑不安的主人解释说，艾玛出了问题。这只狗总是焦虑不安——它不停地吃东西，有时还会突然变得异常兴奋，在墙上乱撞，不停地吠叫。如果把它独自留在家里，它会更加惊慌失措。主人一直用一个词来形容艾玛：过度活跃。她恳求兽医帮她找到解决办法。

The vet she had come to see was a man named Nicholas Dodman, an English immigrant who – over a thirty-year career – had become one of the leading veterinary specialists in the United States, and a professor at Tufts University. At first, Nicholas prescribed for Emma and her owner to go to dog training, where both of them could learn new skills to help them interact. It worked – but not completely. The owner said Emma’s problems dipped by around 30 percent. When he heard this, Nicholas decided that Emma in fact had ADHD – a concept that, until he made his own breakthroughs in interpreting animal behaviour, had only really been applied to humans. He prescribed the stimulant drug Ritalin for the dog, and told Emma’s owner to smush it into her food twice daily. When she came back not long afterwards, the owner was thrilled. The problem, she said, was solved. The dog had stopped bouncing around the house and trying to eat all the time. It was true that Emma still howled terribly when she was left alone, but otherwise, she was the dog her owner had always hoped for.

她去看的兽医名叫尼古拉斯·多德曼，是一位英国移民，三十多年来，他已成为美国顶尖的兽医专家之一，也是塔夫茨大学的教授。起初，尼古拉斯建议艾玛和她的主人一起去参加犬类训练，学习一些新的互动技巧。训练确实有效，但效果并不理想。主人说艾玛的问题减少了大约30%。听到这个消息后，尼古拉斯断定艾玛实际上患有注意力缺陷多动障碍（ADHD）——在他取得动物行为学方面的突破之前，ADHD的概念主要应用于人类。他给艾玛开了利他林这种兴奋剂，并嘱咐主人每天两次将药片混入狗粮中服用。不久之后，主人带着艾玛回来，欣喜若狂。她说，问题解决了。狗狗不再在屋里蹦来蹦去，也不再总是想吃东西了。艾玛独自一人时确实还会发出凄厉的嚎叫，但除此之外，她就是主人一直期盼的那只狗。

By the time I met Nicholas at his home in Massachusetts, this had become a normal day at his clinic. He regularly prescribes Ritalin and other stimulants to animals he diagnoses as having ADHD. Nicholas is a pioneer, and he’s been called the ‘Pied Piper’ of drugging animals for psychiatric problems.

当我在马萨诸塞州尼古拉斯的家中见到他时，这已经成了他诊所的日常。他经常给被诊断患有多动症的动物开利他林和其他兴奋剂。尼古拉斯是这方面的先驱，有人称他为用药物治疗动物精神疾病的“魔笛手”。

I was curious about how he came to take this position. He told me it all began quite by accident, like many scientific breakthroughs. In the mid-1980s he was called as a vet to visit a horse named Poker, who had a problem. Poker was obsessively ‘cribbing’ – a terrible compulsive behaviour that around 8 percent of horses develop when they are shut away in stalls for most of the day. It’s an awkward repetitive action, where the horse will grasp with his teeth onto something solid – like the fence in front of him – then arch his neck, swallow, and grunt hard. He’ll do this again and again, compulsively. The so-called treatments for cribbing at that time were shockingly cruel. Sometimes vets would drill holes into the horse’s face so he couldn’t suck in air, or they would put brass rings in the horse’s lips so he couldn’t grasp the fence. Nicholas was appalled by these practices, and in his search for alternatives, he suddenly had an idea. What if we gave this horse a drug? He decided to inject the horse with naloxone, which is an opioid-blocker. ‘Within a few minutes, the horse just completely stopped,’ he told me. ‘The owner was like, “Oh my God. Oh my God.” ’ After about twenty minutes the horse started cribbing again, but ‘we repeated that [injection] many times with many different horses subsequently, and had exactly the same result’. He said: ‘It fascinated me that you could change behaviour so dramatically by changing brain chemistry … You know, that changed my career.’

我很好奇他是如何走上这条路的。他告诉我，一切都始于偶然，就像许多科学突破一样。上世纪80年代中期，他作为兽医被请去给一匹名叫Poker的马看病，Poker遇到了一个问题。Poker患有严重的“啃咬癖”（cribbing），这是一种可怕的强迫行为，大约8%的马在被关在马厩里大部分时间后会患上这种疾病。这是一种笨拙的重复性动作，马会用牙齿咬住坚硬的东西——比如面前的栅栏——然后弓起脖子，吞咽，发出沉重的哼哼声。它会一遍又一遍地重复这个动作，强迫自己不由自主地这样做。当时所谓的啃咬癖治疗方法极其残忍。有时兽医会在马的脸上钻孔，让它无法吸气，或者在马的嘴唇上戴上黄铜环，让它无法抓住栅栏。尼古拉斯对这些做法感到震惊，在寻找替代方法的过程中，他突然想到了一个主意。如果我们给这匹马注射药物会怎么样？他决定给马注射纳洛酮，这是一种阿片类阻断剂。“几分钟之内，这匹马就完全停止了啃咬，”他告诉我。“马主人惊呼：‘我的天哪！我的天哪！’”大约二十分钟后，这匹马又开始啃咬东西了，但是“之后我们用很多不同的马重复了多次注射，结果都完全一样”。他说：“通过改变大脑化学物质就能如此显著地改变行为，这让我着迷……你知道吗，这改变了我的职业生涯。”

From that point on, Nicholas began to believe you could solve the problems of many animals by responding to them in ways that, until then, had only been applied to humans. For example, he was consulted by Calgary Zoo about a polar bear that was endlessly pacing, and he recommended giving it a massive dose of Prozac. It stopped pacing and began to sit docilely in its cage. Today, thanks in part to Nicholas’s shift in perspective, there are parrots on Xanax and Valium, there are many species from chickens to walruses being given anti-psychotics, and there are cats on Prozac. One of the staff at a leading US zoo told a reporter that psychiatric drugs are ‘definitely a wonderful management tool, and that’s how we look at them. To be able to just take the edge off puts us a little more at ease.’ Nearly half of all zoos in the US now admit giving psychiatric drugs to their animals, and 50 to 60 percent of the owners who come to Nicholas’s clinic are seeking psychiatric meds for their pets. At times, it sounds like One Flew Over the Cuckoo’s Nest for actual cuckoos.

从那时起，尼古拉斯开始相信，可以通过运用此前只应用于人类的方式来解决许多动物的问题。例如，卡尔加里动物园曾就一只不停踱步的北极熊咨询过他的意见，他建议给它服用大剂量的百忧解。北极熊停止了踱步，开始温顺地待在笼子里。如今，部分得益于尼古拉斯的观念转变，鹦鹉开始服用阿普唑仑和地西泮，从鸡到海象等许多物种都在服用抗精神病药物，甚至还有猫在服用百忧解。美国一家知名动物园的工作人员告诉记者，精神类药物“绝对是一种绝佳的管理工具，我们就是这么看待它们的。” “能稍微缓解一下焦虑，让我们安心一些。”美国近一半的动物园现在承认给动物服用精神类药物，而前来尼古拉斯诊所就诊的宠物主人中，有50%到60%的人是来寻求宠物精神类药物治疗的。有时候，这听起来就像是为真正的杜鹃鸟量身打造的《飞越疯人院》。

Before I went to meet Nicholas, I expected him to justify this in one particular way. I thought he would tell me the story that lots of doctors tell parents who have kids with attention problems – that this is a disorder with biological causes, and this is why they need biological solutions in the form of drugs. But he didn’t say that. In fact, his explanation started where his own journey into this science had begun – with cribbing horses. ‘No one’s ever seen a horse in the wild do this. This is a condition of “domestication”, keeping horses in unnatural situations,’ he told me. ‘If they’d never been put in a stall, and they’d never been subjected to that psychological pressure early on, they wouldn’t develop it.’

在去见尼古拉斯之前，我以为他会用某种特定的方式来解释这件事。我以为他会像很多医生告诉那些有注意力缺陷孩子的家长那样，说这是一种有生物学原因的疾病，所以需要用药物这种生物学方法来治疗。但他并没有这么说。事实上，他的解释是从他自己开始研究这门科学的地方说起的——马的啃木癖。“从来没有人见过野马有这种行为。这是‘驯化’造成的，把马放在不自然的环境中，”他告诉我。“如果它们从来没有被关在马厩里，从来没有在早期承受过那种心理压力，它们就不会出现这种症状。”

As he described what happened to these horses, he used a phrase that struck me. He said these horses are suffering from ‘frustrated biological objectives’. Horses want to roam and run and graze. When they can’t express their innate nature, their behaviour and focus go awry, and they start to act out. He told me that ‘the pressure of having your biological objectives thwarted is such that it opens a Pandora’s box’, where you’ll try to find any behaviour that will ‘alleviate this crushing psychological pressure or inability to do anything … Horses spend about 60 percent of their time in the wild grazing, so it’s not surprising that one of the things that gives them release is a sort of fake grazing, which is what cribbing is.’

当他描述这些马的遭遇时，他用了一个让我印象深刻的词。他说这些马正遭受着“生物本能受挫”的折磨。马渴望漫游、奔跑和吃草。当它们无法表达天性时，它们的行为和注意力就会出现偏差，并开始出现异常行为。他告诉我，“生物本能受挫带来的压力就像打开了潘多拉魔盒”，你会试图找到任何能够“缓解这种巨大的心理压力或无所事事的无力感”的行为……马在野外大约有60%的时间都在吃草，所以它们会通过某种假装吃草的方式来释放压力，而啃咬行为正是这种假装吃草的体现，这并不奇怪。

He admitted freely that his approach of drugging animals for what’s dubbed ‘zoochosis’ – the madness animals often develop when they are caged – is an extremely limited solution. I asked him if, for example, drugging the polar bear had solved his problem. ‘No,’ he replied. ‘It’s a Band-aid. The problem is you’ve taken a polar bear out of the polar environment, and you’ve stuck it in a zoo … Polar bears in nature will walk for miles across the Arctic tundra. They look for seal places, and they swim, and they eat seals. The exhibit [the cage where this polar bear was trapped] is nothing like real life. So, just like the guy in jail, they pace to appease the inner pain of being denied a real life … They’ve got all these instincts that are all intact, that they’re unable to utilise.’

他坦言，他用药物治疗动物所谓的“动物园精神病”（动物被囚禁后常出现的疯狂状态）的方法，是一种极其有限的解决方案。我问他，比如给北极熊服用药物是否解决了问题。“没有，”他回答说，“这只是权宜之计。问题在于，你把北极熊从极地环境中带走，关进了动物园……野生北极熊会在北极苔原上跋涉数英里。它们寻找海豹栖息地，它们游泳，它们捕食海豹。动物园里的展馆（这只北极熊被困的笼子）与真实的生活环境截然不同。所以，就像监狱里的人一样，它们来回踱步，以此来缓解被剥夺真实生活的痛苦……它们拥有所有这些完好无损的本能，却无法加以利用。”

The long-term solution is to shut down zoos, he said, and to let all animals live in an environment that is compatible with their natures. He told me about a dog that was unable to focus on anything and spent all its time obsessively chasing its own tail. It lived in a tiny apartment in Manhattan. Then, one day, its owners split up, and it was sent to live on a farm upstate – and its tail-chasing and apparent focus problems went away. All dogs should run for at least an hour off-leash every day, but ‘not many’ pet dogs in the US get that, he told me. They’re frustrated, and it causes problems.

他说，长远之计是关闭动物园，让所有动物生活在与其天性相符的环境中。他给我讲了一个故事：一只狗无法集中注意力，整天痴迷地追着自己的尾巴转。它住在曼哈顿一间狭小的公寓里。后来有一天，它的主人分手了，它被送到纽约州北部的一个农场生活——之后，它追尾巴的毛病和注意力不集中的问题都消失了。他告诉我，所有狗每天至少应该有一个小时的自由奔跑时间，但美国“很少有”宠物狗能做到这一点。它们会感到沮丧，这会导致一些问题。

He can’t magic that world into existence by himself. In the absence of those long-term solutions, he wanted to know, what would I have him do? We discussed this for a long time. I tried to explain to him that while I saw where he was coming from, I felt instinctively uncomfortable with it. These animals are showing these behaviours as a way of expressing distress – Poker the horse hated being shut away, and Emma the beagle hated being left alone, because horses need to run and dogs need a pack. I was worried that by muffling their signals with drugs, he might be encouraging their owners into a kind of fantasy – that they could take a creature, ignore its nature, and make it live a life that fits the owner’s needs, not the animal’s, without any cost. We need to hear the animal’s distress, not suppress it.

他无法凭一己之力创造出那样的世界。在缺乏长远解决方案的情况下，他想知道，我希望他怎么做？我们为此讨论了很久。我试图向他解释，虽然我理解他的想法，但我本能地感到不安。这些动物表现出这些行为是为了表达痛苦——马儿Poker讨厌被关起来，比格犬Emma讨厌独处，因为马需要奔跑，狗需要群体。我担心，他用药物掩盖它们的信号，可能会助长主人的一种幻想——他们可以随意占有动物，无视它们的本性，让它们过上符合主人需求而非动物自身需求的生活，而且无需付出任何代价。我们需要倾听动物的痛苦，而不是压制它们。

He listened thoughtfully, and responded by describing to me pigs who live and die in brutal factory farms, ripped from their mothers as babies, spending their whole lives in carts where they can’t turn around. He asked: ‘I could make this pig a lot better and tolerate this intolerable situation with less psychological pain if I was to put Prozac in the drinking line. Would you be against that?’ But the choices he was confronting me with, I said, with shouldn’t exist. His hypothetical concedes too much – it takes a dysfunctional environment for granted, and assumes that all we can do is try to adapt to it and take the edge off. We need better choices than that. ‘I mean – reality shouldn’t be the choice,’ he replied. ‘It’s what we have, you know? So you have to work with what you’ve got.’

他若有所思地听着，然后向我描述了那些在残酷的工厂化养殖场里苟延残喘、最终死去的猪。它们幼时就被从母亲身边强行带走，一生都被关在无法转身的车厢里。他问道：“如果我在喂猪喝药的路上放点百忧解，就能让这头猪好受些，也能让它在这种难以忍受的处境下少受些心理痛苦。你反对吗？”但我说，他提出的这些选择根本不应该存在。他的假设让步太多了——它把这种糟糕的环境视为理所当然，并假定我们所能做的只是努力适应，尽量减轻痛苦。我们需要更好的选择。“我的意思是——现实不应该成为选择，”他回答说，“这就是我们所拥有的，你知道吗？所以你只能接受现实。”

I began to ask myself – is there any way in which children who struggle to focus are like Emma the beagle, and are being medicated for what is in fact an environmental problem? I learned that scientists fiercely disagree about this. We do know that the huge rise in children being diagnosed with attention problems has coincided with several other big changes in the way children live. Kids are now allowed to run around far less – instead of playing in the streets and in their neighbourhoods, they now spend almost all their time inside their homes or school classrooms. Children are now fed a very different diet – one that lacks many nutrients needed for brain development, and is full of sugars and dyes that negatively affect attention. Children’s schooling has changed, so it now focuses almost entirely on preparing them for high-stress testing, with very little space for nurturing their curiosity. Is it a coincidence that ADHD diagnoses are rising at the same time as these big changes, or is there a connection? I’ve already discussed the evidence that our dramatic changes in diet and rise in pollution are causing a rise in children’s attention problems, and I’ll come to the evidence about how the other changes might be affecting children’s attention in the next chapter.

我开始思考——那些难以集中注意力的孩子，是否就像小猎犬艾玛一样，实际上是因为环境问题而被药物治疗？我发现科学家们对此争论不休。我们确实知道，被诊断为注意力缺陷障碍的儿童人数激增，与儿童生活方式的几项重大变化同时发生。孩子们现在很少有机会奔跑玩耍——他们不再像以前那样在街上和社区里玩耍，而是几乎所有时间都待在家里或教室里。孩子们现在的饮食也大不相同——缺乏大脑发育所需的许多营养物质，却富含糖分和色素，这些都会对注意力产生负面影响。儿童教育也发生了变化，现在几乎完全侧重于让他们为高压考试做准备，而几乎没有空间培养他们的好奇心。多动症诊断率的上升与这些重大变化同时发生，这仅仅是巧合吗？还是两者之间存在某种联系？我已经讨论过饮食习惯的剧烈变化和污染的加剧导致儿童注意力问题增多的证据，下一章我将讨论其他变化可能如何影响儿童注意力的证据。

I want to start, though, with somebody who has pioneered a different way of responding to ADHD in children. Across three years, I repeatedly interviewed Dr Sami Timimi, who is a leading child psychiatrist in Britain, and one of the most prominent and vocal critics in the world of the way we talk about ADHD today. I went to see him in Lincoln, a town that was built over a thousand years ago around a cathedral and seems to have been sighing back into the earth ever since. The old parts of the town have been taken over by chain stores paying minimum wage, and when Sami moved there he discovered his practice was full of people who were really struggling, through no fault of their own, with low wages and little hope. He could see that people in Lincoln needed a lot of practical help – but he was surprised to find that people seemed to expect one thing from him. They thought, as he put it, ‘That a psychiatrist was basically somebody who does medication,’ and he was treated as a pill-dispenser. He inherited from his predecessor twenty-seven kids who were being prescribed stimulant drugs for ADHD, and local schools were pressing for more kids to be put on them. It would have been easy for Sami to just carry on with this approach.

不过，我想先从一位开创了儿童多动症应对新方法的先驱者说起。在过去的三年里，我多次采访了萨米·蒂米米医生。他是英国顶尖的儿童精神科医生，也是当今社会对多动症的讨论方式最杰出、最直言不讳的批评者之一。我去林肯拜访了他。林肯是一座拥有千年历史的小镇，围绕着一座大教堂而建，似乎自那时起就一直默默地沉寂着。小镇的老城区已被支付最低工资的连锁商店占据。萨米搬到那里后发现，他的诊所里挤满了生活拮据的人，他们并非咎由自取，却面临着低收入和绝望的困境。他意识到林肯的人们需要很多实际的帮助，但他惊讶地发现，人们似乎对他只有一种期待。正如他所说，他们认为“精神科医生基本上就是开药的”，而他被当作了发药的。他从前任那里接手了27个患有注意力缺陷多动症（ADHD）并被处方兴奋剂药物的孩子，当地学校也要求更多孩子服用这些药物。萨米完全可以继续沿用这种做法。

But he was pensive. He believed that if he was going to take his responsibility as a doctor to these kids seriously, he had to take time to look in depth at their lives and their environments. One of the children who had been diagnosed with ADHD and given stimulants by Sami’s predecessor was an eleven-year-old boy, who he called Michael to protect his confidentiality. After he was dragged into Sami’s office by his mother, Michael refused to even talk to him. He just sat there, angrily sulking, as his mother explained that she didn’t know what to do. She said that Michael kept kicking off at school, refusing to focus and becoming aggressive. As she explained all this, Michael kept interrupting her, sullenly demanding to leave.

但他陷入了沉思。他认为，如果要认真履行作为医生对这些孩子的责任，就必须花时间深入了解他们的生活和环境。萨米的前任医生曾诊断出一个患有注意力缺陷多动障碍（ADHD）并给他服用兴奋剂的孩子，那是一个十一岁的男孩，为了保护隐私，萨米称他为迈克尔。迈克尔被母亲拖进萨米的办公室后，拒绝和他说话。他只是坐在那里，生气地闷闷不乐，他的母亲解释说她不知道该怎么办。她说迈克尔在学校里总是闹脾气，无法集中注意力，而且变得具有攻击性。在她解释这一切的时候，迈克尔不断打断她，闷闷不乐地要求离开。

Sami refused to decide anything based on just one session. He felt he needed to learn more – so he kept interviewing this mother and son over a period of several months. He wanted to understand when these problems began. As he probed into this, it slowly emerged that two years before, Michael’s dad had moved to another town, and he hardly ever talked to his son any more. It was in the aftermath of this that Michael started acting up at school. Sami wondered if he felt rejected. Sami told me: ‘When you’re a child, you’re not developed intellectually to take a step back and look at things from a more rational, objective point of view … When a father says they’re going to come and see you, but they never turn up, you imagine it’s because there’s something wrong with you. It’s because they don’t want to see you. It’s because you’re not very nice. It’s because you cause problems.’

萨米不愿仅凭一次面谈就下结论。他觉得需要了解更多，于是在接下来的几个月里持续采访这对母子。他想弄明白这些问题是从什么时候开始的。随着调查的深入，他逐渐了解到，两年前，迈克尔的父亲搬到了另一个城镇，之后几乎不再和儿子说话。正是在这段时间之后，迈克尔开始在学校里表现异常。萨米想知道他是否感到被抛弃。萨米告诉我：“当你还是个孩子的时候，你的心智还没有发育成熟，无法冷静地从更理性、客观的角度看待问题……当父亲说要来看你，却从未出现时，你会觉得是自己有问题，是因为他们不想见你，是因为你不讨人喜欢，是因为你惹了麻烦。”

So one day, Sami decided to phone Michael’s dad. He agreed that he would come into the doctor’s office to see Sami, and they talked over the situation. The father was chastened, and decided to come back into his son’s life in a structured and consistent way. Sami called Michael in and told him that there was nothing wrong with him. It wasn’t his fault his dad had disengaged. He didn’t have a disorder. He had been let down, and that wasn’t his fault. Now it was going to change. As Michael reconnected with his dad, over several months they weaned him off his stimulant drugs. Sami did this gradually because the withdrawal effects can be severe and terrible. As time passed, several things changed for Michael. He had a male role model. He knew he wasn’t a bad person who drove his dad away. He stopped acting out at school and started learning again. Sami felt he had identified the underlying problem and solved it – and so the attention problems gradually went away.

有一天，萨米决定给迈克尔的爸爸打电话。他同意来诊所见萨米，两人就此事进行了交谈。父亲幡然醒悟，决定以一种有条理且稳定的方式重新融入儿子的生活。萨米把迈克尔叫来，告诉他他没有任何问题。他父亲疏远他不是他的错。他没有患任何疾病。他只是被父亲辜负了，但这也不是他的错。现在一切都会改变。随着迈克尔与父亲重新建立联系，他们花了几个月的时间逐步让他戒掉兴奋剂药物。萨米采取循序渐进的方式，因为戒断反应可能非常严重。随着时间的推移，迈克尔身上发生了许多变化。他有了男性榜样。他知道自己不是个坏人，不是自己把父亲赶走的。他不再在学校里胡闹，也重新开始学习。萨米觉得他找到了问题的根源并解决了它——于是，迈克尔的注意力问题也逐渐消失了。

Another of the kids brought to Sami was a nine-year-old boy he called Aden, who behaved well at home, but seemed to be behaving badly at school. His teacher said he was hyperactive and kept distracting the other kids, and was urging that he be given stimulants. Sami decided to visit the school, and he was appalled by what he saw. Aden’s teacher spent all her time yelling at the class to be quiet, and irrationally punishing Aden and a few other kids she seemed to have taken a dislike to. The classroom was in chaos, and Aden was being blamed. At first, Sami tried to help the teacher to change her story about Aden, but she wouldn’t listen, so he helped Aden’s parents move him to a new, less chaotic school. Once he got settled in, he started to thrive, and his attention problems also faded.

萨米遇到的另一个孩子是个九岁的男孩，他叫艾登。艾登在家表现很好，但在学校却表现得很差。他的老师说他过度活跃，总是分散其他孩子的注意力，并建议给他服用兴奋剂。萨米决定去学校看看，他所看到的景象让他震惊不已。艾登的老师整天都在冲着全班大喊大叫，让他们安静，还无缘无故地惩罚艾登和其他几个她似乎不喜欢的孩子。教室里一片混乱，而艾登却成了众矢之的。起初，萨米试图帮助老师改变对艾登的指责，但她根本不听，于是萨米帮助艾登的父母把他转到了一所新的、秩序更好的学校。艾登适应新环境后，开始茁壮成长，注意力不集中的问题也逐渐消失了。

Sami does still occasionally continue the prescription of stimulants to children, but it’s rare, it’s short term, and it’s after trying all other options. He said that with the vast majority of cases of kids with attention problems that come into his office, if he listens carefully and offers practical support to change the child’s environment, it almost always reduces or ends the problem they have.

萨米医生偶尔还是会给孩子开兴奋剂，但这很少见，而且只是短期用药，通常是在尝试过所有其他方法之后才会考虑。他说，在他接诊的大多数注意力不集中的儿童病例中，如果他认真倾听并提供切实可行的帮助来改变孩子的生活环境，几乎总能减轻或消除他们的问题。

He told me that when people hear a child has been diagnosed with ADHD, they often imagine this is like a diagnosis of, say, pneumonia – that a doctor has identified an underlying pathogen or illness, and is now going to prescribe something that can deal with that physical problem. But with ADHD, there are no physical tests a doctor can carry out. All she can do is talk to the child, and people who know the child, and see if the kid’s behaviour matches a checklist drawn up by psychiatrists. That’s it. He says: ‘ADHD is not a diagnosis. It’s not a diagnosis. It’s just a description of certain behaviours that sometimes occur together. That’s all it is.’ All you are saying, when a child has been diagnosed with ADHD, is that a child is struggling to focus. ‘It doesn’t tell you anything about the “why” question.’ It’s like being told that a child has a cough, listening to the cough, and then saying – yes, the child has a cough. If a doctor identifies a child with attention problems, that should be the first step in the process – not the last.

他告诉我，当人们听说某个孩子被诊断出患有注意力缺陷多动障碍（ADHD）时，他们常常会想象这就像诊断出肺炎一样——医生找到了潜在的病原体或疾病，然后会开药来治疗这种生理问题。但对于ADHD，医生无法进行任何生理检查。她所能做的只是与孩子以及认识孩子的人交谈，看看孩子的行为是否符合精神科医生制定的清单。仅此而已。他说：“ADHD不是一种诊断。它不是一种诊断。它只是对某些有时会同时出现的行为的一种描述。仅此而已。”当一个孩子被诊断出患有ADHD时，你只能说这个孩子难以集中注意力。“它并没有告诉你‘为什么’这个问题。”这就像有人告诉你一个孩子咳嗽，你听了咳嗽声，然后说——是的，孩子咳嗽。如果医生发现某个孩子有注意力问题，这应该是治疗过程的第一步，而不是最后一步。

I was moved by Sami’s experiences – but I also asked: how do we know if this kind of approach – listening to the child, and trying to solve the underlying problem – actually works, beyond these moving anecdotes? I dug deeply into this question. It turns out there’s a huge number of studies investigating what happens when you give children stimulant drugs (I’ll come to the results of them soon). There are some studies into what happens when you give parenting classes on how to set boundaries, give consistent feedback, and so on (the evidence is mixed, but you often see a mild improvement). But I wanted to know – is there any research into what happens when you intervene in the way Sami does?

萨米的经历深深打动了我，但我同时也在思考：除了这些感人的轶事之外，我们如何才能确定这种方法——倾听孩子的心声，并努力解决根本问题——真的有效呢？我深入研究了这个问题。结果发现，有大量的研究探讨了给孩子服用兴奋剂药物的后果（我稍后会提到这些研究的结果）。也有一些研究探讨了为孩子开设育儿课程，教他们如何设定界限、给予持续的反馈等等（研究结果不一，但通常都能看到一些轻微的改善）。但我更想知道的是——有没有研究探讨过像萨米那样进行干预会产生什么效果？

It turned out that – so far as I could uncover – in the whole world, there seemed to be only one group of scientists who had studied something close to this question, in a remarkable long-term study, so I went to Minneapolis, where they conducted their research, to meet them. In 1973, Alan Sroufe, who became a professor of child psychology there, started a massive collective research project, which was designed to answer a really big question – what factors in your life really shape you? We met in the café of a garden centre in the city’s suburbs. Alan is a gentle, softly spoken scientist who, at the end of our conversation, went to pick up his grandchildren from school. For more than forty years, Alan and his team have been studying the same 200 people, who were all born into poor families. They have been tracked and analysed from birth all the way into middle age. These scientists measured a huge range of factors in these people’s lives – from their bodies to their home lives, from their personalities to their parents. One of the many things they wanted to figure out is: what factors in a person’s life can lead to them developing attention problems?

结果发现——就我所知——全世界似乎只有一组科学家进行过一项与此问题密切相关的研究，而且这项研究历时极长。于是我前往他们开展研究的明尼阿波利斯，与他们会面。1973年，艾伦·斯鲁夫（Alan Sroufe）——后来成为那里的儿童心理学教授——启动了一项庞大的集体研究项目，旨在解答一个真正意义上的重大问题：生活中哪些因素真正塑造了你？我们在城郊一家园艺中心的咖啡馆见面。艾伦是一位温和、说话轻声细语的科学家，谈话结束后，他去学校接孙辈了。四十多年来，艾伦和他的团队一直在研究同一批200名出生于贫困家庭的人。他们从出生一直追踪并分析这些人的生活，直至中年。科学家们测量了这些人生活中的诸多因素——从他们的身体状况到家庭生活，从他们的性格到他们的父母。他们想要弄清楚的众多问题之一是：一个人生活中的哪些因素会导致他出现注意力问题？

At the start, Alan was fairly confident about the answer they would find. He believed – like most scientists at the time – that ADHD was caused entirely by some inborn biological problem in the child’s brain, so he was sure one of the most important measures they took would be of the child’s neurological status at birth. They also measured the baby’s temperament in its first few months, and then, over time, they measured all sorts of other things – like how stressful their parents’ lives were, and how much social support the family got. His eye was keenly fixed on those neurological measures.

一开始，艾伦对他们最终会找到的答案相当有信心。他和当时大多数科学家一样，认为多动症完全是由孩子大脑中某种先天性的生物学问题引起的，因此他确信他们最重要的测量指标之一就是孩子出生时的神经系统状况。他们还测量了婴儿出生后头几个月的性情，然后随着时间的推移，他们测量了各种各样的其他因素——比如父母的生活压力有多大，家庭获得了多少社会支持。他始终密切关注着这些神经系统测量结果。

By the time the kids were three and a half, the scientists started to make predictions about which of them would develop ADHD. They wanted to see: which factors made it more likely? Alan was startled by what they found, as the kids got older and some were indeed diagnosed with attention problems. It turned out their neurological status at birth didn’t help at all in predicting which kids would develop serious attention problems. So what did? They discovered ‘the surrounding context is the most important thing’, Alan told me, and a crucial factor was ‘the amount of chaos in the environment’. If a child is raised in an environment where there is a lot of stress, they are significantly more likely to then develop attention problems and be diagnosed with ADHD. It turns out that the elevated levels of stress in their parents’ lives usually came first. He told me: ‘You could see it unfolding.’

孩子们三岁半的时候，科学家们开始预测他们当中哪些人会患上注意力缺陷多动障碍（ADHD）。他们想看看：哪些因素会增加患病的可能性？随着孩子们长大，一些孩子确实被诊断出注意力问题，他们的发现令艾伦大吃一惊。结果发现，孩子出生时的神经发育状况对预测哪些孩子会发展出严重的注意力问题毫无帮助。那么，究竟是什么因素起作用呢？艾伦告诉我，他们发现“周围环境才是最重要的”，而一个关键因素是“环境中的混乱程度”。如果一个孩子在充满压力的环境中长大，他们患上注意力问题并被诊断出ADHD的可能性就会显著增加。事实证明，父母生活中较高的压力水平通常是先于ADHD出现。他告诉我：“你可以看到这一切是如何发生的。”

But why would a child growing up in a stressful environment be more likely to have this problem? I of course thought back to everything I had learned from Nadine Burke Harris. Alan began to offer an additional layer of explanation – one that is compatible with her findings. He explained that when you’re very young, if you get upset or angry, you need an adult to soothe you, and calm you down. Over time, as you grow up, if you are soothed enough, you learn to soothe yourself. You internalise the reassurance and relaxation your family gave to you. But stressed-out parents, through no fault of their own, find it harder to soothe their children – because they are so amped-up themselves. That means that their children don’t learn how to calm and centre themselves in the same way. Their kids are, as a result, more likely to respond to difficult situations by getting angry or distressed – feelings that wreck their focus. To give an extreme example, he said to me – you try being evicted from your apartment, and then giving your child all the soothing she needs that night. He added – it’s not just poverty that causes this – middle-class parents struggle with stress too. He told me: ‘Many parents are currently overwhelmed with their life circumstances, such that they cannot provide a stable and calm and supportive environment for their children.’ The worst response to this discovery is to ‘point fingers at the parents’. That only causes more stress, and more problems for the kids, and misses the truth: ‘Those parents were doing the best they could. I guarantee you they loved their children.’ Parenting takes place in an environment – and if that environment floods parents with stress, it will inevitably affect their children.

但为什么在压力环境下长大的孩子更容易出现这个问题呢？我当然想起了我从娜丁·伯克·哈里斯那里学到的一切。艾伦开始提供另一种解释——一种与她的研究结果相符的解释。他解释说，当你很小的时候，如果你感到难过或生气，你需要一个成年人来安抚你，让你平静下来。随着时间的推移，当你长大成人，如果你得到了足够的安抚，你就会学会自我安抚。你会将家人给予你的安慰和放松内化于心。但是，压力过大的父母，并非出于自身过错，却发现更难安抚他们的孩子——因为他们自己也情绪激动。这意味着他们的孩子无法以同样的方式学会如何平静下来，集中注意力。结果，他们的孩子更有可能通过生气或沮丧来应对困境——这些情绪会破坏他们的专注力。他举了个极端的例子——你试试看被房东赶出家门，然后还要在当晚安抚孩子。他还说，造成这种情况的不仅仅是贫困——中产阶级父母也同样承受着巨大的压力。他告诉我：“很多父母目前都被生活琐事压得喘不过气来，根本无法为孩子提供一个稳定、平静、充满关爱的环境。” 面对这种情况，最糟糕的反应就是“指责父母”。那样只会给孩子带来更大的压力和更多的问题，而且忽略了真相：“这些父母已经尽力了。我敢保证，他们爱自己的孩子。” 养育子女是在一个特定的环境中进行的——如果父母所处的环境让他们压力重重，那么这必然会影响到他们的孩子。

After gathering evidence on this for decades, Alan concluded that ‘none of what I originally believed turned out to be true’, and a ‘clear majority’ of the kids who were later diagnosed ‘were not born to be ADHD. They developed these problems in reaction to their circumstances.’

经过数十年的收集，艾伦得出结论：“我最初的想法没有一个是真的”，而且后来被诊断出患有注意力缺陷多动症的“绝大多数”孩子“并非天生患有注意力缺陷多动症。他们的这些问题是对他们所处环境的一种反应。”

There was one crucial question, Alan said, that held the key to whether parents overcame these problems – one that seemed to me to tell us a lot about Sami’s work. It was: ‘Is there somebody giving you support?’ The families they studied sometimes got help from people around them. It usually wasn’t from a professional – they just found a supportive partner, or a group of friends. When their social support went up in this way, they found ‘the children are less likely to have problems at the next stage’. Why would this be? Alan wrote: ‘Parents experiencing less stress can be more responsive to their infants; then infants can become more secure.’ This effect was so large that ‘the strongest predictor of positive change was an increase in social support available to the parents during the intervening years.’ Social support is, I reflected, the main thing Sami provides to families whose children struggle with attention.

艾伦说，有一个至关重要的问题，它掌握着父母能否克服这些问题的关键——在我看来，这个问题也深刻地揭示了萨米的工作。这个问题是：“有人在支持你吗？”他们研究的家庭有时会从身边的人那里获得帮助。通常不是来自专业人士——他们只是找到了支持他们的伴侣，或者一群朋友。当他们的社会支持以这种方式增加时，他们发现“孩子在下一阶段出现问题的可能性更小”。这是为什么呢？艾伦写道：“压力较小的父母可以更及时地回应婴儿；这样，婴儿就能更有安全感。”这种影响如此显著，“积极变化的最强预测因素是父母在成长过程中获得的社会支持的增加。”我反思道，社会支持正是萨米为那些孩子注意力难以集中的家庭提供的主要帮助。

Yet there’s a challenge here. There is no question that when you give a child a stimulant like Adderall or Ritalin, their attention will significantly improve in the short term. All the experts I interviewed, wherever they stand on this debate, agreed with this, and I’ve seen it for myself. I knew a little boy who was constantly running around, shouting, and bouncing off the walls, who – when given Ritalin – sat still and was able to look people in the eye with a steady gaze for the first time in his life. The evidence is clear that this effect is real, and due to the drugs. I have plenty of adult friends who use stimulants when they have to blitz a work project, and it has the same effect on them. In Los Angeles in 2019, I caught up with my friend Laurie Penny, who is a British writer on various TV shows there, and she told me she uses prescribed stimulants when she wants to do a big writing job because they help her to concentrate. This seems to me like a reasonable decision for adults to take.

然而，这里存在一个挑战。毫无疑问，给孩子服用像阿德拉或利他林这样的兴奋剂，短期内他们的注意力会显著提高。我采访过的所有专家，无论他们在这个问题上的立场如何，都认同这一点，而且我也亲眼见过。我认识一个小男孩，他以前总是跑来跑去、大喊大叫、精力旺盛，但服用利他林后，他竟然能安静地坐着，生平第一次能够目光坚定地注视别人。证据确凿，这种效果是真实存在的，而且是由药物引起的。我有很多成年朋友在需要集中精力完成工作项目时也会服用兴奋剂，而且效果也一样。2019年在洛杉矶，我遇到了我的朋友劳里·佩妮，她是一位英国编剧，参与过当地多个电视节目的制作。她告诉我，当她需要完成一项重要的写作任务时，她会服用处方兴奋剂，因为这些药物可以帮助她集中注意力。在我看来，成年人这样做是合情合理的。

But there is a reason why most doctors across the world are very cautious about prescribing stimulant drugs to children, and no country (with the solitary exception of Israel) comes close to prescribing them as freely as the US.

但世界上大多数医生对给儿童开兴奋剂药物都非常谨慎是有原因的，而且除了以色列之外，没有哪个国家像美国那样随意开具这类药物。

My concerns about this started to crystallise when I met with a woman named Nadine Ezard, who is the clinical director of alcohol and drug services at St Vincent’s Hospital in Sydney. She’s a doctor who works with people who have addiction problems, and by the time we met in 2015, Aussies were in the middle of a severe spike in methamphetamine addiction. For a while, doctors weren’t sure how to respond. With heroin, there is a drug they could legally prescribe to addicted people that’s a reasonable substitute, methadone – though with meth, there didn’t seem to be one. So Nadine – along with a group of other doctors – was part of a crucial experiment, licensed by the government. They started to give people addicted to meth a stimulant that is prescribed over a million times a year in the US for kids with ADHD – dextroamphetamine.

当我遇到悉尼圣文森特医院酒精和药物服务临床主任纳丁·伊扎德（Nadine Ezard）时，我对这个问题的担忧开始逐渐明朗起来。她是一位专门治疗成瘾问题的医生。2015年我们见面时，澳大利亚正经历着冰毒成瘾人数的急剧上升。一段时间内，医生们不知所措。对于海洛因，有一种可以合法处方给成瘾者使用的合理替代品——美沙酮；但对于冰毒，似乎没有这样的替代品。因此，纳丁和其他一些医生参与了一项由政府批准的关键实验。他们开始给冰毒成瘾者服用一种兴奋剂——右旋安非他明。这种兴奋剂在美国每年被开给治疗儿童多动症的处方超过一百万次。

At the time that I spoke with her, they had already tried it with fifty people, and the results of a bigger experiment are going to be published after this book comes out. She told me that when they are given these stimulants, the people addicted to meth seemed to feel less craving, because it scratched some of the same itch: ‘They say that when they first start on it, it’s the first time in a long time their brain hasn’t been focused completely on meth. That they suddenly feel this freedom.’ Speaking about one patient, she recalled: ‘He would be thinking about meth constantly. He’d be in the supermarket, [or] wherever, [and] his constant decision making would be – “Am I going to have enough money left to buy crystal?” And then [giving him dextroamphetamine] relieved him from that.’ She compared it to giving nicotine patches to smokers.

我跟她交谈时，他们已经对五十人进行了试验，更大规模的实验结果将在本书出版后公布。她告诉我，服用这些兴奋剂后，冰毒成瘾者似乎感觉毒瘾减轻了，因为这些药物缓解了他们毒瘾中的某些症状：“他们说，刚开始服用时，这是他们很久以来第一次大脑不再完全专注于冰毒。他们突然感到一种自由。” 她回忆起一位病人时说：“他总是想着冰毒。他去超市，或者任何地方，脑子里想的都是——‘我剩下的钱够买冰毒吗？’ 然后（给他服用右旋安非他明）就让他摆脱了这种想法。” 她把这比作给吸烟者使用尼古丁贴片。

She is not the only scientist discovering the similarities between methamphetamine and the other amphetamines the US routinely prescribes to children. Later, I went to see Carl Hart, professor of psychology at Columbia University, who had conducted experiments giving Adderall to people who were addicted to meth. When they were given in similar ways in the lab, these people with long-standing meth addictions responded in almost identical ways to Adderall and meth.

她并非唯一一位发现甲基苯丙胺与美国常规给儿童开具的其他苯丙胺类药物之间存在相似之处的科学家。后来，我拜访了哥伦比亚大学心理学教授卡尔·哈特，他曾进行过一项实验，给甲基苯丙胺成瘾者服用阿德拉。当在实验室中以类似方式给他们服用阿德拉时，这些长期甲基苯丙胺成瘾者对阿德拉和甲基苯丙胺的反应几乎完全相同。

Nadine’s programme is a thoughtful, compassionate way to treat people with meth addictions – but I felt unsettled to learn that the drugs we give kids turn out to be a reasonable proxy for meth. Sami told me: ‘It’s a bit bizarre when you start realising that we are prescribing legally the same substances that you are saying on the other hand are very dangerous to take if you take them illicitly … They’re chemically similar. They work in a similar way. They work on very similar neurotransmitters.’ But – as Nadine stressed to me – there are some important differences. They give higher doses to people recovering from meth addiction than children are given for ADHD. They give them as pills, which releases them more slowly into your brain than smoking or injecting. And street drugs – because they are banned and have to be sold by criminals – contain all sorts of contaminants that aren’t in the pills you get from a pharmacist. But still, it made me resolve to research the mass prescription of this drug to children some more.

纳丁的方案是一种体贴周到、充满关怀的冰毒成瘾者治疗方式——但得知我们给孩子们服用的药物竟然是冰毒的合理替代品，我感到很不安。萨米告诉我：“当你意识到我们合法开出的处方药，和你所说的非法服用非常危险的药物一样时，你会觉得有点奇怪……它们的化学成分相似，作用机制也相似，作用于非常相似的神经递质。”但是——正如纳丁向我强调的那样——两者之间存在一些重要的区别。给冰毒成瘾者服用的剂量比给患有注意力缺陷多动症的儿童服用的剂量要高。而且，这些药物是以药片的形式服用，比吸食或注射更缓慢地释放到大脑中。此外，街头毒品——因为它们是违禁品，只能由犯罪分子贩卖——含有各种各样的污染物，而这些污染物在药剂师那里买到的药片中是不存在的。但这件事仍然促使我进一步研究这种药物被大量用于儿童的情况。

For years, lots of parents were told that you could figure out if your child has ADHD in a straightforward way, related to these drugs. Many doctors told them that a normal child would become manic and high if they were given these pills, whereas an ADHD kid would slow down, focus and pay attention. But when scientists actually gave these drugs both to kids with attention problems and kids without attention problems, this turned out to be wrong. All children – indeed, all people – given Ritalin focus and pay attention better for a while. The fact the drug works isn’t evidence that you had an underlying biological problem all along – it’s just proof that you are taking a stimulant. This is why, during the Second World War, radar operators were given stimulants by the army – it made it easier for them to continue to focus on the very boring job of watching a mostly unchanging screen. It’s also why people who snort a line of stimulants then become very boring and go off on long monologues – they become very focused on their own train of thought, and filter out the bored-to-tears look on your face.

多年来，许多家长被告知，可以通过服用某些药物，以简单直接的方式判断孩子是否患有注意力缺陷多动障碍（ADHD）。许多医生告诉他们，正常的孩子服用这些药丸后会变得躁狂兴奋，而患有ADHD的孩子则会放慢速度，集中注意力。但当科学家们将这些药物分别给有注意力问题的孩子和没有注意力问题的孩子服用后，结果证明这种说法是错误的。所有服用利他林的孩子——实际上，所有服用利他林的人——在一段时间内都能更好地集中注意力。药物有效并不意味着你一直存在潜在的生物学问题——它仅仅证明你正在服用兴奋剂。这就是为什么二战期间军队会给雷达操作员服用兴奋剂——这能让他们更容易集中注意力，继续从事这项极其枯燥乏味的工作：盯着几乎一成不变的屏幕。这也是为什么吸食兴奋剂的人会变得非常无聊，并且开始滔滔不绝地自言自语——他们会非常专注于自己的思路，而忽略你脸上无聊到想哭的表情。

There is scientific evidence that there are several risks associated with giving these drugs to kids. The first risk associated with these drugs is physical – there is evidence that taking stimulants stunts a child’s growth. Kids taking a standard dose are about three centimetres shorter, over a three-year period, than they would have otherwise been. Several scientists have also warned that stimulants increase the risk of a child having heart problems and dying as a result. Obviously, heart problems are rare among children – but when millions of kids are taking these drugs, even a small increase in risk means a real rise in deaths.

有科学证据表明，给儿童服用这些药物存在多种风险。首先是生理方面的风险——有证据表明，服用兴奋剂会阻碍儿童的生长发育。服用标准剂量兴奋剂的儿童，在三年内平均身高会比正常情况下矮约三厘米。一些科学家还警告说，兴奋剂会增加儿童患心脏病甚至死亡的风险。当然，儿童心脏病的发病率很低——但当数百万儿童服用这些药物时，即使风险只增加一点点，也会导致死亡人数的显著上升。

But James Li, assistant professor of psychology, who I went to see at the University of Wisconsin in Madison, told me about what I found to be the most worrying thing. He explained: ‘We simply don’t know the long-term effects. That’s a fact.’ Most people assume – I certainly did – that these drugs have been tested and found to be safe, but he explained ‘there hasn’t been a lot of research done on long-term consequences to brain development’. This is especially concerning, he says, since ‘we’re so quick to give them to young kids. Kids are our most vulnerable population, because their brains are developing … These are drugs that operate directly on the brain, right? It’s not an antibiotic.’

但我拜访了威斯康星大学麦迪逊分校的心理学助理教授詹姆斯·李，他告诉我一些最令我担忧的事情。他解释说：“我们根本不了解这些药物的长期影响。这是事实。” 大多数人——当然我也这么认为——都以为这些药物已经过测试，证明是安全的，但他解释说，“关于这些药物对大脑发育的长期影响，目前还没有很多研究。” 他说，这一点尤其令人担忧，因为“我们总是急于给幼儿服用这些药物。儿童是我们最脆弱的群体，因为他们的大脑正在发育……这些药物是直接作用于大脑的，对吧？它们不是抗生素。”

He showed me that the best long-term research we have is in animal studies – where the findings are sobering. I read them, and they show that if you give adolescent rats Ritalin for three weeks – which is the equivalent of giving it to a human for several years – you find that the striatum, a crucial part of the brain that deals with experiencing rewards, shrinks significantly in adolescent rats. He said that you can’t assume that these drugs will affect humans the same way they affect rats, and he stressed there are some benefits to taking these drugs – but we need to be aware ‘there’s the benefit, and there’s the risk. What we currently operate under is the short-term benefit.’

他向我展示了目前最好的长期研究成果来自动物实验——而这些实验的结果令人警醒。我阅读了这些实验报告，报告显示，如果给幼鼠服用利他林三周（相当于给人类服用几年），你会发现幼鼠大脑中负责感知奖赏的关键区域——纹状体——会显著萎缩。他说，你不能想当然地认为这些药物对人类的影响与对老鼠的影响相同，他还强调服用这些药物确实有一些益处——但我们需要意识到“凡事有利必有弊。我们目前关注的只是短期益处。”

When I interviewed other scientists, I also learned that the positive effects of these drugs – while real – are surprisingly limited. At New York University, Xavier Castellanos – a professor of child and adolescent psychiatry – explained to me that the best research on the effects of stimulants found something important. They improve a child’s behaviour on tasks that require repetition, but they do not improve their learning. I frankly didn’t believe him, but then I went and looked it up in the study that the supporters of stimulant prescription had directed me to as the gold standard on ADHD research. After fourteen months on stimulants, kids performed 1.8 percent better on academic tests. But kids who for the same amount of time were simply given guidance on their behaviour improved by 1.6 percent.

当我采访其他科学家时，我也了解到，这些药物的积极作用虽然真实存在，但却出人意料地有限。纽约大学儿童和青少年精神病学教授泽维尔·卡斯特拉诺斯向我解释说，关于兴奋剂效果的最佳研究发现了一个重要的结论：它们可以改善儿童在需要重复性任务中的行为，但并不能提高他们的学习能力。坦白说，我一开始并不相信他，但后来我查阅了那些支持使用兴奋剂的人推荐给我的、被奉为多动症研究黄金标准的研究。结果显示，服用兴奋剂14个月后，孩子们的学业测试成绩提高了1.8%。而同样时间里，仅仅接受行为指导的孩子们，成绩却提高了1.6%。

Just as critically, the evidence suggests that the initial positive effects of stimulants don’t last. Anyone who takes stimulants develops tolerance for the drug – your body gets used to it, so you need a higher dose to get the same effect. Eventually, you hit the maximum dose kids are allowed to take.

同样关键的是，证据表明兴奋剂最初的积极作用并不能持久。任何服用兴奋剂的人都会对药物产生耐受性——身体会逐渐适应，因此需要更高的剂量才能达到相同的效果。最终，你会达到儿童允许服用的最大剂量。

One of the most alarmed scientists I spoke with was Dr Charles Czeisler, the sleep expert at Harvard Medical School, who told me that one of the main effects of taking stimulants is that you sleep less. This, he explained, has very worrying implications for the development of young people’s brains – particularly all the young people he sees using them so they can study longer and longer hours. ‘The pushing of all these amphetamines for these kids reminds me of the opioid crisis, except nobody’s talking about it,’ he said. ‘When I was a kid, if people gave me amphetamines, sold them to children, they would go to jail. But just like the opioid crisis … nobody does anything about it. It’s a dirty little secret in our society.’

我采访的科学家中，最感到担忧的是哈佛医学院的睡眠专家查尔斯·切斯勒博士。他告诉我，服用兴奋剂的主要影响之一就是睡眠减少。他解释说，这对年轻人的大脑发育有着非常令人担忧的影响——尤其是那些他看到为了延长学习时间而服用兴奋剂的年轻人。“向孩子们兜售安非他明让我想起了阿片类药物危机，只不过现在没人谈论这件事，”他说。“我小时候，如果有人给我安非他明，或者卖给孩子，他们就会被送进监狱。但就像阿片类药物危机一样……没人对此采取任何行动。这是我们社会中一个肮脏的小秘密。”

Most of the scientists I interviewed in the US – and I talked with a lot of the most prestigious experts on ADHD – told me that they believe prescribing stimulants is safe and provides a lot of benefits that outweigh the risks. Indeed, many US scientists argue that presenting the counterarguments – as I am doing here – is actively dangerous: it will, they say, make parents less likely to bring their kids forward to be prescribed stimulants, and as a result, those children will needlessly suffer and do worse in their lives. They also believe it may make some people quit these drugs abruptly, which is dangerous – they could go through a horrible physical withdrawal. But in the rest of the world, scientific opinion is more divided, and it’s more common to hear scepticism or outright opposition to this approach.

我采访的大多数美国科学家——其中不乏多动症领域最权威的专家——都告诉我，他们认为处方兴奋剂是安全的，而且其益处远大于风险。事实上，许多美国科学家认为，提出反驳论点——就像我在这里所做的那样——反而会造成危险：他们说，这会让家长更不愿意带孩子来接受兴奋剂治疗，结果就是这些孩子会遭受不必要的痛苦，人生轨迹也会因此变得更糟。他们还认为，这可能会导致一些人突然停药，而这很危险——他们可能会经历可怕的戒断反应。但在世界其他地区，科学界的意见则更为分歧，人们更常听到对这种做法的怀疑甚至公开反对。

There is one decisive reason why many people – like the woman I met on the Amtrak – are persuaded that their child’s attention problems are largely the result of a physical disorder. It is because they have been told that this is a problem caused primarily by their child’s genetic make-up. As I mentioned before, Professor Stephen Hinshaw told me that genes explain ‘75 to 80 percent’ of the problem, and even higher figures are often put forward. If this is a mainly biological problem, then a mainly biological solution intuitively makes sense – and the kind of interventions Sami and others argue for can only ever be additional extras. When I dug into this, I came to believe that the truth is complicated – and doesn’t really fit with the strident claims of either side of this polarised debate.

很多人——比如我在美铁列车上遇到的那位女士——之所以深信孩子的注意力问题主要是生理疾病造成的，原因只有一个：他们被告知，这主要是由孩子的基因构成决定的。正如我之前提到的，斯蒂芬·欣肖教授告诉我，基因可以解释“75%到80%”的问题，而且通常还会提出更高的比例。如果这主要是一个生物学问题，那么主要从生物学角度出发的解决方案似乎也合情合理——而萨米和其他人所主张的那种干预措施，只能算是锦上添花。但当我深入研究这个问题时，我发现真相远比这复杂——而且与这场两极分化的辩论双方的激烈论断并不完全吻合。

I was keen to understand: where do these statistics showing that a very high percentage of ADHD is caused by a genetic disorder come from? I was surprised to learn, from the scientists who put these statistics forward, that they do not come from any direct analysis of the human genome. Almost all of it comes from a much simpler method, known as twin studies. They take a pair of identical twins. If one of them has been diagnosed with ADHD, they ask, Has the other twin been diagnosed with it too? Then they take a pair of non-identical twins. If one of them has been diagnosed with ADHD, they ask, Has the other twin been diagnosed with it? They then repeat this many times, until they have a big enough sample, and they compare the figures.

我很想知道：这些显示高比例多动症是由遗传疾病引起的统计数据究竟来自哪里？令我惊讶的是，提出这些数据的科学家们告诉我，它们并非来自对人类基因组的任何直接分析。几乎所有数据都来自一种更为简单的方法，即双胞胎研究。他们选取一对同卵双胞胎。如果其中一人被诊断出患有多动症，他们会询问：另一人是否也被诊断出患有多动症？然后，他们选取一对异卵双胞胎。如果其中一人被诊断出患有多动症，他们会询问：另一人是否也被诊断出患有多动症？如此反复多次，直到获得足够大的样本量，然后比较数据。

The reason they do this is simple. All sets of twins in these studies – whether they are identical or not – grow up in the same home, with the same family, so they figure if you find a difference between the two types of twin, they reason, it can’t be down to their environment. The difference has to be explained instead by their genes. Identical twins are much more genetically similar to each other than non-identical twins, so if you discover that something is more common among identical twins, the scientists conclude there’s a genetic component. You can figure how much is determined by genes by seeing how big this gap is. This method has been used for years by all sorts of highly reputable scientists.

他们这样做的原因很简单。这些研究中所有的双胞胎——无论是否同卵——都在同一个家庭中长大，因此，如果发现两种双胞胎之间存在差异，他们推断，这不可能是环境造成的。这种差异必然是由基因决定的。同卵双胞胎的基因相似度远高于异卵双胞胎，因此，如果发现某种特征在同卵双胞胎中更为常见，科学家们就会得出结论，认为这种特征存在遗传因素。通过观察这种差异的大小，就可以确定基因决定的程度。多年来，许多享有盛誉的科学家都使用这种方法。

Whenever scientists investigate ADHD in this way, they always find that identical twins are much more likely to both be diagnosed than non-identical twins. Over twenty studies have found this result – it’s consistent. This is where the very high odds on ADHD being genetically determined come from.

每当科学家以这种方式研究多动症时，他们总是发现同卵双胞胎同时被诊断出患有多动症的概率远高于异卵双胞胎。超过二十项研究都得出了这一结论——结果一致。这就是多动症极有可能由基因决定的原因所在。

But a small group of scientists have been asking if there is a serious problem with this technique. I spoke with one of the people who has made this case in the greatest scientific detail, Dr Jay Joseph, who is a psychologist in Oakland, California. He talked me through the facts. It has been proven – in a different set of scientific studies – that identical twins do not actually experience the same environments as non-identical twins. Identical twins spend more time together than non-identical twins. They are treated more alike – by their parents, friends and schools (indeed, often people can’t tell them apart). They are more likely to become confused about their identity and to feel merged with their twin. They are psychologically closer. Jay told me that in most respects, ‘their environment’s more similar … They’re copying each other’s behaviour more. They’re being treated more alike. All of these things lead to more similar behaviour – whatever the behaviour may be.’

但一小部分科学家一直在质疑这种技术是否存在严重问题。我采访了杰伊·约瑟夫博士，他是加州奥克兰的一位心理学家，也是对此问题进行最详尽科学论证的人之一。他向我详细解释了相关事实。另一组科学研究已经证实，同卵双胞胎实际上并不像异卵双胞胎那样生活在相同的环境中。同卵双胞胎相处的时间比异卵双胞胎更长。他们受到的待遇也更相似——父母、朋友和学校都如此对待他们（事实上，人们常常分不清他们）。他们更容易对自己的身份感到困惑，并感觉与自己的双胞胎融为一体。他们在心理上也更亲近。杰伊告诉我，在大多数方面，“他们的环境更相似……他们更倾向于模仿彼此的行为。他们受到的待遇也更相似。所有这些因素都会导致更相似的行为——无论是什么行为。”

So, he explained, there is something other than genes that could explain the gap that’s showing up in all these studies. It could be accounted for by the fact that ‘identical twins grow up in a much more similar behaviour-shaping environment than non-identical twins.’ Their attention problems may be more alike not because their genes are more similar, but because their lives are more similar. If there are factors in the environment causing attention problems, identical twins are more likely to both experience them to the same extent than non-identical twins. So, he explains, ‘Twin studies are unable to disentangle the potential influences of genes and environment.’ This means the statistics we often hear – of 75 to 80 percent of ADHD being due to genetics, for example – are built on an unreliable foundation. Such figures are, Jay says, ‘misleading, and misunderstood’.

所以，他解释说，除了基因之外，还有其他因素可以解释所有这些研究中出现的差异。这可能是因为“同卵双胞胎比异卵双胞胎在更相似的、塑造行为的环境中成长”。他们的注意力问题可能更相似，并非因为他们的基因更相似，而是因为他们的生活更相似。如果环境中存在导致注意力问题的因素，那么同卵双胞胎比异卵双胞胎更有可能在相同程度上经历这些问题。因此，他解释说，“双胞胎研究无法区分基因和环境的潜在影响”。这意味着我们经常听到的统计数据——例如，75%到80%的多动症是由遗传因素造成的——是建立在不可靠的基础上的。杰伊说，这些数据“具有误导性，而且容易被误解”。

It seemed to me implausible that so many prominent scientists would draw on this technique if it was so flawed. I was conscious that in my previous books, I drew on evidence from twin studies myself. But when I asked some scientists who argue that ADHD is primarily genetically driven about the flaws in these studies, many of them readily conceded that these criticisms have some legitimacy, in a way that was disarming. Usually, they would then simply switch the conversation onto other reasons why we should believe this is a genetically based problem. (I’ll come to them in a moment.) I came to believe that twin studies are a kind of zombie technique, which people keep referencing even though they know they can’t fully defend it, because it tells us what we want to hear – that this problem is mostly in our kids’ genes.

在我看来，如果这种方法真的存在如此大的缺陷，那么这么多知名科学家居然会引用它，实在令人难以置信。我意识到，在我之前的著作中，我也曾引用过双胞胎研究的证据。但是，当我询问一些认为多动症主要由基因驱动的科学家，这些研究存在哪些缺陷时，他们中的许多人却欣然承认这些批评有一定的道理，这让我感到有些意外。通常，他们会把话题转移到其他方面，以此来解释为什么我们应该相信这是一个基因问题。（我稍后会谈到这些理由。）我逐渐意识到，双胞胎研究就像一种“僵尸技术”，人们明知无法完全捍卫它，却仍然不断地引用它，因为它迎合了我们想听到的——这个问题主要源于我们孩子的基因。

When you set aside these twin studies, Professor James Li told me, ‘time after time, every single study’ looking at the role any individual gene plays in causing ADHD finds that ‘no matter how you measure [it], it is always small. The effect of the environment is always bigger.’ So as I absorbed all this, I began to ask myself – does this mean genes play no role in ADHD? There are some people who get close to arguing this – and that is where I think the ADHD-sceptics go too far.

詹姆斯·李教授告诉我，撇开这些双胞胎研究不谈，“每一项研究都反复发现”，无论采用何种方法衡量，单个基因在导致多动症中的作用都“微乎其微。环境的影响总是更大。” 因此，在消化了这些信息之后，我开始思考——这是否意味着基因在多动症中完全不起作用？有些人似乎在论证这一点——而我认为，这正是多动症怀疑论者走得太远的地方。

James explained to me that although the twin studies overestimate the role of genes, there’s a new technique called SNP heritability, which figures out how much of a characteristic is genetically driven by using a different method from twin studies. Instead of comparing types of twin, these studies compare the genetic make-up of two totally unrelated people. It could pluck, say, you and me, and see whether match-ups in genes between us correlate with a problem we might both have – like (say) depression or obesity or ADHD. These studies currently find that around 20 to 30 percent of attention problems relate to your genes. James told me that this is a new way of studying the question and it only looks at common variation genes, so in the end the proportion caused by our genetics might end up being somewhat more than that. So it’s wrong, he explained, to dismiss a genetic component – but it’s also wrong to say it’s all or most of the problem.

詹姆斯向我解释说，虽然双胞胎研究高估了基因的作用，但有一种名为SNP遗传力的新技术，它采用与双胞胎研究不同的方法，来确定某种特征有多少是由基因驱动的。这些研究不是比较同类型的双胞胎，而是比较两个完全没有血缘关系的人的基因构成。比如，它可以选取你和我，看看我们之间的基因匹配是否与我们可能共同存在的问题相关——比如抑郁症、肥胖症或注意力缺陷多动障碍（ADHD）。这些研究目前发现，大约20%到30%的注意力问题与基因有关。詹姆斯告诉我，这是一种研究这个问题的新方法，它只关注常见的变异基因，所以最终由基因造成的比例可能比这略高一些。因此，他解释说，忽略基因因素是错误的——但说基因是全部或大部分问题的原因也是错误的。

One of the people who most helped me to understand some aspects of these questions was Professor Joel Nigg, who I interviewed at Oregon Health and Science University in Portland. He is the former president of the International Society for Research in Child and Adolescent Psychopathology, and a leading figure in this field.

在帮助我理解这些问题的某些方面方面，最有发言权的人之一是乔尔·尼格教授，我曾在波特兰的俄勒冈健康与科学大学采访过他。他是国际儿童和青少年精神病理学研究学会的前任主席，也是该领域的领军人物。

He told me it used to be thought that some kids were simply wired by their genes to be different and to develop different brains. But – as he has written – now ‘the science has moved on’. The latest research shows that ‘genes aren’t destiny; rather they affect probability.’ Alan Sroufe, who did the long-term study into what factors cause ADHD, said the same: ‘Genes don’t operate in a vacuum. That’s the main thing we’ve learned from gene studies … Genes are turned on and off in response to environmental input.’ As Joel puts it, ‘our experiences literally get under our skin’ and change how our genes are expressed.

他告诉我，过去人们认为有些孩子天生就与众不同，大脑发育也不同，这是基因决定的。但正如他所写，现在“科学已经取得了进展”。最新的研究表明，“基因并非决定命运，而是影响概率”。长期研究多动症致病因素的艾伦·斯鲁夫也表达了同样的观点：“基因并非孤立存在。这是我们从基因研究中学到的最主要一点……基因会根据环境因素而开启或关闭。”正如乔尔所说，“我们的经历会深深地影响我们”，并改变我们基因的表达方式。

To help me think about how this works, Joel offered me an analogy. He explains: ‘If your child is tired and run down, she will catch a cold at school more easily in the winter. She is more susceptible’ – but ‘if there was no cold virus’, then neither an exhausted kid nor a well-rested one would get a cold. Similarly, your genes might make you more vulnerable to a trigger in the environment – but there still has to be a trigger in the environment. He writes: ‘In some ways, the truly big news about ADHD today is that we’ve revived our interest in the environment.’

为了帮助我理解其中的原理，乔尔举了个例子。他解释说：“如果你的孩子疲惫不堪，冬天在学校就更容易感冒。她更容易感染。”——但“如果没有感冒病毒”，那么疲惫的孩子和休息充足的孩子都不会感冒。同样地，你的基因可能使你更容易受到环境中某种诱因的影响——但环境中仍然必须存在这种诱因。他写道：“在某种程度上，如今关于多动症的真正重大发现是，我们重新开始关注环境因素。”

Joel believes there is some role for stimulants. He says that in a bad situation, he believes they are better than nothing, and can give kids and parents some real relief. ‘I’m splinting a broken bone in a battlefield. I’m not healing it, you know? But at least the guy can walk off, even if he might have a crooked leg the rest of his life.’

乔尔认为兴奋剂有一定的作用。他说，在糟糕的情况下，兴奋剂总比没有强，可以给孩子和家长带来一些真正的缓解。“我就像在战场上给骨折的人固定夹板。我没法治好它，你知道吗？但至少伤者能走下战场，即使他余生可能腿都歪了。”

But if we are going to do that, he said, we crucially also need to ask: ‘Where is the problem located? Do we need to look at what our kids are facing?’ He says that kids at the moment face many large forces that we know harm their attention – stress, poor nutrition, pollution: all things I was going to investigate more after learning about them from him. ‘I would say we should not accept those things. We should not accept that our kids have to grow up in a chemical soup [of pollutants], for example. We shouldn’t accept that they have to grow up with grocery stores that hardly have any food in them that’s really food … That should change … For some kids, there’s actually something wrong with them because their environment has injured them. In that case, it’s a bit criminal to say nothing more than, in effect, “Let’s placate them with medications so that they can cope with this damaging environment we’ve created.” How is that different from giving sedatives to prisoners so they can handle being in prison?’ He believes you can only ethically give out drugs if you are also at the same time trying to solve the deeper problem.

但他表示，如果我们真要这么做，至关重要的是，我们还需要问：“问题出在哪里？我们需要关注孩子们面临的困境吗？” 他说，孩子们目前面临着许多已知会损害他们注意力的强大因素——压力、营养不良、污染：这些都是我从他那里了解到后打算深入研究的问题。“我认为我们不应该接受这些现状。例如，我们不应该接受孩子们必须在充满化学物质（污染物）的环境中长大。我们不应该接受他们必须在几乎没有真正食物的超市里长大……这种情况必须改变……对一些孩子来说，他们的确存在一些问题，因为他们的环境伤害了他们。在这种情况下，如果仅仅说‘让我们用药物安抚他们，让他们能够应对我们创造的这种有害环境’，那就有点罪不可赦了。” “这和给囚犯服用镇静剂让他们能够忍受监狱生活有什么区别？”他认为，只有在试图解决更深层次问题的同时也在努力解决更深层次的问题时，才能合乎道德地发放药物。

He looked sombre, and said: ‘There’s the old metaphor that … villagers are at the river one day, and they notice a dead body come floating down the river. So they do the right thing. They take it out and they give it an appropriate burial. The next day two bodies come down the river and they do the appropriate thing and they bury the bodies. This goes on for a while, and finally they start to wonder – I wonder where these bodies are coming down the river [from], and if we should do something to stop that? So they go up the river to find out.’

他神色凝重，说道：“有个古老的比喻是这样的……有一天，村民们在河边，发现一具尸体顺流而下。于是他们做了该做的事，把尸体捞上来，妥善安葬。第二天，又有两具尸体顺流而下，他们也做了该做的事，把尸体埋葬了。这种情况持续了一段时间，最后他们开始疑惑——这些尸体是从哪里顺流而下的？我们是不是应该做点什么阻止这种情况？于是他们溯河而上，一探究竟。”

He leaned forward in his chair and said: ‘We can treat these kids – but sooner or later, we need to figure out why is this happening.’ I realised it was time for me to go upriver.

他向前倾身坐在椅子上说：“我们可以治疗这些孩子——但迟早，我们需要弄清楚为什么会发生这种情况。”我意识到我该逆流而上了。

# ↩

14 Cause Twelve: The Confinement of Our Children, Both Physically and Psychologically

第十四条原因：对我们孩子的身心限制

A few years ago I was sitting drinking coffee at sunset in a small village at the edge of a forest in Cauca, in the south-west of Colombia. A few thousand people lived there, growing the caffeinated drinks that we glug across the world to keep ourselves alert. I watched them as they slowly unwound for the day. The adults had put tables and chairs out on the street, and they were talking and chatting in the shadow of a lush green mountain. I looked on as they wandered from table to table, when I noticed something that I rarely see in the Western world any more. All across the village, children were playing freely, without adults watching over them. Some had a hoop they were rolling along the ground in a group. Some were chasing each other around at the edge of the forest, and daring each other to run in, only to dash out again thirty seconds later, shrieking and laughing. Even very small children – they seemed to be three or four – were running around with just other kids to look out for them. Occasionally, one of the children would fall over and run back to their mother. The rest only returned home when their parents called for them at eight in the evening, and the streets would finally empty.

几年前，我在哥伦比亚西南部考卡省的一个小村庄里，夕阳西下时分，坐在森林边缘的小村庄里喝咖啡。那里居住着几千人，他们种植咖啡，而我们全世界的人都靠着这些咖啡提神醒脑。我看着他们慢慢地放松下来，结束一天的工作。大人们在街上摆了桌椅，在郁郁葱葱的山峦荫蔽下，他们谈笑风生。我看着他们从一张桌子走到另一张桌子，这时我注意到了一些在西方世界如今已难得一见的景象。整个村庄里，孩子们都在自由自在地玩耍，没有大人照看。有的孩子围着一个圆环在地上滚来滚去。有的孩子在森林边缘追逐嬉戏，互相怂恿着跑进森林，然后又在三十秒后尖叫着、大笑着冲出来。就连很小的孩子——看起来只有三四岁——也和其他孩子一起玩耍，互相照应。偶尔，会有孩子摔倒，然后跑回母亲身边。其余的孩子要等到晚上八点父母呼唤他们回家，街上才会终于空无一人。

It occurred to me that this is what childhood looked like for my parents, in very different places – an Alpine Swiss village, and a working-class Scottish tenement. They ran around freely without their parents for most of the day from when they were quite small, and only returned to eat and sleep. This is, in fact, what childhood looked like for all of my ancestors, so far as I can tell, going back thousands of years. There are periods when some children didn’t live like this – when they were forced to work in factories, for example, or during the living nightmare of chattel slavery – but in the long human story, these are extreme exceptions.

我突然意识到，这或许就是我父母截然不同的童年生活：一个是瑞士阿尔卑斯山的小村庄，一个是苏格兰工人阶级的廉租房。他们从小就经常在外面自由自在地玩耍，只有吃饭睡觉的时候才会回家。事实上，据我所知，我的祖先，可以追溯到几千年前，他们的童年生活也大致如此。当然，也有一些时期，有些孩子的生活并非如此——比如被迫在工厂里做工，或者生活在奴隶制的噩梦之中——但在漫长的人类历史中，这些都只是极端例外。

Today, I don’t know any children who live like that. In the past thirty years there have been huge changes in childhood. By 2003, in the US only 10 percent of children spent any time playing freely outdoors on a regular basis. Childhood now happens, overwhelmingly, behind closed doors, and when they do get to play, they are supervised by grown-ups, or it takes place on screens. The way children spend their time at school has also changed dramatically. The school systems in the US and Britain have been redesigned by politicians so that teachers are forced to spend the majority of their time preparing and drilling children for tests. In the US, only 73 percent of elementary schools now have any form of recess. Free play and free enquiry have fallen off a cliff.

如今，我认识的孩子中，没有一个还过着那样的生活。过去三十年间，儿童的生活发生了翻天覆地的变化。到2003年，美国只有10%的孩子能定期在户外自由玩耍。如今，孩子们绝大多数时间都待在室内，即使有机会玩耍，也往往是在大人的监督下，或者只能对着屏幕。孩子们在学校的学习方式也发生了巨大的改变。美国和英国的教育体系被政客们重新设计，迫使教师们将大部分时间用于备考和训练学生应试。在美国，现在只有73%的小学保留了课间休息时间。自由玩耍和自由探索的机会已经大幅减少。

These changes have happened so quickly, and all at once, that it’s hard to scientifically measure the effects this transformation might be having on children’s ability to pay attention and focus. We can’t randomly assign some kids to live freely in that village in Cauca, and some to live indoors in an American suburb, and come back to see how well they focus. But there is, I believe, a way we can begin to figure out some of the effects of this shift. We can do it if we break down this big transformation into its smaller constituent parts, and see what the science tells us about those effects.

这些变化发生得如此迅速，几乎是同时发生的，以至于很难用科学方法来衡量这种转变对儿童注意力集中能力的影响。我们无法随机安排一些孩子在考卡省的那个村庄自由生活，另一些孩子则住在美国郊区的室内，然后再观察他们的注意力集中情况。但我相信，我们可以通过某种方式来初步了解这种转变的一些影响。我们可以将这种巨大的转变分解成更小的组成部分，然后观察科学对这些组成部分的影响有何解释。

One of the ways I did this was by following the story of a remarkable woman I got to know named Lenore Skenazy. She’s not a scientist. She’s an activist. She was driven to try to understand how this transformation is affecting kids because of a shocking experience she had in her own life. It led her to start to work with some of the best social scientists studying these questions. Together with them, she has pioneered practical proposals to understand why so many more kids seem to be struggling to focus – and how to restore it.

我研究这一问题的方法之一，是关注一位名叫莱诺尔·斯克纳齐（Lenore Skenazy）的杰出女性的故事。她并非科学家，而是一位社会活动家。她之所以致力于了解这种转变对孩子们的影响，是因为她自身的一段痛苦经历。这段经历促使她开始与一些研究这些问题的顶尖社会科学家合作。他们共同提出了许多切实可行的方案，旨在探究为何越来越多的孩子难以集中注意力，以及如何帮助他们恢复注意力。

In the 1960s, in a suburb of Chicago, a five-year-old girl walked out of her house, alone. It was a fifteen-minute walk to Lenore’s school, and every day she did it by herself. When she got to the road near school, she was helped to safely cross by another child, a ten-year-old boy wearing a yellow sash across his chest, whose job was to stop the cars and shepherd the smaller kids across the tarmac. At the end of each school day, Lenore would walk out of the gates, again without an adult, and she would wander the neighbourhood with her friends, or try to spot four-leaf clovers, which she collected. There was often a kickball game going on outside her house that the kids would spontaneously organise and sometimes she would join in. By the time she was nine years old, when she felt like it, she would get on her bike and ride a few miles to the library to pick out books, and then curl up reading them somewhere quiet. At other times, she’d knock on her friends’ doors to see if they wanted to play. If Joel was home, they’d play Batman, and if Betsy was home, they’d play Princess and the Witch. Lenore always insisted on being the witch. Finally, when she was hungry or it started to get dark, she went home.

上世纪六十年代，在芝加哥郊区，一个五岁的小女孩独自走出家门。去莱诺尔的学校要走十五分钟，她每天都独自一人去。走到学校附近的马路时，一个十岁的男孩会帮她安全过马路。男孩胸前系着一条黄色的绶带，他的任务是拦下过往的车辆，引导小一点的孩子们安全过马路。每天放学后，莱诺尔都会独自走出校门，和朋友们在附近闲逛，或者寻找她收集的四叶草。她家门外经常有孩子们自发组织的踢球游戏，有时她也会加入。到了九岁，如果她想读，就会骑上自行车，骑行几英里去图书馆，挑选一些书，然后找个安静的地方蜷缩起来阅读。有时，她会敲朋友家的门，问他们想不想一起玩。如果乔尔在家，他们就玩蝙蝠侠；如果贝茜在家，他们就玩公主和女巫。莱诺总是坚持要当女巫。最后，当她饿了或者天色渐暗时，她就回家了。

To many of us, this scene now seems jarring, or even shocking. Across the US over the past decade, there have been many instances where people have seen children as old as nine walking unaccompanied in the street and they’ve called the police to report it as a case of parental negligence. But in the 1960s, this was the norm all over the world. Almost all children’s lives looked something like this. Being a kid meant you went out into your neighbourhood and you wandered around, found other kids, and made up your own games. Adults had only a vague idea where you were. A parent who kept their child indoors all the time, or walked them to school, or stood over them while they played, and intervened in their games, would have been regarded as crazy.

对我们许多人来说，如今这番景象显得格格不入，甚至令人震惊。过去十年间，美国各地屡屡发生这样的事件：人们看到九岁左右的孩子独自走在街上，于是报警，指控父母疏忽大意。但在上世纪六十年代，这却是世界各地司空见惯的景象。几乎所有孩子的生活都大同小异。孩童时期，他们出门在街区里闲逛，寻找其他孩子，自创游戏。大人对他们的行踪知之甚少。如果父母总是把孩子关在家里，或者送他们上学，或者在他们玩耍时站在一旁干预，都会被视为不正常。

By the time Lenore had grown up and had her own children, in New York City in the 1990s, everything had changed. She was expected to walk her own children to school and wait while they went through the gates, and then pick them up at the end of the day. Nobody let their kids out to play unsupervised, ever. Children stayed in the home all the time, unless there was an adult to watch over them. One time, Lenore took her family to a resort in Mexico, and the kids would gather every morning on the beach and play, usually at whatever game they made up among themselves. It was the only time she had ever seen her son get up before her. He would race to the beach to find the other kids. She had never seen her son so gleeful. Lenore told me: ‘What I realised is that for one week, he had what I had for my entire childhood – which was the ability to go outside, meet up with friends, and play.’

到了上世纪九十年代，莱诺尔在纽约长大成人，有了自己的孩子，一切都变了。她必须亲自送孩子上学，等他们进校门，放学后再去接他们。从来没有人让孩子独自外出玩耍。除非有大人照看，否则孩子们总是待在家里。有一次，莱诺尔带着家人去墨西哥的一个度假村，孩子们每天早上都会聚集在沙滩上玩耍，玩他们自己发明的各种游戏。那是她唯一一次看到儿子比她起得早。他会飞奔到沙滩上去找其他孩子。她从未见过儿子如此快乐。莱诺尔告诉我：“我意识到，在那一周里，他拥有了我整个童年都拥有的东西——可以出门，和朋友们见面，一起玩耍。”

Lenore thought that back home, her nine-year-old son, Izzy, still needed to have some small taste of freedom if he was going to mature. So when, one day, he asked her if he could be taken to a place in New York he’d never been to before and then be left to find his own way home, it struck her as a good idea. Her husband sat on the floor with him and helped him plan out the route he would take, and one sunny Sunday, she took him to Bloomingdales, and – with a little catch in her heart – they parted ways. An hour later, he appeared at the door of their apartment. He had taken a subway and a bus, alone. ‘He was very happy – I’d say he was levitating,’ she recalls. It seemed like such a common-sense thing to do that Lenore – who was a journalist – wrote an article telling this story, so other parents would have the confidence to do the same thing.

莱诺尔觉得，她九岁的儿子伊兹如果想要长大成人，还需要体验一下自由。所以，有一天，伊兹问她能不能带他去纽约一个他从未去过的地方，然后让他自己想办法回家。莱诺尔觉得这个主意不错。她丈夫和伊兹一起坐在地板上，帮他规划路线。在一个阳光明媚的星期天，她带他去了布鲁明戴尔百货公司，然后——带着一丝不舍——他们就此告别。一个小时后，伊兹出现在公寓门口。他独自一人坐地铁和公交车回来了。“他非常高兴——我觉得他高兴得都快飘起来了，”她回忆道。莱诺尔是一位记者，她觉得这样做合情合理，于是写了一篇文章讲述这个故事，希望其他父母也能有信心这样做。

Then something strange happened. Lenore’s article was greeted with horror and revulsion. She was denounced on many of the top news shows in the United States as ‘America’s worst mom’. She was slammed as shamefully neglectful, and she was told that she had put her own child at terrible risk. She was invited to appear on TV shows where they would put her on with a parent whose child had been kidnapped and murdered, as if it was equally likely that your child would ride the subway safely and that he would be killed. Every host would ask her a variant of: ‘But Lenore, how would you have felt if he never came home?’

然后，一件怪事发生了。莱诺尔的文章引起了轩然大波，人们纷纷表示震惊和厌恶。美国许多主流新闻节目都谴责她为“美国最糟糕的妈妈”。她被指责为可耻的疏忽职守，并被告知她让自己的孩子身处险境。她受邀参加电视节目，节目组会安排她与一位孩子被绑架谋杀的家长同台，仿佛孩子乘坐地铁安全抵达和遇害的概率一样高似的。每个主持人都会问她类似这样的问题：“莱诺尔，如果你的孩子再也回不来了，你会作何感想？”

‘I was always flabbergasted,’ Lenore told me when we sat together in her home in Jackson Heights in New York. She told them that she was simply giving her son what she – and all the adults condemning her – had taken for granted when they were kids, just a few decades before. She tried to explain to people that we live in one of the safest moments in human history. Violence against adults and children has dramatically plunged, and your children are now three times more likely to be struck by lightning than to be killed by a stranger. She asked: Would you imprison your child to prevent them being hit by lightning? Statistically, that would make more sense. People responded with disgust to this argument. Other mothers told her that every time they turned their heads, they pictured their kids being snatched. After hearing this a lot, Lenore realised, ‘That was my crime. My crime was not thinking that way. I hadn’t gone to the darkest place first and decided – oh my God, it’s not worth it. To be a good American mom is to think that way now.’ She realised that somehow, we had – in a very short period of time – ended up believing only ‘a bad mom takes her eyes off her kids’.

“我一直都感到震惊，”莱诺尔在纽约杰克逊高地的家中与我交谈时告诉我。她告诉人们，她只是在给她的儿子她——以及所有谴责她的成年人——几十年前还是孩子时习以为常的东西。她试图向人们解释，我们生活在人类历史上最安全的时期之一。针对成人和儿童的暴力事件急剧下降，现在你的孩子被闪电击中的概率是被陌生人杀害的三倍。她问道：你会为了防止孩子被闪电击中而把他们关起来吗？从统计学角度来看，这似乎更合理。人们对这种说法感到厌恶。其他母亲告诉她，她们每次转头，都会想象自己的孩子被掳走的画面。在听到很多这样的话之后，莱诺尔意识到：“这就是我的罪过。我的罪过在于没有那样想。我没有先去思考最黑暗的一面，然后决定——天哪，这不值得。” “现在，做一个好美国妈妈就应该这样想。”她意识到，不知何故，在很短的时间内，我们竟然相信“坏妈妈才会对孩子疏忽大意”。

She noticed that when a DVD of the early episodes of Sesame Street from the late 1960s was released, they had put a warning on the screen at the start. Five-year-olds are shown walking the streets on their own, talking to strangers and playing on vacant lots. The warning says: ‘The following is intended for adult viewing only and may not be suitable for our youngest viewers.’ She realised the change was so dramatic that now it was as if kids couldn’t even be allowed to see what freedom might look like. Lenore was puzzled by how quickly this ‘gigantic shift’ had happened. Children’s lives have come to be dominated by ideas ‘that are very radical and new. The idea that kids can’t play outside without this being dangerous – that has never been the case in human history. Kids have always played together, much of the time without direct adult supervision … That’s been the way for all of humanity. To suddenly say no, it’s too dangerous – it’s like saying kids should sleep upside down.’ It’s an inversion of what every previous human society has thought.
