她注意到，在20世纪60年代末《芝麻街》早期剧集的DVD发行时，开头屏幕上出现了一条警告。画面中，五岁的孩子们独自走在街上，和陌生人交谈，在空地上玩耍。警告写道：“以下内容仅供成人观看，可能不适合年龄较小的观众。”她意识到这种变化如此剧烈，以至于现在孩子们似乎连自由的模样都不能看到了。莱诺尔对这种“巨大转变”发生得如此之快感到困惑。孩子们的生活开始被“非常激进和新颖”的观念所主导。认为孩子们不能在户外玩耍而不感到危险——这在人类历史上从未发生过。孩子们一直都在一起玩耍，很多时候都没有成年人的直接监督……这才是全人类的生存之道。突然说不行，太危险了——这就像说孩子应该倒着睡一样。这完全颠覆了以往所有人类社会的想法。

As I spent a lot of time with Lenore, I came to believe that to understand the effects of this change, we need to break it down into five different components and look at the scientific evidence behind each one. The first is the most obvious. For years, scientists have been discovering a broad body of evidence showing that when people run around – or engage in any form of exercise – their ability to pay attention improves. For example, one study that investigated this found that exercise provides ‘an exceptional boost’ to attention in children. Professor Joel Nigg, who I interviewed in Portland, has summarised the evidence clearly – he explains that ‘for developing children, aerobic exercise expands the growth of brain connections, the frontal cortex, and the brain chemicals that support self-regulation and executive functioning’. Exercise causes changes that ‘make the brain grow more and get more efficient’. The evidence showing this is so broad that these findings should be regarded, he writes, as ‘definite’. The evidence couldn’t be clearer: if you stop kids from acting on their natural desire to run around, on average, their attention, and the overall health of their brains, will suffer.

由于我与莱诺尔相处的时间很长，我逐渐意识到，要理解这种变化的影响，我们需要将其分解为五个不同的组成部分，并考察每个部分背后的科学证据。第一个部分最显而易见。多年来，科学家们发现了大量证据表明，当人们跑步或进行任何形式的运动时，他们的注意力会得到提高。例如，一项研究发现，运动能“显著提升”儿童的注意力。我在波特兰采访的乔尔·尼格教授清晰地总结了这些证据——他解释说，“对于发育中的儿童来说，有氧运动可以促进大脑连接、额叶皮层以及支持自我调节和执行功能的脑化学物质的生长”。运动引起的变化“使大脑生长得更多，效率更高”。他写道，这些证据如此广泛，以至于这些发现应该被视为“确凿无疑的”。证据再清楚不过了：如果你阻止孩子们满足他们奔跑玩耍的自然欲望，平均而言，他们的注意力以及大脑的整体健康都会受到影响。

But Lenore suspected there might be a way this is harming kids that is even deeper. She started to seek out the leading scientists who have studied these questions – including professor of psychology Peter Gray, evolutionary primatologist Dr Isabel Behncke and social psychologist Professor Jonathan Haidt. They taught her that in fact it is when children play that they learn their most important skills – the ones they need for their whole lives.

但莱诺尔怀疑，这种做法可能对孩子造成更深层次的伤害。她开始寻找研究这些问题的顶尖科学家，包括心理学教授彼得·格雷、进化灵长类动物学家伊莎贝尔·贝恩克博士和社会心理学家乔纳森·海特教授。他们告诉她，事实上，孩子们正是在玩耍中学习他们最重要的技能——那些他们一生都需要的技能。

To understand this second component of the change that has taken place – the deprivation of play – picture again that scene on Lenore’s street when she was a child back in that Chicago suburb, or the scene I saw in Colombia. What skills are the kids learning there, as they play freely with each other? For starters, if you’re a kid and you’re on your own with other kids, ‘You figure out how to make something happen,’ Lenore says. You have to use your creativity to come up with a game. You then have to persuade the other kids that your game is the best one they could play. Then ‘you figure out how to read people enough so that the game keeps going’. You have to learn how to negotiate when it’s your turn and when it’s their turn – so you have to learn about other people’s needs and desires, and how to meet them. You learn how to cope with being disappointed, or frustrated. You learn all this ‘through being excluded, through coming up with a new game, through getting lost, through climbing the tree and [then] somebody says, “Climb higher!” and you can’t decide if you will or you won’t. Then you do, and it’s exhilarating, and then you climb a little higher the next time – or you climb a little higher and it’s so scary that you’re crying … And yet: now you’re on top. These are all crucial forms of attention.’

要理解这第二个变化——玩耍的缺失——请再次想象一下莱诺尔小时候在芝加哥郊区街头看到的景象，或者我在哥伦比亚看到的景象。孩子们在那里自由玩耍时，能学到哪些技能呢？首先，如果你是一个孩子，独自和其他孩子在一起，“你会想办法让游戏进行下去，”莱诺尔说。你必须发挥创造力，想出一个游戏。然后，你必须说服其他孩子，你的游戏是他们能玩的最好的游戏。接着，“你得学会如何察言观色，让游戏继续下去”。你必须学会如何协商何时轮到你，何时轮到别人——所以你必须了解他人的需求和愿望，以及如何满足它们。你还要学会如何应对失望或沮丧。你通过被排斥、通过创造新游戏、通过迷路、通过爬树（然后）有人说“爬得更高！”而犹豫不决地决定是爬还是不爬，来学习这一切。然后你爬了上去，感觉很兴奋，然后下次你爬得更高一些——或者你爬得更高一些，却因为太过害怕而哭了起来……然而：现在你站在了顶端。这些都是至关重要的注意力形式。

One of Lenore’s intellectual mentors, Dr Isabel Behncke, the Chilean expert on play, told me when we sat together in Scotland that the scientific evidence we have so far suggests ‘there are three main areas [of child development] where play has a major impact. One is creativity and imagination’ – it’s how you learn to think about problems and solve them. The second is ‘social bonds’ – it’s how you learn to interact with other people and socialise. And the third is ‘aliveness’ – it’s how you learn to experience joy and pleasure. The things we learn from play aren’t trivial add-ons to becoming a functioning human being, Isabel explained. They are the core of it. Play builds the foundation of a solid personality, and everything that adults sit down and explain to the child afterwards builds on this base. If you want to be a person who can pay attention fully, she told me, you need this base of free play.

莱诺尔的一位精神导师，智利游戏研究专家伊莎贝尔·贝恩克博士，曾在苏格兰与我交谈时告诉我，目前已有的科学证据表明，“游戏对儿童发展的三个主要领域有着重大影响。第一是创造力和想象力”——它教会你思考和解决问题。第二是“社会关系”——它教会你如何与他人互动和社交。第三是“活力”——它教会你如何体验快乐和愉悦。伊莎贝尔解释说，我们从游戏中学到的东西并非成为一个健全人格的无关紧要的附加品，而是其核心。游戏构建了稳固人格的基础，之后成年人坐下来向孩子解释的一切都建立在这个基础之上。她告诉我，如果你想成为一个能够全神贯注的人，你需要这种自由游戏的根基。

Yet suddenly, we have been ‘taking all this out of kids’ lives,’ Lenore says. Today, even when children do finally get to play, it’s mainly supervised by adults, who set the rules and tell them what to do. On Lenore’s street when she was a kid, everyone played softball and policed the rules themselves. Today, they go to organised activities where the adults intervene all the time to tell them what the rules are. Free play has been turned into supervised play, and so – like processed food – it has been drained of most of its value. This means that now, as a kid, Lenore said, ‘you’re not getting that [chance to develop these skills] – because you’re in a car being driven to a game where somebody tells you what position you’re playing, and when to catch the ball, and when it’s your time to hit, and who’s bringing the snack, and you can’t bring grapes because they have to be cut into quarters and it’s your mom’s job to do that… That’s a very different childhood, because you haven’t experienced the give-and-take of life that’s going to prepare you for adulthood.’ As a result, kids are ‘not having the problems and the exhilaration of getting there on their own.’ One day, Barbara Sarnecka, an associate professor of cognitive sciences at the University of California, Irvine, told Lenore that today ‘adults are saying: “Here’s the environment. I’ve already mapped it. Stop exploring.” But that’s the opposite of what childhood is.’

然而，莱诺尔说，我们却突然“把这一切都从孩子们的生活中剥夺了”。如今，即使孩子们终于有机会玩耍，也大多是在成年人的监督下，由成年人制定规则，告诉他们该做什么。莱诺尔小时候，在她住的那条街上，大家都在玩垒球，规则都是大家自己遵守的。而现在，孩子们参加各种有组织的活动，成年人却总是插手，告诉他们规则是什么。自由玩耍变成了受监督的玩耍，就像加工食品一样，它失去了大部分价值。这意味着，莱诺尔说，现在的孩子们“没有机会培养这些技能——因为你坐在车里，被送到比赛场地，有人告诉你打什么位置，什么时候接球，什么时候轮到你击球，谁带零食，你不能带葡萄，因为葡萄必须切成四瓣，那是你妈妈的工作……这是一种截然不同的童年，因为你没有体验过生活中那种需要付出和收获的过程，而这种过程会让你为成年做好准备。”结果，孩子们“没有经历解决问题的挑战，也没有体验到独自探索的乐趣”。有一天，加州大学欧文分校认知科学副教授芭芭拉·萨内卡告诉莱诺尔，如今“成年人会说：‘这就是环境。我已经绘制好了地图。别再探索了。’但这与童年的本质截然相反。”

Lenore wanted to know: now that they are effectively under house arrest, what are kids doing with the time they used to spend playing? One study of this found that this time is now overwhelmingly spent on homework (which exploded by 145 percent between 1981 and 1997), screens, and shopping with their parents. A 2004 study found that US kids spent 7.5 hours more each week on academics than they had twenty years before.

莱诺尔想知道：孩子们现在实际上被软禁在家，他们以前用来玩耍的时间都用来做什么了？一项研究发现，这些时间现在几乎全部花在了家庭作业上（1981年至1997年间，家庭作业量激增了145%）、电子屏幕以及和父母一起购物上。2004年的一项研究发现，美国孩子每周花在学习上的时间比20年前多了7.5小时。

Isabel told me the schools squeezing out play are ‘making a huge mistake’. She said: ‘I would first ask them – what is their objective? What are you trying to achieve?’ Presumably, they want children to learn. ‘I just can’t see where these people get their insights from, because all the evidence shows it’s the other way round: our brains are more supple, more plastic, more creative’ when we have had the chance to ‘learn through play. The primary technology for learning is play. You learn to learn in play. And in a world where information is always changing, why do you want to fill their heads with information? We have no idea what the world will be in twenty years. Surely we want to be creating brains that are adaptable, and have the capacity to assess context, and can be thinking critically. All these things are trained through play. So it’s so misguided, it’s unbelievable.’

伊莎贝尔告诉我，那些取消游戏时间的学校“犯了个大错”。她说：“我首先会问他们——他们的目标是什么？你们想达到什么目的？”想必，他们是想让孩子们学习。“我实在不明白这些人是从哪里得出这种结论的，因为所有证据都表明事实恰恰相反：当我们有机会‘通过游戏学习’时，我们的大脑会更灵活、更具可塑性、更有创造力。游戏是学习的主要方式。你在游戏中学会学习。在一个信息瞬息万变的世界里，为什么要把信息塞满他们的脑袋呢？我们根本不知道二十年后世界会变成什么样。我们当然希望培养的是适应性强、能够评估情境、能够批判性思考的大脑。所有这些都是通过游戏来培养的。所以这种做法太荒谬了，简直难以置信。”

This led Lenore to explore the third component of this change. Professor Jonathan Haidt – a leading social psychologist – has argued that there has been a big rise in anxiety among children and teens, in part because of this play deprivation. When a child plays, he learns the skills that make it possible to cope with the unexpected. If you deprive children of those challenges, as they grow up they will feel panicked and unable to cope a lot of the time. They don’t feel they are competent, or can make things happen without older people guiding them. Haidt argues this is one reason why anxiety is sky-rocketing – and there is strong scientific evidence that if you are anxious, your attention will suffer.

这促使莱诺尔去探究这一变化的第三个组成部分。著名社会心理学家乔纳森·海特教授认为，儿童和青少年焦虑症的大幅上升，部分原因在于玩耍时间的匮乏。孩子们在玩耍中学习应对意外情况的技能。如果剥夺了孩子们的这些挑战，他们长大后就会经常感到恐慌和无力应对。他们会觉得自己能力不足，或者无法在没有长辈指导的情况下独立完成事情。海特认为，这正是焦虑症飙升的原因之一——而且有强有力的科学证据表明，焦虑会影响注意力。

Lenore believes there is also a fourth factor at work. To understand it, you have to grasp a discovery that was made by the scientist Ed Deci, a professor of psychology who I interviewed in Rochester in upstate New York, and his colleague Richard Ryan, who I also spoke with. Their research uncovered that all human beings have within us two different kinds of motivation for why we do anything. Imagine you are a runner. If you go running in the morning because you love how it feels – the wind in your hair, the sense that your body is powerful and it’s carrying you forward – that’s an ‘intrinsic’ motive. You’re not doing it to get some other reward further down the line; you’re doing it because you love it. Now imagine you go running not because you love it, but because you have a drill-sergeant dad who forces you to get up and run with him. Or imagine you go running in order to post the videos of you shirtless on Instagram and you’re hooked on getting the hearts and ‘yum, you’re so hot’ comments you receive. That would be an ‘extrinsic’ motive to run. You’re not doing it because the act itself gives you a sense of pleasure or fulfilment – you are doing it because you have been forced to, or to get something out of it further down the line.

莱诺尔认为还有第四个因素在起作用。要理解这一点，你必须了解科学家埃德·德西（Ed Deci）和他同事理查德·瑞安（Richard Ryan）的一项发现。德西是一位心理学教授，我在纽约州北部的罗切斯特采访了他。他们的研究揭示，我们每个人做任何事的动机都有两种。想象一下你是一名跑步爱好者。如果你早上跑步是因为你喜欢跑步的感觉——风吹拂着你的头发，感觉身体充满力量，带着你向前奔跑——这就是一种“内在”动机。你跑步不是为了获得某种回报；你跑步是因为你热爱跑步。现在想象一下，你跑步不是因为热爱跑步，而是因为你有个严厉的父亲，强迫你起床和他一起跑步。或者想象一下，你跑步是为了在Instagram上发布你赤膊的视频，你沉迷于收到的点赞和“哇，你真性感”之类的评论。那是一种“外在”的逃跑动机。你逃跑并不是因为逃跑行为本身给你带来快乐或满足感——而是因为你被迫逃跑，或是为了从中获得某种后续好处。

Richard and Ed discovered that it’s easier to focus on something, and stick at it, if your motives are intrinsic – if you are doing something because it’s meaningful to you – than if your motives are extrinsic, and you’re doing it because you are forced to, or to get something out of it afterwards. The more intrinsic your motivation, the easier it will be to sustain your attention.

理查德和艾德发现，如果你的动机是内在的——也就是你做这件事是因为它对你有意义——那么你更容易专注于某件事并坚持下去；而如果你的动机是外在的，比如被迫去做，或者为了事后获得某种好处，那么你就很难做到这一点。你的动机越是内在的，就越容易保持注意力集中。

Lenore came to suspect that children in this new and radically different model of childhood are being deprived of the chance to develop intrinsic motives. Most people, she said, ‘learn focus by doing something that is either very important or very interesting to them’. You ‘learn the habit of focus by being interested in something enough that you notice what’s going on, and you process it … The way you learn to focus is automatic if there’s something that interests you … or absorbs you, or thrills you.’ But if you are a kid today, you live almost all of your life according to what adults tell you to do. She asked me: ‘How do you find meaning when your day is filled from seven in the morning to nine at night when you go to bed, with somebody else’s idea of what is important? … If you don’t have any free time to figure out what [emotionally] turns you on, I’m not sure you’re going to find meaning. You’re not given any time to find meaning.’

莱诺尔开始怀疑，在这种全新的、截然不同的儿童教育模式下，孩子们被剥夺了发展内在动机的机会。她说，大多数人“通过做对他们来说非常重要或非常有趣的事情来培养专注力”。你“通过对某件事足够感兴趣，从而养成专注的习惯，你会注意到正在发生的事情，并进行思考……如果你对某件事感兴趣……或者让你全神贯注，或者让你兴奋不已，那么你学习专注的方式就是自动的。”但如果你是一个现在的孩子，你几乎一生都在按照成年人的指示生活。她问我：“当你从早上七点到晚上九点睡觉，一天都被别人认为重要的事情填满时，你如何找到意义？……如果你没有自由时间去弄清楚什么能让你（在情感上）兴奋，我不确定你是否能找到意义。你根本没有时间去寻找意义。”

As a child, wandering around her neighbourhood, Lenore had the freedom to figure out what excited her – reading, writing, playing dress-up – and to pursue these things when she wanted to. Other kids learned they loved soccer, or climbing, or little scientific experiments. That was at least one way they learned attention and focus. That route is largely being cut off for kids now. She asked me: if your attention is constantly managed by other people, how can it develop? How do you learn what fascinates you? How do you find your intrinsic motives, the ones that are so important to developing attention?

小时候，莱诺尔在街区里闲逛，可以自由自在地探索自己喜欢的东西——读书、写作、玩角色扮演——并随时去做。其他孩子则发现自己热爱足球、攀岩，或者做一些小实验。这至少是他们培养专注力的一种方式。而现在，孩子们的这条路大多被堵死了。她问我：如果你的注意力总是被别人掌控，它怎么可能发展？你怎么才能发现自己真正感兴趣的是什么？你怎么才能找到内在的动力，那些对培养专注力至关重要的动力？

After learning all this, Lenore was so worried about what we are doing to our kids that she started to tour the country, urging parents to let their children play in a free, unstructured, unsupervised way some of the time. She set up a group named Let Grow, designed to promote free play and freedom to explore for kids. She would say to the parents: ‘I want everybody to think back to your own childhood’ and to describe ‘something that you loved – absolutely loved – to do, that you don’t let your own children do’. Their eyes would light up with memories. They would tell her: ‘ “We built forts. We played manhunt.” I met a guy the other day who played marbles. I said, “What was your favourite marble?” He said, “Oh, it was burgundy, and it was a swirl.” You could just see this love of something from so long ago. It infused him with joy.’ The parents admitted that ‘they all rode their bikes. They all climbed trees. They all went to town and got candy.’ But then they said it was much too dangerous today to allow their kids to do the same.

了解了这一切之后，莱诺尔非常担心我们对孩子们的所作所为，于是她开始在全国巡回演讲，呼吁家长们偶尔让孩子们自由自在、无拘无束地玩耍。她成立了一个名为“让孩子成长”（Let Grow）的组织，旨在推广儿童自由玩耍和探索。她会对家长们说：“我想请大家回想一下自己的童年”，并描述一下“你曾经非常喜欢做，但却不让自己的孩子做的事情”。家长们的眼中会闪烁着回忆的光芒。他们会告诉她：“我们搭堡垒，我们玩捉迷藏。前几天我遇到一个玩弹珠的男孩。我问他：‘你最喜欢哪颗弹珠？’他说：‘哦，是酒红色的，上面有漩涡纹。’你能感受到他对很久以前玩的东西的热爱，那份热爱让他充满了喜悦。”家长们也承认，“他们都骑自行车，他们都爬树。”他们都去镇上买了糖果。但后来他们又说，现在太危险了，不能让自己的孩子也这样做。

Lenore would explain how absolutely minuscule the risk of kidnapping is – and that violence is lower now than when they were young. This is not, she added, because we hide our kids away – we know that because violence against adults has also massively fallen, and they still move around freely. Parents would nod, and keep their kids indoors nonetheless. She would explain the clear benefits of free play. Parents would nod, and still they wouldn’t let their kids out. Nothing seemed to work. She became more and more frustrated. She began to conclude that ‘even the people who are on our side, or who wonder what happened … they can’t let go’. She realised ‘you can’t be the only people [doing it] – because then you’re the crazy person sending your kid’ out alone.

莱诺尔会解释说，绑架的风险微乎其微——而且现在的暴力事件比他们小时候少得多。她补充说，这并不是因为我们把孩子藏起来——我们知道这一点，是因为针对成年人的暴力事件也大幅下降，而他们仍然可以自由活动。父母们会点头，但仍然把孩子关在家里。她会解释自由玩耍的明显好处。父母们会点头，但仍然不让孩子出门。似乎什么方法都不管用。她越来越沮丧。她开始得出结论：“即使是那些站在我们这边的人，或者那些想知道发生了什么事的人……他们也无法放手。”她意识到“你不能是唯一这么做的人——因为那样的话，你就会变成那个把孩子独自送出去的疯子。”

So she asked herself: what if we did this differently? What if we stopped trying to change parents’ minds, and started trying to change their behaviour instead – and what if we tried to change them not as isolated individuals, but as a group? With those thoughts, Lenore became a part of a crucial experiment.

于是她问自己：如果我们换个方式呢？如果我们不再试图改变父母的想法，而是尝试改变他们的行为——而且如果我们不是把他们当作孤立的个体，而是把他们当作群体来改变呢？带着这些想法，莱诺尔参与了一项至关重要的实验。

One day, Roanoke Avenue Elementary, a school on Long Island, decided to take part in something called Global Play Day, where for one day a year, kids are allowed to play freely and create their own fun. The teachers filled four of their classrooms with empty boxes and Lego and some old toys, and they said, Go play. You get to choose what you do. Donna Verbeck, who had been a teacher at the school for more than twenty years, watched the kids, expecting to see glee and laughter – but she quickly realised something was wrong. Some of the kids plunged in and started playing right away, as she’d expected – but a large number of the children just stood there. They stared at the boxes and the Lego and the handful of children who were starting to improvise games, but they didn’t move. They watched, inert, for a long time. Finally one of the kids, puzzled by the experience and unsure what to do, lay down in a corner and went to sleep.

有一天，长岛罗阿诺克大道小学决定参加“全球游戏日”活动。在这一天，孩子们可以自由玩耍，创造属于自己的乐趣。老师们在四个教室里摆满了空纸箱、乐高积木和一些旧玩具，然后说：“去玩吧！你们自己决定玩什么。” 在这所学校任教二十多年的唐娜·维贝克看着孩子们，原本以为会看到欢声笑语——但她很快意识到情况不对劲。正如她所料，一些孩子立刻投入到游戏中——但更多的孩子只是站在那里。他们盯着纸箱、乐高积木，以及少数几个开始即兴游戏的孩子，却一动不动。他们呆呆地看着，很久很久。最后，一个孩子被眼前的景象弄得不知所措，便躺在角落里睡着了。

Suddenly, Donna realised, as she explained to me later: ‘They don’t know what to do. They don’t know how to get involved when somebody else is playing, or how to just start free play by themselves. They just did not know how to do it.’ Thomas Payton, who was the principal, added: ‘And we’re not talking one or two kids. There were a lot of kids like that.’ Donna felt shaken, and sad. She realised that these kids had never been set free to play before. Their attention had been constantly managed for them by adults for their whole lives.

唐娜突然意识到，正如她后来跟我解释的那样：“他们不知道该做什么。当别人在玩的时候，他们不知道该如何融入，也不知道该如何自己开始自由玩耍。他们就是不知道该怎么做。”校长托马斯·佩顿补充道：“而且我们说的不是一两个孩子。有很多孩子都是这样的。”唐娜感到震惊和难过。她意识到，这些孩子以前从未真正自由地玩耍过。他们的注意力从小到大都被大人掌控着。

So Roanoake Avenue Elementary decided to become one of the first schools to sign up to the programme that Lenore leads. Let Grow is based on the idea that if children are going to become adults who can make their own decisions and pay attention, they need to experience increasing levels of freedom and independence throughout their childhood. When a school signs up, they commit that one day a week, or once a month, a child’s ‘homework’ will be to go home and do something new, independently, without adult supervision, and then report back on it. They would choose their own mission. Every child, when they go out into the world, is given a card to show to any adult who stops them to ask where their parents are. It says: ‘I’m not lost or neglected. If you think it’s wrong for me to be on my own, please read Huckleberry Finn and visit letgrow.org. Remember your own childhood. Was your parent with you every second? And with today’s crime rate back to what it was in 1963, it is safer to play outside now than when you were at my age. Let me grow.’

因此，罗阿诺克大道小学决定成为首批加入莱诺尔领导的“让孩子成长”项目的学校之一。“让孩子成长”项目的理念是，如果孩子们想要成长为能够独立做决定、专注思考的成年人，他们需要在整个童年时期体验到不断增强的自由和独立。学校加入该项目后，承诺每周或每月有一天，让孩子们回家后独立完成一项新的、无需成人监督的任务，然后向学校汇报。孩子们可以自由选择自己的任务。每个孩子外出时都会拿到一张卡片，以便向任何拦住他们询问父母下落的成年人出示。卡片上写着：“我没有迷路，也没有被忽视。如果你认为我独自一人是不对的，请读读《哈克贝利·费恩历险记》，并访问letgrow.org网站。想想你自己的童年。你的父母是否每时每刻都陪伴在你身边？如今的犯罪率已经恢复到1963年的水平，所以现在在户外玩耍比你小时候安全多了。”让我成长。

I went to meet the kids who had been taking part in this programme at Roanoke for over a year. It’s in a poor neighbourhood with a lot of parents who are financially struggling, and many who are recent immigrants. The first group I met were nine years old, and they jostled to tell me about what they had done as part of their project with a gleeful energy. One of them set up a lemonade stand on his street. Another had walked down to the local river and collected the trash that had built up there, because she said this would ‘save the turtles’. (A few of the other kids joined in when she said this and shouted, ‘Save the turtles! Save them!’) A little girl told me that, before this project: ‘Well, I’d literally sit in front of a TV all day. It doesn’t really pop into your head to do stuff.’ But for Let Grow, the first thing she did was cook something for her mother on her own. She waved her hands excitedly as she described it. It seemed to have blown her mind – to discover that she could do something.

我去罗阿诺克见了参加这个项目一年多的孩子们。罗阿诺克是一个贫困社区，很多家长经济拮据，其中不乏新移民。我遇到的第一批孩子只有九岁，他们兴高采烈地争先恐后地跟我讲述他们在项目中的所作所为。其中一个孩子在街上摆了个柠檬水摊。另一个孩子走到附近的河边，捡拾河里堆积的垃圾，因为她说这样做可以“拯救海龟”。（她说完后，其他几个孩子也跟着喊：“拯救海龟！拯救它们！”）一个小女孩告诉我，在参加这个项目之前：“我整天就坐在电视机前。根本不会想到要去做点什么。”但参加“让孩子成长”项目后，她做的第一件事就是自己给妈妈做了一顿饭。她一边兴奋地挥舞着双手，一边描述着。她似乎震惊不已——发现自己竟然能做到这件事。

I also wanted with talk to the kids who didn’t immediately volunteer their stories, so I spoke with a pale, rather serious-faced boy. He told me quietly: ‘We have a rope [in our backyard] that’s connected to a tree.’ It had never crossed his mind to try to climb it, ‘But I finally said – well, I could at least try to do it.’ He managed to get a little way up. He offered a sly little beam of a smile as he described how it felt to be climbing for the first time.

我还想和那些没有主动讲述自己故事的孩子们聊聊，于是我和一个脸色苍白、表情略显严肃的男孩交谈起来。他轻声告诉我：“我们后院有一根绳子连着一棵树。”他以前从未想过要爬上去，“但我最终还是决定——好吧，我至少可以试试。”他爬上去一段距离。在描述第一次攀爬的感受时，他脸上露出了一丝狡黠的微笑。

Some of the kids discovered new ambitions. In Donna’s class, there was a boy I’ll call L.B., who wasn’t particularly academic, and had often been distracted or bored in lessons. There was a constant struggle between him and his mom to get him to read or do his homework. He chose as his Let Grow project to build a replica of a boat. He assembled a piece of wood, a foam core, a hot-glue gun, and toothpicks and thread, and he sat night after night, intensely working on it. He tried one set of techniques, and the boat fell apart – so he tried again, and again. Once he had successfully built this small boat and showed it to his friends, he decided he was going to build something bigger – a life-size wagon that he could sleep in, in his yard. He took an old door that was in his garage, and his dad’s wrenches and screwdrivers, and he started to read about how to put all this together. He persuaded his neighbours to give him some old bamboo they had lying around in their garden, to use for the frame. Before long, L.B. had a wagon.

有些孩子发现了新的抱负。在唐娜的班上，有个男孩，我姑且叫他L.B.，他学习成绩不太好，上课经常走神或者觉得无聊。他和他妈妈总是要费一番功夫才能让他看书或做作业。他选择用“放手成长”项目来制作一艘船的模型。他准备了一块木板、一块泡沫板、一把热熔胶枪、牙签和线，然后夜以继日地埋头苦干。他尝试了一种方法，结果船散架了——于是他又试了一遍，一遍又一遍。当他成功地制作出这艘小船并把它展示给朋友们后，他决定要制作一个更大的东西——一辆真人大小的马车，可以睡在里面，放在自家院子里。他从车库里拿出一扇旧门，还有他爸爸的扳手和螺丝刀，开始阅读如何把这些东西组装起来。他劝说邻居们把花园里闲置的一些旧竹子给他，用来做框架。不久之后，L.B.就拥有了一辆马车。

Then he decided he wanted to do something even more ambitious – to build an amphibious wagon, one he could push out onto the ocean. So he started to read about how to build things that float. When I talked with L.B., he described the process of building it in detail. He told me he was going to build another wagon next: ‘I have to figure out how I’m going to cut the hula hoops to go on it, and then I got to lay shrink-wrap over it.’ I asked him how this project made him feel. ‘It’s different because I’m actually using my hands on materials … I think it’s cool to just have your hands on something instead of seeing it on a screen, not really being able to touch it.’ I went to meet his mother, who worked in medical billing, and she told me: ‘I don’t think, as a parent, I realised how much he could do on his own.’ She saw him change: ‘I could see the confidence – and him wanting to do more and more and figure it out his way.’ She glowed with pride. Her struggles to get him to read had ended, because now he was reading all the time about how to build stuff.

然后他决定挑战一个更宏大的目标——造一辆水陆两用车，一辆可以推到海面上的车。于是他开始研究如何制造漂浮物。我和L.B.交谈时，他详细地描述了建造过程。他告诉我接下来他还要造另一辆车：“我得想想怎么把呼啦圈裁好装上去，然后还得在上面包一层收缩膜。”我问他这个项目让他感觉如何。 “这不一样，因为我能亲手操作材料……我觉得能亲手触摸实物比在屏幕上看要酷得多，那种感觉就像触摸到了实物一样。”我去见了他的母亲，她从事医疗账单处理工作。她告诉我：“作为家长，我以前并没有意识到他能独立完成这么多事情。”她亲眼见证了他的变化：“我能感受到他的自信——以及他渴望尝试更多、用自己的方式解决问题的愿望。”她满脸自豪。她之前为了让他爱上阅读而付出的努力终于结束了，因为现在他一直在阅读关于如何动手制作东西的书籍。

It struck me: when L.B. was being told what to do constantly – when he was being forced to act on extrinsic motivations – he couldn’t focus, and he was bored all the time. But when he was given the chance, through play, to find out what interested him – to develop an intrinsic motivation – his ability to focus flourished, and he worked for hours and hours without a break, building his boats and wagons.

我突然意识到：当L.B.总是被告知该做什么——当他被迫受外在激励驱使时——他无法集中注意力，总是感到无聊。但当他有机会通过游戏发现自己的兴趣所在——培养内在动力时——他的专注力就突飞猛进，他可以连续几个小时不停地制作船只和马车。

His teacher, Donna, told me L.B. changed in class after that. His reading hugely improved, and ‘he didn’t consider it to be “reading”, because it was his hobby. It was something he really, really liked.’ He started to gain status among the other kids – whenever they wanted to build anything, the cry would go up to find L.B., because he knew how to do it. She told me that – as with all the deepest learning – ‘Nobody taught him. His mom and dad just let him do it… He just used his own head and really taught himself.’ Gary Karlson, another teacher there, told me: ‘That learning is going to do more for that kid than anything academic that we could’ve brought to him through his time here.’

他的老师唐娜告诉我，L.B.在那之后在课堂上的表现就变了。他的阅读能力突飞猛进，“他不再把阅读当成‘阅读’，因为那是他的爱好。那是他真心喜欢的事情。” 他开始在其他孩子中崭露头角——每当他们想做点什么，都会大声喊着去找L.B.，因为他知道怎么做。唐娜告诉我，就像所有最深刻的学习一样，“没有人教过他。他的父母只是让他自己去学……他完全靠自己，真正地自学成才。” 另一位老师加里·卡尔森告诉我：“这种自学对这个孩子的影响，比我们在这里教给他的任何学术知识都大。”

As I talked with L.B., I thought about another aspect of attention that I had been taught about by scientists – one that is, I think, the fifth way in which we are currently hobbling our children’s attention. In Aarhus in Denmark, Jan Tonnesvang, a Professor of Psychology there, had told me that we all need to have a sense of what he called ‘mastery’ – that we are good at something. It’s a basic human psychological need. When you feel you are good at something, you will find it much easier to focus on it, and if you feel incompetent, your attention will shrivel like a salted snail. When I listened to L.B., I realised that we have a school system right now that is so narrow that it makes a lot of kids (especially boys, I think) feel that they aren’t good at anything. Their experience of school is constantly being made to feel incompetent. But once L.B. started to feel he could master something – that he could become good at it – his focus began to form.

在和L.B.交谈时，我想到了科学家们教给我的关于注意力的另一个方面——我认为这是我们目前正在阻碍孩子注意力发展的第五种方式。在丹麦奥胡斯，心理学教授扬·托内斯旺告诉我，我们都需要一种他称之为“掌控感”的感觉——也就是我们擅长某件事的感觉。这是人类的基本心理需求。当你觉得自己擅长某件事时，你会更容易集中注意力；如果你觉得自己能力不足，你的注意力就会像被腌过的蜗牛一样萎缩。听L.B.讲述时，我意识到我们目前的教育体系过于狭隘，导致很多孩子（尤其是男孩，我想）觉得自己一无是处。他们在学校的经历不断地让他们觉得自己很无能。但是，一旦L.B.开始觉得自己可以掌握某件事——觉得自己可以擅长它——他的注意力就开始集中起来了。

I went to see another aspect of the programme, half an hour’s drive away at a local middle school, in a wealthier part of Long Island. The teacher Jodi Maurici told me she realised her students needed a Let Grow program when thirty-nine out of her 200 students – aged between twelve and thirteen – were diagnosed with anxiety problems in a single year, way more than she’d ever had before. Yet when Jodi explained that their thirteen-year-olds should do something – anything – independently, lots of parents became angry. ‘I had one child tell me they wanted to do the laundry, and [her] mom said, “Absolutely not. You’re not doing the laundry. You may ruin it.” The child was so defeated at that point … When I say defeated, I mean defeated.’ They told Jodi: ‘They don’t even trust me to try on my own.’ She said: ‘They get no confidence, because the small things build confidence.’

我前往半小时车程外的一所当地中学，了解该项目的另一个方面。这所中学位于长岛一个较为富裕的地区。老师乔迪·毛里西告诉我，她意识到她的学生需要“让孩子成长”项目，因为她班上200名学生（年龄在12到13岁之间）中有39名在一年内被诊断出患有焦虑症，远远超过她以往遇到的任何病例。然而，当乔迪解释说，这些13岁的孩子应该独立完成一些事情——任何事情——时，许多家长却很生气。“有个孩子告诉我她想洗衣服，她妈妈说：‘绝对不行。你不能洗衣服。你可能会弄脏衣服。’孩子当时非常沮丧……我说沮丧，是真的非常沮丧。”他们告诉乔迪：“他们甚至不相信我可以自己尝试。”乔迪说：“他们没有建立自信，因为自信是从小事中积累起来的。”

When I talked with Jodi’s students, it was startling to hear how terrified they had been at the start of the programme. A tall, strapping fourteen-year-old boy told me he had always been too frightened of kidnapping and ‘all the ransom calls that happen’ to walk into town. He lives in a place where the French bakery is across the street from the olive-oil store, but he had anxiety levels that would have been appropriate to living in a war zone. The Let Grow programme gave him a taste of independence in small steps. First he did his own laundry. Then, a month later, his parents let him go for a run around the block. Within a year, he had teamed up with his friends and they had built a fort in their local woods, where they now spend a lot of their time hanging out. He told me: ‘We sit there and talk, or we have little competitions. We don’t have our moms. We can’t say, “Hey mom – can you get us this?” It doesn’t work like that. It’s different.’ As I spoke with him, I thought about something the writer Neale Donald Walsch wrote – ‘life begins at the edge of your comfort zone’.

当我与乔迪的学生们交谈时，我震惊地发现他们在项目开始时是多么恐惧。一个身材高大健壮的十四岁男孩告诉我，他一直害怕被绑架，害怕接到“各种勒索电话”，以至于不敢独自进城。他住的地方，法式面包店就在橄榄油店对面，但他的焦虑程度却堪比生活在战区。Let Grow项目让他一步步体验到了独立。首先，他学会了自己洗衣服。一个月后，他的父母允许他绕着街区跑步。不到一年，他就和朋友们一起在附近的树林里建了一个堡垒，现在他们经常在那里玩耍。他告诉我：“我们坐在那里聊天，或者进行一些小比赛。我们没有妈妈。我们不能说，‘嘿，妈妈——你能帮我们拿这个吗？’事情不是这样的。” “情况不一样。”在和他交谈时，我想起了作家尼尔·唐纳德·沃尔什写的一句话——“人生始于舒适区的边缘”。

Lenore met this boy with me, and afterwards she said: ‘Think of history, and prehuman history. We have to chase things to eat. We have to hide from things that want to eat us, and [we have to] seek. We need to build shelter. Everybody does that for a million years, and just this generation, we’ve taken it all away. Kids don’t get to build their shelter, or hide, or seek with a bunch of other kids on their own … And that boy, given the chance, went into the woods and built a shelter.’

莱诺尔和我一起见了这个男孩，之后她说：“想想历史，想想人类出现之前的历史。我们必须追逐猎物才能吃掉它们。我们必须躲避那些想吃掉我们的生物，我们必须寻找食物。我们需要建造庇护所。千百万年来，每个人都这样做，而仅仅这一代人，我们就把这一切都夺走了。孩子们没有机会建造自己的庇护所，没有机会躲藏，没有机会和其他孩子一起寻找食物……而那个男孩，如果有机会，他就会走进森林，建造一个庇护所。”

One day, after a year of growing, and building, and focusing, L.B. and his mom walked down to the ocean, and placed the amphibious wagon he had built onto the water. They pushed it out to sea. They watched it float for a moment – and then it sank. They went home.

一天，经过一年的成长、建设和专注，L.B.和妈妈走到海边，把他造好的水陆两用车放到水里。他们把它推到海里。他们看着它漂浮了一会儿——然后它沉了下去。他们回家了。

‘I felt disappointment, but I was kind of determined to get it afloat. So I siliconed it,’ L.B. told me. They went back to the ocean. This time, the wagon floated, and L.B. and his mother watched it drift away. ‘I felt kind of proud,’ L.B. told me. ‘I was happy to see it float.’

“我当时有点失望，但我决心一定要让它浮起来。所以我用硅胶把它粘住了，”L.B.告诉我。他们又回到了海边。这一次，小车浮了起来，L.B.和他的母亲看着它漂走。“我感到有点自豪，”L.B.告诉我，“我很高兴看到它浮起来了。”

And then they went home, and he started to focus on the next thing he wants to build.

然后他们回家了，他开始专注于他接下来想要建造的东西。

At first, a lot of parents were very nervous about letting their kids take part in the Let Grow experiment. But, Lenore said, ‘When the kid comes through the door proud, and happy, and excited, and maybe a little sweaty or hungry, and they met a squirrel, or they ran into a friend, or they found a quarter,’ the parents see that ‘their kid rose to the occasion’. Once this happens, ‘They are so proud that the parents are rewired. The parents are like – “that’s my boy. Look at him.” That’s what changes them. Not me telling them this is what is going to be good for your kid … The only thing that actually changes the parents is seeing their own kids do something without them watching or helping … People have to see it to believe it. See their kid blossom. And afterward they can’t understand why they didn’t trust their kids sooner. You have to change the picture in people’s heads.’

起初，很多家长都非常担心让孩子参加“放手成长”实验。但莱诺尔说：“当孩子骄傲、快乐、兴奋地走进家门，也许还有些汗流浃背或饿了，他们遇到了一只松鼠，或者碰到了朋友，或者捡到了一枚硬币时”，家长们就会看到“他们的孩子出色地完成了任务”。一旦这种情况发生，“家长们会感到无比自豪，他们的想法也会随之改变。他们会想——‘这是我的孩子，看看他！’这才是真正改变他们的原因。而不是我告诉他们这对孩子有好处……真正能改变家长的，是看到自己的孩子在没有他们监督或帮助的情况下完成某件事……人们必须亲眼所见才能相信。看到自己的孩子茁壮成长。之后，他们会不明白自己为什么没有早点信任自己的孩子。你必须改变人们脑海中的固有观念。”

After everything I had learned from Lenore and the scientists she works with, I began to wonder if our kids are not only more confined at home, but also more confined at school. I started to ask myself – is the way our schools are structured today helping our kids to develop a healthy sense of focus, or in fact hindering it?

从莱诺尔和她合作的科学家们那里了解到很多信息后，我开始思考，我们的孩子不仅在家受到更多限制，在学校也同样如此。我开始自问——如今学校的教学结构究竟是在帮助孩子培养健康的专注力，还是在阻碍这种专注力的培养？

I thought about my own education. When I was eleven years old, I was sitting at a wooden desk in a chilly classroom on my first day at secondary school, which is roughly equivalent to middle school in the US. A teacher placed pieces of paper in front of every kid in the class. I looked down and saw that on this piece of paper, there was a grid, full of little boxes. ‘This is your timetable,’ I remember him saying. ‘It says where you have to be, and at what time, every day.’ I looked at it. It said that on Wednesday at 9 a.m. I would be learning woodwork; at 10 a.m. history; at 11 a.m. geography; and so on. I felt a flush of anger, and looked around me. I thought – wait, what’s happening here? Who are these people to tell me what I will be doing at 9 a.m. on a Wednesday morning? I haven’t committed any crime. Why am I being treated like a prisoner?

我想起了自己的求学经历。十一岁那年，我第一天上中学，坐在教室里一张木桌旁，教室里冷飕飕的。中学大概相当于美国的初中。老师在每个孩子面前都放了一张纸。我低头一看，发现这张纸上画着一个网格，里面布满了小方格。“这是你们的课程表，”我记得老师说，“上面写着你们每天几点到哪儿。”我看了看，上面写着星期三早上九点要上木工课；十点是历史；十一点是地理；以此类推。我顿时怒火中烧，环顾四周。我想——等等，这是怎么回事？这些人凭什么告诉我星期三早上九点要做什么？我又没犯什么罪，为什么我要被当成囚犯一样对待？

I put up my hand and asked the teacher why I had to do these lessons, and not, say, learn about things I found interesting. ‘Because you have to,’ he said. This didn’t seem to me to be a satisfying answer, so I asked him what he meant. ‘Because I say so,’ he said, flustered. In every lesson after that, I asked why we were learning these things. The answers were always the same: because you’ll have a test on it; because you have to; because I tell you so. After a week, I was told to ‘shut up and learn’. When I was at home, choosing my own material, I could read for days on end. At school, I could barely read for five minutes. (This was before the notion of ADHD had spread to Britain, so I was not given stimulants, though I suspect that if I was at school today I would be.)

我举手问老师，为什么我必须上这些课，而不是学习一些我感兴趣的东西。“因为你必须学，”他说。我觉得这个答案并不令人满意，于是又问他是什么意思。“因为我说了算，”他慌乱地说。之后的每一节课，我都问我们为什么要学这些东西。答案总是千篇一律：因为要考试；因为你必须学；因为我说了算。一周后，我被告知“闭嘴好好学”。在家的时候，我可以自己选择学习材料，连续读好几天。但在学校，我连五分钟都读不下去。（那时英国还没有“多动症”的概念，所以我没有服用兴奋剂，但我怀疑如果我现在还在上学，肯定会被开药。）

I always loved learning, and I always hated school. For a long time I thought this was a paradox, until I got to know Lenore. Because it consisted mostly of fragmented rote-learning, very little in my education was meaningful to me, and since I was at school twenty-five years ago, education has been stripped of meaning even more. Across most of the Western world, the school system has been radically restructured by politicians to prioritise testing children much more. Almost everything else has been steadily squeezed out – from play, to music, to breaks. There was never a golden age when most schools were progressive, but there has been a swing towards a school system built around a narrow vision of efficiency. In 2002 George W. Bush signed into law the No Child Left Behind Act, which massively increased standardised testing across the US. In the four years that followed, diagnoses of severe attention problems in children rose by 22 percent.

我一直热爱学习，却又一直厌恶学校。很长一段时间，我都觉得这很矛盾，直到我认识了莱诺尔。因为学校教育大多是零散的死记硬背，对我来说，几乎没有什么意义。而且，自从我二十五年前离开学校以来，教育的意义更是被进一步剥夺了。在西方世界的大部分地区，政客们对学校系统进行了彻底的重组，更加注重对学生的考试。几乎所有其他方面都被逐步挤压——从游戏、音乐到课间休息。虽然从来没有过大多数学校都秉持进步理念的黄金时代，但如今的学校系统却朝着以效率为核心的狭隘愿景发展。2002年，乔治·W·布什签署了《不让一个孩子掉队法案》，该法案大幅增加了美国各地的标准化考试。在接下来的四年里，儿童严重注意力缺陷障碍的诊断率上升了22%。

I thought back over all the factors that I had learned make it possible for kids to develop attention. Our schools allow kids less exercise. They allow kids less play. They create more anxiety, because of the frenzy of tests. They don’t create conditions where kids can find their intrinsic motivations. And for many kids, we don’t give them opportunities to develop mastery – the sense they are good at something. All along, many teachers warned that dragging schools in this direction was a bad idea, but politicians tied financial support for schools to it nonetheless.

我回想起之前学到的所有影响孩子注意力发展的因素。我们的学校减少了孩子的运动量，减少了他们的玩耍时间，考试的压力也加剧了他们的焦虑。学校没有创造条件让孩子找到内在的学习动力。而且，对于很多孩子来说，我们没有给他们机会去培养精通某项技能的成就感——那种觉得自己擅长某件事的感觉。一直以来，很多老师都警告说，把学校往这个方向发展是个糟糕的主意，但政客们却仍然把对学校的财政支持与此挂钩。

I wondered if there was a better way – so I decided to visit places that take a radically different approach to education, to see what I could learn from them. In the late 1960s, a group of Massachusetts parents who were unhappy with their kids’ schooling decided to do something that sounds, at first glance, quite mad. They opened a school that would have no teachers, no classes, no curriculum, no homework and no tests. One of the founders told me their goal was to create a completely new model, from scratch, of how a school could be. It left out almost everything we think of as schooling. More than fifty years later, I arrived at their creation. It is named Sudbury Valley School, and from the outside, it looks like a raddled Downton Abbey – a big, roomy, old-fashioned mansion, surrounded by woods and barns and creeks. It feels like you are stepping into a clearing in a forest, with the scent of pine trees filling every space you enter.

我一直在想是否有更好的方法——于是我决定去拜访一些教育理念截然不同的地方，看看能从中学习到什么。上世纪60年代末，一群对孩子教育不满的马萨诸塞州家长决定做一件乍听起来很疯狂的事：他们创办了一所没有老师、没有课程、没有教材、没有作业、也没有考试的学校。其中一位创始人告诉我，他们的目标是从零开始，创造一种全新的学校模式。这种模式几乎摒弃了我们通常认为的学校教育的一切。五十多年后，我来到了他们创建的这所学校。它名为萨德伯里谷学校（Sudbury Valley School），从外面看，它就像一座破败的唐顿庄园——一座宽敞的老式宅邸，周围环绕着树林、谷仓和小溪。置身其中，仿佛走进了一片森林空地，松树的清香弥漫在每一个角落。

An eighteen-year-old student named Hannah offered to show me around and explain how the school works. We stood at first by the piano room, with kids milling freely around us, and she explained that before she came here, she went to a standard American high school. ‘I just dreaded it. I didn’t want to get up. I was so anxious, and then I’d just go to school, and I’d get through it, and then I’d just get home as fast as I could,’ she said. ‘It was really hard for me to have to sit still and learn stuff that I didn’t think was any good to me.’ So, she told me, when she arrived here, four years before I met her, ‘It was shocking.’ It was explained to her that there is no structure at Sudbury except for the one you create with your fellow students. There’s no timetable or lessons. You learn what you want. You choose how to spend your time. You can ask the staff – who mill around and talk to the kids – to teach you things if you want, but there’s no pressure to do that.

一位名叫汉娜的十八岁学生主动提出带我参观学校，并向我介绍学校的运作方式。我们先站在钢琴教室旁，周围是自由自在的孩子们。她解释说，来这里之前，她上的是一所标准的美国高中。“我当时真是害怕极了。我都不想起床。我焦虑得不行，然后就硬着头皮去上学，熬过这段时间，然后就只想赶紧回家。”她说，“对我来说，被迫静静地坐着学习那些我觉得对我没用的东西，真的太难熬了。”所以，她告诉我，在她来到这里四年后——也就是我认识她之前——“我感到非常震惊”。有人向她解释说，在萨德伯里，除了你和同学们一起建立的规则之外，没有任何固定的制度。这里没有时间表，也没有固定的课程安排。你想学什么就学什么。你可以自由支配自己的时间。你可以请在附近走动并与孩子们交谈的工作人员教你一些东西，但你不会有压力这样做。

So, I asked, what do the kids do all day? From age four to eleven, the kids spend most of their time playing extraordinarily elaborate games they have created, which go on for months, and build up into an epic mythology, like a children’s version of Game of Thrones . They have clans and fight goblins and dragons, and in the school’s extensive grounds, they build forts. Waving towards the rocks, Hannah says that through all these games, ‘I think they’re learning problem-solving, because they’re building these forts, and then there could be a conflict within the group, and they have to figure that out. They’re learning how to be creative and think about things in a different way.’

于是我问，孩子们整天都在干什么？从四岁到十一岁，孩子们大部分时间都在玩他们自己设计的极其复杂的游戏，这些游戏会持续好几个月，最终发展成一部史诗般的奇幻故事，就像儿童版的《权力的游戏》。他们组建部落，与哥布林和巨龙战斗，并在学校广阔的操场上建造堡垒。汉娜指着岩石说，通过这些游戏，“我认为他们在学习解决问题，因为他们要建造这些堡垒，然后团队内部可能会出现冲突，他们必须想办法解决。他们正在学习如何发挥创造力，以及如何用不同的方式思考问题。”

The older students tend to form groups and ask to learn things together – whether it’s cooking, or pottery, or music. People go on learning jags, she says. ‘I’ll find this topic that I’m really interested in, and I’ll just latch onto it, and I’ll research it or I’ll read about it for a week or a few days, and then I move on to the next thing … I’m really interested in medicine, so there’s one speciality of medicine [where] I would read about it intensively and learn everything I could. Then I would go to lizards – lizards are my favourite animal, so I read a lot about lizards. Right now, there’s a bunch of people who have been doing origami all day, which is really cool.’ Hannah had been spending the past year teaching herself Hebrew, with the help of a staff member.

年龄较大的学生往往会结伴学习，一起学习各种各样的东西——无论是烹饪、陶艺还是音乐。她说，人们会不断地钻研某个领域。“我会找到一个自己真正感兴趣的话题，然后就全身心投入进去，花上一周甚至几天的时间去研究或阅读相关资料，之后再转向下一个领域……我对医学很感兴趣，所以我会深入研究医学的某个分支，尽可能多地学习相关知识。然后我又会去研究蜥蜴——蜥蜴是我最喜欢的动物，所以我阅读了很多关于蜥蜴的资料。现在，有一群人一整天都在折纸，这真的很酷。”汉娜在过去一年里一直在自学希伯来语，并得到了一位教职工的帮助。

The fact that you have to create order for yourself doesn’t mean there’s no order at all, she told me as we walked through the grounds. On the contrary: all the school’s rules are created and voted on by a daily meeting. Anyone can turn up and make a proposal, and anyone can vote on it. Everyone – from a four-year-old to the adult staff – has the same say, a single vote. There’s an elaborate legal code that the school has built up over the years. If you are caught breaking the rules, you get tried by a jury that represents the whole age range of kids at the school, and they decide on the punishment. For example, if you break a tree branch, they might decree that you aren’t allowed on the trees for a few weeks. The school is so democratic that the kids even vote on whether the individual staff members get rehired every year.

“你需要自己建立秩序，但这并不意味着这里完全没有秩序，”她一边带我穿过校园一边告诉我。恰恰相反：学校的所有规章制度都是由每日例会制定并投票表决的。任何人都可以参加会议提出提案，任何人都可以投票表决。从四岁的孩子到成年教职工，每个人都拥有同等的发言权，一票之差。学校多年来建立了一套完善的法律体系。如果你违反了校规，将由一个代表全校所有年龄段学生的陪审团进行审判，并由他们决定处罚。例如，如果你折断了树枝，他们可能会判你几周内不得爬树。这所学校非常民主，甚至连教职工是否续聘都由孩子们投票决定。

We walked through the dance room, the computer room, the walls covered with books. At this school, it became clear, kids only do things that are meaningful to them. ‘I think if you’re not getting to use your imagination and be creative, then it’s really putting you in a box,’ Hannah told me. ‘I don’t feel as much pressure to learn every single fact, and I trust that the main idea or the most important things will just stay in my brain, and not having tests also gives me the freedom to take my time learning things.’ Because I – and everyone I know – was raised in such a different system, I found this, at first glance, overwhelmingly weird. Given the freedom to do nothing, wouldn’t most kids go crazy and indulge themselves? There aren’t even formal lessons in reading at Sudbury, though kids can ask the staff, or each other, to show them how reading works. Surely, I thought at first, this produces semi-literates?

我们穿过舞蹈室、电脑室，以及摆满书籍的墙壁。在这所学校里，孩子们只做对他们有意义的事情，这一点显而易见。“我觉得如果你不能发挥想象力和创造力，那真的会把你困在一个盒子里，”汉娜告诉我。“我感觉不到必须记住每一个细节的压力，我相信核心思想或最重要的东西会自然而然地留在我的脑海里，而且没有考试也让我可以自由地慢慢学习。”因为我和我认识的所有人，都是在截然不同的教育体系下长大的，所以乍一看，我觉得这简直匪夷所思。如果孩子们可以自由自在地无所事事，难道他们不会变得疯狂，放纵自己吗？萨德伯里甚至没有正式的阅读课，不过孩子们可以向老师或同学请教阅读方法。我一开始想，这岂不是会培养出半文盲吗？

I wanted to know what the outcome of this kind of education is, so I went to interview Professor Peter Gray, a research psychologist at Boston College who tracked down the alumni of Sudbury Valley School to see how they turned out. Were they undisciplined wrecks who couldn’t function in the modern world? It turned out that over 50 percent went on to higher education, and almost all of them, he has written, have been ‘remarkably successful in finding employment that interested them and earned them a living. They had gone on, successfully, to a wide range of occupations, including business, arts, science, medicine, other service professions, and skilled trades.’ There have been similar results for other kids like them in other places. Peter’s research found that kids who have been ‘unschooled’ like this were more likely to go on to higher education than other kids.

我想了解这种教育方式的最终结果，于是采访了波士顿学院的研究心理学家彼得·格雷教授。他追踪了萨德伯里谷学校的毕业生，想看看他们后来的发展如何。他们是否都是些不守规矩、无法适应现代社会的“问题少年”？结果发现，超过50%的毕业生继续接受了高等教育，而且几乎所有人都“非常成功地找到了自己感兴趣且能维持生计的工作”。格雷教授写道，他们“成功地从事了各种各样的职业，包括商业、艺术、科学、医学、其他服务行业以及技术工种”。其他地方也有类似的例子。彼得的研究发现，像这样接受“非正规教育”的孩子比其他孩子更有可能继续接受高等教育。

How can that be? Peter explained to me that in fact for most of human history, children have learned in the way they do at Sudbury. He studied the evidence that’s been gathered about children in hunter-gatherer societies – the way humans lived until, in evolutionary terms, the day before yesterday. There, kids will play, mill around, imitate adults, ask lots of questions, and slowly, over time, they become competent, without being formally instructed very much. The anomaly isn’t Sudbury, he explained – it’s the modern school, which was designed very recently, in the 1870s, to train children to sit still, shut up and do what they are told, to prepare them to work in factories. He told me that children evolved to be curious and to explore their environment. They naturally want to learn, and they’ll do it spontaneously when they can pursue things that seem interesting to them. They learn primarily by playing freely. His research found that Sudbury was particularly effective with kids who had been told that they had learning problems. Of the eleven students he studied who had been judged to have ‘serious learning difficulties’ before they arrived at Sudbury, four went on to receive college degrees and a fifth was enrolled to get one.

这怎么可能呢？彼得向我解释说，事实上，在人类历史的大部分时间里，孩子们学习的方式都和萨德伯里学校的孩子们一样。他研究了关于狩猎采集社会儿童的证据——从进化论的角度来看，人类的生活方式一直延续到昨天。在那里，孩子们玩耍、四处走动、模仿大人、提出很多问题，随着时间的推移，他们逐渐变得能干，而无需接受太多正式的指导。他解释说，问题不在于萨德伯里学校，而在于现代学校。现代学校是在19世纪70年代才出现的，其目的是训练孩子们安静地坐着、闭嘴，服从命令，为他们将来在工厂工作做好准备。他告诉我，孩子们进化出了好奇心，喜欢探索周围的环境。他们天生渴望学习，当他们能够追求自己感兴趣的事情时，就会自发地学习。他们主要通过自由玩耍来学习。他的研究发现，萨德伯里学校对那些被认为有学习障碍的孩子尤其有效。在他研究的 11 名学生中，有 4 名学生在来到萨德伯里之前就被判定为有“严重的学习困难”，其中 5 名学生后来获得了大学学位，还有 1 名学生正在攻读大学学位。

These findings are important but need to be handled with a bit of caution. Sudbury Valley charges fees between $7,500 and $10,000 a year – so the parents who send their kids there already have more financial advantages than the rest of the population. That means their kids would already – in any circumstances – be more likely to go on to higher education, and the parents themselves are also quite likely to teach their kids some stuff at home. So the success of the kids at Sudbury Valley can’t be attributed solely to the school.

这些发现固然重要，但需要谨慎对待。萨德伯里谷中学每年的学费在7500至10000美元之间——因此，将孩子送入该校的家长本身就比其他家庭拥有更大的经济优势。这意味着，无论在何种情况下，他们的孩子都更有可能继续接受高等教育，而且家长们也很有可能在家辅导孩子学习。所以，萨德伯里谷中学学生的成功不能完全归功于学校本身。

But Peter argues this model is doing something that does boost real learning, in a way conventional schools don’t. To understand why, he says we should look at the evidence for what happens when animals are deprived of play. For example, he told me he started to study this subject after he was struck by a typical study – which I later read myself – which compared two groups of rats. The first was prevented from playing with other rats at all. The second was allowed to play with other rats for one hour a day. The scientists then watched as they grew up, to see if there were any differences. By the time they became adults, the play-deprived rats experienced much more fear and anxiety, and they were much less able to deal with unexpected events. The rats who got to play were braver, more likely to explore, and better able to cope with new situations. They tested both sets of rats for their ability to solve new problems – they set it up so that in order to get food, the rats would have to figure out a new sequence. It turned out the rats who had been allowed to play when they were young were significantly smarter.

但彼得认为，这种模式确实能以传统学校无法做到的方式促进真正的学习。为了理解其中的原因，他建议我们研究动物被剥夺玩耍机会后的表现。例如，他告诉我，他之所以开始研究这个课题，是因为他被一项典型的研究所震撼——后来我自己也读过这项研究——该研究比较了两组老鼠。第一组完全被禁止与其他老鼠玩耍。第二组每天可以与其他老鼠玩耍一小时。科学家们观察它们的成长过程，看看是否存在任何差异。结果发现，成年后，被剥夺玩耍机会的老鼠表现出更多的恐惧和焦虑，并且更难应对突发事件。而那些能够玩耍的老鼠则更加勇敢，更乐于探索，也更能适应新情况。研究人员还测试了两组老鼠解决新问题的能力——他们设置了一个实验，让老鼠必须想出一个新的步骤才能获得食物。结果表明，那些从小被允许玩耍的老鼠要聪明得多。

At Sudbury, Hannah told me that once she was free from the mindless and meaningless grilling of standardised schooling, she found ‘I really appreciate education more, and I’m excited to learn, and I want to pursue different things. Since I don’t feel like I’m being forced to, I’m motivated to do that.’ This fits with a wider body of scientific evidence – the more something is meaningful, the easier it is to pay attention to it and learn, for adults and kids. Standardised schooling too often drains learning of meaning, while progressive schooling tries to infuse it into everything. This is why the best research on this question shows that kids at more progressive schools are more likely to retain what they’ve learned in the long run, more likely to want to carry on learning, and more likely to be able to apply what they’ve learned to new problems. These, it seems to me, are amongst the most precious forms of attention.

在萨德伯里，汉娜告诉我，一旦她摆脱了标准化学校里那种枯燥乏味、毫无意义的“拷问式”教育，她发现“我更加珍惜教育，我渴望学习，也想尝试不同的事物。因为我感觉自己不是被迫学习，所以我更有动力去做。”这与大量的科学证据相符——对成人和孩子来说，事物越有意义，就越容易集中注意力学习。标准化学校教育常常使学习失去意义，而进步的教育方式则力求将意义融入到学习的方方面面。这就是为什么关于这个问题的最佳研究表明，在进步学校就读的孩子更有可能长期记住所学知识，更有可能继续学习，也更有可能将所学知识应用于新的问题。在我看来，这些才是最宝贵的注意力形式。

Standing outside Sudbury, Hannah told me she used to long for the school day to end, but now, ‘I don’t want to go home.’ The other kids I spoke with told me they had a similar point of view, before they ran off to join some collective activity with other children. I found it startling to discover that you can throw out almost everything we regard as schooling – all the testing, all the assessments, even formal teaching – and still produce people who can read, write and function in society. This tells you how much of what we are neurotically putting our kids through is pointless (at best).

站在萨德伯里校外，汉娜告诉我，她以前盼着放学，但现在，“我不想回家”。我跟其他孩子聊了聊，他们也都表达了类似的看法，然后就跑去参加其他孩子的集体活动了。我惊讶地发现，我们几乎可以抛弃所有我们视为学校教育的东西——所有的考试、所有的评估，甚至包括正规的教学——仍然能培养出能读能写、能融入社会的人。这说明，我们神经质地让孩子们经历的很多事情，充其量是毫无意义的。

Personally, my instinct is that Sudbury goes too far. I went to other progressive schools to see if there’s a way you can mix much greater freedom with some adult guidance. One I particularly liked was in Berlin, named the Evangelische Schule Berlin Zentrum. There, the kids decide collectively on a topic they want to investigate – when I visited, it was whether humans can live in space. Then, for a whole term, half of all their lessons are built around investigating this question – they investigate the physics of how to build rockets, the history of going to the moon, the geography of what would grow on other planets. It builds to a big collective project – they were literally building a rocket in their classroom. In this way, subjects that seemed dry and boring when they are broken up and rote-learned were infused for these kids with meaning, and they wanted to know more about them.

就我个人而言，我觉得萨德伯里的做法有点过头了。我去参观过其他一些进步学校，看看能否找到一种方法，既能给予学生更大的自由，又能给予一定的成人指导。我特别喜欢柏林的一所学校，名叫柏林福音学校中心分校（Evangelische Schule Berlin Zentrum）。在那里，孩子们会集体决定一个想要探究的主题——我参观的时候，主题是人类能否在太空生存。然后，整整一个学期，他们一半的课程都围绕着这个问题展开——他们探究火箭的物理原理、登月的历史、其他星球上可能生长的植物等等。最终，他们会完成一个大型的集体项目——他们真的在教室里建造了一枚火箭。这样一来，那些原本枯燥乏味、需要死记硬背的学科，对这些孩子来说就变得意义非凡，他们也渴望了解更多。

Because I had grown up in such a different system, I kept having doubts about these alternatives. But I kept coming back to one key fact: the country that is often judged by international league tables to have the most successful schools in the world, Finland, is closer to these progressive models than anything we would recognise. Their children don’t go to school at all until they are seven years old – before then, they just play. Between the ages of seven and sixteen, kids arrive at school at 9 a.m. and leave at 2 p.m. They are given almost no homework, and they sit almost no tests until they graduate from high school. Free play is at the beating heart of Finnish kids’ lives: by law, teachers have to give kids fifteen minutes of free play for every forty-five minutes of instruction. What’s the outcome? Only 0.1 percent of their kids are diagnosed with attention problems, and Finns are among the most literate, numerate and happy people in the world.

因为我成长于截然不同的教育体系，我对这些替代方案一直心存疑虑。但我始终牢记一个关键事实：芬兰——这个经常被国际排名评为拥有全球最成功学校的国家——比我们所知的任何模式都更接近这些进步的教育模式。芬兰的孩子在七岁之前根本不用上学，在此之前，他们尽情玩耍。七岁到十六岁之间，孩子们早上九点到校，下午两点放学。他们几乎没有家庭作业，直到高中毕业也几乎不用参加任何考试。自由玩耍是芬兰孩子生活的核心：法律规定，教师每授课四十五分钟，就必须给孩子们十五分钟的自由玩耍时间。结果如何呢？只有0.1%的芬兰孩子被诊断出注意力缺陷障碍，芬兰人也是世界上识字率、数学能力和幸福感最高的人群之一。

Hannah told me as I was leaving that when she remembers her time at a conventional high school, ‘I see myself sitting at a desk, and it’s all grey. It’s this weird image.’ She told me she worries about her friends still stuck in that system. ‘They hate it, and I feel bad they don’t have the opportunity to do something else.’

临走时，汉娜告诉我，每当她回忆起在传统高中的时光，“我就会想起自己坐在课桌前，周围一片灰蒙蒙的。那画面很奇怪。”她告诉我，她很担心那些仍然困在那种体制里的朋友们。“他们讨厌那种生活，我为他们感到难过，他们没有机会去做其他的事情。”

When adults notice that children and teens seem to be struggling to focus and pay attention today, we often say it with a weary and exasperated superiority. The implication is – look at this degraded younger generation! Aren’t we better than them? Why can’t they be like us? But after learning all this, I think about it very differently. Children have needs – and it’s our job, as adults, to create an environment that meets those needs. In many cases, in this culture, we aren’t meeting those needs. We don’t let them play freely; we imprison them in their homes, with little to do except interact via screens; and our school system largely deadens and bores them. We feed them food that causes energy crashes, contains drug-like additives that can make them hyper, and doesn’t contain the nutrients they need. We expose them to brain-disrupting chemicals in the atmosphere. It’s not a flaw in them that, as a result, they are struggling to learn attention. It’s a flaw in the world we built for them.

当成年人注意到如今的孩子和青少年似乎难以集中注意力时，我们常常带着一种疲惫而恼怒的优越感说道。言下之意是——看看这代堕落的年轻人！我们难道不比他们强吗？为什么他们不能像我们一样？但在了解了这一切之后，我的想法截然不同。孩子们有他们的需求——而作为成年人，我们的责任是创造一个能够满足这些需求的环境。在很多情况下，在这个社会里，我们并没有满足这些需求。我们不让他们自由玩耍；我们把他们囚禁在家中，除了通过屏幕互动之外，几乎无事可做；我们的学校教育体系在很大程度上麻木了他们，让他们感到无聊。我们给他们吃的食物会导致能量骤降，含有类似药物的添加剂，会让他们变得亢奋，而且缺乏他们所需的营养。我们让他们暴露在空气中扰乱大脑的化学物质中。因此，他们难以集中注意力并不是他们的缺陷，而是我们为他们创造的世界的缺陷。

Now, when Lenore speaks to parents, she still gets them to talk about the happiest moments in their own childhoods. It’s almost always a moment when they were free – building a fort, walking through the woods with friends, playing out in the street. She says to them: ‘We’re scrimping and saving to send them to the dance class,’ but when it comes down to it, ‘You’re not giving them the thing you loved the most.’ We don’t have to continue like this, she tells them. There’s a different childhood waiting for our kids, if we commit, together, to rebuild it – one where they can learn, like L.B. building his boats, to focus deeply again.

现在，每当莱诺尔和家长们交谈时，她仍然会引导他们回忆自己童年最快乐的时光。那些时光几乎总是自由自在的——搭建堡垒、和朋友们在树林里漫步、在街头玩耍。她对他们说：“我们省吃俭用，只为了送他们去上舞蹈课，”但最终，“你们却没能给他们自己最爱的东西。”她告诉他们，我们不必再这样下去了。如果我们齐心协力，共同重建孩子的童年，那么他们就能拥有一个截然不同的童年——一个像L.B.造船一样，重新学会专注的童年。

# ↩

Conclusion

结论

Attention Rebellion

注意力叛逆

If this was a self-help book, I would be able to serve up a delightfully simple conclusion to this story. Those books have a very satisfying structure: the author identifies a problem – usually one he’s had himself – and he talks you through how he personally solved it. Then he says – and now, dear reader, you can do what I have done, and it will set you free. But this is not a self-help book, and what I have to say to you is more complex, and it means starting with an admission: I have not entirely solved this problem in myself. In fact, at this moment, as I write this in lockdown, my attention has never been worse.

如果这是一本自助书籍，我就可以给这个故事一个轻松愉快的结尾。这类书的结构非常令人满意：作者会指出一个问题——通常是他自己也遇到过的问题——然后详细讲述他是如何解决的。接着他会说——亲爱的读者，现在你可以像我一样，获得解脱。但这并非一本自助书籍，我要说的要复杂得多，这意味着我必须先坦白：我并没有完全解决自身的这个问题。事实上，此刻，当我身处封锁之中写下这些文字时，我的注意力从未如此糟糕过。

For me, the collapse came in a strange dream-like month. In February 2020 I walked into Heathrow Airport to board a flight to Moscow. I was on my way to interview James Williams, the former Google strategist who you’ve seen quoted throughout this book. As I hurried through the alienating yellow light of the airport towards my gate, I noticed something strange. Some of the staff were wearing face masks. I had, of course, read in the news about the new virus that had emerged in Wuhan in China, but I assumed – as so many of us did – that like the swine flu or Ebola crises a few years before, this problem would be contained at source before it could become a pandemic. I felt a flicker of irritation at what I saw as their paranoia, and I boarded my flight.

对我而言，崩溃发生在一个如梦似幻的月份。2020年2月，我走进希思罗机场，准备搭乘飞往莫斯科的航班。我此行的目的是采访詹姆斯·威廉姆斯，这位谷歌前战略家，本书中多次引用过他的话。我匆匆穿过机场令人感到疏离的黄色灯光，走向登机口，这时我注意到了一些奇怪的事情。一些工作人员戴着口罩。当然，我之前在新闻上读到过关于中国武汉出现新型病毒的报道，但我当时的想法——就像我们很多人一样——认为就像几年前的猪流感或埃博拉疫情一样，这个问题会在源头得到控制，不会演变成全球大流行。我感到一丝恼火，觉得他们有点过于紧张，然后便登上了飞机。

I landed into a freakishly warm Russian winter. There was no snow on the ground, and people were wearing T-shirts and selling off their fur coats for a pittance. As I strolled through the eerily snowless streets, I felt tiny and disorientated. Everything in Moscow is vast – people live in enormous concrete lumps of apartment blocks, and they work in ugly fortresses, and they trudge between them across eight-lane highways. The city is designed to make the collective seem vast and to make you, the individual, feel like a speck on the wind. James was living in a nineteenth-century Moscow apartment block, and as we sat in front of a huge bookcase filled with Russian classics, I felt like I had stumbled into a Tolstoy novel. He was living there partly because his wife worked for the World Health Organization, and partly because he loved Russian culture and philosophy.

我抵达莫斯科时，正值一个异常温暖的俄罗斯冬季。地上没有积雪，人们穿着T恤，把皮草大衣贱卖。漫步在诡异的无雪街道上，我感到自己渺小而迷茫。莫斯科的一切都无比巨大——人们住在巨大的混凝土公寓楼里，在丑陋的堡垒里工作，在八车道的高速公路上穿梭往来。这座城市的设计旨在营造一种集体庞大的氛围，让你，作为个体，感觉自己就像风中的一粒尘埃。詹姆斯住在莫斯科一栋十九世纪的公寓楼里，我们坐在摆满俄罗斯经典著作的巨大书架前，我感觉自己仿佛走进了托尔斯泰的小说世界。他住在这里，一部分原因是他的妻子在世界卫生组织工作，另一部分原因是他热爱俄罗斯文化和哲学。

He told me that after years of studying focus, he has come to believe that attention takes three different forms – all of which are now being stolen. When we went through them, it clarified for me a lot of what I had learned so far.

他告诉我，经过多年的研究，他逐渐认识到注意力有三种不同的形式——而这三种形式如今都在被窃取。当我们一起探讨这三种形式时，我之前学到的很多东西都豁然开朗了。

The first layer of your attention, he said, is your spotlight . This is when you focus on ‘immediate actions’, like, ‘I’m going to walk into the kitchen and make a coffee.’ You want to find your glasses? You want to see what’s in the fridge? You want to finish reading this chapter of my book? It’s called the spotlight because – as I explained earlier – it involves narrowing down your focus. If your spotlight gets distracted or disrupted, you are prevented from carrying out near-term actions like this.

他说，你注意力的第一层是“聚光灯”。这时你专注于“即时行动”，比如“我要去厨房泡杯咖啡”。你想找眼镜吗？你想看看冰箱里有什么吗？你想读完这本书的这一章吗？之所以称之为“聚光灯”，是因为——正如我之前解释的——它涉及到缩小你的注意力范围。如果你的“聚光灯”被分散或干扰，你就无法执行这些近期行动。

The second layer of your attention is your starlight . This is, he says, the focus you can apply to your ‘longer-term goals – projects over time’. You want to write a book. You want to set up a business. You want to be a good parent. It’s called the starlight because when you feel lost, you look up to the stars, and you remember the direction you are travelling in. If you become distracted from your starlight, he said, you ‘lose sight of the longer-term goals’. You start to forget where you are headed.

你注意力的第二层是你的“星光”。他说，这是你可以用来关注“长期目标——长期项目”的焦点。你想写一本书，你想创办一家公司，你想成为一位好父母。之所以称之为“星光”，是因为当你迷失方向时，你会仰望星空，从而记起自己前进的方向。他说，如果你的注意力从“星光”上转移开来，你就会“忘记长期目标”，你会开始忘记自己要去哪里。

The third layer of your attention is your daylight . This is the form of focus that makes it possible for you to know what your longer-term goals are in the first place. How do you know you want to write a book? How do you know you want to set up a business? How do you know what it means to be a good parent? Without being able to reflect and think clearly, you won’t be able to figure these things out. He gave it this name because it’s only when a scene is flooded with daylight that you can see the things around you most clearly. If you get so distracted that you lose your sense of the daylight, James says, ‘In many ways you may not even be able to figure out who you are, what you wanted to do, [or] where you want to go.’

你注意力的第三层是你的“日光”。这种专注状态让你首先能够了解自己的长期目标。你怎么知道自己想写一本书？你怎么知道自己想创业？你怎么知道做一个好父母意味着什么？如果不能反思和清晰思考，你就无法弄明白这些问题。他之所以这样称呼它，是因为只有当周围环境充满“日光”时，你才能最清晰地看到周围的事物。詹姆斯说，如果你因为分心而失去了对“日光”的感知，“在很多方面，你甚至可能无法弄清楚自己是谁，想做什么，或者想去哪里。”

He believes that losing your daylight is ‘the deepest form of distraction’, and you may even begin ‘decohering’. This is when you stop making sense to yourself, because you don’t have the mental space to create a story about who you are. You become obsessed with petty goals, or dependent on simplistic signals from the outside world like retweets. You lose yourself in a cascade of distractions. You can only find your starlight and your daylight if you have sustained periods of reflection, mind-wandering and deep thought. James has come to believe that our attention crisis is depriving us of all three of these forms of focus. We are losing our light.

他认为，失去专注力是“最深层次的分心”，甚至会导致“意识解体”。这时，你会开始迷失自我，因为你没有足够的精神空间去构建关于“你是谁”的故事。你会执着于琐碎的目标，或者依赖于来自外界的简单信号，比如转发。你会迷失在各种干扰之中。只有持续地进行反思、放空思绪和深入思考，你才能找回属于你的星光和专注力。詹姆斯逐渐意识到，我们当前的注意力危机正在剥夺我们这三种专注方式。我们正在失去自己的光芒。

He said a different metaphor might also help us to understand this. Sometimes, hackers decide to attack a website in a very specific way. They get an enormous number of computers to try to connect to a website all at once – and by doing this, they ‘overwhelm its capacity for managing traffic, to the point where it can’t be accessed by anyone else, and it goes down’. It crashes. This is called a ‘ denial-of-service attack’. James thinks we are all living through something like a denial-of-service attack on our minds. ‘We’re that server, and there’s all these things trying to grab our attention by throwing information at us … It undermines our capacity for responding to anything. It leaves us in a state of either distraction, or paralysis.’ We are so inundated ‘that it fills up your world, and you can’t find a place to get a view on all of it and realise that you’re so distracted and figure out what to do about it. It can just colonise your entire world,’ he said. You are left so depleted that ‘you don’t get the space to push back against it’.

他说，换个比喻或许能帮助我们理解这一点。有时，黑客会选择一种非常特殊的方式来攻击网站。他们会利用大量的计算机同时尝试连接到该网站——通过这种方式，“使网站的流量处理能力不堪重负，以至于任何人都无法访问，网站瘫痪”。这就是所谓的“拒绝服务攻击”。詹姆斯认为，我们所有人都在经历着类似“拒绝服务攻击”的思维攻击。“我们就像那台服务器，各种各样的信息试图通过向我们倾泻信息来吸引我们的注意力……这削弱了我们应对任何事情的能力。它让我们处于一种分心或麻木的状态。” 他说，我们被信息淹没，“信息充斥着你的世界，你找不到一个地方来审视所有信息，意识到自己如此分心，并想办法应对。它会彻底占据你的整个世界。”你会感到精疲力竭，以至于“没有余力去反抗”。

I left James’s apartment and walked the streets of the Russian capital, and I began to wonder if there is, in fact, a fourth form of attention. I would call it our stadium lights – it’s our ability to see each other, to hear each other, and to work together to formulate and fight for collective goals. I could see a creepy example of what happens when this is lost unfolding all around me. I was in Moscow in winter, and people were walking around outside in T-shirts because it was so warm. A heatwave was just starting in Siberia – a sentence I never thought I would write. The climate crisis couldn’t be clearer – Moscow itself, ten years before, had been choked by the smoke from severe wildfires. But there is very little climate activism in Russia, nor – given the scale of the crisis – anywhere in the world. Our attention is occupied with other, less important things. I knew I was more guilty in this than most – I thought about my own horrendous carbon emissions.

我离开詹姆斯的公寓，漫步在俄罗斯首都的街头，开始思考是否真的存在第四种注意力形式。我称之为我们的“体育场灯光”——它让我们能够彼此看见、彼此倾听，并携手制定和争取共同目标。我目睹了一个令人毛骨悚然的例子，它展现了失去这种能力的后果。我身处冬日的莫斯科，人们却穿着T恤衫在户外闲逛，因为天气实在太暖和了。西伯利亚的热浪刚刚开始——我从未想过自己会写下这句话。气候危机再清楚不过了——十年前，莫斯科就曾被严重的野火产生的浓烟笼罩。然而，俄罗斯几乎没有气候行动主义，考虑到危机的规模，世界上任何地方也同样如此。我们的注意力都被其他一些无关紧要的事情占据了。我知道在这方面我比大多数人更有责任——我想到了自己惊人的碳排放量。

As I flew back to London, I felt like on this long journey I had learned a huge amount about attention – and I felt I could fix mine a little, step by step. When I landed, I noticed that everyone who worked at the airport was now wearing a mask, and the newspaper stands were full of images of hospitals in Italy where people were dying on the floor or in the corridors. I didn’t know it then, but these were the last days before air travel all but ceased across the world. Soon after, Heathrow would be empty and echoing.

返回伦敦的途中，我感觉自己在这漫长的旅途中对注意力有了更深的理解——而且我觉得我可以一步一步地改善自己的注意力。飞机落地后，我注意到机场所有工作人员都戴着口罩，报摊上摆满了意大利医院的照片，照片里有人倒在地上或走廊里死去。当时我并不知道，那是全球航空旅行几乎完全停滞前的最后几天。不久之后，希思罗机场就会变得空空荡荡，回荡着空荡荡的回声。

A few days later, I was walking home when I noticed that my teeth were chattering. It was a mild winter in London too, and I assumed I was caught in a cold draught, but by the time I got home half an hour later, I was shivering and shaking. I crawled into bed, and I didn’t get out again, except to go to the bathroom, for three weeks. I had a raging temperature, and I became feverish and almost delusional. By the time I was able to understand what was going on, British Prime Minister Boris Johnson was appearing on television telling everyone that they must not leave their homes, and then, soon after, he was in hospital himself, almost dead. It was like a stress dream, where the walls of reality start to collapse.

几天后，我走在回家的路上，突然感觉牙齿打颤。当时伦敦的冬天比较暖和，我以为是被冷风吹到了，但半小时后到家时，我已经浑身发抖，瑟瑟发抖。我爬上床，除了去洗手间，接下来的三个星期都没下过床。我高烧不退，发烧到几乎神志不清。等我终于明白发生了什么事时，英国首相鲍里斯·约翰逊正在电视上发表讲话，呼吁大家待在家中。不久之后，他自己也进了医院，命悬一线。这一切就像一场噩梦，现实的墙壁开始崩塌。

Up to this point, I had been applying what I’d learned on this journey steadily, step by step, to improve my own attention. I’d made six big changes in my life.

在此之前，我一直在稳步地、一步一步地运用我在这段旅程中学到的知识来提高自己的注意力。我的人生已经发生了六大改变。

One: I used pre-commitment to stop switching tasks so much. Pre-commitment is when you realise that if you want to change your behaviour, you have to take steps now that will lock in that desire and make it harder for you to crack later. One key step for me was buying a kSafe, which – as I mentioned briefly before – is a large plastic safe with a removable lid. You put your phone in it, put the lid back on, and turn the dial at the top for however long you want – from fifteen minutes to two weeks – and then it locks your phone away for as long as you selected. Before I went on this journey, my use of it was patchy. Now I use it every day without exception, and that buys me long stretches of focus. I also use on my laptop a program called Freedom, which cuts it off from the internet for as long as I select. (As I write this sentence, it’s counting down from three hours.)

第一点：我利用预先承诺来减少频繁切换任务。预先承诺是指你意识到，如果你想改变自己的行为，就必须现在就采取行动，巩固这种意愿，让你以后更难破戒。对我来说，关键的一步是购买了一个kSafe，正如我之前简要提到的，它是一个带可拆卸盖子的大型塑料保险箱。你把手机放进去，盖上盖子，然后转动顶部的旋钮，选择你想要的时间——从15分钟到两周不等——它就会把你的手机锁起来，直到你设定的时间结束。在我开始使用kSafe之前，我断断续续地使用它。现在我每天都用，从未间断，这让我能够长时间集中注意力。我还在笔记本电脑上使用一个名为Freedom的程序，它可以切断电脑的网络连接，时间长短由我决定。（我写这句话的时候，它正在倒计时，从三个小时开始。）

Two: I have changed the way I respond to my own sense of distraction. I used to reproach myself, and say – you’re lazy, you’re not good enough, what’s wrong with you? I tried to shame myself into focusing harder. Now, based on what Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi taught me, instead I have a very different conversation with myself. I ask: What could you do now to get into a flow state, and access your mind’s own ability to focus deeply? I remember what Mihaly taught me are the main components of flow, and I say to myself: What would be something meaningful to me that I could do now? What is at the edge of my abilities? How can I do something that matches these criteria now? Seeking out flow, I learned, is far more effective than self-punishing shame.

第二：我改变了应对自己注意力分散的方式。过去，我总是责备自己，说——你太懒了，你不够好，你到底怎么了？我试图用羞愧感来逼自己更加专注。现在，根据米哈里·契克森米哈赖的教导，我与自己进行了截然不同的对话。我会问自己：现在你可以做些什么来进入心流状态，并激发你大脑自身深度专注的能力？我记得米哈里教过我心流的主要组成部分，然后我会问自己：现在我可以做些什么对我来说有意义的事情？什么事情接近我的能力极限？我现在如何才能做到符合这些标准的事情？我发现，主动寻求心流远比自我惩罚和羞愧有效得多。

Three: based on what I learned about the way social media is designed to hack our attention spans, I now take six months of the year totally off it. (This time is divided into chunks, usually of a few weeks). To make sure I stick to it, I always announce publicly when I am going off – I’ll tweet that I am leaving the site for a certain amount of time, so that I will feel like a fool if I suddenly crack and go back a week later. I also get my friend Lizzie to change my passwords.

第三：根据我对社交媒体如何操控我们注意力的了解，我现在每年有六个月完全不使用社交媒体。（这段时间被分成几个小段，通常是几周。）为了确保我能坚持下去，我总是会在离开的时候公开宣布——我会发推特说我要离开一段时间，这样如果我突然忍不住，一周后又回去，我就会觉得自己很傻。我还会让我的朋友莉齐帮我改密码。

Four: I acted on what I learned about the importance of mind-wandering. I realised that letting your mind wander is not a crumbling of attention, but in fact a crucial form of attention in its own right. It is when you let your mind drift away from your immediate surroundings that it starts to think over the past, and starts to game out the future, and makes connections between different things you have learned. Now I make it a point to go for a walk for an hour every day without my phone or anything else that could distract me. I let my thoughts float and find unexpected connections. I found that precisely because I give my attention space to roam, my thinking is sharper, and I have better ideas.

第四：我把学到的关于“走神”重要性的知识付诸实践。我意识到，让思绪游离并非注意力分散，而恰恰是注意力本身至关重要的一种形式。当你让思绪从眼前的环境中抽离出来时，它便开始回顾过去，展望未来，并将你学到的不同事物联系起来。现在，我每天都会抽出一个小时的时间散步，不带手机或其他任何可能分散我注意力的东西。我让思绪自由飘荡，发现意想不到的联系。我发现，正是因为我给了注意力足够的空间去漫游，我的思维才更加敏锐，也更容易产生好的想法。

Five: I used to see sleep as a luxury, or – worse – as an enemy. Now I am strict with myself about getting eight hours every night. I have a little ritual where I make myself unwind: I don’t look at screens for two hours before I go to bed, and I light a scented candle and try to set aside the stresses of the day. I bought a FitBit device to measure my sleep, and if I get less than eight hours, I make myself go back to bed. This made a really big difference.

第五点：我以前觉得睡眠是一种奢侈，甚至更糟——像个敌人。现在我严格要求自己每晚睡足八小时。我养成了一个放松的小习惯：睡前两小时不看任何电子屏幕，点燃一支香薰蜡烛，努力放下白天的压力。我还买了一个Fitbit来监测睡眠，如果睡眠时间不足八小时，我就强迫自己回去睡觉。这真的带来了很大的改变。

Six: I’m not a parent, but I am very involved in the lives of my godchildren and my young relatives. I used to spend a lot of my time with them deliberately doing things – busy, educational activities I would plan out in advance. Now I spend most of my time with them just playing freely, or letting them play on their own without being managed or over-supervised or imprisoned. I had learned that the more free play they get, the more sound a foundation they will have for their focus and attention. I try to give them as much of that as I can.

六：我不是父母，但我非常关心我的教子和年轻亲戚们的生活。过去，我会花很多时间和他们一起做一些精心安排的活动——一些忙碌而又寓教于乐的活动。现在，我大部分时间都只是让他们自由玩耍，或者让他们自己玩，不加管束、不过度监督、也不限制。我发现，他们自由玩耍的时间越多，就越能培养出良好的专注力和注意力。我会尽我所能地给他们这样的机会。

I would like to be able to tell you that I also did other things I learned I should do to improve my focus – cut out processed foods, meditate every day, build in other slow practices like yoga, and take an extra day off work each week. The truth is I struggle with this – so much of how I deal with ordinary anxiety is tied up with comfort eating and overworking.

我很想告诉你，我还做了其他一些我学到的、能提高专注力的方法——戒掉加工食品，每天冥想，加入瑜伽等其他舒缓身心的活动，以及每周多休息一天。但事实上，我在这方面做得并不好——我应对日常焦虑的方式大多是靠暴饮暴食和过度工作来缓解。

But I would estimate that by making these six changes, I had – by the time I went to Moscow – improved my own focus by about 15 to 20 percent, which is a fair whack. It made a real and marked difference to my life. All of these changes are worth trying, and there will probably be other tweaks to your life that you are considering based on what you’ve read in this book. I am strongly in favour of individuals making the changes they can in their personal lives. I am also in favour of being honest about the fact there are limits to how far that can take you.

但我估计，做出这六项改变后，到我去莫斯科的时候，我的专注力提高了大约15%到20%，这可不是个小数目。它给我的生活带来了切实而显著的改变。所有这些改变都值得一试，而且根据你在这本书中读到的内容，你可能还会考虑对生活进行其他一些调整。我强烈支持每个人都能在自己的生活中做出力所能及的改变。我也支持大家坦诚面对这样一个事实：改变的程度是有限的。

As I was recovering from Covid-19, I found myself in a weird mirror image of where I started this journey. I began by going to Provincetown for three months to escape the internet and cellphones. Now I was shut away for three months in my apartment with almost nothing but the internet and cellphones. Provincetown had liberated my focus and attention; the Covid-19 crisis brought it lower than it had ever been. For months, I couldn’t focus on anything. I skipped from news channel to news channel, seeing fear and fever spread across the world. I took to spending hours listlessly watching live webcams of all the places I had been to research this book. It didn’t matter where they were – Memphis or Melbourne, Fifth Avenue in New York or Commercial Street in Provincetown – they were all the same: the streets were almost empty, except for short sightings of masked people scuttling. I was not alone in finding it impossible to focus. Some of what I experienced was likely a biological after-effect of the virus – but many people who hadn’t been infected were reporting a similar problem. There was a 300 percent increase in people googling ‘how to get your brain to focus’. All over social media, people were saying they couldn’t get their mind to work.

在我从新冠肺炎中康复期间，我发现自己陷入了与这段旅程开始时截然相反的怪异境地。最初，我去了普罗温斯敦待了三个月，是为了逃离网络和手机。而现在，我却把自己关在公寓里三个月，几乎除了网络和手机之外什么都没有。普罗温斯敦解放了我的注意力；而新冠疫情危机却让我的注意力跌至谷底。几个月来，我什么都无法集中。我不停地切换新闻频道，看着恐惧和恐慌在全球蔓延。我开始百无聊赖地花几个小时观看我为了写这本书而去过的所有地方的实时网络摄像头。无论它们在哪里——孟菲斯还是墨尔本，纽约的第五大道还是普罗温斯敦的商业街——都一样：街道上几乎空无一人，只有零星几个戴着口罩的人匆匆走过。我并非唯一一个无法集中注意力的人。我经历的某些症状可能是病毒的后遗症——但许多未感染的人也报告了类似的问题。搜索“如何集中注意力”的人数增加了300%。社交媒体上到处都是人们抱怨自己无法集中精力。

But now, I felt, I had the tools to understand why this was happening to us. Your individual efforts to improve your attention can be dwarfed by an environment full of things that wreck it. This had been true for years leading up to Covid-19 – and it was even more true during it. Stress shatters attention, and we were all more stressed. There was a virus we couldn’t see and didn’t fully understand and it was threatening all of us. The economy was tanking and many of us were suddenly even more financially insecure. On top of this, our political leaders often seemed dangerously incompetent, which ramped up the stress further. For all these reasons, many of us were suddenly hypervigilant.

但现在，我觉得我掌握了理解这一切为何发生在我们身上的工具。你个人为提升注意力所做的努力，在充斥着各种破坏注意力因素的环境中，往往显得微不足道。在新冠疫情爆发前的几年里，情况一直如此——疫情期间更是如此。压力会摧毁注意力，而我们所有人当时都承受着更大的压力。一种我们看不见、也不完全了解的病毒，威胁着我们所有人。经济一落千丈，许多人突然间更加缺乏经济保障。雪上加霜的是，我们的政治领导人常常显得极其无能，这进一步加剧了人们的压力。由于所有这些原因，我们中的许多人突然变得异常警惕。

And how did we cope? We turned more heavily than ever before to our Silicon Valley-controlled screens, which were waiting for us, offering connection, or a least a hologram of it. As we used them more, our attention seemed to get worse. In the US, in April 2020, the average citizen spent thirteen hours a day looking at a screen. The number of children looking at screens for more than six hours a day increased sixfold, and traffic to kids’ apps trebled.

我们是如何应对的呢？我们比以往任何时候都更加依赖硅谷掌控的屏幕，它们仿佛在等待着我们，提供着连接，或者至少是连接的幻象。然而，随着我们使用屏幕的时间越来越长，我们的注意力似乎也越来越差。2020年4月，美国公民平均每天花13个小时盯着屏幕。每天看屏幕超过6小时的儿童人数增加了6倍，儿童应用程序的访问量也增加了2倍。

In this respect, Covid gave us a glimpse of the future we were already skidding towards. My friend Naomi Klein, a political writer who has made many strikingly accurate predictions about the future for twenty years, explained to me: ‘We were on a gradual slide into a world in which every one of our relationships was mediated by platforms and screens, and because of Covid, that gradual process went into hyper-speed.’ The tech companies were planning for us to be immersed in their world to such an extreme extent in a decade’s time, not now. ‘The plan was not for it to leap in this way,’ she said. ‘That leaping is an opportunity, really – because when you do something that quickly, it comes as a shock to your system.’ We didn’t slowly acclimatise to it, and get hooked on its increasing patterns of reinforcements. Instead, we got slammed headfirst into a vision of the future – and we realised ‘we hate it. It’s not good for our well-being. We desperately miss each other.’ Under Covid, even more than before, we were living in simulations of social life, not the real thing. It was better than nothing, to be sure – but it felt thinner. And all the while, the algorithms of surveillance capitalism were altering us – tracking and changing us – for many more hours a day.

从这个角度来看，新冠疫情让我们瞥见了我们早已滑向的未来。我的朋友娜奥米·克莱恩是一位政治作家，二十年来她对未来做出了许多惊人准确的预测。她向我解释说：“我们正逐渐滑向一个所有关系都通过平台和屏幕进行媒介的世界，而新冠疫情加速了这一进程。”科技公司原本计划让我们在十年后，而不是现在，如此极端地沉浸于他们的世界。“计划并非如此突飞猛进，”她说，“这种突飞猛进其实是一个机会——因为当你如此迅速地经历某件事时，它会给你的系统带来冲击。”我们并没有慢慢适应，也没有沉迷于它不断强化的模式。相反，我们被一头栽进了未来的景象中——然后我们意识到“我们讨厌它。它对我们的身心健康不利。”我们无比想念彼此。新冠疫情下，我们比以往任何时候都更生活在模拟的社交生活中，而非真实的社交生活中。当然，这总比没有好——但感觉却少了些什么。与此同时，监控资本主义的算法每天都在以更长的时间改变着我们——追踪着我们，改变着我们。

I could see that in the pandemic, the environment changed and this wrecked our ability to focus. For many of us, the pandemic didn’t create new factors that ruined our attention – it supercharged the factors that had already been corroding our attention for years. I saw this when I talked with my godson Adam, who I had taken to Memphis. His attention, which had been deteriorating for some time, was now shattered. He was on his phone almost every waking hour, seeing the world mainly through TikTok, a new app which made Snapchat look like a Henry James novel.

我发现，疫情期间环境发生了变化，这严重影响了我们的注意力。对我们许多人来说，疫情并没有创造新的因素来破坏我们的注意力——它只是加剧了那些多年来一直在侵蚀我们注意力的因素。我和我的教子亚当（我带他去了孟菲斯）交谈时就看到了这一点。他的注意力原本就一直在下降，现在更是彻底崩溃了。他几乎醒着的每一分钟都在玩手机，主要通过TikTok——这款新应用——来了解世界。相比之下，Snapchat在他眼里都像是亨利·詹姆斯的小说一样引人入胜。

Naomi told me that the way we felt when we were spending all day in lockdown on Zoom and Facebook was awful but ‘also kind of a gift’, because it showed us the road we were headed down with such clarity. More screens. More stress. More collapse of the middle class. More insecurity for the working class. More invasive technology. She calls this vision of the future the ‘Screen New Deal’.
