She told me: ‘The ray of hope in all of this is that we are in touch with how much we dislike this vision of the future that we have just trial run … We weren’t going to have a trial run. We were going to have a gradual rollout. But we got a crash course.’

娜奥米告诉我，疫情封锁期间，我们整天泡在Zoom和Facebook上，那种感觉糟透了，但“也算是一种馈赠”，因为它让我们清晰地看到了未来的方向：更多的屏幕，更多的压力，中产阶级的进一步崩溃，工人阶级的不安全感加剧，以及更具侵入性的科技。她把这种未来景象称为“屏幕新政”。她告诉我：“这一切中唯一的希望在于，我们意识到自己有多么厌恶这种我们刚刚试运行过的未来景象……我们原本没有打算试运行，而是计划逐步推广。结果却经历了一场速成班。”

One thing was now very clear to me. If we continue to be a society of people who are severely under-slept and overworked; who switch tasks every three minutes; who are tracked and monitored by social-media sites designed to figure out our weaknesses and manipulate them to make us scroll and scroll and scroll; who are so stressed that we become hypervigilant; who eat diets that cause our energy to spike and crash; who are breathing in a chemical soup of brain-inflaming toxins every day – then, yes, we will continue to be a society with serious attention problems. But there is an alternative. It’s to organise and fight back – to take on the forces that are setting fire to our attention, and replace them with forces that will help us to heal.

现在我非常清楚一件事。如果我们继续生活在一个睡眠严重不足、工作过度的社会；一个每三分钟就要切换任务的社会；一个被社交媒体网站追踪和监控的社会，这些网站旨在找出我们的弱点并操纵我们，让我们不停地滑动屏幕；一个压力过大以至于过度警觉的社会；一个饮食习惯导致能量忽高忽低的社会；一个每天吸入充斥着刺激大脑的化学物质的社会——那么，是的，我们将继续成为一个注意力严重受损的社会。但是，还有另一种选择。那就是组织起来反击——对抗那些正在摧毁我们注意力的力量，并用能够帮助我们恢复的力量取而代之。

I started thinking about why we need to do this with an analogy that seemed to tie together a lot of what I had learned. Imagine you bought a plant and you wanted to help it grow. What would you do? You would make sure certain things were present: sunlight, and water, and soil with the right nutrients. And you would protect it from the things that could damage or kill it: you would plant it far from the trampling feet of other people, and from pests and diseases. Your ability to develop deep focus is, I have come to believe, like a plant. To grow and flourish to its full potential, your focus needs certain things to be present: play for children and flow states for adults, to read books, to discover meaningful activities that you want to focus on, to have space to let your mind wander so you can make sense of your life, to exercise, to sleep properly, to eat nutritious food that makes it possible for you to develop a healthy brain, and to have a sense of safety. And there are certain things you need to protect your attention from, because they will sicken or stunt it: too much speed, too much switching, too much stimuli, intrusive technology designed to hack and hook you, stress, exhaustion, processed food pumped with dyes that amp you up, polluted air.

我开始思考为什么我们需要这样做，并用一个似乎能将我所学到的很多东西联系起来的比喻来解释。想象一下，你买了一株植物，你想帮助它生长。你会怎么做？你会确保它拥有某些必需品：阳光、水和富含营养的土壤。你还会保护它免受伤害或死亡：你会把它种在远离人群踩踏、远离病虫害的地方。我逐渐意识到，你培养深度专注的能力就像一株植物。为了充分发挥你的专注力，它需要某些条件：对孩子来说需要玩耍，对成年人来说需要心流状态；需要阅读书籍；需要发现你想要专注的有意义的活动；需要有空间让你的思绪自由驰骋，从而更好地理解你的人生；需要锻炼；需要充足的睡眠；需要食用营养丰富的食物，从而促进大脑健康发育；还需要安全感。有些事情你需要保护你的注意力，因为它们会损害或阻碍你的注意力：过快的速度、过多的切换、过多的刺激、旨在入侵和让你上瘾的侵入性技术、压力、疲惫、添加了让你兴奋的色素的加工食品、污染的空气。

For a long time we took our attention for granted, as if it was a cactus that would grow in even the most desiccated climate. Now we know it’s more like an orchid, a plant that requires great care or it will wither.

长久以来，我们一直把注意力视为理所当然，仿佛它像仙人掌一样，即使在最干旱的气候下也能生长。现在我们知道，它更像兰花，一种需要精心呵护才能茁壮成长的植物。

With this image in mind, I now had a sense of what a movement to reclaim our attention might look like. I would start with three big, bold goals. One: Ban surveillance capitalism, because people who are being hacked and deliberately hooked can’t focus. Two: Introduce a four-day week, because people who are chronically exhausted can’t pay attention. Three: Rebuild childhood around letting kids play freely – in their neighbourhoods and at school – because children who are imprisoned in their homes won’t be able to develop a healthy ability to pay attention. If we achieve these goals, the ability of people to pay attention would, over time, dramatically improve. Then we will have a solid core of focus that we could use to take the fight further and deeper.

有了这幅画面，我对一场旨在夺回我们注意力的运动有了大致的构想。我会从三个宏大的目标开始。第一：禁止监控资本主义，因为被黑客攻击和人为操控的人无法集中注意力。第二：实行每周四天工作制，因为长期疲惫的人无法集中注意力。第三：重建童年，让孩子们在社区和学校里自由玩耍，因为被禁锢在家中的孩子无法培养健康的注意力。如果我们实现了这些目标，人们的注意力能力会随着时间的推移而显著提高。届时，我们将拥有一个强大的核心力量，可以以此为基础，将这场斗争推向更深层次。

The idea of building a movement sometimes seemed to me still quite hard to picture concretely – so I wanted to talk to people who had built movements around really big, impossible-seeming goals, and actually achieved them. My friend Ben Stewart was the head of communications at Greenpeace UK for years, and when I first met him more than fifteen years ago, he told me about a plan he was drawing up with other environmentalist activists. He explained that Britain was the birthplace of the Industrial Revolution, and this revolution had been powered by one thing: coal. Because coal contributes more than any other fuel to global warming, his team were drawing up a plan to force the government to end all new coal mines and new power stations in Britain, and move rapidly to leaving all the country’s existing coal in the ground to ensure it will never be burned. When he explained it, I literally laughed out loud – Good luck to you, I said, I’m on your side, but you’re being a dreamer.

对我来说，建立一场运动的想法有时仍然很难具体描绘出来——所以我很想和那些围绕着看似不可能的宏大目标建立运动，并且最终实现这些目标的人聊聊。我的朋友本·斯图尔特曾多年担任英国绿色和平组织的传播主管。十五年前我第一次见到他时，他告诉我他正在和其他环保人士一起制定一个计划。他解释说，英国是工业革命的发源地，而这场革命的动力来自一样东西：煤炭。由于煤炭对全球变暖的贡献超过任何其他燃料，他的团队正在制定一项计划，迫使政府停止在英国新建煤矿和发电站，并迅速采取行动，将英国现有的所有煤炭都封存在地下，以确保它们永远不会被燃烧。当他解释完这个计划时，我真的忍不住大笑起来——“祝你好运，”我说，“我支持你，但你真是异想天开。”

Within five years, every single new coal mine and new coal power plant in Britain was stopped, and the government had been forced to set in stone plans to close down all the ones that already existed. As a result of their campaign, the place that launched the world on the road to global warming had begun to seek out a path beyond it.

五年之内，英国所有新建煤矿和燃煤电厂的计划都被叫停，政府也被迫下令关闭所有现有的煤矿和电厂。由于他们的努力，这个曾经将世界推向全球变暖之路的地方，开始寻求摆脱全球变暖的出路。

I wanted to talk to Ben about our attention crisis, and how we could learn from other movements that have succeeded in the past. He said: ‘I agree with you it’s a crisis. It’s a crisis for the human species. But I don’t think it’s being identified [like that] in the same way that structural racism or climate change [are]. I don’t think we’re at that point yet … I don’t think that it’s understood that it’s a societal problem, and that it’s caused by decisions by corporate actors, and that it can change.’ So Ben told me the very first step to building a movement is to create a ‘consciousness-raising breakthrough cultural moment, where people go – “Shit, my brain’s been frazzled by this stuff. It’s why I don’t have some of the pleasures in life I used to have.” ’ How do we do that? The ideal tool, he said, is what he calls ‘a site battle’. This is where you choose a place that symbolises the wider struggle, and begin a non-violent fight there. An obvious example is Rosa Parks taking her seat on a bus in Montgomery, Alabama.

我想和本聊聊我们面临的注意力危机，以及我们如何从过去成功的运动中汲取经验。他说：“我同意你的看法，这确实是一场危机。这是一场人类的危机。但我认为它还没有像结构性种族主义或气候变化那样被人们如此看待。我认为我们还没到那个阶段……我认为人们还没有意识到这是一个社会问题，它是由企业决策造成的，而且它是可以改变的。”所以本告诉我，建立一场运动的第一步是创造一个“意识觉醒的突破性文化时刻”，让人们意识到——“糟了，我的大脑都被这些东西搞得焦头烂额。这就是为什么我失去了以前享受的一些生活乐趣。”我们该如何做到这一点呢？他说，理想的工具是他所谓的“网站攻防战”。在这里，你要选择一个象征着更广泛斗争的地点，并在那里开始一场非暴力抗争。一个显而易见的例子是罗莎·帕克斯在阿拉巴马州蒙哥马利市的公交车上就座。

Think, he said, about how we did it with coal. Man-made global warming is a rapidly unfolding disaster, but – like our attention crisis – it can easily seem pretty abstract, and far away, and hard to get a handle on. Even once you do understand it, it can seem so huge and overwhelming that you are often left feeling powerless to do anything. When Ben first drew up his plans, there was a coal-fired power station in Britain named Kingsnorth, and the government was planning to authorise the construction of another coal station right next to it. This, Ben realised, was the whole global problem in microcosm. So after a lot of planning, with his allies, he broke into the power station and abseiled down its side, painting a warning about the extreme weather events that coal unleashes across the world onto the side of the building.

他说，想想我们当初是怎么用煤炭造成这一切的。人为造成的全球变暖是一场迅速蔓延的灾难，但就像我们面临的注意力危机一样，它很容易显得抽象、遥远，难以捉摸。即使你理解了它，它看起来也如此巨大、如此令人难以承受，以至于你常常感到无能为力。本最初制定计划时，英国有一座名为金斯诺斯的燃煤发电站，政府正计划批准在其旁边建造另一座燃煤发电站。本意识到，这正是整个全球问题的缩影。于是，经过一番周密的计划，他与盟友们一起闯入发电站，用绳索从外墙滑下，在建筑物的侧面喷涂了一幅警示画，警告人们煤炭会在全球范围内引发极端天气事件。

They were all arrested and put on trial – which was part of their plan. They intended to use the justice process – in a ju-jitsu move – as a perfect opportunity to put coal itself on trial. They called some of the leading scientific experts from all over the world to testify, to explain what the burning of coal is doing to the ecosystem. In Britain there’s a law that says that in an emergency, you can break some rules – you don’t get charged with trespassing, for example, if you break into a burning building to save people. Ben and his legal team argued that this was an emergency: they were trying to prevent the planet being set on fire. Twelve ordinary British jurors considered the facts – and they acquitted Ben and the other activists on all counts. It was a sensational story, reported all over the world. In the wake of the negative publicity around coal that emerged out of the trial, the British government abandoned all plans to build new coal-powered stations – and began to shutter the ones that remain.

他们全部被捕并接受审判——这正是他们计划的一部分。他们打算利用司法程序——如同柔术一般——为煤炭本身提供一个绝佳的审判机会。他们邀请了来自世界各地的一些顶尖科学专家作证，解释燃煤对生态系统造成的破坏。在英国，有一项法律规定，在紧急情况下，你可以打破一些规则——例如，如果你闯入着火的建筑物救人，就不会被控非法侵入。本和他的律师团队辩称，这就是一场紧急情况：他们试图阻止地球被点燃。十二名普通的英国陪审员审议了事实——他们宣判本和其他活动人士所有罪名不成立。这是一个轰动一时的新闻，全世界都进行了报道。审判引发了关于煤炭的负面舆论，英国政府放弃了所有新建燃煤电站的计划，并开始关闭现有的燃煤电站。

Ben explained that a site battle makes it possible to ‘tell the story about the wider problem’, and when you do this, ‘it speeds up the national conversation’ by waking up a lot of people to what’s really going on. For this first stage, Ben said, ‘You don’t need millions of people. You need a small group of people that get [what] the problems [are], and know about creative confrontation – to create drama around it, to begin the consciousness-raising … You capture people’s attention, and then enough people feel that it’s a vital issue that they want to give their time and their energy [to], and that there’s a clear direction.’

本解释说，网站攻防战能够“讲述更广泛的问题”，而这样做“能够唤醒更多人，让他们意识到问题的真相，从而加速全国范围内的讨论”。本说，在第一阶段，“你不需要数百万人。你只需要一小群了解问题所在、懂得如何进行创造性对抗的人——围绕问题制造戏剧性，开启意识觉醒……你吸引了人们的注意力，然后足够多的人会觉得这是一个至关重要的问题，他们愿意投入时间和精力，并且找到了明确的方向。”

So Ben asked – should people be surrounding Facebook HQ? Twitter? What’s the site battle here? What’s the issue we start on? This is something activists need to debate and decide on. As I write this, I know one group is considering projecting a video of Holocaust survivors talking about the dangers of super-charging far-right ideas onto the side of Facebook’s HQ. Ben stressed that site battles alone don’t deliver victory – what they do is establish the crisis clearly in the public’s mind, and draw more people into a movement, so they can begin to fight at many different levels and in many different ways. On attention, Ben said, a site battle is an opportunity to explain to people this is a fight ‘about personal liberation’ – about ‘liberating ourselves from people who are controlling our minds without our consent’. That is ‘something that people can coalesce around – and it’s highly motivating as well’. That then becomes a movement millions of people can join. Their participation after that will take many forms. Some of it will be inside the political system, organising within political parties, or lobbying the government. Some of it will continue to be outside the political system, with direct action and persuading other citizens. To succeed, you need both.

所以本问道——人们应该包围Facebook总部吗？Twitter呢？这场网站之战的焦点是什么？我们应该从哪个议题入手？这是行动者们需要辩论和决定的问题。就在我写这篇文章的时候，我知道有一个团体正在考虑将一段大屠杀幸存者讲述极右翼思想被过度渲染的危险的视频投射到Facebook总部大楼的外墙上。本强调，单靠网站之战并不能带来胜利——它的作用在于让公众清楚地认识到这场危机，并吸引更多人加入这场运动，从而让他们能够在不同的层面、以不同的方式展开斗争。关于如何吸引关注，本说，网站之战是一个机会，可以向人们解释这是一场“关于个人解放”的斗争——“将我们从那些未经我们同意就控制我们思想的人手中解放出来”。这是“人们可以团结起来的——而且也极具激励作用”的。然后，这会发展成一场数百万人可以加入的运动。之后，他们的参与将采取多种形式。一部分行动将在政治体制内进行，例如在政党内部组织活动或游说政府。另一部分行动则将继续在政治体制之外进行，例如采取直接行动和说服其他公民。要想成功，两者缺一不可。

As I talked with Ben, I wondered if a movement to achieve these goals should be named Attention Rebellion. He smiled when I suggested it. ‘It is an attention rebellion,’ he said. I realised this requires a shift in how we think about ourselves. We are not medieval peasants begging at the court of King Zuckerberg for crumbs of attention. We are the free citizens of democracies, and we own our own minds and our own society, and together, we are going to take them back.

我和本交谈时，我在想，如果要把实现这些目标的运动命名为“注意力叛乱”，会不会更好。我提出这个建议时，他笑了。“这就是一场注意力叛乱，”他说。我意识到，这需要我们转变对自身的认知。我们不是中世纪的农民，在扎克伯格国王的宫廷里乞求残羹剩饭。我们是民主国家的自由公民，我们拥有自己的思想和社会，我们将携手夺回它们。

At times it seemed to me that this would be a hard movement to get off the ground – but then I remembered that all the movements that have changed your life and my life were hard to get off the ground. For example, when gay people first started organising in the 1890s, they could be put in prison just for saying who they loved. When labour unions started fighting for the weekend, they were beaten by the police and their leaders were shot or hanged. What we face is, in many ways, vastly less challenging than the cliff they had to scale. They didn’t give up. Often, when a person argues for social change, they are called ‘naive’. The exact opposite is the truth. It’s naive to think we as citizens can do nothing, and leave the powerful to do whatever they want, and somehow our attention will survive. There’s nothing naive about believing that concerted democratic campaigning can change the world. As the anthropologist Margaret Mead said, it’s the only thing that ever has.

有时我觉得这场运动很难启动——但后来我想起来，所有改变你我生活的运动，当初启动时都异常艰难。例如，19世纪90年代，当同性恋者开始组织起来时，他们仅仅因为说出自己的爱人就可能被投入监狱。当工会开始争取周末时，他们遭到警察殴打，他们的领导人被枪杀或绞死。我们面临的挑战，在很多方面，远不及他们当年所攀登的悬崖。但他们没有放弃。通常，当有人倡导社会变革时，他们会被指责“天真”。事实恰恰相反。认为我们作为公民可以无所作为，任由当权者为所欲为，而我们的注意力却能继续保持下去，这才是天真。相信团结一致的民主运动能够改变世界，这绝非天真。正如人类学家玛格丽特·米德所说，这是唯一真正改变世界的方式。

I realised that we have to decide now: do we value attention and focus? Does being able to think deeply matter to us? Do we want it for our children? If we do, then we have to fight for it. As one politician said – you don’t get what you don’t fight for.

我意识到我们现在必须做出决定：我们是否重视专注力？深度思考的能力对我们来说重要吗？我们希望我们的孩子也拥有这种能力吗？如果答案是肯定的，那么我们就必须为之奋斗。正如一位政治家所说——你不争取，就得不到。

Even as it became clearer to me what we need to do now, there were some unresolved thoughts that kept nagging at me. Lying beneath so many of the causes of this crisis that I had learned about, there seemed to be one big cause – but I was reluctant to reckon with it because it is so big, and, to be honest, I hesitate to write about it now, in case it daunts you too. Back in Denmark, Sune Lehmann had shown me the evidence that the world is speeding up, and that process is shrinking our collective attention span. He showed that social media is a major accelerant. But he made it clear that this has been happening for a very long time. His study started analysing data from the 1880s, and it showed that every decade since, the way we experience the world has been getting faster, and we have been focusing on any one topic less and less.

即使我越来越清楚我们现在需要做什么，一些未解的疑问仍然萦绕在我心头。在我了解到的这场危机的诸多原因之下，似乎隐藏着一个更大的根源——但我却不愿正视它，因为它实在太大了。说实话，我现在也犹豫要不要写出来，以免它也让你们感到畏惧。在丹麦的时候，苏内·莱曼向我展示了世界正在加速运转的证据，而这一过程正在缩短我们集体的注意力持续时间。他指出，社交媒体是这一趋势的主要加速器。但他明确表示，这种情况已经持续了很长时间。他的研究从19世纪80年代开始分析数据，结果表明，自那时以来，我们体验世界的方式每过十年，节奏就加快一分，我们对任何一个话题的关注度也越来越低。

I kept puzzling away at this question. Why? Why has this been happening so long? This trend far precedes Facebook, or most of the factors I have written about here. What’s the underlying cause stretching back to the 1880s? I discussed it with many people, and the most persuasive answer came from the Norwegian scientist Thomas Hylland Eriksen, who is a professor of social anthropology. Ever since the Industrial Revolution, he said, our economies have been built around a new and radical idea – economic growth. This is the belief that every year, the economy – and each individual company in it – should get bigger and bigger. That’s how we now define success. If a country’s economy grows, its politicians are likely to be reelected. If a company grows, its CEOs are likely garlanded. If a country’s economy or a company’s share price shrinks, politicians or CEOs face a greater risk of being booted out. Economic growth is the central organising principle of our society. It is at the heart of how we see the world.

我一直在苦苦思索这个问题：为什么？为什么这种情况持续了这么久？这种趋势远早于Facebook，甚至早于我在这里提到的绝大多数因素。究竟是什么根本原因可以追溯到19世纪80年代？我与许多人探讨过这个问题，其中最令人信服的答案来自挪威科学家托马斯·海兰德·埃里克森，他是一位社会人类学教授。他说，自工业革命以来，我们的经济一直围绕着一个全新且激进的理念——经济增长——构建。这种理念认为，经济——以及其中的每一家公司——都应该逐年发展壮大。这就是我们现在对成功的定义。如果一个国家的经济增长，其政治家就更有可能连任。如果一家公司发展壮大，其首席执行官就更有可能获得嘉奖。如果一个国家的经济或一家公司的股价下跌，政治家或首席执行官就面临着更大的下台风险。经济增长是我们社会的核心组织原则。它构成了我们看待世界方式的核心。

Thomas explained that growth can happen in one of two ways. The first is that a corporation can find new markets – by inventing something new, or exporting something to a part of the world that doesn’t have it yet. The second is that a corporation can persuade existing consumers to consume more. If you can get people to eat more, or to sleep less, then you have found a source of economic growth. Mostly, he believes, we achieve growth today primarily through this second option. Corporations are constantly finding ways to cram more stuff into the same amount of time. To give one example: they want you to watch TV and follow the show on social media. Then you see twice as many ads. This inevitably speeds up life. If the economy has to grow every year, in the absence of new markets it has to get you and me to do more and more in the same amount of time.

托马斯解释说，增长可以通过两种方式实现。第一种是企业寻找新市场——通过发明新产品，或者将产品出口到世界上尚未拥有的地区。第二种是企业说服现有消费者增加消费。如果你能让人们吃得更多，或者睡得更少，你就找到了经济增长的源泉。他认为，如今我们实现增长主要还是通过第二种方式。企业不断想方设法在相同的时间内提供更多东西。举个例子：他们希望你看电视，并在社交媒体上关注节目。这样一来，你看到的广告数量就会翻倍。这必然会加快生活节奏。如果经济要每年增长，在缺乏新市场的情况下，就必须让你我在相同的时间内做越来越多的事情。

As I read Thomas’s work more deeply, I realised this is one of the crucial reasons why life has accelerated every decade since the 1880s: we are living in an economic machine that requires greater speed to keep going – and that inevitably degrades our attention over time. In fact, when I reflected on it, this need for economic growth seemed to be the underlying force that was driving so many of the causes of poor attention that I had learned about – our increasing stress, our swelling work hours, our more invasive technologies, our lack of sleep, our bad diets.

随着我对托马斯著作的深入研读，我意识到，这正是自19世纪80年代以来生活节奏每十年加速的关键原因之一：我们生活在一个需要更快速度才能运转的经济机器中——而这不可避免地会随着时间的推移削弱我们的注意力。事实上，当我反思时，这种对经济增长的需求似乎正是导致我所了解的诸多注意力不集中原因的根本驱动力——我们日益增长的压力、不断延长的工作时间、日益侵入性的技术、睡眠不足以及不良的饮食习惯。

I thought about what Dr Charles Czeisler had told me back at Harvard Medical School. If we all went back to sleeping as much as our brains and our bodies need, he said, ‘It would be an earthquake for our economic system, because our economic system has become dependent on sleep-depriving people. The attentional failures are just roadkill. That’s just the cost of doing business.’ This is true of sleep – and it’s true of much more than sleep.

我想起了查尔斯·切斯勒博士在哈佛医学院时跟我说过的话。他说，如果我们都能恢复到大脑和身体所需的充足睡眠，“那将对我们的经济体系造成巨大冲击，因为我们的经济体系已经依赖于睡眠不足的人群。注意力不集中造成的损失就像路上的死尸，这就是做生意的代价。” 这句话不仅适用于睡眠，也适用于其他许多方面。

It was intimidating to realise that something so deeply ingrained in our way of life is – over time – an acid on our attention. But I already knew we don’t have to live like this. My friend Dr Jason Hickel, who is an economic anthropologist at the University of London, is perhaps the leading critic of the concept of economic growth in the world – and he has been explaining for a long time that there is an alternative. When I went to see him, he explained that we need to move beyond the idea of growth to something called a ‘steady-state economy’. We would abandon economic growth as the driving principle of the economy and instead choose a different set of goals. At the moment we think we’re prosperous if we are working ourselves ragged to buy things – most of which don’t even make us happy. He said we could redefine prosperity to mean having time to spend with our children, or to be in nature, or to sleep, or to dream, or to have secure work. Most people don’t want a fast life – they want a good life. Nobody lies on their deathbed and thinks about all that they contributed to economic growth. A steady-state economy can allow us to choose goals that don’t raid our attention, and don’t raid the planet’s resources.

意识到我们生活方式中根深蒂固的某些东西，随着时间的推移，竟然会像酸液一样腐蚀我们的注意力，这着实令人感到不安。但我早就知道，我们不必这样生活。我的朋友杰森·希克尔博士是伦敦大学的经济人类学家，他或许是世界上对经济增长概念批判最深刻的人之一——他长期以来一直在阐述另一种选择。我去拜访他时，他解释说，我们需要超越增长的理念，转向一种叫做“稳态经济”的模式。我们将放弃以经济增长为经济驱动力的原则，转而选择一套不同的目标。目前，我们认为，只要拼命工作去购买东西——而这些东西大多并不能给我们带来快乐——我们就算是富裕了。他说，我们可以重新定义富裕，让它意味着有时间陪伴孩子，亲近自然，好好睡觉，做梦，或者拥有一份稳定的工作。大多数人并不想要快节奏的生活——他们想要的是美好的生活。没有人会在临终前回想自己对经济增长做出的所有贡献。稳定的经济状态使我们能够选择那些不会分散我们注意力、也不会消耗地球资源的目标。

As Jason and I talked, in a public park in London in the middle of the Covid-19 crisis, I looked around us, where people were sitting in the middle of a workday under the trees, enjoying nature. This was, I realised, the only time in my life the world had truly slowed down. A terrible tragedy had forced us to do it – but there was also, for many of us, a hint of relief. It was the first time in centuries that the world chose, together, to stop racing, and pause. We decided as a society to value something other than speed and growth. We literally looked up and saw the trees.

在新冠疫情危机期间，我和杰森在伦敦的一个公园里聊天。我环顾四周，人们在工作日的午后坐在树荫下，享受着大自然。我意识到，这是我一生中唯一一次感受到世界真正慢了下来。一场可怕的悲剧迫使我们这样做——但对我们许多人来说，其中也夹杂着一丝解脱。几个世纪以来，世界第一次选择共同停止奔波，停下脚步。作为一个社会，我们决定珍视速度和增长之外的东西。我们抬头望去，看到了树木。

I suspect that, in the long run, it will be ultimately not be possible to rescue attention and focus in a world that is dominated by the belief that we need to keep growing and speeding up every year. I can’t tell you I have all the answers to how we do that – but I believe that if an Attention Rebellion begins, we will, sooner or later, have to take on this very deep issue: the growth machine itself.

我怀疑，从长远来看，在一个被“我们需要每年不断增长和加速”的信念所主导的世界里，我们最终将无法挽回人们的注意力。我无法告诉你所有解决办法——但我相信，如果一场“注意力革命”爆发，我们迟早都将不得不面对这个非常深刻的问题：增长机器本身。

But we will have to do this in any event – for another reason. The growth machine has pushed humans beyond the limits of our minds – but it is also pushing the planet beyond its ecological limits. And these two crises, I was coming to believe, are intertwined.

但无论如何，我们都必须这样做——原因另有其他。经济增长的机器已经将人类推向了思维的极限，同时也把地球推向了生态的极限。我逐渐意识到，这两种危机是相互交织的。

There is one particularly large reason why we need an Attention Rebellion today. It’s stark. Human beings have never needed our ability to focus – our superpower as a species – more than we do at this moment, because we face an unprecedented crisis.

我们今天之所以需要一场注意力革命，有一个特别重要的原因。原因显而易见。人类从未像现在这样需要集中注意力——我们作为物种的超能力——因为我们正面临着一场前所未有的危机。

As I write these words, I am looking at a webcam of San Francisco, showing the streets where I walked with Tristan Harris. He told me there – just over a year before – that his biggest worry about the destruction of our attention is that it will prevent us from dealing with global warming. Right now, on those streets, it’s midday, but you can’t see the sun – it has been blacked out by ash from the massive wildfires ripping across California. One in every thirty-three acres in the state has burned. The house Tristan grew up in, not far away, has been consumed by the flames, and most of his belongings have been destroyed. The streets where I had this conversation about the climate crisis with him have ash flecked across them, and the sky is glowing a low, dark orange.

我写下这些文字时，正看着旧金山的网络摄像头，画面上是我和特里斯坦·哈里斯曾经一起走过的街道。一年多前，他在这里告诉我，他最担心的是，我们注意力分散会让我们无暇应对全球变暖。此刻，在这些街道上，正值中午，却不见阳光——加州肆虐的大规模野火产生的灰烬遮蔽了阳光。加州每33英亩土地中就有1英亩被烧毁。特里斯坦长大的房子就在不远处，已被大火吞噬，他的大部分财物也付之一炬。我和他谈论气候危机的街道上，如今也落满了灰烬，天空泛着低沉的暗橙色光芒。

The three years I worked on this book have been years of fire. Several of the cities I spent time in have been choked by the smoke from huge and unprecedented wildfires – Sydney, Sao Paulo and San Francisco. Like a lot of people, I read about the fires, but only a little – I began to feel quickly overwhelmed. The moment when it became real to me – when I felt it in my gut – was a moment that might seem small when I describe it.

我创作这本书的这三年，简直就是火灾肆虐的三年。我待过的几个城市——悉尼、圣保罗和旧金山——都被史无前例的巨大野火产生的浓烟笼罩。和很多人一样，我也读过一些关于火灾的报道，但只是浅尝辄止——很快我就感到不知所措。真正让我感受到这一切的那一刻——那种发自内心的震撼——或许用语言来描述起来显得微不足道。

Starting in 2019, Australia experienced what became known as its Black Summer, a series of wildfires so vast that they are hard to describe. Three billion animals had to flee or were burned to death, and so many species were lost that Professor Kingsley Dixon, a botanist, called it a ‘biological Armageddon’. Some Australians had to huddle on the beaches, surrounded by a ring of flames, as they wondered if they should try to scramble onto boats to escape. They could hear the fires getting closer. It sounded like a raging waterfall, witnesses said, and it was broken only by the sound of bottles smashing as their houses burned up, one by one. The smoke from the fires was visible 1,200 miles away in New Zealand, where the skies over the South Island turned orange.

从2019年开始，澳大利亚经历了被称为“黑色夏季”的一系列野火，其规模之大难以用语言形容。30亿只动物被迫逃离家园或葬身火海，无数物种消失，以至于植物学家金斯利·迪克森教授称之为“生物末日”。一些澳大利亚人被迫挤在海滩上，周围被火焰包围，他们犹豫着是否应该争先恐后地登上船只逃生。他们能听到火势越来越近。目击者说，那声音如同奔腾的瀑布，只有房屋被烧毁时瓶子破碎的声音才能打破这沉闷的景象。远在1200英里之外的新西兰都能看到火灾产生的浓烟，南岛上空的天空变成了橙色。

About three weeks or so into the fires, I was on the phone to a friend in Sydney when I heard a loud shrieking sound. It was the fire alarm in his apartment. All over the city, in offices and homes, these alarms had started to sound. This was because there was so much smoke in the air travelling in from the wildfires that the smoke alarms believed each individual building was on fire. This meant that one by one, many people in Sydney turned off their smoke alarms, and they sat in the silence and the smoke. I only realised why I found this so disturbing when I talked it over with my friend Bruno Giussani, a Swiss writer. He said to me that they were turning off the warning systems in our homes that are designed to protect us, because the bigger warning systems that are meant to protect us all – our society’s ability to focus on what scientists are telling us, and act on what they say – are not working.

大约三周后，我正在和悉尼的一位朋友通电话，突然听到一声刺耳的尖叫。是他公寓里的火警警报。整个城市，无论是办公室还是民宅，警报都响了起来。这是因为山火带来的浓烟弥漫在空气中，烟雾报警器误以为每栋楼都着火了。这意味着悉尼的许多人一个接一个地关掉了家里的烟雾报警器，然后独自坐在寂静和烟雾之中。直到我和我的朋友，瑞士作家布鲁诺·朱萨尼（Bruno Giussani）谈起这件事，我才明白为什么我对此感到如此不安。他告诉我，人们正在关闭家中那些旨在保护我们的警报系统，因为那些旨在保护我们所有人的更广泛的预警系统——我们社会能够集中精力听取科学家的建议并采取行动的能力——已经失效了。

The climate crisis can be solved. We need to rapidly transition away from fossil fuels and towards powering our societies by clean, green sources of energy. But to do that we will need to be able to focus, to have sane conversations with each other, and to think clearly. These solutions are not going to be achieved by an addled population who are switching tasks every three minutes and screaming at each other all the time in algorithm-pumped fury. We can only solve the climate crisis if we solve our attention crisis. As I contemplated this, I began to think again about something that James Williams wrote: ‘I used to think there were no great political struggles left … How wrong I was. The liberation of human attention may be the defining moral and political struggle of our time. Its success is the prerequisite for the success of virtually all other struggles.’

气候危机是可以解决的。我们需要迅速摆脱化石燃料，转向使用清洁、绿色的能源来驱动我们的社会。但要做到这一点，我们需要集中注意力，彼此进行理智的对话，并保持清晰的思考。如果人们心不在焉，每三分钟就切换任务，在算法驱动的狂怒中互相谩骂，这些解决方案是不可能实现的。只有解决注意力危机，我们才能解决气候危机。在思考这个问题时，我再次想起詹姆斯·威廉姆斯的一段话：“我曾经认为已经没有伟大的政治斗争了……我大错特错了。解放人类的注意力或许是我们这个时代最重要的道德和政治斗争。它的成功是几乎所有其他斗争成功的先决条件。”

When I look now at the orange, fire-scarred skies over San Francisco on this grainy webcam, I keep thinking about the light in Provincetown in the summer I spent there without my phone or the internet, and how pure and perfect it seemed. James Williams was right: our attention is a kind of light, one that clarifies the world and makes it visible to us. In Provincetown I could see more clearly than I ever had before in my life – my own thoughts, my own goals, my own dreams. I want to live in that light – the light of knowing, of achieving our ambitions, of being fully alive – and not in the menacing orange light of it all burning down.

现在，当我透过这台画面模糊的网络摄像头，凝视着旧金山上空被大火烧焦的橙色天空时，我不禁想起夏天在普罗温斯敦度过的时光。那时我没有手机，也没有网络，那里的光线纯净而完美。詹姆斯·威廉姆斯说得对：我们的注意力本身就是一种光，它能照亮世界，让我们看清一切。在普罗温斯敦，我比以往任何时候都看得更清楚——我自己的想法、我自己的目标、我自己的梦想。我想活在那光芒之中——那认知的光芒，那实现抱负的光芒，那鲜活的生命之光——而不是活在那令人不安的、万物燃烧殆尽的橙色光芒之中。

When I hung up on my friend in Sydney so he could unscrew his fire alarm and switch it off, I thought – if our attention continues to shatter, the ecosystem won’t wait patiently for us to regain our focus. It will fall and it will burn. At the start of the Second World War, the English poet W. H. Auden – when he looked out over the new technologies of destruction that had been created by humans – warned: ‘We must love one another, or die.’ I believe that now we must focus together – or face the fires alone.

当我挂断悉尼朋友的电话，让他拧下火警警报器关掉时，我想——如果我们继续分散注意力，生态系统不会耐心等待我们重新集中精力。它会崩溃，会燃烧殆尽。二战初期，英国诗人W·H·奥登在审视人类创造的新型毁灭性技术时发出警告：“我们必须彼此相爱，否则就会灭亡。”我相信，现在我们必须团结一致，否则将独自面对这场灾难。

here something the Spanish writer José Ortega y Gasset said: Original: ‘ La vida no puede esperar a que las ciencias expliquen científicamente el Universo. No se puede vivir ad kalendas graecas . El atributo más esencial de la existencia es su perentoriedad: la vida es siempre urgente. Se vive aquí y ahora sin posible demora ni traspaso. La vida nos es disparada a quemarropa. Ya la cultura, que no es sino su interpretación, no puede tampoco esperar .’ J. Ortega y Gasset, Mission of the University ( Misión de la Universidad ), 1930, translated by H. L. Nostrand (Princeton, Princeton University Press, 1944), p. 73.

以下是西班牙作家何塞·奥尔特加·伊·加塞特的一段话：原文：“生命不能等待科学用科学的方式解释宇宙。人不能按着希腊历生活。存在最本质的属性是它的必然性：生命总是紧迫的。我们活在此时此地，没有丝毫的拖延或推迟。生命被直接抛给我们。文化，作为对生命的诠释，也同样不能等待。” J. Ortega y Gasset，《大学的使命》（Misión de la Universidad），1930年，H. L. Nostrand译（普林斯顿，普林斯顿大学出版社，1944年），第73页。

Dr Wilson has been uncomfortable with how some journalists have written about this study, and I have tried to absorb his criticisms in the text here. here At a conservative estimate, infinite scroll makes you spend 50 percent more of your time: There’s a debate about the precise numbers for this, because it’s inherently hard to measure. One way of measuring it is what’s called ‘bounce rate’ (the number of people who arrive on a site and immediately leave without going to any other page on the website). For example, time.com’s ‘bounce rate’ apparently dropped by 15 percent when they introduced infinite scroll in 2014; Quartz readers view about 50 percent more stories than they would without infinite scroll. Both of these figures come from S. Kirkland, ‘Time.com’s bounce rate down 15 percentage points since adopting continuous scroll’, Poynter , 20 July 2014. https://web.archive.org/web/20150507024326/http://www.poynter.org:80/news/mediawire/257466/time-coms-bounce-rate-down-15-percentage-points-since-adopting-continuous-scroll/

保守估计，无限滚动会让你多花费 50% 的时间：关于这个数字的具体数值尚有争议，因为它本身就很难衡量。一种衡量方法是“跳出率”（即访问网站后立即离开，而没有浏览任何其他页面的用户数量）。例如，time.com 在 2014 年引入无限滚动后，其“跳出率”下降了 15%；Quartz 的读者在使用无限滚动后浏览的文章数量比没有使用时增加了约 50%。这两个数据均来自 S. Kirkland 的文章《Time.com 自采用连续滚动以来跳出率下降 15 个百分点》，发表于 Poynter，2014 年 7 月 20 日。https://web.archive.org/web/20150507024326/http://www.poynter.org:80/news/mediawire/257466/time-coms-bounce-rate-down-15-percentage-points-since-adopting-continuous-scroll/

here The scientists who have studied it discovered that 95 percent of people in our culture who lose weight on a diet regain it within one to five years: The original study finding that 95 percent of diets fail was with one hundred obese patients: A. J. Stunkard and M. McLaren-Hume, ‘The results of treatment for obesity’, AMA Archives of Internal Medicine , 103, 1959, pp. 79–85. Other more recent studies have found very similar outcomes – in this one, only 2 percent of people maintained a greater than 20 kg weight loss two years later: J. Kassirer and M. Angell, ‘Losing weight—an ill-fated New Year’s resolution’, New England Journal of Medicine , 338, 1998, pp. 52–4.

研究此问题的科学家发现，在我们文化中，95%通过节食减肥的人会在一到五年内反弹：最初发现95%的节食减肥失败的研究对象是100名肥胖患者：A. J. Stunkard 和 M. McLaren-Hume，《肥胖症治疗结果》，《美国医学会内科医学档案》，103，1959，第79-85页。其他更新的研究也发现了非常相似的结果——在这项研究中，两年后只有2%的人保持了超过20公斤的减重：J. Kassirer 和 M. Angell，《减肥——一个失败的新年决心》，《新英格兰医学杂志》，338，1998，第52-54页。

Some scientists argue this is too pessimistic or defining success too demandingly. See, for example, R. R. Wing and S. Phelan, ‘Long-term weight loss maintenance’, The American Journal of Clinical Nutrition , vol. 82, issue 1, 2005, pp. 222S–225S. They argue we should define success as somebody who maintains 10 percent weight loss one year after the diet. But even if you use this redefinition, only about 20 percent of dieters can manage it, and 80 percent fail.

一些科学家认为这种观点过于悲观，或者对成功的定义过于苛刻。例如，参见 R. R. Wing 和 S. Phelan 合著的《长期体重维持》（载于《美国临床营养学杂志》，第 82 卷，第 1 期，2005 年，第 222S-225S 页）。他们认为，我们应该将成功定义为节食一年后仍能保持 10% 的体重减轻。但即使采用这种重新定义，也只有大约 20% 的节食者能够做到，而 80% 的人会失败。

A NOTE ON THE AUTHOR

关于作者的说明

Johann Hari is an internationally bestselling author whose books have appeared in 38 languages. His first book, Chasing the Scream , was made into both an Academy Award-nominated film and an eightpart TV series presented by Samuel L Jackson. He was an executive producer of both. His second book, Lost Connections , was a Sunday Times and New York Times bestseller. He has written for the New York Times, Le Monde , the Guardian and others. His TED Talks on addiction and depression have been viewed more than 80 million times.

约翰·哈里是一位国际畅销书作家，他的作品已被翻译成38种语言。他的第一本书《追逐尖叫》（Chasing the Scream）被改编成一部获得奥斯卡提名的电影和一部由塞缪尔·杰克逊主持的八集电视剧。他本人也是这两部作品的执行制片人。他的第二本书《失去的联系》（Lost Connections）荣登《星期日泰晤士报》和《纽约时报》畅销书榜。他曾为《纽约时报》、《世界报》、《卫报》等媒体撰稿。他在TED上关于成瘾和抑郁症的演讲观看次数已超过8000万次。
